#2 [paper] Development of a park and green space service classification to support park prescribing in Korea
Authors: Hyo-Ju Kim, D. Kim, Hyun-jin Jung
Venue: Frontiers in Public Health
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1857595
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Park Prescription—the formalized referral of patients to park- and nature-based activities by healthcare providers—has gained increasing attention as a strategy for chronic disease prevention and health promotion. Despite the expansion of such programs, a structured classification of park and green space services remains lacking, limiting the practical applicability of Park Prescribing. This issue is particularly important in Korea, where the institutional foundation for implementing Park Prescribing remains limited. Accordingly, this study aimed to develop a classification that conceptualizes parks and green spaces as prescribable service resources and to examine its content validity. A preliminary item set was derived through a review of major international Park Prescribing programs and Park Assessment and Observation Tools. Two rounds of modified Delphi survey were subsequently conducted with a panel of 20 experts, comprising 10 Park and Green Space experts and 10 Healthcare experts. The finalized classification comprises three Domains—Park and Green Space Characteristics, Park and Green Space Spatial Components, and Park and Green Space Activities—and includes 11 Major Items, 36 Middle-Level Items, and 101 Sub-Items. Key items were identified as Accessibility and User Convenience within the Characteristics domain, Pedestrian Space and Rest and Interaction Space within the Spatial Components domain, and Physical Health Activities and Passive Recreation Activities within the Activities domain. The proposed classification provides a foundational framework for linking park and green space services to Park Prescribing. It may support the future implementation of Park Prescribing and serve as a basis for health-oriented park planning and management.

#13 [paper] TOURISTS' PERCEPTIONS OF SMART TOURISM SERVICES IN A CHINESE THEME PARK: AN IPA-BASED STUDY OF NINGBO FANGTE ORIENTAL DAWN
Authors: Hongfei Bao
Venue: CACTUS
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.24818/cts/8/2026/1.09
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Smart tourism has become an important means of enhancing the competitiveness and service quality of theme parks. However, limited research has explored how visitors perceive the importance and performance of specific smart service components in Chinese theme parks. This study assesses tourists' perceptions of smart tourism services at Ningbo Fangte Oriental Dawn using a case study approach, a questionnaire survey, and the Importance-Performance Analysis (IPA) framework. A total of 387 valid responses from actual park visitors were analyzed. The results indicate that contactless payments, electronic map updates, ticketing convenience, social media publicity, and intelligent parking were perceived as both important and satisfactory. In contrast, mobile tourism services, online ticket discounts, and visitor-flow diversion were placed in the "Concentrate Here" quadrant, highlighting areas that require managerial attention. The findings provide clear decision-making references for theme park managers to optimize operations and allocate resources effectively, offering valuable practical implications for aligning smart tourism service investments with tourists' perceived value.

#2 [paper] Reply on RC2 Authors: Peihao Yang, Guodong Ye Year: 2026 Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-262-cc1 Still open/current: yes Abstract: Abstract. A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. After training on multiple CMIP6 ensemble members, the constructed models are evaluated for their predictive capacity regarding MHW in the SCS. The results also show that these machine learning-based methods can perform comparably to the existing dynamic models in terms of prediction performance, and in some cases even outperform the latter. Furthermore, by incorporating machine learning interpretability techniques, the key physical processes can also be elucidated from these predictions. That is to say, the new method is not a traditional "black box", but rather an effective tool that can possess certain physical transparency and scientific interpretability.

#3 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. #1 [grant] Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate
Amount: €3,000,000–€15,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2027-01-D1-07
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-03-04
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding, modelling, and predicting extreme events (isolated, compound, or cascading) in a changing climate, including their interaction, likelihood, and impact on resilience.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Utilizing a hierarchy of models (including high-resolution Earth system models and digital twins), data from past and recent climate, AI-based approaches, quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, and case studies to improve prediction, projection, and attribution capabilities across s…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe and globally, encompassing large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena, with specific focus on EU and national/regional actors, low- to middle-income countries, and integration with initiatives like Copernicus and Destination Earth.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

- Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the new Extreme-Events Flagship Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects to be selected under ESA's FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. #3 [paper] Thomson: Continual Learning of Frontier Models for SovereignAI
Authors: Shengzhuang Chen, Jerrod Parker, Yejin Bang, Andrew M. Bean, Nabeel Seedat, S. Winzeck, Daniil Glazko, Jannik Zgraggen
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/25f93a6ad2540697a638a11c5b3b33d30ce29ee8
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The development of frontier models is commonly perceived to be the exclusive remit of a small number of heavily funded players, creating an information, economic and power asymmetry between developers and the diverse user base of modern AI. Recent public discourse acknowledges this concern, calling for SovereignAI (an organisation's capability to independently build, deploy and govern AI use), but offers little concrete advice on how this can be achieved in the short term under a diversity of funding settings. We argue that frontier performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models. Unlike limited approaches such as small-scale fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation of a frozen model, our approach exploits a modern mid-&post-training stack while introducing safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making the minimal number of high-impact interventions on the parameters. This yields gains comparable to those typically seen across multiple successive model generations, at compute and personnel budgets substantially lower than commonly thought, making ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values&data privacy) viable for far more actors. We demonstrate this with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model trained with an enhanced focus on high-stakes professional work. Thomson performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax&multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Evaluations show a distinctive $\pi$-shaped pattern: distinct improvements across a wide range of capabilities, including those not explicitly targeted, while almost completely eliminating the forgetting problem common to narrow domain adaptation.

#5 [paper] Monsoon’s Edge: Rain-Rock & Ruin Western Ghats-The Breaking Point
Authors: Dr NR Jagannath
Venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.55041/ijcope.v2i9.030
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Restoring the hazard-buffering ecosystems of the Western Ghats is essential to re-establish their natural capacity to attenuate runoff, stabilise slopes, and reduce disaster risk in a changing climate. This analytical paper proposes an integrated restoration framework that combines ecological priorities, technical bio-engineering, and institutional-financial reforms to transform fragmented conservation actions into a coherent, range-wide programme with measurable hazard-reduction outcomes. Ecologically, the paper emphasises targeted restoration of shola forests, montane grasslands (shola–grassland mosaics), wetlands, and riparian buffers, which collectively function as a “sponge and net” to delay peak flows and retain soil on steep terrain. It calls for active removal of invasive species such as Eucalyptus and Acacia to enable recovery of native vegetation and habitats, alongside large-scale native-tree planting and fire-prevention measures embedded within national schemes like the National Afforestation Programme and the Green India Mission. These actions aim to rebuild ecosystem mosaics that historically moderated hydrological extremes and maintained slope integrity across the Ghats. On the technical front, the paper advocates native-species bio-engineering on exposed, degraded slopes and road cuts, using deep-rooted indigenous plants to enhance slope cohesion and reduce infrastructure-induced failures at relatively low cost. It further recommends high-resolution, parcel-level GIS mapping to identify, safeguard, and restore critical wildlife corridors and riparian buffers, thereby aligning hazard mitigation with biodiversity connectivity and landscape-scale planning. Institutionally and financially, the analysis argues for replacing isolated, NGO- or division-led initiatives with a coordinated, range-wide ecosystem restoration programme underpinned by explicit hazard-reduction targets and dedicated funding. It proposes mobilising resources from CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management & Planning Authority) and other forestry or climate trusts through a performance-linked fiscal model, where disbursements are contingent on achieving quantifiable ecological indicators such as increases in native canopy cover. To ensure durability and local ownership, the framework integrates restoration with sustainable livelihoods—promoting agroforestry in transition zones and introducing payments for ecosystem services (PES) that provide Gram Sabhas and local communities with a direct economic stake in conservation outcomes. Together, these strategies offer a pathway to rebuild the Western Ghats’ natural hazard-buffering functions while strengthening rural livelihoods, institutional accountability, and climate resilience across one of India’s most critical mountain ecosystems. Keywords: Western Ghats; disaster risk reduction; landslides; Ecologically Sensitive Area; Gadgil report; Kasturirangan report; land-use zoning; cumulative impact assessment; ecosystem restoration; climate resilience; trans-boundary governance; ecological fiscal transfers

#6 [paper] Fair Access to Urban Water: Designing Population‐Sensitive Connection Fees Through a Welfare‐Informed Ability‐to‐Pay Approach
Authors: Seyedhossein Sajadifar, Masoud Alavian Sadr, Shahram Heydarian Samani, Ali Mazyaki, Alireza Pourebrahim
Venue: World Water Policy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1002/wwp2.70115
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
ABSTRACT Setting urban water connection fees is a complex policy problem: Fees must balance affordability, equity, and adequate cost recovery. This study develops a two‐stage framework for setting urban water connection charges in Iran. A bottom‐up engineering model first establishes the full long‐run economic cost of a new connection; a distributive stage then allocates a target provincial average across six city population classes. The distributive stage is stated as a constrained social welfare program and solved exactly; under logarithmic utility, it yields corner solutions rather than a smooth gradient because the fee is a small share of household resources. The recommended schedule is therefore described as what it is: a proportional ability‐to‐pay allocation indexed to city size, whose formal relation to the welfare program is stated explicitly. Revenue neutrality is imposed on a connection‐weighted basis so that the utility collects the intended total rather than an unweighted average of six class fees. Using Household Expenditure and Income Survey data for all 31 provincial capitals, we test rather than assume the population proxy and find an income elasticity of about 0.13 with respect to city size: statistically significant, but explaining a minority of cross‐city variation. Equity claims are correspondingly framed at the intercity level. Applied to a representative province, the schedule is progressive with respect to ability to pay, holds first‐year revenue exactly at the target, and can be adjusted over time using the Consumer Price Index. The approach transfers to other water‐scarce settings under cost‐recovery pressure.

#7 [paper] THE STORIES BEHIND THE DATA: 30 YEARS OF SNOWPACK SURVEYS ON NIWOT RIDGE
Authors: Jennifer Frances Morse
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.15788/1790099397
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
My work is a case study about the co-development of an academic field safety program with a high alpine fine-scale snow depth and snow profile record spanning 30 years in the Front Range of the Southern Rocky Mountains.The Niwot Ridge Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) Project maintains a long-term snow data set through a mid-May snow survey designed to capture peak snowpack.Up to 20 volunteers overnight at a high alpine laboratory (3,505 m) to access the otherwise restricted City of Boulder Watershed.Over three days they record ~ 500 snow depth points and six 2 m snow pit profiles across the upper Green Lakes Valley (3,567 m to 4,042 m).This record has been used to understand how snow redistributes across mountain terrain, develop an index of wind drifting and scouring, inform a model of wind slab release, validate satellite products, and track one of the leading abiotic drivers of a changing mountain watershed.I first joined the survey as a volunteer in 2007.By then, it had run for over a decade in remote, highelevation avalanche terrain, with no formal safety or avalanche protocols or training requirements.Coming from ski patrol, I found this alarming.After several years in academia, I learned it was unremarkable.Field safety provision was, and in places remains, uneven.Programs operating through polar or international logistics organizations had real requirements, while local fieldwork had whatever an individual investigator thought to provide.Field leaders in academia were trained as scientists, not practitioners, with few bridges between the two.Field safety was not taught, if it was addressed at all.Proposal budgets did not include funding for it.When I joined the program in 2010, I brought some knowledge of standard operational practices: protocols, training, and the habit of using close calls as data.Beyond bridging research and practice, this presentation describes the circular evolution between them.Field practice enabled the continuation and consistency of annual data collection in a remote, high-risk environment.The ongoing data collection improved the field practice through building years of experience from which to learn and improve.The results are an increasingly robust field safety program, enabling one of the longest fine-scale records of high alpine snowpack in the Rocky Mountains.

#9 [paper] Lettercraft dataset
Authors: Robert Flierman, Hope Williard, Luka van der Plas, Xander Vertegaal, Sam English, Alexander de Graaf, Wouter Hofland, Ellen Joosten
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22896398
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This dataset was created as part of the project Lettercraft and Epistolary Performance in Medieval Europe, a NWO-Vidi funded project based in the Department of Languages, Literature, and Culture at Utrecht University. The database came about in collaboration with Utrecht University’s Centre for Digital Humanities, who developed the online infrastructure, and with the help of students from Utrecht University Research Master’s Programme in Ancient, Medieval & Renaissance Studies, who joined the project as research apprentices. For more information about the project, visit the Lettercraft website. Here you can also browse the latest version of the data. About the project How did early medieval societies use the letter and who were among its users? The Lettercraft-project approaches the early medieval letter as a performative medium, whose communicative potential was defined principally by non-textual features: its materiality, its ability to be publicly read out and talked over, and its potential quickly to reach wide and diverse audiences. The project submits that the letter was a far more inclusive medium than is commonly assumed on the basis of its textual qualities. Literacy or social status were not required to participate in what the project calls lettercraft, i.e. the various performative actions (e.g. listening, speaking, negotiating, gossiping) that along with writing and reading made up epistolary communication. The project aims to show, moreover, that due to its public nature and social range, the letter was an essential tool of community-building and conflict-resolution in medieval society. As long as it was properly performed, a single letter could persuade an entire community. The project studies the performative potential of the letter in the context of the Merovingian Kingdoms, 476-751 CE, whose communicative networks covered much of Europe. Innovatively, it relies not on the surviving letter-collections, which showcase the literary exploits of elite ecclesiastical men, but rather on descriptions of lettercraft in Merovingian histories and saint-lives. The project proceeds along two complementary pathways. First, it has established an index of Merovingian epistolary terminology that is sensitive to all (textual and non-textual) aspects of lettercraft. This index can be consulted in the glossary provided on the Lettercraft website. We plan to include it in this dataset in the future. Second, the project is developing a new open access dataset of Merovingian epistolary communication, which records descriptions of letter-use documented in Merovingian narrative sources. Significantly, it is a dataset not of letters and their textual contents, but of the non-textual ‘metadata’ surrounding the epistolary process, including references to participants, delivery, performance, gift-giving, materiality, and audience. This enables users to analyses the social contexts in which early medieval epistolary communication took place, the diverse individuals and groups who participated in it, and the actions they performed. About the dataset Corpus – This dataset contains annotations on the use of letters in early medieval narrative texts. The project’s principal source are the eight volumes of Merovingian narrative texts edited by Bruno Krusch and Wilhelm Levison for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica under the header Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum (1885-1951), complemented with a smaller corpus of Merovingian texts not edited in this collection. NB: the annotation of this corpus is still ongoing. Specific information on date, authorship, editions and translations is given with each individual text. In terms of provenance, most of the texts in the dataset can be said to have originated in the Frankish kingdoms under Merovingian rule in the period 450-750, but we have followed the MGH editions in not keeping to a strict chronological or geographical demarcation. #10 [paper] Ten simple rules for preparing and delivering effective funding pitches in competitive grant applications
Authors: Andy Göbel, Tilman D. Rachner
Venue: PLoS Computational Biology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014840
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
In grant applications, oral presentations can be an integral part of the evaluation process. Funding pitches are a specific form of pitch presentations delivered during competitive review procedures to complement a written proposal. Their goal is to convince reviewers of both your project's strength and excellence as well as your suitability as a researcher. This paper offers ten simple rules on how to prepare and deliver effective funding pitches, with a particular focus on content selection, clear structuring, and convincing scientific argumentation. We also highlight the importance of practice and feedback and share practical strategies on how to handle questions and critical discussion professionally.

#13 [paper] Linguistic diversity and theory in psychological science
Authors: Kenny R. Coventry
Venue: Frontiers in Psychology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1866037
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
When it comes to understanding the human mind and behaviour, theory is often generated from and tested via samples that are not representative of the population as a whole. Over twenty years ago, this problem was brought into sharp focus with a number of authors calling for research in the cognitive and psychological sciences to be more aware of diversity and representativeness (e.g. Atran, Medin, & Ross, 2005;Norenzayan & Heine, 2005;Rozin, 2001) -a point also more recently recognised in comparative cognition (Andrews & Monsó, 2025). 'WEIRD' -Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic (Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan, 2010) -was coined as an acronym to raise awareness that most findings in psychological science and related fields are gleaned from studies with limited participant pools. Over a decade later, the extent to which such concerns have resulted in changes to practice can be questioned (e.g. Apicella, Norenzayen, & Henrich, 2020), and a coherent framework to embed linguistic and cultural diversity in psychological theorizing and empirical testing has yet to be established.In tandem with the recognition of a problem with representativeness in psychological science, two other major issues have emerged as ongoing concerns. First, there is the 'reproducibility crisis', pulling together a range of methodological and statistical issues, including worries regarding sample sizes, statistical reporting, questionable research practices (e.g. p-hacking) and publication bias (e.g. Open Science Collaboration, 2015). Second, a range of concerns have been expressed regarding the very nature of theorizing in the psychological sciences. Some have drawn attention to the lack of specificity of theories as one of the origins of the replication crisis itself, calling for more formal theories to be de rigour in the discipline (e.g. Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019;van Dongen et al., 2025), while others point the finger at the absence of an overarching theory formulation framework that may help to constrain theories to become more appropriately testable (e.g. van Rooij & Baggio, 2021,) akin to the 'levels of explanation' approach proposed by Marr (1982).In this article I consider how these three major concerns interconnect in consideration of one of the most essential elements of WEIRDness -the failure to embrace linguistic diversity in both theoretical and empirical psychological science.There are over 7,000 spoken and signed languages across the globe (Ethnologue, 2026), In contrast to the assumption from generative linguistics that languages share universal features (e.g. Chomsky, 1986;Pinker, 1996), a body of (largely) anthropological linguistic studies has shown that languages vary in significant ways, with diversity found at almost every level of linguistic organisation (Evans & Levinson, 2009). For example, languages differ across dimensions including sound systems, phonology, morphology, grammar, orthography, and semantics, leading Evans and Levinson (2009) to conclude that diversity is the most remarkable property of language. If the goal of the cognitive and psychological sciences is to identify and study universal psychological processes, akin to Newton's universal laws of physics (Kroupin, Davis & Henrich, 2025), then such linguistic diversity may challenge the very nature of the focus on universals (see Levinson, 2012 for discussion).In light of this linguistic diversity, one can ask how the cognitive and psychological sciences are doing prior and since Evans and Levinson (2009) in terms of sampling speakers of diverse languages. The answer is not very well. The cognitive and psychological sciences have been dominated with publication in English and testing of English-speaking participants. Abstract:
Associate Professor, Department of Government The rise of far-right antidemocratic actors in many consolidated democracies today poses a unique challenge. Political parties and leaders who enjoy popular support risk tearing apart the democratic fabric through tactics that appear lawful and are often invisible. What options do democracies have to defend themselves against such actors? Democratic self-defence, i.e. actions aimed at preventing, containing, resisting, or repairing democratic backsliding caused by domestic antidemocratic forces, can take many forms: from restrictions on candidacy rights to hate speech laws, and from street protests to welfare reforms. Political parties may exclude antidemocratic parties from coalitions, or they may choose to include them while seeking to moderate their positions. Alternatively, they may focus on expanding social protections in order to address the structural injustices that antidemocratic actors exploit. Such choices raise difficult normative questions. This book offers conceptual tools for making these choices intelligible and brings to light the principles that animate them. Political theorists addressing these issues have paid a great deal of attention to justifying repressive measures. Militant democracy, which includes the pre-emptive restriction of political and civil rights, has received so much attention in the past decade that one would be forgiven for thinking there is no alternative. This book is partly a reaction to this one-sided engagement with repressive measures. It examines less-known approaches to democratic self-defence that prioritise toleration and social integration respectively, strategies that are used as much, if not more, than militant restrictions. The three rationales of democratic self-defence that emerge –militant, tolerant, and social– are presented as ideal types. Unlike much theorising on democratic self-defence, which is prescriptive and advances a single normative framework, this book adopts a deliberately comparative approach that examines the strengths and weaknesses of each ideal type, as well as their connections and contrasts. It proposes conceptual definitions and analyses the normative justifications underpinning each type. The aim is to clarify the principles embodied in practices of democratic self-defence, enabling actors to better understand the normative commitments behind their choices and to make decisions that are ethically justified, democratically legitimate, and consistent with the values they seek to defend. The book also seeks to move the discussion beyond legal instruments and state responses by bringing broader societal and public actors into view. At the same time, it remains focused on agency: on both defenders of democracy and those who seek to undermine it. In doing so, it resists the tendency to portray democracy as a quasi-natural system whose resilience must simply be enhanced. Unlike many studies framed around the concept of democratic resilience, this book foregrounds human agency and the diverse actors who actively defend democracy across multiple spheres. Decisions about whether and how to confront antidemocratic actors do not fall exclusively on any single category of actor. They concern government authorities, courts, state agencies, municipal leaders, business actors, journalists, academics, and others. Democratic self-defence should therefore be understood as a form of agency distributed across a variety of actors. This book grew out of an article I co-authored in 2017 with my dear colleague Ludvig Norman, ‘Three Models of Democratic Self-defence: Militant Democracy and Its Alternatives’ published the year after in Political Studies. In that article, Ludvig and I challenged the dominance of militant democracy in debates on democratic self-defence by exploring two alternative perspectives: a tolerant approach (which we then called liberal-procedural) and a social approach, which we ultimately defended. #15 [paper] Costing global biodiversity framework delivery in megadiverse Australia
Authors: Paul Elton, Sarah Clément, Michelle Ward, Martine Maron
Venue: Journal of Environmental Management
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.130756
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Most nations worldwide face substantial funding gaps to halt biodiversity loss, yet many governments lack comprehensive cost estimates essential for effective budget allocation and implementation planning. This study provides a comprehensive estimate of the costs Australian governments would need to bear to deliver the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework in Australia. Using interpretive principles and evidence from peer-reviewed literature, and spatial analysis, we derived actions, unit costs, and cost factors (the amount of each action required to achieve the GBF's targets). We populated an automated model with these inputs to produce national and jurisdictional government cost estimates to inform planning and cost-sharing between national and subnational governments. Our method captures cost efficiencies from actions that benefit multiple targets. Our model estimates that delivering GBF targets in Australia will cost governments approximately AU$28.5 billion per annum from 2025 to 2050. At 1.1 per cent of GDP, this estimate shows comprehensive biodiversity conservation is arguably fiscally realistic. Our cost factor data can be disaggregated at various scales—such as bioregions, ecosystems, or Indigenous nations—to inform biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning. Our analysis and cost model offer a replicable methodology for other national governments to quantify their financial resourcing requirements for GBF implementation.

#16 [paper] Current state of dementia screening, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to the uptake of evidence-based dementia care in primary healthcare in Africa: a scoping review and call for implementation
Authors: Debela, Mitiku Bonsa, Krell-Roesch, Janina, Geda, Yonas, Bekele, Kebebe, Assefa, Tesfaye, Zenbaba, Demisu, Oljira, Lemessa, Takele, Abulie
Venue: BMC psychiatry
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43026524/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Dementia is a growing public health challenge worldwide, particularly in Africa. Although various screening tools have been used across different settings in the region, evidence on dementia screening practices, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to evidence-based dementia care has not been systematically mapped. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on dementia screening practices, risk reduction approaches, and barriers to dementia care across Africa. METHODS: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The review protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). A comprehensive search of major databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar) and grey literature was conducted. Eligible studies focused on dementia screening, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to evidence-based dementia care in primary healthcare settings across Africa. Study selection and data extraction were independently performed by three reviewers, and findings were synthesized using descriptive mapping. RESULTS: Of the 3,102 records identified, 16 studies met the inclusion criteria. Nine studies reported dementia screening practices using a range of screening tools, most commonly the Brief Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSID) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). The available evidence suggests that dementia screening was largely conducted within research settings rather than as part of routine primary healthcare. Six studies identified barriers to evidence-based dementia screening and care, including workforce shortages, limited infrastructure and funding, inadequate training, low policy prioritization, sociocultural stigma, and limited public awareness. Only one study evaluated the implementation of dementia risk reduction strategies in an African context, highlighting an important evidence gap. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence on dementia screening, risk reduction, and care integration in African primary healthcare remains limited. Key barriers include health system constraints, workforce shortages, inadequate infrastructure and funding, and sociocultural challenges. Future implementation research should evaluate culturally appropriate strategies to strengthen dementia detection, prevention, and integration of dementia services into primary healthcare across Africa.

#17 [paper] Cost-Effectiveness of Annual Atrial Fibrillation Screening Compared with Current Opportunistic Screening in Australian Primary Care: A Model-Based Economic Evaluation
Authors: Ureni Halahakone, Sameera Senanayake, Victoria McCreanor, William Parsonage, David Brain
Venue: Applied Health Economics and Health Policy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40258-026-01073-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although the guidelines recommend opportunistic screening for adults ≥ 65 years, screening for atrial fibrillation (AF) remains underutilised in Australia. The absence of guidance on how often to screen has resulted in variable practice and missed opportunities for AF detection. Previous studies have focused on handheld devices rather than 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) devices that are readily available in primary-care settings, and the evidence supporting an annual AF screening programme in Australia is limited. Therefore, the aim of this study is to compare the cost-effectiveness of an annual, structured, higher‑coverage opportunistic ECG screening approach (annual screening) with current unstructured opportunistic screening (current screening) in older adults in Australia. METHODS: A Markov model was developed to evaluate two strategies for adults ≥ 65 years: (1) annual screening using 12-lead ECG and (2) current opportunistic screening. The model included 11 health states capturing AF treatment and outcomes, and simulations were run using monthly cycles. A health system perspective and 10-year time horizon were applied. To account for uncertainty, a probabilistic sensitivity analysis with 1000 iterations was undertaken and the results were assessed against a cost-effectiveness threshold of 28,000 Australian dollars (AU$) per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Uncertainty was further examined through cost-effectiveness acceptability curves and scenario analyses to test the stability of findings under alternative assumptions. RESULTS: Annual screening increased costs by AU$4213 and gained 0.43 QALYs, yielding an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of AU$9797 per QALY gained. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis demonstrated that 100% of simulations yielded a positive incremental net monetary benefit. Scenario analyses demonstrated that both higher screening costs and less frequent 3-yearly screening were cost-effective in comparison to the current opportunistic screening, with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios below the cost-effectiveness threshold and positive incremental net monetary benefits in all scenarios. CONCLUSION: A structured annual screening approach for AF is likely to be a cost-effective strategy within the Australian primary-care setting. These findings highlight the benefits of more consistent screening practices for early AF detection and stroke prevention.

#20 [paper] Building a PET/CT Program in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Health-System Framework for Financing, Affordability, and Sustainable Implementation.
Authors: Mobit, Paul N, Mourad, Waleed F, Mosse, Wilfried B, Khair, Lana M, Njeh, Christopher F, Folefac, Edmund
Venue: Cancers
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43026854/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background: PET/CT is integral to modern oncology, yet access remains limited in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) because of capital requirements, radiopharmaceutical production complexity, workforce constraints, and weak reimbursement systems. We evaluated the modeled financial feasibility of a cyclotron-based PET/CT program using Cameroon as an illustrative national case and reframed implementation as a health-system planning problem rather than an equipment-purchase decision. Methods: A deterministic scenario model was developed over a 10-year horizon. The model was aligned conceptually with IAEA PET/cyclotron planning guidance, WHO OneHealth ingredients-based costing, and ISPOR principles for transparent decision modeling. The entry-level configuration comprised one PET/CT scanner, an 11-13 MeV negative-ion medical cyclotron, F-18 targetry, two synthesis modules, hot cells, a quality-control laboratory, backup power, and supporting infrastructure. Capital investment was modeled at USD 9 million as a planning estimate, with wide sensitivity analysis. Operating costs were separated into fixed, step-fixed, and variable components. Annual completed scan volumes of 500-5000 were evaluated, together with financing at 3%, 6%, 10%, and 12% APR, public capital support, operating subsidy, equipment availability, disease-specific demand, and alternative generator/satellite strategies. Results: At 6% financing, annual debt service for USD 9 million was USD 1.22 million. Modeled operating expenditure rose with activity from approximately USD 0.93 million at 500 completed scans to USD 1.77 million at 5000 scans because staffing and consumables were activity dependent. Total economic cost per completed scan declined from approximately USD 4311 at 500 scans to USD 598 at 5000 scans. If government provided the capital infrastructure, the operating cost to be recovered declined from USD 1865 to USD 353 per scan over the same activity range. A disease-specific incident-case model based on GLOBOCAN 2022 data for Cameroon showed that pathology confirmation, clinical eligibility, and referral completion materially constrain demand; at 30% histologic confirmation and 80% referral completion, approximately 1005 incident-case PET/CT examinations were generated under the base planning assumptions. Equipment availability of 80%, 90%, and 95% materially changed cost per completed scan in a 3000-slot program. Conclusions: Cyclotron-based PET/CT programs may achieve financial sustainability when patient throughput is sufficient, financing is appropriate, operations are reliable, and the surrounding cancer system can generate and act on evidence-based referrals. The model provides a transparent planning framework rather than empirical proof of sustainability and should be locally calibrated before investment decisions.

#21 [paper] Evaluation of the laboratory assessment process for A Clinically Oriented Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network (ACORN-LAP) in low-income and middle-income countries: a multicountry, cross-sec
Authors: ACORN Laboratory Investigators
Venue: The Lancet. Microbe
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42810374/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-quality microbiology laboratory data underpin effective antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance. Laboratory assessments are useful for ensuring the quality of microbiology data used for AMR surveillance, especially in low-income and middle-income countries where accreditation might not be feasible. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the microbiology laboratory assessment and quality monitoring tools developed to assess laboratories participating in A Clinically Oriented Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network 2 (ACORN2). METHODS: We conducted a multicountry observational study of microbiology laboratories participating in the ACORN2 surveillance project, including a baseline cross-sectional laboratory assessment process (ACORN-LAP) with longitudinal quality monitoring and follow-up. Between Sept 21, 2021, to Nov 25, 2024, all laboratories of hospitals identified as ACORN2 sites identified through investigator networks were invited to complete the ACORN-LAP. These laboratories were from nine countries across Asia and Africa. The assessment included an online REDCap-based assessment, and document-based and video call-based reviews by two selected ACORN assessors. The laboratories participated in quarterly quality monitoring processes, including the review of internal quality control (IQC) and external quality assessment (EQA) results. Anonymous feedback was collected, and an in-person feedback session was conducted during the study. The primary evaluation outcome was the findings of the ACORN-LAP, including the number of key and non-key recommendations identified. Secondary evaluation outcomes included quality monitoring performance, laboratory feedback on the ACORN-LAP and quality monitoring processes, and comparison of the ACORN-LAP and quality monitoring processes with existing laboratory assessment tools. FINDINGS: 20 laboratories completed the ACORN-LAP. The median time from initial contact with the laboratory to issuing recommendations was 3 months (IQR 3-4; range 1-8). The assessors identified 144 recommendations (median 6 per laboratory [IQR 3-8·5]; range 2-21), including 46 key and 98 non-key recommendations. Non-accredited laboratories received more recommendations per laboratory than accredited laboratories (median difference 5 [95% CI 1-11]; p=0·0062 and incidence rate ratio (IRR) 2·5 [95% CI 1·56-4·09]; p=0·0002). Non-accredited laboratories also received more key recommendations per laboratory (median difference 2 [95% CI 1-5]; p=0·0030) and IRR 4·75 [95% CI 2·11-11·84]; p=0·0003). 116 quality monitoring forms were completed (median 6 per laboratory [IQR 4-7]; range 2-9). 115 IQC and 59 scored EQA events were reported. Review of such quality monitoring data identified previously undetected IQC failures and led to improved IQC recording in some laboratories. Feedback showed that laboratories considered the assessment process useful although some laboratories found the assessment process labour intensive. INTERPRETATION: The findings support the use of structured laboratory assessment with ongoing quality monitoring to strengthen AMR surveillance, particularly in non-accredited laboratories. A simple, harmonised global online tool with integrated quality monitoring that assesses against a minimum standard could improve the quality and comparability of AMR surveillance data in low-income and middle-income countries. FUNDING: Wellcome Trust.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

- Integration of quantum computing into data pre-processing pipelines and learning workflows for data-heavy or computationally intensive tasks, demonstrating clear improvements in processing speed, computational complexity, modelling accuracy, and reduced sample requirements at scales achievable with NISQ-era devices,

- Reliable and scalable Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models and algorithms, integrated with existing AI frameworks and pipelines, enabling faster data processing, improved prediction accuracy, and enhanced computational capabilities,

- Validated quantum-enhanced AI methods demonstrating measurable improvements over classical baselines in terms of speed, accuracy, data efficiency, complexity, or scalability, supported by rigorous benchmarking and complexity analysis,

- Robust, noise-aware QML techniques suitable for NISQ hardware, including error-mitigation strategies and algorithmic adaptations that improve reliability, performance, and reproducibility on real quantum processors,

- Demonstrators or proof-of-concept applications showcasing the relevance of QML for real-world challenges (e.g. climate and environmental modelling, Earth observation, healthcare and life sciences, materials discovery, finance, robotics, manufacturing, and cybersecurity),

- Strengthened European leadership and technological sovereignty in quantum computing and trustworthy AI, supported by cross-sector collaboration, knowledge transfer, and contributions to emerging standards, benchmarks and best practices.

- Enhanced collaboration across quantum computing, machine learning and application domains, fostering a coordinated European QML research and innovation community.

Scope:

Proposals are expected to address multiple key research directions in Quantum Machine Learning (QML), targeting both scientific excellence and industrial relevance. Proposals should clearly outline how to contribute to the development, validation and demonstration of quantum-enhanced AI approaches, with clear pathways towards practical applications. The proposed work should strengthen Europe’s scientific and technological capabilities in quantum computing and accelerate the industrial uptake of quantum-enhanced AI solutions.

Activities may include, but are not limited to

- design and analysis of quantum, quantum-inspired or hybrid QML algorithms,

- performance modelling, complexity analysis and benchmarking of quantum-enhanced AI methods,

- development of error-mitigation and noise-aware strategies tailored to QML workloads,

Proposals should advance scalable QML algorithms capable of addressing large-scale, computationally intensive problems, this includes approaches that

- can manage massive data volumes and complex computational tasks,

- enable faster data processing and improved predictive performance in relevant application domains (e.g. hydrologic research, climate modelling, terrain classification from satellite remote sensing, drug discovery, and image-based medical diagnosis).

Many current QML methods remain closely inspired by classical algorithms and therefore do not yet achieve genuine quantum advantage, requiring further developments in

- quantum-native learning models,

- efficient quantum kernels and quantum feature mappings,

- algorithms demonstrating provable or empirical advantages over classical approaches.

Proposals may also include formal complexity analyses, identification of problem classes that can benefit from quantum acceleration.

Developments should address multiple of the following key research directions:

Quantum Supervised Learning (QSL):

Quantum Supervised Learning investigates how quantum algorithms can accelerate or improve the training of supervised learning models, offering novel opportunities to explore quantum–classical learning theories and enabling industry to shorten development cycles and enhance performance in data-intensive domains such as finance, healthcare, and Earth observation.

Abstract:
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has played a crucial role in providing an alternative bioequivalence (BE) approach for generic orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), in addition to comparative clinical endpoint or pharmacodynamic BE studies, as a relatively cost- and time-efficient complement to benchtop and clinical experiments that has been widely used in developing and assessing generic inhaler devices. However, despite the advances in the power of modern computers, there are still some bottlenecks in using CFD due to computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications. Machine learning (ML) has been gaining more attention as a potential tool to alleviate such limitations that arise in CFD. The purpose of this grant is to develop a methodology to integrate ML with CFD models of OIDPs to promote alternative BE studies to enhance and accelerate the development and approval of generic OIDPs.

#1 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#2 [paper] Is guideline-cited evidence keeping pace with the biomedical literature? A cohort analysis, 2008–2025
Authors: Jordan Lewis Fulcher
Venue: Open Science Framework
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/vn9bq
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Biomedical publication volume has grown roughly exponentially, but whether the research that reaches clinical guidelines has grown at the same rate is unknown. This meta-research study follows each annual cohort of research articles in PubMed (2008–2024) to measure how many are later cited by clinical practice guidelines. Guidelines come from two co-primary frames: PubMed's Practice Guideline publication type, and a pre-specified list of 31 named guideline bodies. Reference lists come from the NIH iCite API. Co-primary outcomes: the absolute number of guideline-cited papers per cohort (P1), and the cohort trend in the hazard of first guideline citation (P2, from Kaplan–Meier life tables and a discrete-time hazard model). Secondary analyses: breakpoints, a decomposition into guideline capacity, and a comparison of six high-volume public-data study designs with all other research.

This is a database snapshot of the iCite web service (provided here as a single zipped CSV file, or compressed, tarred JSON files). In addition, citation links in the NIH Open Citation Collection are provided as a two-column CSV table in open_citation_collection.zip. iCite provides bibliometrics and metadata on publications indexed in PubMed, organized into three modules: Influence: Delivers metrics of scientific influence, field-adjusted and benchmarked to NIH publications as the baseline. Field-adjusted, time-adjusted and benchmarked against NIH-funded papers. The median RCR for NIH funded papers in any field is 1.0. An RCR of 2.0 means a paper is receiving twice as many citations per year than the median NIH funded paper in its field and year, while an RCR of 0.5 means that it is receiving half as many citations per year. Calculation details are documented in Hutchins et al., PLoS Biol. 2016;14(9):e1002541. provisional: RCRs for papers published in the previous two years are flagged as "provisional", to reflect that citation metrics for newer articles are not necessarily as stable as they are for older articles. Provisional RCRs are provided for papers published previous year, if they have received with 5 citations or more, despite being, in many cases, less than a year old. All papers published the year before the previous year receive provisional RCRs. The current year is considered to be the NIH Fiscal Year which starts in October. For example, in July 2019 (NIH Fiscal Year 2019), papers from 2018 receive provisional RCRs if they have 5 citations or more, and all papers from 2017 receive provisional RCRs. #6 [paper] Citation accuracy, citation noise, and citation bias: a foundation of citation analysis
Authors: Lutz Bornmann, Christian Leibel
Venue: Scientometrics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-026-05841-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Citation analysis is widely used in research evaluation to assess the impact of scientific papers. These analyses rest on the assumption that citation decisions by authors are accurate, representing the flow of knowledge from cited to citing papers. However, in practice, researchers often cite for reasons that are not related to the fact that there has been (intellectual) input from previous papers. Citations made for rhetorical reasons or without reading the cited work compromise the value of citations as instrument for research evaluation. Past research on threats to the accuracy of citations has mainly focused on citation bias as the primary concern. In this paper, we argue that citation noise—the undesirable variance in citation decisions—represents an equally critical but underexplored challenge in citation analysis. We define and differentiate two types of citation noise: citation level noise and citation pattern noise. Each type of noise is described in terms of how it arises and the specific ways it can undermine the validity of citation-based research assessments. By conceptually differing citation noise from citation accuracy and citation bias, we propose a framework for the foundation of citation analysis. We discuss strategies and interventions to minimize citation noise, aiming to improve the reliability and validity of citation analysis in research evaluation. We recommend that the current professional reform movement in research evaluation such as the Coalition for Advancing Research Assessment (CoARA) pick up these strategies and interventions as an additional building block for careful, responsible use of bibliometric indicators in research evaluation.

Language-model agents that remember across sessions compress what they store: they summarise dialogue, extract facts, or evict cache entries, and then answer later questions from what is left. The compression ratios used to justify these designs come mostly from prompt-compression work in which the question is visible when compression runs. This paper examines whether those results transfer to the memory write, where the compressor must decide what to keep before any question exists. The premise that no one measures this does not survive the literature. The key-value cache line has built query-agnostic compressors and audited query visibility directly: in one matched-budget audit, the method the auditors call the most widely deployed beats a keep-the-start-and-recent-window baseline when it sees the question and loses to it when it does not. The paper argues that what remains open is narrower and harder. Every located "query-agnostic" result is still distribution-aware: the compressor is tuned for, or scored against, questions drawn from the same generator. A memory write has two properties no located protocol scores: its future query distribution is set by events that have not happened, and its compressions compose, because summaries are summarised again and records are overwritten. Published agent-memory evidence is consistent with that reading. Summary units are retrieved with 90.7 percent recall yet answer at 31.5 F1. In a 2024 pilot, two commercial assistants answering from fact stores written during the conversation scored 24.7 to 71.1 percent, where reading the raw history scored 91.8. The paper separates three query-visibility regimes, states what a write-time compression claim would have to report, and names the experiment that would settle the open part. Every arXiv citation was machine-verified against its live arXiv Atom API record, and every other citation against its DOI record, during drafting (title and author list checked against the record returned). No experiment was run and no number in this paper was measured by its author. Table 1 re-presents numbers published by the cited papers, each named on its row; Figure 1 plots published values from three cited papers with no transformation beyond rounding. Longitudinal bibliometric analyses rely on annual citation histories, yet missing annual observations are frequently difficult to distinguish from true zero-citation years. The case study comprises 595 consolidated publications derived from 616 Google Scholar article records, and examines the completed calendar years 2024-2025. Three scenarios are compared: strictly observed annual counts (A), hypothetical zeros for internal gaps only (B), and hypothetical zeros for all missing years within a valid publication interval (C). These findings demonstrate that unchanged indicator values and perfect correlations on a common subset do not guarantee stable rankings when eligibility changes. The zero assignments are hypothetical sensitivity assumptions, not evidence of provider semantics. The results are descriptive and based on a single researcher profile. Abstract:
This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23129310. ## Summary This paper tackles a genuinely important problem in production agent systems: context management as a *learned policy* rather than a length-triggered fallback. The authors augment a coding agent (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, terminal REPL scaffold) with a `compact()` action and train it in two stages: (1) SFT on 1,052 judge-corrected trajectories collected from 379 SWE-rebench tasks, where GPT-5.5-Codex acts as an online judge correcting compaction timing, working-state summaries, and post-compaction actions, with corrections executed in the environment before being used as training data; (2) GRPO-based RL on SWE-Gym with binary task-success rewards, no KL penalty, no entropy bonus, and no compaction-specific reward shaping. The headline result is +9.2% / +5.0% absolute pass-rate gains over the base model on SWE-bench Verified (39.6%) and SWE-PolyBench Verified (24.5%), with gains holding across per-task inference budgets from $0.10 to $4.00. The paper's most distinctive claim is that supervising *what the agent does after compaction* — not just when to compact or what to write in the summary — is the missing piece in prior work, and the online-correction data collection method is the mechanism that delivers it. ## Strengths 1. **The problem framing is correct and under-studied.** The introduction's distinction — compaction tied to *task progress* rather than *context length* — matches production experience: stale exploration (dead hypotheses, verbose tool outputs) degrades agent behavior long before any window limit is hit. The Figure 3(a) result, where proactive compaction helps even in the 256K regime where nothing overflows, is the paper's most practically significant finding. 2. **The data-collection design is the real contribution.** Correcting outputs *before* execution so the trajectory continues from corrected decisions (Section 2.2) is meaningfully different from post-hoc annotation or offline insertion (SWE-Compressor). The AutoCompact-SFT vs. SWE-Compressor comparison (+1.2% / +1.6% with comparable data) is a fair, well-scoped ablation supporting this. 3. **"Summary self-consistency" is a useful new lens.** The Section 3.4 case study (django-13809) — a summary can satisfy coverage checks while proposing a next action incompatible with its own recorded state — names a failure mode I have seen in production agent summaries but rarely seen formalized. That SFT imitates summaries while RL constrains them through downstream success is a clean, honest explanation of the mechanism. 4. **Budget-framed evaluation is the right framing.** Reporting pass rate against dollars-per-task, with explicit token pricing (Alibaba Cloud Model Studio, cached tokens at 20%), treats inference economics as a first-class metric. Too few agent papers do this. ## Major concerns **1. Abstract Bibliometric indicators are widely used to evaluate scientific performance, despite well-known limitations related to disciplinary differences, collaboration practices, and strategic responses to evaluation systems. Traditional metrics such as the H-index are particularly sensitive to the number of co-authors and to the length of reference lists, both of which have exhibited strong historical growth. The purpose of this study is to examine papers in the field of educational technologies published in the Journal of Theory and Practice in Education (EKU) between 2005 and 2025. Using bibliometric analysis, it determines the journal's thematic, methodological, and sample-based publication trends. Seventy papers were identified through a manual systematic review, and citation counts, keyword patterns, study designs, and participant categories were analysed. RAWGraphs and VOSviewer software were then used to visualise the data. The results indicate that the journal underwent a period of rapid growth between 2013 and 2017, a hiatus in publication in 2021, and achieved publication consistency after 2022. Abstract:
A key part of OCEAN ICE is ensuring that the data, models, software, and other research outputs produced by the project remain accessible, discoverable, and useful to the scientific community beyond the project's lifetime. Importantly, as recognised during the SOOS Scientific Steering Committee (SSC) and Data Management Sub-Committee (DMSC) meeting held at SCAR 2026 in Oslo, while the technical support and development of SOOSmap represent a key milestone of OCEAN ICE, the data products generated by the project constitute key assets for SOOSmap and its community. The OCEAN ICE web data portal therefore brings together complementary components that support the discovery, access, visualisation, analysis, and reuse of these resources. The project also provided practical tools and reproducible workflows to facilitate the use of OCEAN ICE outputs. In particular, the OCEAN ICE Literacy environment provides web-executable Jupyter notebooks through Google Colab, enabling researchers and other stakeholders to access, query, process, analyse and visualise OCEAN ICE data programmatically. Combined with SOOSmap, these resources establish a workflow that connects data discovery and visualisation with computational analysis and reproducible reuse, increasing the long-term visibility and scientific value of OCEAN ICE outputs. Together, these components constitute the overall OCEAN ICE Web Data Portal outcomes and provide a practical environment through which project resources can continue to be discovered, accessed and reused beyond the project lifetime. This approach has enabled OCEAN ICE data and products to contribute to international assessments, climate model development and multinational ocean-observing initiatives. OCEAN ICE has therefore not only delivered the planned data-management infrastructure and services, but has also established a practical, reusable framework for integrating, disseminating, and reusing polar oceanographic observations within international marine data infrastructures.

Abstract:
Abstract Marine Spatial Data Infrastructures (MSDI) and Open Science (OS) have reshaped how marine data are managed, shared, and reused, but have largely evolved as separate domains. This integrative review examines how their alignment can advance FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) and sustainable ocean knowledge systems. The study combines a quantitative bibliometric analysis of the broader Spatial Data Infrastructure (SDI) and OS literature with an integrative qualitative synthesis of 54 marine-domain sources, including 41 publications selected through PRISMA screening and 13 additional records identified through snowballing. The bibliometric analysis shows separate development trajectories, but also convergence around metadata, interoperability, standards, ontology, artificial intelligence, big data, reproducibility, and FAIR principles. The qualitative synthesis shows that FAIR provides a practical bridge between MSDI and OS: MSDI contribute technical and institutional foundations for discovery, access, interoperability, stewardship, and preservation, while OS extends these foundations toward transparency, reproducibility, workflow publication, collaborative analysis, and knowledge generation. The Blue-Cloud project illustrates this alignment through federated data infrastructures, virtual research environments, and reusable workflows. We identify four priorities: credible FAIR assessment, semantic and workflow interoperability, enduring governance and maintenance, and a shift beyond data portals toward sustainable ocean knowledge systems.

Abstract:
NASA’s aquatic and marine research enterprise within the overarching NASA Biosphere Program is entering an era of unprecedented data abundance. MODIS and the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission already generate ocean color data at rates that strain legacy processing and archiving workflows, and forthcoming missions will add further volume and complexity. These satellite streams are joined by rapidly growing in situ networks (e.g., BGC-Argo), suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, citizen science, and increasingly high-resolution numerical models. The result is a Big Data regime in which the volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean relevant Earth system data exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches. An important goal is to fully integrate observing workflows, understanding, and models across the terrestrial, aquatic, and atmosphere domains to fully enable understanding of life and the realization of improved information to manage uses of ecosystem services. This white paper addresses Leveraging Ocean Data and Models, a cross-cutting Grand Challenge that underlies and enables progress on the four other foundational grand challenges under the NASA Biosphere, Atmosphere, Cryosphere, and Hydrosphere framework - Global Biosphere, Carbon and the Elements of Life, Interface Habitats, and Transient Events - each of which depends on the ability to acquire, harmonize, and synthesize disparate satellite, suborbital, in situ, and model data streams. We recommend a decadal strategy built on two complementary pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data, covering tiered cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, and machine learning; and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation, covering mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimilation, hybrid approaches, mission emulators, and a NASA Digital Twin Ocean. Without concerted, proactive investment in this cross-cutting infrastructure, the scientific and societal returns on the coming decade’s expanded observing system will be substantially diminished.

Abstract:
The ocean remains critically under-observed, particularly in coastal zones where traditional monitoring is limited by cost, logistical constraints, and competing regulatory priorities. Marine citizen science offers an emerging and powerful complementary approach to addressing these gaps; however, data management challenges currently limit its full integration into scientific and policy data infrastructures. The inaugural workshop of the Marine Citizen Science Data Network (MCSDN), held in February 2026 in Ostend, Belgium, brought together approximately 200 participants from over 30 countries. Attendees included representatives from marine citizen science initiatives, developers of low-cost monitoring devices, data managers, and researchers and data users. Together they identified challenges, opportunities and co-designed recommendations to improve marine citizen science data flows. Workshop discussions highlighted interconnected barriers and enabling factors affecting FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) marine citizen science data. These included fragmented data flows, weak connections between communities, limited participant engagement and feedback mechanisms, the potential of accessible low-cost technologies, and the need for shared practices and standardized documentation. Building on these themes, the workshop produced four concrete recommendations to enhance the reuse and impact of marine citizen science data: (1) develop discipline-specific FAIR guidance, (2) establish minimum metadata standards, (3) create simplified training materials, and (4) support the development and deployment of low-cost sensors. This perspective article presents the EU-funded CS-MACH1 project’s approach to bridging marine citizen science initiatives with European data infrastructures, and highlights the community’s readiness to deliver FAIR, impactful in situ ocean observations.

Abstract:
Using the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework, this research evaluates Taiwan’s oceanographic data management and identifies issues for the prospect of its development. Six databanks were interviewed. Taiwan’s oceanographic data management remains in an orderly chaos. On one hand, it is chaotic because there exist multiple actors with their own data management rules. The fact that these databanks enact their own data management rules and operate accordingly makes the whole context even more fragmented. Therefore, community attributes are a mixture of open data and limited free data usage because revenues of data processing can cover costs of bureaucratic operation and cybersecurity measures. On the other hand, it is orderly because all databanks view open data as a public good while recognizing the importance of data management. The UN initiative of Ocean Decade serves as a strong impetus in advancing Taiwan’s oceanographic data management. Given the situation, it is debated whether integrating oceanographic data and marine-related information to one single databank, National Ocean Database and Sharing System (NODASS) positioned under Ocean Affairs Council (OAC), is economically efficient. OAC also lacks a set of reward-and-punishment rules to enforce data submission to NODASS. Meanwhile, it is also debated whether OAC should be restructured as a ministry and enact a set of generally followed rules of data management. To further develop data management and facilitate data exchange with the international oceanography community, OAC will need to cultivate professional capability while enhancing inter-agency policy coordination.

#6 [paper] Sensoring the Oceans: The Argo Floats Array in the Governance of Science Data Infrastructures
