Abstract:
What role do governance arrangements, background legal rules, and the core infrastructures play in enabling collection and production of oceans data, and other data and knowledge of planetary significance? We explore this by focusing on Argo – an international program of research institutions and state agencies that deploys arrays of autonomous environmental sensor-equipped floats to collect and process ocean observation data that is then made freely available to all. We analyze the techniques and practices involved in planning, testing, calibrating, validating, and error-correcting that ultimately lead to the production, transmission, and dissemination of Argo data. We position Argo within the institutional governance of oceans, weather, climate and, most recently, earth systems to illustrate both the evolution of Argo’s role and its evolving and uneasy position within different governance approaches. In the conclusion, we highlight the advantages of organic network-based open science-data infrastructural initiatives in the development of planetary knowledge and governance, and point to some of the risks and trade-offs if this were to become subsumed into wider and more formalized international data-infrastructure hierarchies.

#7 [paper] Digital Tech Interventions in Marine Ecosystem Monitoring: An Integrative Review

Abstract:
Marine ecosystems are changing faster than the observation systems designed to track them. This article presents an integrative review of digital technology interventions in marine ecosystem monitoring, synthesising peer-reviewed research on sensing platforms, molecular and acoustic methods, machine learning, and ocean data infrastructures published mainly between 2014 and 2026. The review addresses three questions: which classes of digital technology now support marine ecosystem monitoring and what ecological information each supplies; which recurring technical and institutional constraints limit their contribution to sustained, decision-relevant observation; and how these classes can be combined conceptually into an architecture linking sensing to management decisions. The synthesis shows that satellite remote sensing, autonomous platforms, environmental DNA, and passive acoustics have matured within largely separate research streams, each with distinctive observational strengths and each constrained by calibration demands, energy and sensor limits, interpretive uncertainty, or fragmented data practices. Machine learning relieves an analysis bottleneck created by high-volume sensing but introduces its own validation requirements. Building on these findings, the article proposes a four-layer sensing-to-decision architecture that connects observation, analytics, data integration, and governance through explicit feedback loops, using essential ocean variables as the prioritisation logic that binds the layers together. The framework offers monitoring programme designers and ocean governance bodies a structured basis for investment and evaluation decisions, and it identifies cost-effectiveness evidence, cross-domain interoperability, and institutional data governance as priorities for future research.

This review looks at technological and recent innovations along with uses from the Argo and Biogeochemical-Argo programs, satellite remote sensing, autonomous underwater vehicles, and cloud-native data architectures. This review assesses the integration of these systems with Artificial Intelligence, particularly large language models enhanced with vector-database retrieval systems and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This paper discusses the major hindrances to efficient ocean data utilization like data fragmentation, also throwing light on the intricate formats like NetCDF, scalability, and policy barriers. It highlights modern practices such as practical lakehouse architectures, cloud processing, and AI systems with semantic retrieval controls. Furthermore, the review describes and discusses AI prototypes and systems built from case studies designed to assist in disaster response and mitigation, monitor climate, and manage fisheries by transforming data on spectra, profiles, and images into concise answers and easy-to-understand visual response graphics. Abstract:
The International Seabed Authority (ISA) is negotiating rules for commercial exploitation in the Area, with particular significance for the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ), which contains most polymetallic nodule exploration contract areas. The CCZ regional environmental management plan (REMP) is intended to connect the environmental protection mandate in Article 145 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) with decisions on individual projects. Yet adoption alone does not show that a plan can shape mining activity, and ecological outcomes cannot be observed before exploitation begins. This article assesses the plan’s prospective institutional effectiveness through qualitative analysis of ISA instruments, the 2025 standardized procedure for REMPs, draft exploitation regulations, scientific assessments and policy literature across four dimensions: regulatory translation, ecological coherence, implementation capacity and adaptive management. The Agreement under UNCLOS on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), now in force, leaves the ISA legal framework intact while creating a setting in which REMP decision records may support cross-institutional coordination. The analysis finds partial institutional effectiveness. The plan is embedded in ISA decision-making, but it does more to shape whether an application is approved than to define what an approved contractor must do during operations. The network of areas of particular environmental interest (APEIs) has been expanded in response to scientific evidence, yet ecological criteria have only partly shaped spatial allocation, because existing contract and reserved areas constrained network design. Contractor-level supervision is more developed than regional assessment, where cumulative environmental change cannot yet be readily linked to regulatory consequences. Periodic review identifies occasions for reconsideration but does not specify which findings should initiate which responses. These limitations converge at three institutional transmission interfaces between regional objectives and contractor obligations, ecological evidence and spatial allocation, and monitoring findings and authorized decisions. The CCZ case yields three conditions for effective REMPs: contractor-facing regulatory force, ecologically justified spatial protection, and institutionalized monitoring, review and adaptive adjustment. These conditions offer a transferable basis for future REMPs while spatial and regulatory options remain open.

Abstract:
Marine information supports navigation, infrastructure, environmental protection and ocean space allocation. Its availability, however, does not establish its suitability for a particular decision or an institution’s ability to use it responsibly. This working paper examines the institutional conditions under which hydrospatial knowledge can support maritime choices and cooperation. The analysis develops a conceptual framework informed by official hydrographic guidance and ocean information initiatives. Hydrospatial knowledge is treated as a perspective connecting water related information, spatial context and application. The discussion distinguishes geographical coverage from evidential fitness and examines how resolution, provenance, metadata, uncertainty and temporal relevance influence interpretation. GIS, remote sensing and machine learning are considered within this relationship between analytical capability and institutional responsibility. The paper addresses reproducibility, validation and the limits of inference, emphasising that sophisticated processing cannot compensate automatically for unsuitable observations or poorly defined questions. Interoperability is examined alongside governance arrangements, access conditions, procurement and dependence on external expertise. Four dimensions structure the proposed assessment: question definition, evidence suitability, analytical accountability and institutional use. Together, they trace the connection between a decision requirement, the information supporting it, the analytical process and the authority responsible for acting. Hypothetical illustrations concern preliminary cable planning, coastal planning and offshore operations; they demonstrate analytical questions rather than validate particular applications. The contribution is a framework connecting marine data governance with institutional capacity and strategic autonomy. Practical implications include clearer commissioning, documented assumptions, proportionate quality assurance and retained competence to evaluate external services. Cooperation is understood as a means of strengthening informed agency rather than requiring complete technological independence. The paper does not certify datasets, assess surveys or test analytical systems. Comparative research, combining documentary evidence, interviews and specialist review, is proposed to examine whether the framework identifies consequential differences in capability and improves the transparency and defensibility of maritime decisions.

The vast oceans record the impacts of climate change and human activities on the Earth system. Over the past century, oceanographic scientists have collected extensive ocean profile data to reflect variations of oceanic elements, such as dissolved oxygen. However, due to the sophisticated measurements and high costs, historical ocean element observation data remains highly sparse and uneven across the global ocean, with the annual missing rate exceeding 90%. Thus, quantitatively understanding the four-dimensional (4D) spatiotemporal evolution of oceanic elements continues to pose a significant challenge. Machine learning (ML) techniques demonstrate superior capabilities in perceiving spatiotemporal variations within large-scale data, presenting promising opportunities to harness implicit correlations for global reconstruction. However, fragmented data and interdisciplinary differences create barriers to the availability of AI-ready open data, further hindering ML practitioners from designing specialized models. Abstract:
This study aims to analyze the concepts of “library science” and “information science” in the works of philosopher Luciano Floridi, examining his proposed relationship between these disciplines and the philosophy of information. The scope of the research consists of Luciano Floridi’s works available in the Scopus database. The methodology consists of a bibliographic review and content analysis with a posteriori categorization. The data analysis evaluates the concept of library and information science in Floridi’s works and examines the discipline as an applied philosophy of information, its disciplinary characteristics, his argument regarding a crisis of theoretical foundations, and the discipline’s relationships with the philosophy of information and social epistemology as solutions to this crisis. It concludes by presenting the gaps in Floridi’s proposal and suggesting avenues for further research to better understand the field.

#5 [paper] CONSTRUÇÃO DE ESTRATÉGIAS PÚBLICAS PARA A INFORMAÇÃO: A PRODUÇÃO DO IBICT
Authors: Tainá Batista de Assis, Frederico Ramos Oliveira, Graziela Barros Gomes, Raíssa da Veiga de Menêses, Tiago Emmanuel Nunes Braga
Venue: Enancib
Year: 2026
Link: https://enancib.ancib.org/index/article/view/3051
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The Brazilian Institute of Information in Science and Technology (IBICT) announced, in 2026, four guiding concepts for its next Strategic Plan: informational integrity and justice, information for citizenship, Open Science, and informational sovereignty. This study aimed to understand the extent to which the scientific production profile of IBICT researchers aligns with these axes, in order to identify priority areas for internal funding. ScriptLattes was used to extract publications from 48 higher-education-level researchers for the period 2023–2025, followed by manual extraction of the keywords from each document. The terms were classified according to their thematic proximity to the four concepts, and the distribution of researchers across each axis was analyzed. The results show a strong concentration in the axes “information for citizenship” (29 associations) and “Open Science” (26), whereas “informational sovereignty” has the smallest contingent (10), with 90% holding doctoral degrees. The terminological analysis reveals interdisciplinarity with fields such as sociology, law, health, and computing. The study concludes that funding should prioritize informational sovereignty and the integration among concepts, as well as support the qualification of researchers with lower academic degrees.

#6 [paper] CIÊNCIA ABERTA COMO POSSIBILIDADE DE COOPERAÇÃO BRASIL-ANGOLA
Authors: Rafael RAFAEL, Laurindo Virgilio Rafael, Edgar Bisset-Alvarez
Venue: Enancib
Year: 2026
Link: https://enancib.ancib.org/index/article/view/2408
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Within the context of South–South cooperation, understood as a model of cultural and scientific exchange among countries of the Global South, Brazil has played a significant role in technology transfer and human resource development through various initiatives. However, the adoption of open science practices and infrastructures remains a major challenge for enhancing the visibility of scientific production and democratizing access to knowledge, particularly in developing countries. From this perspective, this study aims to discuss open science infrastructures as a means of expanding scientific cooperation between Brazil and Angola within the broader framework of Brazil's scientific partnerships with African countries. To this end, a survey was conducted of the main institutional, policy, legislative, and infrastructural mechanisms that promote open science in Brazil and Angola, serving as a basis for examining opportunities for exchange and collaboration between the two countries. The findings indicate that Brazil has a broad range of policies, legislation, and infrastructures that foster and support open science practices. In contrast, although Angola has not yet established open science as a formal public policy, the country has demonstrated initiatives moving in this direction, albeit still at an early stage of development. In this regard, strengthening targeted cooperation among institutions and their respective open science infrastructures is essential to facilitate the exchange of experiences, promote capacity building, and encourage the sharing of scientific data and knowledge between Brazil and Angola.

#10 [paper] Ethical reflexivity in action: contract researcher strategies and collaborative governance insights from sport for development
Authors: Frank van Eekeren, Chris Noij, Gerolf Pikker
Venue: Sport in Society
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/17430437.2026.2729421
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Ethical tensions arising from conflicting institutional expectations, personal values, and unequal power relations between actors from the Global North and South in Sport for Development (SFD) programs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A qualitative analysis drawing on a critical incident from the authors' roles as contract researchers.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A Dutch-led Sport for Development (SFD) program.
Abstract:
This paper examines how ethical reflexivity can deepen our understanding of contract researcher strategies and collaborative governance in Sport for Development (SFD). Drawing on a critical incident from our role as contract researchers in a Dutch-led SFD program, we explore how ethical tensions emerge from conflicting institutional expectations, personal values, and unequal power relations between actors from the Global North and South. Rather than offering definitive solutions, the study presents ethical reflexivity as a situated practice. Practically, it enables researchers to navigate ambiguity and make sense of tensions as they arise. Epistemologically, it sheds light on the everyday micro-practices that shape collaborative governance. Ethically, it underscores the need for ongoing reflection and accountability in contexts marked by asymmetry and contractual dependency. By foregrounding the moral and political dimensions of research practice, this study contributes to critical debates on power, ethics, and knowledge production in the collaborative governance of SFD.

#12 [paper] Reflective interdisciplinarity in practice: integrating biology and philosophy in studies of individualization
Authors: Marie I. Kaiser, Anton Killin, Barbara A. Caspers, Jürgen Gadau, Sylvia Kaiser, Joachim Kurtz, Caroline Müller, S. Helene Richter
Venue: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-08458-4
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Interdisciplinary research is widely acknowledged as a valuable means of knowledge production and as crucial for addressing complex scientific and societal problems. Interdisciplinary research takes many forms, and this article offers a novel case study of a distinctive form of interdisciplinarity, reflective interdisciplinarity. The article analyzes interdisciplinary research undertaken by philosophers of biology and empirically working biologists studying individualization. This kind of interdisciplinarity is reflective because biology is the target domain that philosophers of biology (and philosophically-minded biologists) reflect upon—as opposed to interdisciplinarity that occurs, for example, when insights from multiple distinct research domains are integrated. To analyze the case study, an analytic framework is developed that distinguishes four dimensions of interdisciplinarity: objects of interdisciplinary research, interdisciplinary research activities, communication of interdisciplinary results, and personal, institutional, and other conditions of interdisciplinary research. The case study shows, first, that reflective interdisciplinarity can involve interdependent, deeply immersive and cooperative interdisciplinary research processes (‘inquiry-embedded integration’) that include a form of knowledge-producing inquiry through which novel epistemic products emerge from joint commitments and goals, shared research questions, and intensive, collaborative discursive practices. The article adapts the notion of a plural subject in characterizing inquiry-embedded integration. Second, the analysis of the case study demonstrates how communicative choices, together with institutional and normative conditions, are partially constitutive of the interdisciplinary process. They shape the content of interdisciplinary products and play decisive roles in interdisciplinary activities such as knowledge integration. Finally, because the case study comprises the authors’ own research processes and publications, the analysis demonstrates that self-reflexive, qualitative analysis of interdisciplinary practice provides a valuable means of theorizing about interdisciplinarity with potential to offer transferable insights.

#13 [paper] Stratégie de science ouverte
Authors: MESRE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.52949/93
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
La Stratégie de science ouverte (SSO) 2026-2033 a pour objectif de consolider les changements initiés avec les deux plans précédents portés à l’échelle nationale en France. Elle couvre huit ans et se structure en ambitions, enjeux, objectifs stratégiques et plans d’action quadriennaux. Les ambitions de la science ouverte sont : un rayonnement et une souveraineté scientifiques accrus, une recherche plus cumulative et collaborative, plus reproductible, responsable et durable, et qui favorise l’innovation et s’ouvre au-delà du monde académique. Parmi les enjeux, la SSO identifie : l’hétérogénéité des pratiques disciplinaires, la résistance au partage des données, la fragilité des infrastructures, les questions de qualité dans l’édition scientifique, la faible valorisation des logiciels de recherche, la communication insuffisante des résultats des essais cliniques. La Stratégie identifie également les leviers pour répondre à ces défis, comme l’évaluation de la recherche et la coordination internationale. L’intelligence artificielle (IA) offre des opportunités, mais aussi des problématiques auxquelles il faut répondre. La SSO vise à concilier la science ouverte avec la protection de la recherche, en appliquant le principe « aussi ouvert que possible, aussi fermé que nécessaire ». Les plans d’action quadriennaux sont inscrits dans huit objectifs stratégiques. Quatre objectifs ciblent les pratiques, la gouvernance et les instruments de la science ouverte, les services et infrastructures, et le positionnement de la France dans le paysage européen et international. Les quatre autres objectifs concernent les publications, les données, les logiciels et les résultats des essais cliniques. Le plan d’action pour la période 2026-2029 décline ces objectifs en 30 actions et 75 mesures. Il engage des nouveaux projets comme une forge nationale pour les logiciels de recherche. Il renforce également les mesures phares comme HAL, Recherche Data Gouv et Software Heritage. La SSO est complétée par le bilan de la politique nationale. Les progrès ont été notables, mais un travail considérable reste à accomplir. La SSO trace une voie ambitieuse, celle d’une recherche française plus transparente, collaborative et souveraine, capable de relever les défis scientifiques du XXIe siècle.

#18 [paper] El realismo pragmatista y la relevancia de la predicción científica en Wenceslao J. González: la búsqueda de la objetividad como ruta para la verdad
Authors: Ana María Alonso Rodríguez
Venue: SCIO Revista de Filosofía
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.46583/scio_2026.30.1272
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): To analyze Wenceslao J. González's pragmatist realism and its emphasis on scientific prediction as a path to objectivity and truth.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Philosophical analysis of González's framework, comparing it to Nicholas Rescher's pragmatic idealism and examining the role of prediction in semantic, epistemological, and ontological aspects.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Current context of Philosophy of Science and Technology, addressing challenges of complexity and historicity.
Abstract:
The predictive success of Science can be regarded as a factor of objectivity. Predictive statements may be correct at the time they are made, but their truth is only verified when the anticipated event occurs. Wenceslao J. Gonzalez’s pragmatist realism emphasises Science understood as an activity and the role of prediction (epistemological, ontological and heuristic) as a path to objectivity, which brings us closer to the truth in three aspects: semantic, epistemological and ontological. Scientific activity is and must be plural. Thus, basic Science explains and predicts, applied Science predicts and prescribes, and the application of Science involves prognosis and specific guidelines for action. This article analyses the novelty offered by pragmatist realism in the current context. It presents it as an alternative to Nicholas Rescher's pragmatic idealism and then delves into the main philosophical and methodological aspects: (i) Conception of Science and the levels of analysis it develops; (ii) Prediction as a factor of objectivity; (iii) Pragmatist realism in the face of the challenges of complexity; and (iv) Objectivity and historicity of scientific activity. Overall, it highlights its potential to address the challenges present in current Philosophy of Science and Technology.

#19 [paper] The PISA high performing systems for tomorrow framework: a decolonial reading of the OECD's future-oriented education for human flourishing
Authors: Saija Volmari, Oshie Nishimura-Sahi
Venue: Journal of International Cooperation in Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1108/jice-09-2025-0061
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Purpose This article critically examines the OECD's High Performing Systems for Tomorrow (HPST) initiative, focusing on how non-Western intellectual traditions – Ubuntu, Confucianism and Buddhism – are referenced in its conceptualisation of education for human flourishing. It investigates the depth of engagement with these traditions through a decolonial conceptual lens. Design/methodology/approach In this study, we employ qualitative content analysis of publicly available OECD documents and webinars. Our analysis is guided by and engages with decolonial scholarship, particularly Moosavi's (2020) proposals to prevent “decolonisation without decolonising”. Findings The findings show that, while the OECD gestures towards epistemic diversity, non-Western traditions are often superficially incorporated and subordinated to dominant Western frameworks. As the initiative moves from a preparatory phase to a more operationally oriented one, such references intermittently recede and later reappear, but without substantive development or influence on the underlying onto-epistemological framework. Instead, they are selectively incorporated into a pre-existing policy agenda structured by measurement, standardisation and global comparison, hence reinforcing existing epistemic hierarchies and marginalising non-Western perspectives. Originality/value This study offers a critical insight into the OECD's flourishing agenda, demonstrating that epistemic inclusion is enacted largely in rhetorical terms, without substantive engagement with non-Western traditions. It contributes to critical discussions on global education governance by exposing the persistence of Western-centric frameworks in shaping educational futures and by advancing the case for more meaningful forms of epistemic pluralism.

Abstract:
Expected Impact:

Through their core operational activities, health NGOs will deliver health promotion, capacity building and networking, and contribute to the optimisation of healthcare activities and practices by providing feedback from patients and facilitating communication with patients.

The beneficiaries are expected to further demonstrate in their proposals the Union added value of their activities and commit to deliver concrete results such as: online materials, webpages, manuals and tools on case studies promoting health in schools, factsheets and relevant literature, materials for teachers on health literacy, and assistance and promotion of twinning with other schools in the Union capacity-building and training activities to reduce the impact of risk factors for non-communicable diseases; new approaches to promote healthy and sustainable diets; expert guidance and peer-to-peer connections; and collaborate in shared areas of activity.

#2 [grant] EIC Pre-accelerator - Widening
Amount: €500,000–€1,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-WIDERA-2027-01-WIDENING-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-11-18
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

This call will increase the innovation potential of deep-tech startups in the Widening countries and enable them to better attract private investments and scale up. It will further strengthen the innovation dimension of the widening component and increase the overall competitiveness of these countries.

The specific outcome expected of this action is increased business, investor, and technology readiness of high potential deep-tech startups in Widening countries to a level where they will:

- be successful in applying and attracting the EIC Accelerator funding and/or;

- manage to secure other private investment and/or;

- attract successfully national or regional funding as alternative funding sources (e.g. through Seal of Excellence programmes).

Scope:

This action focuses on early-stage deep-tech startups which 1) have high-impact innovation technology, product, service, or business model that could create new markets or disrupt existing ones, and 2) have the ambition and commitments to scale up.

The successful applicants need to work on deep tech innovation. Such companies often struggle to attract financing because the technology and investment risks are too high.

In the framework of this call, deep-tech[1] is technology that is based on cutting-edge scientific advances and discoveries and is characterised by the need to stay at the technological forefront by constant interaction with new ideas and results from the lab. Deep-tech innovations are understood to be those that have the potential to deliver transformative solutions, rooted in cutting-edge science, technology, and engineering, including innovation that combines advances in the physical, biological and digital spheres. Deep-tech is distinct from ‘high-tech’ which tends to refer only to R&D intensity[2].

This EIC Pre-accelerator - Widening call is designed to enable promising deep-tech startups to develop further their innovations (from TRL 4 to TRL 5/6)[3], attract the investment amounts needed for scale up in a shorter timeframe and successfully apply and attract funding from EIC Accelerator or other sources.

The applicants are expected to demonstrate in their application that they:

- have completed all elements of TRL 3 (Experimental proof of concept) and therefore the technology is currently at TRL 4 (Technology validated in lab);

- possess the necessary Intellectual Property Rights to ensure freedom to operate and adequate protection of the idea;

- have a clear vision on the intended pathway and route to market. This includes specific milestones together with concrete and verifiable KPIs to assess progress towards the market.

The support will be in awarded by grants max at 70% funding of the eligible costs. 30% co-funding to be covered by the beneficiary through its own resources.

An amount between EUR 500.000 and max EUR 1.000.000 in the form of a lump sum for a period of up to 2 years is considered appropriate.

The requested grant is expected to be used for:

- addressing the investor and market readiness towards commercialisation and deployment (market research, value proposition, business case and business model, prospects for growth, intellectual property protection, competitor analysis etc.) and if relevant, aspects of regulation, certification and standardisation, aimed at getting both the technology and the business idea investment ready and/or;

- the maturation and validation of novel technologies beyond proof of concept to viable demonstrators of the technology in the intended field of application (i.e., from minimum TRL 4 up to TRL 6).

At the end of the EIC Pre-accelerator project, it needs to:

- demonstrate that the technology component of their innovation has at least been validated in a relevant environment (e.g. at least completed all aspects of TRL 5);

- be ready to apply for EIC Accelerator and/or to seek other investors or sources of funding, to enter licensing or collaboration agreements with third parties

#9 [grant] Advancing Screening, Diagnosis, and Referral for Late Talking Children
Amount: $500,000
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/362352
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-10-15
Abstract:
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) Tackling Acquisition of Language in Kids (TALK) initiative intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit research grant applications to improve the earliest steps in clinical practice for late talking children. The overarching purpose of this funding opportunity is to inform, develop, and evaluate evidence-based practices and implementation strategies to (1) effectively and efficiently identify early signs of late talking and (2) successfully guide parents, caregivers, and professionals in supporting the needs of late talking children at the first point of concern.

For this NOFO late talking is defined as a child, usually over the age of 18 months, not meeting expressive language milestones, for any reason. Populations of interest include, but are not limited to, children at higher risk for late talking due to premature birth, exposure to maltreatment or trauma, neurological conditions, motor and sensory disorders, emotional and behavioral disorders, and intellectual and developmental disorders. Children who present as late talkers for no other known reason and with no other symptoms also are of interest for this NOFO.

For this NOFO, the early steps for services for children age birth to three years that are of interest include screening and developmental surveillance of late talking, referral and follow through for specialized services, and in-depth evaluation and diagnosis of language and other contributing delays/disorders. These services typically occur in primary care, specialty care, educational settings, and early childhood community settings. The research will need to be conducted in a relevant setting.

Research focusing on children as well as their parents, caregivers, and supporting community professionals is of interest, including how to support successfully navigating from initial concern to effective care. Community partnerships and community engaged research approaches will be a key requirement for this opportunity.

Applications are not being solicited at this time. Notice is being provided to allow potential applicants sufficient time to develop meaningful collaborations and responsive projects.

Investigators with expertise and insights into early language learning, late talking, early childhood education, early intervention, and primary care are encouraged to begin to consider applying for this new NOFO. In addition, collaborative investigations combining expertise in clinical practice research, dissemination and implementation science, or community engaged research will be encouraged and these investigators should also begin considering applying for this application.

Abstract:
THIS IS NOT A NOTICE OF FUNDING. THIS IS A GENERAL FORECAST ONLY.

Grant and Per Diem (GPD) Program Introduction

The GPD Program is VA’s largest transitional housing program for Veterans experiencing homelessness and is permanently authorized under Public Law 109-461.

Since 1994, the GPD Program has awarded grants to community-based organizations to provide transitional housing with wraparound supportive services to assist vulnerable Veterans move into permanent housing. The grants are designed to meet Veterans at various stages as they move to stable housing. Community-based organizations receiving GPD grants offer focused transitional housing services through a variety of housing models targeted to different populations and needs of Veterans. The GPD program plays a vital role in the continuum of homeless services by providing supportive services to those Veterans who would otherwise be among the unsheltered homeless population. The result of GPD programs is that Veterans achieve residential stability, increase their skill levels and/or income, and obtain greater self-determination.

Types of GPD Grants

Transitional housing grants:

Per Diem Only (PDO) grants provide funding in the form of per diem payments to reimburse grantees for the cost of care provided to Veterans in transitional supportive housing.

Special Need grants target housing and services to specific populations of Veterans (e.g., women, Veterans with chronic mental illness, frail elderly Veterans, Veterans caring for minor dependents, terminally ill Veterans).

Transition-In-Place (TIP) grants offer Veteran residents housing in which supportive services transition out of the residence over time, rather than the resident. Upon completion of the TIP services, the resident retains the unit as their permanent housing with no requirement to move.

Other types of grants:

Case Management grants support Veterans who were previously experiencing homelessness or who are at risk for homelessness so that they may obtain or retain permanent housing.

Capital grants support the costs of acquiring, renovating, or constructing facilities and are only offered intermittently to improve existing facilities or to develop new transitional housing depending on VA's priorities and funding availability.

Lists of current grantees are available on the GPD website.

How to Apply for GPD Funding

Not all grant types are available annually. When available, notices of funding can be found at the following locations: www.grants.gov and https://www.va.gov/homeless/gpd.asp.

Application instructions are provided in each notice of funding.

Each notice of funding will clarify specific eligibility criteria, application requirements, funding limitations, and other requirements.

Applications are submitted through an online portal that is only available when there is an open notice of funding.

Potential applicants who wish to see what was required for previous applications may review past notices of funding, available on the GPD provider website and www.grants.gov. Past notices of funding are not a guarantee of future requirements.

Tentative Estimated GPD Award Schedule

Specific dates are not able to be forecast.

The follow tentative approximations are provided for general planning purposes.

FY 2026

Case Management – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2025 for case management awards starting approximately in FY 2026.

FY 2027

PDO – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2026 for PDO awards starting approximately in FY 2027.

TIP – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2026 for TIP awards starting approximately in FY 2027.

FY 2028

GPD tentatively does not expect to offer a notice of funding for this timeframe. GPD may update this forecast closer to the time.

THIS IS NOT A NOTICE OF FUNDING. THIS IS A GENERAL FORECAST ONLY.

#1 [paper] Between Revelation and Digitality: A Gadamerian Qur’anic Hermeneutics of Prophet Jonah and the #KaburAjaDulu Phenomenon
Authors: Agus Imam Kharomen, Muhammad Makmun, Imam Taufiq
Venue: Tatho
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.70512/tatho.v3i3.201
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The emergence of the hashtag #KaburAjaDulu on various social media platforms represents a manifestation of psychosocial distress, structural criticism and the younger generation’s urge to escape the economic pressures and public policies perceived as failing to prioritise their interests. This qualitative, literature-based study aims to contextualise the Qur’anic narrative of the story of Prophet Jonah in Surah al-Anbiya’, verse 37, using Hans-Georg Gadamer’s hermeneutic framework. By engaging the Qur’an’s historical-textual horizon (ḍiyq al-ṣadr, mughāḍiban, fa ẓanna an la naqdira ‘alaihi, al-ẓulumāt, salaf min al-‘ibādah) with the contemporary horizon of digital netizens. This study found that the act of ‘running away’ without proper preparation risks triggering a new and more severe crisis. The story of Prophet Jonah offers a paradigm shift: the pressures of life must be faced with patience, the cultivation of spirituality through prayer, and the enhancement of one’s capacity through self-purification and the discovery of the truth in one’s choices, so as to subsequently contribute actively to the welfare of the nation. This research highlights a dual responsibility: it urges the government to treat this phenomenon as an early warning indicator to promptly reform the labour market ecosystem and ensure the welfare of human resources in order to prevent the loss of top talent, whilst simultaneously guiding the younger generation to manage personal crises rationally and spiritually.

Authors: Hemopereki Simon
Venue: Te Kaharoa
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.24135/tekaharoa.v19i1.497
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This article examines the Crusaders Super Rugby franchise’s partial rebranding after the 15 March 2019 Christchurch mosque attacks as a case study in how sport reproduces settler/invader colonialism, racial capitalism and white possessive power in Aotearoa New Zealand. While the attacks prompted public scrutiny of the franchise’s name, medieval crusading symbolism and pre-match performance culture, New Zealand Rugby and the Crusaders retained the “Crusaders” name and substituted the horseman logo with koru-inspired branding. Drawing on Aileen Moreton-Robinson’s theorisation of the white possessive, the Doctrine of Discovery, critiques of bicultural containment, and Māori constitutional values, the article analyses media discourse, stakeholder consultation and branding decisions to show how symbolic reform can protect institutional authority while appearing responsive to racial harm. I argue that the rebrand commodified a history of Christian conquest and settler nostalgia for commercial profit, while marginalising Muslim concerns and avoiding deeper accountability for Islamophobia, white supremacy and colonial violence. The deployment of Māori design elements functioned as a settler move to innocence: bicultural aesthetics were used to soften critique, provide cultural legitimacy and redirect attention away from the franchise’s refusal to relinquish the name. Consultation processes similarly operated as performative inclusion, privileging majority sentiment, fan loyalty and brand equity over the experiences of communities most directly affected. By situating the controversy within longer histories of Indigenous dispossession, terra nullius-like logics in Te Waipounamu, racialised capitalism and the containment of mana motuhake, the article demonstrates that the issue was never simply one of branding or public sensitivity. Genuine transformation requires more than a redesigned logo. It requires decolonial accountability, Muslim–Māori solidarity, mana whenua narrative authority, and sporting governance grounded in tikanga, manaakitanga, pono, tika and mana motuhake.

Abstract:
This paper focuses on a way of speaking controversial religious and social truth which can reduce the degree of consequences of directly stated truth, and analyses the use of allegory in William Langland’s Piers Plowman as a relatively safer communication method compared to direct Wycliffite writings. It aims to find out a practical communication function of allegory used by Langland comparing it to the more direct writings of Wycliffe. Piers Plowman also includes dream vision, personification and symbolic figures to find out the distance between the author and the authority in revealing controversial truth. This paper follows a qualitative discourse analysis as well as a comparative method to study Piers Plowman and Wycliffe’s Bible as main sources, and Peter Sutton’s modern verse translation for best results. The findings reflect that Langland’s use of allegory does not make it just a simple literary device. Through dream-vision, personification, symbolic and allegorical events, Langland discusses controversial issues without directly addressing them which provides safer boundary between the author and the corrupt authority. Conversely, the study finds the harsh difficulties faced by Wycliffe as a result for discussing theological and religious communication more directly in his translations. The study does not claim that Wycliffe was punished but that his task became hard for being immediately noticeable to the authorities. This study concludes that allegory can apply a filter between the author and the criticized party to make a difference in the degree of consequences and reveal controversial criticism while keeping the author comparatively safer.

#4 [paper] A new class of inherently efficient SUMOylation substrates
Authors: El hadji Cisse, Laura Visticot, Rafael Cepa, Aanchal Mishra, F Coste, Stephane Goffinont, Lucija Mance, Sarah Battault
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.10.750468
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
SUMOylation is an essential eukaryotic ubiquitin-like post-translational modification that plays a central role in the regulation of various nuclear processes and stress responses. It canonically occurs at lysine residues within ΨKXE consensus motifs that lie in intrinsically disordered regions or loops and interact specifically with the SUMO-conjugating E2 enzyme UBC9. However, many detected SUMOylation sites are found within structured domains, and it remains unclear how these are recognised by UBC9. Here, we investigated the SUMOylation of Lys43 in the BTB domain of human ZBTB38 (ZBTB38BTB), a lysine located within a rigid β-sheet. By combining X-ray crystallography, structural prediction, and in-vitro UBC9 interaction and SUMOylation assays, we show that ZBTB38BTB possesses a dedicated surface that recapitulates the spatial arrangement of residues found in canonical linear consensus motifs. This surface binds UBC9 with mid-micromolar affinity and is predicted to position Lys43 in its active site for efficient SUMOylation. Structural modelling and sequence analyses suggest that this property is shared by BTB domains of five members (10%) of the ZBTB-protein family across vertebrates, revealing a previously unrecognised property of a subset of ZBTBBTB domains. Kinetic analyses reveal that, under the reaction conditions used, the catalytic efficiency of ZBTB38BTB and ZBTB33BTB SUMOylation are closely comparable to that of the C-terminal domain of RANGAP1, the best-characterised and most efficiently SUMOylated substrate known. This defines a new class of inherently efficient, E3 ligase-independent SUMOylation substrates beyond RANGAP1 and suggests that structural pre-organisation of the acceptor lysine and its environment may promote productive UBC9 engagement. Lastly, we demonstrate the presence of higher-molecular-weight, modified forms of ZBTB38 in human cells, consistent with SUMOylation. Together, these results provide a biochemical basis for interpreting existing and designing future studies on the functional impact of ZBTB SUMOylation. More broadly, our findings offer insights into the determinants of efficient SUMOylation, and may facilitate the identification of further inherently efficient targets, and, potentially, the design of SUMOylation modulators.

#6 [paper] Structural determinants for FAT10 activation and transfer from UBA6 to E2 enzymes.
Authors: Ellison, Cara J, Riechmann, Carlos, Dalietou, Evmorfia V, Simmons, Michael D R, Dodd, Emma C, Elliott, Paul R
Venue: Nature communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42733088/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Attachment of the ubiquitin-like protein (UBL) FAT10 onto substrates targets them for proteasomal degradation. Like ubiquitin, FAT10 is activated by the E1 enzyme UBA6 then transferred to E2 enzymes, but mechanisms controlling ubiquitin versus FAT10 activation by UBA6 and FAT10 transfer onto E2s remain unclear. Using cryo-EM, we visualise all stages of FAT10 E1-E2 handover: adenylation, thiolation and transthiolation. We find that FAT10 monopolises UBA6 by out-competing ubiquitin for thiolation and blocking the adenylation domain, preventing further UBL recruitment and promoting FAT10 signalling. We profiled UBA6-compatible E2 enzymes and found FAT10 transfer is restricted to a select subset associated with specific cellular pathways. UBE2Z (USE1) showed highest activity followed by UBE2D2, UBE2J2 and UBE2S. Capturing FAT10 or ubiquitin transfer from UBA6 to UBE2Z reveals UBE2Z is highly specialised for FAT10 transfer. It simultaneously engages both FAT10 domains (UBL1 and UBL2) and co-ordinates the metabolite inositol hexakisphosphate (InsP6) bound within the UBA6 catalytic domain. This InsP6 co-ordination extends to other FAT10 compatible E2s. Together, our structural and biochemical analyses reveal regulatory mechanisms underpinning FAT10 activation and transfer. We define principles governing selective FAT10 transfer, highlighting favourable interactions with FAT10 C-terminal domain (UBL2) and stable UBA6 binding, ensuring controlled conjugation onto substrates.

#9 [paper] Molecular mechanism of HUWE1-HAPSTR1-USP7-mediated ubiquitin chain amplification on nuclear proteins.
Authors: Yatskevich, Stanislau, Mohapatra, Jugal, Mroue, Rana, Phu, Lilian, Leitner, Alexander, Azumaya, Caleigh M, Vandlen, Richard, Cheung, Tommy K
Venue: Molecular cell
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42753704/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Rapid protein turnover is essential for cellular stress adaptation. HUWE1 (HECT, UBA, and WWE domain containing 1), a large HECT-type E3 ligase, regulates many short-lived stress-responsive proteins, yet the mechanisms underlying its substrate selectivity remain unclear. Here, we reveal that HUWE1 functions as a ubiquitin chain amplifier that captures pre-ubiquitinated substrates and amplifies the degradation signal by assembling long ubiquitin chains containing K11-K48 branch points, a process regulated by its partners HUWE1-associated protein stress response 1 (HAPSTR1) and USP7 (ubiquitin-specific-processing protease 7). Structural and biochemical analyses show that HAPSTR1 engages HUWE1's ubiquitin-binding motifs to drive nuclear import and modulate substrate recruitment. A cryo-EM structure of the HUWE1-USP7 complex reveals a bidirectional regulatory mechanism: HUWE1 activates USP7's catalytic activity, while USP7 modulates HUWE1 conformational states. Global proteomic analyses demonstrate that this axis drives extensive remodeling of the short-lived nuclear proteome. These findings establish the HUWE1-HAPSTR1-USP7 complex as a key ubiquitin code modifier, providing a molecular rationale for HUWE1 dysregulation in neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer.

#10 [paper] Three thresholds and a computer-assisted phase diagram for the spectral stability of periodic hydroelastic Whitham waves
Authors: Lingsen Meng
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5zn5j
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
We study the spectral stability of 2π-periodic travelling waves of the hydroelastic Whitham equation, a scalar model with the full linear dispersion relation of water waves under a thin elastic sheet (e.g. a floating ice cover), as a function of the flexural rigidity T. Besides the modulational cluster at the origin, the zero-amplitude spectrum has, on an interval of T, a collision of opposite Krein signature between the carrier and the half-wavenumber mode, and three thresholds with closed forms in tanh(1/2), tanh(1) and tanh(2) organise the picture: waves are modulationally unstable below T0 ≈ 0.16638 (the long-wave/short-wave resonance), unstable through this sideband collision on (T0, T1], T1 ≈ 0.23108, and spectrally stable above T1, so that the stability threshold is T1 and not the modulational threshold T0. We prove this phase diagram for all Bloch parameters, with explicit amplitude windows, by combining analytic reductions with remainder control and a computer-assisted proof in interval arithmetic at finite amplitude. For every amplitude 0 < a ≤ 0.01 (height H ≲ 0.02 of the depth) the waves are unstable for T in [0.0675, 0.16516] ∪ [0.1681, T1] and spectrally stable for T ≥ 0.23108 with an amplitude window that closes linearly at T1, and a rescaling by T^(-1/2) extends the stable statement uniformly to the purely flexural limit. Numerically, our computations reproduce those of Flamarion and Adriazola (2026) and suggest that the instabilities they report for 0.1 < T ≤ 0.7 at larger heights are the finite-amplitude continuation of the sideband collision rather than a modulational instability.

#11 [paper] Scripting the research process: didactic transposition and narrative design for a short documentary film around laboratory analysis of coastal sediments in Uruguay
Authors: Paulina Abre, Francisco Ignacio Lugo, Gonzalo Blanco
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5818
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. Geological literacy is critical for addressing modern socio-environmental challenges, yet geosciences remain marginalized within pre-university curricula globally due to the abstract nature of their processes and significant visualization barriers. This study examines a replicable framework for public science communication through the design, production, and multi-channel evaluation of the 17-minute place-based documentary “Arena negra, un misterio oculto en las playas de Uruguay”. Grounded in Place-Based Education (PBE) and Didactic Transposition frameworks, the scientific script was structured around a multi-scale narrative progression that transitions dynamically from macroscopic coastal landscapes down to laboratory processing (gravimetric and electromagnetic separation) and microscale single-grain mineralogical analysis using an electron microscope. Evaluation metrics over a 566-day digital tracking window yielded 35,704 views and 3124 cumulative playback hours. Algorithmic analysis revealed that 77.2 % of views were driven by YouTube’s Browse Features, indicating that the video successfully bridged a latent content-demand gap regarding regional Earth Sciences. Unexpectedly, hardware, metrics showed that Smart TVs were the dominant playback device (62 %), and demographic data indicated an inverted age profile where citizens ages 65 and older represent the primary consumer group. Qualitative analysis of user comments revealed deep-seated misconceptions regarding sediment color as well as environmental concerns that were successfully mitigated by the videos action-oriented pedagogical strategies and cultural analogies. Ultimately, this intervention demonstrates that translating rigorous laboratory workflows into dynamic, localized storytelling serves as a highly cost-effective, regional environmental awareness in territories with limited formal scientific infrastructure.

Abstract:
Abstract This study investigated how Chilean rural middle school students’ understanding of ecological and nature of science (NOS) concepts and pro-environmental attitudes changed after a place-based socioscientific issues (SSI) curriculum collaboratively developed by USA and Chilean science educators. The SSI curriculum was developed and implemented over 5 days near Valdivia, Chile, focused on red knot migration across the Americas and integrated instruction on the Motus Wildlife Tracking System as a scientific tool. Using a mixed-methods pre-post instruction design, the study demonstrated that after the place-based SSI instruction, students’ understanding of ecological concepts and NOS perspectives notably improved. For instance, students developed a deeper comprehension of factors affecting red knot migration, particularly the human impacts on that ecological phenomenon. Qualitative analysis of students’ open-ended responses demonstrated that students developed more nuanced views regarding several NOS constructs, such as the methods scientists carry out to research environmental issues and the extent to which culture should influence how science is used and conducted. This research highlights the viability of place-based SSI instruction by fostering scientific engagement among diverse student populations and illustrates how international collaborations can bridge educational gaps by connecting local environmental issues to global scientific efforts.

Year: 2026

Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This article explores how the sea is represented in the UK government’s communications by applying corpus linguistic analysis to textual data. The findings reveal a dominant discourse that frames the sea primarily as an economic asset, emphasizing investment and sustainable exploitation understood as resource preservation. Emotional and social dimensions of sustainability are noticeably underrepresented, while narratives surrounding the sea are shaped by managerial, territorial, and threat-based framings. This utilitarian portrayal hinders the development of ocean citizenship, which requires a deeper, emotional connection with the sea. By identifying these narrative imbalances, the article contributes to scholarly discussions on ‘sea blindness’ and ocean citizenship by showing how such a discourse may obscure the sea’s social and environmental significance, limiting public engagement and stewardship. The article argues for a rebalancing of these narratives to include more emotionally resonant and hopeful communication strategies that highlight the intrinsic value of the marine environment beyond its economic value. Key recommendations include shifting from technical to affective language, promoting positive imagery of ocean protection, and favouring the term ‘ocean’ over ‘sea’ to evoke a global sense of stewardship and belonging.

This research is part of a larger goal to capture the heritage, lived experiences, and scientific and cultural capital of Black people in the United States in the science curricula. This research examines the impact of a Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) physics curriculum created for the K-12 classroom, which began with the lived experiences and narratives of an African American engineer. Multimedia and other curriculum products were developed and implemented using best practices in science education pedagogy. Participants were Black homeschoolers ages 3 to 14 and their parents located in the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States. Implementation was virtual, with Black homeschooled children meeting weekly on Zoom for 1 hour for a total of 8 weeks. Schema theory and Funds of Knowledge served as frameworks to explore and explain the large volume of video dialogues and transcripts emerging from this implementation. The study revealed themes and patterns which support best practices in content creation that centers Black narratives and lived experiences in the science curricula. The research has important implications for creating curricula that center cultural and heritage knowledge in meaningful ways in the science and STEM curricula using interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary approaches.

Abstract:
The problem underlying this study was the low Science and Social (IPAS) learning outcomes of Grade 4A students at Bangetayu Wetan 02 Elementary School. The lecture method was still the dominant teaching method used in the learning process. In addition, the learning model and instructional media lacked variety, and students' learning participation was still low. This condition affected the students' learning outcomes, as only 11 out of 30 Grade 4A students (37%) achieved mastery, while 19 students (63%) did not. This study aimed to improve Science and Social (IPAS) learning outcomes through the implementation of the Course Review Horay (CRH) model assisted by Wordwall media. This study employed Classroom Action Research (CAR), which was conducted in two cycles consisting of planning, action, observation, and reflection. The research subjects were 30 Grade 4A students at Bangetayu Wetan 02 Public Elementary School in the 2025/2026 academic year. The data were collected through observation, tests, and documentation and analyzed using descriptive quantitative and qualitative approaches. The results indicated an improvement in Science and Social (IPAS) learning outcomes. The average class score increased from 71.73 in Cycle I to 79.85 in Cycle II, while learning mastery improved from 71.67% to 86.67%. Therefore, the implementation of the Course Review Horay (CRH) model assisted by Wordwall media was able to improve learning outcomes. The implication of this study is that CRH assisted by Wordwall can be used as an alternative learning approach to provide more varied and interactive learning and encourage active student participation.

This study aims to describe and analyze the conceptualization, simulation, and evaluation of the SQUID-MAP (Storytelling and Quick Understanding through Innovative Design) technique within the Al-’Arabiyah lil Aṭfāl course to foster the methodological competence of pre-service Arabic language teachers. Employing a qualitative approach with a descriptive-analytic case study design focused on instructional intervention, this research was conducted in the Arabic Language Education Study Program at the State Islamic University of Madura (UIN Madura). The study examined how higher-education students operationalize pedagogical frameworks to address spatial disorientation and local Madurese phonetic interference in early-childhood Arabic vocabulary learning (Al-Jihat). Data were gathered through participant observation during peer-teaching simulations, semi-structured interviews with the course lecturer and pre-service teachers, and document analysis of lesson plans and instructional media, followed by interactive data analysis using the Miles, Huberman, and Saldana model. The results reveal that pre-service teachers successfully integrated Dual Coding Theory and Meaningful Learning Theory into a hybrid instructional framework that combined tactile floor compass media with immersive local adventure narratives. Through simulated peer teaching, pre-service teachers demonstrated advanced capabilities in establishing consistent visual reference points to eliminate spatial disorientation and in incorporating structured phonetic repetition into storytelling to mitigate regional dialect interference. Evaluative findings confirm a substantial enhancement in pre-service teachers’ Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), transitioning their roles from traditional text-based instructors into adaptive learning experience designers. In conclusion, the SQUID-MAP technique serves as a robust methodological bridge in higher education, equipping future educators with essential conceptual, technological, and sociolinguistically responsive teaching competencies before entering real preschool classrooms.

Venue: Frontiers in Climate
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fclim.2026.1806370
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction This study provides the first comprehensive bibliometric analysis of research on climate change and children’s psychological wellbeing (2001–2025), examining whose children’s experiences are studied and which voices shape this rapidly expanding field through a climate justice lens. Methods We analyzed 1,217 documents from Web of Science and Scopus using co-occurrence, citation, and co-authorship analyses. Results The field exhibited explosive growth (22.52% annually), surging from fewer than 10 publications before 2010 to 262 in 2025. However, profound geographic inequalities revealed epistemic injustice: the United States (740 publications, 60.8%), United Kingdom (396, 32.5%), and Australia (351, 28.8%) dominated production while Small Island Developing States, Sub-Saharan Africa, and climate-vulnerable regions remained severely underrepresented despite experiencing disproportionate impacts. Nine thematic clusters emerged, with eco-anxiety, climate education, and pro-environmental behavior—reflecting Western individualistic frameworks—dominating discourse, while structural themes addressing colonialism, displacement, and systemic violence remained underdeveloped. Collaboration networks exhibited US–Australia–Europe centrality with limited Global South engagement. Discussion This concentration constitutes epistemic injustice wherein nations bearing greatest historical responsibility for emissions while experiencing buffered impacts dominate knowledge production, risking universalization of Western experiences while marginalizing the majority of the world’s climate-affected children. Addressing these inequalities requires systemic transformation: redirecting funding to Global South institutions, diversifying editorial boards, valuing diverse epistemologies, ensuring equitable partnerships, and decolonizing theoretical frameworks. Such transformation represents not merely academic fairness but a climate justice imperative essential for developing knowledge systems that center marginalized voices and inform interventions responsive to realities shaping climate vulnerability globally.

Abstract:
Purpose Conceptual understanding is essential for effective sustainability education, yet students often hold alternative conceptions about key environmental issues. The water footprint (WF), a multifaceted indicator of water use, is increasingly included in sustainability curricula but remains conceptually challenging. This study aims to describe the development and validation of the Water Footprint Diagnostic Instrument (WFDI), a multi-tier diagnostic test designed to assess undergraduate primary education students’ scientific and alternative conceptions of the WF. Design/methodology/approach The construction of the instrument followed Treagust’s principles for developing multi-tier tests and involved three phases: defining propositional knowledge statements, identifying students’ alternative conceptions through two qualitative pilot studies (n = 64; n = 94) and developing the final multi-tier tool. The WFDI was piloted with 56 students, after which minor wording revisions were made before its final administration to 238 students from three Greek universities. Findings The reliability of the WFDI was acceptable (Cronbach’s a = 0.866), and item analysis showed an appropriate spread of difficulty and discrimination values. The results indicate that the tool successfully exposes a sharp misalignment between student accuracy and confidence, revealing that pre-service teachers’ knowledge is often context-dependent and fragmented rather than structurally unified. Practical implications The WFDI provides Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) with a data-driven pathway to reform teacher-training curricula and to target specific sustainability competencies. Specifically, it is valuable for identifying undergraduate students’ initial ideas, developing and evaluating targeted instructional interventions, informing curriculum design and supporting future research on WF-related sustainability topics. Originality/value This study addresses a significant gap in sustainability education by developing the first validated multi-tier diagnostic instrument designed to assess a core and complex sustainability concept, that of Water Footprint. By explicitly linking psychometric data to conceptual change learning theories, the instrument moves beyond purely descriptive testing to reveal structural flaws in future educators’ systemic thinking about complex, global water-use systems.

The second phase, Co-creation of Cultural Anchors, translates these diagnostic insights into tangible cultural artefacts, such as re-signified field songs and digital storytelling installations. Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

Abstract:
Abstract Marine Spatial Data Infrastructures (MSDI) and Open Science (OS) have reshaped how marine data are managed, shared, and reused, but have largely evolved as separate domains. This integrative review examines how their alignment can advance FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) and sustainable ocean knowledge systems. The study combines a quantitative bibliometric analysis of the broader Spatial Data Infrastructure (SDI) and OS literature with an integrative qualitative synthesis of 54 marine-domain sources, including 41 publications selected through PRISMA screening and 13 additional records identified through snowballing. The bibliometric analysis shows separate development trajectories, but also convergence around metadata, interoperability, standards, ontology, artificial intelligence, big data, reproducibility, and FAIR principles. The qualitative synthesis shows that FAIR provides a practical bridge between MSDI and OS: MSDI contribute technical and institutional foundations for discovery, access, interoperability, stewardship, and preservation, while OS extends these foundations toward transparency, reproducibility, workflow publication, collaborative analysis, and knowledge generation. The Blue-Cloud project illustrates this alignment through federated data infrastructures, virtual research environments, and reusable workflows. We identify four priorities: credible FAIR assessment, semantic and workflow interoperability, enduring governance and maintenance, and a shift beyond data portals toward sustainable ocean knowledge systems.

Method (Mycelium's reading): A decadal strategy built on two pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data (cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, machine learning) and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation (mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimila…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): NASA's aquatic and marine research enterprise, including MODIS, PACE mission, and BGC-Argo data streams.
Abstract:
NASA’s aquatic and marine research enterprise within the overarching NASA Biosphere Program is entering an era of unprecedented data abundance. MODIS and the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission already generate ocean color data at rates that strain legacy processing and archiving workflows, and forthcoming missions will add further volume and complexity. These satellite streams are joined by rapidly growing in situ networks (e.g., BGC-Argo), suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, citizen science, and increasingly high-resolution numerical models. The result is a Big Data regime in which the volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean relevant Earth system data exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches. An important goal is to fully integrate observing workflows, understanding, and models across the terrestrial, aquatic, and atmosphere domains to fully enable understanding of life and the realization of improved information to manage uses of ecosystem services. This white paper addresses Leveraging Ocean Data and Models, a cross-cutting Grand Challenge that underlies and enables progress on the four other foundational grand challenges under the NASA Biosphere, Atmosphere, Cryosphere, and Hydrosphere framework - Global Biosphere, Carbon and the Elements of Life, Interface Habitats, and Transient Events - each of which depends on the ability to acquire, harmonize, and synthesize disparate satellite, suborbital, in situ, and model data streams. We recommend a decadal strategy built on two complementary pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data, covering tiered cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, and machine learning; and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation, covering mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimilation, hybrid approaches, mission emulators, and a NASA Digital Twin Ocean. Without concerted, proactive investment in this cross-cutting infrastructure, the scientific and societal returns on the coming decade’s expanded observing system will be substantially diminished.

Abstract:
The ocean remains critically under-observed, particularly in coastal zones where traditional monitoring is limited by cost, logistical constraints, and competing regulatory priorities. Marine citizen science offers an emerging and powerful complementary approach to addressing these gaps; however, data management challenges currently limit its full integration into scientific and policy data infrastructures. The inaugural workshop of the Marine Citizen Science Data Network (MCSDN), held in February 2026 in Ostend, Belgium, brought together approximately 200 participants from over 30 countries. Attendees included representatives from marine citizen science initiatives, developers of low-cost monitoring devices, data managers, and researchers and data users. Together they identified challenges, opportunities and co-designed recommendations to improve marine citizen science data flows. Workshop discussions highlighted interconnected barriers and enabling factors affecting FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) marine citizen science data. These included fragmented data flows, weak connections between communities, limited participant engagement and feedback mechanisms, the potential of accessible low-cost technologies, and the need for shared practices and standardized documentation. Building on these themes, the workshop produced four concrete recommendations to enhance the reuse and impact of marine citizen science data: (1) develop discipline-specific FAIR guidance, (2) establish minimum metadata standards, (3) create simplified training materials, and (4) support the development and deployment of low-cost sensors. Method (Mycelium's reading): Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework; interviews with six databanks.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Taiwan’s oceanographic data management landscape, involving multiple databanks and the Ocean Affairs Council (OAC).
Abstract:
Using the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework, this research evaluates Taiwan’s oceanographic data management and identifies issues for the prospect of its development. Six databanks were interviewed. Taiwan’s oceanographic data management remains in an orderly chaos. On one hand, it is chaotic because there exist multiple actors with their own data management rules. The fact that these databanks enact their own data management rules and operate accordingly makes the whole context even more fragmented. Therefore, community attributes are a mixture of open data and limited free data usage because revenues of data processing can cover costs of bureaucratic operation and cybersecurity measures. On the other hand, it is orderly because all databanks view open data as a public good while recognizing the importance of data management. The UN initiative of Ocean Decade serves as a strong impetus in advancing Taiwan’s oceanographic data management. Given the situation, it is debated whether integrating oceanographic data and marine-related information to one single databank, National Ocean Database and Sharing System (NODASS) positioned under Ocean Affairs Council (OAC), is economically efficient. OAC also lacks a set of reward-and-punishment rules to enforce data submission to NODASS. Meanwhile, it is also debated whether OAC should be restructured as a ministry and enact a set of generally followed rules of data management. To further develop data management and facilitate data exchange with the international oceanography community, OAC will need to cultivate professional capability while enhancing inter-agency policy coordination.

#6 [paper] Sensoring the Oceans: The Argo Floats Array in the Governance of Science Data Infrastructures
