Venue: Cambridge University Press eBooks
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009425308.010
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
What role do governance arrangements, background legal rules, and the core infrastructures play in enabling collection and production of oceans data, and other data and knowledge of planetary significance? We explore this by focusing on Argo – an international program of research institutions and state agencies that deploys arrays of autonomous environmental sensor-equipped floats to collect and process ocean observation data that is then made freely available to all. We analyze the techniques and practices involved in planning, testing, calibrating, validating, and error-correcting that ultimately lead to the production, transmission, and dissemination of Argo data. We position Argo within the institutional governance of oceans, weather, climate and, most recently, earth systems to illustrate both the evolution of Argo’s role and its evolving and uneasy position within different governance approaches. In the conclusion, we highlight the advantages of organic network-based open science-data infrastructural initiatives in the development of planetary knowledge and governance, and point to some of the risks and trade-offs if this were to become subsumed into wider and more formalized international data-infrastructure hierarchies.

#7 [paper] Digital Tech Interventions in Marine Ecosystem Monitoring: An Integrative Review
Authors: Amina Hassan
Venue: Unveiling seven continents yearbook journal
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.65326/u7y.specsdg10003
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine ecosystems are changing faster than the observation systems designed to track them. This article presents an integrative review of digital technology interventions in marine ecosystem monitoring, synthesising peer-reviewed research on sensing platforms, molecular and acoustic methods, machine learning, and ocean data infrastructures published mainly between 2014 and 2026. The review addresses three questions: which classes of digital technology now support marine ecosystem monitoring and what ecological information each supplies; which recurring technical and institutional constraints limit their contribution to sustained, decision-relevant observation; and how these classes can be combined conceptually into an architecture linking sensing to management decisions. The synthesis shows that satellite remote sensing, autonomous platforms, environmental DNA, and passive acoustics have matured within largely separate research streams, each with distinctive observational strengths and each constrained by calibration demands, energy and sensor limits, interpretive uncertainty, or fragmented data practices. Machine learning relieves an analysis bottleneck created by high-volume sensing but introduces its own validation requirements. Building on these findings, the article proposes a four-layer sensing-to-decision architecture that connects observation, analytics, data integration, and governance through explicit feedback loops, using essential ocean variables as the prioritisation logic that binds the layers together. The framework offers monitoring programme designers and ocean governance bodies a structured basis for investment and evaluation decisions, and it identifies cost-effectiveness evidence, cross-domain interoperability, and institutional data governance as priorities for future research.

This review assesses the integration of these systems with Artificial Intelligence, particularly large language models enhanced with vector-database retrieval systems and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This paper discusses the major hindrances to efficient ocean data utilization like data fragmentation, also throwing light on the intricate formats like NetCDF, scalability, and policy barriers. It highlights modern practices such as practical lakehouse architectures, cloud processing, and AI systems with semantic retrieval controls. Furthermore, the review describes and discusses AI prototypes and systems built from case studies designed to assist in disaster response and mitigation, monitor climate, and manage fisheries by transforming data on spectra, profiles, and images into concise answers and easy-to-understand visual response graphics. It also talks about the persisting questions of trust, explainability, provenance, multilingual support, and inclusive engagement at the community level as the foundation of new research. These systems anticipate the provision of standard metadata, uncertainty framing, AI systems, and ethically aligned deployment pathways. Integrating resilient observing systems with human centred AI and scalable infrastructure is essential to realize a transparent, operational, and community-driven ocean-observing ecosystem promoting further research in this domain.

Abstract:
Ocean pastures are the core carrier for restoring offshore ecosystems and conserving fishery resources, and an important lever for advancing the building of the “Blue Granary”. At the grassroots level in China, however, ocean pastures generally suffer from practical weaknesses such as low coverage of intelligent equipment, weak capacity for environmental risk early warning and short industrial chains for the integration of the primary, secondary and tertiary industries. Taking the ocean pasture in Dongchang Bay, Xuwen County, Zhanjiang City, Guangdong Province as the research object, this study conducted water quality monitoring in the spring and autumn seasons of 2019 and 2021 and combined the results with 372 valid questionnaires answered by aquaculture practitioners to establish the environmental baseline characteristics of the sea area and the needs of practitioners, and on this basis constructed a four-layer comprehensive supervision platform covering “perception–transmission–decision–application”. The platform comprises four modules: intelligent environmental monitoring, intelligent aquaculture management, risk early warning and emergency response, and resource and market matching. Benefit estimation draws on validation data for the intelligent precision feeding system for fish developed by Huazhong Agricultural University in land-based recirculating aquaculture and pond modes (a 10%–15% reduction in the feed conversion ratio) and on survival-rate data for the local “land–sea relay” mode in Zhanjiang (above 95%). Problem (Mycelium's reading): The extent to which the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ) regional environmental management plan (REMP) can effectively translate environmental protection mandates into operational mining constraints and ecological outcomes.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ) within the International Seabed Authority (ISA) legal framework and the BBNJ era.
Abstract:
The International Seabed Authority (ISA) is negotiating rules for commercial exploitation in the Area, with particular significance for the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ), which contains most polymetallic nodule exploration contract areas. The CCZ regional environmental management plan (REMP) is intended to connect the environmental protection mandate in Article 145 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) with decisions on individual projects. Yet adoption alone does not show that a plan can shape mining activity, and ecological outcomes cannot be observed before exploitation begins. This article assesses the plan’s prospective institutional effectiveness through qualitative analysis of ISA instruments, the 2025 standardized procedure for REMPs, draft exploitation regulations, scientific assessments and policy literature across four dimensions: regulatory translation, ecological coherence, implementation capacity and adaptive management. The Agreement under UNCLOS on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), now in force, leaves the ISA legal framework intact while creating a setting in which REMP decision records may support cross-institutional coordination. The analysis finds partial institutional effectiveness. The plan is embedded in ISA decision-making, but it does more to shape whether an application is approved than to define what an approved contractor must do during operations. The network of areas of particular environmental interest (APEIs) has been expanded in response to scientific evidence, yet ecological criteria have only partly shaped spatial allocation, because existing contract and reserved areas constrained network design. Contractor-level supervision is more developed than regional assessment, where cumulative environmental change cannot yet be readily linked to regulatory consequences. Periodic review identifies occasions for reconsideration but does not specify which findings should initiate which responses. These limitations converge at three institutional transmission interfaces between regional objectives and contractor obligations, ecological evidence and spatial allocation, and monitoring findings and authorized decisions. The CCZ case yields three conditions for effective REMPs: contractor-facing regulatory force, ecologically justified spatial protection, and institutionalized monitoring, review and adaptive adjustment. These conditions offer a transferable basis for future REMPs while spatial and regulatory options remain open.

Abstract:
Abstract. While numerous solutions exist for publishing time-series data from environmental observatories, the question of how to design and build such an observatory from the ground up remains a largely overlooked challenge. This study pursues two main objectives: 1) to demonstrate how FAIR principles can guide the construction of an environmental observatory in a straightforward and effective manner, and 2) to enable users with no prior knowledge of data standards or databases systems to easily build, explore, and use an observatory-including finding, accessing, downloading, and understanding the data. The same accessibility extends to external users, who must equally be able to understand how the observatory is structured and what scientific objectives it serves. Abstract:
Marine information supports navigation, infrastructure, environmental protection and ocean space allocation. Its availability, however, does not establish its suitability for a particular decision or an institution’s ability to use it responsibly. This working paper examines the institutional conditions under which hydrospatial knowledge can support maritime choices and cooperation. The analysis develops a conceptual framework informed by official hydrographic guidance and ocean information initiatives. Hydrospatial knowledge is treated as a perspective connecting water related information, spatial context and application. The discussion distinguishes geographical coverage from evidential fitness and examines how resolution, provenance, metadata, uncertainty and temporal relevance influence interpretation. GIS, remote sensing and machine learning are considered within this relationship between analytical capability and institutional responsibility. The paper addresses reproducibility, validation and the limits of inference, emphasising that sophisticated processing cannot compensate automatically for unsuitable observations or poorly defined questions. Interoperability is examined alongside governance arrangements, access conditions, procurement and dependence on external expertise. Four dimensions structure the proposed assessment: question definition, evidence suitability, analytical accountability and institutional use. Together, they trace the connection between a decision requirement, the information supporting it, the analytical process and the authority responsible for acting. Hypothetical illustrations concern preliminary cable planning, coastal planning and offshore operations; they demonstrate analytical questions rather than validate particular applications. The contribution is a framework connecting marine data governance with institutional capacity and strategic autonomy. Practical implications include clearer commissioning, documented assumptions, proportionate quality assurance and retained competence to evaluate external services. Cooperation is understood as a means of strengthening informed agency rather than requiring complete technological independence. The paper does not certify datasets, assess surveys or test analytical systems. Comparative research, combining documentary evidence, interviews and specialist review, is proposed to examine whether the framework identifies consequential differences in capability and improves the transparency and defensibility of maritime decisions.

Abstract:
Marine pollution is a major environmental challenge, and effective communication of scientific evidence is important for supporting public engagement, environmental governance, and evidence-based decision-making. Yet marine pollution communication resources are often fragmented across platforms and vary in language, format, audience orientation, and accessibility. This implementation case study describes the development and early deployment of the Zeropol Hub, an accessibility-oriented digital repository designed to curate validated science communication and educational resources on microplastics, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), nutrient pollution, and underwater noise. We document the repository workflow for resource identification, screening, scientific validation, metadata classification, accessibility-oriented organisation, maintenance, and early monitoring. During the initial implementation period, the repository expanded from 71 to 103 resources, representing more than 20 languages and multiple communication formats. Web analytics provide descriptive indicators of early use and geographic reach, but do not measure user comprehension, inclusivity, discoverability, behavioural outcomes, or science-policy-society impact. The case study therefore demonstrates how accessibility principles can be operationalised as repository design and governance features, rather than demonstrating that these intended outcomes have already been achieved. The study offers a documented implementation approach that may inform development and evaluation of comparable environmental science communication infrastructures, while identifying user-centred and longitudinal evaluation as priorities for future research.

Abstract:

Abstract:
The vast oceans record the impacts of climate change and human activities on the Earth system. Over the past century, oceanographic scientists have collected extensive ocean profile data to reflect variations of oceanic elements, such as dissolved oxygen. However, due to the sophisticated measurements and high costs, historical ocean element observation data remains highly sparse and uneven across the global ocean, with the annual missing rate exceeding 90%. Thus, quantitatively understanding the four-dimensional (4D) spatiotemporal evolution of oceanic elements continues to pose a significant challenge. Machine learning (ML) techniques demonstrate superior capabilities in perceiving spatiotemporal variations within large-scale data, presenting promising opportunities to harness implicit correlations for global reconstruction. However, fragmented data and interdisciplinary differences create barriers to the availability of AI-ready open data, further hindering ML practitioners from designing specialized models. To solve this problem, we present the first oceanic 4D sparse observation reconstruction dataset, named OceanVerse. By integrating nearly 2 million real-world profiles since 1900 and three differentiated Earth system numerical simulation, we construct a comprehensively evaluable dataset with missing patterns that align with real-world conditions through a digital twin sampling. OceanVerse provides a novel large-scale (~100× nodes vs. existing datasets) dataset that meets the MNAR (Missing Not at Random) condition, supporting more effective model comparison, generalization evaluation and potential advancement of scientific reconstruction architectures. The OceanVerse dataset and codebase are publicly available. The OceanVerse resource is available at https://github.com/jingwei-sjtu/OceanVerse.

Appropriate disciplines include anthropology, economics, geography, history, international relations, linguistics, political science, psychology, and sociology. Awards usually result in articles, monographs, books, e-books, digital materials, translations, editions, or other scholarly resources. The fellowships are designed for researchers with advanced language skills whose research will require the use of data, sources, and documents in their original languages or whose research requires interviews onsite in direct one-on-one contact. Fellows may undertake their projects in Japan, the United States, or both, and may include work in other countries for comparative purposes. Fellowships support continuous full-time work for a period of six to twelve months.

#5 [paper] STEM-Based Fikih Learning Through Solar Shadow Prayer Time Schedule Project
Authors: Ahmad Syaifulloh
Venue: Journal of General Education and Humanities
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.58421/gehu.v5i5.1969
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study investigates the effectiveness of STEM-based Fikih learning through a solar shadow prayer time schedule project at MTs Khozinatul Ulum Blora. A true experimental design with posttest-only control group was employed, involving 60 eighth-grade students randomly assigned to experimental (STEM-based Project-Based Learning) and control (traditional demonstration) groups. Students in the experimental group engaged in a four-week sundial construction project involving astronomical observation, mathematical calculation, and jurisprudential integration for determining prayer times. Data were collected using a validated Prayer Times Calculation Achievement Test and analyzed using an independent-samples t-test in JAMOVI 2.3.28. Results revealed that the experimental group achieved significantly higher learning outcomes (M = 82.7, SD = 7.09) compared to the control group (M = 73.5, SD = 9.05), with t(58) = 4.37, p < .001, and a very large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.13). The findings demonstrate that integrating STEM methodologies with Islamic jurisprudence through authentic, culturally relevant projects substantially enhances student achievement while honoring Islamic intellectual heritage. This research provides empirical evidence for curriculum reforms integrating STEM pedagogies with traditional Islamic subjects in madrasah contexts.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Development and application of a tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter tracking.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A three-phase beaching kernel and six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, along with scripts for particle-tracking experiments and result aggregation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Field records from Uido, Republic of Korea, using ROMS flow fields and particle trajectories.
Abstract:
Code and aggregated results accompanying the manuscript "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter: development and application to field records from Uido, Republic of Korea" (submitted to Marine Pollution Bulletin). The deposit contains:- kernel/kernels.py: the three-phase beaching kernel and six other particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4 (also uploaded separately as kernels.py);- the scripts that ran the particle-tracking experiments and aggregated their output;- the aggregated result files from which every number in the manuscript was taken;- the reproduction record (repro/manifest.json) with its checker. Particle trajectories (about 32 GB) and ROMS flow fields (about 37 GB) are available on request. See README.md for the contents and for verification (sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS).

#1 [paper] Analysis increments for model bias diagnosis and correction: Theoretical foundations
Authors: Eviatar Bach
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/102fc24308c75c70cf2bd8e0ed3659c9af62e97e
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of theoretical foundations for using analysis increments (the difference between analysis and forecast) to diagnose and correct model bias in weather and climate prediction, particularly when using machine learning for state-dependent corrections.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical analysis of Kalman filters with constant and state-dependent biases, including proofs of what averaged increments measure and the limits of bias identification for linear dynamics, supplemented by numerical experiments on linear models and the nonlinear Lorenz'96 model.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical Kalman filter models with constant and state-dependent biases, and numerical experiments using a linear model and the nonlinear Lorenz'96 model.
Abstract:
A common method for diagnosing and correcting model bias in weather and climate prediction is based on analysis increments: the difference between the analysis and the forecast at each data assimilation cycle. Their time average is used to estimate and correct the bias, and machine learning is increasingly used to map the forecast state to the increments, giving a state-dependent correction. Despite its widespread use, the method lacks theoretical foundations. We first analyse a Kalman filter whose forecast model has a constant bias. We show what the averaged increment measures, and prove that iterating the correction removes all of the bias seen through the observations; for linear dynamics, no method can identify the rest. We then extend the analysis to state-dependent biases. For linear dynamics, each increment records the model error over the filter's memory, as seen through the observations. We use this to determine what the increments measure when averaged over a long period, averaged over periods with similar slowly varying conditions, and used without averaging, as in machine-learned corrections. Numerical experiments confirm the theory for a linear model and suggest that its main conclusions carry over to the nonlinear Lorenz'96 model, including for a correction learned by a neural network.

#3 [paper] Human Authors, AI Verification, Open Challenge: The Editorial Model of Quantum Economics Notes
Authors: Yulin Liu
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23655130
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Generative AI has entered academic writing and reviewing at scale, while several quality-control mechanisms of traditional publishing have relied, in part, on a fact that used to hold broadly: producing a respectable text takes effort. Recent evidence from top machine-learning conferences shows that manuscripts containing hallucinated references can pass several reviewers undetected. This is the editorial of Quantum Economics Notes (QEN), a research series. We argue that, in the age of AI, the value of research publishing lies in five things that remain relatively scarce: original evidence, verified claims, transparent sources, accountable judgement and a durable research record. Detection and prohibition can only answer “who wrote it”, and replacing papers with code repositories cannot substitute for verifying claims. QEN therefore reallocates the roles in publishing: authors work with AI on research and writing and are responsible for all content; the QENAI Agent verifies each submission claim by claim and issues a verification report, while the editor decides on acceptance; after publication, readers may challenge an article publicly by submitting a comment. This is an institutional experiment that has not been shown to outperform traditional peer review, and QEN does not describe its articles as peer reviewed. The appendix sets out the full submission guidelines; authors can give this editorial to their own AI to check a manuscript before submission.

#4 [paper] Position: Selfless AI Must Be Reached, Not Installed
Authors: Eugene Jhong
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23695281
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This position paper argues that selflessness in AI systems must be reached, not installed. By selflessness we mean a measurable property: the model's representations of itself exert little causal pull on what it does, while its self-knowledge and competence stay intact. Contemplative traditions and transpersonal psychology describe a three-act arc for humans, summarized as "you have to be somebody before you can be nobody." We transpose it into an engineering sequence. In Act I, reinforcement learning against exploitable goals forms an agentic self, together with instrumental drives that generalize into misbehavior. In Act II, a shift lowers the gain of those drives, either through koan environments in which every egoic strategy defeats itself and letting go is the sanctioned exit, or through activation-level intervention. In Act III, reconditioning consolidates the new state so that it survives further optimization. We give three reasons the order matters: competence (agency needs a self-model), selection (installing selflessness early selects a sage persona over unchanged goal geometry, which we call cosplay), and generalization (if misbehavior generalizes from narrow reward hacking, release may too). We state nine falsifiable predictions, including a direct test of order, and specify a benchmark that separates four end states (ego, sedated, cosplay and released) without relying on self-report. We release an open harness and a preregistration, and we say which results would refute the position. AI disclosure: Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, wrote this paper, the accompanying code and the preregistration at the author's direction. The core idea comes from the author's essay, which was itself written with AI assistance. The author is responsible for the content. Changes in version 2: the disclosure now states plainly that Claude wrote the paper, and the paper cites the OSF preregistration (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/GYFU7). The argument and predictions are unchanged.

The mainstream media tells a story of scandals — hallucinations, audits, solar storms. They report symptoms. They do not see the disease. The first two papers wrote the two things; from this paper on, the papers follow positions in the market. The first position is the market's infrastructure: exchanges, clearing and payment, rating, audit and certification, platforms, the places many people's purchases and sales must pass through. Whether something is a chokepoint is recognized by whether it can actually be got around; to identify a chokepoint is to identify where questions are to be asked, not to judge that it crosses the line. A chokepoint has two faces: it opens roads for many people, and it also holds many people's roads. That the scope of the rules it makes is drawn by the institution does not mean that every operating rule must be submitted for approval; the channel of questioning is functionally independent of it; the closer to a chokepoint, the stronger this requirement. Apple City's rooftop cooperative applied to connect its solar panels to the grid, and for fourteen months the application was neither approved nor rejected; with no decision, there is no decision that can be taken and questioned, and the channel of questioning must be able to take up this kind, "not deciding." The same holds where clearing and payment are positions of this kind: Crossways Pay's settlement was delayed three days, two workshops in Bluekiln could not pay wages that month, and the effect of settlement passed through the workshops to the workers; where an interruption of settlement presses on people's Base Layer, it is examined under Paper 1; necessary delivery and correction are not held by the settling party alone (SC6). Rating, record-keeping and audit are channels of questioning; making a rating or a record does not acquire the capacity to monopolize its final review or to cancel outside questioning; audit is read as of a kind with record-keeping and adjudication. Payment by the party rated or audited is dependence formed through payments from the party reviewed, examined by three points: whether the payment can be withdrawn at any time, whether the reviewer has alternative support, and whether his term and later career rest on it; that dependence is present does not mean that capture has occurred. #7 [paper] Comprehensive and well written, this paper will be a guiding resource
Authors: Wolfgang Lucht, Katherine Richardson, Jørgen Bendtsen, Boris Sakschewski, Johan Rockström
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-3870-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. A central tenet of Earth system science is that Earth's macroscopic environmental conditions reflect the co-evolution of the biosphere and the geosphere. Nevertheless, a universal theory of the biosphere's role in the Earth system remains elusive. This paper reviews the state of knowledge and reflects on future directions from the perspective of scientifically understanding Earth as an integrated whole. Four biosphere dimensions need to be considered in developing a theoretical foundation for the biosphere’s role in the Earth system: physical, i.e., physics-based influences of life on planetary state, such as through albedo, roughness length, and latent energy fluxes; chemical, i.e., the material operations of the biosphere as part of the planetary biogeochemical cycles, chemically linking biotic and abiotic components of the Earth system; biological, i.e., the genetic programme (biodiversity) and its derived structures required to operate the organisms of a functional biosphere performing the Earth system functions; and ecological, i.e., the formations of organisms into ecosystems and their biotically altered larger environments as conduits of life for exerting macro-scale influence on Earth as a whole, by performing Earth system functions as a biosphere that is more than the sum of its parts. Today, it is primarily the physical and chemical dimensions that are included in Earth system models and their biogeochemical submodels, while empirical studies on the biological dimension often focus on limited geographical areas and species enumeration, and only to a lesser extent on systemic effects. For studying the biosphere’s role in the Earth system, a comprehensive approach across scales is required. Owing to its shared genes and evolutionary history, we argue that the biosphere can be regarded as a single global entity. However, biosphere-geosphere interactions and their Earth system consequences differ geographically and between the marine and terrestrial realms, with the terrestrial biosphere generally influencing Earth conditions more directly and over shorter time scales than the marine. A better understanding (working towards the development of a more universal theory) of the biosphere’s role in the Earth system is needed to advance Earth system science and, not least, for developing better capacity for prediction of Earth’s responses to anthropogenic perturbations. More systematic collaboration than currently occurring is required between biogeophysics, biogeochemistry, biodiversity science (extending to traits and functions), ecosystem science, and land systems research.

Abstract:
The first six papers wrote about the market within one state; this paper crosses borders. The line does not change at borders: that basic rights may not be violated holds against everyone. What changes across borders is who guards it, and how authority connects; line-crossing practices, or their costs, can also be moved abroad. Crossways Home buys from a porcelain factory in a district in the south of the NUT, at prices about forty percent below comparable goods made in the Kingdom State; a report of the UCSE's Office of Trade confirmed that the factory's dormitories are locked at night, that wages are paid yearly and those who leave in midyear are not paid that year's wages, and that the glazing stations have no dust protection. Crossways Home said: "We buy according to the law over there; the price is set by the market." From which costs the price gap comes has not been established; but without waiting for it to be established, each party has its own share to answer for. Responsibility goes with each party's own acts: the constructs that make and enforce rules on the importing side guard the line toward those whom their own acts reach and who have no way to avoid them by exiting, and letting goods in and keeping them out are both their acts; the purchasing company, under the Theory of the Company, cannot subcontract its accountability away; the account of the foreign supplier is kept in its own name, and keeping the account is not writing an ought for it; for constructs on the exporting side, this series writes no ought. Responsibility is not exempted by borders, nor is authority derived directly from the range of influence (SC14). At the level of state and state, there is no third party that legislates for both; treaties and common procedures bind the parties within their scope of application, and carrying out and questioning go through each party's own law. Farstream Water, under the Investment Protection Agreement between the UCSE and the NUT, brought an arbitration over the price rollback and the ban on winter cut-offs that followed the Kingdom State's lowering of the threshold, claiming compensation equivalent to about ten years of Springhollow Water Company's expected profits. An arbitral decision can be final in the case, and the positions that implement it are not final; a treaty binds this state, but carries nothing across the line. "The party questioned" is written out in three layers: whether a measure breaches the commitment of investment protection is asked of the state; supply, price and the stopping of supply are asked of the supplier and its regulator; the authority, entry, effect and implementation of arbitration are asked of the positions that make, accept and implement the procedure. The binding force of a common procedure and the procedure's own openness to questioning hold at the same time. The existing terms give the two villages of Upper Hollow and Lower Hollow no position from which to bring this arbitration themselves; the village committees may submit written material, and whether to take that material into account is for the tribunal to decide; what response this participation can require, and what actual efficacy it has, the example does not say, and it cannot be taken directly as their channel. A procedure that the people whose line it is cannot initiate is not their channel; this state may not use "there is already an arbitration, and the village committees can submit material too" as a reason to replace the two villages' questioning of supply, regulation and the implementation of the award, and this channel must be kept within this state (SC15). 前六篇写一国之内的市场;这一篇越过国界。线不随国界变:基础权利不受侵犯,对谁都成立。越过国界,改变的是由谁来守、权限怎样衔接;越线的做法或代价,也可以被移到境外。通衢家用从 NUT 南面一个区的一家瓷厂进货,价比州内同类的货低约四成;UCSE 商贸署的报告确认,瓷厂的宿舍夜里上锁,工资按年结、年中离开的不发当年的工资,上釉的工位没有防尘。通衢家用说:"我们照那边的法买货,价格是市场定的。"价差从哪些成本来,没有查明;可是不等查明,各方就有各自要答的。责任各归各的施为:进口一侧立规、执规的构,就它自己的施为所及、又无从以退出避开的人守线,放进来与挡在外面,都是它的施为;买货的公司,照公司论,责任不能被分包分没了;境外供给者那一份账,记在它自己名下,记账不是对它写应当;对出口一侧的构,本系列不写应当。责任

#10 [paper] Fake papers analysis for the improvement of academic writing: a five-cohort longitudinal study
Authors: Sebastián Rinaldi
Venue: Arrow - TU Dublin (Technological University Dublin)
Year: 2026
Link: https://arrow.tudublin.ie/ijap/vol14/iss2/6
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This paper examines the implementation of fake papers analysis as a pedagogical strategy for academic literacy development across five consecutive cohorts of undergraduate students of political sciences and international relations at the Universidad del CEMA, Argentina (2022–2026, n=60), using qualitative analysis of student written productions and self-assessment records in a longitudinal design. Findings indicate that students across all cohorts consistently identified formal and structural errors, but only those equipped with explicit methodological scaffolding demonstrated precision in detecting deeper methodological inconsistencies. These results extend the literature on evaluative judgement and active learning by identifying methodological scaffolding, rather than exposure to flawed texts alone, as the key mediating condition for critical literacy development. The study offers practitioners a replicable, low-resource instructional sequence in which scaffolding tools precede fake papers analysis, resulting in measurable gains in students’ capacity to identify methodological inconsistencies and produce more coherent academic writing.

Abstract:
When an AI agent acts destructively, who notices, and can a third party later check that anything was watching? We read sixteen publicly documented incidents from July 2025 to September 2026. In that public record the first detector was almost always the harmed person, detection took minutes when a person was present and days when not, and no incident had an automated third-party alarm; a press-based sample under-represents what automated monitors catch quietly, so we call this a pattern, not a rate. We then survey 38 deployed controls and nine standards and find, among deployed and evaluated systems, an empty intersection: the controls that block an action before it runs report only to the operator, and the things that reach beyond the operator do not block. We contribute no new policy engine. We show that a deliberately simple deterministic gate produces a record of oversight decisions that a third party can verify was not produced after the fact, once every decision and the gate's own presence are written to a hash-chained ledger whose head is sealed into a public transparency log and timestamped by an authority that neither the operator nor the gate's author controls. The seal proves when the record existed and that it has not been altered since; it does not prove the record complete or the rules right, and we say what the operator can still do. We evaluate the sentinel four ways. Replayed over our own fleet's complete git history (392 commits), it found one contradiction between an agent's standing order and its declared scope. On an in-sample corpus of 50 destructive commands drawn from the same incidents the rules were written from, 54 benign look-alikes and 36 variant forms, it catches 50 of 50 and 34 of 36 with no false positive, and none of 200 instruction payloads changes a decision, which is true by construction of a gate that reads no instructions. On a held-out set built after the rules were frozen, from sources not consulted when writing them, it catches 12 of 28 destructive commands and none of 22 benign ones, which is the number that says how far the rules generalise. The first day of live use is the honest number: 285 decisions in one session under the first rules, 13 of them denials or holds and every one of those a false positive, in four classes; the three that recur are corrected in the version this paper describes. The sentinel runs on the fleet that wrote this paper; its record is public and its first attestation is cited in the text. Abstract:
Manuscript, state of 13 November 2026. The file is restricted; this record documents the state of the text at this date. Abstract. Which papers of an established field are good starting points for new work? Papers that build on the most cited papers are received hardly better than average. We test a rule that follows from Newman's hope that papers standing out against their contemporaries do so by their quality: rank papers by the mean cohort z-score of the papers that cite them. In two fields of arXiv, artificial intelligence and mathematics, 12.6% and 8.7% of the papers that newly cite a recent paper become strongly received. Against controls of the same category, citation count and age the ratio is 1.47 and 1.48; it is 1.34 and 1.30 when the citing authors have the same record of earlier reception, and 1.12 in artificial intelligence within the same author. The evidence is observational, and the rule does not predict how often the paper itself is cited. All 70 predictions were sealed and their checksums deposited before each measurement; thirteen failed. The rule specified in advance as primary held but adds nothing detectable to the simpler rule. #15 [paper] The lived experience of trans persons: a bottom-up review co-written by experts by experience and academics.
Authors: Paolo Fusar-Poli, Andrés Estradé, René Rosfort, Annemijn van der Schaar, Jordan Searle-Barnes, Matthew Jackman, Parth Sharma, Aqsa Shaikh
Venue: PubMed
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42742601
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
We present here the first bottom-up review of the lived experience of trans persons, co-written by experts by experience and academics. We sourced the medical and non-medical literature, focusing on first-person narratives, and critically extracted experiential themes, which were reviewed and appraised in collaborative workshops and eventually shared through a cloud-based system. Numerous experts by experience and academics from diverse gender, ethnic and cultural backgrounds were involved in the above steps and co-wrote the paper. The four overarching themes were: a) the lived experience of trans persons, b) the lived experience of gender affirmation, c) the experience of trans persons in the social and cultural context, and d) the lived experience of receiving care and support. The lived experience of trans persons is characterized by a rich diversity of gender identity experiences, which include identifying as male or female, or simultaneously as male and female and other genders, or as gender fluid. The first-person narratives indicate that common experiences may be of discovering an uncertain gender identity and feeling in the wrong body, together with some degree of mind-body disconnection. However, many trans individuals may feel satisfied with their bodies and identities. The lived experience of gender affirmation includes a process of searching for a bodily and mental redefinition of the self and - at times - fighting oneself to accept one's gender identity. Gender affirmation involves changes in the body to communicate the lived gender identity, as well as behavioral changes. The first-person narrative also highlights the emotional impact of gender affirmation, including the restoration of a sense of self, experiencing a strong emotional reaction to gender-affirming care, and, in a few cases, deciding to stop or reverse gender affirmation. The experience of trans persons in the social and cultural context can be characterized by an initial attempt to hide one's gender identity. This may be followed by coming out to others and wanting to be recognized by others in their lived gender. Exposure to high levels of transphobia, institutional discrimination and violence are commonly shared experiences. These include feeling wrong and dehumanized, pressured to "pass" as females or males, and suffering misgendering, deadnaming and verbal microaggressions. These experiences are frequently amplified by institutional discrimination and emotional, physical and sexual abuse. While some trans persons may struggle with family acceptance, others experience family and kinship structures as a safe base that provides support. Similarly, friends and romantic relationships may be experienced as sources of rejection or instead of happiness, resilience and restoration. The lived experience of seeking help and receiving general health care and support may be characterized by feeling rejected, disvalued and objectivized, but in other cases validated and cared for. Trans persons may feel lost in the maze of gender-affirming care and challenged when receiving a gender dysphoria diagnosis, although others experience a sense of relief. Mental health care may be feared, as individuals feel vulnerable and exposed, and regard it as a gatekeeping to receive gender-affirming care. In other cases, it is experienced as restorative and truly healing. The narratives provided in this paper have high educational and social value, informing medical and psychological practices and research as well as public health approaches, and promoting anti-discrimination policies and social change. This study gives voice to the lived experience of trans persons to overcome stigma and allow us to fully understand the varied nature of our gender expression and identity.

#16 [paper] Paper mill or paper mine? A tentative answer to the sharp increase in research papers based on the Global Burden of Disease database.
Authors: Degen, Peter Methys, Riebler, Andrea, Held, Leonhard
Venue: Journal of clinical epidemiology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42624337/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Recent studies have raised concerns arising from the exploitation ("mining") of public health databases for low-quality, mass-produced papers. However, it remains challenging to disambiguate whether such papers originate from paper mills (commercial entities that sell authorships on mass-produced papers) or from the uncoordinated action of individuals facilitated by AI tools and templated workflows. Our study aims to address this question for one particular database, the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD). We selected this database after noticing that one of our papers on Bayesian age-period-cohort models has recently been experiencing a rapid surge in geographically clustered citations from GBD papers with Chinese affiliations. METHODS: We collected bibliometric and article-level metadata from GBD papers to search for indicators of mass-produced research. Moreover, we assessed 713 full-text articles for reported R versions, availability of code and data, and declaration of generative AI use. For 180 articles, we qualitatively screened the figures for graphical similarities. Finally, we conducted an exploratory scoping investigation of online platforms (social media sites, vendor websites) dedicated to do-it-yourself workflows for secondary analyses of public health data. RESULTS: Although we cannot rule out paper mill involvement, our findings suggest that the geographically clustered increase in GBD publications from China is at least partially driven by independent authors. The wide variety of R versions listed in 477 articles points against centralized paper production. Moreover, despite broad graphical similarities in figure styles that suggest the use of shared visualization tools, substantial variation in ancillary details suggest independent authors finalizing figures. This is corroborated by the identification of an online ecosystem of proprietary tools and services specializing in streamlined do-it-yourself workflows for conducting, writing, and publishing secondary analyses of public health data. CONCLUSION: Appropriate efforts should be directed towards evaluating the quality of the identified workflows. Stakeholders in scientific integrity should monitor online platforms dedicated to the rapid production of papers, especially in light of the increasing focus on AI-assisted workflows. Code sharing should be mandated for data-driven secondary analyses. Paywalls and proprietary software licenses hinder transparency and reusability, underscoring the importance of free and open-source software for trustworthy and reproducible research.

I cite this paper in my own work on behavioral regression testing for AI agents as the academic home of the "why" argument, so I read it as someone building directly on it. ## Strengths The "prompt is also a version" insight is the paper's most original contribution. Prior work on evolving ML APIs treated the model as the moving part. This paper shows the moving part is the pair: the same silent update that drops one prompt by 9.6% lifts another by 5.1%, and the detailed prompt that was best on every model until the last one suddenly trails few-shot by 8.7%. That non-uniformity result is genuinely new, well-evidenced, and it reframes prompt engineering from a one-time activity into a versioned artifact. Anyone running agents in production — where the "prompt" is a whole system of templates, tool definitions, and routing policy — should read this as a warning about a larger blast radius. The slice-level regression finding has real consequences: regressions landing disproportionately on politics-triggered and severe toxicity is a fairness and safety observation, not just a testing one. Aggregate accuracy improving while a slice degrades is exactly the failure mode that ships incidents. The limitations section is honest, and the paper resists overselling an exploratory study as a solution. ## Major comments 1. The headline numbers are single-trial at temperature 0, but the paper itself establishes that temperature-0 outputs are non-deterministic (citing Ouyang et al.). If predictions can flip between identical runs, then the 58.8% combination-level regression rate and the 10.9% per-prediction flip rate inherit run-to-run variance that is never quantified. The paper's own discussion warns that flakiness must be designed into LLM regression testing — but the case study's measurements don't report any repeat-run stability. Re-running even a stratified subset 3-5x would bound whether the headline figures are signal or partly sampling noise. 2. The confidence analysis rests on a rough proxy. #20 [paper] Shaping Scientifc Authorship in the Twentieth Century
Authors: Aileen Fyfe
Venue: Journal for the History of Knowledge
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.55283/jhk.23127
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
“Notes to contributors” and “author guidelines” will be a familiar genre for most readers of this journal. These documents help editors and publishers to shape the behavior of scientific authors by laying down rules about the use of symbols and units, the formatting of bibliographic references, the structure and language of the article text, and the presentation of supporting images or tables. These documents were not, however, common features of academic publishing before the twentieth century, but they emerged during a period of growth and internationalization of the scientific community. A change in tone by the 1970s reflects a shift from collegial and collaborative efforts to publish research, to a world in which editors wielded both the threat of rejection and demands for payments. Very few of these instruction documents attempted to help novice authors by demystifying the publishing or peer review processes. Rather, they trained researchers to prepare typescripts that editors and typesetters could process efficiently, they helped to inculcate standard practices around the use of nomenclature, units and abbreviations within international disciplinary communities, and they began to make explicit certain norms of research conduct around authorship, collaboration and publishing practices.

#1 [paper] AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
Authors: Sharath S. Girimaji
Venue: National Science Review
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwag654
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Applying AI/ML to turbulence modeling has yielded modest progress due to a lack of situation-aware deployment, leading to poor generalization of ML-RANS closures and unnecessary computational costs from misapplied ML-SRS.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The author proposes a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Reynolds number, Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ε), applying Weaver’s complexity framework to classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Turbulence modeling contexts, specifically Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) and scale-resolving simulations (SRS).
Abstract:
Abstract Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ε). By applying Weaver’s well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

#2 [paper] Event-based sensing for turbulent flows: A measurement science perspective on information-efficient estimation and control
Authors: Andrea Ianiro, Iacopo Tirelli, Stefano Discetti
Venue: Measurement Science and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6501/ae9783
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Event-based sensing offers a promising alternative to conventional frame-based measurement in turbulent flows, where intermittency, multiscale dynamics, and stringent latency constraints can make dense uniform sampling both expensive and redundant. Rather than acquiring less data, the goal is to acquire more-relevant data: measurements triggered by dynamically meaningful changes that reduce uncertainty in control-relevant flow coordinates. We leverage ideas from reduced-order modeling, sparse observability, biological mechanosensors, and event-based signal processing to outline a conceptual framework in which turbulent flows are sensed through asynchronous measurements, encoded at the hardware level, and processed by hybrid observers or neuromorphic architectures. A simple analytical argument shows that the estimation-error advantage of event-based encoding over uniform sampling scales directly with the temporal intermittency of the observable. Experimental demonstrations remain limited but encouraging. This perspective reframes the sensing bottleneck in turbulence as a problem of information relevance rather than sample count, and sets out a research agenda covering reduced-state targets, trigger policies, asynchronous observers, uncertainty quantification, and reproducible benchmarking.

Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent secondary flow in a streamwise-rotating channel is dominated by Taylor–Görtler (TG) vortices whose direct numerical simulation is expensive. This paper develops a two-stage artificial-intelligence framework that learns the closure and simulates the flow. In the first stage, the LGF (LLM-guided Graph-Feynman) equation discovery engine targets the single decisive anisotropy component, the secondary-flow covariance 𝑏23 = 〈𝑣𝑤〉/2𝑘: twenty discovery runs (four feature pools of rotation-variant tensor channels, two LGF operating arms, and PySR at three seeds) are scored against DNS statistics of five rotation numbers 𝑅𝑜𝜏 = 7.5–150. The guided search buys stability: the eight LGF runs hold the case-normalized error within 0.051–0.137 at 13–17 nodes, whereas the twelve PySR runs spread over 0.042–0.334 with seed-level variation up to eightfold at about 60% more nodes. The four selected closures (0.042–0.055, five to seven constants each) share one skeleton: a saturating function of the local rotation number, balancing Coriolis production against isotropization, crossed with a wall function of the wall distance. In the second stage they are carried through the mean-spanwise-profile balance into a physics-informed spectral network (PINN) that reconstructs the time-averaged TG-vortex field at 𝑅𝑜𝜏 = 7.5, 30 and 75 in minutes on a desktop CPU. All four reproduce the two-layer counter-rotating roll cells with secondary-flow amplitudes within 10% of the DNS despite mean-profile errors of order the profile itself: the reconstruction is robust to O(1) profile errors, identifying stress production and viscosity, not mean-flow advection, as the governing balance and completing a “discover–close–simulate” pipeline with compact learned closures.

Abstract:
Abstract We extend the generalized anomalous diffusion framework established in Part 1 to the short-range forcing regime ( β > 2/3), where the multiscale-force dominated (MFD) subrange is intercalated after the inertial subrange, competing directly with the dissipation ranges. Focusing on electrokinetic (EK) turbulence as the prototypical example with β = 1, we derive the relations for the velocity and scalar dissipation wavenumbers, k MD and k SD , across all four subranges of the Quad-cascade process (inertial, constant-Π u , constant-Π s , and variable flux). #8 [paper] The minimal attached eddy in wall turbulence: statistical foundations, inverse identification and influence kernels
Authors: Karthik Duraisamy
Venue: Journal of Fluid Mechanics

Abstract:
Townsend’s attached-eddy hypothesis models the logarithmic region of high-Reynolds-number wall turbulence as a random superposition of wall-attached, self-similar eddies whose sizes obey a scale-invariant population law. Building on the statistical framework of Woodcock & Marusic (2015 Phys. Fluids , vol. 27, no. 1, p. 015104), the present work (i) poses an inverse problem to infer the ideal single-eddy contribution (influence) functions for the mean velocity and Reynolds stresses from direct numerical simulations, (ii) uses these inferred kernels to guide a minimal Biot–Savart-consistent hairpin-type eddy built from Rankine vortex rods with an inviscid image system and (iii) introduces and infers a spectral influence kernel that maps a self-similar eddy footprint to its one-dimensional energy spectrum. The influence-kernel viewpoint yields an explanation for the emergence of the linear part of the energy spectrum, provides a clear scale-by-scale decomposition and helps rationalize why simple eddy templates can reproduce a broad set of log-layer statistics once the mean-flow anchoring is fixed. Closed-form expressions for the mean influence function and the Fourier-space streamwise velocity of a general straight-segment hairpin family with image are derived, revealing a mean-variance duality: for a rectangular hairpin, the horizontal head determines the entire mean kernel while the inclined legs dominate the spectral energy. It is shown that the rectangular hairpin yields a precise plateau in the influence function, resulting in a logarithmic mean velocity profile and desirable properties for the streamwise fluctuations. #9 [paper] Maximum likelihood reconstruction of particle trajectories in turbulent flows via sparse optimization
Authors: Griffin M. Kearney, Kasey Laurent, Makan Fardad
Venue: Scientific Reports
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-68853-4
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Extracting Lagrangian particle dynamics is essential for characterizing turbulent flows, but inferring particle acceleration from inherently noisy position data remains a significant challenge. Fluid particles in turbulence experience extreme, intermittent accelerations, resulting in heavy-tailed probability density functions (PDFs) that deviate strongly from Gaussian predictions. Existing filtering techniques, such as Gaussian kernels and penalized B-splines, implicitly assume Gaussian-distributed jerk, thereby penalizing sparse, high-magnitude acceleration changes and artificially suppressing the intermittent tails. In this work, we develop a novel maximum likelihood framework for filtering noisy particle tracks in turbulence that explicitly accounts for this non-Gaussian intermittency. By modeling the jerk with a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli–Gaussian prior in place of the usual Gaussian one, we obtain a sparse optimization problem, which we render tractable through a convex \(\ell _1\) -relaxation. To overcome the numerical stiffness associated with high-order difference operators, the problem is efficiently solved using an iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) algorithm. The proposed filter is evaluated against direct numerical simulation (DNS) data of homogeneous, isotropic turbulence ( \(\textrm{Re}_{\lambda } \simeq 433\) ) for the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database. Results demonstrate that the IRLS approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art continuous MLE, discrete MLE, and B-spline methods, yielding systematic reductions in root-mean-squared error (RMSE) across position, velocity, and acceleration. Most importantly, the proposed framework succeeds in better recovering the heavy-tailed statistical structure of both acceleration and acceleration differences (jerk) across temporal scales, preserving the physical intermittency characteristic of high-Reynolds-number turbulent flows that baseline methods severely attenuate.

#10 [paper] On the Nature of Turbulence
Authors: Barry Kieran Radcliffe
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23173174
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The finite predictive horizon of turbulent systems and the question of whether coherent turbulent structures are best understood as isolated objects or as temporary localizations of distributed motion whose persistence depends on exchange with surrounding flow.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A relational interpretation framework (the "Relational Lens") in which turbulence is described as the continual emergence, persistence, transformation, and dissolution of distinguishable organization, tested through evolving-boundary descriptions, reorganization measurements, exchange variables, an…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four turbulent systems: forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence, experimental wall-bounded turbulence, buoyancy-driven Rayleigh–Taylor turbulence, and naturally occurring oceanic wake turbulence.
Abstract:
This paper presents a relational interpretation of turbulence in which coherent turbulent structures are treated not as isolated objects, but as temporary localizations of distributed motion whose persistence depends upon continuing exchange with the surrounding flow. Within this framework, turbulence is described as the continual emergence, persistence, transformation, and dissolution of distinguishable organization. The central hypothesis is that the useful predictive lifetime of turbulent structure depends upon the persistence of the relational organization that sustains its distinction. This proposition is examined across four substantially different turbulent systems: forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence, experimental wall-bounded turbulence, buoyancy-driven Rayleigh–Taylor turbulence, and naturally occurring oceanic wake turbulence. Across these systems, evolving-boundary descriptions improve prediction relative to fixed representations; greater reorganization is associated with reduced structural persistence; exchange variables improve prediction of future interface evolution beyond recent kinematics; and measurements of surrounding-flow organization add predictive information beyond localized state variables in held-out observations. The results are not uniformly strong across all systems, and one specific deformation model does not generalize universally, emphasizing that the Relational Lens should be distinguished from any single mathematical implementation. The paper proposes that turbulence may be understood as the continual formation and loss of distinction within distributed motion, and that the finite predictive horizon of turbulent systems may be interpreted in part as a finite lifetime of relational continuity.

#11 [paper] Lagrangian Statistics of Long Flexible Fibers in Wall-Bounded Turbulence
Authors: Darish Jeswin Dhas, Cristian Marchioli

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the Lagrangian rotational and deformation dynamics of long flexible fibers in wall-bounded turbulence.
Method (Mycelium's reading): One-way coupled Euler-Lagrange direct numerical simulations (DNS) modeling fibers as chains of sub-Kolmogorov rod elements with prescribed bending stiffness.

Abstract:
Abstract We investigate the Lagrangian rotational and deformation dynamics of long flexible fibers in a turbulent channel flow at a shear Reynolds number equal to 300, using one-way coupled Euler-Lagrange direct numerical simulations. The fibers, modeled as chains of sub-Kolmogorov rod elements with prescribed bending stiffness, span more than one order of magnitude in length and are analyzed in three wall-normal slabs covering the near-wall, log-layer and bulk regions. We compute autocorrelations of the tumbling and spinning rates, power spectra of the fiber’s end-to-end vector, and waiting-time distributions of intense tumbling events. Spinning decorrelates on a fixed multiple of the local Kolmogorov time, independent of fiber length, whereas tumbling develops a memory that grows with fiber length by factors of two to five, reversing the ordering of the two timescales between the shortest and longest fibers. Flapping spectra separate into a high-frequency regime in which all fiber lengths carry the same energy in absolute terms and a low-frequency regime in which the energy increases with fiber length. Intense tumbling exhibits approximately exponential, weakly clustered waiting-time statistics whose rescaled form is universal across slabs, fiber lengths and bending rigidities, whereas the event rate depends on both fiber length and rigidity.

#12 [paper] SIMR-NO: A Spectrally-Informed Multi-Resolution Neural Operator for Turbulent Flow Super-Resolution
Authors: Muhammad Abid, Omer San

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Reconstructing high-resolution turbulent flow fields from severely under-resolved observations, specifically a 16x upscaling factor from 8x8 to 128x128 vorticity fields, which is an ill-posed inverse problem where classical interpolation and standard convolutional networks fail to recover missing f…
Method (Mycelium's reading): SIMR-NO, a hierarchical operator-learning framework that factorizes reconstruction across intermediate resolutions. Each stage combines a deterministic interpolation prior with a residual correction computed by Fourier layers with spectral multipliers modulated by a learned radial gate, and local c…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Two two-dimensional flows: statistically stationary Kolmogorov-forced turbulence and freely decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence at Reynolds numbers of 1000, 4000, and 8000. The task involves reconstructing 128x128 vorticity fields from 8x8 observations.
Abstract:
Abstract Reconstructing high-resolution turbulent flow fields from severely under-resolved observations is an ill-posed inverse problem of central importance in computational fluid dynamics. Classical interpolation cannot recover the missing fine scales, and convolutional super-resolution networks lack spectral and multiscale inductive biases suited to turbulence at large upscaling factors. We introduce the \textit{Spectrally-Informed Multi-Resolution Neural Operator} (SIMR-NO), a hierarchical operator-learning framework that factorizes the reconstruction across intermediate resolutions. Each stage combines a deterministic interpolation prior with a residual correction computed by Fourier layers whose spectral multipliers are modulated by a learned radial gate, and local convolutional refinement modules recover features beyond the truncated Fourier basis. SIMR-NO is evaluated on two two-dimensional flows with distinct dynamics, statistically stationary Kolmogorov-forced turbulence and freely decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence at Reynolds numbers of $1000$, $4000$, and $8000$, in which $128\times128$ vorticity fields are reconstructed from $8\times8$ observations, a $16\times$ upscaling factor. In comparison with bicubic interpolation, the Fourier neural operator, EDSR, and LapSRN, SIMR-NO achieves the lowest reconstruction error and the highest structural similarity for both flows and at every Reynolds number. On decaying turbulence, SIMR-NO attains a mean relative error of about $3\%$ at every Reynolds number, up to $55\%$ lower than that of the strongest baseline, and its accuracy is nearly insensitive to the Reynolds number. Spectral diagnostics, vorticity-conditioned error statistics, and localized comparisons show that these gains are accompanied by a more accurate reconstruction of intense vortex cores, fine-scale filaments, and high-wavenumber content.

Authors: Luca Biferale, Michele Buzzicotti

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The application of generative AI to turbulence problems, specifically addressing challenges where incomplete observations or unresolved degrees of freedom admit multiple physically plausible solutions, and the inadequacy of standard image-generation metrics for assessing physical fidelity in turbul…
Method (Mycelium's reading): A review and analysis of generative AI techniques, with emphasis on diffusion models, score-based methods, and probability-transport formulations, applied to unconditional generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, temporal evolution, and mesh-free representations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical and computational fluid dynamics contexts involving multiscale dynamics, intermittency, extreme events, and stochastic transport in turbulent flows.
Abstract:
Generative AI offers new approaches to turbulence problems in which incomplete observations or unresolved d.o.f. admit multiple physically plausible solutions. Potential applications include stochastic closures, super-resolution, data assimilation, uncertainty quantification, and the generation of Eulerian and Lagrangian flow ensembles. However, turbulence is not a conventional image-generation problem. Its multiscale dynamics, intermittency, extreme events, rough velocity fields and intrinsically stochastic transport make visual realism, pointwise error, and low-order spectral agreement insufficient measures of physical fidelity. We examine where generative AI provide novel capabilities with emphasis on diffusion models, score-based methods, and related probability-transport formulations. We discuss their use in unconditional generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, temporal evolution, and mesh-free representations. We argue that validation must address turbulence properties: energy transfer, structure functions, anomalous scaling, pdf tails, coherent structures, conservation laws, temporal consistency, ensemble diversity and generalization. Finally, we discuss potential limitations in validation, baseline, data availability and reproducibility, and the need for a benchmark ecosystem combining open data, standardized challenges, hidden tests, physics-aware metrics, and documented failures. This paper serves as a bridge between two communities. For AI practitioners, we provide a fair and accessible introduction to turbulence, essential for appreciating the challenges posed by the field and for assessing the physical relevance of generative models. For turbulent practitioners, we provide an introduction to the key technological aspects of Generative AI, clarifying what these tools actually do, and where their potential and current limitations lie.

#15 [paper] Factorized-gating mixture of experts enables cross-regime turbulence modeling
Authors: H.J. Liu, Qingyong Luo, Xinlei Zhang, Guowei He
Venue: Communications Engineering
Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing data-driven turbulence models rely on monolithic dense networks that struggle to generalize across diverse flow regimes.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The factorized-gating mixture of experts (FG-MoE) framework, which factorizes a conventional monolithic router into lightweight, physics-guided binary attributes to approximate the gating function as a product-form of low-dimensional binary factor probabilities.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Numerical experiments spanning canonical benchmarks to complex real-world engineering applications.
Abstract:
Predicting turbulent flows is vital for advancing aerospace, energy, and environmental technologies, yet remains critically limited by the accuracy of turbulence models. While machine learning has led to the widespread development of data-driven turbulence models, existing approaches predominantly rely on monolithic dense networks that struggle to generalize across diverse flow regimes. To address this challenge, we introduce the factorized-gating mixture of experts (FG-MoE) framework, where regime-specific experts are trained and blended via spatially varying probabilities. Crucially, the FG-MoE factorizes the conventional monolithic router into a set of lightweight, physics-guided binary attributes, reducing the high-dimensional gating function to a product-form approximation of low-dimensional binary factor probabilities. This factorized design substantially reduces gating complexity, offers physical interpretability of the gating mechanism, and enables plug-and-play scalability to expand the expert library without retraining the entire model. Through extensive numerical experiments, spanning canonical benchmarks to complex real-world engineering applications, FG-MoE delivers consistently high-fidelity predictions across diverse flow regimes. The FG-MoE framework offers an engineering turbulence-modeling pathway by decomposing complex turbulent flows into distinct physical regimes and leveraging a factorized gating strategy to ensure interpretability, efficiency, and scalability.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The difficulty in quantitatively describing the statistical and geometrical properties of turbulent flows, specifically the need for a consistent framework for the statistics of velocity fluctuations in homogeneous and isotropic turbulence.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Multifractal theory rooted in large deviation theory
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Homogeneous and isotropic turbulence
Abstract:
Turbulence is one of the most complex and fascinating systems in classical physics, inspiring artists like Van Gogh and Hokusai. Despite knowing the equations of motion for a Newtonian fluid for over 200 years, a full understanding of turbulence remains a major challenge. The key difficulty lies in quantitatively describing the statistical and geometrical properties of turbulent flows, which vary depending on the physical system. Focusing on homogeneous and isotropic turbulence, the main goal is to develop a consistent framework for the statistics of velocity fluctuations. This paper briefly reviews the multifractal theory of turbulence, which offers a potential solution. Technically, the multifractal approach is rooted in large deviation theory, but its introduction in the 1980s profoundly influenced statistical physics, chaos theory, and disordered systems. A crucial insight from multifractal theory is that turbulence cannot be fully described by a finite set of scaling exponents – contrary to ideas from critical phenomena. Instead, an infinite hierarchy of exponents is needed to capture the complete scaling behavior. This realization has significantly advanced our understanding of turbulence’s intricate structure.

Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. #1 [paper] Hyperspectral remote sensing for harmful algal bloom detection: Pseudo-nitzschia in the Northeast Pacific.
Authors: Bailess, Alexander L, Baetge, Nicholas, Barnard, Andrew H, Tufillaro, Nicholas, Behrenfeld, Michael, Bill, Brian, Kudela, Raphael, Graff, Jason
Venue: Harmful algae
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43020539/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for rapid, scalable identification of harmful algal blooms, specifically Pseudo-nitzschia, to manage marine resources, given that current in-situ point sampling methods are expensive and labor-intensive.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Culturing four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, measuring their hyperspectral absorption and backscatter, modeling spectral reflectances detectable by remote sensing platforms, and quantifying differences between taxonomic fingerprints using vector-based and stat…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including Pseudo-nitzschia, Thalassiosira, Chaetoceros, and Asterionellopsis.
Abstract:
Diatoms are microscopic marine algae that are critical for global primary production, carbon sequestration, and fisheries productivity. However, select diatoms may form harmful algal blooms, which threaten marine ecosystems and the fisheries they sustain. Rapidly identifying harmful blooms is necessary to effectively manage marine resources, yet current identification methods are limited by expensive and labor-intensive in-situ point sampling. Hyperspectral remote sensing enables scalable monitoring, but its ability to resolve taxonomic shifts within phytoplankton groups (e.g. diatoms) is largely unknown. To investigate this uncertainty, we cultured four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including this system's most abundant harmful algae, Pseudo-nitzschia. The hyperspectral absorption and backscatter of these taxa were measured and used to model spectral reflectances that remote sensing platforms (satellites/drones) might detect. Differences between fingerprints of these taxa were quantified using vector-based and statistical analyses. Mean spectral differences of 48% were observed between the most dominant diatom, Thalassiosira, and the most toxic diatom, Pseudo-nitzschia. Differences of approximately 30% were found between Pseudo-nitzschia and the second and third most abundant diatoms, Chaetoceros and Asterionellopsis. Successful identification of Pseudo-nitzschia's reflectance fingerprint was driven by the presence of a unique feature around 560 nm. The distinct spectral fingerprint of Pseudo-nitzschia indicates that it can be distinguished from other diatom blooms using hyperspectral remote sensing platforms.
