#1 [paper] Costing global biodiversity framework delivery in megadiverse Australia
Authors: Paul Elton, Sarah Clément, Michelle Ward, Martine Maron
Venue: Journal of Environmental Management
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.130756
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Most nations worldwide face substantial funding gaps to halt biodiversity loss, yet many governments lack comprehensive cost estimates essential for effective budget allocation and implementation planning. This study provides a comprehensive estimate of the costs Australian governments would need to bear to deliver the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework in Australia. Using interpretive principles and evidence from peer-reviewed literature, and spatial analysis, we derived actions, unit costs, and cost factors (the amount of each action required to achieve the GBF's targets). We populated an automated model with these inputs to produce national and jurisdictional government cost estimates to inform planning and cost-sharing between national and subnational governments. Our method captures cost efficiencies from actions that benefit multiple targets. Our model estimates that delivering GBF targets in Australia will cost governments approximately AU$28.5 billion per annum from 2025 to 2050. At 1.1 per cent of GDP, this estimate shows comprehensive biodiversity conservation is arguably fiscally realistic. Our cost factor data can be disaggregated at various scales—such as bioregions, ecosystems, or Indigenous nations—to inform biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning. Our analysis and cost model offer a replicable methodology for other national governments to quantify their financial resourcing requirements for GBF implementation.

#2 [paper] Halting marine plastic inputs by 2050 is necessary but not sufficient to avoid microplastic accumulation
Authors: Takuro Uehara, Mateo Cordier, Laurent Lebreton
Venue: Communications Earth & Environment
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-026-04054-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic pollution threatens ecosystems, economies, and human health, yet economic literature overlooks the transport of plastic debris across marine ecosystem compartments and its natural breakdown. Here we show, using a system dynamics model, the global physical and economic efforts required to remove buoyant marine plastic debris by 2050. The model simulates the degradation, transport, and cleanup of macroplastics and their breakdown into microplastics across shoreline, coastal, and offshore zones. Scenario analyses explore varying rates of waste input reduction and cleanup intensity. Results indicate that halting new marine plastic inputs by 2050, as outlined in the G20 Implementation Framework for Actions on Marine Plastic Litter, and removing existing buoyant macroplastics may be insufficient to prevent substantial microplastic accumulation. Accelerating cleanup efforts can reduce microplastic generation, albeit at a higher cost. Estimated annual cleanup expenses range from €0.1–5.6 billion, representing 0.3–15.7% of national pollution abatement budgets and 0.0001–0.0052% of global GDP. #1 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

#2 [paper] Reply on RC2 Authors: Peihao Yang, Guodong Ye Year: 2026 Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-262-cc1 Still open/current: yes Abstract: Abstract. A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. After training on multiple CMIP6 ensemble members, the constructed models are evaluated for their predictive capacity regarding MHW in the SCS. The results also show that these machine learning-based methods can perform comparably to the existing dynamic models in terms of prediction performance, and in some cases even outperform the latter. Furthermore, by incorporating machine learning interpretability techniques, the key physical processes can also be elucidated from these predictions. That is to say, the new method is not a traditional "black box", but rather an effective tool that can possess certain physical transparency and scientific interpretability.

#3 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#4 [paper] Model-Based Marine Heatwave Detection with Eddy Diagnostics in the Adriatic Sea: Regional Insights with Global Relevance
Authors: Eurida Liyana, Francesco Memmola, Pierpaolo Falco
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15010054/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intensification, increasing frequency, and duration of marine heatwave (MHW) events, particularly in vulnerable semi-enclosed coastal basins like the Adriatic Sea.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Integration of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm and analysis of long-term observational temperature data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Adriatic Sea (AS).
Abstract:
Marine heatwave (MHW) events are intensifying globally, doubling in frequency and increasing in duration and spatial distribution over recent decades. Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. In this study, we assess the capability of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to detect and simulate MHW events in the AS. We integrate this modeling framework with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm, alongside comprehensive analysis of long-term observational temperature data, to investigate the role of mesoscale eddies in modulating surface and subsurface MHW evolution. Results demonstrate that ROMS effectively reproduces the timing and spatial patterns of historical MHWs in the AS, showing strong agreement between modeled and observed MHWs, with eddy structures frequently coinciding with subsurface thermal anomalies preceding MHWs. These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

#6 [paper] Recent extreme heatwaves are no match for future events
Authors: Philipp Aglas-Leitner, S. Perkins-Kirkpatrick, Lukas Brunner, S. Undorf, F. Aglas-Leitner, E. Fischer, D. Stone
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76809-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21 st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

#7 [paper] Atmosphere-Driven Compound Extremes: Record Marine Heatwave and Phytoplankton Bloom in the Ross Sea During Summer 2022-2023
Authors: Zehao Wang, Shaoyin Wang, Zhu Zhu, Zixin Wei, Fukai Peng
Venue: Environmental Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ae9780
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract We document an extreme marine heatwave (MHW) in the eastern Ross Sea during the 2022–2023 austral summer (DJF), the most intense thermal event in the satellite record. Using satellite-retrieved sea surface temperature (SST), ocean colour, sea ice, and atmospheric-oceanic reanalysis data, we show that the eastern Ross Sea experienced a Category IV (extreme) MHW during this season, with the regional-mean cumulative intensity reaching 127.22 °C·days in January 2023 and summer-mean SST anomalies locally peaking at approximately +2.5 °C above the climatological mean. Summer-mean chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) concentration reached 3.67 mg m⁻³, the highest value observed in the eastern Ross Sea since satellite ocean-colour records began in 1997. The ecological response followed a threshold-dependent sequence: early sea-ice retreat initially removed light limitation, followed later by a strong Chl-a increase as sustained warming and upper-ocean restratification favoured bloom development. In contrast, persistent ice cover in Terra Nova Bay prevented a comparable thermal or biological response. A meridional wind dipole drove divergent ice transport and the early expansion of the eastern Ross Sea polynya, while low-cloud cover decreased by up to 15.43%, increasing downward surface shortwave radiation by 64.09 W m⁻². Subsurface warming remained confined to the upper continental-shelf waters south of approximately 73°S, suggesting that local atmosphere–ice–radiation interactions contributed more strongly to the event than heat transport associated with ocean circulation. These results identify a distinctly polar pathway through which atmospheric forcing can generate compound thermal and biological extremes, highlighting the importance of local sea-ice coupling in shaping future Antarctic coastal productivity.

#9 [paper] Deeper Structure of Marine Heatwaves: Glider-Detected Anomalies in the North Sea
Authors: Charlotte Z. Reed, Victor-Alexandru Darvariu, Nick Hawes, Helen Louise Johnson
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15009434/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Satellite-derived sea surface temperatures cannot always be used to estimate the spatial structure, duration, intensity, and drivers for temperatures below the ocean surface.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Comparison of near-continuous autonomous underwater glider observations with GLORYS12V1 ocean reanalysis and regional heat content analysis.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): North Sea, specifically off the East coast of Scotland and the area between the Shetland and Orkney Islands.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves are often characterized by sea surface temperatures derived from satellite data. However, surface anomalies cannot always be used to estimate the spatial structure, duration, intensity, and drivers for temperatures below the surface. In this study, we use near-continuous autonomous underwater glider observations from a deployment off the East coast of Scotland, accompanied by the GLORYS12V1 ocean reanalysis, to examine recent high temperature anomalies in the North Sea. Glider observations show that warm and cold anomalies can be stronger below the surface than what is represented in the reanalysis, and discrepancies are often associated with differences in the timing and depth of mixed layer depth changes. Regional heat content analysis indicates that anomalies within the mixed layer are strongly influenced by surface heat fluxes, while anomalies below are more closely associated with advective heat transport, particularly inflow from the North Atlantic between the Shetland and Orkney Islands. A prolonged anomaly in 2024-2026 persisted below the surface across multiple seasons, suggesting that subsurface heat storage may hold memory between surface events. Our results demonstrate that marine heatwaves in shelf seas can have substantial subsurface structure, even in a relatively shallow and seasonally well-mixed region. Sustained glider observations can provide key observations alongside satellite and reanalysis products, improving analysis and validation of subsurface temperature anomalies in shelf seas.

#10 [paper] Rethinking Marine Heatwaves: Towards a Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress
Authors: Natalija Dunić, Krešimir Ruić, Ivica Vilibić
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15011394/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard marine heatwave (MHW) definitions rely on statistical temperature anomalies relative to a climatological baseline, which does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic examples used to demonstrate the estimation of response functions from biological observations and the derivation of binary event definitions.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

#11 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#13 [paper] Data and code for: An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system for Mediterranean temperate reefs: forecasting climate-driven mortality under context-dependent local protection
Authors: Jairo Castro‐Gutiérrez, Mar Bosch‐Belmar, Francesco Paolo Mancuso, Sergio Dimarca, Mario Francesco Tantillo, Gianluca Sarà
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Static conservation strategies are outpaced by accelerating marine heatwaves, threatening temperate reefs. There is a need for prospective tools that integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability and support climate-smart Marine Spatial Planning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system using a rigorous modelling framework. It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#14 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

Venue: Geophysical Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026gl122646

Abstract:
Abstract Large populations along Earth's coastlines are exposed to climate hazards including extreme humid heat. Considering observed coastal ocean warming and increased coastal marine heatwave (MHW) activity, we seek to uncover if, how, and where coastal ocean temperatures are linked with heat and humidity on land nearby. We analyze near‐coastal sea surface temperatures (SST) and corresponding land heat characteristics at 1,474 global coastal locations from 1990 to 2023 and find coastal MHW occurrence is associated with positive terrestrial heat/humidity anomalies across seasons, and that warmer coastal SST are associated with more frequent hot/humid extremes on land. We highlight an increase in concurrent marine and terrestrial (THW) heatwave days at many locations, which appears largely driven by MHW trends. Coastal MHW, THW, and concurrent events share similar buildup characteristics, but concurrent and MHW events are more humid than THW and display temperature anomalies which peak at the surface rather than aloft.

#16 [paper] Beyond blocking anticyclones: Iberian cut-off lows amplified early season heat in UK and France 2026

#17 [paper] Comparing Surface and Subsurface Marine Heatwaves in Ocean Reanalyses

Abstract. Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly recognised as major drivers of ecological and socio‑economic disruption, yet their subsurface expression remains poorly constrained due to sparse in situ observations. Here, we characterise properties such as the intensity, duration, and heterogeneity of subsurface MHWs using the Copernicus Global Ocean Reanalysis Ensemble Product (GREP). MHWs are detected across multiple depths (0.5–200 m) using a consistent percentile-based thresholding, applied to three reanalysis members (CGLORSv7, GLORYS2v4, ORAS5) and evaluated against well‑documented historical events. All reanalyses successfully capture the timing and general evolution of major, well-known surface expressions of MHW events when compared against the ESA Climate Change Initiative SST dataset in given areas of interest, such as, for example, events of 2011 in Western Australia, of 2015 in the Northeast Pacific Blob, and of 2006 in the Mediterranean Sea. On a global scale, there is a positive bias of about 15 days in the mean duration for all the events with respect to satellite SST data, consistent with the limited eddy-resolving capability of the eddy-permitting GREP reanalyses, the additional smoothing introduced by ensemble averaging and the difference between the different representative depths of SST in satellite observations and models. Global diagnostics reveal that MHWs extending into the subsurface are more persistent, spatially heterogeneous, and characterised by sharper onset and decline rates than shallow events, particularly in the tropics, western boundary currents, and the Southern Ocean. Mixed‑layer variability strongly modulates the vertical propagation of anomalies, underscoring the role of vertical mixing in shaping subsurface extremes. Our results highlight both the value and limitations of current reanalyses for subsurface MHW characterisation, emphasising the need for ensemble‑based approaches to quantify uncertainty.

Authors: Muhammad Zulhaikal Abdul Razak, Mohammad Hanif Hamden, A. H. M. Din, Fatin Nabihah Syahira Ridzuan, Amalina Izzati Abdul Hamid, Mohd Fadzil Mohd Akhir, Ku Nor Afiza Asnida Ku Mansor, Muhammad Syahrullah Fathulhuda

Abstract:
Heatwaves events is one of the consequences from the global warming and climate change. In a warming ocean temperature, sea level variations are expected to increase in correlation with the temperature fluctuations. Coastal flooding and erosion also occur significantly due to the sea level fluctuation, giving impacts towards economic and marine ecosystem. This study aims to investigate the impacts of heatwaves towards sea level and sea surface temperature using multi-mission satellite altimetry. The satellite altimetry missions derived Sea Level Anomaly (SLA) and Sea Surface Temperature (SST) around the Malaysian Seas from 1993 until 2023. Celebes Sea have showed a mixed correlation coefficient from -0.4223 to 0.8960. Sulu Sea have a small to strong positive correlation with coefficient from 0.2548 to 0.8481. Malacca Straits showed weak to moderate correlation coefficient from -0.020 to 0.4365. South China Sea show a significant and strong negative correlation from -0.5540 to -0.8107. #19 [paper] Mitigating Summertime Marine Heatwaves via Targeted Marine Cloud Brightening
Authors: Matthew T. Luongo, Edward Blanchard‐Wrigglesworth, Kyle Armour, Haruki Hirasawa, Jacob Cohen, Aaron Donohoe
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5kv4t
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) negatively impact marine ecosystems and coastal economies. Here, we evaluate whether a preemptive, short-term, localized surface emission of sea salt aerosols (marine cloud brightening, MCB) can mitigate the impacts of a predicted MHW without creating significant effects beyond the intervention zone. As a case study, we apply MCB to the 2019 Northeast Pacific MHW, "The Blob 2.0," using a global climate model seasonal-to-multiyear predictability ensemble. Initiating MCB in May 2019 mitigates important negative consequences of the event, substantially reducing the MHW magnitude and limiting associated declines in surface oxygen. The impacts of this intervention are mostly local and limited to summer, even when MCB is extended into winter, with nonlocal climate effects smaller than internal variability. By demonstrating local efficacy and minor remote impacts for mitigating the Blob 2.0, this work motivates further study of whether localized and temporary climate interventions can safely and effectively mitigate MHWs.

#20 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

#1 [paper] Satellite-gene abundance fusion reveals global hotspots of ocean ecosystem services
Authors: Baptiste Serandour, Constanza M. Andreani-Gerard, Antoine Bagnaro, Sacha Bourgeois‐Gironde, Samuel Chaffron, Andrés Couve, Roy El Hourany, Lionel Guidi
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The spatial organization of plankton-based ecosystem services, such as functional diversity, net primary productivity, and carbon export, is poorly understood, creating a need for science-based guidance for global ocean governance.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning integration of omics-derived plankton functions and satellite observations with diversity metrics and ecosystem services.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global oceanographic structures, including polar fronts and principal current systems.
Abstract:
The Ocean sustains planetary health through climate regulation, biodiversity, and essential ecosystem services. Plankton underpins these processes by driving primary production, sustaining food webs, and mediating carbon sequestration. Yet the spatial organization of plankton-based ecosystem services remains poorly understood. The High Seas Treaty and the 30% Ocean protection target by 2030 create an urgent need for science-based guidance for global ocean governance. Here, we aim to identify key planktonic areas associated with functional diversity, net primary productivity, and carbon export globally. We used machine learning to integrate omics-derived plankton functions and satellite observations with diversity metric and ecosystem services. Leveraging metagenomic data, we identified molecular functions strongly linked to ecosystem functioning and project their global distributions across seasons. We reveal putative hotspots of functional diversity, net primary productivity, and carbon export. Our analysis pinpoints areas where all three indicators converge synchronously, predominantly along oceanographic structures such as polar fronts and principal current systems. By relying on satellite data as core input, our approach captures the temporal variability of these hotspots, providing a global, dynamic protocol for projections of plankton-based ecosystem services. These findings establish a foundation for developing integrative conservation tools based on ecosystem functioning and inform adaptive management under climate change.

#2 [paper] Leveraging Ocean Data and Models: Building the Data Infrastructure, Workforce, and Modeling Capacity to Synthesize Earth’s Ocean Observations
Authors: Susanne E. Craig, Frank Muller-Karger, Leonid Shumilo, Tzortziou Maria
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5bv4n
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean-relevant Earth system data from satellite streams, in situ networks, suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, and high-resolution numerical models exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A decadal strategy built on two pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data (cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, machine learning) and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation (mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimila…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): NASA's aquatic and marine research enterprise, including MODIS, PACE mission, and BGC-Argo data streams.
Abstract:
NASA’s aquatic and marine research enterprise within the overarching NASA Biosphere Program is entering an era of unprecedented data abundance. MODIS and the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission already generate ocean color data at rates that strain legacy processing and archiving workflows, and forthcoming missions will add further volume and complexity. These satellite streams are joined by rapidly growing in situ networks (e.g., BGC-Argo), suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, citizen science, and increasingly high-resolution numerical models. The result is a Big Data regime in which the volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean relevant Earth system data exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches. An important goal is to fully integrate observing workflows, understanding, and models across the terrestrial, aquatic, and atmosphere domains to fully enable understanding of life and the realization of improved information to manage uses of ecosystem services. This white paper addresses Leveraging Ocean Data and Models, a cross-cutting Grand Challenge that underlies and enables progress on the four other foundational grand challenges under the NASA Biosphere, Atmosphere, Cryosphere, and Hydrosphere framework - Global Biosphere, Carbon and the Elements of Life, Interface Habitats, and Transient Events - each of which depends on the ability to acquire, harmonize, and synthesize disparate satellite, suborbital, in situ, and model data streams. We recommend a decadal strategy built on two complementary pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data, covering tiered cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, and machine learning; and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation, covering mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimilation, hybrid approaches, mission emulators, and a NASA Digital Twin Ocean. Without concerted, proactive investment in this cross-cutting infrastructure, the scientific and societal returns on the coming decade’s expanded observing system will be substantially diminished.

#3 [paper] Ocean surface currents directly imaged from space
Authors: Nicolas G. Rascle, Aurélien Ponte, Frédéric Nouguier, Renaud Binet, Dhruv Balwada, Fabrice Ardhuin, Bertrand Chapron, Bergsma Erwin
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5vv49
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The inability to directly image ocean surface currents from space, which limits understanding of ocean-climate interactions, marine ecosystems, and vertical transport of heat, carbon, and nutrients.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Direct satellite imaging of kilometre-scale surface currents using a tandem configuration of optical satellites that tracks surface wave propagation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Satellite observations of ocean surface dynamics, including coastal jets, equatorial flows, and submesoscale motions.
Abstract:
For more than four decades, satellite images of ocean temperature and colour have revealed jets, swirling eddies, and filaments. Yet the currents that shape these structures have never been directly imaged from space. This observational gap limits our understanding of the ocean's impact on climate and marine ecosystems, as these currents modulate exchanges between the coast and open ocean, vertical transport to the deep sea, and fluxes of heat, carbon, and nutrients. Here we demonstrate the first direct satellite imaging of kilometre-scale surface currents using a tandem configuration of optical satellites that tracks surface wave propagation. This new capability shifts satellite observations beyond the predominantly geostrophic view of ocean circulation, revealing dynamics that have remained largely invisible to satellites - from intense coastal jets and equatorial flows to submesoscale motions just kilometres wide. Across these regimes, the elusive divergence of fronts and internal waves, thought to play a key role in upper-ocean vertical exchange, is concentrated at scales below 5 km, previously unresolved from space. These reference measurements provide a new observational window into the multiscale physics of the upper ocean and its mediating role for the Earth’s climate system and marine life.

#6 [paper] Data-driven coastal nutrients estimation: current status, research gaps, and future developments.
Authors: Ni, Sihan, Qi, Jin, Ran, Xiangbin, Liu, Zhiqiang, Wu, Sensen, Wang, Minyu, Yang, Keyi, Le, Chengfeng
Venue: Water research
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42748610/

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The estimation of coastal nutrients from satellite observations remains a challenge because nutrients lack direct optical properties, and current data-driven methods face issues with interpretability and data scarcity.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A review of the mechanisms governing coastal biogeochemical cycling, the development of data-driven methods for remote sensing retrieval of nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon, and an analysis of the integration of machine learning with marine biogeochemical mechanisms.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global coastal waters and satellite-based remote sensing observations.
Abstract:
Driven by warming and anthropogenic impacts, global coastal waters suffer from the escalating eutrophication crisis, making it essential to understand the dynamics of nutrient discharge and enrichment. While satellites can retrieve surface water optical properties, the estimation of coastal nutrients from space remains a long-standing challenge due to their non-optical properties. Recently, artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning, has enabled the spatiotemporal estimation of surface nutrients from satellite observations, which represents a potential breakthrough for sustainable water management. In this review, we summarize the mechanisms governing coastal biogeochemical cycling and identify the estimation complexity that international scholars have been striving to solve over the past decade. We demonstrate that data-driven methods have shown preliminary success in empowering remote sensing retrieval of nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon. Despite these advances, we note that significant challenges remain for effective monitoring of coastal eutrophication due to the limited interpretability of data-driven estimation and data scarcity. A thorough analysis is provided on the developments and limitations of nutrient retrieval, the potential of integrating data-driven methods with marine biogeochemical mechanisms, and future opportunities to enhance marine ecosystem dynamic models. Ultimately, our aim is to advance satellite observations and data-driven estimation at the forefront of environmental science to develop the precise monitoring, assessment, and protection of coastal waters.

#7 [paper] Integrating anthropogenic hydrodynamics and GOCI satellite observations for water quality retrieval in highly engineered coastal systems: A case study of Saemangeum
Authors: Yejin Lee, Dongjin Kim, Suhwan Kim, Dohee Han, Hyun‐Su Kim, Jonghan Ko, Su-mi Kim, Kyeong-sang Lee

Abstract:
Retrieving water quality parameters in highly engineered coastal systems remains a challenge for standard satellite algorithms due to the complex decoupling of optical properties from natural hydrodynamics. To address the optical complexity of T-P, which lacks direct spectral absorption features, we incorporated Total Nitrogen (T-N) as an operational proxy for nutrient loading, enabling the models to capture the non-linear covariation between nutrients and optically active constituents. Our results demonstrate that incorporating anthropogenic hydrodynamic variables significantly improves retrieval accuracy, with the MLP-Mixer achieving the highest performance (Chl-a R 2 = 0.81; T-P R 2 = 0.83) by effectively learning long-term temporal dependencies. #9 [paper] Characterizing and Predicting Change in the Global Ocean Biosphere: A Four-Dimensional Observing Strategy for the 2028–2037 Decadal Survey
Authors: Susanne Craig, Daniella Asturias, Heather Benway, Leocadio Blanco‐Bercial, Joaquim Goes, Patrick Gray, Hannah Joy-Warren, Sasha Kramer

Method (Mycelium's reading): A phased observing strategy involving the sustenance of hyperspectral ocean color and polarimetric continuity, the addition of ocean-optimized profiling lidar, the expansion of autonomous and suborbital in situ observing networks, and investment in ecosystem models and data assimilation systems.

Abstract:
Ocean ecosystems constitute the largest habitable volume on Earth and regulate climate, support fisheries and a global Blue Economy valued at an estimated $1.5 trillion annually and provide services on which human wellbeing depends. Four decades of satellite ocean color observations have transformed understanding of phytoplankton distribution, biodiversity, and productivity, and NASA's PACE mission is now extending this record with unprecedented hyperspectral and polarimetric capabilities. Yet, passive ocean color remote sensing remains fundamentally two-dimensional – it detects only the optical signature of the uppermost, sunlit ocean; provides little or no coverage during polar night, persistent cloud cover, and low-sun conditions; and offers no independent means of validating its own retrievals. This white paper, submitted in response to the ESAS 2028 Request for Information under the Biosphere sphere, presents the science case and a phased observing strategy for achieving a four-dimensional (three spatial dimensions plus time), pole-to-pole characterization of global ocean ecosystems. The vision presented here draws heavily on Earth’s Living Ocean, the science vision report of NASA’s Ocean Biology and Biogeochemistry Program. We recommend 1) sustaining hyperspectral ocean color and polarimetric continuity, 2) adding a mature, ocean-optimized profiling lidar to resolve water column particle distributions and fill coverage gaps in polar and persistently cloudy regions, 3) expanding autonomous and suborbital in situ observing networks, and 4) investing in ecosystem models and data assimilation systems capable of ingesting these complementary data streams. Together, these elements would resolve a critical, decades-old gap in our ability to characterize, understand, and predict how global ocean ecosystems – from phytoplankton production to the fisheries and top predators they sustain – are responding to compounding natural and human-driven stressors, and whether those ecosystems are approaching thresholds beyond which their structure and function change abruptly and persistently.

Abstract:
ABSTRACT Characterizing open ocean biodiversity at basin scales remains challenging due to sparse sampling and limited opportunities to validate satellite‐derived estimates of plankton community composition. Through the Citizens of the Sea initiative, we deployed standardized environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling kits on 27 sailing vessels during the 2024 Pacific Rally circumnavigating between New Zealand, Tonga, and Fiji, generating 728 surface ocean eDNA samples across 1.5 million km 2 . Using three complementary metabarcoding markers (bacterial 16S rRNA, eukaryotic 18S rRNA and metazoan Cytochrome Oxidase I genes), and following rigorous bioinformatic quality control, we obtained 31,177 unique Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs), providing the first high‐resolution plankton biodiversity assessment of this understudied region. After accounting for human‐derived variation, all metabarcoding markers revealed clear latitudinal patterns in alpha diversity and community composition. ASV richness increased significantly with sea‐surface temperature and community turnover was strongly correlated with gradients in temperature and chlorophyll‐a. Comparisons between eDNA‐inferred phytoplankton functional groups and satellite‐based estimates showed moderate agreement for prokaryote‐dominated communities ( R 2 = 0.27) but a weak correlation for eukaryotic phytoplankton ( R 2 < 0.15), reflecting functional‐type‐specific mismatches between molecular and remote sensing approaches. Our results reinforce that citizen science fleets can generate high‐quality oceanographic eDNA datasets at scales unattainable by research expeditions, while demonstrating the strong potential of these initiatives to bridge molecular observations with satellite‐derived assessments and improve our understanding of open ocean plankton biodiversity.

Abstract:

We analyze the techniques and practices involved in planning, testing, calibrating, validating, and error-correcting that ultimately lead to the production, transmission, and dissemination of Argo data. Setting (Mycelium's reading): Ocean sciences research literature covering physical oceanography, coastal hazards, marine biogeochemistry, ecology, remote sensing, acoustics, marine geology, and applied ocean engineering.
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used in ocean sciences to analyze large, complex, and unevenly sampled datasets from satellites, autonomous platforms, sensors, vessels, and genomic tools. This review examines how AI and ML are being applied across major areas of ocean research, including physical oceanography, coastal hazards, marine biogeochemistry, ecology, remote sensing, acoustics, marine geology, and applied ocean engineering. Using a literature-synthesis workflow supported by Schlitsummarizer and full-text extraction methods, this paper identifies key applications, emerging trends, research gaps, and limitations in ocean-based ML. The review shows that ML is particularly useful for predicting surface currents, reconstructing subsurface ocean conditions, forecasting waves, estimating biogeochemical variables, classifying marine organisms and habitats, improving remote-sensing products, and supporting autonomous observing systems. Emerging trends include the growth of deep learning, physics-informed machine learning, explainable AI, data integration across observing platforms, and management-focused applications related to climate adaptation, coastal planning, fisheries, and environmental monitoring. However, major challenges remain, including sparse and biased ocean observations, limited data from deep-ocean and polar regions, validation bias, poor model transferability, class imbalance in ecological datasets, black-box model behavior, and uncertainty under changing climate conditions. Abstract:
Sea surface nitrate (SSN) monitoring is essential for understanding coastal eutrophication and anthropogenic water cycle. However, SSN is optically inactive, and the mechanisms that enable its retrieval from satellite observations remains unclear, limiting the reliability of large-scale and early diagnosis of coastal eutrophication from space. To address this gap, we employ an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model to identify the latent associations between SSN and individual satellite spectral bands. By estimating daily SSN distributions in the East China Sea, the Pearl River Estuary, and Chesapeake Bay, the XAI model explicitly quantifies the spectral contributions and reveals the optical-biogeochemical association underlying SSN retrieval. In high-turbidity water, strong particle scattering obscures the spectral fingerprint, indicating that satellite-derived SSN estimates should be interpreted with greater caution under highly turbid conditions. These findings highlight the optical-biogeochemical associations underlying satellite nitrate retrieval and provide both an explainable basis and practical guidance for future monitoring of coastal nutrient dynamics from space.

#15 [paper] Writing Nonhuman Agency
Authors: Chak-kwan Ng

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The text explores the conceptual and historical connections between space exploration and oceanography, specifically examining how technological advancements in both fields (sonar, spacecraft) intersected with the American conservation movement and revealed Earth's uniqueness.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): Historical context of the mid-20th century, focusing on US technological developments in oceanography and space exploration.
Abstract:
Although space and the ocean on Earth may seem distant and unrelated, their unexpected connection emerges from the origins of water in the solar nebula that birthed our solar system, which ultimately found its way to our planet in liquid form ( Kunzig 2000 , 14–15). The Big Bang and the subsequent formation of stars and planets reveal the agential creativity of the universe, which is a self-organising dynamism that far exceeds human capacity for understanding. Both the vastness of outer space and the depths of the ocean remain mysterious realms that captivate human curiosity and symbolise the origins of our existence. After the two world wars, the second half of the twentieth century witnessed tremendous advancements in oceanography and space exploration in the United States. The development of the sonar system for seafloor mapping and submarine warfare emerged as a key surveillance technology during World War I. Constantin Chilowsky, a Russian scientist living in Switzerland, proposed using high-frequency sound for underwater detection and collaborated with French physicist Paul Langevin around 1915 to develop hydrophones ( Petersen 2012 , 241–242). In 1931, engineer Otis Barton and naturalist William Beebe became the first hydronauts to explore the depths of the ocean in the bathysphere, descending to a record 1,426 feet off the coast of Nonsuch Island, Bermuda, where they documented fascinating marine life in their natural habitat ( Cerka 2022 ). Sonar technology and deep-sea expeditions laid the foundation for modern oceanography. Post-war technological rivalry spurred efforts to explore outer space, with satellites and spacecraft sending early images of Earth in partial view, the first taken in 1946, followed by others that showcased the planet in its entirety ( Uri 2024 ). Among these, “The Blue Marble”, a well-known colour photograph taken by NASA astronauts on 7 December 1972 during their Apollo 17 mission, epitomised Earth's uniqueness as the only known life-inhabited planet ( Strickland 2022 ). The launch of NASA's Viking missions, which sent spacecraft to explore Mars in 1975 and 1976, was part of a broader initiative that began in the late 1940s and revealed the barrenness of Mars, further affirming Earth's special status ( NASA 2024 ). The scientific breakthroughs intersected with the emergence of the American conservation movement, a co-development that was by no means a coincidence.

#16 [paper] Many knowledges for One Ocean
Authors: Elizabeth Havice, Noella J. Gray, Oscar Hartman Davies, Nadège Legroux, JESSICA LEHMAN, Emily C. Melvin, Kimberley Peters, Teriitutea Quesnot

Abstract:

Drawing on our work on new data technologies, oceans governance, and our participant observation at OOSC and the Third United Nations Oceans Conference, we explore three sites where universalism and difference were evident at the meetings: the propensity to render the oceans technical rather than political; the persistence of gaps as a defining feature of One Ocean Science; and sciences and knowledges incommensurable with One Ocean Science universalism. We highlight that One Ocean Science universalism is, perhaps counterintuitively, constituted through differences and heterogeneities in scientific practices and politics. Manifesting the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development’s goals of ocean science that fosters equity and sustainability will require holding space for difference within One Ocean, including by interrogating and redesigning the epistemological infrastructure of One Ocean Science so that pluralism becomes structural rather than residual.

#17 [paper] The evolving landscape of remote sensing employment: a data-driven analysis of requirements, skills, and responsibilities in earth observation roles
Authors: Christopher A. Ramezan, Ludwig Christian Schaupp, Cadence A. Wright, Aaron E. Maxwell

Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/10106049.2026.2717445

Abstract:

Proposals are expected to address multiple key research directions in Quantum Machine Learning (QML), targeting both scientific excellence and industrial relevance. Proposals should clearly outline how to contribute to the development, validation and demonstration of quantum-enhanced AI approaches, with clear pathways towards practical applications. The proposed work should strengthen Europe’s scientific and technological capabilities in quantum computing and accelerate the industrial uptake of quantum-enhanced AI solutions.

Activities may include, but are not limited to

- design and analysis of quantum, quantum-inspired or hybrid QML algorithms,

- performance modelling, complexity analysis and benchmarking of quantum-enhanced AI methods,

- development of error-mitigation and noise-aware strategies tailored to QML workloads,

- quantum-native learning models,

- efficient quantum kernels and quantum feature mappings,

Proposals may also include formal complexity analyses, identification of problem classes that can benefit from quantum acceleration.

Quantum Supervised Learning (QSL):

#2 [paper] The impact of personalized deadline reminders via Microsoft Teams and Moodle calendar on assignment submission and completion rates
Authors: Ahmad Alfailakawi, Abdulaziz Alenizi
Venue: Frontiers in Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943550
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Objectives This study investigated the effectiveness of two digital deadline reminder strategies—a researcher-authored, friendly-toned announcement delivered through Microsoft Teams and a standard automated calendar/email notification generated by Moodle—compared with a control condition receiving no additional reminders. The study examined differences in on-time assignment submission rates and average submission delays among higher education students. Methodology An A/B/C comparative design with random assignment was employed involving 138 male and female students enrolled in the Introduction to Educational Technology course at the College of Basic Education in Kuwait during the second semester of the 2024–2025 academic year. Participants were allocated equally to three groups: a researcher-authored Microsoft Teams reminder group, an automated Moodle reminder group, and a control group. Five assignments were monitored over a ten-week intervention period, and submission data were obtained from Moodle activity logs. Results Statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups. Students receiving researcher-authored, friendly-toned reminders through Microsoft Teams demonstrated the highest mean on-time submission rate (94.22%) and the shortest mean submission delay (5.18 h). Students receiving automated Moodle reminders recorded an on-time submission rate of 85.65% and an average delay of 15.45 h, while the control group recorded 75.22% and 30.89 h, respectively. The effect sizes were substantial ( η 2 = 0.289 for on-time submission and η 2 = 0.639 for submission delay), although the latter estimate requires cautious interpretation because of the distributional characteristics of the delay variable. Conclusion The findings suggest that proactive digital reminder strategies can support students’ adherence to assignment deadlines. The researcher-authored, friendly-toned reminder strategy delivered through Microsoft Teams was associated with more favorable submission outcomes than the default automated Moodle reminder strategy. However, because the interventions differed simultaneously in communication platform, message content, authorship, and delivery format, the observed differences cannot be attributed to platform characteristics alone. The findings highlight the potential importance of reminder design and delivery practices while emphasizing the need for future research that independently examines the contributions of individual reminder components.

#5 [paper] DESIGN AND SIMULATION OF A TASK REMINDER WITH SPACED REVIEW AND DEADLINE PRESSURE DETECTION
Authors: Hizba Muhammad Falah, Anggi Rizky Windra Putri, Tasiu Abdullahi Yusuf
Venue: International Journal of Cyber Engineering
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.68404/ijce.v2i1.26
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Describe Task reminders commonly indicate when an assignment is due, but deadline counts alone do not describe the effort required before each due date. Moreover, repeated notifications are not equivalent to retrieval-based spaced review. This study develops an explicit scheduling specification for an existing task-reminder prototype and evaluates a separate executable reference engine. The design combines a recall-dependent review rule, a cumulative deadline-pressure calculation, and an event resolver that distinguishes review prompts from deadline checks. Evaluation comprises 23 functional checks, three scripted review sequences, and 300 synthetic workload scenarios containing 1,150 task records. All functional checks passed. At an assumed capacity of two hours per day and a 72-hour horizon, count-based, aggregate-load, and cumulative deadline-pressure rules flagged 100, 100, and 150 scenarios, respectively. In 50 deliberately constructed early-bottleneck scenarios, only the cumulative rule flagged insufficient capacity before the earliest deadline. Conversely, all 50 light clustered workloads triggered the count rule without exceeding the assumed capacity. An independent exhaustive scheduling oracle agreed with the cumulative rule in all 300 scenarios; agreement was 50.0% for the count rule and 83.3% for the aggregate rule. These results verify logic under the stated capacity model. They do not establish improved retention, productivity, or student well-being. The contribution is a reproducible prototype extension with transparent assumptions and an evidence-based separation of reminder functionality from educational effectiveness.

#13 [paper] Do Firms Expect the Deadline to Move? Expiry Dates, Repeated Extensions, and AI Decision-Makers in Japanese Corporate Tax Special Measures
Authors: 勉 矢作
Venue: Open Science Framework
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/dsm7j
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Many tax incentives carry an expiry date. A deadline should pull investment forward into the final year before expiry (a time notch in the sense of Slemrod 2013). If a measure has been extended many times, however, firms may expect another extension, and the deadline may stop working as a deadline. The literature on time notches (Slemrod 2013; House and Shapiro 2008; Cashin and Unayama 2016) and the literature on transition policy (Kaplow 1986, 2003; Shaviro 2000) have developed separately. This study links them by asking whether the history of extensions changes the response to an expiry date. Study 1 uses the annual reports that the Minister of Finance submits to the Diet under the Act on Transparency of Special Tax Measures (2010). These reports give, for each corporate tax special measure, the number of corporations applying it and the amount applied, for fiscal years ending on or after 1 April 2011. Study 2 asks how large language models (LLMs), acting as managers of a small firm, respond to the same kind of deadline. As firms delegate tax and investment decisions to AI, the response to deadlines may change. Study 2 tests the prediction, registered in OSF pw5fz, that LLM agents follow what is written: they respond to the expiry date stated in the statute and ignore an extension history unless it is written in front of them.

#14 [paper] Just Another Manic Monday in the Call Center: When Equal Demand Does Not Produce Equal Service
Authors: Michael Douglas, Eric Kyper
Venue: Archives of Business Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.14738/abr.1410.12332
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Call centers ordinarily explain service-level variation through demand, service time, staffing, routing, and customer patience. Yet performance may also vary systematically by weekday even when workload is comparable. This study examines a Monday effect in operational data from a large U.S. insurance-service organization. The dataset contained 13,024 intraday records across 32 business days, 37 reporting queues, and 20 business groups. Because call counts were cumulative within day, the primary analysis used each queue’s final daily snapshot, producing 1,127 active queue-day observations. Monday service level averaged .658, compared with .715 on Tuesday, although log-transformed call volume did not differ significantly between the two days. Ordinary least squares models with queue-clustered standard errors showed that Monday remained associated with a 5.1-percentage-point reduction in service level after controlling for call volume, average handle time, and business-group fixed effects. The result persisted across all-weekday, logit-transformed, volume-threshold, nonboundary, weighted, paired-queue, and nonparametric sensitivity analyses. The findings distinguish workload effects from weekday effects and suggest that start-of-week operational frictions may impair service beyond what volume alone explains. Because staffing, schedule adherence, absence, backlog, and call-mix measures were unavailable, the analysis identifies a robust temporal pattern rather than a causal mechanism. The study contributes to service-operations research by treating weekday as an operational state variable and offers managers a focused diagnostic agenda for Monday readiness.

#16 [paper] Analysis of Causes and Risk Mitigation for Delivery Delays Based on On-Time In-Full (OTIF) Data in Non-Cement Distribution Using RCA and FMEA Methods at PT XYZ
Authors: Rifki Putra Rahmadhan, Akhmad Wasiur Rizqi
Venue: International Journal Of Science Technology & Management
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.46729/ijstm.v7i6.1522
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Delivery punctuality is an important indicator of logistics service performance, yet non-cement distribution at PT XYZ still experiences delays. On Time In Full (OTIF) data from May to July 2026 recorded that only 54.64% of 14,986 shipments were delivered on time. This study aims to determine the on-time delivery rate, identify the dominant causes and root causes of delay, and determine mitigation priorities. The methods used were Pareto diagram, Root Cause Analysis (RCA) with fishbone and 5 Why, and Failure Mode and Effect Analysis (FMEA), with Severity, Occurrence, and Detection rated by two respondents. The Pareto results show that long parking time (49.9%) and unloading schedule (41.1%) caused 91.0% of the delays. RCA identified the root causes as the absence of a standard maximum stopping time, a joint arrival scheduling mechanism with receivers, a procedure for communicating estimated arrival, and a cargo readiness confirmation procedure. Based on FMEA, the highest Risk Priority Number (RPN) belongs to the absence of a joint arrival scheduling mechanism with receivers (336), followed by the absence of an estimated arrival notification procedure (168) and a standard maximum stopping time (120). Joint arrival scheduling with receivers should be the priority for improvement.

#1 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

#2 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

#3 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#7 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.
