#5 [paper] Two-dimensional simulation of plastic bottles transport in a urban reach of the Arno River
Authors: Gabriella Petaccia, Elisabetta Persi, Francesco Paolo Contò, Diego Ravazzolo, Andrea Fenocchi, Stefano Sibilla, Lorenzo Innocenti, Mirco Mancini
Venue: Digital Water
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/28375807.2026.2724249
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Within the MINOSSE project (ManagINg plastic transpOrt in riverS and coaStal arEas), the 2D hydrodynamic numerical model ORSA2D_WT has been adapted to simulate the transport of plastic bottles, the most common macroplastic item transported in water bodies. Unlike smaller plastics, such as fragments or films, the shape and size of plastic bottles can significantly influence their inertia and fate. They may not follow flow velocity lines, so they must be modelled as discrete items, driven by the flow field and capable of interacting with surrounding elements (riverbed, riverbanks, bridge piers, vegetation, other debris of plastic or different nature). Thanks to the proposed 2D numerical approach, they are modelled as individual items floating on the water surface or being conveyed in the water column. The ORSA2D_WT model has been appled to simullate plastic bottles trajectories in a 7.6 km urban reach of the Arno River, during a winter event. Two different releases points were considered, the Affrco conflunece on the side of the river and a central point of the river close to the upstream section. The results of the model from the release points show a different behaviuor in the trajectories and in the stranding points. These first results qualitatively match the in situ observations, and show that the numerical model can help in identifying hot spots for plastic accumulation.

#6 [paper] PlasticFADE: a predictive model for plastic fragmentation and degradation rates in the environment
Authors: Yibo Tang, Nadim Saadi, Jérôme Lavoie, Anne‐Marie Boulay
Venue: Microplastics and Nanoplastics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00243-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Plastics are widespread across the globe, posing risks to environmental and human health. Fragmentation and degradation are key processes that govern the environmental fate and impacts of plastics, yet their rates remain poorly quantified. Life cycle assessment (LCA) is widely recognized as the standard framework for comprehensively evaluating the environmental performance of products and services. Accurately capturing the fate of plastics in natural environments therefore represents a critical priority for impact assessment modeling. However, the degradation and fragmentation mechanisms governing plastic polymer behavior remain poorly quantified in current life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) models, limiting their capacity to characterize the potential biodiversity impacts arising from plastic emissions to natural environments. In this study, experimental data on plastic fragmentation and degradation were systematically compiled from the literature. Using these data, PlasticFADE was developed as the first iteration of an empirical model to predict polymer-specific rate constants in various environmental compartments. The model predictions reveal that the rate constants vary considerably across polymers and compartments. Estimated lifespans of plastics range from several decades to over a millennium. Beaches are identified as hotspots for both fragmentation and degradation, whereas plastics are most likely to remain intact in the water column. Criteria are proposed for evaluating the reliability of the model outputs, which should be interpreted with due caution. Despite its limitations, the model offers valuable insights into plastic fate processes and offers significant potential for improving current LCIA methods for plastic emissions assessment.

#7 [paper] Sustainable Manufacturing Practices in the Plastic Packaging Industry and Associated Barriers: A Systematic Literature Review
Authors: Anny Jasbleidy Avendaño Avendaño, Fernando Antônio Forcellini
Venue: Circular Economy and Sustainability
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s43615-026-01161-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The plastic packaging industry is a major contributor to environmental impacts due to its intensive use of fossil-based materials and low recycling rates. In this context, Sustainable Manufacturing (SM) has emerged as a strategic approach to mitigate these impacts while balancing environmental, economic, and social dimensions. However, the literature remains fragmented, particularly regarding the integration of practices, barriers, and performance in sustainability. This study aims to systematically identify and analyze SM practices in the plastic packaging industry, examine the barriers to their implementation, and propose an integrated framework that relates practices, barriers, and performance in the dimensions of the Triple Bottom Line (TBL). A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA protocol, searching the Scopus and Web of Science databases without temporal restrictions. A total of 18 peer-reviewed articles were selected for in-depth content analysis. The data were coded and categorized to identify practices, barriers, and their interrelationships. The results indicate a predominance of practices focused on the environmental dimension, such as sustainable design and development, recycling, and resource efficiency, while social practices remain underexplored. Significant barriers include high investment costs, technological limitations, inadequate recycling infrastructure, and regulatory inconsistencies. Based on these findings, this study proposes an integrated framework that captures the relationships among SM practices, barriers to implementation, and performance across TBL dimensions. This framework contributes to advancing theoretical understanding and provides practical support for managers and policymakers in promoting a more systemic and sustainable transition in the plastic packaging industry.

#8 [paper] An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
Authors: Borja Nogué-Algueró, Richard York, Stefano B. Longo, Ekaterina Chertkovskaya, Patrick Trent Greiner
Venue: Ecological Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2026.109264
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This survey synthesizes insights from environmental social sciences to recast the plastics crisis as a structural feature of growth-dependent economies instead of a problem solvable by consumer choice or incremental technologies. Rather than a within-field review of ecological economics, it maps adjacent literatures to specify what this field could study and how, clarifying researchable questions, suitable methods, and tractable indicators. The synthesis foregrounds connections between expansionary political-economic dynamics, globally uneven socio-ecological burdens across the plastics life cycle, and the power and knowledge relations that shape what is produced, measured, and governed. It calls for comparative, mixed-methods, multi-scalar work and for open, standardized data on plastics flows to strengthen causal inference and comparability. Shifting attention upstream—from end-of-pipe fixes to the transformation of provisioning systems—the paper charts lines of inquiry capable of aligning social metabolism with biophysical limits and human needs, providing a roadmap for ecological economics to organize and accelerate research beyond consumer or techno-managerial framings.

#9 [paper] Technological Innovations for Ocean Plastic Waste Management: A Global Bibliometric Analysis of Research Trends, Collaboration Networks, and Emerging Technologies
Authors: Jehu Roeh C. Rubenial Franklin M. Ganancias
Venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.59543/jidmis.v3.1213
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ocean plastic pollution has become one of the most pressing environmental challenges worldwide, driving increasing interest in technology-based solutions for monitoring, prevention, mitigation, and sustainable waste management. Despite the rapid growth of research in this field, a comprehensive understanding of its scientific development, collaboration patterns, and emerging technological directions remains limited. This study presents a global bibliometric analysis of technological innovations for ocean plastic waste management using 12,039 English-language publications retrieved from the Scopus database on 09 July 2026. Bibliographic data were analyzed using Bibliometrix (RStudio) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, influential authors, journals, institutions, countries, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, and thematic evolution. The findings reveal a substantial increase in scientific production, particularly after 2015, demonstrating the rapid expansion of this interdisciplinary research domain. China, the United States, and several European and Asian countries emerged as the leading contributors to scientific productivity and international collaboration, while Marine Pollution Bulletin and Science of the Total Environment ranked among the most productive publication sources. Author keyword co-occurrence analysis identified microplastics, plastic waste, circular economy, recycling, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and remote sensing as dominant research themes. Thematic evolution further revealed a transition from broad marine pollution research toward technology-oriented investigations emphasizing plastic waste management and microplastics. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive knowledge map of the field, highlighting the growing integration of digital technologies and sustainable waste management strategies. The findings offer valuable insights for researchers, policymakers, and environmental practitioners in identifying research priorities, strengthening international collaboration, and advancing technology-driven solutions for sustainable ocean plastic waste management.

#10 [paper] Environmental Impacts and Life Cycle Assessment of Recycled Plastic Bricks
Authors: Sirri Neba Nforsoh, Kayla Kurtz, Marlene Prien, Jitka Bečanová, Šimon Vojta, Rui Wang, Rakesh Paswan, Karla Pozo
Venue: ACS Omega
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.6c04677
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract This study evaluated the mechanical performance, contaminant release, and life-cycle impacts of recycled plastic blocks manufactured from beach-collected and facility-sourced plastic waste. Four formulations combining polyethylene terephthalate, high-density polyethylene, low-density polyethylene, sand, and glass were evaluated. Unweathered blocks had compressive strengths between 20.6–24.3 N/mm2, suitable for paving applications; however, higher plastic fractions led to lower strength and higher porosity. UV weathering reduced strength by 6–12% and increased metal leaching by up to ∼400%. Per- and polyfluorinated concentrations peaked at 13.8 ng/L; concentrations decreased slightly after weathering due to polymer photo-oxidation and embrittlement that enhanced sorption capacity and retention. Formulations with lower plastic content (∼33%) had higher strength and lower leaching. Blocks with higher plastic ratios exhibited greater environmental burdens, matching leaching trends. Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

A fabricated object is exposed to a cue, its outline changes, and the sequence can be shown as a compelling demonstration of adaptive matter. Yet a moving outline is not a complete explanation, and an explanation is not a safe mission. A soft microgripper can close around a bead and still fail to release it; it can return to the same apparent curvature while its contact force has fallen; it can displace an object while losing fragments whose material fate is unmeasured. These cases do not invalidate the study of shape-programmed matter. They reveal that the study needs several distinct endpoints, each owned by an independent measurement pathway. This notebook reorganizes the first five flagships in the STARLI two-hundred-theme blueprint as a scientifically bounded lineage. F001 concerns identifiable stimulus-response geometry. F002 concerns encoded shape memory and loaded recovery. F003 concerns the integrity and mechanics of multi-material interfaces. F004 concerns the ordering of stimuli and the state history of a programmable device. F005 asks whether the complete microhandling mission remains functional after deformation and reconfiguration. None of these endpoints may substitute for another. Their relationship is cumulative but not hierarchical in the sense of guaranteed success: progress in one question may expose failure in the next. Two older research monographs provide the scientific starting point. The first is a 770-page research edition on 4D microrobotic manufacturing and biomedical-environment response. It supplies a repertoire of constitutive baselines, instrument limits, manufacturing variables, adversarial conditions and experimental counterexamples. The second is an 803-page BCI and stroke rehabilitation research atlas. Its most relevant contribution here is methodological: one must not confuse assistance-enabled performance with retained independent function. A bench-scale programmable material is not a stroke intervention, and no inference about patient rehabilitation is made. The analogy merely helps sharpen what counts as an externally supported achievement rather than a capability of the system being studied. All specific experiments in this new family are proposals. The mathematical expressions and numerical surfaces are not new natural laws, and the companion PDF figures are explicitly synthetic. Where published papers are cited, they support a limited background proposition about responsive materials, fabrication, or existing experimental methods; they do not validate this integrated STARLI research program. The scientific achievement sought here is a design of tests that could defeat the program if its premises are wrong. A successor laboratory should be able to reconstruct both an allowed action and a refused action from raw evidence without asking the originating team to supply an unwritten meaning. The narrative uses scientific objects, calibrated units and demanding rival hypotheses. Later investigators are invited to revise the questions rather than inherit their answers. Our analysis reveals that Dutch news articles often omit methodological detail and scientific uncertainties, while emphasizing the timing of an AMOC collapse. Dutch news articles simplify terminology, use types of exaggeration, and localize information to engage a broader public. Although most interviewed scientists consider the media coverage of their research adequate, they identify areas for improvement and propose solutions. #1 [paper] Co-producing urban knowledge in motion: collaborative experimental methods for researching moving infrastructures
Authors: Noel Chung
Venue: Urban Geography
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/02723638.2026.2725759
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Delivery platforms have become ubiquitous in many cities, increasingly governing how things and people move. As contingent, moving infrastructures, they register diverse urban entities in their operations and produce new urban conditions and politics. How, then, can we empirically research the often obscure workings of infrastructures that are also in constant motion? Addressing the diffuse and fleeting nature of moving infrastructures, this paper proposes a methodology that foregrounds movement as both an analytic focus and a mode of enactment. Drawing on a multimethod mobile ethnography with platform delivery workers in Seoul, it shows how the dialogic synthesis of mobile methods helps unravel the infrastructural processes, practices, and politics of making the city through movement. The plurality of data and the collaborative, experimental orientation proved generative while simultaneously raising ethical, logistical, and analytical challenges. Notwithstanding the challenges, the paper demonstrates the value of collectively enacting mobile ethnography to co-produce urban knowledge in motion. It concludes by calling for ongoing collective methodological innovation in response to continually emerging infrastructures in moving and other forms, arguing that embodied, collective, and experimental methods not only contribute to new epistemic practices but also enable us to collectively envision alternative ways of creating infrastructures and cities.

My path to pediatric neurogenetics did not begin in a classroom or specific clinic, but in the inventive chaos of childhood experiments with my brother that turned everyday spaces into laboratories of possibility.My path to becoming a pediatric neurogeneticist was neither linear nor predetermined for me.My earliest scientific "laboratory" was a kitchen table in my childhood home strewn with parts purchased from Radio Shack.My brother (now adult neurologist David Saperstein, M.D.) and I built rudimentary "computers" and explored the mechanics of problem-solving and teamwork.A backyard picnic table was our makeshift anatomy bench, and a cat pelvis (from my 11th-grade physiology course) became a hands-on lesson in structure and function.Those early experiences established a foundational approach to science where curiosity, persistence, and the belief that answers exist if one is willing to take things apart and put them back together again began my journey.Since then, the field of neurogenetics has matured into a recognized discipline with formal clinics, training pathways, and research networks.However, the most transformative moments of my career were driven by serendipity, mentorship, and most profoundly, my patients' stories.Here I describe the influences that shaped my professional journey, the evolution of neuroimaging and biomarkers in metabolic disease, and the enduring lessons of listening, learning, and leadership in the field of rare disease medicine.

#3 [paper] Three steps into agentic AI: a preregistered feasibility study of how non-programmers cross from chatbot to agent to multi-model orchestration (Cohort 1)
Authors: Vadym Chernets
Venue: Open Science Framework
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/x4egq
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ordinary professionals now use AI by talking to a chatbot. Two further steps exist and almost nobody has taken them: running an agent that acts on your own machine, and putting one question to several models in one action instead of visiting them by hand. This study follows a cohort of non-programmers across three specific transitions and records, for each, who crosses, how long it takes, and where the rest stop. The route is unusual and is the reason the study is possible at all. Participants are not installed for. Each receives a text, pastes it into the chatbot they already use, and that chatbot walks them through installing a graphical agent on their own machine. The investigator does not touch anyone's computer. This is a feasibility study of a pathway. It measures crossing, and it records usefulness without claiming to prove it. It has no control group and makes no causal claim. It is Cohort 1 of a programme; later cohorts are registered separately.

#5 [paper] FabLabs as Promissory Organizations: A future-making perspective

Abstract:
This paper examines FabLabs as machine-centred promissory organizations, where futures are not only imagined, but also materially enacted. Drawing on new materialist and process perspectives, we conceptualize FabLabs as promissory assemblages of entangled human and non-human actors, through which future-making is enacted. We show that machines are central agents for the materialization of imagined futures, especially for the boundaries they create between what is possible and what is not possible to actualize. Based on an ethnographic study of 20 FabLabs across nine countries conducted over twelve years, we identify two core processes – fabulation and fabrication – through which the future is first created and then materialized. This study advances research on promissory organizations by revealing their material underpinnings; it also extends future-making research by demonstrating how futures emerge through iterative material-discursive practices, rather than through linear planning. Overall, the paper contributes a machine-centred account of future-making, highlighting how imagination, materiality, and technology co-produce what futures become possible for entrepreneurs.

Abstract:
This paper reviews which actors recent urban freight scholarship recognises as stakeholders and how it represents their roles and interactions in relation to environmental and procedural justice. We conducted a systematic literature review of 54 studies using a deductive–iterative coding approach. #20 [paper] Volumetric Waste: Containing Polymorphous Plastic in Bangkok’s Circular Economies
Authors: Olivia Meyer
Venue: Geoforum
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2026.104858
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This paper examines how volumetric reasoning permeates everyday practices in Bangkok’s circular economies. While circular economies calculate, value, and contain plastic waste, mobile waste flows are hidden from view and often evade regulation. As a result, circular economy initiatives struggle to account for low-value waste, microplastics, and chemicals that proliferate through land, water, air, and blood in bodies. In these instances, waste travels and transforms volumetrically without a traceable latitude and longitude. Similarly, the actual dimensions of plastic objects impact their ability to be valued in the circular economy. Drawing on seventeen months of ethnographic fieldwork in Bangkok, Thailand, this paper documents how circular economy practitioners manage waste that takes on new materialities as it moves through plastic circularity loops. Nonstate waste practitioners invoke volumetric reasoning as they grapple with circular economy solutions (e.g., recovering, repurposing, and upcycling plastics). My argument is twofold: first, I argue that practitioners’ everyday volumetric practices expose the limits of formal circular economy policy. Second, I argue that volumetric reasoning gives practitioners a set of techniques for reclaiming agency over the everyday management of waste. By attending to commonplace yet novel spatial dimensions of plastic circularity, this paper contributes to emerging scholarship at the intersection of political ecology and volumetric analyses of plastic pollution in Asia.

#2 [paper] Gender analysis of the authors of the German-language pharmacy journal Pharmakon from 1972 to 2021
Authors: Mira Ober, Roland Seifert
Venue: Scientometrics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-026-05766-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Women tend to be underrepresented in almost all scientific fields in Germany. This study analyses publications of scientists in a German pharmaceutical non-peer-reviewed journal over a period of 50 years (1972–2021). The journal Pharmakon (previously named Pharmazie in unserer Zeit) is the member journal of the German Pharmaceutical Society (DPhG). We performed a gender analysis of the journal and analysed 1577 articles by 2509 authors. Overall, the percentage of women is 26%. This has changed significantly over time from 5% in the early years to almost 50% in 2020 (Chi 2 -test p = 0.00004). For many years, there were no women as first authors at all, but in 2020, for the first time, there were more female than male first authors. However, at the highest academic rank of professor, female authors are still much less abundant than men. The journal has also changed over the years. The number of authors per article has increased and more articles have been published since the turn of the millennium. Over the years, more non-pharmacists have also published, and interdisciplinary exchange seems to be becoming increasingly important. This study illustrates, for the field of German pharmacy, substantial gender inequalities. These inequalities are mirrored in the gender analysis of authors publishing in Pharmakon . Our study also shows that over the past decades, gender inequalities have become smaller, but they still exist, particularly at the highest-ranking level, i.e. professors. Our study will help politicians, universities and pharmacy associations to implement effective measures for gender equality.

#4 [paper] If You Meet an Author on the Road
Authors: Peter Ayolov
Venue: Knowledge Commons (Lakehead University)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17613/4cesm-mcr45
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The twentieth century repeatedly attempted to dethrone the Author without succeeding in eliminating the cultural desire for authorship. Roland Barthes displaced the writer as the sovereign origin of textual meaning, while Michel Foucault demonstrated that the author persisted as a classificatory, institutional and juridical function even after the metaphysics of individual creation had been destabilised. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence transforms this theoretical dispute into a material problem. Large language models can now perform operations previously treated as visible evidence of authorship: generating sentences, restructuring arguments, imitating genres, proposing metaphors, editing style, producing titles and transforming existing texts. Yet linguistic production does not necessarily establish authorial sovereignty. This article uses the deliberately provocative injunction If You Meet an Author on the Road, Kill Him as a metaphor for the repeated dismantling of every figure elevated into the final source of textual authority. The formulation adapts the Zen logic of destroying attachment to the master rather than advocating the destruction of the person: what must be "killed" is the intellectual idol of the sovereign Author. From this perspective, Barthes's Scriptor, Foucault's author-function, the contemporary Prompter and the generative Model represent successive attempts to relocate rather than finally resolve the problem of textual agency. The article argues that generative AI exposes a fragmentation that had always existed inside the apparently unified act of writing. Intention, research, memory, linguistic formulation, recombination, editing, selection, publication, interpretation and responsibility need not belong to a single agent, and contemporary human–AI production makes their separation increasingly visible. The resulting condition is described as authorship without a centre: a communicative work can emerge through interactions among human intention, inherited language, computational prediction, machine generation, editorial judgement, institutional framing and reader interpretation without any single participant containing the complete causal or semantic origin of the finished text. This does not mean that writers, intentions or responsibility disappear. On the contrary, the dissolution of sovereign authorship makes responsibility more important because distributed production cannot become an excuse for unaccountable publication. The article therefore distinguishes the death of the Author from the disappearance of the human writer and the fragmentation of authorship from the abolition of accountability. Its central claim is that the death of the Author should not be understood as a completed historical event but as a recurring critical operation. Whenever textual culture installs a new sovereign centre—the genius, the Scriptor, the Prompter, the algorithm or the Model—the same theoretical question returns: whether the production of language grants authority over its meaning. In the age of generative AI, the task is therefore not to discover who has inherited the Author's throne, but to question why the text requires a throne at all.

#5 [paper] Author profiles in Web of Science, Scopus, Dimensions, ORCID, ResearchGate, and Google Scholar: a case report.
Authors: Powell, Kimberly R
Venue: Journal of the Medical Library Association : JMLA
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42889833/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aimed to benchmark the availability and accuracy of author profiles for 45 faculty members within the Auburn University College of Nursing. Profile availability in the database platforms Web of Science, Scopus, and Dimensions were analyzed alongside the author-driven platforms ORCID, ResearchGate, and Google Scholar to set an understanding for the potential efforts needed for profile curation, publication tracking, and research impact assessments moving forward. CASE PRESENTATION: Each of the six platforms were manually searched for faculty and name variations alongside both current and past institutional affiliations. All identified profiles were collected. Associated publication counts were recorded and database results were screened for accurate author identification. Among the author-driven platforms, ORCID had the highest adoption rate, with 64% of faculty, while ResearchGate and Google Scholar trailed with 38% and 16% faculty adoption, respectively. Web of Science offered profiles for 82% of faculty; Scopus offered profiles for 80% of faculty, and Dimensions only 53%. However, 53% of the associated publications were misattributed in Web of Science profiles compared to just 1% misattribution in Scopus and none in Dimensions. CONCLUSIONS: Among our faculty, Scopus offered the most efficient author profile platform, balancing profile availability, minimizing misattribution, and including avenues for early identification of new authors. While largely in line with previous study findings, this effort provided important contextual understandings of profile data availability which can be used to inform research impact assessments and library services supporting author profiles for highlighting scholarly influence.

#6 [paper] Another Double Shift? Australian Authors, Digital Media and Gendered Promotional Labor
Authors: Anthea Taylor, Margaret Henderson
Venue: Publishing Research Quarterly
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12109-026-10093-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract With falling revenues from book sales, industry-wide and publishing house restructurings, declining marketing budgets, and the affordances of digital media, the promotional labor associated with books is increasingly being shifted onto individual authors, and usually on an unpaid basis. This article discusses the findings of an all gender online survey of Australian authors conducted in early 2025—the first stage of a larger project on Australian women writers and digital media. We examine the gendered and genre differences in authors’ use of digital media for their careers, including preferred platforms, time spent using digital media, the rationale for using it, the support available, and attitudes towards this work. In addition, we detail respondents’ reported experiences of online harassment and misogyny and how self-censorship becomes a way of negotiating such limitations. Our findings suggest that digital media is an unquestioned, if not necessarily effective, part of the field of literary production, and that its use is highly gendered. Moreover, the early promises of digital media as an expanded and liberated form of public sphere are shown to be hollow, instead subjecting authors to more unpaid work and limiting the types of public conversations in which they can participate.

#7 [paper] The Delegated Author: Generative AI and the Fragmentation of Authorship
Authors: Peter Ayolov
Venue: Knowledge Commons (Lakehead University)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17613/nw55t-gjt09
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence does not merely introduce another instrument into the history of writing; it separates activities that modern culture has traditionally compressed into the single figure of the author. Conceiving an idea, selecting material, researching, composing sentences, structuring an argument, revising language, producing visual representations, judging alternatives and accepting responsibility can now be distributed between human and computational agents. This article proposes the concept of the Delegated Author to describe this emerging condition. Rather than approaching generative AI through the increasingly inadequate opposition between "human-written" and "machine-generated" texts, it examines authorship as a divisible process in which human intention may precede machine execution and human judgement may subsequently select, reject or transform the machine's output. The argument develops from the twentieth-century displacement of the sovereign Author through Roland Barthes's Scriptor and Michel Foucault's author-function towards the contemporary Prompter: a figure capable not merely of recombining inherited language but of delegating part of the linguistic labour of recombination itself. The article tests this theoretical transition through a controlled journalistic experiment derived from an already published human cultural product. The original publication remains unchanged as a control, while a generative Model is permitted to restructure, clarify, compress and visually reinterpret the material. This asymmetrical design deliberately distinguishes machine generation from AI-assisted transformation: the Model receives a problem, research, conceptual direction and textual architecture that already exist rather than beginning from an empty page. The comparison therefore asks not simply whether AI can produce competent language, but what happens when linguistic execution becomes partially detached from intellectual initiation. Particular attention is given to the Paradox of Improvement: the possibility that optimisation may increase clarity, coherence and accessibility while simultaneously reducing stylistic irregularity, ambiguity and recognisable authorial voice. The article argues that generative AI fragments rather than abolishes authorship. The resulting division of creative labour redistributes composition and editing while leaving intention, critical selection, refusal and responsibility unequally distributed. In this emerging configuration, the decisive human contribution may no longer consist in physically producing every sentence. Authorship may increasingly reside in determining why a text should exist, what may be delegated, which machine transformations should survive, where optimisation must stop, and who ultimately answers for what is published.

Abstract:
Background Scientific retractions remain rare but have become increasingly common. We have previously incorporated retraction data into Scopus-based databases of top-cited (top 2%) authors to facilitate linkage of retractions with impact metrics at the individual author level. Here, we set out to explore whether gender disparities in the likelihood of having retractions exist, both among highly-cited authors and among all authors with ≥ 5 publications. Methods We conducted a descriptive cross-sectional bibliometric analysis of a Scopus-based authors database. We used NamSor to assign gender, retaining only results with a confidence > 85%. We examined the demographics of authors with and without retractions among highly cited authors (career-long impact: n = 217,097) and among all other authors (n = 10,361,367). We stratified by publication age, field, country income level, and publication volume, and calculated gender-specific retraction rates and the prevalence ratio (R) of women versus men to have at least one retraction. Multivariable logistic regression were fitted to estimate adjusted associations, reported as odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Gender could be classified for 8,267,888 authors. Among highly cited authors, 3.1% of men and 2.9% of women had at least one retraction; among all authors, the rate was 0.7% for both genders. Differences varied by field: women’s rates of retractions were at least one-third lower than men’s (R < 0.7) in Biology, Biomedical Research, and Psychology (R < 0.7), but higher (R > 1.3) in Economics, Engineering, and Information and Communication Technologies. Among highly cited authors, younger cohorts showed increasingly higher rates of retractions among men (4.2% men vs. 3.0% women in those starting to publish in 2002–2011; 8.7% men vs. 4.9% women in those starting post-2011). In multivariable analyses, differences were minimal, if any, for women versus men in having ≥ 1 retraction (among all authors OR: 0.96, 95% CI: 0.94–0.97; among highly cited authors OR: 0.96, 95% CI: 0.89–1.03). Conclusion Our analysis shows no major gender differences in retraction rates overall, but field-specific differences may exist. Field, career age, country, and publication volume are stronger correlates of retraction. Structural and contextual factors likely drive retraction patterns and warrant further investigation.

#9 [paper] The Right to Be Called an Author: Generative AI, Epistemic Responsibility, and the Duty to Defend
Authors: Victor Frimpong
Venue: Qeios
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.32388/i26t1l.2
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Generative AI has intensified scholarly publishing's need to distinguish formal accountability for a manuscript from the epistemic capacity to answer for it. Existing authorship guidance assigns responsibility to human authors regardless of AI involvement, but assigning responsibility does not establish that it can be meaningfully exercised. This paper addresses that gap by distinguishing nominal from substantive authorship responsibility and introducing the Duty to Defend (DtD): the obligation, internal to the status of scholarly authorship, to retain sufficient epistemic command of one's work to provide a reasonable account of its central claims, methods, evidence, and interpretations when legitimately challenged. Although the expectation that authors can defend their reasoning is already emerging in the literature, the normative question of why authorship itself carries such an obligation remains open. The paper derives this obligation from the reciprocal structure of scholarly credit rather than treating it as an additional compliance requirement and distinguishes it from an AI-detection standard: the relevant question is never whether AI was used, but whether the named author remains capable of standing behind the contribution attributed to them. A conceptual model then identifies three configurations — integrated, attenuated, and displaced authorship — describing how technological assistance can preserve or weaken the connection between credit and human intellectual agency. The paper translates this framework into a graded, trigger-based approach to editorial assurance, in which scrutiny escalates only as substantive scholarly concerns remain unresolved, and examines its own limits, including evidentiary difficulty, unequal capacity to demonstrate understanding, and the risk of converting a safeguard for authorship into a mechanism of suspicion.

Abstract:
In a 1976 interview with Brazilian-Ukrainian author Clarice Lispector, the interviewer asks why Lispector is describing one of her fictional characters as though she is real. Lispector pushes back, claiming “but the person does exist, I see the person, and she orders me around”. Building on Lispector’s interview and the long history of writers detailing the influence of characters and transcendental beings on their craft, this paper puts into question current understandings of collaborative (creative) writing. Abstract:
This survey synthesizes insights from environmental social sciences to recast the plastics crisis as a structural feature of growth-dependent economies instead of a problem solvable by consumer choice or incremental technologies. Rather than a within-field review of ecological economics, it maps adjacent literatures to specify what this field could study and how, clarifying researchable questions, suitable methods, and tractable indicators. The synthesis foregrounds connections between expansionary political-economic dynamics, globally uneven socio-ecological burdens across the plastics life cycle, and the power and knowledge relations that shape what is produced, measured, and governed. It calls for comparative, mixed-methods, multi-scalar work and for open, standardized data on plastics flows to strengthen causal inference and comparability. Shifting attention upstream—from end-of-pipe fixes to the transformation of provisioning systems—the paper charts lines of inquiry capable of aligning social metabolism with biophysical limits and human needs, providing a roadmap for ecological economics to organize and accelerate research beyond consumer or techno-managerial framings.

Abstract:
Abstract As plastic pollution intensifies, questions arise about whether the global plastics crisis (GPC) is being governed, and by whom. While an array of international institutions is often assumed to address this issue, the scholarship has yet to systematically examine who governs plastics and plastic pollution in practice. This article provides an empirical mapping of the GPC governance landscape, finding that multilevel public, civil society, and hybrid institutions incidentally facilitate governance through information dissemination, operational activities, and standard-setting. It identifies focal points that shape the global agenda and powerbrokers that disseminate it, with the United Nations Environment Programme and the Basel Convention emerging as influential. Meanwhile, private actor involvement is limited to multistakeholder partnerships that enable business and industry to feign environmental action while pursuing expansive business-as-usual practices. Abstract Plastic pollution has emerged as a critical global environmental challenge, exacerbating the impacts of climate change and biodiversity loss while posing substantial risks to human health and the economy. Despite a rapid increase in scientific efforts in recent years, our understanding of the characteristics, distribution and environmental consequences of plastic pollution remains incomplete, with many aspects still under debate. This knowledge gap hinders the development and implementation of effective management strategies. In this Review, we provide a comprehensive synthesis of plastic pollution from understanding to combatting, linking the environmental behavior of plastics with their ecological, health, and Earth-system risks. We further discuss mitigation and management strategies across the plastics life cycle. These strategies emphasize upstream prevention through redesign for minimizing production and facilitating reuse, supplemented by measures such as recycling and the implementation of biodegradable and compostable plastics, as well as exposure risk management. We also identify key challenges to address the interlinked triple crises of climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution associated with plastics. The priorities and solutions to end plastic pollution include promoting sustainable production and consumption, minimizing plastic waste and leakage, mitigating plastic pollution and damage, and safeguarding planetary health.

Abstract:

By attending to commonplace yet novel spatial dimensions of plastic circularity, this paper contributes to emerging scholarship at the intersection of political ecology and volumetric analyses of plastic pollution in Asia.

It includes the development of innovative devices, sustainable materials, mooring systems, AI-based condition monit…

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all following expected outcomes:

- Advance in the realisation of the Strategic Energy Technology (SET) Plan’s research and innovation priorities and targets for ocean energy;

- Energy producers and consumers benefit from increased performance of wave and tidal energy technologies with the focus on efficiency and flexibility, reduced cost, improved reliability and sustainability, operation and maintenance, robustness and security during all stages of the lifetime of an ocean energy farm from installation, operation and maintenance to decommissioning;

- Efficient and effective support to ocean energy research and innovation through alignment and cooperation among different actors, avoiding fragmentation of efforts providing effectively a significant developmental boost of wave and tidal energy technologies.

- Increased contribution of ocean energy to the energy system, with minimal impacts on health and the environment (notably biodiversity) and at the lowest possible cost.

Scope:

The action contributes to address the Strategic Energy Technology (SET) Plan’s research and innovation priorities[1] and targets[1] for ocean energy focussing on wave and tidal energy development. It will take into account the input defined in this context by the Implementation Working Group on ocean energy (IWG ocean), the European Technology and Innovation Platform on ocean energy (ETIP Ocean)[3] and the European Energy Research Alliance (EERA) joint programme on ocean energy[4].

The overarching objective is the development and demonstration of cost-effective wave and tidal energy systems that can survive in a harsh ocean or sea environment with minimal impacts on health and the environment and biodiversity. The challenge is open to proposals seeking to steer wave and tidal energy development for different type of resources in an effective way at a European level and to bring these technologies to the market. In this action the following can be considered:

- The development and demonstration in controlled environment of innovative wave energy devices.

- The development and demonstration in controlled environment of innovative next generation tidal energy devices

- The development and demonstration of new sustainable materials in ocean energy converters, moorings and foundations whilst ensuring structural integrity, durability and circularity can be considered.

- The development and demonstration of sustainable tailored mooring and connection of electrical or other power transmission systems (cable system, electrical equipment, ....) for wave and tidal energy devices. Advance combined mooring and electrical connectors or hydraulic power transmission to reduce component cost and number of connection operations, included in systems for sharing an anchor between devices in arrays. Develop novel systems for safe and quick connection/disconnection that do not require large vessels and/or diving teams.

- The instrumentation for condition monitoring and predictive maintenance of ocean energy devices and structures. Apply recent advances in condition and structural health monitoring from other sectors to ocean energy. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in ocean energy technology development.

- Advanced manufacturing of ocean energy devices and structures and auxiliary equipment considering reduced energy, manufacturing costs and materials consumption, high production throughput and optimization of logistics.

- Development of technologies and solutions for the installation, maintenance and decommissioning of wave and tidal energy devices.

The validation and demonstration of new ocean energy technologies should be done in a controlled environment meaning that this is done under monitored and reproducible conditions, using for instance, test rigs and test tanks, semi-enclosed basins, or dedicated real-sea demonstration sites with instrumented monitoring infrastructure.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of robust evidence, governance frameworks, and detection/monitoring capabilities for Solar Radiation Modification (SRM) activities, creating uncertainties regarding risks, effectiveness, and potential for unilateral deployment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Transdisciplinary research leveraging Earth observation (space-borne, ground-based, in-situ data), advanced aerosol and cloud modelling (SAI, MCB, CCT/MCT), and civil society engagement to enhance detection, monitoring, and attribution capabilities without conducting SRM field experiments.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European Union policy and international governance contexts (IPCC, CBD), focusing on global SRM governance, atmospheric chemistry, dynamics, and ecosystem impacts.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Projects are to contribute to all of the following outcomes:

European Union’s, Member States’ and Associated Countries’ policy making is supported with robust evidence and their visibility in deliberations of SRM strengthened. Evidence and new knowledge related to the points below supports the European Union’s, Member States and Associated Countries’ contributions to relevant international review and assessment processes of SRM, notably by the IPCC:

- Civil society, researchers, public authorities as well as policy and decision makers have access to a solid scientific-technological knowledge foundation concerning the detection, attribution and deterrence of SRM activities as a contribution to an emerging multilateral governance system spanning both SRM-related research and technological development.

- The development of a global SRM governance framework is supported through advanced knowledge, generated by desk research, modelling, earth observation, the documentation of development pathways of various SRM technologies and their potential impacts on the earth system and its parts (oceans, large-scale atmospheric circulation, regional climate such as monsoons as well as changes in precipitation), as well as on societies (impact on decarbonisation pathways, livelihood security, nature dependent value chains etc.) and ecosystems. These are considered substantial gaps by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and Group of Chief Scientific Advisors.

- Aerosol and cloud modelling capabilities for global and regional models concerning Stratospheric Aerosol Injection (SAI), Marine Cloud Brightening (MCB) and Cirrus Cloud Thinning (CCT)/Mixed Phase Cloud Thinning (MCT) and their effects on atmospheric chemistry and dynamics are enhanced as a solid scientific-technological base for a detection and deterrence system.

- Policy makers and public authorities have access to robust space-borne, ground-based, air-borne and in-situ EO data (e.g. Copernicus) based on any relevant physical, chemical or social, societal data for the purpose of detection, assessment and attribution for outdoor SRM-development activities. Knowledge about SRM-induced changes to be expected in ecosystems, like shifted precipitation patterns and altered light quality, associated marine and terrestrial net primary production, and on sensitive habitats is enhanced. The knowledge generated shall inform, in the context of SRM technology governance, the detection, monitoring and attribution policy, in the sense of an ecological alert system focused on protecting global biodiversity.

Scope:

Support provided under this topic must not be used to advocate, promote, or support the development of SRM. The conduct of SRM field experiments as well as the conduct of technical and operational SRM research is out of the scope.

The activity aims at enhancing the capabilities to detect, monitor and attribute SRM-related research, innovation or deployment activities. The activity shall be conducted in line with the precautionary approach as outlined by the European Group on Ethics[1], in accordance with the conclusion of SAPEA reports, the IPCC reviews, and build on the decisions of relevant international bodies, mainly CBD and support the ambitions of the Ocean Pact.

evidence.text: #1 [paper] Reply on RC2 Authors: Peihao Yang, Guodong Ye Year: 2026 Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-262-cc1 Still open/current: yes Abstract: Abstract. A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. After training on multiple CMIP6 ensemble members, the constructed models are evaluated for their predictive capacity regarding MHW in the SCS. The results also show that these machine learning-based methods can perform comparably to the existing dynamic models in terms of prediction performance, and in some cases even outperform the latter. Furthermore, by incorporating machine learning interpretability techniques, the key physical processes can also be elucidated from these predictions. That is to say, the new method is not a traditional "black box", but rather an effective tool that can possess certain physical transparency and scientific interpretability.

#3 [paper] Beyond a Better Score: Long-Horizon Agentic ML Development and Evaluation Protocol for Physics Time Series
Authors: Yajun Ma, Lucas Venetoulias, Akbota Assan, A. Li
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23071121
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Physics time-series data are central to fundamental discoveries involving dark matter, neutrinos, and gravitational waves. Machine learning has shown strong potential to recover weak scientific signals buried in complex noise. Recent LLM-agent systems further automate ML development, but existing approaches are often driven primarily by one or a few numerical scores. In pursuit of a better score, agents may exploit shortcuts, trigger mode collapse, or game the evaluation procedure, producing models that achieve high scores but are scientifically invalid. We introduce SIDERIUS, an LLM agent system designed to move beyond a better score toward scientifically valid, long-horizon ML development. SIDERIUS combines contract-defined composable capabilities for flexible orchestration and human-in-the-loop, a multi-layer scientific evaluation protocol that distinguishes valid models from unhealthy or gaming models, and resource-aware exploration for computationally expensive scientific ML. In our TIDMAD benchmark, SIDERIUS with a GPT-based orchestrator achieves the highest Valid-model proposal rate of 63.8% and the best valid denoising score of 2.744, compared with 1.6% and −0.647, respectively, for the same GPT model using the general-purpose Codex coding agent. We further benchmark SIDERIUS on three additional physics time-series datasets, demonstrating its reuse and performance across different tasks. Together, these results suggest that progress in agentic scientific ML should be measured beyond a better score, by how an agent explores and by whether the models it produces can be trusted as science.

#4 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need to synthesize cross-layer integration patterns between observation networks, computational methods, uncertainty-aware decision-support, and standards-based middleware for Flood Early Warning Systems (FEWSs).
Method (Mycelium's reading): Survey and synthesis of IoT-based sensing, communication protocols, data pre-processing, machine learning, data assimilation, and operational platforms, including a case study of a FIWARE/NGSI-LD hydrometeorological monitoring deployment.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): IoT-based sensing and monitoring infrastructures for flood early warning.
Abstract:
Flood Early Warning Systems (FEWSs) increasingly combine heterogeneous observation streams, computational models, and interoperable information infrastructures. This survey reviews how Internet of Things (IoT)-based sensing, communication protocols, data pre-processing, machine learning, data assimilation, and operational platforms contribute to flood monitoring and early warning. Rather than presenting a new forecasting model or claiming end-to-end experimental validation, the paper synthesizes cross-layer integration patterns between observation networks, computational methods, uncertainty-aware decision-support, and standards-based middleware. Particular attention is given to the interface between in situ IoT observations and data-driven or physics-informed modelling approaches, including data assimilation and hyper-local flood simulation. A FIWARE/NGSI-LD hydrometeorological monitoring deployment is included as an infrastructure and interoperability case study, demonstrating the continuous collection and ingestion of sensor observations into the platform, semantic normalization, temporal persistence, and standards-based access to monitoring data.

#7 [paper] How decision-makers trust and use machine learning predictions for managing cold-stunning risks
Authors: Miranda C. White, Christopher D. Wirz, Mariana Goodall Cains, Elisa R. Flores, Julie L. Demuth, Philippe E. Tissot
Venue: Frontiers in Communication
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomm.2026.1816041
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
As extreme weather events increase in frequency and magnitude, science-informed tools are increasingly needed to support effective systems-level management, particularly for high-impact, high-risk, multi-organizational hazards. Cold-stunning events (or periods when water temperatures drop to threatening levels for wildlife) pose substantial risks to coastal systems in Texas. In response, the Texas Marine Coldwater Response Collaborative (TCRC) was established to coordinate cold-stunning response across organizations with diverse priorities and interests. A machine learning (ML) water temperature prediction model has been used to guide the cold-stunning advisory process; however, little is known about how users within the TCRC interpret and act on this information in complex, time-sensitive decision environments. This study examined how different users assess, perceive, trust, and use existing ML-based predictive information to discuss the management of evolving cold-stunning event risks. Structured interviews, which incorporated an interactive activity presenting various forms of predictive information at several stages before and during a simulated cold-stunning event, were conducted with 15 TCRC members, encompassing natural resource managers, coastal economic operators, and weather forecasters. Iterative thematic analysis revealed that users prioritized different predictive signals and information sources according to their operational responsibilities, informational needs, and the evolving decision context. How and when users placed trust in the predictive information also varied across users and decision contexts, shaped by familiarity with the predictive tools, relationships with model developers, consistency with other information sources, and the stakes associated with particular decisions. Overall, these findings highlight the importance of engaging stakeholders throughout the development of predictive tools to account for diverse decision contexts and informational needs. A user-centered, iterative development process can help ensure that predictive tools are not only scientifically robust, but also trusted and applicable within complex, real-world systems-level management.

#8 [paper] Forward ensemble machine learning for grouped source term prediction in nuclear emergency response
Authors: Osamong Gideon Akou, Xuan Wang, Shuhuan Liu, Xinwei Liu, Boyang Liu, Ailing Zhang
Venue: Annals of Nuclear Energy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anucene.2026.112842
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Conventional high-fidelity simulation approaches are computationally expensive and unsuitable for near-real-time decision-making during nuclear emergency response.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A machine learning surrogate framework using three ensemble models (LightGBM, Stacking, and CatBoost) trained on 3000 RASCAL-generated simulation samples, supplemented by SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for feature importance analysis.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A hypothetical containment-bypass scenario for the CAP1400 reactor involving noble gases, iodine, and particulates.
Abstract:
Major nuclear accidents reveal critical limitations in rapid source term prediction during emergency response. Conventional high-fidelity simulation approaches are computationally expensive and unsuitable for near-real-time decision-making. This study develops a machine learning surrogate framework to predict grouped radionuclide source terms-noble gases, iodine, and particulates-under a hypothetical containment-bypass scenario for the CAP1400 reactor. Using 3000 RASCAL-generated simulation samples for training and testing, three ensemble models were evaluated: LightGBM, Stacking, and CatBoost. LightGBM achieved the best overall performance on unseen test data (R 2 = 0.714) with near-instantaneous inference (∼ 0.001 s). Noble gases showed the highest predictive accuracy (test R 2 = 0.762), whereas particulates remained the most challenging target (R 2 = 0.58–0.74). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis identified mass number, core uncovered time and particulate concentration as dominant predictive features. The results demonstrate the potential of machine learning surrogate models to provide rapid and reliable source term estimates for near-real-time nuclear emergency response.

#9 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

#10 [paper] Application of Machine Learning Algorithms for Forecasting Sea Surface Temperature at Hon Dau Station
Authors: Do Thi Thu Ha, Nguyen Quoc Trinh, Nguyen The Duc, Nguyen Van Tung, Nguyen Thieu Hoa
Venue: VNU Journal of Science Earth and Environmental Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.25073/2588-1094/vnuees.5463
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Forecasting Sea Surface Temperature (SST) at Hon Dau station for climate studies, tropical cyclone prediction, and marine resource management.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Time series decomposition followed by the application of ARIMAX, SARIMAX, Prophet, and LSTM models for forecasting, and a linear regression model with Fourier harmonics for long-term projection.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): SST observations at Hon Dau station from 2000–2022.
Abstract:
Sea Surface Temperature (SST) plays a crucial role in climate studies, tropical cyclone prediction, and marine resource management. This study analyzes SST observations at Hon Dau station from 2000–2022 and applies ARIMAX, SARIMAX, Prophet, and LSTM models for SST forecasting. Time series decomposition was conducted to separate trend, seasonal, and residual components to guide model selection. Results indicate that ARIMAX, SARIMAX, and Prophet achieved high accuracy with mean absolute errors (MAE) of 0.82–0.92 °C, while LSTM performed less effectively due to data limitations. For long-term projection, a linear regression model with Fourier harmonics suggests an increase of approximately +1.7 °C in mean annual SST by 2100 relative to 2021, consistent with moderate climate scenarios. These findings highlight the potential of machine learning methods for short-term SST forecasting and emphasize the need for integrating multi-source data with physics-informed deep learning models to improve the reliability of climate and marine applications.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): East China Sea; test set and hindcasts of the 2022 marine heatwave event.
Abstract:
Abstract. Accurate sea surface temperature (SST) prediction in the East China Sea remains challenging because of its highly dynamic oceanic and atmospheric conditions, yet it is essential for regional fisheries management and marine hazard early warning. Here, we propose SwinTrans-ConvLSTM, a spatiotemporal deep-learning framework tailored for SST forecasting in the East China Sea. The model couples the global representation capability of the Swin Transformer with the local temporal-evolution modeling strength of ConvLSTM, incorporates air–sea temperature contrast and vector wind-field features, and is optimized using a curriculum-learning strategy constrained by a physics-informed gradient loss. Experiments show that SwinTrans-ConvLSTM achieves a mean absolute error of only 0.071 °C and a root mean square error of 0.156 °C on the test set, reducing prediction errors by approximately 30 % relative to state-of-the-art baselines. Crucially, hindcasts of the extreme 2022 marine heatwave event further demonstrate that the model can reproduce heatwave occurrence frequency and duration while substantially mitigating the systematic underestimation of extreme SST peaks inherent in purely data-driven models. These results highlight the critical role of thermodynamic-variable reconstruction and training-strategy optimization in improving the robustness of marine extreme-event prediction, and provide a promising technical pathway for high-resolution operational forecasting under complex ocean conditions.

Abstract:
Bleaching of cultured Pyropia (laver) causes losses in Korean seaweed farming. We present a system that forecasts bleaching seven days ahead for farm clusters. OceanTensorCube aligns 32 channels from public marine, meteorological, ocean-model and satellite sources on a 30 m grid, and ST-MMT, a 9.2-million-parameter spatiotemporal transformer with hub-style multi-head cross-attention between variable groups, maps a 14-day input window to a seven-day-ahead bleaching probability. On the validation set, a six-seed ensemble detects every reported positive at a false-alarm rate of at most 3.5%, an upper bound because the report-based labels are positive-unlabeled. A same-date control on separately trained models indicates that the architecture discriminates between clusters when the calendar is held fixed. We also report the system's weaknesses: skill falls steeply as the quarterly nutrient survey ages (ROC-AUC 0.94 at 30 days, 0.53 at 129 days), and a single LSTM on cluster-average series outperforms a single ST-MMT, with only the ensemble leading at the operating point. We describe the labeling procedure, the evaluation protocol and the operational gate that withholds forecasts when inputs are stale. The forecasting service is operated at https://oceantensor.ai.kr.

#20 [paper] Storm surge dynamics in the northern Adriatic Sea: comparing AI emulators with high-resolution numerical simulations
Authors: Rodrigo Campos-Caba, Paula Camus, Andrea Mazzino, Michalis Vousdoukas, Massimo Tondello, Iván Federico, Salvatore Causio, Lorenzo Mentaschi
Venue: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
Year: 2026

Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. Accurate storm surge forecasting is vital for protecting coastal regions, particularly in the northern Adriatic Sea where sea-level rise and increasingly severe storm events pose growing risks. Machine Learning (ML) approaches offer compelling speed and flexibility, yet their ability to emulate high-resolution dynamic models, especially for extreme surge events, has not been sufficiently assessed across methods and loss functions. In this study, a range of ML emulators, from Multivariate Linear Regression (MLR) to Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, is benchmarked against a high-resolution hydrodynamic model optimized for extreme surge representation. We also evaluate the impact of training loss functions, comparing the conventional Mean Squared Error (MSE) with the corrected Mean Absolute Deviation squared (MADc²), designed to better capture surge peaks. Results show that even simple models like MLR, when trained with MADc², achieve performance comparable to advanced neural networks while remaining orders of magnitude faster. These findings demonstrate that with appropriate training strategies, data-driven emulators can rival physics-based models in reproducing extremes. The MLR-MADc² configuration emerges as a practical balance between computational efficiency and accuracy, underscoring the potential of ML emulators for coastal forecasting and risk assessment.

Proposals are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes, in full alignment with the OceanEye initiative:

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.
