Problem (Mycelium's reading): The rise of far-right antidemocratic actors in consolidated democracies, specifically the challenge of defending democracy against actors who use lawful, often invisible tactics, and the normative dilemma of choosing between repressive measures and other strategies.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A comparative normative political theory approach that defines and analyzes three ideal types of democratic self-defence: militant (restrictive), tolerant (liberal-procedural), and social (addressing structural injustices). The method involves providing conceptual definitions, analyzing normative j…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical analysis grounded in contemporary political contexts, with specific reference to the case of the Greek neo-fascist party Golden Dawn and its legal and political trajectory, as well as broader European and global contexts of democratic backsliding.
Abstract:
Associate Professor, Department of Government The rise of far-right antidemocratic actors in many consolidated democracies today poses a unique challenge. Political parties and leaders who enjoy popular support risk tearing apart the democratic fabric through tactics that appear lawful and are often invisible. What options do democracies have to defend themselves against such actors? Democratic self-defence, i.e. actions aimed at preventing, containing, resisting, or repairing democratic backsliding caused by domestic antidemocratic forces, can take many forms: from restrictions on candidacy rights to hate speech laws, and from street protests to welfare reforms. Political parties may exclude antidemocratic parties from coalitions, or they may choose to include them while seeking to moderate their positions. Alternatively, they may focus on expanding social protections in order to address the structural injustices that antidemocratic actors exploit. Such choices raise difficult normative questions. This book offers conceptual tools for making these choices intelligible and brings to light the principles that animate them. Political theorists addressing these issues have paid a great deal of attention to justifying repressive measures. Militant democracy, which includes the pre-emptive restriction of political and civil rights, has received so much attention in the past decade that one would be forgiven for thinking there is no alternative. This book is partly a reaction to this one-sided engagement with repressive measures. It examines less-known approaches to democratic self-defence that prioritise toleration and social integration respectively, strategies that are used as much, if not more, than militant restrictions. The three rationales of democratic self-defence that emerge –militant, tolerant, and social– are presented as ideal types. Unlike much theorising on democratic self-defence, which is prescriptive and advances a single normative framework, this book adopts a deliberately comparative approach that examines the strengths and weaknesses of each ideal type, as well as their connections and contrasts. It proposes conceptual definitions and analyses the normative justifications underpinning each type. The aim is to clarify the principles embodied in practices of democratic self-defence, enabling actors to better understand the normative commitments behind their choices and to make decisions that are ethically justified, democratically legitimate, and consistent with the values they seek to defend. The book also seeks to move the discussion beyond legal instruments and state responses by bringing broader societal and public actors into view. At the same time, it remains focused on agency: on both defenders of democracy and those who seek to undermine it. In doing so, it resists the tendency to portray democracy as a quasi-natural system whose resilience must simply be enhanced. Unlike many studies framed around the concept of democratic resilience, this book foregrounds human agency and the diverse actors who actively defend democracy across multiple spheres. Decisions about whether and how to confront antidemocratic actors do not fall exclusively on any single category of actor. They concern government authorities, courts, state agencies, municipal leaders, business actors, journalists, academics, and others. Democratic self-defence should therefore be understood as a form of agency distributed across a variety of actors. This book grew out of an article I co-authored in 2017 with my dear colleague Ludvig Norman, ‘Three Models of Democratic Self-defence: Militant Democracy and Its Alternatives’ published the year after in Political Studies. In that article, Ludvig and I challenged the dominance of militant democracy in debates on democratic self-defence by exploring two alternative perspectives: a tolerant approach (which we then called liberal-procedural) and a social approach, which we ultimately defended. Abstract:
This dataset was created as part of the project Lettercraft and Epistolary Performance in Medieval Europe, a NWO-Vidi funded project based in the Department of Languages, Literature, and Culture at Utrecht University. The database came about in collaboration with Utrecht University’s Centre for Digital Humanities, who developed the online infrastructure, and with the help of students from Utrecht University Research Master’s Programme in Ancient, Medieval & Renaissance Studies, who joined the project as research apprentices. For more information about the project, visit the Lettercraft website. Here you can also browse the latest version of the data. About the project How did early medieval societies use the letter and who were among its users? The Lettercraft-project approaches the early medieval letter as a performative medium, whose communicative potential was defined principally by non-textual features: its materiality, its ability to be publicly read out and talked over, and its potential quickly to reach wide and diverse audiences. Literacy or social status were not required to participate in what the project calls lettercraft, i.e. the various performative actions (e.g. listening, speaking, negotiating, gossiping) that along with writing and reading made up epistolary communication. The project aims to show, moreover, that due to its public nature and social range, the letter was an essential tool of community-building and conflict-resolution in medieval society. #8 [paper] Fair Access to Urban Water: Designing Population‐Sensitive Connection Fees Through a Welfare‐Informed Ability‐to‐Pay Approach
Authors: Seyedhossein Sajadifar, Masoud Alavian Sadr, Shahram Heydarian Samani, Ali Mazyaki, Alireza Pourebrahim
Venue: World Water Policy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1002/wwp2.70115
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
ABSTRACT Setting urban water connection fees is a complex policy problem: Fees must balance affordability, equity, and adequate cost recovery. This study develops a two‐stage framework for setting urban water connection charges in Iran. A bottom‐up engineering model first establishes the full long‐run economic cost of a new connection; a distributive stage then allocates a target provincial average across six city population classes. The distributive stage is stated as a constrained social welfare program and solved exactly; under logarithmic utility, it yields corner solutions rather than a smooth gradient because the fee is a small share of household resources. The recommended schedule is therefore described as what it is: a proportional ability‐to‐pay allocation indexed to city size, whose formal relation to the welfare program is stated explicitly. Revenue neutrality is imposed on a connection‐weighted basis so that the utility collects the intended total rather than an unweighted average of six class fees. Using Household Expenditure and Income Survey data for all 31 provincial capitals, we test rather than assume the population proxy and find an income elasticity of about 0.13 with respect to city size: statistically significant, but explaining a minority of cross‐city variation. Equity claims are correspondingly framed at the intercity level. Applied to a representative province, the schedule is progressive with respect to ability to pay, holds first‐year revenue exactly at the target, and can be adjusted over time using the Consumer Price Index. The approach transfers to other water‐scarce settings under cost‐recovery pressure.

Abstract:
The median published figure in the Answering Service Price Index is 68.95 USD across 23 sources' own pages (range 5 to 399 USD), read 26 September 2026. Coverage. 23 of the 70 named sources read in full publish a figure; 47 publish none, read 26 September 2026. Methodology. Every row is a verbatim sentence read from the named source's own page through the estate's fetch service on the date shown, hash-pinned to the stored read (the sha of the page's visible text; the raw page is mirrored to R2). 23 of the 70 named sources that could be read published a usable figure; 47 published none and are recorded as not published, never filled in; 3 could not be read (blocked, dead or unreachable) and count nowhere. The headline figures (median, minimum, maximum, quartiles) are over ONE figure per source in USD (a source's median where its page yielded several accepted sentences), so N counts sources, never sentences; 343 candidate sentence(s) were refused by a reviewer with the reason recorded. Derivation as chartered: one row per provider per plan: the base fee, the METER (per minute, per call, per unique caller, per conversation, per agent hour, flat, per seat), the included allowance, the overage rate, the setup fee and whether a contract is required. Across them, the figures nobody publishes: the median and spread of the entry price at each meter; the share of providers publishing a rate AT ALL against the share quoting only, which the harvest already puts near half; the EFFECTIVE cost per answered call at 50, 200 and 500 calls a month, which is the only way plans on five different meters can be compared and which no provider will ever compute because it is the comparison they lose; the AI-priced tier against the human-staffed tier for the same call volume; and the bilingual surcharge, which some providers charge, some bundle and most do not mention. Repriced-since the previous read. One figure per named source, each row dated and pinned to the SHA-256 of the page text it was read from. Computed 2026-09-26. Abstract:
In grant applications, oral presentations can be an integral part of the evaluation process. Funding pitches are a specific form of pitch presentations delivered during competitive review procedures to complement a written proposal. Their goal is to convince reviewers of both your project's strength and excellence as well as your suitability as a researcher. #12 [paper] Valuing education for limited-resource audiences using a willingness to accept experiment
Authors: Russell Tronstad, Ibrahima Sall
Venue: PLoS ONE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0348858
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Education grants often target audiences that have limited-resources relative to their peers, such as beginning farmers, who arguably have the most to gain from more education. Yet, charging even modest fees to these participants is discouraged, creating a challenge for funding entities that desire to have a dollar value for the education provided. To measure this value, we conducted an experiment using a willingness-to-accept (WTA) approach. Participants chose a minimum cash payout from seven different options to voluntarily leave a training session before receiving any instruction or educational materials. The design is constructed so that each option has an equal expected payout. Cash payouts were not advertised or known to any participants before the training. Results show that average WTA values are $277.44 per training (about 4 hours of instruction), which is 2.11 to 4.74 times more than participants' self-reported willingness to pay (WTP), depending on how travel costs and time of participants are valued. WTP consistently and significantly explains much of the variation in WTA. In sharp contrast, detailed travel cost estimates in various forms were consistently insignificant for explaining WTA values. Beginning farmers and ranchers, our targeted limited-resource audience, reported WTA and WTP values that were $81.18 and $22.73 more per training, respectively, than those of non-beginning farmers.

Of these, 9 were associated with >80% and only 2 had ipsilateral strokes. The rates of freedom from >50% and >80% restenosis at 12, 24, and 36 months were 94%, 90%, and 89% and 97%, 96%, and 95%, respectively. The total number of duplex examinations was 938. Based on the Society for Vascular Surgery guideline recommendation that most asymptomatic (>70% to 80%) restenosis should be treated medically and do not need re-intervention, this surveillance would have detected only 2 patients associated with >80% restenosis. # Reviewing a project

1. `projects_get` for goals, confirmed state, blockers, milestones,
   developments in effect and members. Note when the state was last confirmed;
   past thirty days, say it may be out of date.
2. `projects_feed` for the current slate, in rank order, with when each item
   entered. "New this week" means it entered the slate this week.

#2 [paper] Gender analysis of the authors of the German-language pharmacy journal Pharmakon from 1972 to 2021
Authors: Mira Ober, Roland Seifert
Venue: Scientometrics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-026-05766-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Women tend to be underrepresented in almost all scientific fields in Germany. This study analyses publications of scientists in a German pharmaceutical non-peer-reviewed journal over a period of 50 years (1972–2021). The journal Pharmakon (previously named Pharmazie in unserer Zeit) is the member journal of the German Pharmaceutical Society (DPhG). We performed a gender analysis of the journal and analysed 1577 articles by 2509 authors. Overall, the percentage of women is 26%. This has changed significantly over time from 5% in the early years to almost 50% in 2020 (Chi 2 -test p = 0.00004). For many years, there were no women as first authors at all, but in 2020, for the first time, there were more female than male first authors. However, at the highest academic rank of professor, female authors are still much less abundant than men. The journal has also changed over the years. The number of authors per article has increased and more articles have been published since the turn of the millennium. Over the years, more non-pharmacists have also published, and interdisciplinary exchange seems to be becoming increasingly important. This study illustrates, for the field of German pharmacy, substantial gender inequalities. These inequalities are mirrored in the gender analysis of authors publishing in Pharmakon . Our study also shows that over the past decades, gender inequalities have become smaller, but they still exist, particularly at the highest-ranking level, i.e. professors. Our study will help politicians, universities and pharmacy associations to implement effective measures for gender equality.

#4 [paper] If You Meet an Author on the Road
Authors: Peter Ayolov
Venue: Knowledge Commons (Lakehead University)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17613/4cesm-mcr45
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The twentieth century repeatedly attempted to dethrone the Author without succeeding in eliminating the cultural desire for authorship. Roland Barthes displaced the writer as the sovereign origin of textual meaning, while Michel Foucault demonstrated that the author persisted as a classificatory, institutional and juridical function even after the metaphysics of individual creation had been destabilised. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence transforms this theoretical dispute into a material problem. Large language models can now perform operations previously treated as visible evidence of authorship: generating sentences, restructuring arguments, imitating genres, proposing metaphors, editing style, producing titles and transforming existing texts. Yet linguistic production does not necessarily establish authorial sovereignty. This article uses the deliberately provocative injunction If You Meet an Author on the Road, Kill Him as a metaphor for the repeated dismantling of every figure elevated into the final source of textual authority. The formulation adapts the Zen logic of destroying attachment to the master rather than advocating the destruction of the person: what must be "killed" is the intellectual idol of the sovereign Author. From this perspective, Barthes's Scriptor, Foucault's author-function, the contemporary Prompter and the generative Model represent successive attempts to relocate rather than finally resolve the problem of textual agency. The article argues that generative AI exposes a fragmentation that had always existed inside the apparently unified act of writing. Intention, research, memory, linguistic formulation, recombination, editing, selection, publication, interpretation and responsibility need not belong to a single agent, and contemporary human–AI production makes their separation increasingly visible. The resulting condition is described as authorship without a centre: a communicative work can emerge through interactions among human intention, inherited language, computational prediction, machine generation, editorial judgement, institutional framing and reader interpretation without any single participant containing the complete causal or semantic origin of the finished text. This does not mean that writers, intentions or responsibility disappear. On the contrary, the dissolution of sovereign authorship makes responsibility more important because distributed production cannot become an excuse for unaccountable publication. The article therefore distinguishes the death of the Author from the disappearance of the human writer and the fragmentation of authorship from the abolition of accountability. Its central claim is that the death of the Author should not be understood as a completed historical event but as a recurring critical operation. Whenever textual culture installs a new sovereign centre—the genius, the Scriptor, the Prompter, the algorithm or the Model—the same theoretical question returns: whether the production of language grants authority over its meaning. In the age of generative AI, the task is therefore not to discover who has inherited the Author's throne, but to question why the text requires a throne at all.

#5 [paper] Author profiles in Web of Science, Scopus, Dimensions, ORCID, ResearchGate, and Google Scholar: a case report.
Authors: Powell, Kimberly R
Venue: Journal of the Medical Library Association : JMLA
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42889833/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aimed to benchmark the availability and accuracy of author profiles for 45 faculty members within the Auburn University College of Nursing. Profile availability in the database platforms Web of Science, Scopus, and Dimensions were analyzed alongside the author-driven platforms ORCID, ResearchGate, and Google Scholar to set an understanding for the potential efforts needed for profile curation, publication tracking, and research impact assessments moving forward. CASE PRESENTATION: Each of the six platforms were manually searched for faculty and name variations alongside both current and past institutional affiliations. All identified profiles were collected. Associated publication counts were recorded and database results were screened for accurate author identification. Among the author-driven platforms, ORCID had the highest adoption rate, with 64% of faculty, while ResearchGate and Google Scholar trailed with 38% and 16% faculty adoption, respectively. Web of Science offered profiles for 82% of faculty; Scopus offered profiles for 80% of faculty, and Dimensions only 53%. However, 53% of the associated publications were misattributed in Web of Science profiles compared to just 1% misattribution in Scopus and none in Dimensions. CONCLUSIONS: Among our faculty, Scopus offered the most efficient author profile platform, balancing profile availability, minimizing misattribution, and including avenues for early identification of new authors. While largely in line with previous study findings, this effort provided important contextual understandings of profile data availability which can be used to inform research impact assessments and library services supporting author profiles for highlighting scholarly influence.

#6 [paper] Another Double Shift? Australian Authors, Digital Media and Gendered Promotional Labor
Authors: Anthea Taylor, Margaret Henderson
Venue: Publishing Research Quarterly
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12109-026-10093-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract With falling revenues from book sales, industry-wide and publishing house restructurings, declining marketing budgets, and the affordances of digital media, the promotional labor associated with books is increasingly being shifted onto individual authors, and usually on an unpaid basis. This article discusses the findings of an all gender online survey of Australian authors conducted in early 2025—the first stage of a larger project on Australian women writers and digital media. We examine the gendered and genre differences in authors’ use of digital media for their careers, including preferred platforms, time spent using digital media, the rationale for using it, the support available, and attitudes towards this work. In addition, we detail respondents’ reported experiences of online harassment and misogyny and how self-censorship becomes a way of negotiating such limitations. Our findings suggest that digital media is an unquestioned, if not necessarily effective, part of the field of literary production, and that its use is highly gendered. Moreover, the early promises of digital media as an expanded and liberated form of public sphere are shown to be hollow, instead subjecting authors to more unpaid work and limiting the types of public conversations in which they can participate.

#7 [paper] The Delegated Author: Generative AI and the Fragmentation of Authorship
Authors: Peter Ayolov
Venue: Knowledge Commons (Lakehead University)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17613/nw55t-gjt09
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence does not merely introduce another instrument into the history of writing; it separates activities that modern culture has traditionally compressed into the single figure of the author. Conceiving an idea, selecting material, researching, composing sentences, structuring an argument, revising language, producing visual representations, judging alternatives and accepting responsibility can now be distributed between human and computational agents. This article proposes the concept of the Delegated Author to describe this emerging condition. Rather than approaching generative AI through the increasingly inadequate opposition between "human-written" and "machine-generated" texts, it examines authorship as a divisible process in which human intention may precede machine execution and human judgement may subsequently select, reject or transform the machine's output. The argument develops from the twentieth-century displacement of the sovereign Author through Roland Barthes's Scriptor and Michel Foucault's author-function towards the contemporary Prompter: a figure capable not merely of recombining inherited language but of delegating part of the linguistic labour of recombination itself. The article tests this theoretical transition through a controlled journalistic experiment derived from an already published human cultural product. The original publication remains unchanged as a control, while a generative Model is permitted to restructure, clarify, compress and visually reinterpret the material. This asymmetrical design deliberately distinguishes machine generation from AI-assisted transformation: the Model receives a problem, research, conceptual direction and textual architecture that already exist rather than beginning from an empty page. The comparison therefore asks not simply whether AI can produce competent language, but what happens when linguistic execution becomes partially detached from intellectual initiation. Particular attention is given to the Paradox of Improvement: the possibility that optimisation may increase clarity, coherence and accessibility while simultaneously reducing stylistic irregularity, ambiguity and recognisable authorial voice. The article argues that generative AI fragments rather than abolishes authorship. The resulting division of creative labour redistributes composition and editing while leaving intention, critical selection, refusal and responsibility unequally distributed. In this emerging configuration, the decisive human contribution may no longer consist in physically producing every sentence. Authorship may increasingly reside in determining why a text should exist, what may be delegated, which machine transformations should survive, where optimisation must stop, and who ultimately answers for what is published.

#8 [paper] Gender imbalances of retraction prevalence among highly cited authors and among all authors
Authors: Stefania Boccia, Antonio Cristiano, Angelo Maria Pezzullo, Jeroen Baas, Guillaume Roberge, John P. A. Ioannidis
Venue: Research Integrity and Peer Review
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1186/s41073-026-00254-7
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background Scientific retractions remain rare but have become increasingly common. We have previously incorporated retraction data into Scopus-based databases of top-cited (top 2%) authors to facilitate linkage of retractions with impact metrics at the individual author level. Here, we set out to explore whether gender disparities in the likelihood of having retractions exist, both among highly-cited authors and among all authors with ≥ 5 publications. Methods We conducted a descriptive cross-sectional bibliometric analysis of a Scopus-based authors database. We used NamSor to assign gender, retaining only results with a confidence > 85%. We examined the demographics of authors with and without retractions among highly cited authors (career-long impact: n = 217,097) and among all other authors (n = 10,361,367). We stratified by publication age, field, country income level, and publication volume, and calculated gender-specific retraction rates and the prevalence ratio (R) of women versus men to have at least one retraction. Multivariable logistic regression were fitted to estimate adjusted associations, reported as odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Gender could be classified for 8,267,888 authors. Among highly cited authors, 3.1% of men and 2.9% of women had at least one retraction; among all authors, the rate was 0.7% for both genders. Differences varied by field: women’s rates of retractions were at least one-third lower than men’s (R < 0.7) in Biology, Biomedical Research, and Psychology (R < 0.7), but higher (R > 1.3) in Economics, Engineering, and Information and Communication Technologies. Among highly cited authors, younger cohorts showed increasingly higher rates of retractions among men (4.2% men vs. 3.0% women in those starting to publish in 2002–2011; 8.7% men vs. 4.9% women in those starting post-2011). In multivariable analyses, differences were minimal, if any, for women versus men in having ≥ 1 retraction (among all authors OR: 0.96, 95% CI: 0.94–0.97; among highly cited authors OR: 0.96, 95% CI: 0.89–1.03). By contrast, retractions were strongly associated with publication volume (per +1 unit log10 papers: OR: 8.69, 95% CI: 8.54–8.85; OR: 11.36, 95% CI: 10.40–12.40), non-high-income countries (OR: 4.17, 95% CI: 4.10–4.24; OR: 2.56, 95% CI: 2.39–2.75), and recent career age, especially first publication ≥ 2012 (OR: 2.91, 95% CI: 2.83–2.99; OR: 4.67, 95% CI: 3.89–5.62) among all authors and among highly cited authors, respectively. Compared with Clinical Medicine, most fields had lower adjusted odds, with Biomedical Research among highly cited authors being a notable exception (OR: 1.36, 95% CI: 1.25–1.47). Conclusion Our analysis shows no major gender differences in retraction rates overall, but field-specific differences may exist. Field, career age, country, and publication volume are stronger correlates of retraction. Structural and contextual factors likely drive retraction patterns and warrant further investigation.

#9 [paper] The Right to Be Called an Author: Generative AI, Epistemic Responsibility, and the Duty to Defend
Authors: Victor Frimpong
Venue: Qeios
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.32388/i26t1l.2
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Generative AI has intensified scholarly publishing's need to distinguish formal accountability for a manuscript from the epistemic capacity to answer for it. Existing authorship guidance assigns responsibility to human authors regardless of AI involvement, but assigning responsibility does not establish that it can be meaningfully exercised. This paper addresses that gap by distinguishing nominal from substantive authorship responsibility and introducing the Duty to Defend (DtD): the obligation, internal to the status of scholarly authorship, to retain sufficient epistemic command of one's work to provide a reasonable account of its central claims, methods, evidence, and interpretations when legitimately challenged. Although the expectation that authors can defend their reasoning is already emerging in the literature, the normative question of why authorship itself carries such an obligation remains open. The paper derives this obligation from the reciprocal structure of scholarly credit rather than treating it as an additional compliance requirement and distinguishes it from an AI-detection standard: the relevant question is never whether AI was used, but whether the named author remains capable of standing behind the contribution attributed to them. A conceptual model then identifies three configurations — integrated, attenuated, and displaced authorship — describing how technological assistance can preserve or weaken the connection between credit and human intellectual agency. The paper translates this framework into a graded, trigger-based approach to editorial assurance, in which scrutiny escalates only as substantive scholarly concerns remain unresolved, and examines its own limits, including evidentiary difficulty, unequal capacity to demonstrate understanding, and the risk of converting a safeguard for authorship into a mechanism of suspicion.

#15 [paper] Non-material beings and the excesses of collaborative writing
Authors: Oscar Davis
Venue: TEXT
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.52086/001c.173380
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
In a 1976 interview with Brazilian-Ukrainian author Clarice Lispector, the interviewer asks why Lispector is describing one of her fictional characters as though she is real. Lispector pushes back, claiming “but the person does exist, I see the person, and she orders me around”. Building on Lispector’s interview and the long history of writers detailing the influence of characters and transcendental beings on their craft, this paper puts into question current understandings of collaborative (creative) writing. Collaborative writing provides many opportunities to expand and challenge dominant Western and capitalist understandings of authorship, and yet, contemporary scholarship on collaborative writing tends to focus on human-to-human relations. Drawing on theories, ambiguities and gaps within feminist and post-humanist critiques of authorship and Donna Lee Brien and Tess Brady’s 12 overlapping categories of collaborative writing in “Collaborative Practice” (2003), this paper aims to expose the metaphysics of substance that determines who and what is seen as collaborator. Ultimately, I argue that collaborative writing should not be understood as a voluntary mode to enter or leave, but rather as a lens or intrinsic ethical component of authorship that needs to be continuously unearthed and expanded.

The deeper question is: How can a system move from physical measurement to interpretation, state estimation, decision, authorized action, verification, and recovery without losing traceability, uncertainty, human authority, or the ability to reconstruct what happened? The book couples two research lineages. The first lineage treats AI-interpreted quantum health as a metrology and reproducibility problem. AI denoising, quantum machine learning, digital twins, calibration, reference standards, manufacturing variation, versioning, data provenance, and interlaboratory reproducibility are treated as parts of one measurement chain. The second lineage treats quantum autonomous infrastructure as a bounded operational system. Its core loop is: Sense-> Interpret-> Decide-> Act-> Verify-> Recover Autonomy is therefore not defined as maximum independence. It is defined through explicit authority envelopes, stop conditions, fallback paths, human override, reversibility, runtime assurance, and recovery. The flagship three-coupling is: Measurement TraceabilityxAuthority EnvelopexRecovery Closure A central research heuristic is: AQHI=(Tm x Dq x Va x Rc)/(1 + Fa + Ul + Pb) where Tm represents measurement traceability, Dq decision quality, Va verified action, and Rc recovery capacity. The denominator penalizes false action, unpropagated uncertainty, provenance breaks, and related burdens. Raw physical observation is kept separate from deterministic preprocessing, learned correction, inference, recommendation, authorization, execution, verification, and recovery. Every transformation should preserve enough provenance to allow independent replay. Every model update should preserve enough version history to distinguish physical change from calibration change, algorithmic change, policy change, and unresolved residual. Every autonomous capability should declare what it is allowed to do, what evidence it requires, when it must abstain, when it must escalate, and how it returns to a known-safe state. The book gives particular attention to uncertainty. Uncertainty is not treated as a number attached only to the final measurement. It must propagate through the entire chain. Measurement uncertainty affects state estimation. State uncertainty affects action thresholds. Action consequence affects proof burden. Irreversible actions therefore require stronger evidence than reversible ones. This produces an important principle: Autonomy should become more conservative as uncertainty and irreversibility increase. The book also develops digital twins as uncertainty-aware operational belief states rather than replicas of reality. Digital twins may support prediction, counterfactual measurement planning, and state estimation, but they must remain distinguishable from the physical system they represent. Model mismatch, residuals, out-of-distribution conditions, retirement, reset, and reinitialization are treated as first-class research problems. Failure science forms another major part of the volume. Abstract:
This chapter asks what kind of entity a news text is when it emerges from the interaction of a journalist and a generative artificial intelligence system, and who or what can be said to have written it. Drawing on the posthumanist ontologies of Haraway, Latour, and Barad, the chapter argues that the inherited distinction between real and artificial news has ceased to sort GenAI assisted texts reliably, because such texts have no author in the sense journalism has traditionally assumed. Through a four stage conceptual analysis, the chapter develops hybrid journalism ontology as a framework in which the journalist, the model, the training data, and the platform together produce a text belonging to none of them alone. #1 [paper] Hyperspectral remote sensing for harmful algal bloom detection: Pseudo-nitzschia in the Northeast Pacific.
Authors: Bailess, Alexander L, Baetge, Nicholas, Barnard, Andrew H, Tufillaro, Nicholas, Behrenfeld, Michael, Bill, Brian, Kudela, Raphael, Graff, Jason
Venue: Harmful algae
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43020539/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for rapid, scalable identification of harmful algal blooms, specifically Pseudo-nitzschia, to manage marine resources, given that current in-situ point sampling methods are expensive and labor-intensive.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Culturing four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, measuring their hyperspectral absorption and backscatter, modeling spectral reflectances detectable by remote sensing platforms, and quantifying differences between taxonomic fingerprints using vector-based and stat…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including Pseudo-nitzschia, Thalassiosira, Chaetoceros, and Asterionellopsis.
Abstract:
Diatoms are microscopic marine algae that are critical for global primary production, carbon sequestration, and fisheries productivity. However, select diatoms may form harmful algal blooms, which threaten marine ecosystems and the fisheries they sustain. Rapidly identifying harmful blooms is necessary to effectively manage marine resources, yet current identification methods are limited by expensive and labor-intensive in-situ point sampling. Hyperspectral remote sensing enables scalable monitoring, but its ability to resolve taxonomic shifts within phytoplankton groups (e.g. diatoms) is largely unknown. To investigate this uncertainty, we cultured four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including this system's most abundant harmful algae, Pseudo-nitzschia. The hyperspectral absorption and backscatter of these taxa were measured and used to model spectral reflectances that remote sensing platforms (satellites/drones) might detect. Differences between fingerprints of these taxa were quantified using vector-based and statistical analyses. Mean spectral differences of 48% were observed between the most dominant diatom, Thalassiosira, and the most toxic diatom, Pseudo-nitzschia. Differences of approximately 30% were found between Pseudo-nitzschia and the second and third most abundant diatoms, Chaetoceros and Asterionellopsis. Successful identification of Pseudo-nitzschia's reflectance fingerprint was driven by the presence of a unique feature around 560 nm. The distinct spectral fingerprint of Pseudo-nitzschia indicates that it can be distinguished from other diatom blooms using hyperspectral remote sensing platforms.

#2 [paper] Global and National Dynamics of Scopus-Indexed Data Paper Publishing: A Bibliometric Analysis With Evidence From Ukraine

Abstract:
Abstract This article examines the global evolution and national differentiation of Data Papers in the context of the development of open science, with a particular focus on Ukraine. The aim of the study was to determine the temporal dynamics, geographic and disciplinary distribution, major publishing platforms, and the characteristics of Ukraine’s positioning within the global research data publication landscape. The analysis was conducted based on Scopus data using the distinct “Data Paper” document type. Publications from 2014 to 2026 were analyzed on a global scale, and those from 2016 to 2026 were analyzed for Ukraine; subject areas, journals, open access models, and mechanisms for waiving publication fees were examined separately. An overall upward global trend in Data Papers was observed, with a peak annual figure of approximately 2,300 documents in 2024. At the same time, Ukrainian activity remains low in volume and volatile: only 57 documents were identified during the study period, with a maximum of 10 publications in 2022. Global publication activity is concentrated primarily in the United States, China, and leading European research systems. The Ukrainian landscape is characterized by a unique combination of computer science, mathematics, social sciences, management and analytics, and natural sciences. The results indicate that Ukraine is already integrated into the Data Paper segment; however, its trajectory differs significantly from the global one in terms of scale and stability. Abstract:
Career anxiety amongst students has emerged as a rather topical issue in the realm of psychology and education; however, at present, there is no comprehensive bibliometric analysis that would allow tracing the evolution of knowledge in this field. The purpose of this paper is to present the results of the bibliometric analysis of 525 peer-reviewed scientific papers on career anxiety amongst students, published freely in electronic form during 2016 – 2025. The search was carried out in the search engine Dimensions.ai using a search by title and abstract. The analysis was conducted taking into account the trends of publications and citations, subject areas, geographic distribution, institutional affiliation, and collaborative networks. It was found that the number of papers increased exponentially from 11 papers in 2017 to 168 papers in 2025, generating 1,550 citations in 2025. China has a considerable number of papers (61), but Poland, France, and the Netherlands have much greater impact per paper due to international collaboration. The Field-Weighted Citation Ratio decreased from 3.57 in 2018 to 1.46 in 2024, and only 33.33% of the papers in 2025 received citations, showing lower impact due to accelerated production. No institution published more than four papers, and there are no inter-institutional collaborations. There is a need in this area for creating international collaborations, bridging computing and economics disciplines, establishing research centers, and conducting research at different institutions in order to accumulate knowledge from the disjunctive output.

The purpose of this study is to examine papers in the field of educational technologies published in the Journal of Theory and Practice in Education (EKU) between 2005 and 2025. Using bibliometric analysis, it determines the journal's thematic, methodological, and sample-based publication trends. Seventy papers were identified through a manual systematic review, and citation counts, keyword patterns, study designs, and participant categories were analysed. #5 [paper] New visual culture of science: analysis of graphical abstracts in the life science journal “Cell”

Abstract:
Driven by the shift towards online journal publishing, many academic journals have introduced graphical abstracts (GAs) since the 2000s to convey the primary findings of research papers. This study investigated this visual culture in life sciences by analyzing GAs with focus on content, representation, and background. In total, 333 GAs were collected from articles published in the journal Cell in 2021 and analyzed. Among these, 295 GAs (88.6%) explained the results and models and succinctly presented the key findings, and 251 GAs (75.4%) used a layout that divided the area into two or more sections. New graphics that were not present in the main text were featured in 222 GAs (66.7%), indicating substantial investment in their creation. The GAs shared commonalities with modern infographics commonly seen on the internet, which emphasize clarity. The increased used of GAs may be attributed to the need for "instant comprehension," which is an epistemic virtue reinforced by authors, readers, and journals and driven by the scientific self of "surviving researchers and journals" in a competitive scientific environment.

#7 [paper] High Article Processing Charges and the Expansion of Predatory Publishing in the Generative AI Era: Implications for Research Integrity and Global Scholarly Inclusion

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intersection of high article processing charges (APCs), generative AI-driven publication pressures, and the expansion of predatory publishing, and their impact on research integrity and global scholarly inclusion.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A critical review based on a purposive selection of interdisciplinary literature in scholarly communication, higher education, information science, research ethics, and science policy, utilizing reference snowballing and thematic relevance.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Interdisciplinary literature in scholarly communication, higher education, information science, research ethics, and science policy.
Abstract:
Abstract The transition to open access publishing was intended to democratize knowledge, yet the dominance of article processing charge models has created new financial stratifications that disproportionately affect researchers in low- and middle-income countries. Concurrently, generative artificial intelligence has lowered barriers to manuscript production while amplifying editorial overload and predatory publishing vulnerabilities. This critical review examines the interconnected dynamics among article processing charge inflation, generative artificial intelligence-driven publication pressures, predatory publishing expansion, and global scholarly inequality, with alignment to Sustainable Development Goals 4, 9, 10, 16, and 17. The review is based on a purposive selection of interdisciplinary literature in scholarly communication, higher education, information science, research ethics, and science policy. Literature was selected through reference snowballing and thematic relevance to the five research objectives rather than systematic database searching. Findings indicate that global spending on article processing charges has escalated significantly, with average charges for high-impact journals exceeding several thousand United States dollars, creating conditions that increase susceptibility to predatory journals. The rise of generative artificial intelligence further complicates scholarly communication through accelerated manuscript production, paper mills, and concerns regarding epistemic reliability. Predatory publishing should be understood not merely as a problem of unethical journals but as a structural consequence of inequitable academic publishing systems intensified by artificial intelligence-era publication pressures. Policy reforms centered on diamond open access models, ethical artificial intelligence governance, research integrity education, and strengthened international collaboration are proposed.

#9 [paper] Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciências: past, present, and future.

Abstract:
National flagship journals play a strategic yet often undervalued role in scientific systems outside the core centers of global knowledge production. This study analyzes the Annals of the Brazilian Academy of Sciences, Brazil's oldest continuously published scientific journal, to examine how long-standing multidisciplinary journals in emerging research systems navigate internationalization, evaluation regimes, and societal relevance. Using bibliometric and network analysis of Scopus and Web of Science data (1945-2025) we assess publication trends, thematic evolution, collaboration patterns, citation performance, and non-academic impact through policy and patent citations. A paper that takes a year to reach print may describe tools, policies and evidence that have already been superseded. This article describes an experiment in doing things differently. The article sets out the motivation for the experiment, including the author's long interest in educational innovation and his concerns about the economics of academ‐ ic publishing. It describes the venue and its strengths and limitations, the source corpus, the workflow and the division of labour between human and AI, and the verification process, which found and corrected more than two dozen errors, unverifiable claims and one retracted study carried over from the newsletters. It reports the actual publication timeline. It then discusses the risks of the approach, including "research slop", weakened rigour and researchers becoming editors of machine-written text, and argues that these risks are real but manageable when the human remains responsible for judgement and the process is transparent. It closes with a replicable workflow for others.

#13 [paper] The disclosure gap: why mandating AI transparency without protecting honesty is a leadership failure
Authors: Damola Usman Onaolapo
Venue: Frontiers in Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1966879
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Universities and journals have answered generative artificial intelligence (AI) with one main instrument: mandatory disclosure. Ask researchers to declare what they used, and transparency should follow. The evidence says it does not. Across 5,114 journals and 5.2 million papers, about 70% of journals now require disclosure, yet only around 0.1% of papers published since 2023 declare AI use, and journals with policies show no less AI adoption than journals without them. Submission data from two major publishers tell the same story: 5.7 and 3.3% disclosure, against surveys where between 28 and 76% of researchers say they use these tools. This Perspective argues that the gap is not a compliance failure to be fixed with firmer rules. It is what happens when institutions ask people to volunteer information that carries a real cost, and then do nothing about that cost. Experiments show that AI users are judged less competent and less motivated; researchers have named the effect AI shaming and the punishment of honesty. The paper argues that this cost falls unevenly, that the evidence on how it falls is messier than a simple centre-periphery story allows, and that the problem belongs to institutional leaders rather than journal editors. It sets out what owning it would mean.

#16 [paper] Signed and anonymous referee reports and AI-associated language in open peer review: a within-manuscript difference-in-differences study of Copernicus journals
Authors: Fazıl Akdağ
Venue: Open Science Framework
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/jz6bt

Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are now used to write scientific papers and peer review reports. Corpus-level studies have estimated their footprint in abstracts (Kobak et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2025) and in reviews for machine learning conferences (Liang et al., 2024; Russo et al., 2025). Sharma et al. (2026) examined whether LLM-assisted reviews treat LLM-assisted papers differently and found that an apparent interaction disappears once paper quality is controlled. Publishers have responded with rules. The AI policy of Copernicus journals does not allow referees to have AI tools generate their comments or reports, allows assistance with language, and asks referees not to upload manuscripts or reports to AI tools (for example, Ocean Science AI policy). One proposed safeguard is open identity: a referee who signs a report is personally accountable for its content. Accountability theory predicts that identifiable people take more care over their judgements (Lerner and Tetlock, 1999), and signed reviews have long been studied for their quality, tone and recommendations (van Rooyen et al., 1999; Bravo et al., 2019; van Sambeek and Lakens, 2021). The same theory also predicts more attention to how one appears to an audience, and a named referee may have more reason to polish the language of a report. Signed and anonymous reviews have also been compared for tone in journals where referees choose to sign (Sahakyan and AlShebli, 2025). To our knowledge no study has compared AI-associated vocabulary in signed and anonymous referee reports (literature searches to 28 October 2026). Copernicus journals allow this comparison. Their interactive public discussion publishes every referee report, and each referee chooses whether to sign or to remain anonymous. Signed and anonymous reports therefore appear side by side on the same manuscripts, and this has been the case since well before ChatGPT was released on 30 November 2022 (Bornmann et al., 2010, used the same system to study peer review). Crossref holds structured metadata for every report, including the referee's recommendation and the link to the final article. The study compares, within the same manuscript, the change in AI-associated vocabulary between signed and anonymous referee reports from before to after the release of ChatGPT. Comparing reports on the same manuscript holds the manuscript, its quality, its topic and its authors constant. The measure is lexical: it captures LLM-styled text, which includes text generated, polished or translated with LLM tools, and it cannot tell these uses apart.

Background The University Grants Commission (UGC) announced the discontinuation of the UGC-CARE Reference List through a Public Notice dated 11 February 2025, following the Commission's decision taken at its 584th meeting on 3 October 2024, marking a major shift in India's approach to research quality governance. Introduced in 2019 to address predatory publishing, the UGC-CARE framework provided a centralized mechanism for identifying credible publication venues. The transition to quality-oriented research assessment emphasizing publication ethics, peer review integrity, editorial transparency, and institutional accountability has generated considerable debate, yet its implications for research integrity and health professions education remain insufficiently explored. Methods A narrative policy analysis was conducted using publicly available UGC policy documents, regulatory reports, international responsible research assessment frameworks, and peer reviewed literature. Guided by Walt and Gilson's Policy Analysis Triangle, the analysis examined the policy context, content, process, and key actors associated with India's transition from the UGC-CARE framework to quality-oriented research assessment. Evidence was synthesized into four thematic domains: journal quality governance, research integrity, stakeholder implications, and educational implications. Results The findings were organized into four thematic domains. First, the post-CARE framework reflects a transition from centralized journal vetting to decentralized quality governance. Second, greater emphasis is placed on researcher responsibility, institutional accountability, and publication literacy. Third, the reform has important implications for researchers, institutions, and research assessment practices. Fourth, it creates opportunities to strengthen publication ethics, journal evaluation, and responsible scholarly communication within medical and dental education. Based on these findings, publication literacy is proposed as a competency supporting competency-based medical education (CBME). Conclusions India's post-CARE reforms represent an evolution toward responsible research assessment and institutional accountability rather than a return to the pre-CARE era. Strengthening publication literacy, research integrity culture, and faculty development may support successful implementation of the emerging quality-oriented research assessment framework.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Recent studies have raised concerns arising from the exploitation ("mining") of public health databases for low-quality, mass-produced papers. However, it remains challenging to disambiguate whether such papers originate from paper mills (commercial entities that sell authorships on mass-produced papers) or from the uncoordinated action of individuals facilitated by AI tools and templated workflows. Our study aims to address this question for one particular database, the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD). We selected this database after noticing that one of our papers on Bayesian age-period-cohort models has recently been experiencing a rapid surge in geographically clustered citations from GBD papers with Chinese affiliations. METHODS: We collected bibliometric and article-level metadata from GBD papers to search for indicators of mass-produced research. Moreover, we assessed 713 full-text articles for reported R versions, availability of code and data, and declaration of generative AI use. For 180 articles, we qualitatively screened the figures for graphical similarities. Finally, we conducted an exploratory scoping investigation of online platforms (social media sites, vendor websites) dedicated to do-it-yourself workflows for secondary analyses of public health data. RESULTS: Although we cannot rule out paper mill involvement, our findings suggest that the geographically clustered increase in GBD publications from China is at least partially driven by independent authors. The wide variety of R versions listed in 477 articles points against centralized paper production. Moreover, despite broad graphical similarities in figure styles that suggest the use of shared visualization tools, substantial variation in ancillary details suggest independent authors finalizing figures. This is corroborated by the identification of an online ecosystem of proprietary tools and services specializing in streamlined do-it-yourself workflows for conducting, writing, and publishing secondary analyses of public health data. CONCLUSION: Appropriate efforts should be directed towards evaluating the quality of the identified workflows. Stakeholders in scientific integrity should monitor online platforms dedicated to the rapid production of papers, especially in light of the increasing focus on AI-assisted workflows. Code sharing should be mandated for data-driven secondary analyses. Paywalls and proprietary software licenses hinder transparency and reusability, underscoring the importance of free and open-source software for trustworthy and reproducible research.

Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

Two research mothers / one 200-theme family blueprint 82 source-anchored scientific investigations / five interlocking but distinct flagship questions Prospective nonclinical science / not a clinical or medical device claim Author: White Rainbow Epoch / 33 x STARLI Scientific Working Edition v1.0 / 13 November 2026 Scientific position: the difference between an event and an inference The intellectual temptation of four-dimensional manufacturing is unusually clear. A fabricated object is exposed to a cue, its outline changes, and the sequence can be shown as a compelling demonstration of adaptive matter. Yet a moving outline is not a complete explanation, and an explanation is not a safe mission. A soft microgripper can close around a bead and still fail to release it; it can return to the same apparent curvature while its contact force has fallen; it can displace an object while losing fragments whose material fate is unmeasured. These cases do not invalidate the study of shape-programmed matter. They reveal that the study needs several distinct endpoints, each owned by an independent measurement pathway. This notebook reorganizes the first five flagships in the STARLI two-hundred-theme blueprint as a scientifically bounded lineage. F001 concerns identifiable stimulus-response geometry. F002 concerns encoded shape memory and loaded recovery. F003 concerns the integrity and mechanics of multi-material interfaces. F004 concerns the ordering of stimuli and the state history of a programmable device. F005 asks whether the complete microhandling mission remains functional after deformation and reconfiguration. None of these endpoints may substitute for another. Their relationship is cumulative but not hierarchical in the sense of guaranteed success: progress in one question may expose failure in the next. Two older research monographs provide the scientific starting point. The first is a 770-page research edition on 4D microrobotic manufacturing and biomedical-environment response. Abstract:
Abstract. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC) may be approaching a tipping point, with potentially significant environmental and societal consequences. Here, we examine the framing and accuracy of Dutch news articles reporting on the AMOC slowdown or potential collapse using peer-reviewed scientific research papers. Abstract:
Abstract The transition to open access publishing was intended to democratize knowledge, yet the dominance of article processing charge models has created new financial stratifications that disproportionately affect researchers in low- and middle-income countries. Concurrently, generative artificial intelligence has lowered barriers to manuscript production while amplifying editorial overload and predatory publishing vulnerabilities. This critical review examines the interconnected dynamics among article processing charge inflation, generative artificial intelligence-driven publication pressures, predatory publishing expansion, and global scholarly inequality, with alignment to Sustainable Development Goals 4, 9, 10, 16, and 17. The review is based on a purposive selection of interdisciplinary literature in scholarly communication, higher education, information science, research ethics, and science policy. Literature was selected through reference snowballing and thematic relevance to the five research objectives rather than systematic database searching. Findings indicate that global spending on article processing charges has escalated significantly, with average charges for high-impact journals exceeding several thousand United States dollars, creating conditions that increase susceptibility to predatory journals. The rise of generative artificial intelligence further complicates scholarly communication through accelerated manuscript production, paper mills, and concerns regarding epistemic reliability. Predatory publishing should be understood not merely as a problem of unethical journals but as a structural consequence of inequitable academic publishing systems intensified by artificial intelligence-era publication pressures. Policy reforms centered on diamond open access models, ethical artificial intelligence governance, research integrity education, and strengthened international collaboration are proposed.

#1 [grant] Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate
Amount: €3,000,000–€15,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2027-01-D1-07
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-03-04
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding, modelling, and predicting extreme events (isolated, compound, or cascading) in a changing climate, including their interaction, likelihood, and impact on resilience.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Utilizing a hierarchy of models (including high-resolution Earth system models and digital twins), data from past and recent climate, AI-based approaches, quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, and case studies to improve prediction, projection, and attribution capabilities across s…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe and globally, encompassing large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena, with specific focus on EU and national/regional actors, low- to middle-income countries, and integration with initiatives like Copernicus and Destination Earth.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

- Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the new Extreme-Events Flagship Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects to be selected under ESA's FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. results.name: corpus_item
results.content:
#1 [paper] An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast.
Authors: Zhang, Xiang, Cui, Yingzhe, Li, Furong, Zhou, Shenghui, Wu, Guangnan, Jing, Zhao, Wu, Lixin
Venue: Science advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43024702/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

#3 [paper] Integrating Generative AI and Data Science into General Chemistry Laboratories
Authors: Chun-I Wang, Sara Busharar, Anthony Fosu, Julian Rivera Ortiz, Gustavo López, Donna McGregor, Pamela A. Mills
Venue: ChemRxiv
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv.15011508/v1

Abstract:
The emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini is reshaping research, education, and industry. Recent workforce data indicate a widening gap between declining junior-level opportunities and rising demand for senior-level expertise, underscoring the urgent need to adapt undergraduate chemistry curricula to prepare students for an AI-enabled workforce. To address this challenge, we designed a series of Python-based laboratory experiments for General Chemistry that integrate generative AI with instructor guidance to enhance student learning. The modules focus on (1) using AI tools to support conceptual understanding, (2) applying AI-assisted coding for data visualization and analysis, and (3) introducing machine learning workflows to solve real-world chemistry problems. All activities are implemented in Google Colaboratory, a cloud-based programming platform now integrated with Gemini, which helps students, particularly those without prior programming experience, complete coding tasks with step-by-step instructor guidance. We compare student attitudes toward the use of AI and programming at the beginning and end of the semesters, observing a more positive attitude toward AI use and increased confidence in programming. To demonstrate scalability, three PhD graduate students, two of whom had no prior programming background, successfully led the laboratory sessions using these AI-supported materials, confirming that instructors across a wide range of computational skill levels can teach the experiments. This work demonstrates how generative AI can create more prosperous and equitable learning experiences, equipping students with transferable skills essential for research and industry careers, as well as the evolving STEM workforce.

#15 [paper] Embedding Responsible AI in a Technical Machine Learning Course
Authors: Stefania Zourlidou, Frank Hopfgartner
Venue: European Conference on e-Learning
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.34190/ecel.25.1.5151
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) courses in higher education usually emphasise mathematical foundations and algorithmic methods, while ethical and societal questions are often treated as separate or optional topics. This paper reports a small-scale practice-based evaluation of a blended design that embedded responsible AI within a Master’s-level ML and Data Mining course at a German university in winter semester 2025/26. The design combined fifteen on-campus lectures on core ML topics, including one lecture on fairness as a technical topic, fifteen optional weekly assignments discussed in tutorials, and an eight-module microlearning course on AI literacy and responsible AI. Completion of at least half of the microlearning and a mandatory practical assignment were required for exam eligibility. The study analyses an anonymous end-of-course survey, using only responses from students who explicitly consented to research use (n=35). Student perceptions were generally positive: 78% reported a good balance between theory and practice, 75% found the weekly assignments important for understanding, and 59% judged the microlearning to fit well with the on-campus lectures. For responsible AI, around two thirds reported greater confidence in identifying fairness issues, feeling better prepared to discuss ethics professionally, or perceiving ethics as integrated rather than added on. 75% intended to consider fairness and ethical implications in future ML projects, with no respondent disagreeing. Open responses suggested perceived transfer, with students naming hiring systems, facial recognition, student-risk prediction and credit or loan decision-making, and often using technical vocabulary such as training data, optimisation objectives and evaluation metrics. The paper does not claim causal impact, and findings should be interpreted in light of the small voluntary sample, the single-cohort single-institution setting, and the possibility of social-desirability bias on an end-of-course survey on ethics. Instead, it offers descriptive evidence that a lightweight microlearning layer, combined with a technical fairness lecture, can be a feasible way to connect technical ML learning with ethical reflection in practice. It also identifies revisions for the next iteration: reduce workload tension, add explicit ethical-reflection prompts to assignments, and include more practical coding work.

#16 [paper] Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
Authors: Elhocine Mansouri, Eiki Kimura, Masatoshi Koga, Keigo Arai
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/cecdb34a7d3e95180e270f1fb1888def6a606b1c
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.
