#18 [paper] MIRA: Towards a General AI Scientist
Authors: Deep Principle
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21930641
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence now reaches into much of scientific practice, yet a gap persists between systems that answer scientific questions and systems that advance science. Scientific discovery is not a single response but an iterative loop that runs from hypothesis generation through execution to interpretation, carried out under uncertainty and accountable to reproducible evidence. We present MIRA, an AI scientist tailored for the physical sciences, to operationalize this loop end to end. MIRA is organized as a squad of agents with different harnesses and tools that mirror how a human research team divides and coordinates its work. It frames research directions and mines the published literature and a team’s internal data to propose grounded, testable hypotheses; it executes pre- or user-defined simulation workflows on cloud compute infrastructure; and it drives physical experiments through our in-house automated laboratory, the AI Materials Factory, carrying a hypothesis from plan to bench. MIRA consolidates results into calibrated conclusions, states its uncertainty explicitly, and compiles each completed project into a persistent memory and a maintained scientific wiki, so that reasoning, provenance, and negative results remain available to later work. On two external benchmarks MIRA attains the highest score at the lowest cost per task among seven agents compared, and leads four of five task categories on a specialized drug-discovery suite, exceeding agents purpose-built for that domain. This report details MIRA’s architecture and stage-by-stage design, and demonstrates it across chemistry, materials, and energy as a generalist that accelerates research and discovery while remaining reliable and auditable.

#19 [paper] Machine Learning – Supported Pedagogy in Computer Engineering: A Proposed Framework for Learner Modeling, Adaptive Support, and Controlled Empirical Evaluation
Authors: Hillary Mae De Guzman
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23126048
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Students in Computer Engineering courses often progress unevenly across diverse subject areas, and instructors lack sufficient time to provide individual feedback.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A pedagogical framework that converts course records and learning-activity data into learner features, employs a lightweight predictive model to estimate mastery and flag students needing help, and uses a recommender to suggest targeted support activities for instructor review.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Computer Engineering courses combining programming, digital logic, mathematics, and hardware laboratories.
Abstract:
Computer Engineering courses combine programming, digital logic, mathematics, and hardware laboratories, so students often progress unevenly and instructors have little time for individual feedback. Machine Learning (ML) has recently been explored to predict student performance, personalize learning support, and provide scalable feedback. This paper presents the design of an ML-supported pedagogical framework in which course records and learning-activity data are converted into learner features, a lightweight predictive model estimates mastery and flags students who may need help, and a recommender suggests targeted support activities that the instructor reviews before use. Effectiveness is evaluated in a controlled comparison with conventional instruction using concept assessments, normalized learning gain, prediction quality, and fairness checks across student subgroups. Privacy, informed consent, human oversight, and verification of any generative-AI output are treated as hard constraints rather than optional features. The study is structured for validation in a real course and does not claim measured improvement until the experiments are completed.

Method (Mycelium's reading): A pedagogical framework that converts course records and learning-activity data into learner features, uses a lightweight predictive model to estimate mastery and flag students needing help, and employs a recommender to suggest targeted support activities for instructor review.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Computer Engineering courses involving programming, digital logic, mathematics, and hardware laboratories.
Abstract:
Computer Engineering courses combine programming, digital logic, mathematics, and hardware laboratories, so students often progress unevenly and instructors have little time for individual feedback. Machine Learning (ML) has recently been explored to predict student performance, personalize learning support, and provide scalable feedback. This paper presents the design of an ML-supported pedagogical framework in which course records and learning-activity data are converted into learner features, a lightweight predictive model estimates mastery and flags students who may need help, and a recommender suggests targeted support activities that the instructor reviews before use. Effectiveness is evaluated in a controlled comparison with conventional instruction using concept assessments, normalized learning gain, prediction quality, and fairness checks across student subgroups. Privacy, informed consent, human oversight, and verification of any generative-AI output are treated as hard constraints rather than optional features. The study is structured for validation in a real course and does not claim measured improvement until the experiments are completed.

Abstract:
The Graduate College's Dean’s Doctoral Fellowship (DDF) supports the recruitment of academically talented students whose educational pathways and experiences may include financial, institutional, or other barriers to graduate education. The fellowship reflects the Graduate College’s commitment to expanding access to graduate education and strengthening the Illinois graduate community by recruiting students from many educational, geographic, and familial backgrounds. The DDF provides financial support to students who demonstrate strong potential for success in graduate study and whose pathways to graduate education reflect significant barriers or nontraditional routes. Through this recruitment fellowship, the Graduate College seeks to expand opportunities for talented students to pursue doctoral education at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and to connect fellowship recipients with programs and resources that support their transition to and success in graduate education. Eligibility and Selection Criteria DDFs are intended as recruitment fellowships. To that end, only those students who are seeking admission to a doctoral program at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (Illinois) are eligible. Generally, this includes students at either one of two stages of study: students seeking first-time admission to a doctoral program, or students who have completed a master’s at Illinois and are now applying for admission to a doctoral program here at Illinois. Students in approved cost-recovery or self-supporting programs are not eligible for nomination. The list of such programs can be found here . Only those students intending to enter during the 2027-28 academic year are eligible. For students intending to enter in Spring 2028, their fellowship will not begin until Fall 2028. Full-time Illinois employees are ineligible. Students who have previously received a Graduate College Equity Master's Fellowship (EMF) or an Aspire Master's Fellowship remain eligible for consideration for the Dean’s Fellowship, provided they meet all other eligibility requirements. Candidates must be U.S. citizens, permanent residents, or approved domestic applicants . (If the student is tagged in Slate as "domestic," the student meets this criterion.) The Dean’s Doctoral Fellowship is open to newly admitted students in an Illinois doctoral degree program who: Demonstrate academic achievement and potential for success in graduate study (as assessed by the nominating department, transcript, honors, or other designation); and Have experienced financial hardship, are first generation in their families to attend college, experienced barriers to educational access, or followed a non-traditional path to graduate education; and Have demonstrated their ability to contribute to a community characterized by inclusion, belonging, respect, and productive collaboration. Candidates should provide an example of how they have engaged with students, colleagues, or communities with different perspectives, abilities, and experiences to achieve a positive outcome and reflect on what they learned from the experience. Award Structure – Two Versions: The DDF pays $75,000 in total stipend over the duration of the fellowship. However, there are two versions of the fellowship, each with its own payment structure. At the time of nomination, the department must select which version to offer the student. If awarded, students may not switch to the other version. Version 1: $25,000 annual stipend for three years, plus a full tuition waiver. This option is primarily for departments that intend for the fellowship to serve as the student’s main source of funding for the three “on fellowship” years. This version of the fellowship offers flexibility in that recipients have a five-year window within which to use the three years of support. The window begins with the 2027-28 academic year and ends with the 2031-32 academic year. The three funded years are called “on fellowship” yea

#1 [grant] Integrating Machine Learning with Computational Fluid Dynamics Models of Orally Inhaled Drug Products (U01) Clinical Trials Not Allowed
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/351059
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Bottlenecks in using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), including computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Developing a methodology to integrate machine learning (ML) with CFD models of OIDPs.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs) and generic inhaler devices.
Abstract:
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has played a crucial role in providing an alternative bioequivalence (BE) approach for generic orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), in addition to comparative clinical endpoint or pharmacodynamic BE studies, as a relatively cost- and time-efficient complement to benchtop and clinical experiments that has been widely used in developing and assessing generic inhaler devices. However, despite the advances in the power of modern computers, there are still some bottlenecks in using CFD due to computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications. Machine learning (ML) has been gaining more attention as a potential tool to alleviate such limitations that arise in CFD. The purpose of this grant is to develop a methodology to integrate ML with CFD models of OIDPs to promote alternative BE studies to enhance and accelerate the development and approval of generic OIDPs.

Amount: €2,000,000–€3,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-JU-EUROHPC-2026-QML-07-01
Still open/current: yes

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need to integrate quantum computing into data pre-processing and learning workflows to address data-heavy or computationally intensive tasks, specifically aiming to demonstrate improvements in processing speed, computational complexity, modelling accuracy, and reduced sample requirements at sca…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The development, validation, and demonstration of quantum-enhanced AI approaches, including the design of quantum, quantum-inspired, or hybrid QML algorithms, performance modelling, complexity analysis, benchmarking, and the development of error-mitigation and noise-aware strategies tailored to QML…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The text describes a call for proposals for a research project rather than a specific dataset or cohort. The intended setting includes NISQ-era devices and application domains such as climate and environmental modelling, Earth observation, healthcare, materials discovery, finance, robotics, manufac…
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

- Integration of quantum computing into data pre-processing pipelines and learning workflows for data-heavy or computationally intensive tasks, demonstrating clear improvements in processing speed, computational complexity, modelling accuracy, and reduced sample requirements at scales achievable with NISQ-era devices,

- Reliable and scalable Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models and algorithms, integrated with existing AI frameworks and pipelines, enabling faster data processing, improved prediction accuracy, and enhanced computational capabilities,

- Validated quantum-enhanced AI methods demonstrating measurable improvements over classical baselines in terms of speed, accuracy, data efficiency, complexity, or scalability, supported by rigorous benchmarking and complexity analysis,

- Robust, noise-aware QML techniques suitable for NISQ hardware, including error-mitigation strategies and algorithmic adaptations that improve reliability, performance, and reproducibility on real quantum processors,

- Demonstrators or proof-of-concept applications showcasing the relevance of QML for real-world challenges (e.g. climate and environmental modelling, Earth observation, healthcare and life sciences, materials discovery, finance, robotics, manufacturing, and cybersecurity),

- Strengthened European leadership and technological sovereignty in quantum computing and trustworthy AI, supported by cross-sector collaboration, knowledge transfer, and contributions to emerging standards, benchmarks and best practices.

- Enhanced collaboration across quantum computing, machine learning and application domains, fostering a coordinated European QML research and innovation community.

Scope:

Proposals are expected to address multiple key research directions in Quantum Machine Learning (QML), targeting both scientific excellence and industrial relevance. Proposals should clearly outline how to contribute to the development, validation and demonstration of quantum-enhanced AI approaches, with clear pathways towards practical applications. The proposed work should strengthen Europe’s scientific and technological capabilities in quantum computing and accelerate the industrial uptake of quantum-enhanced AI solutions.

Activities may include, but are not limited to

- design and analysis of quantum, quantum-inspired or hybrid QML algorithms,

- performance modelling, complexity analysis and benchmarking of quantum-enhanced AI methods,

- development of error-mitigation and noise-aware strategies tailored to QML workloads,

Proposals should advance scalable QML algorithms capable of addressing large-scale, computationally intensive problems, this includes approaches that

- can manage massive data volumes and complex computational tasks,

- enable faster data processing and improved predictive performance in relevant application domains (e.g. hydrologic research, climate modelling, terrain classification from satellite remote sensing, drug discovery, and image-based medical diagnosis).

Many current QML methods remain closely inspired by classical algorithms and therefore do not yet achieve genuine quantum advantage, requiring further developments in

- quantum-native learning models,

- efficient quantum kernels and quantum feature mappings,

- algorithms demonstrating provable or empirical advantages over classical approaches.

Proposals may also include formal complexity analyses, identification of problem classes that can benefit from quantum acceleration.

Developments should address multiple of the following key research directions:

Quantum Supervised Learning (QSL):

Quantum Supervised Learning investigates how quantum algorithms can accelerate or improve the training of supervised learning models, offering novel opportunities to explore quantum–classical learning theories and enabling industry to shorten development cycles and enhance performance in data-intensive domains such as finance, healthcare, and Earth observation.

Under the area of Using Space on Earth related to SatCom and EO, below this topic focusses on the Low to Mid TRL level developments of key technologies[1] required to strengthen competitiveness in these domains with a dedicated focus on synergies between Earth observation and Satellite telecommunication technologies.

The areas of R&I, which needs to be addressed to tackle the above-mentioned expected outcomes are:

In this topic, the integration of the gender dimension (sex and gender analysis) in research and innovation content should be addressed only if relevant in relation to the objectives of the research effort.

Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13082

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsurface hazard detection systems suffer from a 'collect everything' bottleneck, where static, pre-programmed sensor scripts flood tactical networks with raw data, ignore environmental degradation of sensor modalities, and lack the real-time adaptability to optimize sensor tasking and rou…
Method (Mycelium's reading): An adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine utilizing probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods (such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) to dynamically queue, activate, or inhibit sensor payload…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned aerial and ground platforms conducting standoff reconnaissance for subsurface WMD devices, chemical/biological munitions, and radiological dispersal device components in diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
Abstract:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.

A proactive system is required to answer:

"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"

This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.

#45 [grant] Multi-Fidelity Transfer Learning for Defense Applications
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13096
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Computational cost, limited availability, and security restrictions of high-fidelity simulation environments constrain the development of robust AI/ML agents for missile defense and aerospace applications.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Multi-fidelity transfer learning, involving a staged approach where agents are pretrained on low-fidelity models or unclassified representations before being adapted and optimized in high-fidelity or classified environments.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): United States missile defense system (MDS) and aerospace applications.
Abstract:
Rapid Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration into the MDS is required for the United States to properly defend itself against its adversaries. The development of robust Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) agents for complex missile defense and aerospace applications is often constrained by the computational cost, limited availability, and security restrictions of high-fidelity simulation environments. Transfer learning provides a critical pathway to overcoming these barriers. By initially training agents on low-fidelity models or unclassified representations—where data is abundant and computational demands are reduced—core behaviors, strategies, and decision-making frameworks could be efficiently developed and refined. These pretrained models could then be adapted and optimized in high-fidelity and/or environments at higher classification levels, allowing the agent to leverage its foundational knowledge while rapidly acquiring the nuanced performance required for operational deployment. This staged approach significantly reduces training time, minimizes resource expenditure, and mitigates the risk of overfitting to scarce high-fidelity/classified data. Moreover, it enables iterative development cycles where low-fidelity environments serve as agile testbeds for innovation, and high-fidelity environments refine and validate for mission-readiness. Leveraging transfer learning in this manner not only accelerates capability delivery but also ensures that AI/ML systems achieve the precision, resilience, and adaptability necessary for real-world mission success.

Scope:

Understanding the mechanisms and drivers of land (including inland waters) and ocean carbon sinks and sources is crucial for accurate climate models and scenarios and informing climate mitigation strategies. However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

The ocean’s capacity to act as a carbon sink is determined by a variety of factors, including changes in climate, atmospheric composition (in particular CO2 concentration) and chemical, physical and biological processes of the ocean, all influenced by human activities. Projects are expected to improve the understanding and quantification of the various mechanisms involved, with a focus on the behaviour of the ocean sink under past (including palaeo records), present and future conditions and various climate change and emission scenarios. #50 [grant] Compact Unmanned Aerial System for Marine Species Monitoring
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13133
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing UAS for marine species monitoring are often prohibitively expensive, lack integrated high-resolution photogrammetry capabilities, or fail to meet specific operational requirements (size, duration, and NDAA compliance) for field-based research.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of a prototype compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS integrating a high-resolution flat zoom lens camera with a gimbal, a LiDAR altimeter/range finder (50m+), and a lightweight battery system (<100 Wh).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Small boat-based operations in wet conditions (IP45 rating) with temperatures ranging from -20 to +40 degrees Celsius.
Abstract:
A major remaining hurdle with marine species management is to know if, and when, measurable short-term behavioral and/or physiological responses of marine species to sound exposure results in biologically significant or meaningful effects on individuals and/or their populations. Advances in UAS methods and technology present unprecedented opportunities to improve the capacity to collect this robust data with minimal disturbance to marine species. However, while UAS methods have led to significant advances in our understanding of marine species’ behavior, health, and body condition, thus far many obstacles remain including cost, flight duration, size, and image resolution.

This STTR topic seeks to develop a compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS and payloads designed to collect high-resolution photogrammetry imagery to improve marine mammal monitoring, health measurements, and behavioral sequencing. In particular, the prototype device should contain the following technical parameters: high resolution flat zoom lens camera integrated with a gimbal system; highly maneuverable and flexible payload system; lightweight batteries less than 100 Watt hours; an accurate Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) altimeter and range finder integrated with the camera and capable of measuring distances up to 50m or more; and a monitor that is operational in direct sunlight and with polarized sunglasses;. It should be designed for flight times as much as or greater than 40 minutes; be compact and portable in both size and weight such that the UAS and case can fit airline luggage restrictions; have the ability to be quickly calibrated, launched, and caught by hand during small boat-based operations and to tolerate temperature range of -20 degrees to +40 degrees Celsius; and have a minimum weather resistant rating of IP45 to allow for operations in wet conditions; be capable of dynamic home point positioning; and produces minimal noise.

While there are several existing NDAA-compliant drones available in the marketplace, the desired components and capabilities only exist in piecemeal and further, these UAS are prohibitively expensive for the field. The DON seeks to develop a prototype device to be designed and optimized for marine species monitoring, encompassing all the above technical parameters. Critically, this device must be affordable for the marine research community with the target market price between $10,000 - $15,000.

#53 [grant] Persistent, Geochemically-Driven Low-Temperature Power Systems for Subsea Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13137
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsea ISR nodes and UUV docking stations rely on lithium-chemistry batteries that suffer from capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess toxic chemistries, and require resource-intensive physical replacement in contested or ice-covered environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters that generate electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between anoxic marine sediment and oxygenated overlying seawater, utilizing abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode …
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Sub-zero Arctic subsea environments, specifically the interface between marine sediment and overlying seawater.
Abstract:
The Department of the Navy’s expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries. These legacy power sources present severe logistical and operational limitations: they suffer from rapid capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess highly toxic/hazardous chemistries, and require frequent, resource-intensive physical replacement (battery swapping) in highly contested or ice-covered environments.

To achieve persistent, logistics-free ISR, the Navy has a critical need for an environmentally benign, deploy-and-forget power architecture. This STTR topic seeks the development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters to generate continuous electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between the anoxic marine sediment (mud) and the oxygenated overlying seawater. The proposed approach must demonstrate a credible path to 5W power and 24-month endurance in sub-zero Arctic conditions through a ruggedized seabed electrochemical power-harvesting architecture that maximizes long-term energy extraction while using only indigenous sediment microbial communities and naturally occurring geochemical gradients. Proposed solutions may use abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode design, power management, and optimum emplacement.

Biocatalytic Prioritization & Environmental Strictures:

While purely abiotic electrochemical approaches will be considered, approaches that leverage biologically-mediated processes (e.g., utilizing natural biocatalysis to enhance electron transfer at the anode) will be prioritized due to their potential for higher power density and self-renewing longevity.

However, to prevent any risk of ecological disruption to fragile Arctic ecosystems, solutions must strictly rely on harnessing the naturally occurring, indigenous populations already present in the local sediment. The introduction, deployment, or seeding of any exogenous, synthetic, lab-grown, or non-native biological agents (microbes/bacteria) is strictly prohibited.

By utilizing advanced electrode materials that naturally synergize with the local subsea environment, the system must reduce or avoid reliance on deployable primary batteries for the supported payload while ensuring operational viability in extreme cold and high-pressure conditions.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Bottlenecks in using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), including computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Developing a methodology to integrate machine learning (ML) with CFD models of OIDPs.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs) and generic inhaler devices.
Abstract:
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has played a crucial role in providing an alternative bioequivalence (BE) approach for generic orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), in addition to comparative clinical endpoint or pharmacodynamic BE studies, as a relatively cost- and time-efficient complement to benchtop and clinical experiments that has been widely used in developing and assessing generic inhaler devices. However, despite the advances in the power of modern computers, there are still some bottlenecks in using CFD due to computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications. Machine learning (ML) has been gaining more attention as a potential tool to alleviate such limitations that arise in CFD. The purpose of this grant is to develop a methodology to integrate ML with CFD models of OIDPs to promote alternative BE studies to enhance and accelerate the development and approval of generic OIDPs.

#56 [grant] Distributed Multispectral Event-Driven Integrated Sensing and Communications
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13104
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current frame-based processing for remote passive sensors generates large data volumes, causing high energy consumption, processing bottlenecks, and communication delays that hinder time-critical battlespace awareness in resource-limited hardware platforms.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of Multispectral Integrated Neuromorphic Sensing and Communications (MINSC), an event-driven, asynchronous sensing and processing framework utilizing neuromorphic computing for energy-efficient edge inference and low-probability-of-intercept (LPI) data transmission.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Navy Aegis Combat System (ACS) and Aegis Test Bed (ATB) environments for cross-domain operations and remote passive sensing.
Abstract:
The Navy Aegis Program Office is interested in expanding battlespace awareness to support cross-domain operations through the integration of remote passive sensors. Currently, these sensors rely on real-time frame-based processing that generates large volumes of data, requiring significant processing power and energy and creating constraints for resource-limited hardware platforms with finite battery life, processing capabilities, and memory. In addition, transmitting large volumes of data over dynamic communication links can introduce delays and encounter bandwidth limitations that cannot meet time-critical operational needs. The complexity of the battlespace and electromagnetic environment further presents challenges for robust detection, classification, and identification. Advanced remote passive-sensor technologies that enable efficient and distributed sensing and processing will support multidomain operations by providing timely and resilient battlespace awareness. Successful technologies will be transitioned to the Aegis Combat System (ACS) to enhance distributed sensing, accelerate decision-making, and enable cross-domain operations.

The Navy is seeking to develop Multispectral Integrated Neuromorphic Sensing and Communications (MINSC) technology to support endurant remote sensing capability. MINSC is an event-driven sensor featuring low-probability-of-intercept (LPI) data transmission that can timely identify a wide range of objects and transmit the information to remote platforms to integrate into the existing decision-making process. Neuromorphic computing can provide energy efficient, parallel processing, and low-latency framework for passive sensing, edge computing, and remote inference.

Neuromorphic sensors deliver high temporal resolution, asynchronous, energy and bandwidth efficient data inspired by biological vision. The Navy seeks to build an Event-Driven Energy-Efficient Ecosystem to support Endurant Long-Range Sensing and Communications capability. Solutions can be software, neuromorphic hardware, and/or end-to-end neuromorphic system that can deliver robust information and fuse with existing sensors to provide improved tracking, detection, classification, and identification. The Navy is open to innovative ideas of novel system design that can make decisions locally and communicate sparingly or timely send out the event-driven information for remote inference. The intended capability is an integrated remote passive-sensing capability that performs event-driven local sensing and processing, communicating only the information necessary to enhance remote awareness, and fuses with existing sensors to improve tracking, detection, classification and identification.

Distributed MINSC will provide advantages in dynamic environment and resilience to noise and debris associated with military applications. Incorporating event-based multispectral remote sensors with onboard sensors will expand operational battlespace, contribute to robust Common Operational Picture (COP) and enhance situational awareness. It will integrate with the Aegis and permit realistic testing of all threat types and configurations in a dynamic testing environment. Track visualization will be delivered through the existing ACS console Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs). The solution will support current operator track management and decision-making and integrate with the AEGIS Test Bed (ATB) to facilitate system evaluation against more advanced threats. The solution will provide an enhanced capability to address targets in all configurations and optimal engagement options to the sailors, which will increase mission capability and effectiveness against the latest threats.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Advancing basic research in the marine geosciences regarding climate, environmental, crustal, and observatory science objectives.

Abstract:
International Ocean Discovery Program Operations

The International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) serves to advance basic research in the marine geosciences and is supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and its international partners. The science plan, Illuminating Earth's Past, Present, and Future: The International Ocean Discovery Program Science Plan for 2013-2023, provides justification for the United States' participation in the IODP and reflects the top priorities of the international science community. A multi-platform approach is required to address the goals outlined in the IODP science plan, including a non-riser vessel to collect widely-distributed high-resolution cores to address climate, environmental, crustal and observatory science objectives; a heavy riser-equipped vessel to reach the deep sedimentary and crustal layers; and mission-specific platforms to support high-latitude and shallow-water projects.

Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13145

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current Electronic Support (ES) systems rely on Pulse Descriptor Words (PDWs) to detect enemy electronic signals, but modern adversary radar systems using Artificial Intelligence (AI) create complex waveforms that are difficult to identify and characterize using PDWs alone.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of novel machine learning (ML) methods for dynamic and scalable signal representation and compression to describe complex waveforms in a compressed format for RF spectrum knowledge sharing and network-level information dissemination.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Radio frequency (RF) spectrum environments involving emitter detection, classification, and geolocation, with implementation constrained by size, weight, and power (SWaP) requirements.
Abstract:
Current ES systems are designed to detect enemy electronic signals by extracting Pulse Descriptor Words (PDWs) from these signals. Modern radar systems used by adversaries increasingly employ Artificial Intelligence (AI) and it is becoming increasingly difficult to identify, characterize, and represent their waveforms using PDWs alone. To deploy effective Electronic Countermeasures (ECM), there is a need to develop novel methods, including machine learning (ML) [1,2] to enable dynamic and scalable data representation and compression methods that represent complex waveforms, which can be efficiently shared with other nodes in the network. The main goal of this project is to develop advanced techniques for dynamic and scalable signal representation to describe complex waveforms in a compressed format for radio frequency (RF) spectrum knowledge sharing and support network level information dissemination for emitter detection, classification and geolocation representative of activity segmentation [3]. Operational size, weight and power (SWaP) constraints should be determined to implement the proposed algorithms on hardware platforms and the developed techniques should be evaluated and demonstrated with hardware-in-the-loop experiments in relevant spectrum environments.

#61 [grant] Improved Ionosphere D-region Specification for High Frequency Propagation
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13111
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing D-region ionosphere models (D-RAP, IRI, NIMO) fail to capture day-to-day variability, nighttime high-latitude conditions, and the precise shape of the lower D-region (60-70 km), which are necessary for reliable VLF propagation and HF absorption predictions.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of improved measurement techniques, data exploitation, and modeling to specify electron density in the 60-70 km and 80-90 km altitude regions, with a goal of 10% error or 75% improvement over existing models.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ionosphere, specifically the D-region (60-90 km altitude), with emphasis on high latitudes and nighttime conditions.
Abstract:
HF and VLF skywave propagation depend on knowledge of the altitudinal structure of the ionosphere for reliable system operation. The D-region ionosphere, a region typically between 60-90 km altitude above the Earth’s surface, is particularly challenging to predict with sufficient fidelity for skywave mission planning because the region is difficult to measure with in situ measurements. Remote sensing methods provide a limited dataset from which to develop detailed physical and assimilative models that can reliably produce the regional behavior on a day-to-day basis.

Operational models like the D-Region Absorption Product (D-RAP) produce maps of outage areas as a function of radio frequency (RF) to inform HF system users of anticipated degradation or blackouts due to radiation increases. These predictions primarily address HF absorption due to solar X-ray flares at low and mid-latitudes and do not address the VLF propagation use case. While solar X-ray flares are important effects with Navy relevance, the effects of flares typically only last for a few hours and occur 10-20 times a year. For sufficient use in HF absorption and VLF propagation applications, a D-region ionosphere is required to capture seasonal, solar cycle, and day-to-day variability at all latitudes in addition to solar flare phenomenology.

The intended capability is improved D-region specification and forecast in the 60-70 km and 80-90 km altitude regions for VLF propagation and HF absorption, particularly day-to-day variability and in the high latitude regions at night.

Climatological models like the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) produce an altitude profile at D-region altitudes. The IRI model is based on about a hundred historical rocket profiles, so it captures some of the basic day/night, latitudinal, and seasonal variations in the D-region ionosphere but the model does not capture day-to-day variations or solar X-ray flare events. The model may be sufficient for some HF propagation applications but has been shown to be severely deficient in the high latitude region and during nighttime. In addition, the observations used to create the model do not accurately capture the shape of the lower D-region, which is required for VLF propagation applications.

The Next-generation Ionospheric Model for Operations (NIMO) is an assimilative geospace model developed to address operational USN space weather needs in the ionosphere. NIMO harnesses contributions from both near real-time data and state-of-the-art implementation of ionospheric theory to provide hindcasts, nowcasts, and forecasts for operational or research purposes. NIMO is currently configured to assimilate various types of electron density measurements through the Ionospheric Data Assimilation Four-Dimensional (IDA-4D) data assimilation schema. The D-region is not included in the data assimilation process but is simply added in post processing to the bottom of the electron density grid. The D-region model includes influence from changes in the solar conditions, but uses a climatological model for the neutral atmosphere, so it does not capture the day-to-day variability that is seen in the ionosphere.

Key performance Metrics/Goals:

Techniques to improve the global specification and forecast of the D-region ionosphere is sought with particular emphasis on the low latitudes ( 60 degrees). Note: Any measurement techniques should provide measurements or any model should ingest measurements of the D-region and demonstrate improvement over existing models in two key altitude regions: 60-70 km altitude and 80-90 km altitude, which are required for VLF propagation and HF absorption, respectively.

Key parameters include

1. Specify electron density in the 60-70km and 80-90km regions within 10% error. Alternatively, an improvement 75% of the time over existing models is sought.

2. Specification at a temporal cadence of 5-15 minutes

3. Specification at a spatial resolution of 5 degrees in latitude

Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13097

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Conventional Electronic Support Measures (ESM) and wideband radiometer/energy-detection receivers fail to detect stealth radar transmissions, covert datalinks, and distributed sensor relays that use Low Probability of Intercept and Low Probability of Detection (LPI/LPD) techniques to depress emissi…
Method (Mycelium's reading): An AI-driven signal processing framework utilizing sub-noise-floor cyclostationary analysis (spectral correlation density/cyclic autocorrelation), time-frequency deep learning architectures (Wigner-Ville Distributions or Continuous Wavelet Transforms processed by CNN/RNN), adaptive multi-channel de…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Dense electromagnetic operational environments involving covert, highly agile adversarial emissions in naval contexts.
Abstract:
The Navy faces acute operational challenges in intercepting and characterizing covert, highly agile adversarial emissions across dense electromagnetic operational environments. Modern threat systems increasingly utilize Low Probability of Intercept and Low Probability of Detection (LPI/LPD) techniques—such as Direct-Sequence Spread Spectrum (DSSS), ultra-fast frequency hopping (UFLH), wideband Linear Frequency Modulation (LFM), Costas frequency coding, and polyphase pulse compression (e.g., Frank, P1–P4 codes)—deliberately depressing emission power densities below the thermal noise floor [Refs 1, 2]. Consequently, conventional Electronic Support Measures (ESM) and wideband radiometer/energy-detection receivers exhibit severe performance degradation, failing to detect stealth radar transmissions, covert datalinks, and distributed sensor relays. This visibility shortfall undermines the tactical sensor-to-shooter timelines foundational to Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control (CJADC2) and Distributed Maritime Operations (DMO).

To counter advanced stealth emitters, an AI-driven signal processing framework can draw upon several modular algorithmic pathways and candidate techniques, such as:

Sub-Noise-Floor Cyclostationary Analysis: For instance, computing the spectral correlation density (SCD) or cyclic autocorrelation can expose covert signal periodicities (e.g., symbol rates, chipping sequences, and carrier modulation artifacts), isolating structured LPI/LPD waveforms from stationary thermal background noise and Gaussian interference [Refs 3, 4].

Time-Frequency Deep Learning Architectures: As an example for intra-pulse modulation recognition, raw wideband In-phase/Quadrature (I/Q) samples can be transformed into high-resolution time-frequency representations—such as Wigner-Ville Distributions (WVD) or Continuous Wavelet Transforms (CWT)—and processed by deep convolutional or recurrent neural networks (CNN/RNN) to classify polyphase or frequency-coded pulses without requiring prior waveform templates [Refs 5, 6].

Adaptive Multi-Channel De-interleaving: For high-density pulse environments, candidate approaches include reinforcement-learning-guided spectral search or adaptive filter banks to isolate agile hopping channels and separate co-channel, overlapping LPI signals across wide instantaneous bandwidths [Ref 7].

Calibrated Operator Decision Metrics: To support tactical watchstanders, Bayesian neural networks or conformal prediction methods can be applied to generate uncertainty bounds alongside extracted parameters (e.g., pulse repetition intervals, modulation bandwidths, chirp rates), providing validated, interpretable indicators of stealth emitter activity.

SWaP-Constrained Edge Optimization: Potential implementation paths for tactical platforms include neural network quantization, weight pruning, and tensor acceleration to facilitate low-latency inference on Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP)-constrained naval edge computing hardware.

#1 [paper] Funding deadlines act as a zeitgeber for science
Authors: Haining Wang, Jing Su
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.10.758253
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Funders decide which science is paid for. Whether they also shape when it becomes public has been hard to test. Across 376,542 preprints on bioRxiv and medRxiv, the US share rose by 2.3 to 2.7 percentage points in the four weeks before due dates for the main research grant of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and dropped on the date. About one in eleven US preprints in those weeks was attributable to the deadline, and fields that depend least on NIH rose least. Among 15,906 funded investigators, the share of preprints posted in the four weeks before their own deadline was 9% higher than in other four-month cycles, and these preprints resembled the later grant without being more highly cited. Repeated before every due date, this individual surge matches the national peak's timing within a week. NIH's application calendar, like its funding, shapes when US biomedical science becomes public.

#6 [paper] Alternative futures for laboratory medicine in 2050: scenarios and signposts for diagnostic capability contraction.
Authors: Yuji, Koichiro, Yuji, Wakako, Ohnishi, Hiroaki
Venue: Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42723619/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Laboratory medicine has begun to describe its own future, and the images it produces are almost uniformly expansionary. What they rarely contain is a collapse scenario: a future in which the field delivers less than today. A profession planning for 2050 needs one. CONTENT: We summarise what structured foresight offers a clinical readership, entering through the threats quadrant of a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) analysis, and treat the standard taxonomy of futures as a lens, not a required method. We define diagnostic capability contraction as progressive degradation rather than catastrophic disappearance, distinct from retiring tests that add nothing. Six drivers are specified: loss of laboratory-developed tests, reduced test availability, workforce attrition, supplier dependency, geographical access and payment. Evidence comes from three jurisdictions, including Japan, where one regulatory driver produced different outcomes in the same period. We set out four scenarios for 2050, one per generic image, and propose signposts as early-warning indicators, with action thresholds, for the contraction scenario. Estimates of likelihood attach to the indicators, not the futures. SUMMARY: The evidence base is uneven across drivers, and informatively so: what is not anticipated is not measured. The argument applies to our own prior work, expansionary in the same way. OUTLOOK: A set containing a contraction branch gives laboratory leadership what an expansionary set cannot: what to watch for, and when to act. A preferred future chosen without it comes from a shorter list than the field faces. Building a balanced set is work that no small group of authors can do alone.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The current knowledge of food chemical complexity is limited to a narrow set of approximately 150 components, leaving over 100,000 compounds and contaminants ('nutrient dark matter') unquantified and underexplored, creating a bottleneck for predictive nutrition and food safety.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development and testing of validated AI algorithms capable of interpreting and annotating high-throughput foodomics data (e.g., untargeted mass-spectrometry or nuclear magnetic resonance) and predicting/inferring compound presence and concentration via innovative approaches like phylogenetic relati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): High-throughput foodomics data involving hundreds of thousands of compounds across thousands of foods.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- an Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool able to accelerate the analysis of complex foodomics data to speed up the identification, structural characterisation, and quantification of chemicals present in food;

- improving capacity and synergies in foodomics research between academia, research infrastructures and industry.

Scope:

Through food and beverages, the population is exposed to an immense variety of chemicals (as contaminants and as ingredients). The “foodome” is the complete set of compounds present in a food sample at a given time; it includes both endogenous biomolecules (produced through a species' metabolic processes) and exogenous compounds (natural and synthetic substances from production, processing, handling, and packaging). The current knowledge is largely confined to a narrow set of approximately 150 food components catalogued by traditional databases. These components represent only a very small fraction of the total chemical complexity present in foods, while thousands (>100,000) of compounds and contaminants remain largely unquantified and underexplored. Understanding this “nutrient dark matter” would require identifying, cataloguing and quantifying the full spectrum of substances present in our food and present in accessible, AI-ready databases. The need for such information is today a bottleneck to make the nutrition field predictive and data driven, and has the potential to make food processing more efficient in bringing new foods items on the market. Efforts to create such datasets are underway but owing to the quantity of samples (hundreds of thousands of compounds across thousands of foods), such databases often rely on high-throughput experimental methods which do not allow a precise characterisation of the molecules identified.

Proposals should address the following activities:

- develop and test validated AI algorithms capable of interpreting and annotating high-throughput foodomics data, for instance from untargeted mass-spectrometry or nuclear magnetic resonance;

- the AI algorithms should be capable to predict or infer the presence and concentration of compounds based on (incomplete) foodomics data via innovative approaches, for instance by considering phylogenic relationships between species. Moreover, this should help identify analytical methods and potential food safety hazards based on their similarity to known compounds;

- develop a European research and innovation network between Member States and Associated Countries in food exposome research to support the development, standardization, valorisation and dissemination of the AI results and considering existing initiatives such as the Centre for Excellence in the Periodic Table of Food Initiative from Wageningen University.

The multi-actor approach is encouraged. Proposals should include industry in the consortia and academia, startups, SMEs and international initiatives. Collaboration with international partners is encouraged as well as with existing private companies in the EU/Associated countries.

Technology Readiness Level - Technology readiness level expected from completed projects

Activities are expected to start from TRL 5 in order to achieve TRL 7 by the end of the project – see General Annex B.

#20 [paper] CY 2027 Medicare PFS and OPPS proposed rules: key implications for wound care across facility and non-facility settings
Authors: William H Tettelbach, Luis Arencibia, Diane Weiss
Venue: International Journal of Tissue Repair
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.63676/eya7yd09
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) CY 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) proposed rule contains several provisions with direct implications for wound care delivery. The proposals include lower physician conversion factors, a new 50% payment reduction when separately identifiable office/outpatient evaluation and management (E/M) services are furnished on the same day as 0-, 10-, or 90-day global procedures, replacement of HCPCS G2211 with percentage-based modifiers, continued evolution of cellular, acellular, and matrix-like product (CAMP) payment, national valuation of real-time bacterial fluorescence wound imaging, practice-expense reform, and changes to remote physiologic and therapeutic monitoring. The same-day E/M proposal is especially important for wound clinicians because interventions such as sharp surgical debridement are commonly performed and medically necessary during wound care encounters. Importantly, as currently drafted, the proposal is limited to office/outpatient E/M services, which in wound care are commonly furnished in private physician offices and hospital outpatient departments (HOPDs). It does not currently extend to appropriately reported home/residence or nursing-facility E/M services, including those furnished in POS 12, 13, 31, and 32. CMS is seeking comment on whether the policy should later extend to other E/M categories. Facility and non-facility effects also differ because hospital outpatient departments receive separate facility reimbursement while independent office and mobile practices bear practice expense directly. This summary reviews the proposed policies most relevant to wound care and distinguishes their expected application across common sites of service.

Abstract:
Abstract Each new lightweight YOLO release reports higher COCO accuracy and lower CPU latency, and applied studies commonly build on the newest release. Recent multi-dataset comparisons show that a newer release need not win downstream, but they rarely separate a model difference from training-seed and test-set variability. We trained six nano-scale generations with three seeds on floating-debris and PASCAL VOC subsamples and three generations on VisDrone (49 runs), and compared them with paired test-image resampling. YOLO26n led YOLOv8n by 5.98 percentage points of mAP@0.5:0.95 on VOC but trailed it by 1.62 points on floating debris and 0.69 points on VisDrone, with all three bootstrap intervals excluding zero. The floating-debris deficit occurred in every object-size stratum and persisted under the default training recipe. These pairwise contrasts were stable, whereas the complete six-model ranking survived in only 55.1% and 16.4% of resamples. On three CPUs, randomized interleaved timing gave latency reductions of 1–12% from YOLOv8n to YOLO11n and 14–22% from YOLO11n to YOLO26n, against about 30% and 31% implied by the published tables. A release-level gain is therefore a hypothesis to test on the target data and processor. Pairwise intervals, not full rankings, should decide an upgrade or a baseline.

The project consists of a 21-episode video series produced during an 18-day, 4500-km field campaign to service a network of mineral dust collectors deployed across alpine, desert, and urban environments in Utah, Nevada, and Idaho as part of the NSF-funded DUST^2 Critical Zone project. Each episode in the Tour is anchored to a specific site and task, such as arriving at a collector, observing the surrounding landscape, and retrieving samples, and uses that moment to introduce focused concepts related to mineral dust, soil formation, snow–hydrology interactions, climate variability, ecosystem function, and human influence. This approach foregrounds scientific process, uncertainty, and interdisciplinarity, allowing viewers to observe how geoscience knowledge is generated in real settings. The communication strategy emphasizes authenticity, continuity across episodes, and visual engagement with landscapes, transforming a routine monitoring campaign into a coherent outreach narrative. Mineral dust serves as a unifying theme through which otherwise disparate environments and disciplines are connected, illustrating the Critical Zone as a laterally linked system rather than a set of isolated sites. The Collectors Tour also reflects lessons learned from long-term communication efforts, including the value of consistency, the power of storytelling grounded in genuine field practice, and the importance of acknowledging collaboration, logistics, and uncertainty. As a case study, the Collectors Tour offers a replicable model for integrating science communication into ongoing field research and contributes to broader discussions on effective strategies for communicating Earth and space science to diverse publics.

#20 [paper] Research Priorities for a Circular Economy for Plastic Sustainability in the Caribbean
Authors: Anne Marie Mozrall, Jessica P. Feliz Garrido, P. Tejada-Tejada, Akeem Mohammed, Brigitte Mildred Roldán Ramírez, Alana Malinde S.N. Lancaster, Iris Odett Atencio, Diego Batista
Venue: Environmental Science & Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5c16637
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Caribbean countries bear a disproportionate burden of marine plastic pollution because of their small landmass, high population density, and insufficient waste management infrastructure. Many Caribbean nations depend on informal, unmanaged landfills, underscoring an urgent need for more resilient, sustainable systems. This perspective synthesizes existing data to map the region’s plastic waste landscape and leverages regional expertise to identify key research priorities. This work emerged from interdisciplinary international professionals and members of the CEPlaSt (circular economy for plastic sustainability) network. A major barrier to circularity is the lack of reliable data on waste composition and flows, alongside stark infrastructure disparities across the wider Caribbean region. Addressing these gaps through targeted investment and region-specific planning is essential to modernize waste systems, reduce plastic emissions, and advance a sustainable Caribbean plastic circular economy.

Abstract:
The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the problem of the mandatory publication of scientific results in journals indexed in the international scientometric databases Scopus and Web of Science, in the context of modern Ukrainian scientific discourse. The relevance of the study is due to the fact that these databases are increasingly perceived not only as a tool for integrating Ukrainian science into the global academic space, increasing the visibility of research results and ensuring certain quality standards, but also as a de facto mandatory condition for a scientific career, certification, accreditation of educational programs and defense of dissertations. Under such conditions, bibliometric indicators often begin to replace a substantive assessment of scientific novelty, methodological soundness and social significance of research, and publication activity itself becomes an end in itself. The paper proves that the problem of mandatory publication in Scopus and Web of Science cannot be considered only as a technical or administrative issue. It has a deep theoretical, methodological, institutional and ethical dimension. On the one hand, international indexing contributes to the openness of science, its inclusion in global communication networks, increased citations and dissemination of research results. On the other hand, excessive formalization of publication requirements creates risks of commodification of knowledge, when a scientific result is evaluated not so much by its truth, novelty or benefit to society, but by its ability to meet market and bureaucratic criteria. This, in turn, contributes to the spread of practices of academic capitalism, the emergence of a shadow market for intermediary services, as well as the intensification of the activities of so-called "predatory" publications that imitate scientific communication without proper peer review and compliance with ethical standards. Particular attention is paid to the methodological imbalance in the assessment of science. It is shown that a unified approach, based mainly on quantitative metrics - the number of publications, citations, Hirsch index, impact factor of journals, grant funding amounts - does not take into account the specifics of individual fields of knowledge. First of all, this applies to socio-humanitarian, artistic and some social disciplines, which are characterized by local issues, national and cultural conditioning of the subject, the importance of Ukrainian studies discourse and the need to use national languages ​​and professional publications. In such cases, focusing exclusively on English-language international journals is not always methodologically justified, and sometimes even narrows the possibilities of fully presenting research results that are important for national security, cultural identity and development of the state. The article also analyzes the institutional consequences of the introduction of strict requirements for publications in Scopus/WoS. It is established that the transformation of publication from a tool of scientific communication into a formal bureaucratic marker leads to a distortion of researchers' motivation, increased publication pressure, fragmentation of results, an increase in the number of formal or insignificant articles, as well as inefficient spending of budgetary and private funds. For many scientists, especially young researchers, postgraduate students and teachers, such a system creates additional barriers to reach academic recognition, forcing them to adapt to formal criteria that do not always adequately reflect the real scientific value of the work. Emphasis is placed on the financial pressures that accompany the modern publishing model. The text emphasizes that significant author's fees for publication in international journals, long review periods, as well as limited deadlines for the completion of scientific topics create unequal conditions for Ukrainian researchers. #7 [paper] Autonomy without immunity: conventionality control and the limits of sporting sovereignty in the Inter-American system
Authors: Roberto Leonardo Cruz-Núñez, Hugo Armando Aguilar Brito, Andherson Jhordan Aguirre-Lanegra, Nuccia Seminario-Hurtado
Venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2026.1949642
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Professional athletes and clubs can compete only if they accept the jurisdiction of an arbitral tribunal seated outside their own country. International federations rely on that arrangement to claim immunity from judicial review; this article calls that claim sporting sovereignty. European courts have narrowed it by holding that compulsory sports arbitration must satisfy fair-trial guarantees, but protection there still depends on the courts of the state where the federation is seated and on a narrow reading of public policy, so the substance of a discrimination complaint may go unexamined. This article asks how far Articles 8 and 25 of the American Convention on Human Rights limit the rule-making authority of transnational sports organisations in states parties, through conventionality control, the duty of every domestic authority to test the rules it applies against the treaty. It proceeds by doctrinal legal analysis and by comparing the European and Inter-American standards of review, and it examines four jurisdictions: Peru, Colombia, Chile and Brazil. Inter-American judicial guarantees attach to the function a body exercises rather than to its formal character; they reach private power through the state's duty to ensure rights; and every domestic authority must apply them of its own motion, wherever the federation is seated. The comparison shows that Brazil and Chile channel contractual and employment disputes between player and club to the state courts, and that Colombia protects players through the constitutional action of tutela, so that closure is confined to disciplinary, eligibility and competition matters; Peru is the exception, having legislated the primacy of federation rules without such limits. In the Peruvian and Colombian cases examined, the delays that harmed a club and a player came from federation bodies overrunning their own deadlines, which undermines the argument that speed requires exemption from review. Sporting sovereignty is thus a delegated and conditioned authority. The article proposes a criterion of conditioned autonomy under which the power of federations is legitimate where it pursues a permissible aim, observes procedural guarantees, decides while a decision can still serve the person affected, and respects the substantive limit of human dignity and non-discrimination.

#13 [paper] Point-of-Care Ultrasound After Medical Screening Exam Reduces Time to Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy Diagnosis and Surgery
Authors: Victoria L. Morris, Michael Vu, Yongsu Lee, Evelyn Park, Ravi Soni, Ryan Walsh, Rachel Bower, John Waller-Delarosa
Venue: Western Journal of Emergency Medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.53932
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction: Ectopic pregnancy remains the leading cause of first-trimester maternal mortality. Delays in diagnosis and operative management increase morbidity and may be exacerbated by emergency department (ED) crowding. We evaluated whether integration of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) into the medical screening exam of pregnant patients—the obstetric medical screening exam—was associated with improved timeliness of care for patients with surgically managed ectopic pregnancy. Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of adult patients undergoing operative management for ruptured ectopic pregnancy between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2023, at a county safety-net hospital. The obstetric screening exam was implemented July 12, 2021, and incorporated focused transabdominal pelvic and right upper quadrant ultrasound into the initial ED evaluation, often prior to bed assignment. The primary outcome was time from ED arrival to operating room (OR). Secondary outcomes included time to obstetric consultation, time to hospital admission, ED length of stay (LOS), and POCUS use. Nonparametric testing was used for skewed time data. Logistic regression evaluated the odds of reaching the OR within four hours. Patient-level interrupted time series analysis assessed temporal trends. Results: A total of 150 patients were included (87 pre- and 63 post-implementation). Median arrival-to-OR time decreased from 516 minutes (interquartile range [IQR] 324–709.5) to 391 minutes (IQR 220–619), a 125-minute reduction (P = .020; bootstrap 95% CI, 8–233). The proportion of patients reaching the OR within four hours increased from 16.1% to 31.8% (odds ratio 2.42; 95% CI, 1.11–5.29; P = .02). Time to obstetric consultation (210 vs 146 minutes; P = .003), time to hospital admission (345 vs 250 minutes; P = .005), and ED LOS (451 vs 367 minutes; P = .03) were all reduced. Point-of-care ultrasound use increased from 41.4% to 66.7% (P < .001), while the remainder underwent radiology ultrasound. Interrupted time series analysis demonstrated no significant immediate change after implementation (P = .790), but a significant postintervention trend toward reduced arrival-to-OR time (−0.45 minutes/day, P = .01). Conclusion: Embedding POCUS into the medical screening examination in triage was associated with sustained improvement in operative timeliness for ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Early diagnostic integration within ED workflow may mitigate system-level delays in time-sensitive obstetric emergencies.

#14 [paper] Generating ACGME-constraint-aware surgery residency call schedule software with the assistance of agentic coding large language models

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s44186-026-00601-8
