Abstract:
Abstract Background Manual creation of a surgery residency call schedule is a labor-intensive process that adds to the administrative burden of a chief resident while often producing suboptimal fairness and work distribution. While commercial scheduling software exists, many programs struggle with inflexibility, high costs, and an inability to accommodate program-specific constraints. Methods We developed a scheduling software platform using AI-assisted development tools (Codex, Claude Code), both commercially available agentic coding environments. The system applies a rule-based, weekend-first assignment hierarchy with randomized tie-breaking under a search budget fixed in advance, then performs iterative weekday assignment, accommodating vacation requests and discrete call-shift swapping. The validation roster modeled a single general surgery residency program: 55 residents (32 categorical and 2 preliminary general surgery residents spanning PGY 1 through PGY 6; 20 off-service rotators from other programs; and 1 fellow) distributed across 10 call pools. Three prespecified call-related ACGME constraints were enforced (at least 4 days off per 28-day period, call no more frequently than every third night averaged over 4 weeks, and no consecutive 24-hour call). The 80-hour weekly maximum and the 24-hour period free of all clinical and educational responsibility were not evaluated, as both depend on activity the call calendar does not capture. We evaluated the system with 100 independent full-year runs (July 1 to June 30), each generated end-to-end across all call pools and months under an independently randomized vacation distribution. Compliance and fairness were evaluated at the level of the individual call-pool month (service-month), the unit at which a monthly schedule is produced; fairness and workload metrics were computed across the program’s in-program surgery residents. Results We generated 12,000 service-month schedules over 100 independent full-year runs. 99.2% (11,906) satisfied all prespecified call-related constraints with no violations detected by the internal validation engine. Forty-five of the 100 full-year runs required no manual intervention in any service-month, and none required it in more than 4 of its 120. Manual review of 120 randomly selected service-months by two authors, without reference to the validator’s output, agreed with it in 120 of 120 cases. Monthly fairness, defined within each call pool and month as the range (maximum minus minimum) of call shifts or weekends assigned per resident, showed a shift range ≤ 1 in 65.4% of service-months (mean 1.84, SD 2.15) and perfect weekend equity (range = 0) in 42.5%, with 86.6% achieving a weekend range ≤ 1 (mean 0.71, SD 0.70). Mean full-year generation time was 108.8 s (SD 59.1). Residents averaged 18.65 weekends (SD 3.13) and 78.23 call days (SD 5.49) per year. Conclusions This automated scheduling system generates resident call schedules that satisfy the prespecified call-related ACGME constraints, optimizes fairness across multiple dimensions, accommodates complex vacation requirements, handles cross-pool coordination, and flags the service-months it cannot resolve within its search budget rather than emitting a non-compliant schedule. These results provide construct validity evidence that optimization algorithms combined with careful constraint specification can eliminate the great majority of the administrative burden of manual scheduling while improving schedule quality and equity.

#15 [paper] Just Another Manic Monday in the Call Center: When Equal Demand Does Not Produce Equal Service
Authors: Michael Douglas, Eric Kyper
Venue: Archives of Business Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.14738/abr.1410.12332
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Call centers ordinarily explain service-level variation through demand, service time, staffing, routing, and customer patience. Yet performance may also vary systematically by weekday even when workload is comparable. This study examines a Monday effect in operational data from a large U.S. insurance-service organization. The dataset contained 13,024 intraday records across 32 business days, 37 reporting queues, and 20 business groups. Because call counts were cumulative within day, the primary analysis used each queue’s final daily snapshot, producing 1,127 active queue-day observations. Monday service level averaged .658, compared with .715 on Tuesday, although log-transformed call volume did not differ significantly between the two days. Ordinary least squares models with queue-clustered standard errors showed that Monday remained associated with a 5.1-percentage-point reduction in service level after controlling for call volume, average handle time, and business-group fixed effects. The result persisted across all-weekday, logit-transformed, volume-threshold, nonboundary, weighted, paired-queue, and nonparametric sensitivity analyses. The findings distinguish workload effects from weekday effects and suggest that start-of-week operational frictions may impair service beyond what volume alone explains. Because staffing, schedule adherence, absence, backlog, and call-mix measures were unavailable, the analysis identifies a robust temporal pattern rather than a causal mechanism. The study contributes to service-operations research by treating weekday as an operational state variable and offers managers a focused diagnostic agenda for Monday readiness.

#17 [paper] Do Firms Expect the Deadline to Move? Expiry Dates, Repeated Extensions, and AI Decision-Makers in Japanese Corporate Tax Special Measures
Authors: 勉 矢作
Venue: Open Science Framework
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/dsm7j

Abstract:
Many tax incentives carry an expiry date. A deadline should pull investment forward into the final year before expiry (a time notch in the sense of Slemrod 2013). If a measure has been extended many times, however, firms may expect another extension, and the deadline may stop working as a deadline. The literature on time notches (Slemrod 2013; House and Shapiro 2008; Cashin and Unayama 2016) and the literature on transition policy (Kaplow 1986, 2003; Shaviro 2000) have developed separately. This study links them by asking whether the history of extensions changes the response to an expiry date. Study 1 uses the annual reports that the Minister of Finance submits to the Diet under the Act on Transparency of Special Tax Measures (2010). These reports give, for each corporate tax special measure, the number of corporations applying it and the amount applied, for fiscal years ending on or after 1 April 2011. Study 2 asks how large language models (LLMs), acting as managers of a small firm, respond to the same kind of deadline. As firms delegate tax and investment decisions to AI, the response to deadlines may change. Study 2 tests the prediction, registered in OSF pw5fz, that LLM agents follow what is written: they respond to the expiry date stated in the statute and ignore an extension history unless it is written in front of them.

A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#7 [paper] Comparing Surface and Subsurface Marine Heatwaves in Ocean Reanalyses

Abstract. Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly recognised as major drivers of ecological and socio‑economic disruption, yet their subsurface expression remains poorly constrained due to sparse in situ observations. Here, we characterise properties such as the intensity, duration, and heterogeneity of subsurface MHWs using the Copernicus Global Ocean Reanalysis Ensemble Product (GREP). MHWs are detected across multiple depths (0.5–200 m) using a consistent percentile-based thresholding, applied to three reanalysis members (CGLORSv7, GLORYS2v4, ORAS5) and evaluated against well‑documented historical events. All reanalyses successfully capture the timing and general evolution of major, well-known surface expressions of MHW events when compared against the ESA Climate Change Initiative SST dataset in given areas of interest, such as, for example, events of 2011 in Western Australia, of 2015 in the Northeast Pacific Blob, and of 2006 in the Mediterranean Sea. Here, it is also shown that anomalies frequently penetrate below the mixed layer, down to 100–150 m. On a global scale, there is a positive bias of about 15 days in the mean duration for all the events with respect to satellite SST data, consistent with the limited eddy-resolving capability of the eddy-permitting GREP reanalyses, the additional smoothing introduced by ensemble averaging and the difference between the different representative depths of SST in satellite observations and models. Global diagnostics reveal that MHWs extending into the subsurface are more persistent, spatially heterogeneous, and characterised by sharper onset and decline rates than shallow events, particularly in the tropics, western boundary currents, and the Southern Ocean. Mixed‑layer variability strongly modulates the vertical propagation of anomalies, underscoring the role of vertical mixing in shaping subsurface extremes. Our results highlight both the value and limitations of current reanalyses for subsurface MHW characterisation, emphasising the need for ensemble‑based approaches to quantify uncertainty.

#9 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event

Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

#2 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly

Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#3 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le

Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

This study validated a forecasting tool for heatwave-related emergency department (ED) demand across four clusters comprising the emergency care network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland. Methods: This retrospective, ecological, time-series study modeled daily mean temperature and ED presentations using a distributed lag non-linear model framework with autoregressive and calendar adjustment components. Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) negatively impact marine ecosystems and coastal economies. Here, we evaluate whether a preemptive, short-term, localized surface emission of sea salt aerosols (marine cloud brightening, MCB) can mitigate the impacts of a predicted MHW without creating significant effects beyond the intervention zone. As a case study, we apply MCB to the 2019 Northeast Pacific MHW, "The Blob 2.0," using a global climate model seasonal-to-multiyear predictability ensemble. By demonstrating local efficacy and minor remote impacts for mitigating the Blob 2.0, this work motivates further study of whether localized and temporary climate interventions can safely and effectively mitigate MHWs.

Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Headline accuracy in disaster early-warning studies often masks class imbalance, temporal drift, and spatial extrapolation error.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A leakage-aware evaluation protocol using chronological splits and spatial hold-outs, applying logistic regression for flood severity and histogram-based gradient boosting for heat-event proxies.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Two modules: 4,548 flood events from 155 gauges (split by time) and a heat-event proxy based on IMD gridded daily maximum temperature (1° grid, 1951–2024) across 338 eligible cells.
Abstract:
Disaster early-warning studies often report headline accuracy, which can hide class imbalance, temporal drift and spatial extrapolation error. This paper applies a leakage-aware evaluation protocol to two research modules. The first is flood severity classification among 4,548 recorded flood events from 155 gauges, evaluated with a chronological split (training before 2010, validation 2010–2014, test 2015–2020). The second is a heat-event proxy built from IMD gridded daily maximum temperature (1° grid, 1951–2024). A grid-cell day is positive when it belongs to a run of at least three consecutive hot days, where a hot day exceeds the cell's 1961–1990 calendar-day 90th percentile and its baseline climatological Tmax exceeds 35 °C. The proxy covers 338 eligible cells, April–June target dates and 1991–2024. It is not an official IMD declaration. For flood severity, validation PR-AUC selected logistic regression, which achieved test balanced accuracy 0.6445 and ROC-AUC 0.6483 against a majority-class balanced accuracy of 0.5000. For the heat-event proxy, histogram-based gradient boosting was selected by validation PR-AUC (0.5811). On the 2020–2024 test period it achieved balanced accuracy 88.82%, recall 90.36%, ROC-AUC 0.9548 and PR-AUC 0.5813, but produced 18,415 false positives at threshold 0.50. A simple persistence rule had higher F1 (0.591 against 0.457) and fewer false positives. A spatial hold-out over 51 unseen cells gave balanced accuracy 87.33%. Attributions are associations, not causes, and these results do not establish operational early-warning performance.

Nano, Small and Micro Enterprises (NSMEs), represent the final linkage within last-mile delivery of food, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) commodities, in Kenya's arid and semi-arid regions; however, these entities remain excluded from formal disaster risk management and project planning frameworks. The objective of this study was to determine the extent to which Community Based Early Warning Systems (CBEWS) influence Resilience-Oriented Project Planning amongst NSMEs in Marsabit County, specifically regarding access to early warning information, translation of that information into preparedness, and mechanisms that enable such transition. The findings of the study indicated that while drought and flood forecasts have Increased their reach to Marsabit's trading community; access does not consistently translate into planning: fewer than half of the enterprises participated in the study used climate information to prepare for shocks, and almost none had written continuity plans. Successful translation occurred primarily when scientific forecasting was integrated with locally trusted Indigenous Technical Knowledge, disseminated via trader networks and radio broadcasts, and coupled with trigger-based financing protocols. #15 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5

Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

#16 [paper] Atmosphere-Driven Compound Extremes: Record Marine Heatwave and Phytoplankton Bloom in the Ross Sea During Summer 2022-2023

Abstract:
Abstract We document an extreme marine heatwave (MHW) in the eastern Ross Sea during the 2022–2023 austral summer (DJF), the most intense thermal event in the satellite record. Using satellite-retrieved sea surface temperature (SST), ocean colour, sea ice, and atmospheric-oceanic reanalysis data, we show that the eastern Ross Sea experienced a Category IV (extreme) MHW during this season, with the regional-mean cumulative intensity reaching 127.22 °C·days in January 2023 and summer-mean SST anomalies locally peaking at approximately +2.5 °C above the climatological mean. Summer-mean chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) concentration reached 3.67 mg m⁻³, the highest value observed in the eastern Ross Sea since satellite ocean-colour records began in 1997. The ecological response followed a threshold-dependent sequence: early sea-ice retreat initially removed light limitation, followed later by a strong Chl-a increase as sustained warming and upper-ocean restratification favoured bloom development. In contrast, persistent ice cover in Terra Nova Bay prevented a comparable thermal or biological response. A meridional wind dipole drove divergent ice transport and the early expansion of the eastern Ross Sea polynya, while low-cloud cover decreased by up to 15.43%, increasing downward surface shortwave radiation by 64.09 W m⁻². Subsurface warming remained confined to the upper continental-shelf waters south of approximately 73°S, suggesting that local atmosphere–ice–radiation interactions contributed more strongly to the event than heat transport associated with ocean circulation. These results identify a distinctly polar pathway through which atmospheric forcing can generate compound thermal and biological extremes, highlighting the importance of local sea-ice coupling in shaping future Antarctic coastal productivity.

Abstract:

#1 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

#2 [paper] Reply on RC2 Authors: Peihao Yang, Guodong Ye Year: 2026 Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-262-cc1 Still open/current: yes Abstract: Abstract. A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. After training on multiple CMIP6 ensemble members, the constructed models are evaluated for their predictive capacity regarding MHW in the SCS. The results also show that these machine learning-based methods can perform comparably to the existing dynamic models in terms of prediction performance, and in some cases even outperform the latter. Furthermore, by incorporating machine learning interpretability techniques, the key physical processes can also be elucidated from these predictions. That is to say, the new method is not a traditional "black box", but rather an effective tool that can possess certain physical transparency and scientific interpretability.

#3 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#4 [paper] Model-Based Marine Heatwave Detection with Eddy Diagnostics in the Adriatic Sea: Regional Insights with Global Relevance
Authors: Eurida Liyana, Francesco Memmola, Pierpaolo Falco
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15010054/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intensification, increasing frequency, and duration of marine heatwave (MHW) events, particularly in vulnerable semi-enclosed coastal basins like the Adriatic Sea.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Integration of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm and analysis of long-term observational temperature data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Adriatic Sea (AS).
Abstract:
Marine heatwave (MHW) events are intensifying globally, doubling in frequency and increasing in duration and spatial distribution over recent decades. Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. In this study, we assess the capability of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to detect and simulate MHW events in the AS. We integrate this modeling framework with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm, alongside comprehensive analysis of long-term observational temperature data, to investigate the role of mesoscale eddies in modulating surface and subsurface MHW evolution. Results demonstrate that ROMS effectively reproduces the timing and spatial patterns of historical MHWs in the AS, showing strong agreement between modeled and observed MHWs, with eddy structures frequently coinciding with subsurface thermal anomalies preceding MHWs. These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

#5 [paper] A robust framework for evaluating marine heatwave risk in surface and seafloor waters.
Authors: Stephanie Helen Woolley, Moninya Roughan, Robert Mason, Nicholas R. Perkins, Timothy C. Ingleton, Skipton N. C. Woolley, Joel Williams
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10915846/v1
Still open/current: yes

#6 [paper] Recent extreme heatwaves are no match for future events
Authors: Philipp Aglas-Leitner, S. Perkins-Kirkpatrick, Lukas Brunner, S. Undorf, F. Aglas-Leitner, E. Fischer, D. Stone
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76809-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21 st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

#7 [paper] Atmosphere-Driven Compound Extremes: Record Marine Heatwave and Phytoplankton Bloom in the Ross Sea During Summer 2022-2023
Authors: Zehao Wang, Shaoyin Wang, Zhu Zhu, Zixin Wei, Fukai Peng
Venue: Environmental Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ae9780
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract We document an extreme marine heatwave (MHW) in the eastern Ross Sea during the 2022–2023 austral summer (DJF), the most intense thermal event in the satellite record. Using satellite-retrieved sea surface temperature (SST), ocean colour, sea ice, and atmospheric-oceanic reanalysis data, we show that the eastern Ross Sea experienced a Category IV (extreme) MHW during this season, with the regional-mean cumulative intensity reaching 127.22 °C·days in January 2023 and summer-mean SST anomalies locally peaking at approximately +2.5 °C above the climatological mean. Summer-mean chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) concentration reached 3.67 mg m⁻³, the highest value observed in the eastern Ross Sea since satellite ocean-colour records began in 1997. The ecological response followed a threshold-dependent sequence: early sea-ice retreat initially removed light limitation, followed later by a strong Chl-a increase as sustained warming and upper-ocean restratification favoured bloom development. In contrast, persistent ice cover in Terra Nova Bay prevented a comparable thermal or biological response. A meridional wind dipole drove divergent ice transport and the early expansion of the eastern Ross Sea polynya, while low-cloud cover decreased by up to 15.43%, increasing downward surface shortwave radiation by 64.09 W m⁻². Subsurface warming remained confined to the upper continental-shelf waters south of approximately 73°S, suggesting that local atmosphere–ice–radiation interactions contributed more strongly to the event than heat transport associated with ocean circulation. These results identify a distinctly polar pathway through which atmospheric forcing can generate compound thermal and biological extremes, highlighting the importance of local sea-ice coupling in shaping future Antarctic coastal productivity.

#8 [paper] Depth-Resolved Marine Heatwave Prediction in the Levantine Basin
Authors: D. N. H. Weerasinghe, S. Viswakula
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24030956
Still open/current: yes

#9 [paper] Deeper Structure of Marine Heatwaves: Glider-Detected Anomalies in the North Sea
Authors: Charlotte Z. Reed, Victor-Alexandru Darvariu, Nick Hawes, Helen Louise Johnson
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15009434/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Satellite-derived sea surface temperatures cannot always be used to estimate the spatial structure, duration, intensity, and drivers for temperatures below the ocean surface.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Comparison of near-continuous autonomous underwater glider observations with GLORYS12V1 ocean reanalysis and regional heat content analysis.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): North Sea, specifically off the East coast of Scotland and the area between the Shetland and Orkney Islands.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves are often characterized by sea surface temperatures derived from satellite data. However, surface anomalies cannot always be used to estimate the spatial structure, duration, intensity, and drivers for temperatures below the surface. In this study, we use near-continuous autonomous underwater glider observations from a deployment off the East coast of Scotland, accompanied by the GLORYS12V1 ocean reanalysis, to examine recent high temperature anomalies in the North Sea. Glider observations show that warm and cold anomalies can be stronger below the surface than what is represented in the reanalysis, and discrepancies are often associated with differences in the timing and depth of mixed layer depth changes. Regional heat content analysis indicates that anomalies within the mixed layer are strongly influenced by surface heat fluxes, while anomalies below are more closely associated with advective heat transport, particularly inflow from the North Atlantic between the Shetland and Orkney Islands. A prolonged anomaly in 2024-2026 persisted below the surface across multiple seasons, suggesting that subsurface heat storage may hold memory between surface events. Our results demonstrate that marine heatwaves in shelf seas can have substantial subsurface structure, even in a relatively shallow and seasonally well-mixed region. Sustained glider observations can provide key observations alongside satellite and reanalysis products, improving analysis and validation of subsurface temperature anomalies in shelf seas.

#10 [paper] Rethinking Marine Heatwaves: Towards a Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress
Authors: Natalija Dunić, Krešimir Ruić, Ivica Vilibić
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15011394/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard marine heatwave (MHW) definitions rely on statistical temperature anomalies relative to a climatological baseline, which does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic examples used to demonstrate the estimation of response functions from biological observations and the derivation of binary event definitions.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

#11 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). #1 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

#2 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

These results highlight the importance of the climate reference framework when interpreting how heatwave lifecycle characteristics may change under continued warming.

Abstract:
Abstract. Wind-driven upwelling of subsurface ocean waters to the surface ensures nutrient-rich waters reach the epipelagic zone, supporting some of the most diverse ecosystems and largest fish stocks in the global ocean. In early 2025, the Gulf of Panama experienced a collapse of the local upwelling system not previously observed in historical records, with notable impacts on regional physical and biogeochemical conditions. Predictability of upwelling collapse in relatively local systems on seasonal timescales has yet to be assessed. Here, the predictability of upwelling in the Gulf of Panama is explored in an operational seasonal forecasting system. First, the extreme weakening of the northerly jets driving upwelling and the corresponding extreme sea surface temperatures of 2025 are shown to have been accurately predicted a season in advance. By validating against a high-resolution global ocean reanalysis, an increase in temperature forecast skill with depth is uncovered, making the case for exploiting subsurface information for improved early-warning and description of upwelling events. Lastly, the occurrence of warm upwelling, specifically in 1998, raises a discussion of the most suitable upwelling indicators for the region. The seasonal forecast system sufficiently resolves wind stress-derived Ekman Pumping and the exceptionally weak vertical ocean velocity in 2025. This study demonstrates the capability of seasonal forecasts to provide early warning of upwelling collapse.

#2 [paper] Funding deadlines act as a zeitgeber for science
Authors: Haining Wang, Jing Su
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.10.758253
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Funders decide which science is paid for. Whether they also shape when it becomes public has been hard to test. Across 376,542 preprints on bioRxiv and medRxiv, the US share rose by 2.3 to 2.7 percentage points in the four weeks before due dates for the main research grant of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and dropped on the date. About one in eleven US preprints in those weeks was attributable to the deadline, and fields that depend least on NIH rose least. Among 15,906 funded investigators, the share of preprints posted in the four weeks before their own deadline was 9% higher than in other four-month cycles, and these preprints resembled the later grant without being more highly cited. Repeated before every due date, this individual surge matches the national peak's timing within a week. NIH's application calendar, like its funding, shapes when US biomedical science becomes public.

Authors: Crislaine Zurilda Silveira, Camila de Azevedo Gibbon, Patrícia da Silva Neubert, Fabio Lorensi do Canto

Abstract:
The time elapsed between the submission and publication of an article is an indicator of a journal's editorial workflow speed. This study aims to analyze the publication time of journals in the SciELO Brazil Collection, considering the stages of submission, acceptance, and publication, across different subject areas. The research is exploratory and descriptive in nature, based on data extracted from SciELO Analytics regarding 18.540 articles published in 2025 by 326 journals. Descriptive statistics were used to measure editorial times, alongside qualitative analyses to compare the results with existing literature. The results indicate that the average time between submission and acceptance was 192.4 days, and between acceptance and publication on SciELO, it was 165.5 days. The complete publication cycle ranged from 234.9 days in Engineering to 418.7 days in the Humanities, with an overall average of 357.9 days, exceeding the 180-day limit recommended by SciELO. The Humanities and Applied Social Sciences areas showed greater heterogeneity and timeframes exceeding 12 months, whereas Engineering and Biological Sciences demonstrated greater uniformity and shorter durations. It is concluded that the editorial workflows of the SciELO Brazil collection still face challenges related to delays in the review and production processes.

Abstract:
For surgical trainees embarking on a period of laboratory research, the transition from operating theatre to bench science can be both rewarding and disorienting. This annotation is written specifically for clinicians entering a wet laboratory environment, typically on an out-of-programme research placement, who may be unfamiliar with the realities of experimental science. Drawing on the first-hand experiences of a multidisciplinary orthopaedic research team, it explains why laboratory timelines are often longer than expected, and offers practical guidance for working effectively alongside PhD-level scientists, postdoctoral researchers, research technicians, and their trainees - collaborators whose technical expertise is indispensable to experimental success. Wet lab work involves complex protocols, tissue handling, assay optimization, and regulatory approvals, all of which can significantly extend project timelines. Effective communication, realistic planning, and mutual respect are crucial to manage unforeseen challenges and ensure that experiments are reliable, reproducible, and clinically meaningful.

#12 [paper] Divergent responses to AI-era submission pressure: a comparative analysis of medicine and computer science, 2015–2026
Authors: KangWei Wang, Ce Shi
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11412416/v1

Abstract:
Abstract ChatGPT's release in late 2022 and the arrival of agentic AI systems from 2025 coincided with reports of rising manuscript volumes and editorial strain. Whether this pressure is uniform across research fields, or absorbed differently by each, has not been tested comparatively. We contrast two ecosystems with sharply different barriers to entry: computer science (CS), where submission carries almost no procedural cost, and medicine, where ethics review and data governance constrain what can be produced. Using open data for 2015–2026 — monthly submission and output volumes from arXiv, medRxiv, bioRxiv and PubMed; submission and acceptance figures for thirteen CS conferences; and review times for 38 medical journals — we measured AI-associated writing with a 95-word excess-vocabulary detector applied identically to 30,000 CS abstracts and 13,000–24,000 PubMed abstracts per year. CS preprint submissions rose 99.3% between 2022 and 2025, against 38–41% for the life-science preprint servers and 5.5% for PubMed-indexed output, and several medical specialties contracted; the divergence holds within arXiv itself. CS conferences absorbed the surge by expanding capacity, with NeurIPS submissions up 195% at an unchanged acceptance rate. AI-associated writing rose sharply from 2023 in both fields, the proportional increase nearly identical from a higher CS baseline, with the break appearing in all eight medical specialties tested. Review time for accepted papers showed no aggregate change. Medicine and CS therefore experienced comparable growth in AI-associated writing but opposite responses: CS expanded output and review capacity, while biomedicine held output flat and routed the pressure into editorial triage.

#18 [paper] The impact of presentations in scientific conferences: Publication and citation rates in trauma surgery.
Authors: Touponse, Gavin, Bidwell, Serena, Shank, Amei, Tai, Jesse, Poe, James, Berg, Alexander, Khan, Hason, Tian, Lu
Venue: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42912484/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Understanding the publication rates and citation patterns of conference abstracts is critical for program committees and investigators alike. However, the downstream scholarly outcome of conference abstracts remains poorly characterized. We hypothesized that across contemporary US trauma-related scientific meetings, a substantial proportion of conference abstracts would not progress to peer-reviewed publications, and that publication rates and citation patterns would vary by presentation format and conference. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of abstracts presented at four major US trauma surgery conferences from 2017 to 2019. We identified peer-reviewed manuscripts associated with conference abstracts via Google Scholar and PubMed. We collected presentation format, publishing journal, 2024 journal impact factor, and citation count. A cohort of directly submitted peer-reviewed manuscripts was also analyzed. Mixed-effects Poisson regression models assessed the association between presentation and citation counts, adjusting for publication timing. RESULTS: Of 1,157 abstracts, 762 (66%) were published as peer-reviewed manuscripts. Most manuscripts were published in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery (JTACS) (55%), with 5 in journals with a higher-impact factor than JTACS. On regression analysis, abstracts presented as oral presentations, and published in journals with an impact factor higher than JTACS, were associated with a greater number of citations. When comparing manuscripts presented as abstracts to directly submitted peer-reviewed manuscripts, abstract presentation was associated with 22% more citations (incidence rate ratio: 1.22; 95% CI [1.16-1.29]; p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This cross-sectional study of four trauma societies found that approximately a third of presented abstracts did not progress to peer-reviewed publication, with publication rates varying by conference and presentation format. Exploratory analyses found that among those published in JTACS, published manuscripts originating from presented abstracts demonstrated a modestly higher citation count compared with directly submitted manuscripts. Our findings highlight an opportunity to better understand how conference time and investigator effort translate into downstream scholarly output. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/Epidemiological; Level IV.

#1 [paper] Leveraging Ocean Data and Models: Building the Data Infrastructure, Workforce, and Modeling Capacity to Synthesize Earth’s Ocean Observations
Authors: Susanne E. Craig, Frank Muller-Karger, Leonid Shumilo, Tzortziou Maria
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5bv4n

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean-relevant Earth system data from satellite streams, in situ networks, suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, and high-resolution numerical models exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A decadal strategy built on two pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data (cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, machine learning) and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation (mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimila…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): NASA's aquatic and marine research enterprise, including MODIS, PACE mission, and BGC-Argo data streams.
Abstract:
NASA’s aquatic and marine research enterprise within the overarching NASA Biosphere Program is entering an era of unprecedented data abundance. MODIS and the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission already generate ocean color data at rates that strain legacy processing and archiving workflows, and forthcoming missions will add further volume and complexity. These satellite streams are joined by rapidly growing in situ networks (e.g., BGC-Argo), suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, citizen science, and increasingly high-resolution numerical models. The result is a Big Data regime in which the volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean relevant Earth system data exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches. An important goal is to fully integrate observing workflows, understanding, and models across the terrestrial, aquatic, and atmosphere domains to fully enable understanding of life and the realization of improved information to manage uses of ecosystem services. This white paper addresses Leveraging Ocean Data and Models, a cross-cutting Grand Challenge that underlies and enables progress on the four other foundational grand challenges under the NASA Biosphere, Atmosphere, Cryosphere, and Hydrosphere framework - Global Biosphere, Carbon and the Elements of Life, Interface Habitats, and Transient Events - each of which depends on the ability to acquire, harmonize, and synthesize disparate satellite, suborbital, in situ, and model data streams. We recommend a decadal strategy built on two complementary pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data, covering tiered cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, and machine learning; and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation, covering mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimilation, hybrid approaches, mission emulators, and a NASA Digital Twin Ocean. Without concerted, proactive investment in this cross-cutting infrastructure, the scientific and societal returns on the coming decade’s expanded observing system will be substantially diminished.

#2 [paper] A comprehensive examination of the current AI landscape in ocean sciences: applications, challenges, and emerging trends
Authors: Tiara Mulder, Spencer Bialek, Shen Molloy, Alexi Baccardax Westcott, Shayla Fitzsimmons
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1890995
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): To examine the current landscape of AI and machine learning applications in ocean sciences, identifying key uses, emerging trends, and challenges.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Literature-synthesis workflow supported by Schlitsummarizer and full-text extraction methods.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Ocean sciences research literature covering physical oceanography, coastal hazards, marine biogeochemistry, ecology, remote sensing, acoustics, marine geology, and applied ocean engineering.
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used in ocean sciences to analyze large, complex, and unevenly sampled datasets from satellites, autonomous platforms, sensors, vessels, and genomic tools. This review examines how AI and ML are being applied across major areas of ocean research, including physical oceanography, coastal hazards, marine biogeochemistry, ecology, remote sensing, acoustics, marine geology, and applied ocean engineering. Using a literature-synthesis workflow supported by Schlitsummarizer and full-text extraction methods, this paper identifies key applications, emerging trends, research gaps, and limitations in ocean-based ML. The review shows that ML is particularly useful for predicting surface currents, reconstructing subsurface ocean conditions, forecasting waves, estimating biogeochemical variables, classifying marine organisms and habitats, improving remote-sensing products, and supporting autonomous observing systems. Emerging trends include the growth of deep learning, physics-informed machine learning, explainable AI, data integration across observing platforms, and management-focused applications related to climate adaptation, coastal planning, fisheries, and environmental monitoring. However, major challenges remain, including sparse and biased ocean observations, limited data from deep-ocean and polar regions, validation bias, poor model transferability, class imbalance in ecological datasets, black-box model behavior, and uncertainty under changing climate conditions. Overall, this review argues that AI and ML are valuable tools for expanding ocean observation and prediction, but they must be used alongside oceanographic knowledge, careful validation, and transparent interpretation to ensure reliable scientific and management outcomes.

#1 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#3 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.

Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#6 [paper] Understanding ecosystem responses to recurrent marine heatwaves
Authors: Emily Lester, Stanley Mastrantonis, Sharyn M. Hickey, Anna Lafratta, Jessica A. Benthuysen, Eben Afrifa-Yamoah, Arani Chandrapavan, martial depczynski
Venue: Biological Conservation
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2026.112016
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) have emerged as an increasingly severe disturbance to global marine ecosystems, with documented intensifications in both frequency and magnitude over the past century. Western Australia has experienced some of the most severe MHWs on record, causing widespread ecological impacts, including coral bleaching and mortality, local species extinctions, and socioeconomic impacts such as fishery closures, making the region a critical case study of climate-driven change in the marine domain. Most recently, a severe MHW during summer 2024/2025 has caused widespread disruption to marine life, reinforcing the region's vulnerability to repeated extreme events. While extensive research has documented the impacts of these events, most studies have examined individual heatwaves or specific taxonomic groups in isolation, limiting our understanding of cumulative and cascading effects across the ecosystem. Here, we combine a scoping review of published and emerging evidence with oceanographic analyses to assess the cumulative ecological impacts of MHWs across Western Australia. Using iconic MHWs as case studies, we reveal widespread ecological consequences, spanning habitat degradation, mass invertebrate mortality events, food web disruption, and spatial redistribution of fisheries' indicator species. Accordingly, we propose adaptive management strategies for future MHWs. These strategies include the relocation of vulnerable species, implementation of adaptive fisheries management frameworks, and development of rapid response monitoring programs targeting key benthic indicator groups. We emphasise that the successful implementation of such strategies hinges upon the accurate and timely prediction of future MHW events.

#7 [paper] Comparing Surface and Subsurface Marine Heatwaves in Ocean Reanalyses
Authors: Vincenzo de Toma, Andrea Storto, Ronan McAdam, Antonietta Capotondi, Chunxue Yang

Abstract. Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly recognised as major drivers of ecological and socio‑economic disruption, yet their subsurface expression remains poorly constrained due to sparse in situ observations. Here, we characterise properties such as the intensity, duration, and heterogeneity of subsurface MHWs using the Copernicus Global Ocean Reanalysis Ensemble Product (GREP). MHWs are detected across multiple depths (0.5–200 m) using a consistent percentile-based thresholding, applied to three reanalysis members (CGLORSv7, GLORYS2v4, ORAS5) and evaluated against well‑documented historical events. All reanalyses successfully capture the timing and general evolution of major, well-known surface expressions of MHW events when compared against the ESA Climate Change Initiative SST dataset in given areas of interest, such as, for example, events of 2011 in Western Australia, of 2015 in the Northeast Pacific Blob, and of 2006 in the Mediterranean Sea. Here, it is also shown that anomalies frequently penetrate below the mixed layer, down to 100–150 m. On a global scale, there is a positive bias of about 15 days in the mean duration for all the events with respect to satellite SST data, consistent with the limited eddy-resolving capability of the eddy-permitting GREP reanalyses, the additional smoothing introduced by ensemble averaging and the difference between the different representative depths of SST in satellite observations and models. Global diagnostics reveal that MHWs extending into the subsurface are more persistent, spatially heterogeneous, and characterised by sharper onset and decline rates than shallow events, particularly in the tropics, western boundary currents, and the Southern Ocean. Mixed‑layer variability strongly modulates the vertical propagation of anomalies, underscoring the role of vertical mixing in shaping subsurface extremes. Our results highlight both the value and limitations of current reanalyses for subsurface MHW characterisation, emphasising the need for ensemble‑based approaches to quantify uncertainty.

#11 [paper] Marine heatwave exposure is changing unevenly across Scottish aquaculture sites
Authors: Camila Toledo-Jaime, Jennifer A. Graham, Ben Hudson, David Andrew Moffat, Bryony L. Townhill, Steven J. Palmer

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1963854

Abstract:
Introduction Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are an increasing climate hazard for coastal aquaculture, yet regional assessments may not resolve how exposure varies across the locations where farms operate. Methods Here, we analysed daily ~5-km OSTIA sea surface temperature data from 1990 to 2025 at the locations of 361 active Scottish finfish and shellfish farms, represented by 218 unique grid cells, and compared satellite temperatures with in situ records from eight farms.
