#1 [paper] An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
Authors: Borja Nogué-Algueró, Richard York, Stefano B. Longo, Ekaterina Chertkovskaya, Patrick Trent Greiner
Venue: Ecological Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2026.109264
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This survey synthesizes insights from environmental social sciences to recast the plastics crisis as a structural feature of growth-dependent economies instead of a problem solvable by consumer choice or incremental technologies. Rather than a within-field review of ecological economics, it maps adjacent literatures to specify what this field could study and how, clarifying researchable questions, suitable methods, and tractable indicators. The synthesis foregrounds connections between expansionary political-economic dynamics, globally uneven socio-ecological burdens across the plastics life cycle, and the power and knowledge relations that shape what is produced, measured, and governed. It calls for comparative, mixed-methods, multi-scalar work and for open, standardized data on plastics flows to strengthen causal inference and comparability. Shifting attention upstream—from end-of-pipe fixes to the transformation of provisioning systems—the paper charts lines of inquiry capable of aligning social metabolism with biophysical limits and human needs, providing a roadmap for ecological economics to organize and accelerate research beyond consumer or techno-managerial framings.

#2 [paper] Who is governing the global plastics crisis? Mapping the global plastics governance landscape
Authors: Babet de Groot
Venue: International Environmental Agreements Politics Law and Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10784-026-09734-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract As plastic pollution intensifies, questions arise about whether the global plastics crisis (GPC) is being governed, and by whom. While an array of international institutions is often assumed to address this issue, the scholarship has yet to systematically examine who governs plastics and plastic pollution in practice. This article provides an empirical mapping of the GPC governance landscape, finding that multilevel public, civil society, and hybrid institutions incidentally facilitate governance through information dissemination, operational activities, and standard-setting. It identifies focal points that shape the global agenda and powerbrokers that disseminate it, with the United Nations Environment Programme and the Basel Convention emerging as influential. Meanwhile, private actor involvement is limited to multistakeholder partnerships that enable business and industry to feign environmental action while pursuing expansive business-as-usual practices. This article thereby establishes an empirical baseline for understanding GPC governance in the absence of a global plastics treaty, demonstrating that legal and regime-based classifications of institutional relevance offer an incomplete account.

#3 [paper] doi:10.33490/jklm.v4i2
Venue: Jurnal Kesehatan Lingkungan Mapaccing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.33490/jklm.v4i2
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study aimed to explore the communication barriers faced by the waste picker community in reducing plastic waste in Maros Regency, South Sulawesi, Indonesia.A qualitative case study design was conducted from March to May 2025.Seven informants, comprising five active waste pickers, one waste collector, and one official of the Maros Regency Environmental Agency, were selected purposively.Data were collected through participant observation and in-depth interviews and analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña.Trustworthiness was established through source and method triangulation and member checking.Five barriers were identified: (1) varied and generally low environmental literacy; (2) a mismatch between the communication channels used and the community's access and habits, as digital media were rarely accessible; (3) overly technical messages that were difficult to understand and apply; (4) low community participation; and (5) inadequate waste-handling infrastructure.These findings indicate that communication barriers occur at the levels of the message, the channel, and the receiver, and are reinforced by structural constraints.Plastic waste reduction programs should therefore use interpersonal and participatory communication through trusted intermediaries such as waste collectors, deliver simple and visual messages, and be accompanied by improved sorting facilities.

#4 [paper] Selecting Materials Outreach Topics from Community Repair Demand: Organizational Weighting, Temporal Transfer and Local Fit
Authors: Chahn Yong Jung
Venue: Journal of Materials Education (Electronic)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.71448/jme2026346
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Community repair events bring materials science into contact with familiar products, but outreach teams must decide which objects deserve limited preparation time. This study evaluates topic selection under two representation rules: equal influence for each recorded repair attempt and equal influence for each repair group. The Open Repair Alliance collection contains 48,669 attempts. Selection used 17,805 attempts from 95 groups, followed by evaluation on 18,802 attempts from 126 groups. The four topics selected by attempt weighting were laptops, lamps, separate audio equipment and coffee makers. Group weighting replaced the latter two with mobile phones and small kitchen appliances. Its selection-period advantage in average group coverage contracted from 3.09 to 0.43 percentage points in the following year. Network-stratified group resampling gave a 95% interval of −1.29 to 2.28 points for that contrast, while attempt coverage decreased by 3.27 points. Local differences had opposing signs: 58 groups gained coverage, 63 lost coverage and five were unchanged. Resampling the selection groups recovered the complete topic sets in only 19.28% and 35.84% of draws. Increasing the kit to eight topics made the two rules select identical categories; ten topics were needed to exceed one-half of average group demand. These results establish the consequences of representation choices without attributing learning gains to category matching. A shared materials kit therefore requires an explicit intended beneficiary, host-specific preparation and an educational assessment independent of repair completion.

#5 [paper] Public knowledge of plastic-related chemical risks and intention to reduce exposure: a secondary analysis of an international randomized controlled trial
Authors: Danya Sandler, Rivka Green, Carly Goodman, Christine Till, Bruce Lanphear
Venue: BMC Public Health
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-29140-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Background Endocrine-disrupting chemicals in plastics are linked to earlier puberty, adverse birth outcomes, and reduced cognitive function, yet public awareness of these risks remains low. We examined whether a brief educational video could increase knowledge about plastic-related hazards and intention to reduce plastic use. Methods This secondary analysis draws from a parallel-group randomized controlled trial [1] in which 15 761 participants aged 18–45 were recruited from Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, India, and Australia via CloudResearch's Prime Panels®. After completing baseline demographic and knowledge measures, participants were randomly assigned to watch a 7-minute educational video about toxic chemicals and neurodevelopment (n = 9135) or to view a blank screen (n = 6626). Immediate outcomes included three plastic-related knowledge items and one behavioural intention item assessing their likelihood of reducing plastic use in the next month. Following exclusions, 12 818 participants were included in analyses (intervention: n = 6427; control: n = 6391). Six weeks later, 3879 participants completed a follow-up assessing prevention attitudes and self-reported behaviour change. Results Participants who viewed the video were significantly more likely to report that plastics are harmful, disrupt hormone activity, and affect children’s cognitive development (rank-biserial r = .34–.38, all p < .001). They also reported greater intention to reduce plastic compared with controls (51% vs. 44.8%, (rank-biserial r = .06, p < .001). Intention was most strongly predicted by the belief that plastic chemicals disrupt hormone activity (OR = 1.99, p < .001). At six-week follow-up, higher baseline intention predicted greater self-reported reductions in plastic use (OR = 1.56, p < .001), with no significant difference by group. Effects varied across demographic subgroups, with stronger responses among participants in India, urban residents, South Asian participants, those with higher education or fewer children, and right-leaning participants. Conclusions A brief educational video improved plastics-related knowledge and short-term intentions to reduce exposure. However, behaviour change at follow-up was more strongly associated with baseline intention than with intervention status, highlighting the role of motivation and contextual factors in sustained behaviour change. Future interventions should consider baseline motivation and structural barriers alongside educational content.

#6 [paper] Tackling the global plastic pollution crisis
Authors: Guibing Zhu, Changchao Li, Peng Wang, Peixiu Chen, Jingjing Peng, Ziyang Tang, Lei Zhong, Chunlei Liu
Venue: National Science Review
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwag582
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Plastic pollution has emerged as a critical global environmental challenge, exacerbating the impacts of climate change and biodiversity loss while posing substantial risks to human health and the economy. Despite a rapid increase in scientific efforts in recent years, our understanding of the characteristics, distribution and environmental consequences of plastic pollution remains incomplete, with many aspects still under debate. This knowledge gap hinders the development and implementation of effective management strategies. In this Review, we provide a comprehensive synthesis of plastic pollution from understanding to combatting, linking the environmental behavior of plastics with their ecological, health, and Earth-system risks. We further discuss mitigation and management strategies across the plastics life cycle. These strategies emphasize upstream prevention through redesign for minimizing production and facilitating reuse, supplemented by measures such as recycling and the implementation of biodegradable and compostable plastics, as well as exposure risk management. We also identify key challenges to address the interlinked triple crises of climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution associated with plastics. The priorities and solutions to end plastic pollution include promoting sustainable production and consumption, minimizing plastic waste and leakage, mitigating plastic pollution and damage, and safeguarding planetary health.

#7 [paper] Technological Innovations for Ocean Plastic Waste Management: A Global Bibliometric Analysis of Research Trends, Collaboration Networks, and Emerging Technologies
Authors: Jehu Roeh C. Rubenial Franklin M. Ganancias
Venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.59543/jidmis.v3.1213
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ocean plastic pollution has become one of the most pressing environmental challenges worldwide, driving increasing interest in technology-based solutions for monitoring, prevention, mitigation, and sustainable waste management. Despite the rapid growth of research in this field, a comprehensive understanding of its scientific development, collaboration patterns, and emerging technological directions remains limited. This study presents a global bibliometric analysis of technological innovations for ocean plastic waste management using 12,039 English-language publications retrieved from the Scopus database on 09 July 2026. Bibliographic data were analyzed using Bibliometrix (RStudio) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, influential authors, journals, institutions, countries, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, and thematic evolution. The findings reveal a substantial increase in scientific production, particularly after 2015, demonstrating the rapid expansion of this interdisciplinary research domain. China, the United States, and several European and Asian countries emerged as the leading contributors to scientific productivity and international collaboration, while Marine Pollution Bulletin and Science of the Total Environment ranked among the most productive publication sources. Author keyword co-occurrence analysis identified microplastics, plastic waste, circular economy, recycling, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and remote sensing as dominant research themes. Thematic evolution further revealed a transition from broad marine pollution research toward technology-oriented investigations emphasizing plastic waste management and microplastics. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive knowledge map of the field, highlighting the growing integration of digital technologies and sustainable waste management strategies. The findings offer valuable insights for researchers, policymakers, and environmental practitioners in identifying research priorities, strengthening international collaboration, and advancing technology-driven solutions for sustainable ocean plastic waste management.

#8 [paper] Closing the gap between micro- and nano plastics science and policy
Authors: A. Nejadhashemi, Eeswaran Rasu, M. Mahmoudi
Venue: npj Emerging Contaminants
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/dafb8d14911c1f334a54f571e73cc204b3dcd7b3
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) are increasingly being identified across environmental matrices, the food chain, and drinking water, with documented effects on human health, yet policy on how to translate this evidence into pollution-reduction action lags well behind the pace at which the underlying data are being generated. This Comment synthesizes the current state of environmental MNP data collection across oceanic, freshwater, and cryospheric matrices, showing that ocean surveys currently offer the most robust field datasets, while lake, river, soil, food, and polar measurements remain comparatively sparse and methodologically heterogeneous. Building on this assessment, we outline a forward-looking research and policy agenda for translating improved data into action once more comprehensive datasets become available. This agenda spans three interconnected priorities: advancing analytical precision and ecosystem-level research, from reference materials and machine-learning-assisted detection to toxicology and biogeochemical impacts; harmonizing global policy frameworks, including regulatory standards, extended producer responsibility, and the emerging Global Plastics Treaty; and addressing the equity and governance trade-offs that arise when translating MNP science into practice, particularly through a One Health lens that links environmental, plant, animal, and human health. Together, these sections aim to bridge the gap between what we currently know about MNP occurrences in the environment, the more broadly documented human health evidence, and what must be done, scientifically and politically, to manage the risks they pose.

#10 [paper] Plastic Waste Utilization in Sustainable Construction Materials: A Sustainable Approach for Waste Management and Green Construction
Authors: Anshika Yadav, Hemant Agrawal, Ashutosh Luhania, Vijay Saini
Venue: Iconic Research and Engineering Journals
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64388/irev10i2-1722396
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The rapid increase in plastic consumption has resulted in significant environmental challenges due to improper disposal and accumulation of plastic waste. Conventional disposal methods such as landfilling and incineration contribute to environmental degradation and greenhouse gas emissions. The construction industry offers a promising solution through the utilization of plastic waste in building materials. This study reviews the potential of incorporating plastic waste into concrete, asphalt pavements, bricks, blocks, and composite materials. The environmental, economic, and engineering benefits of plastic-modified construction materials are analyzed. Results from previous studies indicate that plastic waste can improve durability, reduce material costs, and minimize environmental pollution while promoting sustainable construction practices. The study concludes that plastic waste utilization can play a significant role in achieving circular economy objectives and reducing the environmental footprint of the construction sector.

#12 [paper] Advances in technologies across the marine plastic value chain in Europe: A critical review
Authors: Eimear Magee, Matheus C. dos Santos, Meriem Stimade, Jose Alvarez, Gerard Dooly, Vincent Mallet, Michel Bakni, Douglas Marques
Venue: Cleaner Engineering and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clet.2026.101352
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine plastic pollution (MPP) driven by unsustainable production, ineffective waste management, and plastic persistence, requiring technologies to advance a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A critical review evaluating state-of-the-art technologies across the marine plastics value chain, including remote sensing, robotic platforms, machine-vision systems, downstream sorting (electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging, AI-driven classification), and mechanic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe
Abstract:
Marine Plastic Pollution (MPP) is widely recognised as a significant global challenge, driven by unsustainable plastic production, ineffective waste management, and the long-term persistence of plastics in marine environments. MPP has become increasingly widespread across oceans, along coastlines and on the seafloor, resulting in an urgent need for the development of technologies capable of advancing a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products. Advances in cleaner production technologies, including satellite and drone-based remote sensing, autonomous robotic platforms, and machine-vision systems, have improved the efficiency of plastic debris identification, classification, and recovery in complex marine environments. Similarly, innovations in downstream sorting, such as electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven classification, are enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of processing MPP. The review evaluates mechanical recycling methods with particular emphasis on recent advances in extrusion, moulding technologies, and additive manufacturing for converting MPP into high-value secondary materials in a CE framework in Europe. These technological developments demonstrate the potential for establishing viable and scalable valorisation routes. Overall, the review outlines key opportunities to strengthen a sustainable CE and guide future research and industrial adoption. In doing so, it provides a comprehensive examination of state-of-the-art technologies across the entire marine plastics value chain in Europe, from detection and recovery to separation, identification, and recycling.

#14 [paper] Volumetric Waste: Containing Polymorphous Plastic in Bangkok’s Circular Economies
Authors: Olivia Meyer
Venue: Geoforum
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2026.104858
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This paper examines how volumetric reasoning permeates everyday practices in Bangkok’s circular economies. While circular economies calculate, value, and contain plastic waste, mobile waste flows are hidden from view and often evade regulation. As a result, circular economy initiatives struggle to account for low-value waste, microplastics, and chemicals that proliferate through land, water, air, and blood in bodies. In these instances, waste travels and transforms volumetrically without a traceable latitude and longitude. Similarly, the actual dimensions of plastic objects impact their ability to be valued in the circular economy. Drawing on seventeen months of ethnographic fieldwork in Bangkok, Thailand, this paper documents how circular economy practitioners manage waste that takes on new materialities as it moves through plastic circularity loops. Nonstate waste practitioners invoke volumetric reasoning as they grapple with circular economy solutions (e.g., recovering, repurposing, and upcycling plastics). My argument is twofold: first, I argue that practitioners’ everyday volumetric practices expose the limits of formal circular economy policy. Second, I argue that volumetric reasoning gives practitioners a set of techniques for reclaiming agency over the everyday management of waste. By attending to commonplace yet novel spatial dimensions of plastic circularity, this paper contributes to emerging scholarship at the intersection of political ecology and volumetric analyses of plastic pollution in Asia.

#15 [paper] Sustainable Production and Consumption of Single‐Use Plastic Packaging in Aotearoa New Zealand: Expert Interpretations and Major Supermarket Representations
Authors: Maria Rebecca Ross, Trisia Angela Farrelly, Samantha Gardyne, Glenn Banks
Venue: Kōtuitui New Zealand Journal of Social Sciences Online
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1002/kot2.70067
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Supermarkets trade a plethora of products wrapped in single‐use plastic packaging (SUPP), which is a key driver of plastics production and consumption. Harmonised criteria to assess the sustainable production and consumption (SPC) of plastics are critical for policy development that effectively protects human and environmental health. However, the spaces where actors make decisions and produce knowledge allow for broad interpretations of SPC and the criteria by which it may be assessed. We examine the supermarket duopoly's representations of SPC and the potential for these to influence the effectiveness of Aotearoa New Zealand's plastic pollution framework. Critical discourse analysis of interviews with local experts and publicly available major supermarket sustainability documents were used to highlight power, language and knowledge relationships. We found that current SUPP production and consumption was generally understood by local experts as unsustainable. While access to information was viewed as critical to transparent trade of safe and sustainable SUPP, there are currently no globally harmonised criteria and definitions and, therefore, no universal standards for data transparency across the full life cycle of plastics. Major supermarket representations of safe, sustainable and essential uses of SUPP generally reflected dominant discourses that perpetuate the status quo. Narratives of SUPP ‘recycling’ and ‘recyclability’ dominate the supermarket duopoly's sustainability documents. However, local experts offered transformational ideas that challenge business as usual. The study highlights that empowering a range of independent experts to participate in the development of harmonised criteria is crucial to transition to the safer and more SPC of SUPP.

#16 [paper] Public awareness and behaviors regarding plastic consumption, recycling, and microplastics among residents of Tehran, Iran
Authors: Shaghayegh Zolghadri, Amir Hossein Hamidian, Fatemeh Abdi
Venue: Discover Public Health
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1186/s12982-026-03164-7
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract This cross-sectional study examined plastic consumption, recycling and littering behaviors, perceived plastic-related risks, and microplastic awareness among 300 Tehran residents aged 15–60 years. Participants were recruited through non-probability convenience and self-selection sampling using an online questionnaire distributed through Instagram, Telegram, and personal networks. Data were analyzed using Pearson’s χ², Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis H, Dunn–Bonferroni post hoc, and Spearman correlation tests, as appropriate. Women reported greater intention to participate in waste segregation (χ²(4) = 12.733, p = .013, Cramer’s V = 0.206) and more positive feelings about environmental participation (χ²(4) = 14.554, p = .006, Cramer’s V = 0.220) than men. Microplastic awareness showed a weak positive association with educational attainment (Spearman’s ρ = 0.186, p = .001), and social networks were the preferred source of environmental information about plastic pollution and recycling (69.7%). A marked difference in perceived risks was observed: 53.7% selected the highest response category for plastic-related animal mortality, whereas only 3.4%, 11.6%, and 11.7% selected this category for cancer, hormonal disorders, and respiratory problems, respectively. Residential-area category was unrelated to most outcomes. However, plastic-bag consumption differed across housing-price categories (H(2) = 6.469, p = .039, ε² = 0.015), with higher consumption in middle- than upper-housing-price areas (adjusted p = .037). Among 296 disposable-mask users, 60.8% discarded masks with household waste, 29.1% with recyclable waste, and 10.1% through medical-waste channels; disposal methods did not differ significantly by gender, education, or residential-area category. These findings indicate uneven perceptions of ecological and potential human-health implications of plastics and support clear, evidence-based public communication about microplastics and appropriate waste disposal. Because the study relied on online convenience sampling and self-reported responses, the findings should not be generalized to all Tehran residents without caution.

#17 [paper] Changes in University Students’ Understanding of Plastic Challenges and Sustainability Competencies Following Internships
Authors: Maren Skjelstad Fredagsvik, Bernt Rønning, Hilde Ervik
Venue: Education Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16111865
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study explores changes in university students’ understanding of plastic-related environmental challenges and sustainability competencies following internships. Using a qualitative pre-post design, we analysed questionnaire responses from 16 students who completed six-week internships in Norwegian companies working with plastic challenges. Thematic analysis showed changes in knowledge related to environmental, societal, and economic impacts of marine plastics, and potential solutions and challenges. We identified changes in expressed knowledge related to disciplinary, critical and normative, creative and strategic, systems, and interpersonal and communication competencies. Students primarily demonstrated practice-oriented knowledge, such as familiarity with technologies, sustainability principles and stakeholder engagement, while reflective, ethical, and global dimensions remained less evident in students’ responses. These findings suggest that real-world learning may support the development of applied knowledge and professional skills, while underscoring the need for integrating internships with academic reflection to support competence-related knowledge concerning systemic sustainability challenges. Engagement with authentic sustainability challenges was associated with increased expression of scientific knowledge aligned with scientific literacy, suggesting that internships may serve as learning experiences associated with sustainability competencies. We argue that higher education institutions should strengthen experiential learning and industry collaboration to link theory and practice and prepare students to contribute to sustainability work in practice.

#18 [paper] Research on modeling of public perception construction of low-carbon infrastructure under new media path
Authors: Wenyan Qu
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1117/12.3123405
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The construction of low-carbon infrastructure is a key carrier for achieving the "dual carbon" strategy, but its public perception bias often leads to the dilemma of avoiding neighbors. The evolution of new media from visualization to participatory approach provides a new window for cognitive construction. This article is based on the Chinese context and the theories of cognitive dual processing and media richness. Setting (Mycelium's reading): Spaceborne HSRL systems, hyperspectral sensors, and the Biogeochemical-Argo (BGC-Argo) in situ network.
Abstract:
Most of the ocean's life and biogeochemical activity is hidden from our satellite view, occurring in a vast vertical dimension that fundamentally governs marine ecosystems, the global carbon cycle, and Earth's climate. For decades, oceanography from space has been limited to a 2D surface perspective, with early light detection and ranging (lidar) offering tantalizing but quantitatively flawed glimpses into the ocean's interior. Here, we review the significant advancement driven by high-spectral-resolution lidar (HSRL), a technology that resolves this long-standing uncertainty. By directly measuring depth-resolved optical properties, HSRL transitions ocean profiling from estimation to quantitative measurement. The recent launches of the first spaceborne HSRL systems mark a major development in this new era. This technological step enables a "virtual constellation" in which HSRL provides the vertical backbone, hyperspectral sensors add biological complexity, and the Biogeochemical-Argo (BGC-Argo) network provides in situ biogeochemical context. This synergistic system is paving the way for 4D (3D space + time) ocean monitoring, providing the essential data streams to build a predictive "ocean digital twin"-a critical tool to advance our understanding of the ocean's response to climate change and to support global efforts in sustainable development.

High-resolution oceanographic monitoring is essential for managing the Mediterranean Sea, a major climate-change hotspot and a hub of socio-economic activity. The Balearic Islands Coastal Observing and Forecasting System (SOCIB) addresses this need through an integrated multiplatform network, including autonomous gliders, HF radars, and metocean buoys. This work describes SOCIB’s operational observing framework and evaluates its contribution to assessing the physical and biogeochemical variability of the Western Mediterranean. SOCIB provides real-time metocean data such as currents, waves, and winds essential for optimizing maritime operations, enhancing safety, and supporting regulatory compliance. Furthermore, integrating these datasets into numerical models and AI-based predictive systems improves risk mitigation and early warning systems for coastal hazards. Looking ahead, SOCIB aims to expand its spatial coverage, deploy new autonomous platforms, and contribute to a Digital Twin of the Mediterranean, ensuring safe and sustainable marine operations.

Abstract:
Ocean ecosystems constitute the largest habitable volume on Earth and regulate climate, support fisheries and a global Blue Economy valued at an estimated $1.5 trillion annually and provide services on which human wellbeing depends. Four decades of satellite ocean color observations have transformed understanding of phytoplankton distribution, biodiversity, and productivity, and NASA's PACE mission is now extending this record with unprecedented hyperspectral and polarimetric capabilities. Yet, passive ocean color remote sensing remains fundamentally two-dimensional – it detects only the optical signature of the uppermost, sunlit ocean; provides little or no coverage during polar night, persistent cloud cover, and low-sun conditions; and offers no independent means of validating its own retrievals. This white paper, submitted in response to the ESAS 2028 Request for Information under the Biosphere sphere, presents the science case and a phased observing strategy for achieving a four-dimensional (three spatial dimensions plus time), pole-to-pole characterization of global ocean ecosystems. The vision presented here draws heavily on Earth’s Living Ocean, the science vision report of NASA’s Ocean Biology and Biogeochemistry Program. We recommend 1) sustaining hyperspectral ocean color and polarimetric continuity, 2) adding a mature, ocean-optimized profiling lidar to resolve water column particle distributions and fill coverage gaps in polar and persistently cloudy regions, 3) expanding autonomous and suborbital in situ observing networks, and 4) investing in ecosystem models and data assimilation systems capable of ingesting these complementary data streams. Together, these elements would resolve a critical, decades-old gap in our ability to characterize, understand, and predict how global ocean ecosystems – from phytoplankton production to the fisheries and top predators they sustain – are responding to compounding natural and human-driven stressors, and whether those ecosystems are approaching thresholds beyond which their structure and function change abruptly and persistently.

Abstract:

Ultimately, this framework demonstrates a transferable modeling concept for monitoring human-modified aquatic environments, showing that explicitly accounting for anthropogenic forcing can improve satellite-based water-quality retrieval, particularly in managed systems where operational auxiliary measurements (e.g., near-real-time nutrient proxies) are available.

#11 [paper] Three gaps for foundation models to address in satellite remote sensing of inland waters

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5151t

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Discontinuities and trade-offs in satellite mission continuity, spectral/spatial/temporal coverage, and retrieval algorithm generalization constrain inland water remote sensing records.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Quantification of three gaps (mission, coverage, and generalization), definition of progress criteria for each, and assessment of 100 recent machine learning studies against these criteria.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 100 recent machine learning studies related to inland water remote sensing and existing generic Earth observation Foundation Models.
Abstract:
Long-term Earth observation of inland waters depends on continuity between satellite missions, adequate combinations of spectral, spatial and temporal resolution, and representative calibration and validation datasets. Discontinuities and trade-offs in these components constrain the records available for studying inland waters and their change. We examine three gaps affecting inland water remote sensing: a mission gap between comparable 300 m ocean colour observations from MERIS and OLCI during 2012–2016, a coverage gap in spectral, spatial and temporal sampling, and a generalisation gap when retrieval algorithm accuracy declines beyond bio-optical properties and atmospheric conditions represented during development. Foundation models (FMs) could help address these gaps by learning reusable representations from satellite archives before adaptation to a particular retrieval task. We hypothesise that relationships learned across overlapping satellite missions can support reconstruction of what a sensor would have measured during the mission gap, that combining complementary sensors can extend usable observation coverage, and that pretraining on satellite archives, which cover more water bodies and a wider range of bio-optical properties and atmospheric conditions than available field datasets, can improve retrieval algorithm generalisation. Testing these hypotheses requires criteria that define progress. We quantify the three gaps, define a progress criterion for each and assess 100 recent machine learning studies against the criteria. For the mission gap, three studies address continuity across sensor eras, and none recovers a record from a withheld mission period. For the coverage gap, 23 studies combine complementary observations, but only three test them on withheld water bodies or periods. For the generalisation gap, only seven studies withhold whole water bodies or later periods from all model development. Across all three gaps, none of the six studies that use pretraining compares it with the same architecture trained without pretraining on independent water bodies. The assumption common to all three hypotheses, that archive pretraining adds information beyond established methods, therefore remains untested. Applying the criteria to existing generic Earth observation FMs, then to FMs pretrained on inland waters, would determine which gaps pretraining can reduce.

Abstract:
High-resolution (HR) satellite imagery is essential for coastal mapping, ocean analysis, and long-term environmental monitoring; however, acquiring it is constrained by hardware limitations and high costs. Freely available low-resolution (LR) archives, such as those from Sentinel-2 (S2), offer global coverage and frequent revisits, but their 10 m native resolution is insufficient for fine-scale analysis. This study presents HARBOR (Harmonization-based Adaptive Resolution Boosting for Optical Remote sensing), an integrated harmonization-based workflow that combines established radiometric harmonization and sub-pixel convolutional super-resolution (SR) components and adapts them to four-band coastal S2–PlanetScope (PS) data. Rather than proposing a new network architecture, HARBOR addresses a gap in the way satellite SR is commonly assembled, where network optimization receives most of the attention and cross-sensor radiometric inconsistency is treated as a preprocessing detail. The workflow consists of four interconnected stages: (1) a same-day, close-time data preparation approach for temporally consistent cross-sensor learning, (2) statistical radiometric harmonization to reduce cross-sensor reflectance differences, (3) the synthetic generation of S 2 like imagery to expand limited supervised datasets, and (4) a customized Efficient Sub-Pixel Convolutional Neural Network (ESPCN) adapted for multispectral satellite imagery using a fused loss formulation. In a coastal case study of Galveston Island, Texas, USA, PS imagery resampled from 3 m to 5 m served as the HR reference for reconstructing S2 inputs from 10 m to 5 m. Because only 18 same-day, close-time S2 and PS pairs were available for direct cross-sensor training, a harmonization model calibrated on those pairs was used to generate synthetic S 2 like imagery from PS, expanding the supervised training set to 191 temporally consistent pairs. A component ablation separates the three elements of the workflow, namely statistical radiometric harmonization, synthetic S 2 like expansion of the training set, and the fused loss. Compared at a fixed training-set size, radiometric harmonization is the largest single contributor to reconstruction quality, ahead of the fused loss, while synthetic expansion is what makes supervised training feasible given the scarcity of real same-day pairs. The harmonization parameters and trained weights are calibrated to a single study site and require re-estimation on local same-day pairs before use elsewhere; what transfers is the end-to-end workflow itself, which integrates cross-sensor data preparation, radiometric harmonization, synthetic S 2 like generation, and neural network-based reconstruction into a single transferable pipeline, rather than the Galveston-calibrated model. Enhanced S2 archives of this kind could in future support coastal monitoring, environmental assessment, and the monitoring of Nature-Based Solutions (NbS) for coastal flood resilience, though no downstream task of that type is demonstrated.

#13 [paper] Satellite Remote Sensing of Methane Point Sources: A Review of Capabilities and Applications
Authors: Daniel Cusworth, Daniel J. Varon, Dylan Jervis, Jason McKeever, Alexander J. Turner, Christian Frankenberg, John R. Worden, Andrew K. Thorpe
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-6060

Abstract:
Abstract. The ability to remotely sense methane point sources continues to grow, driven by new satellite launches, newly discovered detection capabilities in satellites not originally intended for methane observation, and increasingly mature data processing and delivery pipelines. We review current and anticipated satellite remote sensing capabilities, including a description of instrument specifications, sampling strategies, and data availability. We detail algorithms that drive general methane plume processing pipelines and associated validation experiments across multiple product levels. We describe categories of stakeholder and science driven use cases that use satellite point source datasets. In particular, we detail several mitigation programs that use satellite point source detections to inform leak detection and verification (e.g., IMEO Methane Alert and Response System; California Satellite Methane Project). We also summarize research to date that incorporates point source datasets to inform practices to reduce emissions and aid aggregate accounting of emissions from facilities to regional scales. Continued work to establish common validation standards and reference sites to make detection and quantification performance comparable across instruments is recommended for building increased confidence in plume datasets. However, the successful integration of satellite point source imager observations into stakeholder workstreams demonstrates that these datasets are equipped today to support climate policy, operator response, and emissions accounting.

#15 [paper] Infrared‐Guided Super‐Resolution of Remotely Sensed Passive Microwave Sea Surface Temperature

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026jh001333

Abstract:
Abstract High‐resolution sea surface temperature (SST) is essential for weather forecasting and climate applications. Passive microwave (MW) SST offers largely cloud‐penetrating coverage but is coarse and spatially smoothed, whereas infrared (IR) SST resolves fine‐scale structures but is frequently cloud‐obscured. Using IR as auxiliary guidance for MW super‐resolution is challenging due to cross‐modality discrepancies in effective resolution and radiometric consistency; unconstrained IR injection can introduce spurious textures and local biases. We propose MambaIR‐MSP, a MW‐anchored, IR‐guided super‐resolution framework. A multi‐source prior (MSP) module combines spatial‐frequency alignment (SA) in the frequency domain with physics‐aware affine fusion (PAAF) in the temperature domain to regulate IR guidance, suppress modality‐induced bias, and preserve the MW radiometric baseline. In addition, a channel–frequency attention block (CFAB) selectively enhances gradient‐relevant components while avoiding unstable high‐frequency amplification. Experiments on 1‐year AMSR2–VIIRS collocations over the Kuroshio Extension and an independent Gulf Stream test set show that MambaIR‐MSP achieves competitive RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM relative to representative CNN, Transformer, and SSM baselines, while improving structural fidelity in high‐gradient regions, as reflected by gains in high‐frequency energy ratio, gradient variance ratio, and frontal overlap.

Today, 67 countries contribute to physical and biogeochemical ocean observations at sea through 17 GOOS observing networks monitored by OceanOPS. Satellites complement these measurements with observations from space, while a diverse community of initiatives collects vital data on marine life and ecosystems. Together, these observations underpin weather forecasting, climate monitoring, maritime and coastal risk management, biodiversity conservation and sustainable ocean economies. Observing capacity is unevenly distributed around the world, and many networks face challenges in securing the sustained funding needed to maintain and expand their observations. Strengthening coordination, improving data sharing and broadening international participation will be essential to build a more comprehensive, resilient and sustainable system. Continued investment and stronger collaboration across countries and observing communities are crucial to ensure that ocean observations can meet growing scientific, operational and societal needs. For more than four decades, satellite images of ocean temperature and colour have revealed jets, swirling eddies, and filaments. Here we demonstrate the first direct satellite imaging of kilometre-scale surface currents using a tandem configuration of optical satellites that tracks surface wave propagation. #1 [paper] Co-producing urban knowledge in motion: collaborative experimental methods for researching moving infrastructures
Authors: Noel Chung
Venue: Urban Geography
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/02723638.2026.2725759
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Delivery platforms have become ubiquitous in many cities, increasingly governing how things and people move. As contingent, moving infrastructures, they register diverse urban entities in their operations and produce new urban conditions and politics. How, then, can we empirically research the often obscure workings of infrastructures that are also in constant motion? Addressing the diffuse and fleeting nature of moving infrastructures, this paper proposes a methodology that foregrounds movement as both an analytic focus and a mode of enactment. Drawing on a multimethod mobile ethnography with platform delivery workers in Seoul, it shows how the dialogic synthesis of mobile methods helps unravel the infrastructural processes, practices, and politics of making the city through movement. The plurality of data and the collaborative, experimental orientation proved generative while simultaneously raising ethical, logistical, and analytical challenges. Notwithstanding the challenges, the paper demonstrates the value of collectively enacting mobile ethnography to co-produce urban knowledge in motion. It concludes by calling for ongoing collective methodological innovation in response to continually emerging infrastructures in moving and other forms, arguing that embodied, collective, and experimental methods not only contribute to new epistemic practices but also enable us to collectively envision alternative ways of creating infrastructures and cities.

Abstract:
My path to pediatric neurogenetics did not begin in a classroom or specific clinic, but in the inventive chaos of childhood experiments with my brother that turned everyday spaces into laboratories of possibility.My path to becoming a pediatric neurogeneticist was neither linear nor predetermined for me.My earliest scientific "laboratory" was a kitchen table in my childhood home strewn with parts purchased from Radio Shack.My brother (now adult neurologist David Saperstein, M.D.) and I built rudimentary "computers" and explored the mechanics of problem-solving and teamwork.A backyard picnic table was our makeshift anatomy bench, and a cat pelvis (from my 11th-grade physiology course) became a hands-on lesson in structure and function.Those early experiences established a foundational approach to science where curiosity, persistence, and the belief that answers exist if one is willing to take things apart and put them back together again began my journey.Since then, the field of neurogenetics has matured into a recognized discipline with formal clinics, training pathways, and research networks.However, the most transformative moments of my career were driven by serendipity, mentorship, and most profoundly, my patients' stories.Here I describe the influences that shaped my professional journey, the evolution of neuroimaging and biomarkers in metabolic disease, and the enduring lessons of listening, learning, and leadership in the field of rare disease medicine.

#3 [paper] Three steps into agentic AI: a preregistered feasibility study of how non-programmers cross from chatbot to agent to multi-model orchestration (Cohort 1)
Authors: Vadym Chernets
Venue: Open Science Framework
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/x4egq
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ordinary professionals now use AI by talking to a chatbot. Two further steps exist and almost nobody has taken them: running an agent that acts on your own machine, and putting one question to several models in one action instead of visiting them by hand. This study follows a cohort of non-programmers across three specific transitions and records, for each, who crosses, how long it takes, and where the rest stop. The route is unusual and is the reason the study is possible at all. Participants are not installed for. Each receives a text, pastes it into the chatbot they already use, and that chatbot walks them through installing a graphical agent on their own machine. The investigator does not touch anyone's computer. This is a feasibility study of a pathway. It measures crossing, and it records usefulness without claiming to prove it. It has no control group and makes no causal claim. It is Cohort 1 of a programme; later cohorts are registered separately.

#4 [paper] From Web Data to DIY Ideas: Material-Based Project Generation Systems

Abstract:
This article investigates and explores the prototype of a material based project generation system, aiming to transform online DIY content into structured design knowledge for sustainable reuse. Based on an unfinished system developed by the author in his early years, this work reviews the methods of collecting unstructured data from the Internet, extracts key information through lightweight natural language processing, and normalizes it into a unified model suitable for automatic generation. Discussed baseline strategies for retrieving and editing project generation, as well as evaluation metrics that consider constraint satisfaction, feasibility, and user experience. The paper also investigates practical applications in personal creativity support, maker education, and community recycling, supported by initial human in the loop implementation and interactive segmentation code that links material understanding with basic robot operations. The challenges of multimodal alignment, richer constraint modeling, and robust dataset construction have been identified, highlighting opportunities for future integration with digital twins and automated assembly. Although the original system is still incomplete, the study concludes that a practical and impactful pipeline is achievable, demonstrating how artificial intelligence can help users recycle materials more effectively and contribute to sustainable, resource-saving designs.

#5 [paper] FabLabs as Promissory Organizations: A future-making perspective
Authors: Maria Rita Micheli, Marta Gasparin, Daniel Hjorth, Mario Campana, Amanda Shantz
Venue: Organization Studies
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1177/01708406261488577
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This paper examines FabLabs as machine-centred promissory organizations, where futures are not only imagined, but also materially enacted. Drawing on new materialist and process perspectives, we conceptualize FabLabs as promissory assemblages of entangled human and non-human actors, through which future-making is enacted. We show that machines are central agents for the materialization of imagined futures, especially for the boundaries they create between what is possible and what is not possible to actualize. Based on an ethnographic study of 20 FabLabs across nine countries conducted over twelve years, we identify two core processes – fabulation and fabrication – through which the future is first created and then materialized. Fabulation refers to narratively performed imagination leading to the creation of imagined futures, while fabrication concerns the material experimentation and prototyping to test and eventually materialize imagination. This study advances research on promissory organizations by revealing their material underpinnings; it also extends future-making research by demonstrating how futures emerge through iterative material-discursive practices, rather than through linear planning. Overall, the paper contributes a machine-centred account of future-making, highlighting how imagination, materiality, and technology co-produce what futures become possible for entrepreneurs.

#6 [paper] Urban freight and procedural justice: who do we recognise as stakeholders?
Authors: Oliver Olmedo, Otgondulam Boldbaatar, Carla Tejada, Travis Fried, Paul Buijs, Sarah Dennis-Bauer, Anne Goodchild
Venue: Transport Reviews
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/01441647.2026.2725113
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This paper reviews which actors recent urban freight scholarship recognises as stakeholders and how it represents their roles and interactions in relation to environmental and procedural justice. We conducted a systematic literature review of 54 studies using a deductive–iterative coding approach. We identified 19 stakeholders and organised them into five overarching categories: government, private sector, general public, academia, and labour & civil society. Results show that government and private-sector actors are consistently foregrounded and often positioned as central decision-makers or implementers, whereas the general public and labour & civil society, despite often being disproportionately affected, are less consistently recognised in the literature. We conclude by outlining how urban freight research can make stakeholder identification more transparent and reflexive, thereby supporting policy guidance that is both operationally effective and procedurally equitable.

#20 [paper] Volumetric Waste: Containing Polymorphous Plastic in Bangkok’s Circular Economies
Authors: Olivia Meyer
Venue: Geoforum
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoforum.2026.104858
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This paper examines how volumetric reasoning permeates everyday practices in Bangkok’s circular economies. While circular economies calculate, value, and contain plastic waste, mobile waste flows are hidden from view and often evade regulation. As a result, circular economy initiatives struggle to account for low-value waste, microplastics, and chemicals that proliferate through land, water, air, and blood in bodies. In these instances, waste travels and transforms volumetrically without a traceable latitude and longitude. Similarly, the actual dimensions of plastic objects impact their ability to be valued in the circular economy. Drawing on seventeen months of ethnographic fieldwork in Bangkok, Thailand, this paper documents how circular economy practitioners manage waste that takes on new materialities as it moves through plastic circularity loops. Nonstate waste practitioners invoke volumetric reasoning as they grapple with circular economy solutions (e.g., recovering, repurposing, and upcycling plastics). My argument is twofold: first, I argue that practitioners’ everyday volumetric practices expose the limits of formal circular economy policy. Second, I argue that volumetric reasoning gives practitioners a set of techniques for reclaiming agency over the everyday management of waste. By attending to commonplace yet novel spatial dimensions of plastic circularity, this paper contributes to emerging scholarship at the intersection of political ecology and volumetric analyses of plastic pollution in Asia.

#1 [paper] A BIBLIOTECONOMIA E A CIÊNCIA DA INFORMAÇÃO NAS OBRAS DE LUCIANO FLORIDI: UMA ANÁLISE DE CONTEÚDO

Abstract:
This study aims to analyze the concepts of “library science” and “information science” in the works of philosopher Luciano Floridi, examining his proposed relationship between these disciplines and the philosophy of information. The scope of the research consists of Luciano Floridi’s works available in the Scopus database. The methodology consists of a bibliographic review and content analysis with a posteriori categorization. The data analysis evaluates the concept of library and information science in Floridi’s works and examines the discipline as an applied philosophy of information, its disciplinary characteristics, his argument regarding a crisis of theoretical foundations, and the discipline’s relationships with the philosophy of information and social epistemology as solutions to this crisis. It concludes by presenting the gaps in Floridi’s proposal and suggesting avenues for further research to better understand the field.

#5 [paper] CONSTRUÇÃO DE ESTRATÉGIAS PÚBLICAS PARA A INFORMAÇÃO: A PRODUÇÃO DO IBICT
Authors: Tainá Batista de Assis, Frederico Ramos Oliveira, Graziela Barros Gomes, Raíssa da Veiga de Menêses, Tiago Emmanuel Nunes Braga
Venue: Enancib
Year: 2026
Link: https://enancib.ancib.org/index/article/view/3051
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The Brazilian Institute of Information in Science and Technology (IBICT) announced, in 2026, four guiding concepts for its next Strategic Plan: informational integrity and justice, information for citizenship, Open Science, and informational sovereignty. This study aimed to understand the extent to which the scientific production profile of IBICT researchers aligns with these axes, in order to identify priority areas for internal funding. ScriptLattes was used to extract publications from 48 higher-education-level researchers for the period 2023–2025, followed by manual extraction of the keywords from each document. The terms were classified according to their thematic proximity to the four concepts, and the distribution of researchers across each axis was analyzed. The results show a strong concentration in the axes “information for citizenship” (29 associations) and “Open Science” (26), whereas “informational sovereignty” has the smallest contingent (10), with 90% holding doctoral degrees. The terminological analysis reveals interdisciplinarity with fields such as sociology, law, health, and computing. The study concludes that funding should prioritize informational sovereignty and the integration among concepts, as well as support the qualification of researchers with lower academic degrees.

#6 [paper] CIÊNCIA ABERTA COMO POSSIBILIDADE DE COOPERAÇÃO BRASIL-ANGOLA
Authors: Rafael RAFAEL, Laurindo Virgilio Rafael, Edgar Bisset-Alvarez
Venue: Enancib
Year: 2026
Link: https://enancib.ancib.org/index/article/view/2408
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Within the context of South–South cooperation, understood as a model of cultural and scientific exchange among countries of the Global South, Brazil has played a significant role in technology transfer and human resource development through various initiatives. However, the adoption of open science practices and infrastructures remains a major challenge for enhancing the visibility of scientific production and democratizing access to knowledge, particularly in developing countries. From this perspective, this study aims to discuss open science infrastructures as a means of expanding scientific cooperation between Brazil and Angola within the broader framework of Brazil's scientific partnerships with African countries. To this end, a survey was conducted of the main institutional, policy, legislative, and infrastructural mechanisms that promote open science in Brazil and Angola, serving as a basis for examining opportunities for exchange and collaboration between the two countries. The findings indicate that Brazil has a broad range of policies, legislation, and infrastructures that foster and support open science practices. In contrast, although Angola has not yet established open science as a formal public policy, the country has demonstrated initiatives moving in this direction, albeit still at an early stage of development. In this regard, strengthening targeted cooperation among institutions and their respective open science infrastructures is essential to facilitate the exchange of experiences, promote capacity building, and encourage the sharing of scientific data and knowledge between Brazil and Angola.

#10 [paper] Ethical reflexivity in action: contract researcher strategies and collaborative governance insights from sport for development
Authors: Frank van Eekeren, Chris Noij, Gerolf Pikker
Venue: Sport in Society
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/17430437.2026.2729421
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Ethical tensions arising from conflicting institutional expectations, personal values, and unequal power relations between actors from the Global North and South in Sport for Development (SFD) programs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A qualitative analysis drawing on a critical incident from the authors' roles as contract researchers.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A Dutch-led Sport for Development (SFD) program.
Abstract:
This paper examines how ethical reflexivity can deepen our understanding of contract researcher strategies and collaborative governance in Sport for Development (SFD). Drawing on a critical incident from our role as contract researchers in a Dutch-led SFD program, we explore how ethical tensions emerge from conflicting institutional expectations, personal values, and unequal power relations between actors from the Global North and South. Rather than offering definitive solutions, the study presents ethical reflexivity as a situated practice. Practically, it enables researchers to navigate ambiguity and make sense of tensions as they arise. Epistemologically, it sheds light on the everyday micro-practices that shape collaborative governance. Ethically, it underscores the need for ongoing reflection and accountability in contexts marked by asymmetry and contractual dependency. By foregrounding the moral and political dimensions of research practice, this study contributes to critical debates on power, ethics, and knowledge production in the collaborative governance of SFD.

#12 [paper] Reflective interdisciplinarity in practice: integrating biology and philosophy in studies of individualization
Authors: Marie I. Kaiser, Anton Killin, Barbara A. Caspers, Jürgen Gadau, Sylvia Kaiser, Joachim Kurtz, Caroline Müller, S. Helene Richter
Venue: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-08458-4
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Interdisciplinary research is widely acknowledged as a valuable means of knowledge production and as crucial for addressing complex scientific and societal problems. Interdisciplinary research takes many forms, and this article offers a novel case study of a distinctive form of interdisciplinarity, reflective interdisciplinarity. The article analyzes interdisciplinary research undertaken by philosophers of biology and empirically working biologists studying individualization. This kind of interdisciplinarity is reflective because biology is the target domain that philosophers of biology (and philosophically-minded biologists) reflect upon—as opposed to interdisciplinarity that occurs, for example, when insights from multiple distinct research domains are integrated. To analyze the case study, an analytic framework is developed that distinguishes four dimensions of interdisciplinarity: objects of interdisciplinary research, interdisciplinary research activities, communication of interdisciplinary results, and personal, institutional, and other conditions of interdisciplinary research. The case study shows, first, that reflective interdisciplinarity can involve interdependent, deeply immersive and cooperative interdisciplinary research processes (‘inquiry-embedded integration’) that include a form of knowledge-producing inquiry through which novel epistemic products emerge from joint commitments and goals, shared research questions, and intensive, collaborative discursive practices. The article adapts the notion of a plural subject in characterizing inquiry-embedded integration. Second, the analysis of the case study demonstrates how communicative choices, together with institutional and normative conditions, are partially constitutive of the interdisciplinary process. They shape the content of interdisciplinary products and play decisive roles in interdisciplinary activities such as knowledge integration. Finally, because the case study comprises the authors’ own research processes and publications, the analysis demonstrates that self-reflexive, qualitative analysis of interdisciplinary practice provides a valuable means of theorizing about interdisciplinarity with potential to offer transferable insights.

#13 [paper] Stratégie de science ouverte
Authors: MESRE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.52949/93
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
La Stratégie de science ouverte (SSO) 2026-2033 a pour objectif de consolider les changements initiés avec les deux plans précédents portés à l’échelle nationale en France. Elle couvre huit ans et se structure en ambitions, enjeux, objectifs stratégiques et plans d’action quadriennaux. Les ambitions de la science ouverte sont : un rayonnement et une souveraineté scientifiques accrus, une recherche plus cumulative et collaborative, plus reproductible, responsable et durable, et qui favorise l’innovation et s’ouvre au-delà du monde académique. Parmi les enjeux, la SSO identifie : l’hétérogénéité des pratiques disciplinaires, la résistance au partage des données, la fragilité des infrastructures, les questions de qualité dans l’édition scientifique, la faible valorisation des logiciels de recherche, la communication insuffisante des résultats des essais cliniques. La Stratégie identifie également les leviers pour répondre à ces défis, comme l’évaluation de la recherche et la coordination internationale. L’intelligence artificielle (IA) offre des opportunités, mais aussi des problématiques auxquelles il faut répondre. La SSO vise à concilier la science ouverte avec la protection de la recherche, en appliquant le principe « aussi ouvert que possible, aussi fermé que nécessaire ». Les plans d’action quadriennaux sont inscrits dans huit objectifs stratégiques. Quatre objectifs ciblent les pratiques, la gouvernance et les instruments de la science ouverte, les services et infrastructures, et le positionnement de la France dans le paysage européen et international. Les quatre autres objectifs concernent les publications, les données, les logiciels et les résultats des essais cliniques. Le plan d’action pour la période 2026-2029 décline ces objectifs en 30 actions et 75 mesures. Il engage des nouveaux projets comme une forge nationale pour les logiciels de recherche. Il renforce également les mesures phares comme HAL, Recherche Data Gouv et Software Heritage. La SSO est complétée par le bilan de la politique nationale. Les progrès ont été notables, mais un travail considérable reste à accomplir. La SSO trace une voie ambitieuse, celle d’une recherche française plus transparente, collaborative et souveraine, capable de relever les défis scientifiques du XXIe siècle.

On the other hand, the training programs offered by Portugal are few, but institutions such as the University of Coimbra and NOVA University Lisbon provide specific training in humanities and digital curation. To conclude, France possesses a more advanced, accessible, and developed open science system compared to Portugal, which is still in process.

#18 [paper] El realismo pragmatista y la relevancia de la predicción científica en Wenceslao J. González: la búsqueda de la objetividad como ruta para la verdad
Authors: Ana María Alonso Rodríguez
Venue: SCIO Revista de Filosofía
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.46583/scio_2026.30.1272
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): To analyze Wenceslao J. González's pragmatist realism and its emphasis on scientific prediction as a path to objectivity and truth.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Philosophical analysis of González's framework, comparing it to Nicholas Rescher's pragmatic idealism and examining the role of prediction in semantic, epistemological, and ontological aspects.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Current context of Philosophy of Science and Technology, addressing challenges of complexity and historicity.
Abstract:
The predictive success of Science can be regarded as a factor of objectivity. Predictive statements may be correct at the time they are made, but their truth is only verified when the anticipated event occurs. Wenceslao J. Gonzalez’s pragmatist realism emphasises Science understood as an activity and the role of prediction (epistemological, ontological and heuristic) as a path to objectivity, which brings us closer to the truth in three aspects: semantic, epistemological and ontological. Scientific activity is and must be plural. Thus, basic Science explains and predicts, applied Science predicts and prescribes, and the application of Science involves prognosis and specific guidelines for action. This article analyses the novelty offered by pragmatist realism in the current context. It presents it as an alternative to Nicholas Rescher's pragmatic idealism and then delves into the main philosophical and methodological aspects: (i) Conception of Science and the levels of analysis it develops; (ii) Prediction as a factor of objectivity; (iii) Pragmatist realism in the face of the challenges of complexity; and (iv) Objectivity and historicity of scientific activity. Overall, it highlights its potential to address the challenges present in current Philosophy of Science and Technology.

#19 [paper] The PISA high performing systems for tomorrow framework: a decolonial reading of the OECD's future-oriented education for human flourishing
Authors: Saija Volmari, Oshie Nishimura-Sahi
Venue: Journal of International Cooperation in Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1108/jice-09-2025-0061
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Purpose This article critically examines the OECD's High Performing Systems for Tomorrow (HPST) initiative, focusing on how non-Western intellectual traditions – Ubuntu, Confucianism and Buddhism – are referenced in its conceptualisation of education for human flourishing. It investigates the depth of engagement with these traditions through a decolonial conceptual lens. Design/methodology/approach In this study, we employ qualitative content analysis of publicly available OECD documents and webinars. Our analysis is guided by and engages with decolonial scholarship, particularly Moosavi's (2020) proposals to prevent “decolonisation without decolonising”. Findings The findings show that, while the OECD gestures towards epistemic diversity, non-Western traditions are often superficially incorporated and subordinated to dominant Western frameworks. As the initiative moves from a preparatory phase to a more operationally oriented one, such references intermittently recede and later reappear, but without substantive development or influence on the underlying onto-epistemological framework. Instead, they are selectively incorporated into a pre-existing policy agenda structured by measurement, standardisation and global comparison, hence reinforcing existing epistemic hierarchies and marginalising non-Western perspectives. Originality/value This study offers a critical insight into the OECD's flourishing agenda, demonstrating that epistemic inclusion is enacted largely in rhetorical terms, without substantive engagement with non-Western traditions. It contributes to critical discussions on global education governance by exposing the persistence of Western-centric frameworks in shaping educational futures and by advancing the case for more meaningful forms of epistemic pluralism.

The definition of surgical success has changed profoundly over the past century. For much of surgical history, success was measured by the technical accomplishment of the operation and its immediate outcome: whether the patient survived the procedure, whether the operation could be completed safely, and whether major postoperative complications could be avoided. Today, surgical success extends far beyond the surgical theatre: it encompasses long-term survival, durable disease control, functional recovery, and quality of life, shifting attention from the surgery itself to the life that follows.Few developments illustrate this evolution more clearly than organ transplantation. More than a technical achievement, transplantation raised questions that began only after the surgery was completed: could a transplanted organ function for years? Could recipients return to normal life? Could a single operation become a durable therapy? Answering these questions transformed transplantation from an isolated surgical procedure into a model of lifelong care.Dr. Joseph E. Murray played a key role in this transition. Widely remembered as the pioneer of organ transplantation, the surgeon who performed the first successful human kidney transplant in 1954, and the recipient of the 1990 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (1), Murray's contributions go beyond the advancements of organ transplantation, introducing a concept that re-defined surgical success.The first successful human organ transplantation marked a turning point for the field of surgery. In 1954, Richard Herrick was dying of end-stage renal disease when his twin brother Ronald offered gave him one of his kidneys (2). Their genetic identity provided a unique opportunity to overcome the immunological barrier that had defeated previous attempts. On December 23, Joseph Murray and his team performed the first clinical transplantation, successfully replacing a failing organ (2) (Fig. 1). What made the achievement remarkable was not only the technical success but the broad potential it carried forward.By the mid-twentieth century, surgery had already significantly advanced, with major progress in vascular, thoracic, and neurosurgical procedures (3). Yet, surgical achievements were still largely judged by what could be accomplished safely in the operating room. The Herrick case transformed transplantation from an experimental concept into a viable surgical therapy. Richard Herrick survived for eight years after the procedure, demonstrating that the success of surgery could be measured not only by what was accomplished during an operation, but by the life that operation made possible afterward. Indeed, Richard used his eight years effectively, married his recovery room nurse and together they had two children (4). Yet, this exceptional success also exposed a fundamental limitation of transplantation: even the most technically successful operation could fail if the pathophysiology of the underlying disease was not understood or the post-operative treatment was not meeting the specific biological needs.This next challenge lay not in the operation itself, but in the recipient's response to the transplanted organ. During the 1950s, Peter Medawar established that graft rejection was an active immunological response to genetically different tissue, providing the biological explanation for why transplantation beyond identical twins remained so difficult (5). #7 [paper] Valuing education for limited-resource audiences using a willingness to accept experiment
Authors: Russell Tronstad, Ibrahima Sall
Venue: PLoS ONE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0348858
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Education grants often target audiences that have limited-resources relative to their peers, such as beginning farmers, who arguably have the most to gain from more education. Yet, charging even modest fees to these participants is discouraged, creating a challenge for funding entities that desire to have a dollar value for the education provided. To measure this value, we conducted an experiment using a willingness-to-accept (WTA) approach. Participants chose a minimum cash payout from seven different options to voluntarily leave a training session before receiving any instruction or educational materials. The design is constructed so that each option has an equal expected payout. Cash payouts were not advertised or known to any participants before the training. Results show that average WTA values are $277.44 per training (about 4 hours of instruction), which is 2.11 to 4.74 times more than participants' self-reported willingness to pay (WTP), depending on how travel costs and time of participants are valued. WTP consistently and significantly explains much of the variation in WTA. In sharp contrast, detailed travel cost estimates in various forms were consistently insignificant for explaining WTA values. Beginning farmers and ranchers, our targeted limited-resource audience, reported WTA and WTP values that were $81.18 and $22.73 more per training, respectively, than those of non-beginning farmers.

#9 [paper] How Much is a Human Right Worth? ECtHR-NPD: A Benchmark for Predicting Non-Pecuniary Damage Awards
Authors: Yanyi Pu, Damián A. González-Salzberg, Zheng Yuan, Nikolaos Aletras
Venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2609.18908
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Existing legal benchmarks cover diverse tasks, while continuous monetary remedies remain comparatively underexplored. We introduce ECtHR-NPD, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for predicting non-pecuniary damage (NPD) awards at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) from case information when no statutory formula or explicit calculation rule determines the amount. ECtHR-NPD contains 14,575 cases with case-level awards in nominal euros, chronological splits, and a protocol separating target construction from model input. We evaluate a battery of methods, including constant predictors, gradient-boosted trees, retrieval methods, fine-tuned encoder language models (LMs), prompted decoder LMs, and knowledge-augmented agents. Our results show that more sophisticated LM and agentic approaches do not consistently outperform the strongest feature-based baseline. All model families struggle to identify zero awards and to calibrate high-award predictions, with further degradation on the Challenging test view, making ECtHR-NPD a challenging testbed for current state-of-the-art open-weight and proprietary LMs.
