#5 [paper] Generating ACGME-constraint-aware surgery residency call schedule software with the assistance of agentic coding large language models
Authors: Isaac H. Lies, Meredith G. Rippy, Syamal Dave Bhattacharya, Wesley H. Giles
Venue: Global Surgical Education - Journal of the Association for Surgical Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s44186-026-00601-8
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Background Manual creation of a surgery residency call schedule is a labor-intensive process that adds to the administrative burden of a chief resident while often producing suboptimal fairness and work distribution. While commercial scheduling software exists, many programs struggle with inflexibility, high costs, and an inability to accommodate program-specific constraints. Methods We developed a scheduling software platform using AI-assisted development tools (Codex, Claude Code), both commercially available agentic coding environments. The system applies a rule-based, weekend-first assignment hierarchy with randomized tie-breaking under a search budget fixed in advance, then performs iterative weekday assignment, accommodating vacation requests and discrete call-shift swapping. The validation roster modeled a single general surgery residency program: 55 residents (32 categorical and 2 preliminary general surgery residents spanning PGY 1 through PGY 6; 20 off-service rotators from other programs; and 1 fellow) distributed across 10 call pools. Three prespecified call-related ACGME constraints were enforced (at least 4 days off per 28-day period, call no more frequently than every third night averaged over 4 weeks, and no consecutive 24-hour call). The 80-hour weekly maximum and the 24-hour period free of all clinical and educational responsibility were not evaluated, as both depend on activity the call calendar does not capture. We evaluated the system with 100 independent full-year runs (July 1 to June 30), each generated end-to-end across all call pools and months under an independently randomized vacation distribution. Compliance and fairness were evaluated at the level of the individual call-pool month (service-month), the unit at which a monthly schedule is produced; fairness and workload metrics were computed across the program’s in-program surgery residents. Results We generated 12,000 service-month schedules over 100 independent full-year runs. 99.2% (11,906) satisfied all prespecified call-related constraints with no violations detected by the internal validation engine. Forty-five of the 100 full-year runs required no manual intervention in any service-month, and none required it in more than 4 of its 120. Manual review of 120 randomly selected service-months by two authors, without reference to the validator’s output, agreed with it in 120 of 120 cases. Monthly fairness, defined within each call pool and month as the range (maximum minus minimum) of call shifts or weekends assigned per resident, showed a shift range ≤ 1 in 65.4% of service-months (mean 1.84, SD 2.15) and perfect weekend equity (range = 0) in 42.5%, with 86.6% achieving a weekend range ≤ 1 (mean 0.71, SD 0.70). Mean full-year generation time was 108.8 s (SD 59.1). Residents averaged 18.65 weekends (SD 3.13) and 78.23 call days (SD 5.49) per year. Conclusions This automated scheduling system generates resident call schedules that satisfy the prespecified call-related ACGME constraints, optimizes fairness across multiple dimensions, accommodates complex vacation requirements, handles cross-pool coordination, and flags the service-months it cannot resolve within its search budget rather than emitting a non-compliant schedule. These results provide construct validity evidence that optimization algorithms combined with careful constraint specification can eliminate the great majority of the administrative burden of manual scheduling while improving schedule quality and equity.

#6 [paper] Comparison of Sizing Methods to Optimize Device Selection for Percutaneous Closure of Atrial Septal Defects.
Authors: Vural, Çağdaş, Baykan, Ali, Doğan, Alper, Kum, Yunus Emre, Akay, Özge Pamukçu, Üzüm, Kazım, Narin, Nazmi
Venue: Cardiology research and practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42824356/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Accurate sizing of atrial septal defects (ASDs) is crucial for appropriate device selection during percutaneous transcatheter closure. Despite the availability of multiple imaging and sizing techniques, no consensus exists on the optimal method for determining device size. This study aimed to compare preprocedural ASD measurements obtained using different techniques with the final device waist diameter and to identify the measurement method demonstrating the most favorable agreement and reproducibility. METHODS: This retrospective study included 149 pediatric patients (64 males, 85 females) who underwent percutaneous transcatheter ASD closure. Preprocedural defect sizing was performed using transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), balloon sizing, and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). TEE measurements were obtained in the four-chamber, aortic, and bicaval views. In addition to individual diameters, the arithmetic mean, cube root-derived diameter, and maximal TEE-measured diameter were calculated and compared with the final device waist diameter. The final device waist diameter, measured fluoroscopically after deployment, was used as the reference comparator, reflecting operator-selected device sizing rather than true anatomical defect dimensions. RESULTS: Among TEE-based measurements, both the cube root-derived diameter and the arithmetic mean of TEE measurements demonstrated high reproducibility and favorable agreement with the final device waist diameter, with only marginal numerical differences between the two methods. Bland-Altman analysis supported these findings by showing minimal bias and narrow limits of agreement, whereas TTE and balloon sizing demonstrated lower, though statistically significant, concordance with the final device waist diameter. CONCLUSION: Combining multiple measurement techniques improves agreement with the operator-selected device size during percutaneous ASD closure. While TTE alone may be sufficient in patients with simple defects and adequate acoustic windows, integrated approaches incorporating TEE and multiaxis measurements showed favorable agreement characteristics, particularly in anatomically heterogeneous defects or resource-limited settings. These findings should be interpreted as reflecting agreement with operator-selected device sizing rather than anatomical sizing accuracy, given the inherent circularity of using implanted device size as a reference standard.

#7 [paper] Frequent Callers to Emergency Medical Services: an observational cohort study from Region Zealand, Denmark (2018-2025).
Authors: Thiele-Nygaard, Amalie Elisabeth, Møller, Thea Palsgaard, Blomberg, Stig Nikolaj Fasmer, Andersen, Lars Bredevang, Jensen, Josefine Tangen, Ersbøll, Annette Kjaer, Christensen, Helle Collatz
Venue: BMC emergency medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43021062/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Frequent callers to Emergency Medical Services represent a small group of citizens who account for a substantial number of calls. Despite their impact, little is known about their characteristics and patterns of EMS use. This study aimed to examine frequency, dispatch outcomes, and characteristics of frequent callers in a prehospital setting. METHODS: We conducted an observational cohort study of calls to the Emergency Medical Dispatch Center in Region Zealand, Denmark, between 2018 and 2025. Calls without a civil register number and individuals younger than 18 years were excluded. Frequent callers were defined as individuals contacting 1-1-2 five or more times within 12 consecutive months. Calls from frequent callers were categorized as pre-frequent calls (before reaching the threshold) and post-threshold calls (from the fifth call onward). Descriptive statistics were used to compare frequent callers with non-frequent callers, as well as subgroups of frequent callers based on call frequency. RESULTS: Overall, 214 091 individuals made 443 977 calls. Of these, 3.0% (n = 6 415) were frequent callers, accounting for 19.9% (n = 88 260) of all calls. "Unclear problem" was the most common contact cause across all groups, whereas "Alcohol/intoxication/overdose" and "Psychiatry - Suicidal" were only among the five most common contact causes in the post-threshold groups with the highest call volumes. High-priority dispatch was assigned to 89.6% of non-frequent calls, 84.3% of pre-frequent calls, and 73.1% of post-threshold calls. Telephone resolution without ambulance dispatch increased across groups (7.3%, 12.5%, and 23.8%, respectively), as did non-conveyance after dispatch (19.2%, 20.8%, and 27.4%). Differences became more pronounced with increasing post-threshold call volume. CONCLUSIONS: Frequent callers accounted for a substantial proportion of contacts to the Emergency Medical Dispatch Center. While pre-frequent calls resembled calls from non-frequent callers, post-threshold calls were more often resolved over the phone and less often resulted in hospital transport. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Approval for performance of the study was given by the Emergency Medical Services in Region Zealand (p202519525).

#9 [paper] Knowing Your Number Is Not Permission to Call: Authorization-to-Reach for Spam-Free, Privacy-First Communication in the 6G and AI-Agent Era
Authors: Sangam Das
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23729617
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Robocalls, spam texts, and scam calls all exploit one design assumption: anyone who knows a phone number, SIP URI, or messaging handle can attempt contact. Once a number is shared with a business, a marketplace seller, a delivery driver, or a directory listing, it becomes a permanent, reusable route, and leaked or brokered contact data keeps that route open for anyone who obtains it. Existing defences answer different questions. STIR/SHAKEN verifies who is calling, not whether that caller is permitted to reach this recipient now. Virtual and masked numbers hide the real number but stay dialable while active. OAuth delegates API access but defines no telecom reachability rules. Spam scoring and call screening judge an attempt only after it has already been routed and signaled. This disclosure describes an authorization-to-reach model that separates knowing a contact identifier from permission to make contact. Each inbound call, message, or notification is held as a candidate request until an enforcement point, such as a session border controller, SIP application server, IMS node, or CPaaS gateway, validates a recipient-scoped grant bound to sender, recipient, purpose or transaction, channel, expiry, attempt quota, revocation epoch, and audience, with replay protection and sender binding so that a copied grant is not a bearer credential. Only then does the phone ring or the message get delivered; otherwise the request is rejected (for example with SIP 403) before any communication takes effect. Three deployment profiles, blocked path, pre-routing authorization, and absent path, allow incremental rollout over existing E.164 numbering, SIP, IMS, and PSTN infrastructure, while emergency calls (911/112) and lawful intercept remain unaffected. The gap grows as AI agents and AI-native 6G networks originate contact at machine speed. The record includes use cases (map and directory enquiries, marketplaces, ride and delivery, AI assistants), a comparison with existing approaches, a candidate grant format, possible STIR/PASSporT, SIP, and OAuth encodings, security and privacy analysis, a 58-question telecom engineering FAQ, and five workflow charts. A reference implementation is publicly available. Its central principle: possession of a communication identifier is not, by itself, permission to communicate. Download the full PDF to review the workflow charts, grant format, deployment profiles, and complete FAQ. Keywords: robocall prevention; spam call blocking; scam calls; SMS spam; caller ID spoofing; STIR/SHAKEN; PASSporT; SIP; IMS; session border controller; CPaaS; number masking; virtual numbers; privacy relay; consent to contact; contact data leakage; telecom fraud prevention; authorization-to-reach; purpose-scoped authorization; revocable grant; capability token; non-bearer token; OAuth RAR; DPoP; replay protection; zero-trust telecom; 6G; IMT-2030; AI-native networks; AI agents; machine-originated traffic; emergency call routing; TCPA; GDPR

#1 [paper] Bibliometric performance and uncertainty in heterogeneous research groups: trends in authorship and fractional citation indicators
Authors: Paolo Castellini, Alessia Caputo, alberto scocco
Venue: Scientometrics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-026-05830-8
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Bibliometric indicators are widely used to evaluate scientific performance, despite well-known limitations related to disciplinary differences, collaboration practices, and strategic responses to evaluation systems. Traditional metrics such as the H-index are particularly sensitive to the number of co-authors and to the length of reference lists, both of which have exhibited strong historical growth. This study analyzes the temporal evolution of authorship, referencing, and productivity patterns in six research populations (four Italian Scientific Disciplinary Sectors in engineering and two international conference communities), covering 1,286 researchers and 86,351 publications. The results reveal systematic increases in authors per article, references per article, and documents per author, with structural changes that coincide with technological developments and the introduction of bibliometric criteria in national evaluation policies. Building on fractional counting, we propose a new citation-based indicator in which publication credit is shared among co-authors and each incoming citation is weighted by the inverse of the number of references in the citing article. Comparisons with the H-index show strong overall correlations, but indicate that the proposed indicator attenuates the advantage associated with hyper-authorship and inflated reference lists and reduces variability across heterogeneous research groups. Adopting a measurement-theoretic perspective, we further assess the uncertainty of bibliometric indicators by analyzing linear trends with researcher seniority and the dispersion of individual data around these trends. The proposed indicator exhibits a slightly more homogeneous trend across heterogeneous research groups and shows strong overall correlation with the H-index, suggesting that it may provide a more comparable representation of scientific performance across diverse research communities.

Authors: Zhu, Ling, Wu, Tong, Zhang, Liang-Jie, Liu, Qin-Yuan, Zhang, Liang-Liang, Song, Bin, Zhu, Yu-Long, Hua, Lei

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Wilson's disease (WD) is a genetic disorder of copper (Cu) metabolism that causes Cu accumulation in multiple organs, particularly the liver and brain, resulting in progressive multisystem damage. This study investigated glymphatic system function and its associated factors in patients with WD. METHODS: Seventy-one patients with WD (19 hepatic, 52 neurological) and 15 healthy controls (HCs) were enrolled. The analysis along the perivascular space (ALPS) index was quantified using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI-ALPS). Comparisons were performed between patients and than HCs, and across WD phenotypes, and correlations with clinical characteristics were analyzed. RESULTS: Compared with HCs, patients with WD exhibited significantly reduced ALPS index (p < 0.001). Patients with neurological WD had a significantly lower ALPS index than those with hepatic WD (p = 0.018) and HCs (p < 0.001). No significant difference was observed between patients with hepatic WD and HCs (p = 0.077). In neurological WD, the ALPS index was significantly higher on the left side than that on the right (p < 0.001), whereas no significant interhemispheric differences were found in hepatic WD or HCs (p > 0.05). In neurological WD, the ALPS index correlated positively with albumin, fasting blood glucose, and the white matter volume-to-total intracranial volume ratio (V_WM/TIV ratio), and negatively with age, alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), and the unified WD rating scale-part I (UWDRS-I) score. Multiple regression identified age, AST, and the UWDRS-I score as independent predictors of reduced ALPS index. CONCLUSIONS: Neurological WD was associated with impaired glymphatic system function and altered lateralization. Age, AST, and the UWDRS-I score were independently associated with dysfunction.Glymphatic function, assessed by DTI-ALPS index, was impaired in neurological WD compared with the hepatic phenotype and controls. Age, AST, and UWDRS-I score independently predicted dysfunction, linking neurodegeneration, liver injury, and altered glymphatic activity.

Non-flood seasons generally exhibited better compliance conditions than flood seasons, while several monitoring sections showed persistently lower compliance stability. Indicator-level analysis suggests that DO and COD contributed strongly to spatial–temporal differentiation within the monitoring dataset. Compared with the conventional WQI, the WQCI provided additional information on whether similar overall water quality scores corresponded to different compliance pressures under different target classes. The WQCI framework used in this study offers a practical approach for linking routine monitoring results with regulatory objectives and identifying priority areas for river basin management.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

#1 [paper] Advances in technologies across the marine plastic value chain in Europe: A critical review
Authors: Eimear Magee, Matheus C. dos Santos, Meriem Stimade, Jose Alvarez, Gerard Dooly, Vincent Mallet, Michel Bakni, Douglas Marques
Venue: Cleaner Engineering and Technology
Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine plastic pollution (MPP) driven by unsustainable production, ineffective waste management, and plastic persistence, requiring technologies to advance a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A critical review evaluating state-of-the-art technologies across the marine plastics value chain, including remote sensing, robotic platforms, machine-vision systems, downstream sorting (electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging, AI-driven classification), and mechanic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe
Abstract:
Marine Plastic Pollution (MPP) is widely recognised as a significant global challenge, driven by unsustainable plastic production, ineffective waste management, and the long-term persistence of plastics in marine environments. MPP has become increasingly widespread across oceans, along coastlines and on the seafloor, resulting in an urgent need for the development of technologies capable of advancing a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products. Advances in cleaner production technologies, including satellite and drone-based remote sensing, autonomous robotic platforms, and machine-vision systems, have improved the efficiency of plastic debris identification, classification, and recovery in complex marine environments. Similarly, innovations in downstream sorting, such as electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven classification, are enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of processing MPP. The review evaluates mechanical recycling methods with particular emphasis on recent advances in extrusion, moulding technologies, and additive manufacturing for converting MPP into high-value secondary materials in a CE framework in Europe. These technological developments demonstrate the potential for establishing viable and scalable valorisation routes. Overall, the review outlines key opportunities to strengthen a sustainable CE and guide future research and industrial adoption. In doing so, it provides a comprehensive examination of state-of-the-art technologies across the entire marine plastics value chain in Europe, from detection and recovery to separation, identification, and recycling.

Authors: Kozhikkodan Veettil, Bijeesh, Amangeldy, Nurzada, Puri, Vikram, Phuong, Tran Thi Nhu

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Traditional solid waste monitoring methods are cost-effective and limited in spatial and temporal scope, necessitating more efficient monitoring solutions.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A comprehensive review and synthesis of remote sensing applications in solid waste management, covering technological developments over the past 20 years, including sensor platforms, data processing, machine learning workflows, and integration with GIS and IoT.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global solid waste management context, reviewing literature and applications from the last two decades.
Abstract:
The rapid growth of solid waste generation carries significant environmental and public health challenges globally. Traditional waste monitoring methods are not cost-effective and are limited in spatial and temporal scope. Remote sensing, encompassing satellite, aerial, and unmanned platforms, has emerged as a transformative approach to identify, monitor, and manage solid waste sites. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the state-of-the-art in remote sensing applications for solid waste monitoring and management, covering technological developments in the past 2 decades. We examine sensor platforms (optical, hyperspectral, thermal, synthetic aperture radar, light detection and ranging), data processing and machine learning workflows, major application domains (landfill mapping, illegal dumping detection, volumetric assessment, thermal anomaly detection, greenhouse gas monitoring, marine plastic tracking), and integration with geographic information system and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. The present study also evaluates operational successes, methodological challenges, policy implications, and outlines a research roadmap for enhancing the accuracy, scalability, and real-world adoption of remote sensing in waste management.

#4 [paper] UAV-based deep learning and spatial analysis for mapping coastal plastic debris distribution
Authors: Elnur Safarov, Эмиль Р. Байрамов, S.H. Safarov, Etibar Gahramanov, Saida Aliyeva, Zaur Imrani
Venue: Geocarto International
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/10106049.2026.2736384
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Plastic waste accumulation in enclosed and semi-enclosed coastal basins with restricted hydrodynamic exchange.
Method (Mycelium's reading): UAV imagery, YOLOv4-based detection, GPS field validation, and spatial analysis.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Neftchala shoreline of the western Caspian Sea.
Abstract:
Plastic waste accumulation is a major environmental challenge in enclosed and semi-enclosed coastal basins where restricted hydrodynamic exchange can promote long-term litter retention. This study assesses surface macroplastic litter along the Neftchala shoreline of the western Caspian Sea using UAV imagery, YOLOv4-based detection, GPS field validation, and spatial analysis. A total of 7,192 litter items were detected within approximately 0.385 km2, corresponding to an average density of 18,684 items/km2, while hotspot densities exceeded 60,000 items/km2. The distribution was strongly clustered, with a Nearest Neighbour Index of 0.49 and three shore-parallel accumulation zones. Detected litter was spatially associated with shoreline proximity, low-relief terrain, and reed-dominated vegetation, particularly desiccated reed belts exposed by recent Caspian Sea-level decline. Because the survey represents a single-date observation, these relationships are interpreted as spatial associations rather than direct causal mechanisms. The workflow supports targeted cleanup and monitoring across semi-enclosed coastal environments and broader evidence-based environmental management.

#5 [paper] CLEAR-RUN : AUTONOMOUS RUNWAY FOD DETECTION AND REMOVAL
Authors: Umair Raza
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23573169

Abstract:
CLEAR-RUN is a multi-phase research and engineering initiative at the National University of Sciences & Technology (NUST), aimed at transforming runway safety through intelligent, autonomous Foreign Object Debris (FOD) detection and removal. Moving beyond conventional detection-only systems, CLEAR-RUN integrates an AI-enabled aerial platform with RGB and thermal sensing, precision geolocation, a centralized ground control station, and an autonomous ground rover capable of locating and physically retrieving debris. The system employs edge AI, multi-agent coordination, and vision-guided retrieval to establish a complete detection-to-removal pipeline. Initial hardware development and field trials have demonstrated detection across 23 FOD classes and 93.3% retrieval success across 30 pickup trials. Subsequent phases aim to enhance localization accuracy, validate round-the-clock operational capability, and scale coordinated robotic deployment, advancing toward a cost-effective, operationally viable solution for autonomous runway clearance.

Abstract:
Marine pollution has emerged as a significant environmental challenge, with millions of tons of waste flowing intooceans each year, causing disruptions in marine ecosystems. Traditional methods for monitoring and addressing thispollution are inadequate in dealing with its ineffable complexity. Researchers are thoroughly investigating the potentialof artificial intelligence (AI) as a revolutionary tool for tracking and reducing ocean pollution. This literature reviewexplores the application of cutting-edge technology in tracking and mitigating marine pollution, such as plastic waste,oil spills, and wastewater contamination. A comprehensive review of recent research was performed, concentrating ontechniques that employ advanced technology for the detection, forecasting, and elimination of marine debris. Researchshows that advanced computer vision and machine learning techniques significantly boost the efficiency and precisionof pollution detection, such as recognizing plastic waste through satellite images, and improving clean-up strategies bydirecting collection vessels for maximum effectiveness. Efforts are underway to form partnerships among governmententities, industry players, and academic scholars to advance these data-centric solutions. However, obstacles persist;AI systems typically demand significant amounts of data and are subject to time limitations, and it is essential toconsider the environmental impacts of AI deployment, including energy use and electronic waste. This paper bringstogether current applications, assesses their effectiveness and limitations, and highlights gaps in the existing research.The ability of AI to transform ocean waste management is substantial; however, achieving its complete potentialnecessitates collaboration across disciplines, strict data governance, and thoughtful attention to sustainability in AIresearch.

#7 [paper] Infrared-visible space debris perception and detection with light-boosting convolution and cross-modal attention fusion
Authors: Yongqing Yang, Dalei Yao, Fan Bu, Yan Wen, Rongli Chen
Venue: Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fspas.2026.1930223
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction Space debris poses an increasing threat to the safety of spacecraft because reliable perception under complex illumination remains challenging for autonomous on-orbit operations. Existing visible-light methods are highly susceptible to low-light degradation, whereas infrared images preserve thermal information but lack sufficient structural details. Methods To address these limitations, we propose the Space Debris Perception and Detection Network (SPDNet), an end-to-end infrared-visible framework that jointly performs image enhancement, cross-modal feature fusion, and object detection. Specifically, a Light-Boosting Convolution module restores degraded visible features under weak illumination, a Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) module progressively exchanges complementary infrared and visible information during hierarchical feature extraction, and a Multi-Scale Adaptive Fusion (MSAF) module adaptively integrates multi-scale semantic features to improve both overall detection and small-object recognition. Experiments are conducted on a paired infrared-visible space debris dataset constructed from publicly available visible images and geometrically aligned simulated infrared imagery. Abstract:

Masks were created in CVAT and verified through a primary annotator, a second cross-checking annotator, a third adjudicator, and a final quality-control pass. #9 [paper] Quantifying the long-term evolution of post-earthquake debris-flow activity in the epicentral area of the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, China
Authors: Qingyun Shi, Weihua Zhang, Chuan Tang, Yucai Ma, Wei Zhou, Jiang Xiong, Yu Tie
Venue: Natural Hazards
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08494-y
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The 2008 Wenchuan earthquake triggered widespread coseismic landslides and supplied large volumes of loose material on hillslopes and channels, resulting in persistent post-earthquake debris flow activity near the epicentral area. Quantifying the long-term evolution of this activity is important for geohazard assessment, but remains challenge because debris flows are jointly controlled by sediment supply, topography, and rainfall. In this study, a catchment-scale framework was developed to evaluate debris flow activity intensity in 44 catchments affected by the Wenchuan earthquake. Multi-temporal landslide inventories from 2008 to 2019 were used to calculate landslide sediment supply potential (LSSP), which integrates landslide areal density, spatial distribution indices, and channel gradient. LSSP was then combined with representative hourly rainfall intensities from documented debris flow triggering events to derive a debris flow activity intensity index (AI DF ). The results show that active landslide area decreased from 122.05 km² in 2008 to 30.55 km² in 2019, while recovery areas expanded progressively. LSSP increased sharply immediately after the earthquake and then declined over time, with a rapid decrease during 2008–2011 followed by a slower adjustment phase. Nevertheless, sediment supply in many catchments remained above the pre-earthquake level in 2019. AI DF showed an overall decline after its post-earthquake peak, although temporary increases occurred during major rainfall events. Comparison with documented debris flow events indicates that AI DF captures the main temporal pattern of observed activity. The fitted long-term trend suggests three stages of post-earthquake debris flow activity: an active period from 2008 to 2013, a recession period from 2013 to 2048, and a relatively stable period after 2048. These results indicate that debris flow activity in the Wenchuan earthquake-affected area may persist for several decades, mainly controlled by the gradual depletion and redistribution of landslide-derived sediment under rainfall forcing.

Abstract:
Purpose: This review asks whether, and under what conditions, combining satellite remote sensing with machine learning, and ensemble learning in particular, improves the mapping of illegal-dumpsite susceptibility, and where the evidence for that claim is still missing, with emphasis on sub-Saharan Africa and Nigeria. Methodology: A structured narrative review with a non-systematic, purposive selection of studies was carried out. Candidate studies published from 2000 to 2026 were identified through targeted keyword searches of scholarly databases and search engines (Google Scholar, Scopus-indexed journals and African Journals Online), combining dumping terms (illegal dump, illegal landfill, dumpsite) with remote-sensing, susceptibility and machine-learning terms, and through citation chasing from recent surveys. Only one study used spatial cross-validation, none used a stacking ensemble, and no Nigerian study has modelled susceptibility predictively. #14 [paper] How Emerging Technologies Transform Disaster Debris Management: Generative AI, Digital Twins, and Cyber-Physical-Social Systems for Circular Recovery

Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Method (Mycelium's reading): Collection and georeferencing of litter across twenty-five beaches, application of the Brand Audit approach, estimation of item age, and evaluation of the relationship with maritime activities.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Twenty-five beaches in the state of Pará, Brazilian Amazon coast.
Abstract:
Marine debris remains a critical environmental challenge due to its multiple impacts on ecosystems. The Amazonian coast of Pará is one of the most biodiverse coastal environments in the world; however, it is affected by the presence of both local and foreign litter. It is necessary to understand the origin and source of marine debris to design effective mitigation strategies. In this context, the objective of this study is to analyze the presence of allochthonous litter along the Amazonian coast to determine its characteristics and infer its potential sources. Maritime activities constitute a plausible pathway/source contributing to the occurrence of foreign-identified litter along the Pará coast. To achieve this objective, litter was collected and georeferenced at twenty-five beaches in the state of Pará; subsequently, the Brand Audit approach was applied, the age of the items was estimated, and the possible relationship with maritime activities was evaluated. A total of 2368 items were collected, predominantly plastic bottles associated with products from Mauritania (25%) and China (18%). Among the subset of items for which age could be estimated (n = 1042; 44% of the total), 75% were manufactured less than 24 months before collection. The results indicate that maritime activities represent a plausible source requiring further investigation. The presence of international litter may be influenced by cleanup activities and beach geomorphology. The study highlights the presence of foreign-identified litter in areas of high environmental, cultural, and economic value, and emphasizes the importance of strengthening monitoring and litter-management measures.

#3 [paper] Spatial Patterns of Marine Litter on a Remote South Atlantic Ocean Island: Setting Baselines for Monitoring

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Characterizing the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter on Trindade Island, a remote South Atlantic island, to establish baselines for monitoring before the establishment of marine protected areas.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Systematic sampling of seven beaches with varying exposure to wind and substrate; quantification of litter items, categorization by purpose, and calculation of pollution indices (Clean Coast Index and Plastic Abundance Index).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Seven beaches on Trindade Island, South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland; characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates.
Abstract:
Abstract Marine plastic litter is a major environmental problem across all oceans, including remote regions. Here, we described the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter stranded on the beaches of Trindade Island, in the South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland, before the establishment of marine protected areas and the initiation of a long-term research program on the island. Seven beaches differing in exposure to wind and substrate were sampled. A total of 1317 litter items were recorded, with plastics as the main litter (81.9%), mostly hard plastic fragments. Although Lixo Beach had the smallest surveyed area (425 m 2 ), it exhibited the highest litter density (0.74 items/m 2 ) and highest litter-covered area (2.2% of the sampled beach area). Domestic and household purpose items composed the bulk of identifiable items (28.9%), followed by naval (22.5%) and fishery (17.7%) pieces. Litter distribution among beaches differed, with leeward beaches accumulating significantly more and larger litter items than windward beaches, revealing substantial local-scale variation patterns in debris retention. These beaches are characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates rather than sand. Our analysis of pollution indices demonstrated that the Clean Coast Index ( CCI ) and the Plastic Abundance Index ( PAI ) are strongly correlated and suitable for long-term monitoring. This study confirms that oceanic islands are prone to accumulating marine litter, while contrasting results from other studies on Trindade Island emphasize the need for simple yet standardized protocols to support long-term monitoring of plastic pollution in remote environments.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine litter contamination and its impact on ocean ecosystems and human societies.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A concise overview of impacts, solutions, and causes, including the use of deep learning algorithms to analyze images and video footage from drones or underwater cameras, and debris analysis utilizing publicly available datasets.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Marine environments; analysis of publicly available datasets generated by previous studies.
Abstract:
Marine litter contamination causes a tremendous environmental issue with a high influence on the consequences for ocean ecosystems and human societies. This study offers a concise overview of the impacts, potential solutions, and causes to address this complex problem with Artificial Intelligence. The sources of marine pollution encompass a wide range of human activities, including oil spills, chemical discharges, plastic waste, nutrient runoff, sewage disposal, and atmospheric deposition. These pollutants pose significant threats to marine life, biodiversity, and ecosystem health. While deep learning technologies have shown promise in various environmental applications, including pollution monitoring and management, their direct application to solving marine pollution is limited. Deep learning algorithms can be used to analyze images and video footage from drones or underwater cameras to identify and track plastic pollution. This study additionally provides debris analysis utilizing publicly available datasets generated by a few studies. The several approaches that are being considered can be applied to the creation and efficient management of litter in the future, preserving our ecology. Collaborative efforts between environmental scientists, engineers, and data scientists are crucial to developing robust and effective deep-learning solutions for marine pollution management.

#5 [paper] Out of sight, hidden into the deep: Marine litter in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon (southwestern Atlantic) revealed by ROV survey
Authors: Valeria Teso, Diego Urteaga, Graziella Bozzano, Gregório Bigatti, Martín Brogger, Francisco Brusa, Rodrigo Calderón, NADIA CERINO
Venue: PLoS ONE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0357098
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The deep sea is increasingly recognized as vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures, including marine litter, yet large geographic gaps remain in our understanding of litter distribution and ecological interactions. Submarine canyon systems can act as conduits and accumulation zones for anthropogenic material, but data from the southwestern Atlantic are scarce. Here, we present the first characterization of deep-sea marine macro-litter in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon (Argentina), based on 240 hours of remotely operated vehicle (ROV) video collected during 17 dives (878-3,820 m depth) aboard the R/V Falkor (too) in July-August 2025. Litter was observed during 10 dives, comprising 29 items distributed between 1,120 and 3,820 m. Plastic was the dominant material (27 items), followed by rubber (2 items). Most litter consisted of plastic sheets and bags, food wrappers, and commercial fishing-related gear, including lines, ropes, and cables. Litter was observed in multiple settings, including buried or degraded items, resting on the seabed, and trapped among rocks or drifting near the bottom. Most items were located within the canyon domain, forming localized clusters along the canyon axis and walls. Litter-fauna interactions were documented for seven items and included both sessile colonization and associations with mobile fauna, mainly on partially buried plastic items and entangled fishing-related gear. These patterns suggest that substrate stability and residence time may influence sessile colonization. The composition and distribution of debris indicate that maritime activities, particularly fisheries, are the most likely sources and further support the role of submarine canyons as accumulation zones for marine litter. This study provides critical baseline data in an understudied region and highlights the need for improved monitoring programs and management strategies for marine litter to reduce impacts in submarine canyon systems.

#6 [paper] Assessing oceans’ health through biopsy sampling in free-ranging marine mammals: a systematic review (2014–2024)
Authors: Suelen Goulart, Giulia Galani, Lucas Fazardo de Lima, Isadora Nicole Lara Piccinin, Felipe da Silva Valente, Aline Nunes, Eduardo Pires Renault-Braga, Marcelo Maraschin
Venue: Environmental Science and Pollution Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-026-38163-3
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine mammals are ecological sentinels of ocean health. As apex predators, they can bioaccumulate contaminants through aquatic food webs. In this context, this systematic review evaluates the role of minimally invasive biopsy sampling in assessing contaminant exposure across free-ranging populations. Following PRISMA guidelines, 31 studies were evaluated, covering the period from 2014 to 2024, and sourced from the CAPES Periodicals Portal database. Results indicate a primary focus on persistent organic pollutants (POPs; 74.19%), such as PCBs and DDTs, with a notable geographic bias toward cetaceans in the Northern Hemisphere (47.4% in the Americas). Cetaceans, especially bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus), were significantly overrepresented (93.94% of studies), while studies on the Carnivora order, focused on pinnipeds, were scarce (6.06%). Inorganic contaminants were underrepresented, despite concerning mercury levels in dolphins and chromium-induced genotoxicity in fin whales. Interestingly, emerging contaminants, like phthalates, were detected in only two studies. DEHP, a hazardous plasticizer, was detected in three cetacean species. Thus, the urgent need to expand monitoring efforts to underrepresented regions and to integrate biopsy analysis with other approaches (e.g., multi-omics, isotopic analyses), long-term research, and satellite telemetry to map pollution hotspots is emphasized. Standardizing protocols and establishing global biobanks are essential for data harmonization. This work highlights the critical role of biopsies within the One Health framework, connecting marine pollution data to human and ecosystem resilience. Graphical Abstract

#7 [paper] Evaluation of micro-litter pollution in the Antarctic asteroid Odontaster validus Koehler, 1906 at Deception Island (South Shetland Islands)
Authors: Marina Aldana-Martínez, Conxita Ávila, Tomás Azcárate-García
Venue: Marine Pollution Bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marpolbul.2026.120412
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Micro-litter (ML) pollution is increasingly being reported in Antarctic benthic ecosystems and the organisms inhabiting them. In this study, we assessed ML abundance and characteristics in the Antarctic asteroid Odontaster validus at Deception Island (South Shetland Islands), an area with significant human presence. Additionally, we considered the potential influence of local factors, including proximity to research stations and the bay entrance, as well as depth (5 and 15 m), on ML pollution. Approximately 63% of the specimens exhibited at least one item, all of which were fibers, with a mean abundance of 1.10 ± 1.05 items individual −1 and 0.77 ± 1.31 items g −1 WW. Spatial variability in ML abundance was detected, notably at 15 m depth, with specimens collected at BAE (3.15 ± 2.46 items g −1 WW), the sampling station nearest to research stations, exhibiting significantly higher abundances than those from sampling stations near the bay entrance. Our results are consistent with previous studies suggesting that Antarctic research stations may act as local ML sources, leading to higher ML abundances in benthic invertebrates inhabiting nearby areas. Although no significant differences were observed between sampling stations at 5 m depth or between depths, variations in ML abundances were also detected. Our results provide critical new insights into ML pollution in this key Antarctic asteroid species and how it is influenced by local factors. This study also supports the potential use of O. validus as a bioindicator of ML pollution in Antarctic benthic ecosystems, contributing to future monitoring and conservation efforts.

#10 [paper] Bioprospecting Marine Invertebrate-Associated Bacteria for Polyethylene Biodegradation in Indonesian Coastal Waters
Authors: Etin Diah Permanasari, Hanifah Sriamelia
Venue: Science Get Journal.
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.69855/science.v3i4.850
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Polyethylene (PE) persists in marine environments because of its chemical inertness. Marine invertebrate-associated bacteria may provide enzymes capable of transforming this polymer, but their potential in Indonesian waters remains underexplored. This study isolated, identified, and evaluated bacteria associated with sponges, ascidians, and holothurians from four coastal sites in West Sumatra. Thirty-seven distinct isolates were recovered from 34 of 42 specimens using enrichment culture with PE film as the only added carbon source. Seven representative isolates were identified through 16S rRNA gene sequencing as Bacillus, Pseudomonas, Rhodococcus, and Vibrio. After 60 days, SSP-03 (Rhodococcus sp.) exhibited the highest PE weight loss (22.3 ± 1.8%), followed by SBB-07 (Bacillus sp., 18.9 ± 1.6%) and SAM-12 (Pseudomonas sp., 14.6 ± 1.4%), compared with 1.3 ± 0.3% in the control. Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy revealed increased carbonyl indices, indicating surface oxidation. These findings demonstrate PE biodeterioration, not complete biodegradation, and highlight marine invertebrate-associated bacteria as promising biocatalyst candidates.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Manual identification and collection of marine litter on Arctic beaches is labor-intensive; there is a need for automated, large-scale monitoring methods.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Training a YOLOv8s Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) in Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) configuration to detect and classify marine litter types (plastic, metal, fishing gear, wood, etc.) from high-resolution aerial photography.

Abstract:
Marine litter beach accumulation is a pressing issue not only for urban coastal areas but also for remote and uninhabited regions such as the Arctic. Existing manual litter collection and identification methods remain labor-intensive. An assessment of the volume and composition of marine litter was conducted for the Russian Arctic coastlines using high-resolution airphotos. The method is based on training the You Only Look Once (YOLOv8, 2023) convolutional neural network (CNN) in the Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) configuration to recognize plastic, metal, fishing gear, wood, and other types of marine litter on images. #13 [paper] Material design for artificial reef restoration: a novel calcium carbonate biocomposite
Authors: Beth O’Sullivan, Roderick Bamford, Mark Shannon, Jennie Mallela, Adam W. Periman
Venue: Research Directions Biotechnology Design
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/s2977905726100808
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Artificial reefs offer potential for urgent coral reef restoration, yet are frequently fabricated from materials of opportunity, without accounting for the dynamic and temporal processes necessary for a healthy reef system. We introduce a novel calcium carbonate biocomposite designed as a living artefact supporting recruitment while enabling bioerosion and recycling by reef organisms. By recognising material agentic capacity, how material properties influence organism behaviour, we consider substrate design as more-than-human design practice distinct from conventional approaches. Rather than finished objects, we reconceptualise substrates as active participants in sympoietic processes where organisms and materials mutually constitute reef ecosystems. An 8.8-month in-situ reef study shows the CaCO 3 biocomposite supported early-stage colonisation but did not yet develop communities equivalent to natural coral rubble, requiring further research and analysis of more mature benthic communities. This research demonstrates that designing with organisms as active partners, grounded in material agency, enables collaborative reef restoration practice.

#14 [paper] Towards circularity in shellfish aquaculture: stimulating mussel shell dissolution in marine sediments
Authors: Cedric Goossens, Steven Bouillon, Filip J. R. Meysman, Sebastiaan van de Velde
Venue: Biogeosciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/bg-23-6447-2026
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE) is receiving considerable attention as a carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) removal strategy, and novel approaches to increase the total alkalinity ( A T ) of the surface ocean are being explored. In bivalve aquaculture, calcification during shell growth consumes A T , thus leading to CO 2 emissions. After consumption, shells are typically landfilled or incinerated, which can generate additional CO 2 emissions. Here, we investigate how the CO 2 footprint of shellfish aquaculture can be reduced by using bivalve shells as a resource for mineral-based OAE. The idea is to grind the calcium carbonate (CaCO 3 ) shells to increase the reactive surface area and distribute them into permeable, oxygen-rich sediments, where their dissolution produces A T that could then compensate the CO 2 emitted during calcification. To evaluate this concept, we conducted microcosm incubations of sediments amended with crushed mussel shells (∼ 8 wt %), and monitored the sediment geochemistry and sediment-water exchange over 24 weeks. Control sediments exhibited low and constant CaCO 3 dissolution rates ( R diss = 0.9 ± 0.5 mmolm-2d-1) and A T fluxes ( F AT = 3.2 ± 1.1 mmolm-2d-1). In contrast, shell-amended sediments showed markedly higher R diss and F AT values, which exhibited a transient response modulated by oxygen and organic matter availability. Initially, shell dissolution was restricted, most likely by oxygen availability due to the intense mineralization of shell-associated organic matter. Subsequently, following gradual sediment reoxygenation, dissolution rates increased, reaching a maximum R diss of 22.7 ± 2.6 mmolm-2d-1 after 9 weeks, corresponding to a measured F AT of 43.0 ± 6.0 mmolm-2d-1. After that, CaCO 3 dissolution rates declined as organic matter availability decreased, approaching control rates, with a slightly elevated R diss of 2.2 ± 1.1 mmolm-2d-1 at the end of the experiment. After 24 weeks, ∼ 6 % of the initial shell mass had dissolved, and extrapolation of the dissolution rate at the end of the experiment suggests that complete dissolution would require ∼ 38 years. Our results suggest that organic matter availability limits CaCO 3 dissolution in the permeable sediment investigated. This constraint, however, can be alleviated by targeting environments with high organic matter deposition for in-situ applications, such as sediments beneath mussel farms, thereby promoting mussel aquaculture circularity.

#15 [paper] From Marine Byproducts to Biomaterials: A Governed Model for Centralized Quality Control and Distributed Manufacturing
Authors: Mohammed Alhalees
Venue: Industrial Biotechnology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1177/15509087261495500
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine fishery and aquaculture processing generate substantial volumes of biological byproducts—fish skin, bone, scales, and viscera—that remain underutilized as feedstocks for higher-value bio-based materials. The gap between feedstock availability and quality-controlled manufacturing capacity in many coastal economies is not solely scientific; the scientific characterization of marine-derived biomaterials is comparatively more developed than the governance literature addressing their distributed manufacture. It is a governance gap: The absence of a framework capable of transmitting sufficient process knowledge to geographically distributed manufacturing entities while retaining intellectual property integrity, capturing local adaptation learning, and maintaining quality coherence across nodes and biological input sources. Existing organizational models—centralized production and conventional technology licensing—each address part of this challenge but leave important governance problems unresolved. This review examines the governance and technology transfer literature bearing on distributed biomanufacturing, identifies the specific design gap those literatures leave open, and proposes a platform governance model in which intellectual property, research and development authority, feedstock qualification, and quality standards are maintained centrally while geographically defined industrial nodes conduct local sourcing, manufacturing, and regulatory engagement. The central argument is that, for biologically variable feedstocks, governance architecture may function as a technical control mechanism—not merely a commercial arrangement—for reproducibility, quality assurance, and responsible technology transfer. The model is presented as a conceptual framework requiring proof-of-concept validation, regulatory classification, quality system development, and partner governance design before any operational, regulatory, or commercial claims can be made. Governance risks, implementation considerations, and a staged pathway to node deployment are discussed.

#16 [paper] Global compilation of in situ particulate organic carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus concentrations in coastal and open ocean waters
Authors: Alain Fumenia, Hubert Loisel, Thierry Moutin, Jamee C. Adams, Hélène Agogué, Lihini I. Aluwihare, Kevin Robert Arrigo, Marcel Babin
Venue: Scientific Data
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-026-08413-7
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Lack of a comprehensive, global collection of in situ marine particulate organic matter (POM) concentrations to support biogeochemical modeling and satellite-derived estimates.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Compilation of measurements from multiple sources with systematic assembly of metadata regarding sampling strategies, filtration protocols, filter types, and analytical techniques to address methodological heterogeneity.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean waters (surface to 6009 m depth), including 25,944 independent stations (52% in coastal waters <200 m bottom depth) from 1988 to 2025.
Abstract:
We present a global compilation of in situ marine particulate organic carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus concentrations (POC, PON, and POP, respectively), from multiple sources to provide one of the most comprehensive collections of marine particulate organic matter (POM) to date. The dataset includes 155137 measurements (70586 POC, 69290 PON, and 15261 POP) from 25944 independent stations, more than doubling the number of previously available observations. Observations span more than three decades (1988–2025) and cover the global ocean from the surface to 6009 m depth. Notably, 52% of stations are located in shallow, coastal waters (<200 m bottom depth), enhancing coverage of productive nearshore regions and improving representation of dynamic coastal biogeochemistry. To address methodological heterogeneity among the compiled datasets, detailed metadata describing sampling strategies, filtration protocols, filter types, and analytical techniques were systematically assembled for each measurement whenever available. This dataset provides a resource for quantifying the spatial and temporal variability of POM distributions, and the elemental stoichiometry of marine particles, supporting biogeochemical modeling efforts. The dataset will also enable the development and validation of both bio-optical models and satellite-derived estimates of POM, including applications to the Sentinel-3 and the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) missions.

#17 [paper] Sustained algal-bacterial interactions promote accumulation of recalcitrant particulate carbon with accelerated radiocarbon aging signatures
Authors: Hanshuang Zhao, Zenghu Zhang, Xiuting Feng, Shailesh Nair, Huamao Yuan, Jinming Song, Xiuzhen Li, Nianzhi Jiao
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-77300-x
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Algal-bacterial interactions regulate the production and fate of marine particulate organic carbon (POC), yet their capacity to generate long-lived carbon sinks remains unclear. Using a two-year, nutrient-self-sustaining co-culture of Synechococcus and its mutualistic microbiota, we demonstrate that sustained algal-bacterial interactions promote the progressive accumulation of recalcitrant POC. Continuous release of algal-derived organic substrates, coupled with repeated microbial enzymatic reworking, produced inert organic particles, with ~26% resisting remineralization and forming a stable recalcitrant particulate carbon pool. Radiocarbon (Δ14C) analyses revealed an apparent age offset exceeding 400 years for POC formed within only two-year experiment. This “aged” signature likely results from algal assimilation of fossil-fuel-14C-depleted atmospheric CO2 followed by accumulation in generated recalcitrant POC. By demonstrating that apparent radiocarbon age can become decoupled from actual residence time, these results provide insights into the interpretation of “old” marine POC and highlight the important roles of algal-bacterial interactions in ocean particulate carbon sequestration. Sustained algae-bacteria interactions generate recalcitrant particulate organic carbon with aged radiocarbon signatures within years, revealing an overlooked ocean carbon storage pathway and complicating interpretations of old marine carbon pools.

#18 [paper] Monitoring seagrass meadow health using coastal bird fecal fatty acid biomarkers
Authors: David A. Gold, Christopher Mulligan
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.01.748668
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Lipids have the potential to trace trophic interactions through an ecosystem, but their use has been largely limited to predator/prey-scale studies. Carnivore fecal lipids offer an unexplored way to strategically monitor the health and spatial distribution of ecosystems that are difficult to access. This hypothesis is explored here in seagrass meadows, which are a globally significant long-term carbon storage reservoir. This study tested the hypothesis that lipids can be used to passively monitor seagrass meadow health by tracing fatty acids transferred up the food chain and onto nearby beaches via coastal bird stool. By comparing the lipids produced by seagrasses and those made by diverse microbial eukaryotes, such as diatoms and dinoflagellates, our analysis could distinguish between healthy and collapsed meadows in a pilot dataset. A metabolite that is produced by the seagrass wasting disease pathogen was also recovered in our data, providing a potential diagnostic for seagrass health. The advantages to this non-invasive monitoring approach using lipids are that beaches are far more accessible than seagrass meadows, and birds spatially ‘sample’ a larger area than researchers could do efficiently. Although this pilot study was limited in samples and field sites, our results provide compelling reasons to pursue carnivorous fecal dietary lipids as a source of ecosystem data.

#19 [paper] Technological Innovations for Ocean Plastic Waste Management: A Global Bibliometric Analysis of Research Trends, Collaboration Networks, and Emerging Technologies
Authors: Jehu Roeh C. Rubenial Franklin M. Ganancias
Venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.59543/jidmis.v3.1213
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ocean plastic pollution has become one of the most pressing environmental challenges worldwide, driving increasing interest in technology-based solutions for monitoring, prevention, mitigation, and sustainable waste management. Despite the rapid growth of research in this field, a comprehensive understanding of its scientific development, collaboration patterns, and emerging technological directions remains limited. This study presents a global bibliometric analysis of technological innovations for ocean plastic waste management using 12,039 English-language publications retrieved from the Scopus database on 09 July 2026. Bibliographic data were analyzed using Bibliometrix (RStudio) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, influential authors, journals, institutions, countries, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, and thematic evolution. The findings reveal a substantial increase in scientific production, particularly after 2015, demonstrating the rapid expansion of this interdisciplinary research domain. China, the United States, and several European and Asian countries emerged as the leading contributors to scientific productivity and international collaboration, while Marine Pollution Bulletin and Science of the Total Environment ranked among the most productive publication sources. Author keyword co-occurrence analysis identified microplastics, plastic waste, circular economy, recycling, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and remote sensing as dominant research themes. Thematic evolution further revealed a transition from broad marine pollution research toward technology-oriented investigations emphasizing plastic waste management and microplastics. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive knowledge map of the field, highlighting the growing integration of digital technologies and sustainable waste management strategies. The findings offer valuable insights for researchers, policymakers, and environmental practitioners in identifying research priorities, strengthening international collaboration, and advancing technology-driven solutions for sustainable ocean plastic waste management.

#20 [paper] Environmental regulation and disruption of shell biomineralization in bivalves and gastropods: a mechanistic review
Authors: Wenxiao Guo, Hao Li, Dongfang Li, Peiyao Sun, Ran Zhao
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1909510
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Molluscan shells are increasingly threatened by a complex array of environmental stressors—climate-related drivers, changes in seawater chemistry, contaminants, and biotic cues. This review provides a mechanistic synthesis of how these stressors disrupt the biomineralization process across life stages. We develop a conditional hierarchical response framework from the reviewed evidence. The framework links ionoregulatory and acid-base disturbances with molecular, microstructural, and shell-level responses, while allowing for compensatory, nonlinear, species-specific, and life-stage-specific outcomes. This molecular disruption manifests as defects in calcium carbonate (CaCO 3 ) crystalline microstructure, which may in turn compromise shell macro-scale physical properties (strength, hardness, growth). We synthesize combined and context-dependent effects of co-occurring stressors and distinguish formally tested interactions from qualitative comparisons of combined treatments. Future research must leverage integrated multi-omics, advanced in vivo imaging, and multi-stressor experimental designs to unravel candidate molecular and physiological thresholds and predict adaptive potential. This framework may help identify testable mechanisms, evidence gaps, and context-dependent vulnerabilities relevant to conservation.
