#1 [paper] Advances in technologies across the marine plastic value chain in Europe: A critical review
Authors: Eimear Magee, Matheus C. dos Santos, Meriem Stimade, Jose Alvarez, Gerard Dooly, Vincent Mallet, Michel Bakni, Douglas Marques
Venue: Cleaner Engineering and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clet.2026.101352
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine plastic pollution (MPP) driven by unsustainable production, ineffective waste management, and plastic persistence, requiring technologies to advance a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A critical review evaluating state-of-the-art technologies across the marine plastics value chain, including remote sensing, robotic platforms, machine-vision systems, downstream sorting (electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging, AI-driven classification), and mechanic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe
Abstract:
Marine Plastic Pollution (MPP) is widely recognised as a significant global challenge, driven by unsustainable plastic production, ineffective waste management, and the long-term persistence of plastics in marine environments. MPP has become increasingly widespread across oceans, along coastlines and on the seafloor, resulting in an urgent need for the development of technologies capable of advancing a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products. Advances in cleaner production technologies, including satellite and drone-based remote sensing, autonomous robotic platforms, and machine-vision systems, have improved the efficiency of plastic debris identification, classification, and recovery in complex marine environments. Similarly, innovations in downstream sorting, such as electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven classification, are enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of processing MPP. The review evaluates mechanical recycling methods with particular emphasis on recent advances in extrusion, moulding technologies, and additive manufacturing for converting MPP into high-value secondary materials in a CE framework in Europe. These technological developments demonstrate the potential for establishing viable and scalable valorisation routes. Overall, the review outlines key opportunities to strengthen a sustainable CE and guide future research and industrial adoption. In doing so, it provides a comprehensive examination of state-of-the-art technologies across the entire marine plastics value chain in Europe, from detection and recovery to separation, identification, and recycling.

#2 [paper] Modeling dispersal and beaching of urban plastic waste along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire.
Authors: Amemou, Hilaire, Cecchi, Philippe, Koné, Vamara, Penven, Pierrick, Lett, Christophe
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42735662/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The processes governing the fate, dispersal, and coastal retention of urban plastic debris along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, which is vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO) to simulate the dispersal and beaching of plastic particles.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically focusing on the region around Abidjan and the broader Ivorian coast.
Abstract:
Plastic pollution is a growing concern in West Africa's marine environment, yet the processes governing its fate remain poorly understood. The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). We provide the first regional-scale assessment of seasonal beaching dynamics along the Ivorian coast using a high-resolution coupled hydrodynamic-Lagrangian framework. Simulations show that while a large fraction of particles is transported offshore (~52%), a substantial proportion (~48%) remains nearshore and beaches at least once. Persistent accumulation hotspots are identified around Abidjan, regardless of the release location. Seasonal variability strongly controls debris pathways. During the minor upwelling season (January-April), beaching occurs predominantly west of Abidjan, associated with weaker currents and enhanced coastal retention. In contrast, during the major upwelling season (June-September), intensified currents and mesoscale activity promote wider dispersal and shift beaching eastward. From October to December, beaching intensifies along the eastern coastline. These results highlight the dominant role of regional hydrodynamics in shaping marine debris distribution and demonstrate the value of high-resolution Lagrangian modeling for identifying pollution hotspots and supporting mitigation strategies in data-scarce coastal regions.

#3 [paper] International legal regulation of marine plastic pollution: basic theories, specific issues, and China’s responses
Authors: Yuanhong Shi
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1930536
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic pollution (MPP) is among the gravest environmental issues of the international community and is directly linked with the shared interests of humanity. The current international legal frameworks that regulate MPP primarily involve the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and other international conventions and other soft-law instruments. Nevertheless, there is still no fully developed international legal regulatory framework of MPP. According to the basic theories of the international regulation of MPP, this paper identifies the unresolved problems in the current process of governance, including the limitations of existing international conventions, the difficulty in negotiating the Global Plastics Treaty, the insufficient compliance capacity of relevant States, and the inadequate oversight mechanisms. Based on the experience of the representative countries, regions, and other international organizations, this paper suggests that China should pursue a holistic approach to governance of MPP by enhancing its domestic laws, encouraging the implementation of the Global Plastics Treaty, facilitating and supporting international governance mechanisms to increase state compliance, and enhancing regulatory and enforcement capabilities.

#4 [paper] Halting marine plastic inputs by 2050 is necessary but not sufficient to avoid microplastic accumulation
Authors: Takuro Uehara, Mateo Cordier, Laurent Lebreton
Venue: Communications Earth & Environment
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-026-04054-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic pollution threatens ecosystems, economies, and human health, yet economic literature overlooks the transport of plastic debris across marine ecosystem compartments and its natural breakdown. Here we show, using a system dynamics model, the global physical and economic efforts required to remove buoyant marine plastic debris by 2050. The model simulates the degradation, transport, and cleanup of macroplastics and their breakdown into microplastics across shoreline, coastal, and offshore zones. Scenario analyses explore varying rates of waste input reduction and cleanup intensity. Results indicate that halting new marine plastic inputs by 2050, as outlined in the G20 Implementation Framework for Actions on Marine Plastic Litter, and removing existing buoyant macroplastics may be insufficient to prevent substantial microplastic accumulation. Accelerating cleanup efforts can reduce microplastic generation, albeit at a higher cost. Estimated annual cleanup expenses range from €0.1–5.6 billion, representing 0.3–15.7% of national pollution abatement budgets and 0.0001–0.0052% of global GDP. Stopping new marine plastic inputs and removing buoyant macroplastics by 2050 may still leave substantial microplastic accumulation, and rapid cleanup to reduce microplastic generation would cost 0.1–5.6 billion euros annually, according to a system dynamics model.

#5 [paper] PlasticFADE: a predictive model for plastic fragmentation and degradation rates in the environment
Authors: Yibo Tang, Nadim Saadi, Jérôme Lavoie, Anne‐Marie Boulay
Venue: Microplastics and Nanoplastics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00243-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Plastics are widespread across the globe, posing risks to environmental and human health. Fragmentation and degradation are key processes that govern the environmental fate and impacts of plastics, yet their rates remain poorly quantified. Life cycle assessment (LCA) is widely recognized as the standard framework for comprehensively evaluating the environmental performance of products and services. Accurately capturing the fate of plastics in natural environments therefore represents a critical priority for impact assessment modeling. However, the degradation and fragmentation mechanisms governing plastic polymer behavior remain poorly quantified in current life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) models, limiting their capacity to characterize the potential biodiversity impacts arising from plastic emissions to natural environments. In this study, experimental data on plastic fragmentation and degradation were systematically compiled from the literature. Using these data, PlasticFADE was developed as the first iteration of an empirical model to predict polymer-specific rate constants in various environmental compartments. The model predictions reveal that the rate constants vary considerably across polymers and compartments. Estimated lifespans of plastics range from several decades to over a millennium. Beaches are identified as hotspots for both fragmentation and degradation, whereas plastics are most likely to remain intact in the water column. Criteria are proposed for evaluating the reliability of the model outputs, which should be interpreted with due caution. Despite its limitations, the model offers valuable insights into plastic fate processes and offers significant potential for improving current LCIA methods for plastic emissions assessment.

#6 [paper] Research Priorities for a Circular Economy for Plastic Sustainability in the Caribbean
Authors: Anne Marie Mozrall, Jessica P. Feliz Garrido, P. Tejada-Tejada, Akeem Mohammed, Brigitte Mildred Roldán Ramírez, Alana Malinde S.N. Lancaster, Iris Odett Atencio, Diego Batista
Venue: Environmental Science & Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.5c16637
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Caribbean countries bear a disproportionate burden of marine plastic pollution because of their small landmass, high population density, and insufficient waste management infrastructure. Many Caribbean nations depend on informal, unmanaged landfills, underscoring an urgent need for more resilient, sustainable systems. This perspective synthesizes existing data to map the region’s plastic waste landscape and leverages regional expertise to identify key research priorities. This work emerged from interdisciplinary international professionals and members of the CEPlaSt (circular economy for plastic sustainability) network. A major barrier to circularity is the lack of reliable data on waste composition and flows, alongside stark infrastructure disparities across the wider Caribbean region. Addressing these gaps through targeted investment and region-specific planning is essential to modernize waste systems, reduce plastic emissions, and advance a sustainable Caribbean plastic circular economy.

#7 [paper] Two-dimensional simulation of plastic bottles transport in a urban reach of the Arno River
Authors: Gabriella Petaccia, Elisabetta Persi, Francesco Paolo Contò, Diego Ravazzolo, Andrea Fenocchi, Stefano Sibilla, Lorenzo Innocenti, Mirco Mancini
Venue: Digital Water
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/28375807.2026.2724249
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Within the MINOSSE project (ManagINg plastic transpOrt in riverS and coaStal arEas), the 2D hydrodynamic numerical model ORSA2D_WT has been adapted to simulate the transport of plastic bottles, the most common macroplastic item transported in water bodies. Unlike smaller plastics, such as fragments or films, the shape and size of plastic bottles can significantly influence their inertia and fate. They may not follow flow velocity lines, so they must be modelled as discrete items, driven by the flow field and capable of interacting with surrounding elements (riverbed, riverbanks, bridge piers, vegetation, other debris of plastic or different nature). Thanks to the proposed 2D numerical approach, they are modelled as individual items floating on the water surface or being conveyed in the water column. The ORSA2D_WT model has been appled to simullate plastic bottles trajectories in a 7.6 km urban reach of the Arno River, during a winter event. Two different releases points were considered, the Affrco conflunece on the side of the river and a central point of the river close to the upstream section. The results of the model from the release points show a different behaviuor in the trajectories and in the stranding points. These first results qualitatively match the in situ observations, and show that the numerical model can help in identifying hot spots for plastic accumulation.

#8 [paper] Groundings of drifters in the Wadden Sea inform the transport of floating macroplastic
Authors: Marc Schneiter, Rolf Hut, Erik van Sebille
Venue: Ocean science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3595-2026
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the transport and coastal interaction dynamics of floating macroplastic in intertidal regions, specifically through the analysis of drifter groundings.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Field campaign involving the release and tracking of 24 shallow surface drifters in the Dutch Wadden Sea; manual and statistical automatic detection of drifter groundings; characterization of groundings relative to wind conditions, tides, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Dutch Wadden Sea, an intertidal region driven by semi-diurnal tides and wind.
Abstract:
Abstract. We study floating marine macro plastic pollution with a dedicated campaign where we released and tracked 24 shallow surface drifters in the Dutch Wadden Sea, an intertidal region where water dynamics are driven by semi-diurnal tides and wind. The campaign captured water surface transport patterns, and around 150 observations of the drifters interacting with the coast and mudflats, where groundings of varying durations occurred. We identify these transitions in the recorded trajectories from both manual inspection and by formulating and evaluating a statistical approach for automatic detection. We then characterize the transitions by relating them to the coinciding wind conditions and tides, and with the duration of the groundings. The results of this analysis generally agree with the intuitions that wind towards the coast increases the frequency of interactions and that the drifters are rarely re-floated during falling tides. Furthermore, we find that groundings tend to be shorter duration when they occur shorter before the next high tide. We present multiple visualizations that characterize the groundings in more detail. The results provide a statistical characterization of coastal interactions that can be integrated in models and used for the planning of beach-cleanups. They may be improved by considering the specific environmental conditions of the campaign, and by analyzing the influence of the weight and size of the drifters, which are both larger than typical floating macroplastic.

#9 [paper] Spatial Patterns of Marine Litter on a Remote South Atlantic Ocean Island: Setting Baselines for Monitoring
Authors: Fernanda Caminha Leal Valls, Leandro Bugoni
Venue: Thalassas An International Journal of Marine Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s41208-026-01266-2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Characterizing the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter on Trindade Island, a remote South Atlantic island, to establish baselines for monitoring before the establishment of marine protected areas.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Systematic sampling of seven beaches with varying exposure to wind and substrate; quantification of litter items, categorization by purpose, and calculation of pollution indices (Clean Coast Index and Plastic Abundance Index).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Seven beaches on Trindade Island, South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland; characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates.
Abstract:
Abstract Marine plastic litter is a major environmental problem across all oceans, including remote regions. Here, we described the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter stranded on the beaches of Trindade Island, in the South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland, before the establishment of marine protected areas and the initiation of a long-term research program on the island. Seven beaches differing in exposure to wind and substrate were sampled. A total of 1317 litter items were recorded, with plastics as the main litter (81.9%), mostly hard plastic fragments. Although Lixo Beach had the smallest surveyed area (425 m 2 ), it exhibited the highest litter density (0.74 items/m 2 ) and highest litter-covered area (2.2% of the sampled beach area). Domestic and household purpose items composed the bulk of identifiable items (28.9%), followed by naval (22.5%) and fishery (17.7%) pieces. Litter distribution among beaches differed, with leeward beaches accumulating significantly more and larger litter items than windward beaches, revealing substantial local-scale variation patterns in debris retention. These beaches are characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates rather than sand. Our analysis of pollution indices demonstrated that the Clean Coast Index ( CCI ) and the Plastic Abundance Index ( PAI ) are strongly correlated and suitable for long-term monitoring. This study confirms that oceanic islands are prone to accumulating marine litter, while contrasting results from other studies on Trindade Island emphasize the need for simple yet standardized protocols to support long-term monitoring of plastic pollution in remote environments.

#10 [paper] Tracing microplastic footprints in beach sediments along the Qatar coast: A risk-based approach to pollution assessment
Authors: Samah Dib, Rana Al- Absi, S. Veerasingam, V M Aboobacker, Jassim Al-Khayat, P. Vethamony
Venue: Marine Pollution Bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.marpolbul.2026.120409
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Surface and subsurface sediments from twenty representative beaches along the Qatar coast were analyzed following standardized NOAA protocols, including sieving, density separation, microscopic observation, and ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, to investigate the horizontal and vertical distribution, physical characteristics, polymer composition, and environmental risks of microplastics (MPs). MPs were detected at concentrations ranging from 0 to 855 MPs kg −1 dry sediment. Fragments and pellets were the dominant morphologies, representing 42.98% and 38.96% of the total count, respectively. Polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) were the dominant polymers, together comprising 60% of identified MPs, reflecting their extensive use in consumer products and packaging. MP abundance decreased with depth; however, given the shallow core depth (25 cm) and dynamic intertidal conditions, this gradient primarily reflects surface enrichment from recent inputs and physical mixing rather than a definitive historical record. Risk assessment using the pollution load index (PLI), polymer hazard index (PHI), coefficient of microplastic impact (CMPI), environmental status index (ESI), potential ecological risk index (PERI), and microplastic pollution index (MPPI) revealed spatial variation in contamination levels. Al Wakrah and Zekreet showed the highest pollution and hazard levels, while northern sites such as Ras Rakan showed relatively moderate contamination. Overall, the findings highlight the ecological threat of MPs along the Qatar coast and the need for targeted mitigation and integrated coastal management to reduce plastic leakage into the marine environment.

#11 [paper] Mainstreaming surf conservation and management into coastal governance: collective reflections from the 2026 world surfing conservation conference
Authors: Ana Manero, Shane Orchard, Scott Atkinson, Yehuda Ben-Hamo, Carolina Butrich, Serge Dedina, Patricio Mekis, Zac Plopper
Venue: Ocean & Coastal Management
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocecoaman.2026.108407
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Surf breaks are increasingly recognized as valuable coastal resources that support recreation, culture, local economies, and human wellbeing. Over the past two decades, research and practice on surf conservation have expanded considerably across disciplines such as coastal and environmental management, tourism and oceanography. While formal mechanisms for surf break management have evolved in some jurisdictions, they are often absent or weakly integrated into formal coastal governance. There is a need for both surf-specific legal instruments and stronger alignment with existing environmental laws and planning frameworks. This Short Communication reflects on key perspectives from the 2026 World Surfing Conservation Conference, held on the Gold Coast, Australia, February 13th-19th 2026. The event convened a diverse international community including researchers, policymakers, practitioners, Indigenous representatives, advocates, athletes and industry stakeholders. In lieu of formal proceedings this article offers a thematic analysis of the 131 conference presentations and recommendations for further embedding a focus on surf resources within mainstream coastal management. The analysis identifies surf protection initiatives and governance gaps as dominant themes alongside opportunities to better connect surf conservation with biodiversity protection. Four priorities are identified: (1) Mainstream surf management within formal coastal governance frameworks, recognizing the spatial and socio-cultural dimensions of surf breaks as natural resources; (2) Leverage existing governance instruments that are already in place for the protection and sustainable management of other natural resources; (3) Apply community values and economic valuation frameworks to support decision-making on surf break management; (4) Ensure that responsibility and accountability for the long-term protection of surf resources is provided and maintained by the relevant governmental authorities.

#12 [paper] Eco Awareness Movement at Payum Beach, Merauke: Participatory Environmental Education, Beach Cleanup, and Mangrove Planting
Authors: Mulkhaeri Ikram, Wa Ode Sitti Mardiana, Firda Weri, Wilhelmina Jeujanan, Umiyati Haris, Rachmat Agung Puank Parukka
Venue: Devotion Jurnal Pengabdian Kepada Masyarakat
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.62282/devotion.v4i1.45-56
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Payum Beach, Merauke Regency, faces coastal environmental concerns related to waste management and the need for continued attention to coastal vegetation. This community service program involved 50 participants in a three-hour activity conducted on 11 September 2026. The program integrated environmental education, beach cleanup, mangrove planting, discussion, and a sustainability commitment through a participatory approach. Preparation and coordination, initial field observation, activity implementation, documentation, and descriptive evaluation were used to organize the program. The activity included education on coastal ecosystems, waste reduction, environmentally responsible behavior, and the ecological functions of mangroves; direct cleanup of the beach; planting of 50 mangrove seedlings; and a post-activity discussion on environmental problems, waste management, mangrove maintenance, and possible follow-up actions. The available records document participation, activity duration, and the number of seedlings planted, but do not provide quantitative measurements of waste volume, pre- and post-activity knowledge, behavioral change, or seedling survival. Accordingly, the program is interpreted as an initial participatory environmental education and action activity rather than evidence of long-term behavioral or ecological outcomes. The activity demonstrates the feasibility of combining education and direct environmental action while highlighting the need for standardized baseline data, participant profiling, and follow-up monitoring in subsequent activities.

#13 [paper] Comparative policy analysis of urban microplastic pollution and water quality management toward sustainable environmental governance in Malaysian cities
Authors: Muhammad Zakwan Anas Abd Wahid, Amirah Sariyati Mohd Yahya, Mohamad Syazmin Sulaiman, Muhamad Nazarwin Zainal Abidin, Mohamed Syazwan Osman
Venue: Discover Cities
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s44327-026-00378-x
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Rapid urbanization in Southeast Asia has intensified microplastic (MP) pollution in city water bodies, urban drainage systems, and coastal environments, posing significant threats to urban water quality and public health. This study employs a comparative policy analysis to evaluate how global, regional, and national legislative frameworks address MP pollution as a critical urban water management challenge, with emphasis on ASEAN member states and Malaysia’s cities. Malaysian urban centres, particularly densely populated coastal cities such as Penang, Kuala Lumpur, and Johor Bahru, exhibit alarming MP contamination across urban water bodies, with reported concentrations ranging from 0.14 particles/L in coastal surface waters to 29,174 pieces/kg in urban sediments — values that reflect two different environmental media (water column versus sediment) and are therefore not directly comparable in magnitude, but together illustrate the pervasiveness of MP contamination across compartments driven by inadequate urban waste management infrastructure and insufficient stormwater governance. Despite Malaysia ranking third globally in marine plastic pollution contributions (73,098 metric tons annually), cities lack dedicated MP-specific urban water management legislation. This governance gap is particularly critical given MP contamination documented across urban Malaysian water bodies and sediments. The study identifies four critical urban governance challenges: (1) legislative fragmentation and weak enforcement in urban environmental management, (2) economic-environmental trade-offs in plastic-dependent urban economies, (3) insufficient municipal solid waste and wastewater infrastructure addressing MP sources, and (4) limited urban public awareness and multi-stakeholder engagement. Through systematic analysis of international regulatory models and ASEAN city-level initiatives, this research proposes an integrated urban environmental governance framework encompassing legislative amendments to the Environmental Quality Act 1974, establishment of city-scale MP monitoring protocols aligned with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 11, implementation of Extended Producer Responsibility schemes for urban plastic waste, and enhancement of regional cooperation mechanisms. The findings offer actionable policy recommendations to improve urban water quality, strengthen sustainable municipal solid waste management, and promote resilient and sustainable cities, providing a replicable model for rapidly urbanizing developing nations facing similar urban environmental governance challenges.

#14 [paper] From edge defense to distributed resilience: A biomimicry framework for coastal governance architecture.
Authors: Hammond, Lisa M
Venue: Journal of environmental management
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43025139/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Coastal cities worldwide are investing heavily in seawall elevation, enforcement, and maintenance as a primary response to accelerating sea-level rise. Miami Beach, Florida, estimates $80.3 million for its seawall program alone within a $500 million total adaptation investment, with 91% of seawalls located on private property. A 2026 study in Nature further reveals that approximately 90% of coastal hazard assessments underestimate baseline sea levels by an average of 0.3 m due to measurement mismatches between sea and land elevation systems, meaning the risk these governance systems are calibrated to address is itself systematically understated. While seawall investments address real and urgent flood risk, they reflect a governance architecture that concentrates resilience at the parcel boundary, fragments responsibility across isolated private actors, and designs for resistance rather than recovery. This paper argues that the limitations of current coastal governance are architectural rather than engineering, rooted in a single-boundary compliance model that concentrates stress at one edge rather than distributing protective function across layered systems. Drawing on biomimicry methodology, the paper abstracts three functional principles from healthy coastal ecosystems, distributed load-bearing, staged energy reduction, and recovery orientation, and translates them into four governance propositions addressing distributed load-bearing, staged compliance architecture, recovery-oriented governance, and coordinated signaling across layers. The framework is illustrated through analysis of Miami Beach policy, ordinance, and spending data. The paper contributes to the literature by extending biomimicry from engineering application to governance architecture.

#15 [paper] Large-Scale Flume Experiments on Solitary Wave–Structure–Sediment Interactions, in Collaborative Research: Hybrid Flow-Sediment-Structure Interaction Analysis of Extreme Scour due to Coastal Flooding
Authors: Ali Farhadzadeh, Majid Ghayoomi, Tian-Jian Hsu, Seyedalireza Mirghafouri, Ahmad Klait, Pedro Lomónaco, Timothy B. Maddux
Venue: Texas Advanced Computing Center
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17603/ds2-71f8-sm86
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the interactions among extreme flood flow, soil, and structure that lead to foundation scour and failure in complex urban settings, including the effects of unsaturated soil mechanics and wave action.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A hybrid approach combining large-scale wave flume physical modeling, geotechnical centrifuge modeling, and numerical simulation (specifically enhancing an open-source Eulerian two-phase modeling framework with an extended effective stress-based sub-model and a revised solver for slight water compr…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Laboratory experiments (wave flume and geotechnical centrifuge) simulating extreme coastal flooding conditions, involving single and arrays of structures in low fines content soils of varying properties (composition, relative density, initial water content) and unsaturated ground.
Abstract:
Foundation scour is one of the primary causes of structural damage in coastal communities during flooding events. This project will leverage state-of-the-art in wave flume physical modeling, geotechnical centrifuge modeling, and numerical simulation to answer a number of critical and open questions related to the interactions among extreme flood flow, soil, and structure which lead to scour and foundation failure?shifting the paradigm in the current understanding of key physical processes in flood-induced scouring process in complex urban setting. Enhancement of open-source multi-physics computational tool for coastal hazard mitigation will provide a strong multi-disciplinary modeling platform to the broader civil and coastal engineering research community. The new parameterization set for extreme scour-liquefaction resulted from the fundamental knowledge-gain will benefit region-scale nearshore morphodynamic modeling and the state of foundation design in flood-prone areas. The education and outreach efforts will broaden the participation at all levels including: (1) recruitment, retention, and education of underrepresented students in three collaborating institutions; (2) engaging science teachers in three coastal states with different urban settings and population, in coastal infrastructure and community resiliency training; and (3) enhancing the well-being of the coastal residents through changing the design and hazard mitigation protocols. This project will bridge the state-of-the-art in sediment transport and scour, unsaturated and saturated soil mechanics, and hydrodynamics of flood flow. This goal will be achieved by correlating the spatiotemporal variations of scouring and loading with the dynamics of shallow flood flows within complex urban setting and water hysteresis in unsaturated soils around and underneath surface structures. The research objectives of this project are to understand: (1) scouring patterns of single and array of structures, under various flow and soil states; (2) initiation and progression of foundation scouring in low fines content soils of varying properties (i.e., composition, relative density, initial water content); (3) soil-foundation interaction response under simultaneous wave action and hydraulically-induced excess pore pressure; (4) rocking response of shallow foundations in unsaturated ground; (5) enhancement of an open-source Eulerian two-phase modeling framework for a complete description of seabed stability and scour; and (6) incorporating an extended effective stress-based sub-model and a revised solver for slight water compressibility to simulate soil behavior in partially drained and unsaturated condition with high overburden. The long-term goal of this project is to create public-domain tools for reliable scour predictions of complex urban and non-urban settings, under extreme coastal flooding conditions.

#16 [paper] Long-Term Shoreline Dynamics and Their Implications for Coastal Spatial Management
Authors: Dessy Mayasari, Ida Zubaidah, I Gede Wyana Lokantara, Robby Firmansyah
Venue: Journal La Sociale
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.37899/journal-la-sociale.v7i4.5208
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Coastal development increasingly takes place in environments where dynamic shoreline processes undermine the permanence of spatial planning and infrastructure. This research investigates long-term shoreline change along the Tanjung Pandan coast, Indonesia, and assesses its implications for coastal management, with Tanjung Pendam serving as a strategic urban waterfront. A quantitative spatial-descriptive methodology, combined with planning interpretation, was employed using multi-temporal shoreline data from 2000, 2013, and 2025. Abrasion and accretion were spatially delineated and proportionally quantified, while the Integrated City Planning framework was used to analyze coastal-management conditions and planning trajectories. Results indicate that abrasion constitutes 91.86% of the total mapped shoreline-change area, whereas accretion accounts for only 8.14%, revealing a significant imbalance in coastal transformation. At Tanjung Pendam, shoreline dynamics coincide with tidal flooding and spatially variable coastal protection, underscoring a gap between coastal mobility and relatively static planning decisions. The findings do not directly attribute observed shoreline change to sea-level rise but highlight its significance as a future adaptation factor. This research demonstrates that historical shoreline data can serve as a practical foundation for adaptive coastal spatial management by enhancing the integration of shoreline monitoring, spatial planning, and differentiated coastal-management strategies.

#17 [paper] Marine plastic pollution: ecological risks, environmental distribution, and sustainable mitigation perspectives
Authors: F. A. Samiul Islam
Venue: EQA - International Journal of Environmental Quality
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.60923/issn.2281-4485/25086
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic pollution has become a major environmental challenge affecting marine biodiversity, ecosystem stability, environmental quality, and human well-being across coastal and oceanic ecosystems. Increasing plastic production, ineffective waste management, urbanization, and transboundary transport processes have accelerated the accumulation of macroplastics, microplastics, and nanoplastics in aquatic environments. This review critically evaluates the major sources, transport pathways, environmental distribution, ecological impacts, socio-economic implications, and mitigation strategies associated with marine plastic contamination. Plastic pollutants primarily originate from municipal waste discharge, riverine transport, fisheries, aquaculture, industrial activities, wastewater effluents, and maritime operations, followed by widespread redistribution through hydrodynamic and atmospheric processes. Major ecological consequences include entanglement, ghost fishing, ingestion, trophic transfer, oxidative stress, endocrine disruption, habitat degradation, pathogen dispersal, and biodiversity decline. Plastic contamination additionally threatens fisheries productivity, seafood safety, tourism economies, public health, and ecosystem-service sustainability. Current mitigation approaches increasingly emphasize circular-economy transition, extended producer responsibility, international governance frameworks, ecosystem-based management, and advanced environmental monitoring technologies. However, substantial challenges remain regarding policy implementation, recycling efficiency, technological inequality, and transboundary waste leakage. Integrated environmental governance, sustainable production systems, scientific monitoring, and evidence-based mitigation strategies are therefore essential for improving long-term marine environmental quality and reducing global plastic contamination.

#18 [paper] Compliance and non-compliance patterns among listed and non-listed ship recycling facilities: a comparative assessment of 22 facilities evaluated for the EU List
Authors: Newton Narciso Pereira, Camila Aparecida Maciel da Silveira, Kauã Costa dos Santos Paula, Camila Aguiar Diniz
Venue: Environmental Science and Pollution Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-026-38259-w
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ship recycling plays a central role in the circular economy of the maritime industry, yet significant disparities persist in safety, environmental performance, and regulatory compliance across global Ship Recycling Facilities (SRFs). This study analyzes 22 official inspection reports conducted by DNV for the European Commission under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation (EU SRR 1257/2013), comparing listed and non-listed facilities. Using a structured qualitative framework, the findings suggest that differences between listed and non-listed facilities are reflected not only in overall compliance levels but also in the nature and distribution of non-conformities across regulatory dimensions. While most facilities showed relatively high levels of conformity in infrastructure-related requirements, more pronounced differences between the groups were observed in environmental monitoring, institutional governance, traceability systems, and intertidal zone control. Non-listed SRFs showed recurring deficiencies in environmental monitoring, documentation, emergency preparedness, and hazardous waste management, whereas listed facilities generally showed stronger governance and risk-management capabilities despite minor shortcomings. A sensitivity analysis excluding facilities employing dismantling methods prohibited under the EU SRR identified two non-listed facilities with performance profiles comparable to several listed SRFs, indicating that structural eligibility alone does not account for all observed differences between the groups. The results further suggest that environmental verification, traceability, and institutional governance are among the dimensions in which recurrent differences between the two groups were observed. These findings provide new insights into patterns associated with different listing outcomes and highlight areas that may support the modernization and regulatory alignment of ship recycling facilities.

Authors: OSPAR Beach Litter Expert Group (BLEG)
Year: 2026

#20 [paper] Technological Innovations for Ocean Plastic Waste Management: A Global Bibliometric Analysis of Research Trends, Collaboration Networks, and Emerging Technologies
Authors: Jehu Roeh C. Rubenial Franklin M. Ganancias
Venue: Journal of Intelligent Decision Making and Information Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.59543/jidmis.v3.1213
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Ocean plastic pollution has become one of the most pressing environmental challenges worldwide, driving increasing interest in technology-based solutions for monitoring, prevention, mitigation, and sustainable waste management. Despite the rapid growth of research in this field, a comprehensive understanding of its scientific development, collaboration patterns, and emerging technological directions remains limited. This study presents a global bibliometric analysis of technological innovations for ocean plastic waste management using 12,039 English-language publications retrieved from the Scopus database on 09 July 2026. Bibliographic data were analyzed using Bibliometrix (RStudio) and VOSviewer to examine publication trends, influential authors, journals, institutions, countries, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, and thematic evolution. The findings reveal a substantial increase in scientific production, particularly after 2015, demonstrating the rapid expansion of this interdisciplinary research domain. China, the United States, and several European and Asian countries emerged as the leading contributors to scientific productivity and international collaboration, while Marine Pollution Bulletin and Science of the Total Environment ranked among the most productive publication sources. Author keyword co-occurrence analysis identified microplastics, plastic waste, circular economy, recycling, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and remote sensing as dominant research themes. Thematic evolution further revealed a transition from broad marine pollution research toward technology-oriented investigations emphasizing plastic waste management and microplastics. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive knowledge map of the field, highlighting the growing integration of digital technologies and sustainable waste management strategies. The findings offer valuable insights for researchers, policymakers, and environmental practitioners in identifying research priorities, strengthening international collaboration, and advancing technology-driven solutions for sustainable ocean plastic waste management.

Of the eight grants currently in the lab's feed, none of them state their funding in US dollars. Here's what each one shows:

- **#10** A stronger Global Ocean Observing System — €50,000,000
- **#11** Innovative Solutions for mitigating the environmental impact of waterborne transport (ZEWT) — €2,000,000–€13,500,000
- **#12** Green, circular and resilient harbours — €1,000,000–€8,925,000
- **#13** Field-Friendly Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Systems — no amount stated (it's an SBIR/STTR topic)
- **#14** Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination — no amount stated (NSF OTIC program)
- **#15** Preparing demonstration missions for collaborative Earth Observation (Space Partnership) — €1,500,000–€15,000,000
- **#16** Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity — €3,000,000–€8,000,000
- **#17** Geosciences Research: GEO Core — no amount stated (NSF program announcement)

So the slate is split between EU-funded calls (all in euros) and US-funded programs (NSF, SBIR) that don't list a dollar figure in the feed. None of the eight explicitly states a USD amount.

Note: this covers the first 8 of 32 grants in the lab's slate. If you'd like, I can page through the rest to check whether any of the remaining 24 state their funding in dollars.

- public authorities prioritise investments on infrastructures and capacity building to advance ocean research, protect and restore ocean health and biodiversity and provide critical services through a global ocean observing system and data delivery that is fit-for purpose, cost efficient and designed across all its components;

- increased EU leadership and strategic autonomy in global ocean observation capabilities, in support of EU climate and biodiversity goals, strengthening the EU’s contribution to and influence within GOOS, and reducing the risk of critical dependencies, notably for key services (i.e. Copernicus Services);

- enhanced collaboration between observation communities, marine research infrastructures, European SMEs and technology providers, maritime industries, and service operators, actionably contributing to the validation, procurement readiness, uptake and large-scale deployment of innovative ocean observing technologies and approaches, in particular for biodiversity observations, while reinforcing the long-term sustainability of the global ocean observing system.

The EU has committed to global leadership in climate action, biodiversity protection and ocean governance, notably through the EU Ocean Pact, the EU Ocean Observation Initiative “OceanEye”, the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, the EU Mission Restore our Ocean and Waters, the EU Climate Law, and international commitments such as the Global Biodiversity Framework and Agreement on Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ). Achieving these objectives requires sustained, global, interoperable and open ocean observations, as well as the knowledge and the capacity to use these observations.

Sustained and resilient ocean observation is crucial for marine biodiversity conservation and restoration under a changing climate, meaning that maintaining an optimised global ocean observing system is very important to achieve biodiversity goals.

Evolving geopolitical dynamics and reduced engagement by key international partners pose significant risks to the continuity, openness and resilience of global ocean observing systems, in particular in areas beyond national jurisdictions, highlighting the need for reinforced European action to safeguard scientific sovereignty and long-term, reliable observations and predictions. Amount: €2,000,000–€13,500,000

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The decarbonization of waterborne transport using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels introduces new, unexplored risks to marine and aquatic ecosystems, including pollution from normal operations and accidental spills, threatening the achievement of Good Environmental and Ecological Status in Europ…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The project aims to evaluate and forecast environmental impacts, model pollution sources, and develop, demonstrate, and test innovative prevention, abatement, and mitigation systems and strategies (targeting TRL 5) for managing spills and reducing harmful impacts of zero-emission fuels.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European marine waters, inland waterways, and port areas, focusing on waterborne transport operations using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes.

- Improved water resilience and good environmental and good ecological status in European waters and contribute to the achievement of the European Union's environmental targets, including the European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Innovative prevention, abatement and mitigation systems and strategies for reducing and eliminating the harmful impacts of waterborne transport on waters.

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Actions should address all of the following aspects:

- Evaluate and forecast the environmental impacts of waterborne transport operations on marine, rivers and other aquatic ecosystems, in particular regarding the effects of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels (with particular attention to accidental spills) and related technologies. The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

- Modelling scenarios on water and air pollution sources from each ship types and services running on renewable low and zero carbon fuels.

- Develop and demonstrate innovative and cost-effective abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to prevent, eliminate and reduce the harmful impacts of the use of renewable low and zero carbon fuels. Relevant TRL5 demonstration of such systems should be done.

- Identifying training needs and skills requirements to deploy developed solutions, as well as in relation to the management and use of renewable low carbon fuels in ports and on vessels in marine and inland waters, including relevant emergency response preparedness.

#13 [grant] Field-Friendly Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Systems
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13129
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current DNN architectures suffer from 'Black Box' vulnerabilities, excessive computational scaling, lack of transparency, and a dependency on high-cost GPU infrastructure.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of an alternative to CNN-based architectures that maps parameter count to performance, replaces distributed neural layers with interpretable logic similar to standard programming code, and incorporates reliability metrics to identify when an output is unreliable.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): CNN-based image classification evaluated using MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets, comparing against ResNet-18 and larger architectures on CPU and embedded edge hardware.
Abstract:
Current DNN architectures suffer from inherent "Black Box" vulnerabilities, demanding massive computational scaling and offering no clear link between parameter count and performance. The proposed model must address these shortfalls:

- Optimized Resource Utilization: Unlike DNNs that heuristically overparameterize to boost accuracy, the proposed model must quantitatively map parameter count to expected performance and enable users to identify the minimum configuration required for mission success, significantly reducing computational overhead, complexity, and deployment costs.

- Transparency: The model must replace opaque, distributed neural layers with novel methods for interpretability and trust that go beyond the current post-hoc techniques. By making input-output logic similar to standard programming code, the model should ensure decisions are easily explainable, verifiable, and compliant with auditing standards.

- Reliability: The model must recognize whether it can provide a reliable output for a given problem instance, which will address another well-known criticism of DNNs wherein performance is typically measured as an average, e.g., average accuracy, over many instances of a problem and will help build user trust and acceptability of the model vs DNNs, particularly in sensitive areas like person identification in a crowd video and identifying the source of a cyber-security violation.

The model must deliver DNN-level performance with superior speed and a reduced memory footprint, optimized for lean, secure processing on low-cost CPU and embedded edge hardware. By eliminating cloud-dependence, the model will maximize data privacy and operational security while substantially reducing power consumption compared to GPU-reliant models. It must operate flexibly across mixed CPU-GPU environments, allowing operators to dynamically balance throughput against computational cost. Beyond standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the model’s architecture must be extensible to transformer-based and multimodal models handling text, image, and video.

The metrics below establish outer-edge targets specifically for CNN-based image classification. While satisfying every metric is not mandatory, the model will be evaluated on the number of targets achieved and the viability of the engineering trade-offs.

1. Comparison with Base Architecture of ResNet-18 and larger

2. Comparison of the Number of Classes 10 and 100 using 3 datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, having different combinations of numbers of classes and total number of image pixels (number of channels*number of pixels per image)

3. Mean Average Accuracy of Classification: Same as DNNs or higher

4. Number of Parameters (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less

5. Training MFLOPs/Image (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less

6. Training Memory Size (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less

7. Inference MFLOPs/Image: 50% of DNNs or less

8. Rate of Growth of Metrics (5), (6), and (7): Sublinear

In Phase II, similar metrics and their extensibility and relevance to transformers and multimodality scenarios (images and videos as well as their combinations with text to form LLMs and VLMs) will need to be provided and their implementation explained.

This STTR topic requires combinations of research and development, and proposers must demonstrate a strong partnership between the small business and a research institution.

The proposed solution should eliminate the dependency on complex computing infrastructure (e.g., GPUs) by delivering comparable performance on standard off-the-shelf hardware (CPUs, edge devices). It should optimize the cost-to-performance ratio, balancing accuracy with reductions in time, storage, and computational cost. - enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

#1 [paper] Hyperspectral remote sensing for harmful algal bloom detection: Pseudo-nitzschia in the Northeast Pacific.
Authors: Bailess, Alexander L, Baetge, Nicholas, Barnard, Andrew H, Tufillaro, Nicholas, Behrenfeld, Michael, Bill, Brian, Kudela, Raphael, Graff, Jason

Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for rapid, scalable identification of harmful algal blooms, specifically Pseudo-nitzschia, to manage marine resources, given that current in-situ point sampling methods are expensive and labor-intensive.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Culturing four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, measuring their hyperspectral absorption and backscatter, modeling spectral reflectances detectable by remote sensing platforms, and quantifying differences between taxonomic fingerprints using vector-based and stat…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including Pseudo-nitzschia, Thalassiosira, Chaetoceros, and Asterionellopsis.
Abstract:
Diatoms are microscopic marine algae that are critical for global primary production, carbon sequestration, and fisheries productivity. However, select diatoms may form harmful algal blooms, which threaten marine ecosystems and the fisheries they sustain. Rapidly identifying harmful blooms is necessary to effectively manage marine resources, yet current identification methods are limited by expensive and labor-intensive in-situ point sampling. Hyperspectral remote sensing enables scalable monitoring, but its ability to resolve taxonomic shifts within phytoplankton groups (e.g. diatoms) is largely unknown. To investigate this uncertainty, we cultured four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including this system's most abundant harmful algae, Pseudo-nitzschia. The hyperspectral absorption and backscatter of these taxa were measured and used to model spectral reflectances that remote sensing platforms (satellites/drones) might detect. Differences between fingerprints of these taxa were quantified using vector-based and statistical analyses. Mean spectral differences of 48% were observed between the most dominant diatom, Thalassiosira, and the most toxic diatom, Pseudo-nitzschia. Differences of approximately 30% were found between Pseudo-nitzschia and the second and third most abundant diatoms, Chaetoceros and Asterionellopsis. Successful identification of Pseudo-nitzschia's reflectance fingerprint was driven by the presence of a unique feature around 560 nm. The distinct spectral fingerprint of Pseudo-nitzschia indicates that it can be distinguished from other diatom blooms using hyperspectral remote sensing platforms.

#1 [paper] FISolver: Data-Driven Discovery of First Integrals via Backward Generation and Guided Reinforcement Learning
Authors: Jingfeng Zhong, Zhengxiang Liu, Zhijie Wang, Shuai Li
Venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3799682.3840846
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The discovery of first integrals is of fundamental scientific importance for understanding conservation laws in dynamical systems. However, existing symbolic computation tools and Large Language Models (LLMs) remain limited on this task because high-quality training data are scarce and successful solutions often depend on mathematical intuition. This paper presents FISolver, an LLM-based solver developed to address this challenge. First, we introduce a "Backward Generation" algorithm that systematically builds large-scale datasets of (differential equation, first integral) pairs by deriving differential equations from sampled integrals, thereby alleviating the data scarcity bottleneck. Second, we apply supervised fine-tuning to a compact mathematical model and further improve its performance through reinforcement learning with a Levenshtein Distance-based shaped reward. In addition, we design data synthesis and blending strategies that support effective adaptation to difficult problem families from sparse examples. Experiments show that FISolver, while requiring substantially lower computational cost, significantly outperforms larger mathematical LLMs and commercial solvers such as Mathematica on challenging benchmarks, indicating a new data-driven route for automated discovery of first integrals.

#2 [paper] Physics-Informed Stochastic Configuration Machine: A Backpropagation-Free Neural Network with Fast Training for Nonlinear Differential Equations
Authors: Yue-Hao Song, Zhong Chen, Li-Hui Cen, Liang Wu, Kai Zhang School Of Automation, Central South University, Changsha, China
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/be209dbb441023a8f62dba9895d123bd1460da64
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
While Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a transformative paradigm for solving complex differential equations, their reliance on backpropagation-based gradient descent and automatic differentiation (AD) imposes significant computational bottlenecks and severe non-convex optimization challenges. To overcome these fundamental limitations, we propose the Physics-Informed Stochastic Configuration Machine (PI-SCM), a novel backpropagation-free framework for both forward and inverse problems in differential equations. The core mathematical contribution lies in the analytical evaluation of local Jacobians for nonlinear differential operators, which facilitates a linearized representation of the physical loss and projects it into a unified, linearized algebraic subspace. This reformulation allows for the explicit determination of optimal network weights via a sequence of generalized linear least squares solvers, effectively bypassing the iterative traps of traditional nonlinear optimizers. We develop a progressive algorithmic suite comprising localized construction (PI-SC-I), sliding-window updating (PI-SC-II), and global updating (PI-SC-III), and rigorously establish their universal approximation properties. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PI-SCM achieves high-fidelity predictive accuracy and robust parameter identification while accelerating the training process by orders of magnitude compared to standard PINNs. Our work provides a highly efficient and scalable foundation for next-generation, real-time Scientific Machine Learning applications.

#4 [paper] Variational Parameter Dynamics: The Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy Depth Catastrophe and Relativistic Momentum in Neural Networks
Authors: Shubham Barmase

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard deep learning optimization heuristics (SGD, momentum, Nesterov) are discrete update maps that suffer from momentum overshoot on steep cliffs and stall on non-convex landscapes; deep feedforward networks exhibit a severe Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) stiffness catastrophe due to exponential…
Method (Mycelium's reading): Elevating parameter optimization to continuous variational mechanics governed by Hamilton's Principle of Stationary Action over configuration trajectories θ(t). The approach uses a Lagrangian formulation L(θ, dθ/dt, t) and isotropic Euler-Lagrange dynamics. It introduces relativistic velocity clamp…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Neural networks, specifically deep feedforward networks and non-layered architectures (continuous spatial wave fields, coupled recurrent graphs). Empirical evaluation on non-convex landscapes.
Abstract:
Standard deep learning optimization heuristics—such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD), Polyak heavy-ball momentum, and Nesterov acceleration—are conventionally formulated as discrete update maps. In this paper, we elevate parameter optimization to continuous variational mechanics governed by Hamilton's Principle of Stationary Action over configuration trajectories θ(t) in R^D: S[θ] = ∫ L(θ, dθ/dt, t) dt. We establish three primary theoretical and empirical discoveries: 1. Relativistic Velocity Clamping: Momentum, Nesterov acceleration, and gradient clipping are exact physical manifestations of Euclidean mass, Bregman Lagrangian criticality (γ(t) = 3/t), and Lorentz-invariant relativistic velocity clamping (||dθ/dt|| < c). Under relativistic kinetic energy, parameter velocity is strictly bounded below c, eliminating momentum overshoot on steep cliffs and attaining machine-precision convergence (1.67e-20) on non-convex landscapes where standard SGD stalls at 0.195. 2. The CFL Depth Catastrophe: Deep feedforward networks exhibit an exponential block-hierarchical Hessian condition gap (κ ≈ 1.42e5), inducing a severe Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) stiffness catastrophe that freezes isotropic Euler-Lagrange dynamics. 3. Non-Layered Spectral Remedy: Non-layered architectures—specifically continuous spatial wave fields and coupled recurrent graphs—compress this condition number by up to 6,140x (κ ≈ 23.1), allowing un-preconditioned isotropic Euler-Lagrange optimization to converge directly to target boundaries. #5 [paper] Machine Learning Applications to Physical Processes
Authors: W.D. Charles
Venue: Washington University in St. Louis Libraries
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.7936/6avb-db95
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This thesis demonstrates how machine learning techniques can solve computationally challenging problems across diverse areas of physics, from high-energy astrophysics to condensed matter systems, accelerating traditional computation. My first contribution addresses the computational expense of Monte Carlo calculations for radiative processes in relativistic plasmas. I develop a neural network sampling method that enables fast sampling from an arbitrary probability density, and demonstrate the method on inverse Compton scattering, achieving a speedup of up to an order of magnitude beyond standard methods. My second contribution addresses the structure and radiation of neutron star magnetospheres. I use physics-informed neural networks to model the axisymmetric pulsar magnetosphere, then reproduce twisted magnetar equilibria with the same framework, and finally present a GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo transport code for resonant Compton scattering which shows that photons paradoxically escape an optically thick twisted magnetar magnetosphere after undergoing only one or two scatterings. My third contribution addresses predicting magnetic properties in condensed matter. I first train an ensemble learning method to predict uranium-based compound magnetic order using only structural information, bypassing expensive density functional theory calculations. This work is then extended using transformer-based models to predict individual atomic magnetic properties within crystals. Together these contributions show that machine learning can be integrated with physical understanding to enable investigations that were previously computationally intractable.

#8 [paper] Machine learning of nonlinear waves: data-driven methods for computer-assisted discovery of equations, symmetries, conservation laws, and integrability
Authors: Jimmie Adriazola, P. G. Kevrekidis, V. Koukouloyannis, Wei Zhu
Venue: Nonlinearity
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6544/ae73dc
