#6 [paper] MERLIN SCIENCE — Media Index Lacks Extractable Mathematical Equations or Constants — E8 Intelligence Research
Authors: Andrew Stewart Caldin
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23939196
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The finding is simple: a search for mathematical evidence returned a media index, not a corpus of equations, and no constants or ratios could be extracted from titles alone. Here is the context. We ran a retrieval looking for primary mathematical structure — equations, constants, ratios — and got back a list of documentary and video titles. That is metadata, not evidence. The only mathematically substantive item was a reference to the oldest math text, which almost certainly means Plimpton 322, the Old Babylonian tablet from around 1800 BCE. The rest was cosmic-cycle numerology and named topics with no derivable content attached. The reasoning a scientist can evaluate is this. Plimpton 322 encodes Pythagorean triples through reciprocal pairs. Take a number x and its reciprocal, form a equals x minus one over x, c equals x plus one over x, b equals two, scale as needed, and you recover a squared plus b squared equals c squared. That is real, and it is sexagesimal, base sixty. Base six Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

#7 [paper] RISE: A Rust Library for Inverted Index Search Engines
Authors: Angelo Savino, Rossano Venturini
Venue: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3799682.3840184
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Inverted indexes are a crucial data structure for efficient information retrieval in large text corpora. They enable fast full-text search by mapping each term to the documents in which it appears, on top of which efficient algorithms quickly retrieve the documents relevant to a user query. We present RISE, a novel inverted index library implemented in Rust, designed to deliver high performance and efficiency for information retrieval tasks. RISE leverages Rust's safety and performance to provide a robust solution for building and querying inverted indexes, while offering accessible extensibility through its expressive trait system. While developing RISE, we revisited the inverted-index literature, thereby reproducing numerous prior works using this new test bench. We evaluated RISE against existing libraries, demonstrating competitive query performance across various datasets and workloads, with speedups of up to 2x over the current state of the art. Our results indicate that RISE is a promising tool for researchers and practitioners in the field of information retrieval.

#8 [paper] Structural validity of the German WISC-V beyond primary assessment: a factor-analytical approach to the ancillary index scales.
Authors: Pauls, Franz, Daseking, Monika
Venue: Frontiers in psychology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42756111/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Aligning with the factor-analytical procedure already established for the original test version, the present study examined the structural validity and diagnostic viability of the German Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Fifth Edition (WISC-V) ancillary index scales on an extended standardization sample of children and adolescents aged between 6 and 16 years (N = 1,466). METHODS: Representing the first comprehensive investigation into the ancillary index structure of the German WISC-V, competing hierarchical and bifactor model solutions were systematically evaluated via confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) and supplemented by model-based reliability analyses. RESULTS: The results provided structural support for the retention of the Auditory Working Memory index (AWM) as a structurally identifiable yet psychometrically redundant scale, whereas a subordinate factor for the Quantitative Reasoning index (QR) was completely unviable due to estimation failures and non-convergence across both model frameworks. A hierarchical model solution confirmed that the Nonverbal Index (NVI) represents a valid multidimensional construct, though model-based reliability analyses indicated that its underlying specific subscales lack the structural stability for independent interpretation beyond the NVI composite score. Furthermore, model-fit evaluations established that the General Ability Index (GAI) and the Cognitive Proficiency Index (CPI) are best represented by a second-order oblique four-factor model solution. While the GAI and CPI are reflected by plausible latent dimensions, their profound statistical proximity to the Full Scale Intelligence Quotient (FSIQ) and the underlying subscales' lack of sufficient statistical stability underscore the risk of profile misinterpretation. DISCUSSION: Consequently, study limitations and boundaries for evidence-based assessment are discussed, emphasizing that subsequent diagnostic decision-making in clinical practice based on the ancillary index scales alone should be approached with caution absent further cross-cultural and clinical validation.

#9 [paper] Estimating the Tail Index of Pareto-Type Distributions from Geometric Records
Authors: Martín Alcalde, Raúl Gouet, Miguel Lafuente, F. Javier López, Gerardo Sanz
Venue: Journal of Statistical Theory and Applications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s44199-026-00190-x
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
In this paper, we develop a novel inferential approach based on geometric records for estimating the tail index of heavy-tailed distributions. We construct a maximum likelihood estimator for the Pareto model and establish strong consistency and asymptotic normality, providing also an explicit expression for the asymptotic variance. These results are then extended to a broad class of Pareto-type distributions. The performance of the estimator is assessed via Monte Carlo simulation and compared with classical estimators from the literature. The proposed method is particularly well suited for settings where data arrive sequentially, as it yields smooth estimation trajectories. It is also especially advantageous in applications such as destructive testing, where measuring each item is costly. In this context, the estimator achieves a comparable level of estimation accuracy to Hill’s estimator, but with a considerably lower number of fully measured items. An application to the analysis of the distribution of fluctuations of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJI) is also presented.

#10 [paper] A fatty liver index-based sequential strategy for identifying hepatic steatosis in individuals with suspected steatotic liver disease.
Authors: Yang, Yan, Feng, Xiongcai, Deng, Hong, Dong, Zhiyong, Xu, Lishu, Feng, Shiting, Liao, Bing, Shao, Congxiang
Venue: BMC gastroenterology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42958515/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Fatty liver index (FLI) is widely used as a non-invasive tool for identifying hepatic steatosis but performs poorly in lean individuals and leaves a substantial proportion of individuals within an indeterminate range. This cross-sectional study evaluated whether combination strategies could improve identification of hepatic steatosis in a selected referred population with suspected steatotic liver disease (SLD). METHODS: In a derivation cohort of 1648 subjects with suspected SLD who underwent MRI-PDFF assessment between January 2015 and January 2022, we evaluated five non-invasive indices (FLI, hepatic steatosis index [HSI], liver fat score [LFS], visceral adiposity index [VAI], and triglyceride-glucose index [TyG]). Four FLI-based sequential strategies were developed and further validated in an independent biopsy-based cohort of 426 patients from five tertiary centers in South China. RESULTS: FLI performed best in identifying hepatic steatosis among the five non-invasive indices, with an AUROC of 0.75, but showed a high missed-identification rate exceeding 90% in individuals with BMI < 23 kg/m². In Strategy 4, the FLI-LFS sequential algorithm improved identification performance in lean individuals. In the derivation cohort, sensitivity increased from 9.4% to 78.6%, the missed-identification rate decreased from 90.6% to 21.4%, and accuracy increased from 30.0% to 73.1%. A similar improvement in missed identification was observed in the validation cohort. CONCLUSIONS: Compared with FLI alone, the sequential FLI-LFS algorithm substantially improved the identification of hepatic steatosis among lean individuals with suspected SLD. The strategy may help identify individuals who require further imaging and etiological evaluation but should not be regarded as a stand-alone tool for determining the subtype or cause of SLD.

#11 [paper] RWEB-CWBI: A Reliability-Weighted, Empirical-Bayes-Shrunk Composite Estimator for Multidimensional Child Well-Being, with Cross-Survey Validation in Egypt
Authors: Mariam Magdy Kamal, Mohamed Naguib, Noura Anwar Abdel-Fatah
Venue: Stats
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/stats9050102
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background: Composite well-being indicators are typically built by aggregating dimension scores with subjectively elicited or transferred weights, computed on raw sample means without formal reliability checks. Methods: We propose the Reliability-Weighted, Empirical-Bayes-Shrunk Composite (RWEB-CWBI), which shrinks each dimension’s group-level mean via the dimension-specific DerSimonian–Laird random-effects models, derives aggregation weights from a group-level principal component analysis of the shrunk dimension matrix, and rescales each loading by its empirical area-level reliability ratio (RR), automatically reducing the influence of dimensions with lower estimated reliability, and thus providing an alternative to automatic exclusion. RWEB-CWBI is applied within a broader Child Well-Being Index (CWBI) framework, building on participatory CWBI1-CWBI5 specifications estimated on a 10-governorate Takaful-beneficiary sample (n = 8716 households; the 2016 UNICEF sample), and evaluated alongside data-driven weighting, empirical Bayes shrinkage, and machine-learning benchmarking on an independent, nationally representative sample (EFHS-2021; n = 49,936 children, 26 governorates). Results: Participatory CWBI4 and CWBI5 showed the strongest alignment with the available subjective well-being measures. RWEB-CWBI down-weighted the least reliable EFHS dimension (RR = 0.75) automatically, while preserving close agreement with the simpler indices’ governorate rankings (ρ = 0.988–0.989). Gradient boosting improved cross-validated R2 over OLS by 2.5 points (0.798 vs. 0.773), with urban residence dominating permutation importance. The EFHS-UNICEF ranking correlation stayed weak and non-significant under every specification, including RWEB-CWBI (ρ = 0.14–0.19, n = 10, p ≥ 0.60). Conclusion: RWEB-CWBI is presented as a statistically motivated methodological proposal for handling heterogeneous dimension-level precision and availability. The persistence of the weak EFHS-UNICEF correlation across conventional, data-driven, and reliability-weighted specifications indicates that the finding is robust to the choice of weighting method, although contributions from population differences, measurement differences, and survey-design differences cannot be distinguished conclusively.

#12 [paper] The prognostic value of triglyceride glucose–waist height ratio index in patients with heart failure after acute myocardial infarction: a retrospective study
Authors: Hongru Fan, Qingjun Jiang, Liqun He
Venue: Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fcvm.2026.1762185
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background Heart failure (HF) after acute myocardial infarction (AMI) remains a major clinical challenge. The triglyceride glucose-waist-to-height ratio (TyG-WHtR) integrates metabolic and obesity indices, yet its prognostic value for AMI-HF is unclear. Methods This retrospective study enrolled 738 AMI patients undergoing PCI from January 2019 to June 2024. Baseline TyG-WHtR was calculated pre-discharge. The primary outcome was HF occurrence within 1-year follow-up. Multivariate logistic regression and restricted cubic splines (RCS) assessed associations. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and DeLong tests compared TyG-WHtR against the GRACE score and other metabolic indices. Subgroup analyses were performed based on AMI-to-PCI time and ESC-defined HF classifications. Results A total of 136 patients (18.4%) developed HF. TyG-WHtR was an independent predictor of AMI-HF (adjusted OR = 1.192, 95% CI: 1.021∼1.392, p = 0.026), persisting after adjusting for the post-PCI GRACE score. RCS revealed a positive nonlinear dose-response relationship (p-nonlinear=0.034). TyG-WHtR demonstrated good discrimination (AUC=0.769, 95% CI: 0.726∼0.811), outperforming TyG-WC and TyG-BMI (both p &lt; 0.05). Notably, TyG-WHtR showed superior predictive value in HFpEF (AUC=0.815) compared to GRACE (AUC=0.761, p = 0.012), whereas GRACE performed better in HFrEF. The predictive value was consistent across AMI-to-PCI time strata (p-interaction=0.584). Baseline TyG-WHtR correlated inversely with 1-year LVEF (r = −0.327, p &lt; 0.001) in HF patients. Conclusion TyG-WHtR is an independent risk factor for 1-year AMI-HF, particularly in HFpEF phenotypes. It provides incremental prognostic value beyond the GRACE score and may guide early risk stratification in post-PCI AMI patients.

#13 [paper] Association between the albumin-bilirubin score and gallstone prevalence: evidence from NHANES and an independent hospital-based cohort.
Authors: Sun, Qi, Gao, Xizhuang, Zhang, Hanning, Song, Yuanjian
Venue: Frontiers in medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42787026/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the association between the albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score and gallstone prevalence, and to develop machine-learning-based classification models for identifying participants with gallstones. METHODS: Data from NHANES 2017-March 2020, including adults with complete albumin, bilirubin, and gallstone-status information, were analyzed. Weighted multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic spline models were used to examine the association between ALBI score and gallstone prevalence. Fifteen feature-selection and machine-learning combinations were implemented to build classification models, with external validation conducted in a hospital-based cohort. Model performance was assessed using ROC curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis. RESULTS: A total of 5,090 participants were included, including 490 with gallstones (9.63%, crude proportion). In the fully adjusted survey-weighted logistic regression model, continuous ALBI score was positively associated with gallstone prevalence (OR = 2.89; 95% CI: 1.68-4.99; P = 0.002). Restricted cubic spline analyses, stratified by sex, revealed a significant nonlinear association in women (P = 0.004) but not in men (P = 0.261), with a positive dose-response relationship when the ALBI score exceeded -2.60. In the machine-learning analysis, the leading cross-validated AUC values ranged from 0.718 to 0.720 across the top configurations, with internal test-set AUC values of 0.703 to 0.708; these differences were within the expected variability of the cross-validation procedure and the models should be regarded as indistinguishable in discriminative performance. In the external validation cohort, the AUC values ranged from 0.701 to 0.710, but the confidence intervals around these estimates are wide (approximately 0.62-0.80) owing to the small number of events (n = 42), and the external results provide only preliminary support for generalizability. CONCLUSION: In a national sample of US adults, a higher ALBI score remained associated with higher odds of gallstone disease after multivariable adjustment. Machine-learning models incorporating ALBI achieved moderate discrimination (cross-validated AUC up to 0.720; internal test AUC up to 0.708), with preliminary external-validation support that requires confirmation in larger cohorts.

#14 [paper] Laboratory indicators combined with liver function scores for predicting suboptimal hepatobiliary phase imaging during gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI
Authors: Fuhe Qiu, Fuling Huang, Haihui Pan, Jiancong Li, Feichen Lu
Venue: Frontiers in Medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1945459
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background Suboptimal hepatobiliary-phase (HBP) enhancement may limit the diagnostic quality of gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI. We investigated whether routinely available laboratory indicators and liver function scores could identify patients at increased risk of suboptimal HBP imaging. Methods This retrospective study included 555 patients with focal liver lesions who underwent gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI, including 460 with good and 95 with suboptimal HBP image quality. Associations between laboratory indicators, liver function scores, and HBP image quality were evaluated using correlation and logistic regression analyses. Model discrimination, calibration, internal validation, and potential clinical utility were assessed using ROC analysis, bootstrap resampling, calibration analysis, and decision-curve analysis. Results The ALBI score (OR=2.391, 95% CI: 1.364–4.190), GGT (OR=1.003, 95% CI: 1.001–1.004), TBA (OR=1.010, 95% CI: 1.003–1.017), and Hb (OR=0.982, 95% CI: 0.971–0.993) were independently associated with suboptimal HBP imaging. The combined model yielded an AUC of 0.758 (95% CI: 0.701–0.816), with 63.16% sensitivity and 78.70% specificity. Bootstrap internal validation that repeated the entire model-development procedure yielded a mean AUC optimism of 0.044 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.714, indicating that moderate discrimination was retained after correction for model-development optimism. The apparent and optimism-corrected Brier scores were 0.116 and 0.128, respectively. Conclusions A model combining the ALBI score, GGT, TBA, and Hb showed moderate discrimination for suboptimal HBP imaging. These routinely available indicators may assist pre-MRI risk stratification, but external validation is required before clinical implementation.

#16 [paper] Dissociable associations of free-water fraction and DTI-ALPS index with disease manifestation and mutation carrier status in Parkinson's disease.
Authors: Liu, Chang, Liu, Xi, Dong, Meng, Li, Wenze, Zhang, Hongfa, Zhang, Lu, Zhang, Yuqing, Chen, Yangmei
Venue: Japanese journal of radiology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42911531/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
PURPOSE: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a biologically heterogeneous disorder. Diffusion MRI-derived free-water fraction (FWf) and DTI-ALPS index have been proposed as biomarkers of PD-related brain alterations; however, their relationships with clinical disease manifestation and genetic susceptibility remain unclear. This study investigated whether substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) FWf and DTI-ALPS indices show different associations with disease status and mutation carrier status across the PD continuum. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Diffusion MRI data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative were analyzed, including healthy controls (HCs), non-manifesting mutation carriers (NMCs), and patients with sporadic or genetic PD. A 2 × 2 factorial analysis of covariance was performed to assess the effects of disease status and mutation carrier status on SNc FWf and DTI-ALPS indices. Exploratory longitudinal associations between baseline imaging measures and 4-year clinical outcomes were examined using multivariable linear regression with adjustment for the corresponding baseline clinical measures. RESULTS: Among 284 participants (63 HCs, 48 NMCs, 126 sporadic PD patients, and 47 genetic PD patients), mean SNc FWf showed a significant main effect of disease status, whereas mutation carrier status and the interaction effect were not significant. Sporadic PD patients exhibited higher SNc FWf than HCs and NMCs. In contrast, the left-sided DTI-ALPS index was associated with mutation carrier status. NMCs had lower left-sided DTI-ALPS indices than HCs and sporadic PD patients. In the exploratory longitudinal analysis, higher baseline mean SNc FWf was associated with a higher 4-year MDS-UPDRS Part II score, although this association was not significant when the analysis was restricted to participants with manifest PD. CONCLUSIONS: SNc FWf and DTI-ALPS may capture complementary aspects of PD heterogeneity. SNc FWf appears more closely related to clinical disease expression, whereas DTI-ALPS index may reflect differences associated with genetic susceptibility. Further validation in larger mutation-stratified and longitudinal cohorts is warranted.

#17 [paper] Dual-Hypergraph Indexing: Bridging Knowledge Islands for Multi-Hop Reasoning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/d995118624560cc893b6d381d0db5a682b38955d
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing hypergraph-based RAG paradigms treat extracted hyperedges as isolated factual assertions, creating 'knowledge islands' that hinder multi-hop causal inference, temporal tracking, and narrative synthesis.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Dual-Hypergraph Indexing (DHI), a hierarchical representation framework that couples a foundational entity-relation factual hypergraph ($H_K$) with an elevated deep-insight hypergraph ($H_D$) using a dual-pathway aggregation algorithm consisting of importance-driven hub aggregation and temporal chu…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Five benchmarks, including the multidisciplinary Mix benchmark and complex medical pathology reasoning tasks.
Abstract:
While hypergraph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively captures higher-order multi-entity correlations, existing paradigms treat extracted hyperedges as isolated factual assertions. This structural fragmentation engenders rigid"knowledge islands"that bottleneck multi-hop causal inference, temporal tracking, and narrative synthesis. To systematically address these challenges, we introduce Dual-Hypergraph Indexing (DHI), a hierarchical representation framework that elevates discrete facts into structured analytical insights. DHI couples a foundational entity-relation factual hypergraph ($H_K$) with an elevated deep-insight hypergraph ($H_D$) via a dual-pathway aggregation algorithm. Specifically, DHI employs: (1) importance-driven hub aggregation via 5-metric topological profiling and adaptive thresholding to capture spatial semantic clusters; and (2) temporal chunk-chain progressive aggregation via sliding-window greedy exploration to track chronological evolutions. Across five benchmarks, DHI achieves state-of-the-art performance, boosting logical coherence by +1.53 on the multidisciplinary Mix benchmark and scoring 85.78\% on complex medical pathology reasoning tasks. DHI provides a robust architecture for next-generation multi-hop RAG.

#18 [paper] 低垂的果实(第三辑):六条 OEIS 猜想——命题来源、逻辑证明与 Lean 4 源码(Low-Hanging Fruit, Vol. III: Six OEIS Conjectures: Sources, Proofs, and Lean 4 Sources)

Abstract:
Longitudinal bibliometric analyses rely on annual citation histories, yet missing annual observations are frequently difficult to distinguish from true zero-citation years. #1 [paper] AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
Authors: Sharath S. Girimaji
Venue: National Science Review
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwag654
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Applying AI/ML to turbulence modeling has yielded modest progress due to a lack of situation-aware deployment, leading to poor generalization of ML-RANS closures and unnecessary computational costs from misapplied ML-SRS.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The author proposes a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Reynolds number, Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ε), applying Weaver’s complexity framework to classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Turbulence modeling contexts, specifically Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) and scale-resolving simulations (SRS).
Abstract:
Abstract Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ε). By applying Weaver’s well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

#2 [paper] Event-based sensing for turbulent flows: A measurement science perspective on information-efficient estimation and control
Authors: Andrea Ianiro, Iacopo Tirelli, Stefano Discetti
Venue: Measurement Science and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6501/ae9783
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Event-based sensing offers a promising alternative to conventional frame-based measurement in turbulent flows, where intermittency, multiscale dynamics, and stringent latency constraints can make dense uniform sampling both expensive and redundant. Rather than acquiring less data, the goal is to acquire more-relevant data: measurements triggered by dynamically meaningful changes that reduce uncertainty in control-relevant flow coordinates. We leverage ideas from reduced-order modeling, sparse observability, biological mechanosensors, and event-based signal processing to outline a conceptual framework in which turbulent flows are sensed through asynchronous measurements, encoded at the hardware level, and processed by hybrid observers or neuromorphic architectures. A simple analytical argument shows that the estimation-error advantage of event-based encoding over uniform sampling scales directly with the temporal intermittency of the observable. Experimental demonstrations remain limited but encouraging. This perspective reframes the sensing bottleneck in turbulence as a problem of information relevance rather than sample count, and sets out a research agenda covering reduced-state targets, trigger policies, asynchronous observers, uncertainty quantification, and reproducible benchmarking.

#3 [paper] Modeling and simulating turbulent secondary flow in a streamwise-rotating channel with LLM-guided symbolic regression and physics-informed neural networks
Authors: Wei Zhang, Benlong WANG, Zheng Ma, Bing Zhu
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11375175/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The high computational expense of direct numerical simulation (DNS) for turbulent secondary flow in a streamwise-rotating channel, specifically the need for efficient closure models and flow simulation methods.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A two-stage AI framework: (1) LLM-guided Graph-Feynman (LGF) equation discovery to learn a closure for the secondary-flow covariance b23, compared against PySR; (2) Physics-informed spectral neural networks (PINNs) using the discovered closures to reconstruct the time-averaged Taylor–Görtler vortex…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Turbulent secondary flow in a streamwise-rotating channel; DNS statistics for rotation numbers Roτ = 7.5–150; simulation reconstruction at Roτ = 7.5, 30, and 75 on a desktop CPU.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent secondary flow in a streamwise-rotating channel is dominated by Taylor–Görtler (TG) vortices whose direct numerical simulation is expensive. This paper develops a two-stage artificial-intelligence framework that learns the closure and simulates the flow. In the first stage, the LGF (LLM-guided Graph-Feynman) equation discovery engine targets the single decisive anisotropy component, the secondary-flow covariance 𝑏23 = 〈𝑣𝑤〉/2𝑘: twenty discovery runs (four feature pools of rotation-variant tensor channels, two LGF operating arms, and PySR at three seeds) are scored against DNS statistics of five rotation numbers 𝑅𝑜𝜏 = 7.5–150. The guided search buys stability: the eight LGF runs hold the case-normalized error within 0.051–0.137 at 13–17 nodes, whereas the twelve PySR runs spread over 0.042–0.334 with seed-level variation up to eightfold at about 60% more nodes. The four selected closures (0.042–0.055, five to seven constants each) share one skeleton: a saturating function of the local rotation number, balancing Coriolis production against isotropization, crossed with a wall function of the wall distance. In the second stage they are carried through the mean-spanwise-profile balance into a physics-informed spectral network (PINN) that reconstructs the time-averaged TG-vortex field at 𝑅𝑜𝜏 = 7.5, 30 and 75 in minutes on a desktop CPU. All four reproduce the two-layer counter-rotating roll cells with secondary-flow amplitudes within 10% of the DNS despite mean-profile errors of order the profile itself: the reconstruction is robust to O(1) profile errors, identifying stress production and viscosity, not mean-flow advection, as the governing balance and completing a “discover–close–simulate” pipeline with compact learned closures.

Abstract:
Abstract We extend the generalized anomalous diffusion framework established in Part 1 to the short-range forcing regime ( β > 2/3), where the multiscale-force dominated (MFD) subrange is intercalated after the inertial subrange, competing directly with the dissipation ranges. Focusing on electrokinetic (EK) turbulence as the prototypical example with β = 1, we derive the relations for the velocity and scalar dissipation wavenumbers, k MD and k SD , across all four subranges of the Quad-cascade process (inertial, constant-Π u , constant-Π s , and variable flux). By incorporating Golestanian’s predicted anomalous diffusion regimes for electrolytes, we construct comprehensive phase diagrams showing how the relative magnitudes of k MD and k SD are governed by the scale-dependent anomalous Schmidt number Sc Z . We identify two new spectral subranges that emerge exclusively in this short-range forcing regime: (i) the convective-forcing-viscous subrange ( k MU ≪ k ≪ k CFVD ) for either Sc Z ≫ 1 or Sc Z ≪ 1 with γ > α , where the scalar field drives viscous flow through electric body force; and (ii) the diffusive-forcing-convective subrange ( k MU ≪ k ≪ k DFCD ) for Sc Z ≪ 1 and γ ≤ α , where the scalar structure dominated by diffusion determines electric body force, which in turn cause momentum convection. These results provide a complete analytical map of EK turbulence under anomalous diffusion, revealing how external parameters such as electric field strength and ionic diffusivity determine the cascade topology.

#8 [paper] The minimal attached eddy in wall turbulence: statistical foundations, inverse identification and influence kernels
Authors: Karthik Duraisamy
Venue: Journal of Fluid Mechanics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2026.12182
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Townsend’s attached-eddy hypothesis models the logarithmic region of high-Reynolds-number wall turbulence as a random superposition of wall-attached, self-similar eddies whose sizes obey a scale-invariant population law. Building on the statistical framework of Woodcock & Marusic (2015 Phys. Fluids , vol. 27, no. 1, p. 015104), the present work (i) poses an inverse problem to infer the ideal single-eddy contribution (influence) functions for the mean velocity and Reynolds stresses from direct numerical simulations, (ii) uses these inferred kernels to guide a minimal Biot–Savart-consistent hairpin-type eddy built from Rankine vortex rods with an inviscid image system and (iii) introduces and infers a spectral influence kernel that maps a self-similar eddy footprint to its one-dimensional energy spectrum. The influence-kernel viewpoint yields an explanation for the emergence of the linear part of the energy spectrum, provides a clear scale-by-scale decomposition and helps rationalize why simple eddy templates can reproduce a broad set of log-layer statistics once the mean-flow anchoring is fixed. Closed-form expressions for the mean influence function and the Fourier-space streamwise velocity of a general straight-segment hairpin family with image are derived, revealing a mean-variance duality: for a rectangular hairpin, the horizontal head determines the entire mean kernel while the inclined legs dominate the spectral energy. It is shown that the rectangular hairpin yields a precise plateau in the influence function, resulting in a logarithmic mean velocity profile and desirable properties for the streamwise fluctuations. The model is further extended by calibrating the eddy population density as a function of scale, yielding accurate descriptions of mean velocity and streamwise variance across italic Re Subscript tau Baseline equals 6000 minus 20 000 Re τ = 6000 − 20 000 $\textit{Re}_{\tau }=6000{-}20\,000$ .

#9 [paper] Maximum likelihood reconstruction of particle trajectories in turbulent flows via sparse optimization
Authors: Griffin M. Kearney, Kasey Laurent, Makan Fardad
Venue: Scientific Reports
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-68853-4
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Extracting Lagrangian particle dynamics is essential for characterizing turbulent flows, but inferring particle acceleration from inherently noisy position data remains a significant challenge. Fluid particles in turbulence experience extreme, intermittent accelerations, resulting in heavy-tailed probability density functions (PDFs) that deviate strongly from Gaussian predictions. Existing filtering techniques, such as Gaussian kernels and penalized B-splines, implicitly assume Gaussian-distributed jerk, thereby penalizing sparse, high-magnitude acceleration changes and artificially suppressing the intermittent tails. In this work, we develop a novel maximum likelihood framework for filtering noisy particle tracks in turbulence that explicitly accounts for this non-Gaussian intermittency. By modeling the jerk with a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli–Gaussian prior in place of the usual Gaussian one, we obtain a sparse optimization problem, which we render tractable through a convex \(\ell _1\) -relaxation. To overcome the numerical stiffness associated with high-order difference operators, the problem is efficiently solved using an iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) algorithm. The proposed filter is evaluated against direct numerical simulation (DNS) data of homogeneous, isotropic turbulence ( \(\textrm{Re}_{\lambda } \simeq 433\) ) for the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database. Results demonstrate that the IRLS approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art continuous MLE, discrete MLE, and B-spline methods, yielding systematic reductions in root-mean-squared error (RMSE) across position, velocity, and acceleration. Most importantly, the proposed framework succeeds in better recovering the heavy-tailed statistical structure of both acceleration and acceleration differences (jerk) across temporal scales, preserving the physical intermittency characteristic of high-Reynolds-number turbulent flows that baseline methods severely attenuate.

#10 [paper] On the Nature of Turbulence
Authors: Barry Kieran Radcliffe
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23173174
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The finite predictive horizon of turbulent systems and the question of whether coherent turbulent structures are best understood as isolated objects or as temporary localizations of distributed motion whose persistence depends on exchange with surrounding flow.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A relational interpretation framework (the "Relational Lens") in which turbulence is described as the continual emergence, persistence, transformation, and dissolution of distinguishable organization, tested through evolving-boundary descriptions, reorganization measurements, exchange variables, an…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four turbulent systems: forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence, experimental wall-bounded turbulence, buoyancy-driven Rayleigh–Taylor turbulence, and naturally occurring oceanic wake turbulence.
Abstract:
This paper presents a relational interpretation of turbulence in which coherent turbulent structures are treated not as isolated objects, but as temporary localizations of distributed motion whose persistence depends upon continuing exchange with the surrounding flow. Within this framework, turbulence is described as the continual emergence, persistence, transformation, and dissolution of distinguishable organization. The central hypothesis is that the useful predictive lifetime of turbulent structure depends upon the persistence of the relational organization that sustains its distinction. This proposition is examined across four substantially different turbulent systems: forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence, experimental wall-bounded turbulence, buoyancy-driven Rayleigh–Taylor turbulence, and naturally occurring oceanic wake turbulence. Across these systems, evolving-boundary descriptions improve prediction relative to fixed representations; greater reorganization is associated with reduced structural persistence; exchange variables improve prediction of future interface evolution beyond recent kinematics; and measurements of surrounding-flow organization add predictive information beyond localized state variables in held-out observations. The results are not uniformly strong across all systems, and one specific deformation model does not generalize universally, emphasizing that the Relational Lens should be distinguished from any single mathematical implementation. The paper proposes that turbulence may be understood as the continual formation and loss of distinction within distributed motion, and that the finite predictive horizon of turbulent systems may be interpreted in part as a finite lifetime of relational continuity.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the Lagrangian rotational and deformation dynamics of long flexible fibers in wall-bounded turbulence.
Method (Mycelium's reading): One-way coupled Euler-Lagrange direct numerical simulations (DNS) modeling fibers as chains of sub-Kolmogorov rod elements with prescribed bending stiffness.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Turbulent channel flow at a shear Reynolds number of 300, analyzing fibers spanning more than one order of magnitude in length across near-wall, log-layer, and bulk regions.
Abstract:
Abstract We investigate the Lagrangian rotational and deformation dynamics of long flexible fibers in a turbulent channel flow at a shear Reynolds number equal to 300, using one-way coupled Euler-Lagrange direct numerical simulations. The fibers, modeled as chains of sub-Kolmogorov rod elements with prescribed bending stiffness, span more than one order of magnitude in length and are analyzed in three wall-normal slabs covering the near-wall, log-layer and bulk regions. We compute autocorrelations of the tumbling and spinning rates, power spectra of the fiber’s end-to-end vector, and waiting-time distributions of intense tumbling events. Spinning decorrelates on a fixed multiple of the local Kolmogorov time, independent of fiber length, whereas tumbling develops a memory that grows with fiber length by factors of two to five, reversing the ordering of the two timescales between the shortest and longest fibers. Flapping spectra separate into a high-frequency regime in which all fiber lengths carry the same energy in absolute terms and a low-frequency regime in which the energy increases with fiber length. Intense tumbling exhibits approximately exponential, weakly clustered waiting-time statistics whose rescaled form is universal across slabs, fiber lengths and bending rigidities, whereas the event rate depends on both fiber length and rigidity.

#12 [paper] SIMR-NO: A Spectrally-Informed Multi-Resolution Neural Operator for Turbulent Flow Super-Resolution
Authors: Muhammad Abid, Omer San
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11514570/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Reconstructing high-resolution turbulent flow fields from severely under-resolved observations, specifically a 16x upscaling factor from 8x8 to 128x128 vorticity fields, which is an ill-posed inverse problem where classical interpolation and standard convolutional networks fail to recover missing f…
Method (Mycelium's reading): SIMR-NO, a hierarchical operator-learning framework that factorizes reconstruction across intermediate resolutions. Each stage combines a deterministic interpolation prior with a residual correction computed by Fourier layers with spectral multipliers modulated by a learned radial gate, and local c…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Two two-dimensional flows: statistically stationary Kolmogorov-forced turbulence and freely decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence at Reynolds numbers of 1000, 4000, and 8000. The task involves reconstructing 128x128 vorticity fields from 8x8 observations.
Abstract:
Abstract Reconstructing high-resolution turbulent flow fields from severely under-resolved observations is an ill-posed inverse problem of central importance in computational fluid dynamics. Classical interpolation cannot recover the missing fine scales, and convolutional super-resolution networks lack spectral and multiscale inductive biases suited to turbulence at large upscaling factors. We introduce the \textit{Spectrally-Informed Multi-Resolution Neural Operator} (SIMR-NO), a hierarchical operator-learning framework that factorizes the reconstruction across intermediate resolutions. Each stage combines a deterministic interpolation prior with a residual correction computed by Fourier layers whose spectral multipliers are modulated by a learned radial gate, and local convolutional refinement modules recover features beyond the truncated Fourier basis. SIMR-NO is evaluated on two two-dimensional flows with distinct dynamics, statistically stationary Kolmogorov-forced turbulence and freely decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence at Reynolds numbers of $1000$, $4000$, and $8000$, in which $128\times128$ vorticity fields are reconstructed from $8\times8$ observations, a $16\times$ upscaling factor. In comparison with bicubic interpolation, the Fourier neural operator, EDSR, and LapSRN, SIMR-NO achieves the lowest reconstruction error and the highest structural similarity for both flows and at every Reynolds number. On decaying turbulence, SIMR-NO attains a mean relative error of about $3\%$ at every Reynolds number, up to $55\%$ lower than that of the strongest baseline, and its accuracy is nearly insensitive to the Reynolds number. Spectral diagnostics, vorticity-conditioned error statistics, and localized comparisons show that these gains are accompanied by a more accurate reconstruction of intense vortex cores, fine-scale filaments, and high-wavenumber content.

#14 [paper] Generative AI in Turbulence: Foundations, Applications, Validations and Benchmarks
Authors: Luca Biferale, Michele Buzzicotti
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/5d11e451fde866572ad78443a7d7eab94b6b8f2f
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The application of generative AI to turbulence problems, specifically addressing challenges where incomplete observations or unresolved degrees of freedom admit multiple physically plausible solutions, and the inadequacy of standard image-generation metrics for assessing physical fidelity in turbul…
Method (Mycelium's reading): A review and analysis of generative AI techniques, with emphasis on diffusion models, score-based methods, and probability-transport formulations, applied to unconditional generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, temporal evolution, and mesh-free representations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical and computational fluid dynamics contexts involving multiscale dynamics, intermittency, extreme events, and stochastic transport in turbulent flows.
Abstract:
Generative AI offers new approaches to turbulence problems in which incomplete observations or unresolved d.o.f. admit multiple physically plausible solutions. Potential applications include stochastic closures, super-resolution, data assimilation, uncertainty quantification, and the generation of Eulerian and Lagrangian flow ensembles. However, turbulence is not a conventional image-generation problem. Its multiscale dynamics, intermittency, extreme events, rough velocity fields and intrinsically stochastic transport make visual realism, pointwise error, and low-order spectral agreement insufficient measures of physical fidelity. We examine where generative AI provide novel capabilities with emphasis on diffusion models, score-based methods, and related probability-transport formulations. We discuss their use in unconditional generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, temporal evolution, and mesh-free representations. We argue that validation must address turbulence properties: energy transfer, structure functions, anomalous scaling, pdf tails, coherent structures, conservation laws, temporal consistency, ensemble diversity and generalization. Finally, we discuss potential limitations in validation, baseline, data availability and reproducibility, and the need for a benchmark ecosystem combining open data, standardized challenges, hidden tests, physics-aware metrics, and documented failures. This paper serves as a bridge between two communities. For AI practitioners, we provide a fair and accessible introduction to turbulence, essential for appreciating the challenges posed by the field and for assessing the physical relevance of generative models. For turbulent practitioners, we provide an introduction to the key technological aspects of Generative AI, clarifying what these tools actually do, and where their potential and current limitations lie.

#15 [paper] Factorized-gating mixture of experts enables cross-regime turbulence modeling
Authors: H.J. Liu, Qingyong Luo, Xinlei Zhang, Guowei He
Venue: Communications Engineering
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44172-026-00802-5
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing data-driven turbulence models rely on monolithic dense networks that struggle to generalize across diverse flow regimes.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The factorized-gating mixture of experts (FG-MoE) framework, which factorizes a conventional monolithic router into lightweight, physics-guided binary attributes to approximate the gating function as a product-form of low-dimensional binary factor probabilities.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Numerical experiments spanning canonical benchmarks to complex real-world engineering applications.
Abstract:
Predicting turbulent flows is vital for advancing aerospace, energy, and environmental technologies, yet remains critically limited by the accuracy of turbulence models. While machine learning has led to the widespread development of data-driven turbulence models, existing approaches predominantly rely on monolithic dense networks that struggle to generalize across diverse flow regimes. To address this challenge, we introduce the factorized-gating mixture of experts (FG-MoE) framework, where regime-specific experts are trained and blended via spatially varying probabilities. Crucially, the FG-MoE factorizes the conventional monolithic router into a set of lightweight, physics-guided binary attributes, reducing the high-dimensional gating function to a product-form approximation of low-dimensional binary factor probabilities. This factorized design substantially reduces gating complexity, offers physical interpretability of the gating mechanism, and enables plug-and-play scalability to expand the expert library without retraining the entire model. Through extensive numerical experiments, spanning canonical benchmarks to complex real-world engineering applications, FG-MoE delivers consistently high-fidelity predictions across diverse flow regimes. The FG-MoE framework offers an engineering turbulence-modeling pathway by decomposing complex turbulent flows into distinct physical regimes and leveraging a factorized gating strategy to ensure interpretability, efficiency, and scalability.

#19 [paper] Anomalous Scaling in Fully Developed Turbulence
Authors: Angelo Vulpiani, Roberto Benzi
Venue: Cambridge University Press eBooks
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009709620.010
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The difficulty in quantitatively describing the statistical and geometrical properties of turbulent flows, specifically the need for a consistent framework for the statistics of velocity fluctuations in homogeneous and isotropic turbulence.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Multifractal theory rooted in large deviation theory
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Homogeneous and isotropic turbulence
Abstract:
Turbulence is one of the most complex and fascinating systems in classical physics, inspiring artists like Van Gogh and Hokusai. Despite knowing the equations of motion for a Newtonian fluid for over 200 years, a full understanding of turbulence remains a major challenge. The key difficulty lies in quantitatively describing the statistical and geometrical properties of turbulent flows, which vary depending on the physical system. Focusing on homogeneous and isotropic turbulence, the main goal is to develop a consistent framework for the statistics of velocity fluctuations. This paper briefly reviews the multifractal theory of turbulence, which offers a potential solution. Technically, the multifractal approach is rooted in large deviation theory, but its introduction in the 1980s profoundly influenced statistical physics, chaos theory, and disordered systems. A crucial insight from multifractal theory is that turbulence cannot be fully described by a finite set of scaling exponents – contrary to ideas from critical phenomena. Instead, an infinite hierarchy of exponents is needed to capture the complete scaling behavior. This realization has significantly advanced our understanding of turbulence’s intricate structure.

#20 [paper] Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI
Authors: Jiawei Chen, Xiang I. A. Yang, Ping He
Venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.29850
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. Four large language model (LLM) agents then propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations and generate scripts for CFD simulations. The Discovery Agent infers the vortex axis from various vortex-identification methods. The candidates are tested on four cases spanning canonical and engineering flows: a flat plate, a backward-facing step, a free shear layer, and an iced airfoil. For all test cases, the best candidate consistently outperforms the standard length scale based on the maximum cell size. Its accuracy is similar to, or slightly better than, that of the expert-designed shear-layer-adapted length scale. Each agentic discovery run takes about 25 minutes on average, excluding the CFD simulations. These results show that LLM-based reasoning can significantly accelerate the discovery of physically interpretable turbulence models and reduce reliance on manual expert formulation.

Abstract:
THIS IS NOT A NOTICE OF FUNDING. THIS IS A GENERAL FORECAST ONLY.

Grant and Per Diem (GPD) Program Introduction

The GPD Program is VA’s largest transitional housing program for Veterans experiencing homelessness and is permanently authorized under Public Law 109-461.

Since 1994, the GPD Program has awarded grants to community-based organizations to provide transitional housing with wraparound supportive services to assist vulnerable Veterans move into permanent housing. The grants are designed to meet Veterans at various stages as they move to stable housing. Community-based organizations receiving GPD grants offer focused transitional housing services through a variety of housing models targeted to different populations and needs of Veterans. The GPD program plays a vital role in the continuum of homeless services by providing supportive services to those Veterans who would otherwise be among the unsheltered homeless population. The result of GPD programs is that Veterans achieve residential stability, increase their skill levels and/or income, and obtain greater self-determination.

Types of GPD Grants

Transitional housing grants:

Per Diem Only (PDO) grants provide funding in the form of per diem payments to reimburse grantees for the cost of care provided to Veterans in transitional supportive housing.

Special Need grants target housing and services to specific populations of Veterans (e.g., women, Veterans with chronic mental illness, frail elderly Veterans, Veterans caring for minor dependents, terminally ill Veterans).

Transition-In-Place (TIP) grants offer Veteran residents housing in which supportive services transition out of the residence over time, rather than the resident. Upon completion of the TIP services, the resident retains the unit as their permanent housing with no requirement to move.

Other types of grants:

Case Management grants support Veterans who were previously experiencing homelessness or who are at risk for homelessness so that they may obtain or retain permanent housing.

Capital grants support the costs of acquiring, renovating, or constructing facilities and are only offered intermittently to improve existing facilities or to develop new transitional housing depending on VA's priorities and funding availability.

Lists of current grantees are available on the GPD website.

How to Apply for GPD Funding

Not all grant types are available annually. When available, notices of funding can be found at the following locations: www.grants.gov and https://www.va.gov/homeless/gpd.asp.

Application instructions are provided in each notice of funding.

Each notice of funding will clarify specific eligibility criteria, application requirements, funding limitations, and other requirements.

Applications are submitted through an online portal that is only available when there is an open notice of funding.

Potential applicants who wish to see what was required for previous applications may review past notices of funding, available on the GPD provider website and www.grants.gov. Past notices of funding are not a guarantee of future requirements.

Tentative Estimated GPD Award Schedule

Specific dates are not able to be forecast.

The follow tentative approximations are provided for general planning purposes.

FY 2026

Case Management – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2025 for case management awards starting approximately in FY 2026.

FY 2027

PDO – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2026 for PDO awards starting approximately in FY 2027.

TIP – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2026 for TIP awards starting approximately in FY 2027.

FY 2028

GPD tentatively does not expect to offer a notice of funding for this timeframe. GPD may update this forecast closer to the time.

Abstract:
Through this Disaster NOFO, EDA will award investments in regions experiencing severe economic distress or other economic harm resulting from hurricanes, wildfires, tornadoes, floods, and other natural disasters occurring in calendar years 2023 and 2024. EDA’s goal under this NOFO is to assist communities recovering from a disaster by realizing opportunities to recover and change the economic trajectory of the community for the better. In other words, EDA funding seeks to help communities recover and set them on a path to exceed their previous pre-disaster baseline. EDA seeks projects that are responsive to community needs post-disaster by engaging all aspects of the community, with special focus on private industry partners.

This Disaster NOFO provides funding through three pathways:

Readiness Path – Standalone non-construction projects designed to increase a community’s readiness to apply for or implement disaster recovery funding from private and public sources including, but not limited to, future EDA NOFOs and the Implementation or Industry Transformation Paths under this NOFO. Projects will fund strategy development, capacity building, and/or predevelopment costs necessary for future recovery projects.

Implementation Path – Standalone construction or non-construction projects designed to address the economic challenges faced by a community recovering from a natural disaster and improve economic trajectories beyond pre-disaster economic conditions.

Industry Transformation Path – Led by a coalition of regional stakeholders, a portfolio of large-scale, multicomponent construction and non-construction projects designed to fundamentally transform the economic trajectory of a region through the development or acceleration of an industry.

Abstract:
UPDATED NOTICE - PLEASE READ: April 6, 2023

EDA is excited to announce the launch of its new grants management platform: the Economic Development Grants Experience (EDGE). EDGE was developed to streamline the application and grants management process by implementing a single platform with increased transparency, improved user experience, higher data quality, and more efficiency throughout the entire grant lifecycle.

As of April 6th, 2023, applications can no longer be submitted on Grants.gov, and will ONLY be accepted through EDGE. To apply in EDGE, please go to: sfgrants.eda.gov. More information on how to apply is provided in the full NOFO.

PARTNERSHIP PLANNING program instructions: Please note that applicants will be invited to submit applications through EDGE for the Partnership Planning program. For more information, please reach out to your EDA point of contact.

Program Description:

EDA makes planning and local technical assistance investments to support economic development, foster job creation, and attract private investment in economically distressed areas of the United States.

Under the Planning program, EDA makes Partnership Planning, Short-Term Planning, and State Planning awards to eligible recipients to create and implement regional economic development plans designed to build capacity and guide the economic prosperity and resiliency of an area or region. More specifically, EDA makes Partnership Planning investments to designated planning organizations (i.e., District Organizations) serving EDA-designated Economic Development Districts and to Indian Tribes to facilitate the development, implementation, revision, or replacement of Comprehensive Economic Development Strategies (CEDS), which articulate and prioritize the strategic economic goals of recipients’ respective regions. EDA also makes Short-Term and State Planning awards for economic development planning activities that guide the eventual creation and retention of high-quality jobs, particularly for the unemployed and underemployed in the Nation’s most economically distressed regions.

Under the Local Technical Assistance program, EDA makes awards to strengthen the capacity of local or State organizations, institutions of higher education, and other eligible entities to undertake and promote effective economic development programs through projects such as feasibility studies, impact analyses, disaster resiliency plans, and project planning.

**Please note: While the published Notice of Funding Opportunity (available under "Related Documents") states that the ED900A form and the SF424B form are both required for a complete application, these forms are no longer required and have therefore been removed from the package template.

#20 [grant] Advancing Screening, Diagnosis, and Referral for Late Talking Children
Amount: $500,000
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/362352
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-10-15
Abstract:
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) Tackling Acquisition of Language in Kids (TALK) initiative intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit research grant applications to improve the earliest steps in clinical practice for late talking children. The overarching purpose of this funding opportunity is to inform, develop, and evaluate evidence-based practices and implementation strategies to (1) effectively and efficiently identify early signs of late talking and (2) successfully guide parents, caregivers, and professionals in supporting the needs of late talking children at the first point of concern.

For this NOFO late talking is defined as a child, usually over the age of 18 months, not meeting expressive language milestones, for any reason. Populations of interest include, but are not limited to, children at higher risk for late talking due to premature birth, exposure to maltreatment or trauma, neurological conditions, motor and sensory disorders, emotional and behavioral disorders, and intellectual and developmental disorders. Children who present as late talkers for no other known reason and with no other symptoms also are of interest for this NOFO.

For this NOFO, the early steps for services for children age birth to three years that are of interest include screening and developmental surveillance of late talking, referral and follow through for specialized services, and in-depth evaluation and diagnosis of language and other contributing delays/disorders. These services typically occur in primary care, specialty care, educational settings, and early childhood community settings. The research will need to be conducted in a relevant setting.

Research focusing on children as well as their parents, caregivers, and supporting community professionals is of interest, including how to support successfully navigating from initial concern to effective care. #7 [paper] Valuing education for limited-resource audiences using a willingness to accept experiment
Authors: Russell Tronstad, Ibrahima Sall
Venue: PLoS ONE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0348858
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Education grants often target audiences that have limited-resources relative to their peers, such as beginning farmers, who arguably have the most to gain from more education. Yet, charging even modest fees to these participants is discouraged, creating a challenge for funding entities that desire to have a dollar value for the education provided. To measure this value, we conducted an experiment using a willingness-to-accept (WTA) approach. Participants chose a minimum cash payout from seven different options to voluntarily leave a training session before receiving any instruction or educational materials. The design is constructed so that each option has an equal expected payout. Cash payouts were not advertised or known to any participants before the training. Results show that average WTA values are $277.44 per training (about 4 hours of instruction), which is 2.11 to 4.74 times more than participants' self-reported willingness to pay (WTP), depending on how travel costs and time of participants are valued. WTP consistently and significantly explains much of the variation in WTA. In sharp contrast, detailed travel cost estimates in various forms were consistently insignificant for explaining WTA values. Beginning farmers and ranchers, our targeted limited-resource audience, reported WTA and WTP values that were $81.18 and $22.73 more per training, respectively, than those of non-beginning farmers.

#10 [paper] An economic analysis of postoperative cataract consultation using remote self-assessment
Authors: Casper van der Zee, Janneau L. J. Claessens, Rudy M. M. A. Nuijts, Rob Wouters, Nicolaas J. Reus, Karl Boden, Oliver Findl, Saskia M. Imhof
Venue: PLOS Digital Health
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pdig.0001617
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
To evaluate the potential savings realized by replacing the 4-6 weeks consultation following cataract surgery with remote self-assessment. In addition, we evaluated the costs associated with adverse events (AEs) from a societal perspective and evaluated the current cost of AEs based on published literature and publicly available datasets. We determined the cost reduction when replacing the in-person 4-6-week postoperative consultation visit with remote self-assessment using our previous clinical trial, publicly available healthcare resource databases, and threshold analysis to determine the effect on cost if the incidence of AEs is affected by conducting an online self-assessment. We collected AE probabilities and costs of AEs based on published literature and databases. and performed a threshold analysis to demonstrate the financial impact if the incidence of AEs is altered versus the savings due to replacing the 4-6 weeks in-person consultation with remote self-assessment. Remote self-assessments resulted in an average savings between -€83 and -€92 per patient. Physical consultations were less costly only if >80% of remote self-assessments warranted an in-person follow-up. The mean cost of AEs per patient was estimated to be €16.35 and were attributed primarily to rare but severe complications, including endophthalmitis and retinal detachment. Having patients participate in a remote self-assessment following cataract surgery is expected to reduce costs under a wide range of assumptions. Due to the lack of published data regarding the utility loss due to AEs, quality of life was not included in our analysis; nevertheless, these cost savings should be balanced by the clinical impact of potentially missing relatively rare AEs. These findings contribute to the ongoing discussion regarding appropriate care following cataract surgery.

#11 [paper] Death by a thousand cuts: Short-sighted attacks on the academic mission.
Authors: Hassanein, Salma, Chu, Linda C, Patel, Kirang, Rowe, Steven P, Fishman, Elliot K
Venue: Clinical imaging
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42849173/

Abstract:
In recent years, the increasing financial pressures on academic institutions have led to a gradual diminution of departmental and institutional funding of important supporting aspects of the academic mission. We specifically note that funding for travel to academic meetings, payment of article processing charges, and the support of lunches and team building activities have all been curtailed. Such an approach threatens to undermine the academic mission and decrease the downstream benefits such as departmental and institutional prestige, participation in cooperative group endeavors, and external/federal funding. In an era where clinical volumes and the difficulty of cases are constantly increasing, and recruiting and retaining academic faculty is an uphill battle against markedly high salaries and more flexible scheduling available in private practice, academic institutions are only hurting themselves by making ultimately trivial cuts in the funding of the academic mission. Academic institutions need to fund the academic mission - to do otherwise is to ultimately surrender that mission and scuttle the emerging careers of talented junior faculty.

#12 [paper] What Will My Gift Buy? How Effectiveness Signals Shape the Perceived Price of Giving and Donations
Authors: Minjung Kim
Venue: Journal of Philanthropy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1002/nvsm.70073
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
ABSTRACT Perceptions of a nonprofit's effectiveness shape charitable giving, but less is understood about the route by which an effectiveness signal becomes a gift. This study asks whether one specific belief, the perceived price of giving, helps account for that relationship. Perceived price is how much a donor believes it costs, in dollars given, to deliver a dollar of program benefit to the organization's beneficiaries, and it rises as more of a gift is expected to go to overhead. Prior work shows that both effectiveness signals and overhead ratios shape giving, yet few studies test whether effectiveness signals work by way of donors' beliefs about the price of their gift. In partnership with a small, newly established nonprofit, an online survey experiment was conducted (total N = 1862). The experiment manipulated reputational effectiveness across control, low, and high conditions and measured the perceived price of giving, giving intentions, and a small‐stakes incentivized donation decision. The perceived price of giving mediated the response to the low‐effectiveness (reach) cue, but there was little evidence that it mediated the response to the high‐effectiveness (outcome) cue; the mediation was clearest for stated giving intentions and weaker for the amount donors were willing to give and for the small‐stakes donation decision. Because the high and low conditions differed in dimension as well as in valence, we do not attribute this asymmetry to the sign of the signal alone. For fundraising practice, how an organization communicates its effectiveness can shift what donors believe a gift will accomplish (a lever available even to organizations without audited financial figures), though this belief is one mechanism among several rather than the whole story.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe
Abstract:
Marine Plastic Pollution (MPP) is widely recognised as a significant global challenge, driven by unsustainable plastic production, ineffective waste management, and the long-term persistence of plastics in marine environments. MPP has become increasingly widespread across oceans, along coastlines and on the seafloor, resulting in an urgent need for the development of technologies capable of advancing a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products. Advances in cleaner production technologies, including satellite and drone-based remote sensing, autonomous robotic platforms, and machine-vision systems, have improved the efficiency of plastic debris identification, classification, and recovery in complex marine environments. Similarly, innovations in downstream sorting, such as electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven classification, are enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of processing MPP. The review evaluates mechanical recycling methods with particular emphasis on recent advances in extrusion, moulding technologies, and additive manufacturing for converting MPP into high-value secondary materials in a CE framework in Europe. These technological developments demonstrate the potential for establishing viable and scalable valorisation routes. Overall, the review outlines key opportunities to strengthen a sustainable CE and guide future research and industrial adoption. In doing so, it provides a comprehensive examination of state-of-the-art technologies across the entire marine plastics value chain in Europe, from detection and recovery to separation, identification, and recycling.

#7 [paper] Infrared-visible space debris perception and detection with light-boosting convolution and cross-modal attention fusion
Authors: Yongqing Yang, Dalei Yao, Fan Bu, Yan Wen, Rongli Chen

Abstract:
Introduction Space debris poses an increasing threat to the safety of spacecraft because reliable perception under complex illumination remains challenging for autonomous on-orbit operations. Existing visible-light methods are highly susceptible to low-light degradation, whereas infrared images preserve thermal information but lack sufficient structural details. Methods To address these limitations, we propose the Space Debris Perception and Detection Network (SPDNet), an end-to-end infrared-visible framework that jointly performs image enhancement, cross-modal feature fusion, and object detection. Specifically, a Light-Boosting Convolution module restores degraded visible features under weak illumination, a Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) module progressively exchanges complementary infrared and visible information during hierarchical feature extraction, and a Multi-Scale Adaptive Fusion (MSAF) module adaptively integrates multi-scale semantic features to improve both overall detection and small-object recognition. Experiments are conducted on a paired infrared-visible space debris dataset constructed from publicly available visible images and geometrically aligned simulated infrared imagery. Results The proposed SPDNet achieves an average gradient (AG) of 88.9, spatial frequency (SF) of 87.286, mutual information (MI) of 5.946, and Chen-Blum metric (QCB) of 0.941 for image fusion. For debris detection, SPDNet obtains 78.48% mAP, 98.74% mAP50, and 40.27% APsmall, outperforming representative image fusion methods under a unified detection framework. Discussion These results demonstrate that jointly optimized cross-modal feature enhancement and adaptive multi-scale fusion provide an effective solution for autonomous space debris perception under challenging illumination conditions.

#8 [paper] Multi-Task UAV Dataset for Floating Plastic Waste Detection in the Kashmir Region (AquaPlasticWaste 2026)
Authors: Veningston K, Ahsan Ul Haq, Shafiya Mushtaq, Dinesh Kumar R
Venue: Mendeley Data
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17632/zshjxgfmc3.1
