Abstract:
AquaPlasticWaste 2026 — Multi-Task UAV Dataset for Floating Plastic Waste Detection in the Kashmir Region — is a 5,000-image UAV aerial imagery dataset for automated plastic waste monitoring on Dal Lake, an ecologically important Himalayan freshwater lake in Srinagar, Kashmir, India, facing severe pollution pressure. Images were captured with a consumer-grade quadrotor UAV flown at a consistent altitude across open water, shoreline, houseboat clusters, and floating garden zones, under varied lighting conditions. It is the first multi-task, polygon-annotated UAV dataset targeting plastic pollution on a Himalayan lake surface. All images carry polygon-based instance segmentation masks, rather than bounding boxes, to capture the irregular shapes of floating litter (e.g., flattened bags, torn wrappers). Masks were created in CVAT and verified through a primary annotator, a second cross-checking annotator, a third adjudicator, and a final quality-control pass. Two labeling schemes are provided from the same masks: binary (plastic vs. non-plastic) and seven-class (background, bottle, cap, foam, polythene, shoe, wrapper). Annotations are exported in both COCO JSON and YOLO polygon/segmentation formats for direct use in standard detection and segmentation frameworks. Of the 5,000 images, 4,692 (93.8%) contain plastic and 308 (6.2%) are plastic-free, with 30,166 polygon instances annotated in total. Wrapper is the most common class (35.4% of instances, present in 63.2% of images); shoe is rarest (1.1% of instances, 4.8% of images). Mean plastic pixel coverage is 1.40% per image (median 0.55%, max 33.31%), and median instance size is 1,448 pixels, well below typical benchmark object sizes (e.g., MS-COCO) — a genuine small-object challenge. Imbalance is reported at three levels for different loss-function needs: 31.9:1 by instance count (wrapper vs. shoe), 44.8:1 by pixel area among foreground classes (polythene vs. cap), and 70.4:1 between plastic and background pixels overall. A single annotation source supports four downstream tasks: image classification, litter-density regression, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation, enabling multi-task and cross-task benchmarking without repeated labeling effort. Existing waste-detection datasets such as TrashNet, TACO, UAVVaste, and TrashCan are ground-level, underwater, or single-task; none target a freshwater lake surface from the air. AquaPlasticWaste 2026 fills this gap, offering a realistic, class-imbalanced, small-object benchmark relevant to environmental monitoring, lake-conservation planning, and edge-deployable UAV vision systems.

#9 [paper] Quantifying the long-term evolution of post-earthquake debris-flow activity in the epicentral area of the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, China
Authors: Qingyun Shi, Weihua Zhang, Chuan Tang, Yucai Ma, Wei Zhou, Jiang Xiong, Yu Tie
Venue: Natural Hazards
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11069-026-08494-y
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The 2008 Wenchuan earthquake triggered widespread coseismic landslides and supplied large volumes of loose material on hillslopes and channels, resulting in persistent post-earthquake debris flow activity near the epicentral area. Quantifying the long-term evolution of this activity is important for geohazard assessment, but remains challenge because debris flows are jointly controlled by sediment supply, topography, and rainfall. In this study, a catchment-scale framework was developed to evaluate debris flow activity intensity in 44 catchments affected by the Wenchuan earthquake. Multi-temporal landslide inventories from 2008 to 2019 were used to calculate landslide sediment supply potential (LSSP), which integrates landslide areal density, spatial distribution indices, and channel gradient. LSSP was then combined with representative hourly rainfall intensities from documented debris flow triggering events to derive a debris flow activity intensity index (AI DF ). The results show that active landslide area decreased from 122.05 km² in 2008 to 30.55 km² in 2019, while recovery areas expanded progressively. LSSP increased sharply immediately after the earthquake and then declined over time, with a rapid decrease during 2008–2011 followed by a slower adjustment phase. Nevertheless, sediment supply in many catchments remained above the pre-earthquake level in 2019. AI DF showed an overall decline after its post-earthquake peak, although temporary increases occurred during major rainfall events. Comparison with documented debris flow events indicates that AI DF captures the main temporal pattern of observed activity. The fitted long-term trend suggests three stages of post-earthquake debris flow activity: an active period from 2008 to 2013, a recession period from 2013 to 2048, and a relatively stable period after 2048. These results indicate that debris flow activity in the Wenchuan earthquake-affected area may persist for several decades, mainly controlled by the gradual depletion and redistribution of landslide-derived sediment under rainfall forcing.

Candidate studies were identified via targeted keyword searches in Google Scholar, Scopus-indexed journals, and African Journals Online, combined with citation chasing. The review synth…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global empirical studies (16 international) and Nigerian studies (5), with specific focus on sub-Saharan Africa (including Dakar and Blantyre) and Nigeria.
Abstract:
Purpose: This review asks whether, and under what conditions, combining satellite remote sensing with machine learning, and ensemble learning in particular, improves the mapping of illegal-dumpsite susceptibility, and where the evidence for that claim is still missing, with emphasis on sub-Saharan Africa and Nigeria. Methodology: A structured narrative review with a non-systematic, purposive selection of studies was carried out. Candidate studies published from 2000 to 2026 were identified through targeted keyword searches of scholarly databases and search engines (Google Scholar, Scopus-indexed journals and African Journals Online), combining dumping terms (illegal dump, illegal landfill, dumpsite) with remote-sensing, susceptibility and machine-learning terms, and through citation chasing from recent surveys. Empirical studies that detected dumpsites or mapped dumping susceptibility with remote-sensing or GIS predictors and reported a validation outcome were included, and each was appraised for source type and validation design. Twenty-one empirical studies (16 international detection and susceptibility studies and 5 Nigerian studies) were synthesised, supported by methodological literature. Findings: Susceptibility studies outside Africa report strong discrimination with comparatively simple models (logistic regression, overall accuracy 92–94%; discriminant analysis, AUC 0.97–0.98), and the largest head-to-head comparison (seven classifiers on the same data) found AUC values within a narrow range (0.86–0.89). The two African susceptibility studies (Dakar, Blantyre) used expert-weighted multicriteria analysis rather than machine learning. Only one study used spatial cross-validation, none used a stacking ensemble, and no Nigerian study has modelled susceptibility predictively. Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: Unlike recent surveys that focus on detecting waste in imagery, this review compares susceptibility-mapping methods on their reported performance and validation practice, maps the regional evidence gap for Nigeria, and sets out minimum standards (simple-model baselines, spatial validation and treatment of pseudo-absences) that future ensemble studies must meet before ensembles can be recommended to waste-management authorities.

#11 [paper] Fuel debris detection system using in-situ measurements of gamma rays and neutrons for investigation of fuel debris distribution
Authors: 上野克宜, Yuichiro Ueno, Koichi Okada, Yosuke Takatori, Satoshi Okada, Yutaka Kometani
Venue: Journal of Nuclear Science and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/00223131.2026.2741954
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This paper presents a compact, integrated system for in-situ detection of fuel debris via simultaneous gamma-ray and neutron measurements, developed for application within the primary containment vessel (PCV) of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station Unit 1. The system combines a miniaturized CdTe detector with 100-ns signal processing for gamma-ray spectroscopy and a compact B-10 proportional counter structually designed to suppress its gamma-ray response, both enclosed in a shielded container weighing less than 8 kg. Performance was validated through laboratory experiments with sealed sources, functional verification using a spent fuel assembly under simulated PCV conditions, and in-situ demonstration using a swimming remotely operated vehicle (ROV). The system reliably detected Eu-154 gamma rays and neutrons under dose rates exceeding 10 Gy/h, achieving an energy resolution of 41 keV at 1274 keV. Field deployment suggested the presence of fuel debris-derived material at most measurement locations near the sediment surface. These findings establish the system’s suitability for decommissioning support in severe radiation environments.

#12 [paper] Spatial Patterns of Marine Litter on a Remote South Atlantic Ocean Island: Setting Baselines for Monitoring
Authors: Fernanda Caminha Leal Valls, Leandro Bugoni
Venue: Thalassas An International Journal of Marine Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s41208-026-01266-2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Characterizing the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter on Trindade Island, a remote South Atlantic island, to establish baselines for monitoring before the establishment of marine protected areas.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Systematic sampling of seven beaches with varying exposure to wind and substrate; quantification of litter items, categorization by purpose, and calculation of pollution indices (Clean Coast Index and Plastic Abundance Index).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Seven beaches on Trindade Island, South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland; characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates.
Abstract:
Abstract Marine plastic litter is a major environmental problem across all oceans, including remote regions. Here, we described the characteristics and spatial distribution of marine litter stranded on the beaches of Trindade Island, in the South Atlantic Ocean, 1200 km off the South American mainland, before the establishment of marine protected areas and the initiation of a long-term research program on the island. Seven beaches differing in exposure to wind and substrate were sampled. A total of 1317 litter items were recorded, with plastics as the main litter (81.9%), mostly hard plastic fragments. Although Lixo Beach had the smallest surveyed area (425 m 2 ), it exhibited the highest litter density (0.74 items/m 2 ) and highest litter-covered area (2.2% of the sampled beach area). Domestic and household purpose items composed the bulk of identifiable items (28.9%), followed by naval (22.5%) and fishery (17.7%) pieces. Litter distribution among beaches differed, with leeward beaches accumulating significantly more and larger litter items than windward beaches, revealing substantial local-scale variation patterns in debris retention. These beaches are characterized by coarse, large pebble substrates rather than sand. Our analysis of pollution indices demonstrated that the Clean Coast Index ( CCI ) and the Plastic Abundance Index ( PAI ) are strongly correlated and suitable for long-term monitoring. This study confirms that oceanic islands are prone to accumulating marine litter, while contrasting results from other studies on Trindade Island emphasize the need for simple yet standardized protocols to support long-term monitoring of plastic pollution in remote environments.

#13 [paper] Design and Experimental Characterization of a Solar-Powered Multi-Sensor Instrumentation System for Smart Dumpster Monitoring and GPS Tracking
Authors: Abdul-wasiu Alani Olowosebioba, Fatai Sunday Akingbade, Isaiah Olaoluwapo Andrew
Venue: Iconic Research and Engineering Journals
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64388/irev10i4-1723922
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study presents the design and experimental characterization of a solar-powered multi-sensor instrumentation system for smart waste monitoring and GPS tracking. The developed system integrates an ultrasonic sensor for waste-level measurement, a GPS module for location tracking, a GSM communication unit for remote notification, and a photovoltaic power subsystem for autonomous operation. An Arduino-based controller was employed for data acquisition, processing, and communication. Experimental evaluation was conducted to determine the performance of the sensing, communication, positioning, and power-management subsystems. Results showed a waste-level measurement accuracy of 99.1% with an average sensor error of 0.28 cm, demonstrating high reliability for real-time monitoring applications. The GPS subsystem achieved an average positioning accuracy of 3.3 m, enabling effective location identification and tracking of the waste bin. The solar-energy subsystem delivered a maximum output power of 40 W, while the battery backup system sustained continuous operation for approximately 15.6 h under test conditions. The servo-actuated lid mechanism exhibited an average response time of 0.81 s, ensuring prompt system operation. Furthermore, the GSM communication module achieved a 100% message transmission success rate during the experimental trials. The results demonstrate that the prototype instrumentation system provides reliable sensing, communication, and energy autonomy for intelligent waste-management applications. The integration of renewable energy, multi-sensor monitoring, and wireless communication offers a practical and sustainable solution for smart-city dumpster-monitoring infrastructure.

#14 [paper] How Emerging Technologies Transform Disaster Debris Management: Generative AI, Digital Twins, and Cyber-Physical-Social Systems for Circular Recovery
Authors: Mojtaba Parsaee, Tarlan Abazari, Mahdi Ghafoori, Mohsen Goodarzi
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1061/9780784486955.022
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This paper explores how emerging technologies can transform disaster debris management from linear clear-and-dispose practices toward circular, environmentally sustainable recovery. Climate-related disasters generate massive volumes of construction and demolition (C&D) debris, yet practice remains dominated by rapid landfilling with limited use of artificial intelligence (AI), digital twins (DTs), or cyber-physical-social systems (CPSS), leaving major circularity and climate-mitigation opportunities unrealized. This paper proposes a framework that couples large language model-based generative AI agents with archetype-driven life cycle assessment (LCA) inside a DT- and CPSS-oriented environment. Using the 2023 tornado in Sullivan, Indiana, as a benchmark, the framework classifies damaged buildings into archetypes, links material inventories to a proxy LCA library, and simulates linear, moderately circular, and enhanced circular debris pathways. Results indicate that circular strategies can divert about 46% of C&D debris from landfills and reduce embodied greenhouse gas emissions by roughly 28% compared to conventional landfilling. An interactive web interface converts high-dimensional outputs into charts and narrative explanations that help stakeholders explore trade-offs between debris management scenarios. Overall, the work establishes a transferable foundation for AI-enabled DTs and CPSS that treat disaster debris as a material resource and embed circular economy principles into disaster governance and supply chains.

#15 [paper] LAND-MAP sensor-fusion simulation: synthetic landfill survey generator, spatial-validation classifiers, value-of-information economic layer, and sensor-selection and decision-viability maps
Authors: Leon Sandler
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22984667
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
A simulation-based methodology paper. No field, laboratory or test-bed data were used; every performance figure is a model prediction from a synthetic, physically motivated but unvalidated model. Submitted to Environmental Monitoring and Assessment. An architecture for pre-excavation landfill characterisation — a magnetometer, electromagnetic induction, ground-penetrating radar (GPR), thermal imaging and a gas array, fused by spatial machine learning into material and gas-hazard probabilities and coupled to an explicit value-of-information (VOI) economic layer — is evaluated against the specific, falsifiable questions it raises rather than the claims originally made for it. Under a spatially blocked, non-leaky validation protocol, an XGBoost classifier reaches pooled F1 of 0.99 (metal), 0.98 (organic) and 0.87 (construction and demolition debris), against 0.32 (plastic) and 0.24 (glass); random per-cell splitting did not detectably inflate performance relative to spatial blocking (95% CI including zero for all three classifiers tested), a tested null result rather than an assumption. The paper's central finding is that predictive utility is not decision utility, and that the economically optimal sensor is not a fixed property of the architecture: ground- penetrating radar contributes most to classification accuracy, but only the magnetometer shows a reliably positive incremental value of information at baseline economics — and that ranking itself changes under deliberately different, still economically nameable site compositions (polymer-rich, C&D-rich, glass-rich), shifting the economically preferred sensor to GPR or EMI. A two-dimensional decision-viability map over sensing-degradation and economic-adversity severity shows the resulting VOI-zero boundary is considerably more sensitive to adverse secondary-material markets than to sensor degradation itself. Pooling 40 independent survey realisations, the simulated survey has positive median VOI ($924) and a median break-even survey cost of $1,451. A field validation and falsification plan with pre-specified acceptance criteria, and a Status of Claims and Assumptions table classifying every result by evidentiary status, are given.

#16 [paper] Modeling dispersal and beaching of urban plastic waste along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire.
Authors: Amemou, Hilaire, Cecchi, Philippe, Koné, Vamara, Penven, Pierrick, Lett, Christophe
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42735662/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The processes governing the fate, dispersal, and coastal retention of urban plastic debris along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, which is vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO) to simulate the dispersal and beaching of plastic particles.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically focusing on the region around Abidjan and the broader Ivorian coast.
Abstract:
Plastic pollution is a growing concern in West Africa's marine environment, yet the processes governing its fate remain poorly understood. The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). We provide the first regional-scale assessment of seasonal beaching dynamics along the Ivorian coast using a high-resolution coupled hydrodynamic-Lagrangian framework. Simulations show that while a large fraction of particles is transported offshore (~52%), a substantial proportion (~48%) remains nearshore and beaches at least once. Persistent accumulation hotspots are identified around Abidjan, regardless of the release location. Seasonal variability strongly controls debris pathways. During the minor upwelling season (January-April), beaching occurs predominantly west of Abidjan, associated with weaker currents and enhanced coastal retention. In contrast, during the major upwelling season (June-September), intensified currents and mesoscale activity promote wider dispersal and shift beaching eastward. From October to December, beaching intensifies along the eastern coastline. These results highlight the dominant role of regional hydrodynamics in shaping marine debris distribution and demonstrate the value of high-resolution Lagrangian modeling for identifying pollution hotspots and supporting mitigation strategies in data-scarce coastal regions.

#17 [paper] Landfill: time capsule of plastic waste but microplastic generation source
Authors: Qiujie Huang, Hui Wang, Changfu Yang, Jicui Cui, Muhammad Amjad Farooq, Zhaowen Cheng, Xiaoming Wang, Zhiyong Han
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76905-6
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Landfills act as critical terrestrial sources of microplastics, functioning as “leaky time capsules” continuously releasing pollutants into surrounding ecosystems. Here, we establish a prediction model to dynamically quantify microplastic generation in landfills. By calibrating 31 years of in-situ tracking at a large-scale landfill together with a nationwide field investigation across 37 landfills, we systematically identify the spatial patterns of microplastic generation in China. East China acts as a primary hotspot contributing 45.6% of the total microplastic stock. Landfills in coastal areas account for nearly one-third of the national microplastic stock despite representing only 8.3% of the total sites. Although aggressive source reduction and in-situ remediation reduce the national microplastic by 46.4% by 2050, high-risk landfills in coastal areas remain insensitive to these measures. These findings highlight the necessity of differentiated regional control measures to effectively mitigate landfill-sourced microplastic pollution. This study dynamically models microplastic generation in China’s landfills, identifying East China and coastal sites as hotspots. Aggressive mitigation could reduce national stocks by 46.4% by 2050, though high-risk coastal sites remain insensitive.

#18 [paper] Hyperspectral Classification Strategies for Robotic Sorting of Non-Contaminated Hospital Plastic Waste: A System Design and Methodology Framework
Authors: Holger Neumann, Marc Krech, Daniel Fiß, Jens Friedrich, Christian Vogel
Venue: Recycling
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/recycling11100185
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Non-contaminated plastic waste from healthcare facilities is largely non-infectious and rich in recoverable polymers, yet it is routinely incinerated because no automated sorting process suited to the clinical setting has been established. This paper presents the design of a sensor fusion system and a hyperspectral classification methodology for this stream; experimental results are not yet available and will be reported in a follow-up study. Near-infrared hyperspectral imaging, an RGB line-scan camera, and an inductive metal sensor are integrated on a collaborative robot platform and combined in a late-fusion pipeline for polymer identification, object detection, and metal discrimination. Two hyperspectral classification strategies are specified: reference-spectrum distance matching, which requires no labeled training data, and supervised machine learning, which depends on a labeled dataset. A conceptual comparison based on their methodological properties and on published evidence leads to their use as successive development phases, with the first strategy helping to build the training set for the second. An analytical assessment based on sensor datasheet values indicates the sensor specification required for production line speeds, which the pipeline accommodates without changes to the classification methodology. The regulatory scope of the recoverable fraction under German waste legislation is treated as a design input that determines the target material classes and the open-set rejection behavior required of the classifiers. Open design parameters and a staged validation pathway are identified.

#19 [paper] Detecting Nighttime Anomalies from NASA Black Marble Using a Generalized Spatio-Temporally Robust Framework of Machine Leaning Ensembles
Authors: S. Chakraborty
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/49f8ffab26efb5f3fecd6a4a0287d64f4341bfff
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Nighttime lights from NASA's Black Marble product suite capture thermal and light emission signals from anomalous events including fires, volcanic eruptions, and gas flaring. Existing detection approaches rely primarily on thermal bands, limiting sensitivity to weaker signals. We propose a novel machine learning framework that jointly models Black Marble M-band and Day/Night Band (DNB) signals to derive a generalized, spatio-temporally robust ensemble of anomaly detectors. The framework iteratively builds detectors that scale across regions, seasons, anomaly classes, and extends over land and ocean. Detection sets at varying confidence levels are derived based on relevant bands and detector agreement. The approach improves true detection rate while reducing spurious detections and results demonstrate strong generalizability with applications in natural hazard monitoring and energy extraction.

#20 [paper] Post-event information in calendar-year satellite products inflates landslide susceptibility assessments
Authors: Yifan Du, Tianhe Zheng, Peiyan Yang, Yibo Li, J. Zhou, Kun Yang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5rb93
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Annual satellite products, such as the AlphaEarth Foundations and TESSERA embeddings, summarize a calendar year, so the product of a landslide's event year also contains post-event observations. We audited this post-event information in 18 dated events (7 earthquakes, 11 rainstorms; 61,402 landslides), changing only the input year within each event and keeping the points, spatial folds, models and bootstrap clusters fixed. Replacing the prior-year AlphaEarth product with the event-year product raised the out-of-fold AUC by 0.087 (95% CI 0.065–0.110; all 18 events) for a point model and by 0.071 (0.048–0.093) for a patch CNN. The point-model gain was 0.085 after subtracting each event's drift between two pre-event years. On complete maps, the event-year input added on average 0.21–0.22 of the landslide area to the map's top 10% (9 of 9 events; up to 0.46). A training-year × prediction-year decomposition traced the inflation to models that learn the event's surface changes, chiefly its landslide scars; event-year inputs used only at prediction did not inflate within-event scores on average. The inflation grew with the post-event fraction of the year, reaching half its full size when 23–39% of the year followed the event; this relation survived corrections for recovery. TESSERA and plain Sentinel-2 composites behaved alike. In forward tests in three regions, models trained on earlier landslides scored 0.02–0.11 higher AUC on the new event with event-year inputs, whereas legitimate pre-event embeddings helped mainly near earlier landslides. Studies should use only products whose year ends before the event.

Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-BIODIV-01

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsurface hazard detection systems suffer from a 'collect everything' bottleneck, where static, pre-programmed sensor scripts flood tactical networks with raw data, ignore environmental degradation of sensor modalities, and lack the real-time adaptability to optimize sensor tasking and rou…
Method (Mycelium's reading): An adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine utilizing probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods (such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) to dynamically queue, activate, or inhibit sensor payload…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned aerial and ground platforms conducting standoff reconnaissance for subsurface WMD devices, chemical/biological munitions, and radiological dispersal device components in diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
Abstract:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.

A proactive system is required to answer:

"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"

This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.

Project results are expected to contribute to some of the following outcomes:

#10 [grant] Multi-Modal Luminescent Paint Systems for Underwater Surface Diagnostics
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13134
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current luminescent paint systems for underwater surface diagnostics fail to provide accurate, simultaneous, and uncoupled measurements of pressure, temperature, and skin friction due to oxygen diffusion inhibition, breakdown of Taylor's frozen-flow hypothesis, low luminous efficiency of MLPs, and …
Method (Mycelium's reading): Proposed use of innovative material architectures, such as multi-color mechano-luminescent particles or multi-core/shell dye structures, integrated with an optical processing suite to decouple cross-sensitivities.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Hydrodynamic testing in water, specifically focusing on boundary layer interactions along hydrodynamic surfaces.
Abstract:
Quantifying coupled boundary layer interactions along hydrodynamic surfaces require non-intrusive, full-field imaging of surface pressure, temperature, and skin friction (shear stress). While optical diagnostics have revolutionized aerodynamic testing, adapting luminescent paints to hydrodynamic testing in water introduces fundamental physical and application constraints that current state-of-the-art systems cannot overcome:

• Pressure-Sensitive Paint (PSP): Conventional PSP relies on oxygen-quenching physics. When submerged, oxygen diffusion into the polymer binder is severely inhibited by the liquid boundary layer and low oxygen solubility, rendering standard PSPs insensitive or plagued by extremely slow response times. Furthermore, severe temperature cross-sensitivity corrupts the pressure signal.

• Temperature-Sensitive Paint (TSP): Accurate dynamic temperature measurements are crippled by the standard utilization of Taylor’s frozen-flow hypothesis, which inaccurately assumes turbulent structures remain unchanged as they advect. In water, non-equilibrium flow, high thermal mass and rapid localized diffusion cause this hypothesis to break down, failing to capture true high-frequency temperature fluctuations.

• Mechano-Luminescent Paint (MLP): MLPs offer a direct optical pathway to map shear stress via mechanical deformation. However, current MLP formulations are in their technological infancy, suffering from poor dynamic range, low luminous efficiency, and signal degradation from material fatigue and hydrostatic pressure cross-talk.

In addition to the above challenges, current formulations are difficult to apply uniformly over large areas. Existing techniques fail to maintain a consistent, repeatable coating thickness on complex, curved, or non-flat surfaces. This inconsistency skews calibration and compromises measurement reliability across large-field hydrodynamic models. Innovative material architectures, such as utilizing distinct, multi-color mechano-luminescent particles or multi-core/shell dye structures, may enable simultaneous, uncoupled optical separation of pressure, shear, and temperature in all flow environments, i.e. gas, liquid, and multiphase flows.

This STTR topic seeks an integrated material, application, and optical processing suite. The system must decouple cross-sensitivities and deliver simultaneous, high dynamic range, full-field quantitative maps of the wall pressure, shear, and temperature fluctuations.

#1 [paper] An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
Authors: Borja Nogué-Algueró, Richard York, Stefano B. Longo, Ekaterina Chertkovskaya, Patrick Trent Greiner
Venue: Ecological Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2026.109264
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This survey synthesizes insights from environmental social sciences to recast the plastics crisis as a structural feature of growth-dependent economies instead of a problem solvable by consumer choice or incremental technologies. Rather than a within-field review of ecological economics, it maps adjacent literatures to specify what this field could study and how, clarifying researchable questions, suitable methods, and tractable indicators. The synthesis foregrounds connections between expansionary political-economic dynamics, globally uneven socio-ecological burdens across the plastics life cycle, and the power and knowledge relations that shape what is produced, measured, and governed. It calls for comparative, mixed-methods, multi-scalar work and for open, standardized data on plastics flows to strengthen causal inference and comparability. Shifting attention upstream—from end-of-pipe fixes to the transformation of provisioning systems—the paper charts lines of inquiry capable of aligning social metabolism with biophysical limits and human needs, providing a roadmap for ecological economics to organize and accelerate research beyond consumer or techno-managerial framings.

#2 [paper] Who is governing the global plastics crisis? Mapping the global plastics governance landscape
Authors: Babet de Groot
Venue: International Environmental Agreements Politics Law and Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10784-026-09734-z
Still open/current: yes

Abstract Plastic pollution has emerged as a critical global environmental challenge, exacerbating the impacts of climate change and biodiversity loss while posing substantial risks to human health and the economy. Despite a rapid increase in scientific efforts in recent years, our understanding of the characteristics, distribution and environmental consequences of plastic pollution remains incomplete, with many aspects still under debate. This knowledge gap hinders the development and implementation of effective management strategies. In this Review, we provide a comprehensive synthesis of plastic pollution from understanding to combatting, linking the environmental behavior of plastics with their ecological, health, and Earth-system risks. We further discuss mitigation and management strategies across the plastics life cycle. These strategies emphasize upstream prevention through redesign for minimizing production and facilitating reuse, supplemented by measures such as recycling and the implementation of biodegradable and compostable plastics, as well as exposure risk management. We also identify key challenges to address the interlinked triple crises of climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution associated with plastics. The priorities and solutions to end plastic pollution include promoting sustainable production and consumption, minimizing plastic waste and leakage, mitigating plastic pollution and damage, and safeguarding planetary health.

The goal of the Micro/Nanoplastics (M/NPs) Research and Resource Coordination Center initiative is to establish a robust center that will coordinate and advance multidisciplinary efforts among biomedical and material science researchers to gain a comprehensive understanding of the health effects of M/NPs. NIEHS will provide support (U24) to an eligible institution to launch a new coordination center to address the above-mentioned goals.

#1 [grant] Developing novel recycling technologies for complex plastic materials applying biotech solutions
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-CIRCBIO-03
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The difficulty of recycling complex plastic materials (multi-material, multi-layer, and composites) in sectors such as packaging, construction, renewable energy infrastructure, and transport.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development and pilot-scale demonstration of biotech solutions, specifically the application of microbes and enzymes for enhanced plastic degradation, integrated with the Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design framework and lifecycle assessments.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Industrial value chains within the European Union, targeting a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 4-5.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- environment and society at large benefit from recyclable plastic products which can be recycled back into high value applications;

- industrial value chains introduce circular plastic products on the market through enhanced design for recycling and solutions for effective sorting and recycling on a large scale;

- industrial value chains are equipped with improved characterisation of waste from complex plastic materials to enable its recycling.

Scope:

The topic supports the European Green Deal, the Regulation on Packaging and Packaging Waste, the Waste Shipment Regulation, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, the upcoming Circular Economy Act and contributes to Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products. It also contributes to the new EU bioeconomy strategy, the Life Sciences Strategy and the EU Biotech Act and is relevant to the European Commission’s communication: ‘Building the future with nature: Boosting Biotechnology and Biomanufacturing in the EU’.

Proposals should:

- advance novel biotech solutions for recycling of complex plastic materials and products (multi-material/multi-layer/composites), namely in the sectors of packaging, construction, renewable energy infrastructure and transport;

- propose recommendations towards fit-for-purpose regulatory risk assessments for novel materials and recycling technologies (i.e. hazard identification, methodological updates) and take into account the Safe-and-Sustainable-by-Design framework;

- consider the latest solutions in material innovation while developing novel recycling solutions e.g. by application of microbes and enzymes for enhanced degradation of plastics;

- demonstrate the solutions on a pilot scale involving the whole value chain.

Successful proposals are expected to evaluate the feasibility, effectiveness and impact of the demonstrated solutions using robust evaluation methods (including lifecycle assessments such as product environmental footprint, where relevant) and present data and evidence about the economic, environmental and social costs and benefits of the developed solutions.

Industrial value chains are expected to take part in the proposed consortia to enable a demonstration of the proposed solution and involve all relevant stakeholders.

Clustering with other relevant Horizon Europe projects is encouraged.

Technology Readiness Level - Technology readiness level expected from completed projects

Activities are expected to achieve TRL 4-5 by the end of the project – see General Annex B. Activities may start at any TRL.

#2 [grant] Innovative circular solutions for end-of-life footwear through collection, sorting and recycling
Amount: €3,000,000–€8,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL6-2027-01-CIRCBIO-05
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- all relevant stakeholders, including consumers, economic and social economy operators and waste managers, have an improved understanding of the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits to circularity in the footwear industry;

- economic operators and waste managers are provided with evidence-based, innovative, cost-effective, and scalable solutions that improve the management of end-of-life footwear products, valorise post-consumer footwear waste materials and increase the circularity of the value chain;

- consumers have access to user-friendly solutions to correctly dispose of end-of-life footwear, thus reducing landfill, improving sustainability practices, supporting them in making more conscious choices, and contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation by reducing waste and promoting circular economy practices.

Scope:

The transition to a circular economy requires innovative solutions to manage end-of-life products, including footwear, which can have significant environmental and climate impacts if landfilled and not properly collected, sorted, and recycled. In line with the EU's ambitious circular economy targets and policies, such as the Waste Framework Directive and the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, this topic aims at improving the circularity of the footwear value chain and reducing the environmental footprint of end-of-life post-consumer footwear, whilst promoting a more regenerative and restorative approach to the footwear value chain.

Proposals should:

- assess the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits linked to the transition of the footwear industry towards circularity, particularly in the collection, sorting and recycling of post-consumer footwear waste;

- develop and test new methods and technologies that facilitate the collection, sorting, preparation for reuse and recycling of post-consumer footwear products, integrating digital tools (including AI) and the use of the Digital Product Passport to enable reuse and recycling, and minimise the release of hazardous chemicals and microplastics during the recycling process;

- explore and develop innovative business models that enable the transition towards a circular and sustainable footwear value chain, promote the uptake of design for preparing for reuse and recycling, enable the development of take-back solutions and stimulate informed consumer choices and sustainable consumption patterns;

- develop and test innovative solutions that facilitate the collaboration between the relevant stakeholders, including footwear manufacturers, retailers, consumers and waste managers, to ensure the effectiveness and uptake of the proposed solutions, including strategies for managing hazardous chemicals and microplastics in footwear waste.

Successful proposals should bring together all relevant stakeholders active in the footwear value chain, namely industry representatives, SMEs, brand owners, producers, retailers, local authorities, waste managers, economic operators, consumer organisations, researchers, and NGOs.

The topic supports EU policies, particularly the European Green Deal, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, as well as the zero pollution action plan. The proposed solutions should also be consistent with the Waste Framework Directive, the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for textiles, the Clean Industrial Deal and the EU Circular Economy Act, supporting Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products.

This topic requires the effective contribution of SSH disciplines and the involvement of SSH experts, institutions as well as the inclusion of relevant SSH expertise, in order to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related research activities.

Amount: €200,000–€12,500,000

Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-02-02
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

- Increased economically viable and functionally equivalent renewable material and sustainable chemical solutions used in large scale textile applications, including apparel, home and technical textiles;

- A realistic pathway for an absolute reduction of the use of virgin fossil-based materials and chemicals used to produce textile products for the EU market by 2035, contributing to enhance the preservation of human health, biodiversity and ecosystems, whether aquatic or terrestrial ecosystem preservation and emission reduction;

- Uptake of business models and system approaches that allow for the scale up of sustainable textile material and chemical alternatives as competitive alternatives to conventional approaches.

Scope:

Innovative renewable textile fibres and sustainable chemical solutions today face almost insurmountable cost disadvantages compared to extremely cost-competitive and industrially entrenched fibres and chemicals based on virgin fossil resources. To allow for the scale up of the use of innovative renewable materials and sustainable chemicals by the textile industry, improved processability of materials, suitable processing technology, deeper technical knowledge and smart phase-in approaches such as material blending or drop-in solutions are required. Specific emphasis must be placed on resulting final product quality, their durability and functionality to avoid negative user/consumer perception of products made with renewable materials and sustainable chemicals. As not all cost and quality challenges may be immediately overcome by technological innovation, accompanying business models and systems approaches are needed to enable equitable cost and risk sharing among all involved stakeholders in the textile value chain.

Attributes such as recyclability, recycled material content, and resource efficiency as well as reduced carbon and environmental footprint are expected to be part of the textile-specific requirements under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation.

Proposals should specifically address:

- Innovative processing technologies to facilitate the efficient use of recycled, regenerated and bio-based fibres as well as sustainable processing and functionalising chemicals across all major stages of the textile manufacturing value chain, such as spinning, weaving, knitting, dyeing or finishing;

- Quantification of biodiversity outcomes associated to new processes by using existing Monitoring, Reporting and Validation (MRV) methodologies, adapting and testing them if needed;

- Characterisation, quality assurance and mitigation strategies for the most common processing and functionality challenges and limitations of the sustainable materials and chemicals targeted;

- Development of best practices and training materials targeted at designers, manufacturers, brands, end of life managers and end users, working with the targeted materials and chemicals;

- Strategies and tools to practically implement collective risk sharing and smart scaling approaches.

Proposals should actively involve suppliers of renewable materials and sustainable chemicals, brands, commercial end users and developers/manufacturers of relevant processing technology and industrial partners with the capacity to commercially scale up production with the targeted materials and chemicals. The involvement of partners beyond the manufacturing supply chain, such as product designers, brands, commercial end users and end of life managers including collectors, sorters, recyclers and remanufacturers is particularly encouraged. Proposals should carry out research and innovation to develop missing elements and achieve the necessary integration, including economic viability. Hence, synergies with, or using results from, other projects may be appropriate. The mere integration of existing technologies or processes is outside the scope of this topic.

Amount: €200,000–€12,500,000

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Slow adoption of innovative advanced materials designed for circularity in products and the need for resilient supply networks and resource efficiency in strategic value chains.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A full-innovation-cycle approach encompassing design for circularity, development, scale-up (including recovery and valorisation), and demonstration via industrial use cases, guided by the Safe and Sustainable by Design (SSbD) framework and supported by digital tools, AI, and FAIR data practices.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European strategic value chains, specifically in the fields of energy and construction, focusing on recyclable polymers, composites, magnets, and metal alloys for additive manufacturing.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

- Innovative advanced materials designed for circularity are adopted in products faster, through accelerated production and technology uptake;

- Business models become available to enhance the use of circular advanced materials in strategic value chains; and

- Resource efficiency (materials and energy) is increased significantly through a focus on circular advanced materials.

- Quality standards, harmonisation and regulatory requirements are addressed facilitating simplified market transition.

Scope:

The focus of this topic is on enabling circularity and resilient supply networks through R&I in advanced materials, in particular recyclable polymers and composites, magnets and metal (alloys) for additive manufacturing, and on accelerating their pathway to market. Proposals should develop new innovative advanced materials (IAMs) with superior or novel functionalities designed for circularity. The scope includes necessary developments of related processes and technologies to ensure integration in industrial manufacturing facilitating uptake of the developed solutions. Proposals should also develop circular business models considering the cost of changes needed along the life cycle of these new materials to facilitate their uptake.

The scope covers the full innovation cycle from the design for circularity and functional integration (new materials designs), development and scaleup (including scalable recovery, recycling and valorisation at end of life), to demonstration of industrial uptake and integration into products. The transformative potential of the developed solutions is to be showcased by demonstrators and industrial use cases. Projects should also explore possibilities to transfer developed solutions to other applications or sectors.

The SSbD framework[1] should guide the innovation process towards safer and more sustainable chemicals and advanced materials. Where relevant data generated within the proposal may be shared with the Common Data Platform for Chemicals. The new alternatives to be developed should meet the technical functions required in the specific applications while aligning their innovation process decision making with such framework.

Best use of digital tools and FAIR data, including AI and data-driven approaches throughout the innovation process should support the circular transition for industry and circular product design. This includes sharing FAIR and interoperable data and tools across supply networks and value chains, to foster circularity, including data needed for materials and component development, production and circular product design.

The approach should foster collaboration among stakeholders along the innovation chain and industrial value networks to accelerate the development and adoption of new circular solutions.

Projects should build on, or seek collaboration with, existing projects in EU Member States and Associated Countries and develop synergies with other relevant European, national or regional initiatives, funding programmes and platforms, in particular with the Materials Commons for Europe.

Proposals should support strategic value chains in the fields of energy and construction. The portfolio approach will be used to fund at least one proposal from each of these two. Proposers should declare in their proposal the main application area of their proposal (i.e., energy or construction).

Proposals should include a business case and exploitation strategy, as outlined in the introduction to this Destination.

This topic implements the co-programmed European Partnerships Innovative Advanced Materials for the EU (IAM4EU) and Made in Europe (MiE).

Technology Readiness Level - Technology readiness level expected from completed projects

Authors: Zhang, Xiang, Cui, Yingzhe, Li, Furong, Zhou, Shenghui, Wu, Guangnan, Jing, Zhao, Wu, Lixin

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

#2 [paper] Is guideline-cited evidence keeping pace with the biomedical literature? A cohort analysis, 2008–2025
Authors: Jordan Lewis Fulcher
Venue: Open Science Framework
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/vn9bq

Abstract:
Biomedical publication volume has grown roughly exponentially, but whether the research that reaches clinical guidelines has grown at the same rate is unknown. This meta-research study follows each annual cohort of research articles in PubMed (2008–2024) to measure how many are later cited by clinical practice guidelines. Guidelines come from two co-primary frames: PubMed's Practice Guideline publication type, and a pre-specified list of 31 named guideline bodies. Reference lists come from the NIH iCite API. Co-primary outcomes: the absolute number of guideline-cited papers per cohort (P1), and the cohort trend in the hazard of first guideline citation (P2, from Kaplan–Meier life tables and a discrete-time hazard model). Secondary analyses: breakpoints, a decomposition into guideline capacity, and a comparison of six high-volume public-data study designs with all other research.

#6 [paper] Citation accuracy, citation noise, and citation bias: a foundation of citation analysis
Authors: Lutz Bornmann, Christian Leibel
Venue: Scientometrics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-026-05841-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Citation analysis is widely used in research evaluation to assess the impact of scientific papers. These analyses rest on the assumption that citation decisions by authors are accurate, representing the flow of knowledge from cited to citing papers. However, in practice, researchers often cite for reasons that are not related to the fact that there has been (intellectual) input from previous papers. Citations made for rhetorical reasons or without reading the cited work compromise the value of citations as instrument for research evaluation. Past research on threats to the accuracy of citations has mainly focused on citation bias as the primary concern. In this paper, we argue that citation noise—the undesirable variance in citation decisions—represents an equally critical but underexplored challenge in citation analysis. We define and differentiate two types of citation noise: citation level noise and citation pattern noise. Each type of noise is described in terms of how it arises and the specific ways it can undermine the validity of citation-based research assessments. By conceptually differing citation noise from citation accuracy and citation bias, we propose a framework for the foundation of citation analysis. We discuss strategies and interventions to minimize citation noise, aiming to improve the reliability and validity of citation analysis in research evaluation. We recommend that the current professional reform movement in research evaluation such as the Coalition for Advancing Research Assessment (CoARA) pick up these strategies and interventions as an additional building block for careful, responsible use of bibliometric indicators in research evaluation.

#7 [paper] Compressed Once, Read Many Times: Why Prompt-Compression Results Do Not Transfer to Agent Memory, What the Query-Agnostic Line Already Showed, and the Two Properties of a Memory Write No Protocol Yet
Authors: Pranay M. Mahendrakar
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22969434
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
(c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Language-model agents that remember across sessions compress what they store: they summarise dialogue, extract facts, or evict cache entries, and then answer later questions from what is left. The compression ratios used to justify these designs come mostly from prompt-compression work in which the question is visible when compression runs. This paper examines whether those results transfer to the memory write, where the compressor must decide what to keep before any question exists. The premise that no one measures this does not survive the literature. The key-value cache line has built query-agnostic compressors and audited query visibility directly: in one matched-budget audit, the method the auditors call the most widely deployed beats a keep-the-start-and-recent-window baseline when it sees the question and loses to it when it does not. The paper argues that what remains open is narrower and harder. Every located "query-agnostic" result is still distribution-aware: the compressor is tuned for, or scored against, questions drawn from the same generator. A memory write has two properties no located protocol scores: its future query distribution is set by events that have not happened, and its compressions compose, because summaries are summarised again and records are overwritten. Published agent-memory evidence is consistent with that reading. Summary units are retrieved with 90.7 percent recall yet answer at 31.5 F1. In a 2024 pilot, two commercial assistants answering from fact stores written during the conversation scored 24.7 to 71.1 percent, where reading the raw history scored 91.8. The paper separates three query-visibility regimes, states what a write-time compression claim would have to report, and names the experiment that would settle the open part. The literature search, drafting and citation verification for this paper were carried out with AI assistance under the author's direction. Every arXiv citation was machine-verified against its live arXiv Atom API record, and every other citation against its DOI record, during drafting (title and author list checked against the record returned). Every quantitative claim is taken from the abstract, full text or a table of the source credited with it; full-text numbers were read from the sources' own HTML renderings rather than from summaries. No experiment was run and no number in this paper was measured by its author. Table 1 re-presents numbers published by the cited papers, each named on its row; Figure 1 plots published values from three cited papers with no transformation beyond rounding. The three-regime classification, Algorithm 1 and the reporting protocol in Section 10 are original conceptual synthesis by the author, not empirical results, and are presented as such. Three psychology references are cited for terminology only; their full texts were not available to the verification step and no finding is attributed to them.

Abstract:
Manuscript, state of 13 November 2026. The file is restricted; this record documents the state of the text at this date. Abstract. Which papers of an established field are good starting points for new work? Papers that build on the most cited papers are received hardly better than average. We test a rule that follows from Newman's hope that papers standing out against their contemporaries do so by their quality: rank papers by the mean cohort z-score of the papers that cite them. In two fields of arXiv, artificial intelligence and mathematics, 12.6% and 8.7% of the papers that newly cite a recent paper become strongly received. For the top 2% by our rule the shares are 20.6% and 16.5%; by Newman's z-score 13.8% and 10.9%; by time-rescaled PageRank 12.6% and 8.8%. Against controls of the same category, citation count and age the ratio is 1.47 and 1.48; it is 1.34 and 1.30 when the citing authors have the same record of earlier reception, and 1.12 in artificial intelligence within the same author. The evidence is observational, and the rule does not predict how often the paper itself is cited. All 70 predictions were sealed and their checksums deposited before each measurement; thirteen failed. The rule specified in advance as primary held but adds nothing detectable to the simpler rule. The checksums of the sealed analysis plans and of the programs are deposited separately: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24138400 (all versions).

#13 [paper] PREreview of "(Why) Is My Prompt Getting Worse? Rethinking Regression Testing for Evolving LLM APIs"

Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

Abstract:
This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23214938. ## Summary This paper makes the case that LLM APIs need their own regression-testing discipline, and backs it with an exploratory case study: toxicity detection across five GPT-3.5 models (text-davinci-002 through gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct, spanning 18 months), two datasets (Civil Comments, GitHub Discussions), and four prompting strategies (simple, instruction-last, detailed, few-shot). The headline results: 58.8% of prompt+model combinations lose accuracy across API updates (70.2% of those by more than 5 points); 55% of updates help some prompts while hurting others, so the "best" prompt changes from version to version; 10.9% of individual predictions regress even when aggregate accuracy improves; and regressions concentrate on data slices — 90% land on toxic discussions, disproportionately politics-triggered, code-targeting, and severe ones. From this the authors derive three rethinks for LLM regression testing: slice-level granularity (a new correctness notion), versioning prompts alongside models, and handling non-determinism. I cite this paper in my own work on behavioral regression testing for AI agents as the academic home of the "why" argument, so I read it as someone building directly on it. ## Strengths The "prompt is also a version" insight is the paper's most original contribution. Prior work on evolving ML APIs treated the model as the moving part. This paper shows the moving part is the pair: the same silent update that drops one prompt by 9.6% lifts another by 5.1%, and the detailed prompt that was best on every model until the last one suddenly trails few-shot by 8.7%. That non-uniformity result is genuinely new, well-evidenced, and it reframes prompt engineering from a one-time activity into a versioned artifact. Anyone running agents in production — where the "prompt" is a whole system of templates, tool definitions, and routing policy — should read this as a warning about a larger blast radius. The slice-level regression finding has real consequences: regressions landing disproportionately on politics-triggered and severe toxicity is a fairness and safety observation, not just a testing one. Aggregate accuracy improving while a slice degrades is exactly the failure mode that ships incidents. The limitations section is honest, and the paper resists overselling an exploratory study as a solution. ## Major comments 1. The headline numbers are single-trial at temperature 0, but the paper itself establishes that temperature-0 outputs are non-deterministic (citing Ouyang et al.). If predictions can flip between identical runs, then the 58.8% combination-level regression rate and the 10.9% per-prediction flip rate inherit run-to-run variance that is never quantified. The paper's own discussion warns that flakiness must be designed into LLM regression testing — but the case study's measurements don't report any repeat-run stability. Re-running even a stratified subset 3-5x would bound whether the headline figures are signal or partly sampling noise. 2. The confidence analysis rests on a rough proxy. Entropy is estimated from n=20 samples at t=0.7 because APIs don't expose probabilities — a reasonable workaround, but 20 samples is a noisy estimate of a distribution, and the striking "63.8% of regressions happen at entropy=0" claim depends on it. The paper finds models differ in self-consistency yet doesn't connect this back: a model whose calibration shifts under update arguably needs calibration regression as its own test dimension. 3. Slice discovery is the load-bearing recommendation with the thinnest scaffolding. The slice finding depends on author-provided metadata the paper admits "may not be available for many datasets." #14 [paper] Assessing the Reliability of Longitudinal Bibliometric Rankings under Incomplete Citation Histories
Authors: João Paulo Papa
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/7d7287a7ccc671aeefd130c67e5bad5887620413
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Longitudinal bibliometric analyses rely on annual citation histories, yet missing annual observations are frequently difficult to distinguish from true zero-citation years. We present a reproducible case-study framework for auditing citation-history gaps, tracing retrieval provenance, and quantifying the sensitivity of longitudinal indicators and rankings to explicit missing-data assumptions. The case study comprises 595 consolidated publications derived from 616 Google Scholar article records, and examines the completed calendar years 2024-2025. Three scenarios are compared: strictly observed annual counts (A), hypothetical zeros for internal gaps only (B), and hypothetical zeros for all missing years within a valid publication interval (C). The number of publications with computable growth and acceleration indicators increases from 196 (A) to 257 (B) and 490 (C); the corresponding counts for a revival indicator are 131, 152, and 177. Although the ordering of publications eligible under both compared scenarios is unchanged (Spearman and Kendall correlations equal to 1.0), complete-ranking positions and Top-K membership may change markedly. In particular, acceleration exhibits a Jaccard overlap of 0.563 at K=50 between A and C, while revival exhibits 0.667 at K=10. These findings demonstrate that unchanged indicator values and perfect correlations on a common subset do not guarantee stable rankings when eligibility changes. The zero assignments are hypothetical sensitivity assumptions, not evidence of provider semantics. The results are descriptive and based on a single researcher profile. A reusable Google Scholar Tracker software workflow supports the audit and sensitivity analysis; version 1.8.5 is publicly available on GitHub and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24170285).

#15 [paper] Axel Dieter Becke: Not just the “B” in “B3LYP”
Authors: Mark E. Casida
Venue: Electronic Structure
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1088/2516-1075/aeb1a4
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract There is hardly anyone doing electronic structure calculations on molecules who has not used the famous B3LYP functional. Many will even know that the “B” in B3LYP stands for Becke, but how many know the history of the B3LYP functional? Behind this functional, Axel Becke has two of the most highly cited papers in both chemistry and physics—both with several tens of thousands of citations—and many less cited, but arguably equally important accomplishments, that led to B3LYP, as well as continued developments in building ever better density-functional approximatons after the appearance of B3LYP. Axel has received much recognition and many honors for his work. In particular, in 2015, Axel was awarded Canada’s highest honor for science and engineering—namely the Gerhard Herzberg Gold Medal. Achievements like this require more than “just” brilliance; they require being the right person in the right place at the right time. I will argue that Axel did indeed fulfill these requirements. At the same time, I will try to give some flavor of the field of electronic structure as seen through my own eyes and those of a few others during the period from the beginning of Axel’s career up until very recent times.
