Abstract:
This study presents a comprehensive, multidimensional bibliometric assessment of the journal Scientometrics (Springer/Akadémiai Kiadó), which was founded in 1978 and is evaluated here using a Scopus-derived dataset of 7,779 records covering the publication years 1979-2025-the full span of Scopus-indexed content available as of 8 May 2026.The investigation systematically analyses research output dynamics, authorship patterns, citation behaviour, institutional and country-level contributions, major funding sponsors, document typology, and evolving research themes.The total publication output grew from 16 papers in 1979 to a peak of 450 in 2021, accumulating 295,024 citations and yielding an overall dataset h-index of 179.The Degree of Collaboration increased markedly from 33.33% in the 1979-1988 period to 86.83% in 2019-2025, evidencing the globalisation of quantitative science studies.Four and A Half Decades of Quantitative Science Studies: A Multidimensional Bibliometric Assessment of the Journal Scientometrics (1978-2025) https://iaeme.com/Home/journal/IJSIM 2 editor@iaeme.comChina (16.71%) and the United States (13.82%) collectively lead national contributions.The most cited paper in the corpus-the VOSviewer software survey by van Eck and Waltman (2010) with 16,764 citations-underscores the central role of bibliometric instrumentation in shaping the field's citation landscape.Keyword analysis reveals sustained dominance of bibliometrics, citation analysis, and the hindex, with emerging themes including altmetrics, open access, and research integrity.The findings collectively affirm the journal's status as the pre-eminent international venue for quantitative science studies and provide a longitudinal empirical baseline for future editorial and policy assessments.

#17 [paper] PREreview of "AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents"
Authors: Karmendra Pandey
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026

Abstract:
This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23129310. ## Summary This paper tackles a genuinely important problem in production agent systems: context management as a *learned policy* rather than a length-triggered fallback. The authors augment a coding agent (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, terminal REPL scaffold) with a `compact()` action and train it in two stages: (1) SFT on 1,052 judge-corrected trajectories collected from 379 SWE-rebench tasks, where GPT-5.5-Codex acts as an online judge correcting compaction timing, working-state summaries, and post-compaction actions, with corrections executed in the environment before being used as training data; (2) GRPO-based RL on SWE-Gym with binary task-success rewards, no KL penalty, no entropy bonus, and no compaction-specific reward shaping. The headline result is +9.2% / +5.0% absolute pass-rate gains over the base model on SWE-bench Verified (39.6%) and SWE-PolyBench Verified (24.5%), with gains holding across per-task inference budgets from $0.10 to $4.00. The paper's most distinctive claim is that supervising *what the agent does after compaction* — not just when to compact or what to write in the summary — is the missing piece in prior work, and the online-correction data collection method is the mechanism that delivers it. ## Strengths 1. **The problem framing is correct and under-studied.** The introduction's distinction — compaction tied to *task progress* rather than *context length* — matches production experience: stale exploration (dead hypotheses, verbose tool outputs) degrades agent behavior long before any window limit is hit. The Figure 3(a) result, where proactive compaction helps even in the 256K regime where nothing overflows, is the paper's most practically significant finding. 2. **The data-collection design is the real contribution.** Correcting outputs *before* execution so the trajectory continues from corrected decisions (Section 2.2) is meaningfully different from post-hoc annotation or offline insertion (SWE-Compressor). The AutoCompact-SFT vs. SWE-Compressor comparison (+1.2% / +1.6% with comparable data) is a fair, well-scoped ablation supporting this. 3. **"Summary self-consistency" is a useful new lens.** The Section 3.4 case study (django-13809) — a summary can satisfy coverage checks while proposing a next action incompatible with its own recorded state — names a failure mode I have seen in production agent summaries but rarely seen formalized. That SFT imitates summaries while RL constrains them through downstream success is a clean, honest explanation of the mechanism. 4. **Budget-framed evaluation is the right framing.** Reporting pass rate against dollars-per-task, with explicit token pricing (Alibaba Cloud Model Studio, cached tokens at 20%), treats inference economics as a first-class metric. Too few agent papers do this. ## Major concerns **1. The judge is load-bearing but unvalidated.** GPT-5.5-Codex reviews every proposed action during data collection and rewrites flawed outputs — yet the paper reports no judge agreement rates, no human audit of corrections, and not even the *correction rate* (what fraction of proposed actions were rewritten?). The 24%/53%/23% split across correction types describes the collected data, not the judge's reliability. This matters because the SFT stage imitates judge-written outputs: to the extent the judge's compaction preferences are idiosyncratic, AutoCompact-SFT distills GPT-5.5-Codex's priors as much as it learns compaction. A modest human audit (e.g., 100 sampled corrections rated by the authors) would substantially strengthen the paper. **2. #18 [paper] Bibliometric performance and uncertainty in heterogeneous research groups: trends in authorship and fractional citation indicators
Authors: Paolo Castellini, Alessia Caputo, alberto scocco
Venue: Scientometrics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11192-026-05830-8
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Bibliometric indicators are widely used to evaluate scientific performance, despite well-known limitations related to disciplinary differences, collaboration practices, and strategic responses to evaluation systems. Traditional metrics such as the H-index are particularly sensitive to the number of co-authors and to the length of reference lists, both of which have exhibited strong historical growth. This study analyzes the temporal evolution of authorship, referencing, and productivity patterns in six research populations (four Italian Scientific Disciplinary Sectors in engineering and two international conference communities), covering 1,286 researchers and 86,351 publications. The results reveal systematic increases in authors per article, references per article, and documents per author, with structural changes that coincide with technological developments and the introduction of bibliometric criteria in national evaluation policies. Building on fractional counting, we propose a new citation-based indicator in which publication credit is shared among co-authors and each incoming citation is weighted by the inverse of the number of references in the citing article. Comparisons with the H-index show strong overall correlations, but indicate that the proposed indicator attenuates the advantage associated with hyper-authorship and inflated reference lists and reduces variability across heterogeneous research groups. Adopting a measurement-theoretic perspective, we further assess the uncertainty of bibliometric indicators by analyzing linear trends with researcher seniority and the dispersion of individual data around these trends. The proposed indicator exhibits a slightly more homogeneous trend across heterogeneous research groups and shows strong overall correlation with the H-index, suggesting that it may provide a more comparable representation of scientific performance across diverse research communities.

#19 [paper] From Fabricated Citations to Unverified Journal Matches: Problems and Solutions in LLM Assisted Manuscript Generation
Authors: Indri Anjar Kartika Sari, Onno Widodo Purbo, Abi Julian Saputra Pratama, Rahardian Dwi Saputra
Venue: INNOVASI JURNAL INOVASI PENDIDIKAN
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64540/jyrkxj90
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The growing use of large language models (LLMs) in scholarly writing introduces risks of fabricated references, unsupported claims, and unreliable journal recommendations. Evidence gating addresses these risks by allowing outputs only when verifiable conditions are met and requiring explicit abstention otherwise. This study evaluates evidence gating through a design science research approach, examining scopus-jurnal, an open-source Python multi-agent pipeline that retrieves literature, drafts IMRaD sections, validates citations, reviews manuscripts, and recommends journals. Five evaluation episodes combined traceability audits and white-box experiments covering 46 in-text citations, 122 verification cases, 14 reviewer output formats, and 40 journal-matching probes. Results show that although the pipeline abstained when evidence was absent, weaknesses emerged between LLM outputs and deterministic code. Two of 17 specified phases lacked implementation, restricting the pipeline to drafting framing sections. Citation detection resolved only 31.6% of valid APA citations, while fabricated citations were sometimes accepted. Title matching accepted all 14 fabricated near-miss titles and rejected eight of nine legitimate short titles. Reviewer-score parsing failed on seven of ten plausible formats. A revised verification rule reduced false acceptance from 33.3% to 2.4% and false rejection from 43.1% to 0%. Journal-matching experiments showed that scope evidence without a score threshold enabled safe abstention, whereas introducing a threshold eliminated abstention. These findings emphasize tool-level evaluation and contribute an audit protocol, seven design principles, a reference architecture, eight integrity-preserving solutions, and five future research priorities.

#21 [paper] Bibliometric Analysis of the 20-Year Transformation of Educational Technology Articles: A Case Study of the Journal of Theory and Practice in Education
Authors: ÖZDEN ŞAHİN İZMİRLİ, Asmin Murat, Tülay Akbıyık Koç, Giunai Abdulla Kyzy, Sarvinoz Abdinazarova, Ege İnal
Venue: Eğitimde Kuram ve Uygulama
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17244/eku.1982476
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The purpose of this study is to examine papers in the field of educational technologies published in the Journal of Theory and Practice in Education (EKU) between 2005 and 2025. Using bibliometric analysis, it determines the journal's thematic, methodological, and sample-based publication trends. Seventy papers were identified through a manual systematic review, and citation counts, keyword patterns, study designs, and participant categories were analysed. RAWGraphs and VOSviewer software were then used to visualise the data. The results indicate that the journal underwent a period of rapid growth between 2013 and 2017, a hiatus in publication in 2021, and achieved publication consistency after 2022. Keyword analyses revealed clusters centred on technology, distance education, virtual reality, and multimedia. However, the study reveals a relative scarcity of cross-disciplinary integration. From a methodological perspective, qualitative and quantitative studies were shown to occur with similar frequency, while mixed designs remained relatively limited. Participants were primarily pre-service teachers. This study reveals the 20-year evolution of the EKU Journal in the field of educational technologies and provides evidence-based guidance for editors and researchers.

#5 [paper] Mapping Global Trends in Higher Education Admission Strategies Over the Last Decade: A Bibliometric Analysis
Authors: Noormawanti -, Agus Pahrudin, Eti Hadiati, Muhammad Afif Amrullah
Venue: Journal Human Research in Rehabilitation
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21554/hrr.092604
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study examines global trends and thematic developments in research on higher education student admission strategies from 2016 to 2025, amid increasingly complex selection policies and expanding digital influence. Using a bibliometric analysis of 487 Scopus-indexed documents, metadata were refined with OpenRefine and analyzed using Biblioshiny R and VOSviewer to map publication patterns, collaborations, and keyword networks. Results show a significant rise in publications since 2018, peaking in 2024. Leading sources include Academic Medicine and ASEE Annual Conference Proceedings, with prominent contributors such as Glazer, James-Maceachern, Nesterov, and Sin. Five main thematic clusters emerged: student recruitment policy, professional education, cultural diversity, educational psychology, and academic evaluation. Emerging topics include machine learning applications, sustainability-oriented admissions, and digital justice. These developments highlight the growing need to integrate technological innovation with social equity to promote inclusive and transparent global admission practices.

#6 [paper] Factors Associated With Interview Offer Rates in Otolaryngology Residency Applications.
Authors: Nanu, Douglas P, Maley, Grace E, Khan, Sofia, Ibrahim, Alexa F, Nguyen, Shaun A, Carr, Michele M
Venue: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery
Year: 2026

Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association of preference signaling on interview offer rates in otolaryngology residency applications, comparing applicant type (MD vs DO), geographic status (in-state vs out-of-state), and international status (US vs non-US IMGs) across US programs and regions. STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional analysis. SETTING: All US otolaryngology residency programs with interview data participating in the 2024 to 2025 match cycle. METHODS: Data were obtained from the AAMC Residency Explorer Tool. Programs reporting interview rates for both signaled and nonsignaled applicants were included. Mean rates (±SD) were compared using Welch's t-tests. Effect sizes were calculated with Cohen's d. Regional differences (Midwest, South, Northeast, West) were analyzed using one-way ANOVA. RESULTS: Of 133 programs, 82 (61.7%) reported complete data. Programs invited signaled applicants at markedly higher rates than nonsignaled applicants (41.8% vs 5.0%, P < .001). Programs demonstrated significantly higher interview offer rates for MD and in-state applicants than DO and out-of-state applicants, respectively, across all regions (all P < .01). Differences between US and non-US IMGs were smaller and less consistent. No significant regional differences were observed in the magnitude of these effects. CONCLUSION: Preference signaling and applicant background were strongly associated with interview offer rates in the 2024 to 2025 OHNS cycle, with programs demonstrating significantly higher interview offer rates for MD, in-state, and signaled applicants across all regions. These findings highlight disparities in interview selection observed in the 2024 to 2025 cycle and emphasize the continued influence of both signaling and applicant characteristics on residency competitiveness.

Factors other than greenhouse gas emissions have caused observed warming to date of 1.2°C . No. Global warming is causing a diverse range of climate risks such as greater frequency and intensity of heat waves, shifting precipitation patterns (which puts at risk water systems, agriculture, and ecosystems), droughts, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes—these risks are escalating because warming causes more energy and water vapor in the atmosphere. Higher atmospheric CO 2 concentrations also eat away at the minerals used by marine life to build their shells and skeletons. And there is an escalating risk of crossing (poorly understood) tipping points in the Earth’s climate system such as permafrost melting (which could turn on an unstoppable gas tap of CO 2 and methane), long-term collapse of major ice sheets (which could raise global sea levels several meters), changes in ocean circulation (which could radically change temperature and precipitation patterns around the world), and forest dieback (which could transform the Amazon into dry savanna) (see Chapter 2 ). If the required emissions reductions are not achieved by 2030, emissions will need to be cut even more drastically after 2030, rapidly raising the costs of low-carbon energy transitions and potentially putting temperature goals permanently beyond reach (see Chapters 2 and 9 ). #8 [paper] The impact of presentations in scientific conferences: Publication and citation rates in trauma surgery.
Authors: Touponse, Gavin, Bidwell, Serena, Shank, Amei, Tai, Jesse, Poe, James, Berg, Alexander, Khan, Hason, Tian, Lu
Venue: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42912484/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Understanding the publication rates and citation patterns of conference abstracts is critical for program committees and investigators alike. However, the downstream scholarly outcome of conference abstracts remains poorly characterized. We hypothesized that across contemporary US trauma-related scientific meetings, a substantial proportion of conference abstracts would not progress to peer-reviewed publications, and that publication rates and citation patterns would vary by presentation format and conference. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of abstracts presented at four major US trauma surgery conferences from 2017 to 2019. We identified peer-reviewed manuscripts associated with conference abstracts via Google Scholar and PubMed. We collected presentation format, publishing journal, 2024 journal impact factor, and citation count. A cohort of directly submitted peer-reviewed manuscripts was also analyzed. Mixed-effects Poisson regression models assessed the association between presentation and citation counts, adjusting for publication timing. RESULTS: Of 1,157 abstracts, 762 (66%) were published as peer-reviewed manuscripts. Most manuscripts were published in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery (JTACS) (55%), with 5 in journals with a higher-impact factor than JTACS. On regression analysis, abstracts presented as oral presentations, and published in journals with an impact factor higher than JTACS, were associated with a greater number of citations. When comparing manuscripts presented as abstracts to directly submitted peer-reviewed manuscripts, abstract presentation was associated with 22% more citations (incidence rate ratio: 1.22; 95% CI [1.16-1.29]; p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This cross-sectional study of four trauma societies found that approximately a third of presented abstracts did not progress to peer-reviewed publication, with publication rates varying by conference and presentation format. Exploratory analyses found that among those published in JTACS, published manuscripts originating from presented abstracts demonstrated a modestly higher citation count compared with directly submitted manuscripts. Our findings highlight an opportunity to better understand how conference time and investigator effort translate into downstream scholarly output. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/Epidemiological; Level IV.

#9 [paper] A Decision Support System for Conference Session Selection using Natural Language Processing and Machine Learning
Authors: Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, Tillman Erb, SLO Cal Poly, Puneet Agarwal, Sumona Mukhopadhyay
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21872/annual2025_6180
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Conference attendees are often faced with selecting from hundreds of presentations and sessions in pursuit of new findings and methods relevant to their area of interest, an overwhelming amount of information from which to clearly make a decision. To address this, we aim to develop a tool leveraging machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) techniques such as topic modeling (BERTopic) and semantic matching. By creating and matching embeddings of conference presentation abstracts and titles, the tool will provide improved query matching compared to keyword searching. Attendees can select from a variety of input types, including keyword selection and natural language query, and receive a collection of presentations with abstracts semantically matching the input. Notably, users can input an abstract of a paper most relevant to their area of interest and receive a collection of relevant conference presentations. We hope that this tool will enable academics and practitioners to rapidly identify relevant presentations, fostering knowledge exchange and professional network exploration.

#10 [paper] Fair, Explainable Early Warning for First-Year Student Dropout: Accuracy, Group Equity and Support Allocation
Authors: FNU Sumaiya
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23487386
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Working paper (v1.0, October 2026). Not peer reviewed; results are preliminary and may contain errors. Colleges use early-warning systems to decide which students receive outreach, tutoring and advising, yet published audits show these tools can be inaccurate and unequal across student groups. This working paper asks three questions an institution should answer before relying on such a tool: Is a transparent model accurate enough? Is it equally accurate for every student group? And who should receive support when capacity is limited? Using public records for 4,424 students (UCI Predict Students’ Dropout and Academic Success), we compare transparent logistic and multinomial-logit models, built at enrollment and after the first semester, against a grades-only baseline. We audit their errors across four student groups, and we formulate the allocation of limited support as an optimization problem with fairness quotas, proving that a simple greedy rule solves it optimally. Key findings (means across five data splits): A first-semester model that never sees demographic attributes reached AUC 0.897 and caught 66.8% of eventual dropouts at a 5.5% false-alarm rate. Entry grades alone reached AUC 0.564. The model under-detected dropouts among scholarship holders by 27 percentage points and among younger students by 25 points, consistently across splits. Group-specific thresholds narrowed these gaps but sharply increased false alarms. With support capacity for 10% of students, model-based targeting reached three times as many eventual dropouts as random selection. Fairness quotas cost about 2 of 132 support slots. Files: the working paper (PDF), and fair-early-warning.zip, which contains R code that reproduces every table and figure (base R only). The data are available from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.24432/C5MC89) and are not redistributed here.

#12 [paper] Reapplication and Credential Completion Among Non-Selected Community College Health Science Applicants: A Social Stratification Perspective
Authors: Donna G Whitehouse
Venue: Digital Commons - East Tennessee State University (East Tennessee State University)
Year: 2026
Link: https://dc.etsu.edu/etd/4736
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Reapplication and Credential Completion Among Non-Selected Community College Health Science Applicants: A Social Stratification Perspective by Donna Whitehouse Community colleges serve as primary access points for healthcare workforce preparation, yet thousands of qualified applicants are not selected for competitive admission health science programs each year. Research on what happens to these students following non-selection is limited, and existing studies focus almost exclusively on nursing, leaving allied health programs largely absent from the literature. This study addressed that gap by examining the reapplication behavior and credential completion outcomes among 2,604 applicants to three competitive admission health science programs, Nursing, Occupational Therapy Assistant, and Surgical Technology, at a single public, urban, community college in the southeastern United States. Social stratification theory, rooted in the frameworks of Weber (1946) and Bourdieu (1986), provided the theoretical foundation for this study. This perspective holds that educational institutions, such as community colleges with open access missions, can still function as sites where existing social hierarchies are reproduced through seemingly neutral selection processes. Social stratification theory suggests that competitive admission processes, while operationally necessary given program capacity constraints, may function as filters whose consequences fall unevenly across demographic groups, reflecting pre-existing structural inequalities rather than 6 academic potential alone. This study examined whether that pattern was observable in the reapplication and credential completion outcomes of non-selected applicants. Using a descriptive longitudinal design and binary logistic regression, the study tracked student outcomes over a three-year window following initial application. Pell grant eligibility emerged as the most consistent predictor across every research question, with Pell-eligible applicants reapplying and completing credentials at higher rates than their non-Pell-eligible peers, a counterintuitive finding that resists straightforward theoretical explanation. Race and ethnicity were associated with lower odds of credential completion among Black and Other/Unknown applicants relative to White applicants, particularly in models with sufficient statistical power to detect the effect. Selection status was the strongest predictor of credential completion, with selected applicants more than five times more likely to complete a credential within three years than non-selected peers. Findings suggest that competitive admission processes at community colleges may unintentionally replicate broader societal stratification patterns. Implications for enrollment management practice, institutional data tracking, and equitable access to health science education are discussed.

#13 [paper] Enrollment, Graduation, and Dropout Trends in Nepalese Higher Education: A Mathematical and Statistical Analysis
Authors: Kranti Thakur, Suresh Kumar Sahani
Venue: MASALIQ
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.58578/masaliq.v6i6.12248
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Rapid enrolment growth in Nepalese higher education has coincided with persistently weak graduation and completion outcomes. This study examined enrolment trends, faculty and funding capacity, pass and graduation rates, and dropout dynamics across central and provincial universities. Secondary data from University Grants Commission Nepal Education Management Information System reports, national newspapers, and peer-reviewed studies were analysed using ordinary least-squares regression and log-linear exponential growth models. A four-state absorbing Markov chain representing active enrolment, delayed or repeated study, graduation, and dropout was calibrated to Tribhuvan University’s reported aggregate pass rate of 29.3%. Enrolment increased from approximately 371,000 students in 2016/17 to over 633,000 in 2023/24. The linear model showed a strong fit (R² = 0.933), while the estimated enrolment compound annual growth rate was 7.93%, compared with 3.81% for faculty and 11.07% for government funding. The Markov model estimated a long-run dropout absorption probability of approximately 43% for first-attempt cohorts. Additional analyses characterized institutional fragmentation through the distribution of affiliated colleges by enrolment size and examined outbound student mobility, with more than 100,000 students annually obtaining No-Objection Certificates for overseas study. The findings indicate that enrolment growth has outpaced faculty expansion, while completion outcomes remain weak despite increased government funding. The study provides an integrated quantitative assessment to inform policies addressing imbalances between enrolment expansion, institutional capacity, and completion efficiency.

#14 [paper] Emergency Ultrasound Fellowship Match Outcomes: Unfilled Positions and Implications over Eight Years.
Authors: Boivin, Zachary, Coneybeare, Di, Salerno, Alexis, Werner, Sandra, She, Trent

Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Advanced emergency ultrasound (AEMUS) fellowships recently experienced an unexpected decrease in the number of positions filled in the match. Our study aimed to characterize this trend over an eight-year period. METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional observational study of AEMUS fellowships participating in the National Resident Matching Program (NRMP) from the 2019-2026 match cycles, cross-referencing the publicly available database from the Society of Clinical Ultrasound Fellowships. The primary outcome was both the proportion of AEMUS fellowship positions filled and a program complement fill percentage. Secondary outcomes included stratification by geography and duration since program establishment. RESULTS: We included a total of 138 of the 141 programs listed in the NRMP Match. From 2019 to 2026, there was a 28.2% increase in the number of programs and a 34.5% increase in available positions. There was a general increase in the percentage of positions filled from 2019 to 2022, with 53.7% (87/162) of positions filled to 74.4% (145/195), peaking at 81.1% (137/169) in 2021. This upward trend reversed in 2023 with a decrease to 65.1% (142/218). The percentage of positions filled has continued to decrease through 2026, with a fill rate of only 56.0% (122/218). In the eight years of NRMP data, 97 of the 138 programs (70.3%) went unfilled at least once. Programs participating in the Match for a longer period had a statistically significant higher fill percentage, with 27 programs in the 1- to 4-year group with a total fill percentage of 46.0%, 32 programs in the 5- to 7-year group with a fill percentage of 59.0%, and 79 programs in the ≥ 8-year group with a fill percentage of 72.8% (P < .01) using a Kruskal-Wallis test. Spearman correlation analysis found no association between geographic proximity and likelihood of a program being fully filled. CONCLUSION: This cross-sectional study of NRMP data showed a decrease in the percentage of positions filled for adult AEMUS fellowships starting in 2023, which continued through 2026. Programs with greater longevity exhibited higher fill percentages, showing resilience in the face of this pattern.

Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Securing peer reviewers for scholarly manuscripts is essential to journal operations but has become increasingly challenging. We sought to describe trends in acceptance of reviewer invitations and review completion at two journals sponsored by the Society of Teachers of Family Medicine: PRiMER and Family Medicine. METHODS: We conducted retrospective quality assurance of reviewer invitation outcomes for research manuscripts submitted to either journal from January 2010 to April 2026. Data were extracted from ScholarOne. We calculated odds ratios (ORs) for agreement to review and for review completion for each year via binary logistic regression, employing the generalized estimating equation to control for individual reviewer behavior, journal, and article type. RESULTS: We included 16,905 discrete invitations to review 2,574 manuscripts. Agreement rates at Family Medicine ranged from 70.99% in 2010, to a low of 41.80% in 2025, and 37.99% through April 2026; PRiMER agreement ranged from 74.36% in 2016, to 42.79% in 2025, and 20.23% in partial 2026. Combined completion rates dropped from 89.90% in 2010, to 82.20% in 2025, and to 73.90% in partial 2026. Using 2010 as the reference year, ORs for agreement to review dropped markedly, with the odds of accepting a review invitation in 2026 only 15.9% of the 2010 (2026: OR = 0.159, P<0.001) and the odds of review completion in 2026 falling to 32.9% of 2010 (OR = 0.329, P<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Reviewer engagement is declining across both journals. New, innovative strategies to recruit, engage, and incentivize reviewers will be necessary to sustain peer review.

#17 [paper] Cutoff Trend Prediction for Engineering Admis-sions Using Machine Learning
Authors: Mule Darshan Dipak, Bhosale Sachin Bajirao, Bangar Abhishek Popat
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23801960
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Engineering admission in Maharashtra is carried out through merit-based Centralised Admission Process (CAP) rounds, in which every college, branch and reservation category closes at a different cutoff percentile each year. Students usually rely on the previous year's cutoff list to decide their preference order, but cutoffs move from year to year because of changes in seat matrices, examination difficulty, branch demand and category-wise competition. Existing college-predictor tools mostly compare a candidate's score with last year's closing val-ues and rarely model how the cutoff itself is changing. This paper reviews five selected studies on admission prediction, cutoff-based college prediction and time-series forecasting, and iden-tifies gaps in temporal modelling, validation and uncertainty reporting. Based on these findings, a Machine Learning Framework for Cutoff Trend Prediction is proposed. The framework con-verts official CAP cutoff lists into a structured dataset of about 239,840 records, derives lag-based and trend features for every college-branch-category-round combination, and trains re-gression models such as Ridge regression, Random Forest and gradient boosting, with LSTM and ARIMA considered as optional time-series baselines. The forecast cutoff for the coming year is compared with a student's percentile to group colleges as Safe, Target or Dream. A pro-totype web application with search, prediction and history modules has been developed to de-liver the results. The framework aims to improve the accuracy, transparency and practical use-fulness of cutoff information for engineering aspirants. Quantitative evaluation of the proposed models is identified as future work.

#18 [paper] Predictive Validity of Entrance Selection Tests for Academic Performance and Study Completion in Postgraduate Education
Authors: Sendi Ramdhani, Amalia Saprıatı, Kristanti Ambar Puspitasari
Venue: International Journal of Education and Teaching Zone
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.57092/ijetz.v5i3.843

Abstract:
This study examined the predictive validity of postgraduate entrance-test scores for cumulative grade point average (GPA) and study duration at the Postgraduate School of Universitas Terbuka, Indonesia. Using retrospective institutional records, the study included 112 alumni admitted under comparable testing procedures implemented from 2021 onward; analyses involving English proficiency were based on 111 cases because one score was recorded on a non-comparable scale. Pearson correlations and multiple linear regression were used to assess predictive relationships. Numerical reasoning showed the strongest bivariate association with GPA (r = .227, p = .016), followed by verbal reasoning (r = .195, p = .040). No entrance-test component was significantly associated with study duration. In the multivariable model, English proficiency (β = −.233, p = .011), numerical reasoning (β = .271, p = .017), and figural reasoning (β = −.286, p = .004) were significant predictors of GPA, with the model explaining 17.9% of its variance (adjusted R² = .139). However, after adjustment for study program, only numerical reasoning remained statistically significant (β = .230, p = .044). Entrance-test scores provided little evidence of predictive utility for study duration after program adjustment. Overall, the findings indicate limited and component-specific predictive validity, with program-level heterogeneity influencing the observed relationships. These results highlight the need to evaluate entrance-test components in relation to specific academic outcomes and institutional contexts rather than treating aggregate test performance as a uniformly reliable predictor of postgraduate success.

#19 [paper] Divergent responses to AI-era submission pressure: a comparative analysis of medicine and computer science, 2015–2026

Abstract:
Abstract ChatGPT's release in late 2022 and the arrival of agentic AI systems from 2025 coincided with reports of rising manuscript volumes and editorial strain. Whether this pressure is uniform across research fields, or absorbed differently by each, has not been tested comparatively. We contrast two ecosystems with sharply different barriers to entry: computer science (CS), where submission carries almost no procedural cost, and medicine, where ethics review and data governance constrain what can be produced. Using open data for 2015–2026 — monthly submission and output volumes from arXiv, medRxiv, bioRxiv and PubMed; submission and acceptance figures for thirteen CS conferences; and review times for 38 medical journals — we measured AI-associated writing with a 95-word excess-vocabulary detector applied identically to 30,000 CS abstracts and 13,000–24,000 PubMed abstracts per year. CS preprint submissions rose 99.3% between 2022 and 2025, against 38–41% for the life-science preprint servers and 5.5% for PubMed-indexed output, and several medical specialties contracted; the divergence holds within arXiv itself. CS conferences absorbed the surge by expanding capacity, with NeurIPS submissions up 195% at an unchanged acceptance rate. AI-associated writing rose sharply from 2023 in both fields, the proportional increase nearly identical from a higher CS baseline, with the break appearing in all eight medical specialties tested. Review time for accepted papers showed no aggregate change. Medicine and CS therefore experienced comparable growth in AI-associated writing but opposite responses: CS expanded output and review capacity, while biomedicine held output flat and routed the pressure into editorial triage.

#21 [paper] Predicting Timely Graduation for Evidence-Based Higher Education Management: An Explainable Machine Learning Approach
Authors: Sunda Ariana, Devi Udariansyah, Bosya Perdana, Rosmiani Aprian
Venue: International Journal of Engineering Science and Information Technology

Link: https://doi.org/10.52088/ijesty.v6i4.1977

Abstract:
Higher education institutions increasingly use predictive analytics to identify students who may require academic support, yet predictive accuracy alone does not determine how model outputs should inform responsible management action. This study evaluates an explainable machine-learning framework for timely graduation decision support using routine academic records through Semester 4 and proposes a Role-Differentiated Action Translation Layer (R-ATL). Historical academic records were reconstructed into student-level trajectories, with timely graduation defined as completion by the end of the eighth semester. The analytical sample comprised 1,711 students from the 2019–2021 cohorts. Models were developed using the 2019–2020 cohorts and temporally tested on the untouched 2021 cohort. Random Forest achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.755, balanced accuracy of 0.670, and Brier score of 0.190, while XGBoost achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.761, with the small difference not statistically resolved. TreeSHAP identified a mixed performance–progression profile dominated by weighted IPS, Semester-4 IPS, early credit accumulation, and Semester-3 IPS. Informative missingness in the 2024 cohort limited complete-trajectory scoring to 438 of 604 students; these results were therefore treated as a current-cohort scoring demonstration rather than external validation. R-ATL translates explanation patterns into proposed role-specific information for students, academic advisors, program managers, and institutional leaders while retaining human review. The framework received complete content validity agreement from six experts. External validation, end-user usability and actionability testing, and intervention-outcome evaluation remain necessary for further empirical assessment and confirmation of the framework’s practical effectiveness across diverse higher education contexts and student populations

- **Amount:** €1,500,000–€40,000,000
- **Deadline:** 2027-06-15
- **Still open:** yes

This is a Horizon Europe research infrastructure access call. It funds "access programme like" projects providing transnational and/or virtual access to integrated research infrastructure installations and services. Proposals must address one of three ESFRI-based areas (Physical Sciences & Engineering / Data & Computing; Health & Food / Social Sciences & Humanities; Environment / Energy) and include at least two ESFRI Landmark and/or ERIC beneficiaries.

The next largest in the feed is #4 (EIC STEP Defence, up to €30 million), which falls short of the €40 million threshold.

#1 [grant] EIC Pre-accelerator - Widening
Amount: €500,000–€1,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-WIDERA-2027-01-WIDENING-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-11-18
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

This call will increase the innovation potential of deep-tech startups in the Widening countries and enable them to better attract private investments and scale up. It will further strengthen the innovation dimension of the widening component and increase the overall competitiveness of these countries.

The specific outcome expected of this action is increased business, investor, and technology readiness of high potential deep-tech startups in Widening countries to a level where they will:

- be successful in applying and attracting the EIC Accelerator funding and/or;

- manage to secure other private investment and/or;

- attract successfully national or regional funding as alternative funding sources (e.g. through Seal of Excellence programmes).

Scope:

This action focuses on early-stage deep-tech startups which 1) have high-impact innovation technology, product, service, or business model that could create new markets or disrupt existing ones, and 2) have the ambition and commitments to scale up.

The successful applicants need to work on deep tech innovation. Such companies often struggle to attract financing because the technology and investment risks are too high.

In the framework of this call, deep-tech[1] is technology that is based on cutting-edge scientific advances and discoveries and is characterised by the need to stay at the technological forefront by constant interaction with new ideas and results from the lab. Deep-tech innovations are understood to be those that have the potential to deliver transformative solutions, rooted in cutting-edge science, technology, and engineering, including innovation that combines advances in the physical, biological and digital spheres. Deep-tech is distinct from ‘high-tech’ which tends to refer only to R&D intensity[2].

This EIC Pre-accelerator - Widening call is designed to enable promising deep-tech startups to develop further their innovations (from TRL 4 to TRL 5/6)[3], attract the investment amounts needed for scale up in a shorter timeframe and successfully apply and attract funding from EIC Accelerator or other sources.

The applicants are expected to demonstrate in their application that they:

- have completed all elements of TRL 3 (Experimental proof of concept) and therefore the technology is currently at TRL 4 (Technology validated in lab);

- possess the necessary Intellectual Property Rights to ensure freedom to operate and adequate protection of the idea;

- have a clear vision on the intended pathway and route to market. This includes specific milestones together with concrete and verifiable KPIs to assess progress towards the market.

The support will be in awarded by grants max at 70% funding of the eligible costs. 30% co-funding to be covered by the beneficiary through its own resources.

An amount between EUR 500.000 and max EUR 1.000.000 in the form of a lump sum for a period of up to 2 years is considered appropriate.

The requested grant is expected to be used for:

- addressing the investor and market readiness towards commercialisation and deployment (market research, value proposition, business case and business model, prospects for growth, intellectual property protection, competitor analysis etc.) and if relevant, aspects of regulation, certification and standardisation, aimed at getting both the technology and the business idea investment ready and/or;

- the maturation and validation of novel technologies beyond proof of concept to viable demonstrators of the technology in the intended field of application (i.e., from minimum TRL 4 up to TRL 6).

At the end of the EIC Pre-accelerator project, it needs to:

- demonstrate that the technology component of their innovation has at least been validated in a relevant environment (e.g. at least completed all aspects of TRL 5);

- be ready to apply for EIC Accelerator and/or to seek other investors or sources of funding, to enter licensing or collaboration agreements with third parties

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for large-scale demonstration of protection, restoration, and management of blue forest ecosystems (marine and coastal vegetated habitats) within European sea basins to meet EU climate, biodiversity, and restoration goals.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Innovative multidisciplinary projects integrating active and passive restoration, conservation efforts (e.g., managing Marine Protected Areas), innovative financing mechanisms (e.g., nature credits), multi-sensor research and monitoring, and community engagement, tailored to specific sea basins.

- Enhanced capacity of marine vegetated habitats/blue carbon ecosystems to support biodiversity and fisheries;

- Established novel financing and incentive mechanisms that support conservation, restoration and management of blue forest ecosystems projects;

- Raised public awareness and improved community participation in blue forest ecosystems protection, restoration and management activities, ensuring long-term involvement.

Scope:

This topic seeks innovative multidisciplinary projects that will advance large-scale demonstration of protection, restoration and management of blue forest ecosystems, focusing on the assessment of ecological interactions, restoration of degraded ecosystems, conservation, and sustainable management within European sea basins. The direct involvement of relevant authorities and stakeholders in the consortium is strongly encouraged.

Proposals should target the development and implementation of comprehensive strategies that integrate blue carbon ecosystems into marine biodiversity frameworks, in particular in the implementation of the national restoration plans under the Nature Restoration Regulation.

Proposals are expected to show how their activities and results will help achieve the Mission’s objectives and targets. Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/CREA-MEDIA-2027-CODEV
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-03-02
Abstract:
Scope:

The objective of the support to European co-development is to support the cooperation among European production companies that are developing works with a strong international audience potential.

Expected results

-
Increased collaboration at development stage between European production companies from different countries and from different markets and consequently an increased number of co-productions.

-
Increased quality, feasibility, cross-border potential and market value of selected projects.

-
A stronger position on European and international markets for companies selected under European co-development.

-
Increased international cooperation, including collaborations between European and Korean professionals, in line with the audiovisual entitlement appended to the Protocol on Cultural Cooperation between the EU and Korea.

Description of the activities to be funded

The European co-development action shall provide support to the development of a single project for commercial exploitation intended for cinema release, television broadcasting or commercial exploitation on digital platforms or a multi-platform environment in the following categories: animation, creative documentary or fiction. The project must be co-developed by at least two European independent production companies, having signed a co-development agreement specifying the division of tasks and the collaboration on creative aspects.

The aim is to provide funds to audiovisual production companies to develop works with high creative value and cultural diversity and wide cross-border exploitation potential. Companies are encouraged to develop strong and innovative collaborations at creative and financing level and to develop strategies for marketing and distribution from the outset of the development phase thus improving the potential to reach audiences at a European and international level.

Applications should present adequate strategies to ensure a more sustainable and more environmentally-respectful industry and to ensure gender balance, inclusion, diversity and representativeness.

Still open/current: yes

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to some or all of the following expected outcomes:

- Development of a mature technological solution addressing EU security policy priorities in the areas addressed by the Cluster 3 work programme and in particular the destination of fighting crime and terrorism, disaster resilient societies, border management and resilient infrastructure;

- Facilitate increased and sustained collaboration between small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), public research partners, and academia, leading to improved knowledge transfer within the European innovative SME ecosystem;

- Mitigate difficulties in access to finance and new international markets, thereby enhancing the growth and expansion of European innovative SMEs.

Scope:

Europe’s 25 million small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are the backbone of the EU economy. SMEs can bring innovation to societal challenges, including the security of EU citizens. Innovative SMEs and high-tech start-ups can transform and modernise EU security capabilities.

However, despite the innovation capacity of EU SMEs, these often experience difficulties in finding their way to the public markets. These include red tape in public contracts, access to new customers, access to finance, industrial competition and Intellectual Property (IP) valorisation. These difficulties are exacerbated in markets that show restrictions of different kind, as it is the case of security.

Knowing that SMEs require additional support to reach the security buyers and that the collaboration opportunities offered by the projects of the Pillar II of Horizon Europe can be a catalyst for uptake, this topic aims to offer a collaborative environment for small and medium innovators to tailor their innovations to the specific needs of civil security end-users, taking into account the urge to address the diverse needs of all citizens, regardless of gender, age or ability.

Applicants are invited to submit proposals for technology development along with the following principles:

- Focus on mature technological solutions addressing EU security policy priorities in the areas addressed by the Cluster 3 Work Programme;

- Fostering collaboration between SMEs from different Member States and Associated Countries;

- Involving security end-users in the role of validator and potential first-adopter of the proposed innovations;

- Fostering collaboration schemes between small companies and research and technology organisations and/or big industrial players aimed at fostering innovative technology transfer or creating innovative business models that facilitate access to market and strengthen the innovation capacity of EU SMEs and start-ups in the domain of civil security.

Examples of activities to plan in the proposed projects include, but are not limited to: assimilating market requirements; facilitating access to additional funding; approaching potential public buyers; assess competitive landscape; supporting in innovation management (methodological and process innovation, business model innovation, market innovation); assist in IP management and exploitation; provide guidance for expansion to future markets, etc.

The participation of research and technology organisations should not focus on own technology development but on supporting the small industrial players in accelerating the technology transfer of innovative security solutions for their further development and production.

It is encouraged that one SME takes the coordinator role[1]. If the coordinator is not an SME, this should be duly justified.

The projects should have a maximum estimated duration of 2 years.

Under this topic, projects should address one of the following areas addressed by the Cluster 3 work programme: Fighting Crime and Terrorism (FCT, Option A), Disaster-Resilient Society (DRS, Option B), Resilient Infrastructure (INFRA, Option C), Border Management (BM, Option D).

#8 [grant] Framework Loans
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/JTM-2026-PSLF-FRAMEWORK-LOANS
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-22
Abstract:
Objective:

This topic targets projects linked to a framework loan to address serious social, economic and environmental challenges deriving from the transition towards the EU’s 2030 climate and energy targets and the EU’s 2050 objective of climate neutrality, for the benefit of the EU territories identified in the Territorial Just Transition Plans.

- The projects must be linked to an EIB framework loan. Framework loans by other banks or EIB financial intermediaries (including EIB Intermediated Framework Loans or Multi-Beneficiary Intermediated Loans) cannot benefit from PSLF funding under this topic.

Scope:

Projects related to a wide range of sustainable investments may be funded, such as:

- investments in renewable energy and green and sustainable mobility, including the promotion of green hydrogen

- efficient district heating networks

- public research

- digitalisation

- environmental infrastructure for smart waste and water management

- sustainable energy, energy efficiency and integration measures, including renovations and conversions of buildings

- urban renewal and regeneration

- the transition to a circular economy

- land and ecosystem restoration and decontamination, taking into account the ‘polluter pays’ principle

- biodiversity, as well as

- up-skilling and re-skilling, training, and

- social infrastructure, including care facilities and social housing.

Infrastructure development may also include cross-border projects and solutions leading to enhanced resilience to withstand ecological disasters, in particular those accentuated by climate change. A comprehensive investment approach should be favoured, in particular for territories with important transition needs.

Investments in other sectors may also be supported, if they are consistent with the approved Territorial Just Transition Plans.

The following sectors are clearly excluded from the scope of the JTM PSLF support:

- decommissioning or the construction of nuclear power stations

- manufacturing, processing and marketing of tobacco and tobacco products

- help to undertakings in difficulty, as defined in point (18) of Article 2 of Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 (18), unless authorised under temporary State aid rules established to address exceptional circumstances or under de minimis aid to support investments reducing energy costs in the context of the energy transition process

- investments related to the production, processing, transport, distribution, storage or combustion of fossil fuel.

The project activities must benefit a territory covered by an approved Territorial Just Transition Plan and must be consistent with this Plan and the sectors and thematic areas it sets out.

Expected Impact

Proposals must describe in Part B of the application (section 1, relevance and impact) how the project will achieve a measurable impact in addressing serious social, economic and environmental challenges deriving from the transition towards the EU’s 2030 climate and energy targets and the EU’s 2050 objective of climate neutrality. In particular, and when relevant, key performance indicators (KPIs) on greenhouse gas emission (GHG) reductions, job creation per gender, number of people reached are to be provided in part C of the application.

Applicants are recommended to use the EIB methodology for assessing project GHG reductions and emissions variations “EIB Project Carbon Footprint Methodologies”.

Applicants are also recommended to take into account the guidance provided in the publication “Considering gender in regional transformations: A toolkit for just transition regions” in order to identify gender challenges relevant to their project.

For more information about the EIB lending policy, see Regional development & cohesion (eib.org).

#9 [grant] Pilot access schemes to Technology Infrastructures for European startups, scaleups and innovative SMEs (CSA)
Amount: €200,000–€12,500,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL4-2027-01-MAT-PROD-47
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-02-02
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Proposals should demonstrate the following expected outcomes:

- A sound understanding of the specific needs of industrial users (including but not limited to innovative SMEs, startups and scaleups) for Technology infrastructure services in specific priority areas including but not limited to advanced materials, clean energy, or health and biotechnology;

- Increased opportunities for industrial users for development, testing, up-scaling and deployment of new technologies via the use of services offered by Technology Infrastructures;

- Strengthened innovation and technology development capacity of European SMEs, startups and scaleups via improved access to Technology Infrastructures;

- Attractiveness and effectiveness of the developed access schemes for broadening the range of Technology Infrastructures users, especially for startups and scaleups, including with transnational access.

Scope:

Startups, scaleups and other innovative SMEs require access to state-of-the-art research and technology facilities, equipment and expertise to test, upscale, validate new products and technologies, shortening the time-to-market and increasing the chances for a successful commercialisation. Access mechanisms to Technology Infrastructures as well as access contracts and collaboration or service provision agreements are often complex, while the costs of using such infrastructures can significantly surpass the financial capacities of growing innovative companies.

The action will develop and test pilot multi-site access schemes for startups, scaleups and other innovative SMEs, involving a critical mass of Technology Infrastructures operators and users in priority areas (including but not limited to advanced materials, clean energy, or health and biotechnology). It should build on existing initiatives with already developed single access points to a comprehensive set of facilities and services in a selected technology area, like for example Open Innovation Test Beds or other integrated networks, that allow for a quick deployment of a common access scheme.

The action should include setting-up a pilot centrally managed and funded access programme, allowing companies quick access to the needed services, with simplified and standardised access conditions applicable across the EU, to be coordinated and in line with the work on the envisaged European Charter of access for industrial users to research and technology infrastructures. While the focus shall be the provision of access and support services to companies, the action can also include enhancing the accessibility and usability of technology infrastructure services to ensure that they meet the evolving needs of users.

The action should aim at significant broadening of the user base of the technology infrastructures to address the needs of startups and scaleups that do not have access to such facilities in their local ecosystems. To this end, proposals should include the development and implementation of activities to increase the visibility and promote and demonstrate the uptake of technology infrastructures services provided to users across the EU.

Furthermore, proposals should aim to enhance transnational and multisite collaboration among Technology Infrastructures fostering the building of technology infrastructures ecosystems, the sharing of experience, resources, and best practices in management, service offer, staff exchange and networking. Proposals may also benefit, especially for communication and dissemination activities, from sharing best practices and taking stock of what other relevant projects are developing in the field of Technology Infrastructures.

Abstract:

Project results are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- Interdisciplinarity and sharing of information, knowledge and technologies across scientific fields with due attention to research security; better management, including implementing FAIR data principles, of the continuous flow of data collected or produced by research infrastructures.

#11 [grant] TV and online content Fiction projects
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/CREA-MEDIA-2027-TVONLINE-3
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-02-10
Abstract:
Scope:

The objective of the support to TV and online content is to increase the capacity of audiovisual producers to develop and produce strong projects with significant potential to circulate throughout Europe and beyond, and to facilitate European and international co-productions within the television and online sector.

The action aims to strengthen the independence of producers in relation to broadcasters and digital platforms, to enhance collaboration between operators, including independent producers, broadcasters, digital platforms and sales agents, from different countries participating in the MEDIA strand, including from low capacity countries, in order to produce high quality programming aimed at wide international distribution and promoted to a wide audience including commercial exploitation in the multi-platform environment. Particular attention will be given to projects presenting innovative aspects in the content and in the financing that show a clear link with the envisaged distribution strategies. Supported projects can also have associated partners from countries not participating in the MEDIA Strand, though these cannot be beneficiaries. These partners can come from non-European countries to foster wider international cooperation and market access: a case in point is Korea pursuant to the audiovisual entitlement appended to the Protocol on Cultural Cooperation between the EU and Korea.

Expected results

- Increased production of high quality European works for linear and non-linear broadcasting including on digital platforms, as well as an increase in the number of co-productions.

- Enhanced cooperation between operators from different countries participating in the MEDIA Strand, including between broadcasters.

- Increased audience for European works through linear and non-linear broadcasting including on digital platforms.

- Increased international cooperation, including collaborations between European and Korean professionals, in line with the audiovisual entitlement appended to the Protocol on Cultural Cooperation between the EU and Korea.

Description of the activities to be funded

#12 [grant] Strengthening the remembrance of LGBTIQ+ victims and other victims
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/CERV-2026-CITIZENS-REM-GENCRIME-2
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-02-24
Abstract:
Objective:

3. Strengthening the remembrance of the Holocaust, acts of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity to strengthen democracy in the EU.

Projects under this topic should focus on the non-Jewish victims of the Holocaust as well as other genocides, war crimes and crimes against humanity of the 20th century’s Europe.

Projects under this topic should NOT address the Holocaust against Jewish people which are covered by Topic 2.

CERV-2026-CITIZENS-REM-GENCRIME-2 - Priority 2: Strengthening the remembrance of LGBTIQ+ victims and other victims

Projects under this priority should not address projects focusing on the remembrance of Roma victims (Projects focussing on the remembrance of Roma victims should apply under Priority 1).

Europe’s 20th century was marked by horrific crimes, genocides, war crimes and crimes against humanity as well as the crimes committed under authoritarian and totalitarian regimes, including those of communist and fascist dictatorships. The remembrance of these gravest crimes committed on European soil plays a critical role in upholding these values.

Despite growing efforts to preserve the memory of the victims of these crimes, the experiences of many groups remain overlooked, marginalised or insufficiently recognised in public memory. This includes, among others, LGBTIQ+ people and other communities targeted on the basis of their identity, beliefs or perceived social status.

Throughout history, LGBTIQ+ people have faced systemic persecution under a wide range of political and social regimes, often shaped by prevailing religious, cultural, and legal norms. Under the Nazi regime, it is estimated that 50000 gay and bisexual men were subject to ‘severe jail sentences in brutal conditions’, with around 10-15000 being sent to concentration camps. Lesbian women, transgender people, and others whose identities did not conform to Nazi ideals of gender and sexuality also faced surveillance, discrimination, violence, and social exclusion, with their experiences largely unrecognized for decades.

As a result, the history of LGBTIQ+ persons in Europe is marked by both struggle and resilience. The preservation and recognition of LGBTIQ+ history and memory are essential to building an inclusive European identity rooted in dignity, diversity, and human rights. Remembering and recognising these atrocities is essential to restore justice as underlined in the LGBTIQ+ equality strategy 2026-2030.

Greater awareness of all these histories contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of the causes, mechanisms and consequences of mass atrocities and contributes not only to preventing their recurrence but also to reinforcing democratic resilience, fostering civic engagement, and building a common European culture of remembrance.

Projects under this topic could focus on:

- Addressing how genocides, war crimes and crimes against humanity were organised, which actors were involved and how they were committed, the roles of collaborators, perpetrators and bystanders.

- Finding new ways of remembering, educating and teaching about these crimes to protect society against resurging threats of hatred. They can include artistic work on memory projects, as well as stimulating memory activism. These new methods should be inclusive, where applicable participatory and create an enabling learning environment.

- Fostering awareness raising, mutual learning or training activities that accurately reflect the persecution of LGBTIQ+ people, and other minorities throughout history.

- Countering historical falsification and memory competition related to the persecution of LGBTIQ+ people, genocides, war crimes and crimes against humanity, especially among Europeans that shared a common history but have divergent views on their common past.

Amount: €3,500,000–€5,380,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-NEB-2027-01-PARTICIPATION-02
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-12-01
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Demonstrated methodology is used by architects, spatial planners, designers and other relevant actors to identify the extent to which neighbourhoods[1] and communities[1] are intergenerational[1].

- Demonstrated solutions for intergenerational neighbourhoods and communities are available to public authorities, public/private real estate developers and owners, and stakeholders involved in the green transition[1] of neighbourhoods.

- The demonstrated solutions make a significant contribution to intergenerational living and measurably advance the green transition in the neighbourhoods (for example in the field of sustainable mobility, accessibility, climate-resilience, water resilience, and/or biodiversity conservation).

Scope:

Research shows that countries with lower age-related inequalities have higher levels of life satisfaction overall[5], and that governments that balance the needs and interests of the present and future generations have higher levels of trust[6].

There is an increasing body of research on solutions such as ‘independent living’, ‘age-friendly housing’ and ‘smart multi-generational neighbourhoods’ and their benefits. Although different more cost-efficient solutions have been developed over the years, the focus of investments remains on costly age-segregated housing and communities for older adults (such as large nursing homes and large assisted living facilities).

This topic will support the development of intergenerational neighbourhoods and communities that better address the needs of the different age groups, while simultaneously tackling various local challenges (including, but not limited to the demographic transition, climate change, pollution, biodiversity loss, loss of cultural heritage, feelings of insecurity).

Proposals are expected to address all of the following:

- Demonstrate a methodology to measure and monitor the extent to which neighbourhoods and communities are intergenerational. These may include digital platforms, smart sensing systems, or participatory data collection methods that enhance inclusiveness[1], accessibility, and real-time insight. Among others, the methodology is expected to:

- Identify barriers (e.g. legal, regulatory, institutional) to intergenerational living in neighbourhoods and communities.

- Explore perceptions of the different generations.

- Determine the role of informal services (including culture, social and health care, and education), in fostering intergenerational neighbourhoods and communities.

- Demonstrate at least three solutions that promote intergenerational living in at least three neighbourhoods (in urban, peri-urban and rural areas) located in different Member States and/or Associated Countries. The solutions are expected to:

- Redesign neighbourhood spaces, functions and/or services, where possible building upon the cultural and creative sectors and analysing users’ perception. This includes multisensory perceptions as well as perceived beauty.

- Be adaptable to different local contexts.

- Monitor, evaluate, and document the demonstrated solutions. Based on the evidence, propose recommendations for their adaptation and uptake.

Proposals are expected to follow a participatory[1] and transdisciplinary[1] approach through the integration of different actors and disciplines.

This topic requires the effective contribution of social sciences and humanities (SSH)[1] disciplines and the involvement of SSH experts, institutions as well as the inclusion of relevant SSH expertise, in order to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related research activities.

In order to achieve the expected outcomes, international cooperation[11] is encouraged.

#16 [grant] Structurally addressing homelessness through coordinated social infrastructure and services in neighbourhoods
Amount: €3,500,000–€6,300,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-NEB-2026-01-BUSINESS-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2026-12-01
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Evidence of the structural social infrastructure[1] and services needed to address homelessness[1] at neighbourhood[1] level is made available to stakeholders involved in tackling homelessness.

- Improved availability and accessibility of key social infrastructure and services for homeless groups in the targeted neighbourhoods.

Scope:

Based on 2024 data, over 1.2 million people are estimated to experience homelessness in Europe[4], with a significant proportion (45%) of surveyed homeless individuals finding themselves in a situation of chronic homelessness for over two years[5].

While housing-led approaches[1] are crucial to tackle homelessness, addressing the structural and multidimensional causes of homelessness also requires systemic interventions focusing on social infrastructure and services in neighbourhoods. Social infrastructure and services include the physical places as well as public and community[1] sector facilities and services that support and enable access to healthcare, employment, education, community integration, and other social services. They must be developed and made available in a coordinated manner that mitigates the interconnected root causes of homelessness in the long term and supports the reintegration and social inclusion of individuals in communities by avoiding long-term dependence on emergency support. This is especially important considering that chronic homelessness is often accompanied by a complex mix of needs and physical and psychological functional variations.

Research is required on how to analyse the interconnected, contextual conditions that drive and mitigate homelessness at the neighbourhood level and how to inform strategies to structurally address homelessness.

Proposals are expected to address all of the following:

- Develop a system-based approach to mitigate homelessness and support the reintegration of individuals in communities by coordinating key social infrastructure and services (including healthcare, education, employment, community integration and other relevant social services) at neighbourhood level. The approach must cover at least the following:

- Analysis of local neighbourhood context and existing built environment[1] in terms of availability and equitable access to relevant social infrastructures and services, particularly for chronic homelessness and marginalised groups or those in a vulnerable situation.

- Assessment of the impact and potential correlation between infrastructure and service design in the built environment and the degree of homelessness in neighbourhoods.

- Development of strategies to overcome challenges of coordinating key social infrastructure and services at neighbourhood level (such as data limitations and fragmentation, siloed and fragmented social service systems, and funding challenges for scalability).

- Analysis of the views, willingness, and ability of homeless groups, especially those experiencing chronic homelessness, to engage with and benefit from the provided social infrastructures and services.

- Assessment of the potential impacts on community (re)integration and participation[9], well-being, social cohesion, and a sense of belonging in neighbourhoods for both homeless groups and the broader community in neighbourhoods.

- Assessment of the socioeconomic impact of the system-based approach through measurable indicators on social infrastructure and service accessibility and use.

- Provision of recommendations and guidance to apply the approach in other neighbourhoods, considering contextual factors such as unequal geographical distribution of and access to social infrastructure and services (considering factors including gender, sexual orientation, age, physical and psychological functional variations, or other relevant social factors), and local homelessness conditions.

Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-04-06
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Projects results are expected to contribute to the following outcomes:

For supported doctoral candidates

- Deeper and more diverse set of research-related and transferable skills and competences;

- Improved employability and career prospects both within academia and beyond;

- New mind-sets and approaches to R&I work forged through international, inter-sectoral and interdisciplinary experience;

For participating organisations

- Enhanced quality and sustainability of research training;

- Increased global attractiveness, visibility and reputation of the participating organisation(s);

- Stronger R&I capacity and output among participating organisations;

- Increased contribution of the participating organisations to the local, regional and/or national socio-economic ecosystems;

Scope:

Applicants submit proposals for new or existing doctoral programmes with an impact on the enhancement of human resources in R&I at regional, national or international level. These programmes will be co-funded by MSCA COFUND.

The doctoral programmes should develop substantial training modules, addressing key transferable skills and competences common to all fields, including digital ones (e.g. generative AI) and fostering the culture of Open Science, knowledge valorisation[1], and when applicable innovation and entrepreneurship as well as good scientific conduct such as research integrity. In particular, doctoral programmes should adequately prepare doctoral candidates to pursue a career in research and adequately prepare them for increased research collaboration and information-sharing made possible by new (digital) technologies (e.g. collaborative tools, opening access to publications and to other research outputs including data, FAIR data management, societal engagement and citizen science, etc.).

On top of compulsory international mobility, applicants are encouraged to include elements of cross-sectoral mobility and interdisciplinarity into their programmes. Collaboration with a wider set of associated partners, including from the non-academic sector, will be positively taken into account during the evaluation. These organisations may provide hosting or secondment opportunities or training modules in research or transferable skills.
