#19 [grant] Addressing homelessness through housing-led approaches aligned with the New European Bauhaus
Amount: €3,500,000–€6,300,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-NEB-2026-01-PARTICIPATION-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2026-12-01
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Housing-led approaches[1] aligned with the NEB are made available to stakeholders involved in tackling homelessness[1].

- Robust evidence on NEB-aligned housing-led approaches tackling homelessness (including people temporarily hosted by acquaintances and family) to inform the development and/or update of policies and services for prevention and early intervention in the context of the green transition[1] in neighbourhoods[1].

Scope:

Social and affordable housing is being advanced in the EU, including through the Affordable Housing Initiative[5]. Despite efforts, current policies for the green transition are failing to adequately address the housing crisis. Homelessness remains a structural challenge across Europe, with negative impacts on both individuals experiencing it (e.g. physical and mental health, social and economic conditions) and neighbourhood communities[1] (e.g. pressure on public services, erosion of social fabric[1], etc.).

Research and innovation gaps in tackling homelessness range from data collection (i.e. the variety of approaches to defining, measuring and monitoring homelessness), to integrating housing-led approaches with resilience strategies for homeless populations in a climate-changing world.

Housing-led approaches cover diverse policy responses to homelessness that provide immediate and permanent access to housing, targeted prevention, and needs-based, person-centred support services across several areas of the individual’s life while giving homeless populations a high degree of choice and control.

This topic focuses on developing and/or updating housing-led approaches that apply NEB values[1] and principles[1]. Such approaches are expected to cover measures ranging from upstream preventive measures to those giving access to green, low-carbon, climate-resilient, health-promoting and socially inclusive housing that ensures quality of experience for homeless populations across neighbourhoods in urban, peri-urban and rural areas.

Proposals are expected to address all of the following:

- Refine and demonstrate at least three housing-led approaches in at least three neighbourhoods (in urban, peri-urban and rural areas) located in different Member States and/or Associated Countries, that:

- Are adapted to the specific characteristics of the neighbourhoods where the approaches will be applied (e.g. existing local/national regulations, composition of the population, cultural differences, existing infrastructure, etc.).

- Provide permanent housing to homeless people, as defined by the European Typology of Homelessness and Housing Exclusion[10], complemented by services that (re-)integrate homeless populations in their local community.

- Integrate plans for the green transition of the permanent housing, taking into consideration climate mitigation and adaptation aspects (for instance, through the inclusion of renewable energy solutions and/or nature-based solutions[11]) and the social dimension of living conditions for a conflict-minimised cohabitation of different social groups.

- Are co-created[1] with the targeted homeless populations, paying special attention to families with minor children, and people temporarily hosted by acquaintances and family.

- Include measures to address the institutional barriers that hinder access to housing in the selected neighbourhoods.

- Present the highest potential for replication and adaptability to local specificities.

- Develop and implement a methodology to monitor, analyse and document the effectiveness of the selected approaches in reducing homelessness compared to conventional approaches, building upon the European Typology of Homelessness and Housing Exclusion[10]. The methodology is expected to ensure the comparability of data and results across neighbourhoods.

#20 [grant] European slate development
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/CREA-MEDIA-2027-DEVSLATE
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2026-12-01
Abstract:
Scope:

The objective of the European slate development support is to foster the competitiveness of European independent production companies and to increase their economic weight on the market. The aim is also to increase the capacity of audiovisual producers to develop projects with the potential to circulate throughout Europe and beyond, and to facilitate European and international coproduction.

The support will also provide an entry point for emerging talent, giving them the opportunity to direct a short film supported by the strong foundation provided by experienced companies.

Expected results

- A stronger position on European and international markets for companies selected under European slate development.

- Increased quality, feasibility, cross-border potential and market value of European works supported.

Description of the activities to be funded

Support will be given to independent European production companies able to develop a slate of 3 to 5 audiovisual works (fiction, animation, creative documentary). This should allow production companies to reduce risks and increase their capacity to attract and retain talents.

The European slate development shall provide support to the development of minimum 3 and maximum 5 works for commercial exploitation intended for cinema release, television broadcasting or commercial exploitation on digital platforms or a multi-platform environment in the following categories: animation, creative documentary or fiction. Applicants may add a short film by emerging talent to their slate (optional).

The aim is to provide funds to audiovisual production companies to develop work with high creative value and cultural diversity and wide cross-border exploitation potential. Companies are encouraged to develop strategies for marketing and distribution from the outset of the development phase thus improving the potential to reach audiences at a European and international level.

Greater cooperation, including co-development, between operators from different countries participating in the MEDIA Strand is also pursued as well as strengthening the competitiveness of European audiovisual production companies by consolidating their capacity for investment in the development phase and expanding companies’ activities and their innovation capacity to explore new fields and markets.

Special attention will be given to applications presenting adequate strategies to ensure a more sustainable and more environmentally-respectful industry and to ensure gender balance, inclusion, diversity and representativeness.

# Reviewing a project

1. `projects_get` for goals, confirmed state, blockers, milestones,
   developments in effect and members. Note when the state was last confirmed;

2. `projects_feed` for the current slate, in rank order, with when each item
   entered. "New this week" means it entered the slate this week.
3. Tie items to blockers: for each open blocker, which slate item (if any)
   speaks to it, and why. Cite both by #n.
4. End with what the team might do next, phrased as suggestions. You cannot
   change the project; point to the app for edits.

Abstract:
The Fulbright-Hays DDRA Fellowship Program, funded by the U.S. Department of Education (ED) and administered by the International and Foreign Language Education (IFLE) Office, provides opportunities for graduate students to conduct full-time dissertation research abroad in modern foreign languages and area studies. ED defines "area studies" as a "program of comprehensive study of the aspects of a society or societies, including the study of their geography, history, culture, economy, politics, international relations, and languages." Eligible Regions and Countries: Allowable projects are those that focus on one or more of the following geographic areas: Africa, East Asia, Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands, South Asia, the Near East, Central and Eastern Europe and Eurasia, and the Western Hemisphere (excluding the United States and its territories). Projects Not Allowable: Applications for research focused on the following countries are not eligible: Andorra, Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, San Marino, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom, and Vatican City. Note that it may be possible to conduct research in Western Europe, provided the project itself is focused on another world region. Projects in countries designated as "closed" by Fulbright-Hays are ineligible. See the "Maintenance Allowances" section in the FY 2025 DDRA Application Instructions for details. Applications for projects in countries currently designated by the Department of State with a Level 4 travel advisory may be submitted, but awardees may end up having their travel plans delayed or canceled due to travel restrictions. Applicants may propose research projects lasting from 6 to 12 consecutive months. Projects may begin as early as January 1, 2026 and must end by March 31, 2027. Students do not apply directly to the Department of Education for these awards. Instead, applications must be submitted on behalf of the applicant by the student's institution of higher education (IHE). Students must therefore work closely with their IHE for an application to be submitted successfully.

#14 [paper] OTOLens: Development and validation of a mobile application for assessment of tympanic membrane and middle ear pathology.
Authors: Prakairungthong, Sarun, Limviriyakul, Siriporn, Thitisomboon, Wipaluk, Bhabhatsatam, Bhattaraprot, Thongyai, Kanthong, Atipas, Suvajana, Suvarnsit, Kanokrat

Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42790172/

Abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVE: Diagnosing tympanic membrane and middle ear pathology in primary care is challenging due to anatomical complexity, overlapping presentations, and limited access to specialized equipment. We developed and externally validated OTOLens, a smartphone-based mobile application classifying otoscopic images using deep learning. METHODS: In this prospective development and validation study, OTOLens combined three ResNet-based image classifiers (OME, TMP, and MYR) with a parallel gradient-boosted tabular classifier operating on PCA-reduced image features, integrated by a per-condition maximum and a 0.5 decision threshold (Apple Core ML/Create ML); the system was trained on 1011 annotated otoscopic images across five categories: normal tympanic membrane (n = 251), otitis media with effusion (OME; n = 227), myringitis (MYR; n = 210), other pathology (n = 197), and tympanic membrane perforation (TMP; n = 126), labeled by three fellowship-trained otolaryngologists via majority consensus. External validation used 180 prospectively acquired images reviewed independently by three otolaryngologists. Performance metrics included sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, F1 score, and AUROC; inter-rater reliability was assessed by Fleiss' κ; application agreement by Cohen's κ. RESULTS: Internal testing demonstrated class-wise accuracy of 58-81% with AUROC up to 0.89. External validation achieved 52.8% overall accuracy (Cohen's κ = 0.417; moderate agreement). Class-specific sensitivity was 86.7% for TMP, 48.9% for OME, 40.0% for MYR, and 35.6% for normal tympanic membrane; specificity was 100% for normal tympanic membrane and MYR. Expert inter-rater reliability was substantial (Fleiss' κ = 0.681, 95% CI: 0.619-0.738). CONCLUSIONS: OTOLens achieved high sensitivity for TMP, supporting its potential as a primary care triage aid. Generalizability was constrained by domain shift, class imbalance, and limited TMP representation; multicenter validation with expanded datasets is required prior to clinical deployment.

#1 [paper] Satellite-gene abundance fusion reveals global hotspots of ocean ecosystem services
Authors: Baptiste Serandour, Constanza M. Andreani-Gerard, Antoine Bagnaro, Sacha Bourgeois‐Gironde, Samuel Chaffron, Andrés Couve, Roy El Hourany, Lionel Guidi
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The spatial organization of plankton-based ecosystem services, such as functional diversity, net primary productivity, and carbon export, is poorly understood, creating a need for science-based guidance for global ocean governance.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning integration of omics-derived plankton functions and satellite observations with diversity metrics and ecosystem services.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global oceanographic structures, including polar fronts and principal current systems.
Abstract:
The Ocean sustains planetary health through climate regulation, biodiversity, and essential ecosystem services. Plankton underpins these processes by driving primary production, sustaining food webs, and mediating carbon sequestration. Yet the spatial organization of plankton-based ecosystem services remains poorly understood. The High Seas Treaty and the 30% Ocean protection target by 2030 create an urgent need for science-based guidance for global ocean governance. Here, we aim to identify key planktonic areas associated with functional diversity, net primary productivity, and carbon export globally. We used machine learning to integrate omics-derived plankton functions and satellite observations with diversity metric and ecosystem services. Leveraging metagenomic data, we identified molecular functions strongly linked to ecosystem functioning and project their global distributions across seasons. We reveal putative hotspots of functional diversity, net primary productivity, and carbon export. Our analysis pinpoints areas where all three indicators converge synchronously, predominantly along oceanographic structures such as polar fronts and principal current systems. By relying on satellite data as core input, our approach captures the temporal variability of these hotspots, providing a global, dynamic protocol for projections of plankton-based ecosystem services. These findings establish a foundation for developing integrative conservation tools based on ecosystem functioning and inform adaptive management under climate change.

#2 [paper] Leveraging Ocean Data and Models: Building the Data Infrastructure, Workforce, and Modeling Capacity to Synthesize Earth’s Ocean Observations
Authors: Susanne E. Craig, Frank Muller-Karger, Leonid Shumilo, Tzortziou Maria
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5bv4n
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean-relevant Earth system data from satellite streams, in situ networks, suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, and high-resolution numerical models exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A decadal strategy built on two pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data (cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, machine learning) and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation (mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimila…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): NASA's aquatic and marine research enterprise, including MODIS, PACE mission, and BGC-Argo data streams.
Abstract:
NASA’s aquatic and marine research enterprise within the overarching NASA Biosphere Program is entering an era of unprecedented data abundance. MODIS and the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission already generate ocean color data at rates that strain legacy processing and archiving workflows, and forthcoming missions will add further volume and complexity. These satellite streams are joined by rapidly growing in situ networks (e.g., BGC-Argo), suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, citizen science, and increasingly high-resolution numerical models. The result is a Big Data regime in which the volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean relevant Earth system data exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches. An important goal is to fully integrate observing workflows, understanding, and models across the terrestrial, aquatic, and atmosphere domains to fully enable understanding of life and the realization of improved information to manage uses of ecosystem services. This white paper addresses Leveraging Ocean Data and Models, a cross-cutting Grand Challenge that underlies and enables progress on the four other foundational grand challenges under the NASA Biosphere, Atmosphere, Cryosphere, and Hydrosphere framework - Global Biosphere, Carbon and the Elements of Life, Interface Habitats, and Transient Events - each of which depends on the ability to acquire, harmonize, and synthesize disparate satellite, suborbital, in situ, and model data streams. We recommend a decadal strategy built on two complementary pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data, covering tiered cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, and machine learning; and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation, covering mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimilation, hybrid approaches, mission emulators, and a NASA Digital Twin Ocean. Without concerted, proactive investment in this cross-cutting infrastructure, the scientific and societal returns on the coming decade’s expanded observing system will be substantially diminished.

#3 [paper] Ocean surface currents directly imaged from space
Authors: Nicolas G. Rascle, Aurélien Ponte, Frédéric Nouguier, Renaud Binet, Dhruv Balwada, Fabrice Ardhuin, Bertrand Chapron, Bergsma Erwin
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5vv49
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The inability to directly image ocean surface currents from space, which limits understanding of ocean-climate interactions, marine ecosystems, and vertical transport of heat, carbon, and nutrients.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Direct satellite imaging of kilometre-scale surface currents using a tandem configuration of optical satellites that tracks surface wave propagation.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Satellite observations of ocean surface dynamics, including coastal jets, equatorial flows, and submesoscale motions.
Abstract:
For more than four decades, satellite images of ocean temperature and colour have revealed jets, swirling eddies, and filaments. Yet the currents that shape these structures have never been directly imaged from space. This observational gap limits our understanding of the ocean's impact on climate and marine ecosystems, as these currents modulate exchanges between the coast and open ocean, vertical transport to the deep sea, and fluxes of heat, carbon, and nutrients. Here we demonstrate the first direct satellite imaging of kilometre-scale surface currents using a tandem configuration of optical satellites that tracks surface wave propagation. This new capability shifts satellite observations beyond the predominantly geostrophic view of ocean circulation, revealing dynamics that have remained largely invisible to satellites - from intense coastal jets and equatorial flows to submesoscale motions just kilometres wide. Across these regimes, the elusive divergence of fronts and internal waves, thought to play a key role in upper-ocean vertical exchange, is concentrated at scales below 5 km, previously unresolved from space. These reference measurements provide a new observational window into the multiscale physics of the upper ocean and its mediating role for the Earth’s climate system and marine life.

#6 [paper] Data-driven coastal nutrients estimation: current status, research gaps, and future developments.
Authors: Ni, Sihan, Qi, Jin, Ran, Xiangbin, Liu, Zhiqiang, Wu, Sensen, Wang, Minyu, Yang, Keyi, Le, Chengfeng
Venue: Water research
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42748610/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The estimation of coastal nutrients from satellite observations remains a challenge because nutrients lack direct optical properties, and current data-driven methods face issues with interpretability and data scarcity.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A review of the mechanisms governing coastal biogeochemical cycling, the development of data-driven methods for remote sensing retrieval of nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon, and an analysis of the integration of machine learning with marine biogeochemical mechanisms.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global coastal waters and satellite-based remote sensing observations.
Abstract:
Driven by warming and anthropogenic impacts, global coastal waters suffer from the escalating eutrophication crisis, making it essential to understand the dynamics of nutrient discharge and enrichment. While satellites can retrieve surface water optical properties, the estimation of coastal nutrients from space remains a long-standing challenge due to their non-optical properties. Recently, artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning, has enabled the spatiotemporal estimation of surface nutrients from satellite observations, which represents a potential breakthrough for sustainable water management. In this review, we summarize the mechanisms governing coastal biogeochemical cycling and identify the estimation complexity that international scholars have been striving to solve over the past decade. We demonstrate that data-driven methods have shown preliminary success in empowering remote sensing retrieval of nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon. Despite these advances, we note that significant challenges remain for effective monitoring of coastal eutrophication due to the limited interpretability of data-driven estimation and data scarcity. A thorough analysis is provided on the developments and limitations of nutrient retrieval, the potential of integrating data-driven methods with marine biogeochemical mechanisms, and future opportunities to enhance marine ecosystem dynamic models. Ultimately, our aim is to advance satellite observations and data-driven estimation at the forefront of environmental science to develop the precise monitoring, assessment, and protection of coastal waters.

#7 [paper] Integrating anthropogenic hydrodynamics and GOCI satellite observations for water quality retrieval in highly engineered coastal systems: A case study of Saemangeum
Authors: Yejin Lee, Dongjin Kim, Suhwan Kim, Dohee Han, Hyun‐Su Kim, Jonghan Ko, Su-mi Kim, Kyeong-sang Lee
Venue: Remote Sensing of Environment
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2026.115700
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Retrieving water quality parameters in highly engineered coastal systems is challenging for standard satellite algorithms due to the complex decoupling of optical properties from natural hydrodynamics.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A physics-aware, data-driven framework that integrates anthropogenic structural drivers (seawater-exchange fluxes controlled by sluice-gate operations) with spectral data, using Random Forest, XGBoost, Transformer, and MLP-Mixer architectures, and incorporating Total Nitrogen (T-N) as an operationa…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Saemangeum Reservoir, using decadal Geostationary Ocean Color Imager (GOCI) data (2011–2020).
Abstract:
Retrieving water quality parameters in highly engineered coastal systems remains a challenge for standard satellite algorithms due to the complex decoupling of optical properties from natural hydrodynamics. This study develops a physics-aware, data-driven framework to retrieve chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) and total phosphorus (T-P) in the Saemangeum Reservoir, a representative dike-enclosed waterbody, using decadal Geostationary Ocean Color Imager (GOCI) data (2011−2020). Unlike conventional approaches relying solely on spectral data, we explicitly integrate anthropogenic structural drivers—specifically, seawater-exchange fluxes controlled by sluice-gate operations—into the modeling architecture. We systematically evaluated 255 spectral-hydrodynamic input combinations across four architectures: Random Forest, XGBoost, Transformer, and MLP-Mixer. To address the optical complexity of T-P, which lacks direct spectral absorption features, we incorporated Total Nitrogen (T-N) as an operational proxy for nutrient loading, enabling the models to capture the non-linear covariation between nutrients and optically active constituents. Our results demonstrate that incorporating anthropogenic hydrodynamic variables significantly improves retrieval accuracy, with the MLP-Mixer achieving the highest performance (Chl-a R 2 = 0.81; T-P R 2 = 0.83) by effectively learning long-term temporal dependencies. However, spatial cross-validation revealed that ensemble tree-based models offer superior generalization in spatially heterogeneous zones, suggesting a trade-off between temporal precision and spatial robustness. Explainable AI analysis further confirmed that thermal forcing, nutrient coupling, and anthropogenic hydrodynamic variables are key contributors to water-quality variability. Ultimately, this framework demonstrates a transferable modeling concept for monitoring human-modified aquatic environments, showing that explicitly accounting for anthropogenic forcing can improve satellite-based water-quality retrieval, particularly in managed systems where operational auxiliary measurements (e.g., near-real-time nutrient proxies) are available.

#1 [paper] Web data portal v.2.0 (Deliverable D7.10)
Authors: Antonio Novellino, Rachele Bordoni
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22961127
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Ensuring that research outputs (data, models, software) produced by the OCEAN ICE project remain accessible, discoverable, and useful to the scientific community beyond the project's lifetime.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of the OCEAN ICE web data portal, which integrates data discovery and visualization with the OCEAN ICE Literacy environment (web-executable Jupyter notebooks via Google Colab) to facilitate programmatic access, querying, processing, and analysis.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): OCEAN ICE project outputs and SOOSmap data products.
Abstract:
A key part of OCEAN ICE is ensuring that the data, models, software, and other research outputs produced by the project remain accessible, discoverable, and useful to the scientific community beyond the project's lifetime. Importantly, as recognised during the SOOS Scientific Steering Committee (SSC) and Data Management Sub-Committee (DMSC) meeting held at SCAR 2026 in Oslo, while the technical support and development of SOOSmap represent a key milestone of OCEAN ICE, the data products generated by the project constitute key assets for SOOSmap and its community. The OCEAN ICE web data portal therefore brings together complementary components that support the discovery, access, visualisation, analysis, and reuse of these resources. The project also provided practical tools and reproducible workflows to facilitate the use of OCEAN ICE outputs. In particular, the OCEAN ICE Literacy environment provides web-executable Jupyter notebooks through Google Colab, enabling researchers and other stakeholders to access, query, process, analyse and visualise OCEAN ICE data programmatically. Combined with SOOSmap, these resources establish a workflow that connects data discovery and visualisation with computational analysis and reproducible reuse, increasing the long-term visibility and scientific value of OCEAN ICE outputs. Together, these components constitute the overall OCEAN ICE Web Data Portal outcomes and provide a practical environment through which project resources can continue to be discovered, accessed and reused beyond the project lifetime. This approach has enabled OCEAN ICE data and products to contribute to international assessments, climate model development and multinational ocean-observing initiatives. OCEAN ICE has therefore not only delivered the planned data-management infrastructure and services, but has also established a practical, reusable framework for integrating, disseminating, and reusing polar oceanographic observations within international marine data infrastructures.

#2 [paper] Aligning Marine Spatial Data Infrastructures and Open Science for FAIR and sustainable ocean knowledge systems
Authors: Telmo Dias, Vânia Lima, João Vitorino, Ana Cristina Costa, Márcia L. Baptista
Venue: npj Ocean Sustainability
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44183-026-00246-6
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine Spatial Data Infrastructures (MSDI) and Open Science (OS) have largely evolved as separate domains, and their alignment is needed to advance FAIR and sustainable ocean knowledge systems.
Method (Mycelium's reading): An integrative review combining a quantitative bibliometric analysis of the broader Spatial Data Infrastructure (SDI) and Open Science (OS) literature with an integrative qualitative synthesis of 54 marine-domain sources (41 publications selected through PRISMA screening and 13 additional records i…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The broader Spatial Data Infrastructure (SDI) and Open Science (OS) literature, specifically focusing on 54 marine-domain sources.
Abstract:
Abstract Marine Spatial Data Infrastructures (MSDI) and Open Science (OS) have reshaped how marine data are managed, shared, and reused, but have largely evolved as separate domains. This integrative review examines how their alignment can advance FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) and sustainable ocean knowledge systems. The study combines a quantitative bibliometric analysis of the broader Spatial Data Infrastructure (SDI) and OS literature with an integrative qualitative synthesis of 54 marine-domain sources, including 41 publications selected through PRISMA screening and 13 additional records identified through snowballing. The bibliometric analysis shows separate development trajectories, but also convergence around metadata, interoperability, standards, ontology, artificial intelligence, big data, reproducibility, and FAIR principles. The qualitative synthesis shows that FAIR provides a practical bridge between MSDI and OS: MSDI contribute technical and institutional foundations for discovery, access, interoperability, stewardship, and preservation, while OS extends these foundations toward transparency, reproducibility, workflow publication, collaborative analysis, and knowledge generation. The Blue-Cloud project illustrates this alignment through federated data infrastructures, virtual research environments, and reusable workflows. We identify four priorities: credible FAIR assessment, semantic and workflow interoperability, enduring governance and maintenance, and a shift beyond data portals toward sustainable ocean knowledge systems.

#3 [paper] Leveraging Ocean Data and Models: Building the Data Infrastructure, Workforce, and Modeling Capacity to Synthesize Earth’s Ocean Observations
Authors: Susanne E. Craig, Frank Muller-Karger, Leonid Shumilo, Tzortziou Maria
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5bv4n
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean-relevant Earth system data from satellite streams, in situ networks, suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, and high-resolution numerical models exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A decadal strategy built on two pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data (cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, machine learning) and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation (mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimila…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): NASA's aquatic and marine research enterprise, including MODIS, PACE mission, and BGC-Argo data streams.
Abstract:
NASA’s aquatic and marine research enterprise within the overarching NASA Biosphere Program is entering an era of unprecedented data abundance. MODIS and the Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission already generate ocean color data at rates that strain legacy processing and archiving workflows, and forthcoming missions will add further volume and complexity. These satellite streams are joined by rapidly growing in situ networks (e.g., BGC-Argo), suborbital campaigns, genomic surveys, citizen science, and increasingly high-resolution numerical models. The result is a Big Data regime in which the volume, variety, and acquisition rate of ocean relevant Earth system data exceed the capacity of legacy processing, storage, and synthesis approaches. An important goal is to fully integrate observing workflows, understanding, and models across the terrestrial, aquatic, and atmosphere domains to fully enable understanding of life and the realization of improved information to manage uses of ecosystem services. This white paper addresses Leveraging Ocean Data and Models, a cross-cutting Grand Challenge that underlies and enables progress on the four other foundational grand challenges under the NASA Biosphere, Atmosphere, Cryosphere, and Hydrosphere framework - Global Biosphere, Carbon and the Elements of Life, Interface Habitats, and Transient Events - each of which depends on the ability to acquire, harmonize, and synthesize disparate satellite, suborbital, in situ, and model data streams. We recommend a decadal strategy built on two complementary pillars: Access and Utility of Ocean Observational Data, covering tiered cloud-based facilities, workforce training, international data sharing, and machine learning; and Numerical Models and Data Assimilation, covering mechanistic and statistical models, coupled physical-biogeochemical assimilation, hybrid approaches, mission emulators, and a NASA Digital Twin Ocean. Without concerted, proactive investment in this cross-cutting infrastructure, the scientific and societal returns on the coming decade’s expanded observing system will be substantially diminished.

#4 [paper] Advancing data integration in marine citizen science: insights from a collaborative workshop
Authors: Emilie Brévière, Nancy Fockedey, Peter Thijsse, Antonio Novellino, Patrick Gorringe, Sigmund Kluckner, Laura Khatib, Juan Martinez-Osuna
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1894836
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine citizen science data management challenges limit its full integration into scientific and policy data infrastructures, particularly due to fragmented data flows, weak community connections, and limited participant engagement.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A collaborative workshop (Marine Citizen Science Data Network) involving approximately 200 participants from over 30 countries, including initiative representatives, developers, data managers, researchers, and data users, to identify challenges and co-design recommendations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The inaugural workshop of the Marine Citizen Science Data Network (MCSDN), held in February 2026 in Ostend, Belgium, as part of the EU-funded CS-MACH1 project.
Abstract:
The ocean remains critically under-observed, particularly in coastal zones where traditional monitoring is limited by cost, logistical constraints, and competing regulatory priorities. Marine citizen science offers an emerging and powerful complementary approach to addressing these gaps; however, data management challenges currently limit its full integration into scientific and policy data infrastructures. The inaugural workshop of the Marine Citizen Science Data Network (MCSDN), held in February 2026 in Ostend, Belgium, brought together approximately 200 participants from over 30 countries. Attendees included representatives from marine citizen science initiatives, developers of low-cost monitoring devices, data managers, and researchers and data users. Together they identified challenges, opportunities and co-designed recommendations to improve marine citizen science data flows. Workshop discussions highlighted interconnected barriers and enabling factors affecting FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) marine citizen science data. These included fragmented data flows, weak connections between communities, limited participant engagement and feedback mechanisms, the potential of accessible low-cost technologies, and the need for shared practices and standardized documentation. Building on these themes, the workshop produced four concrete recommendations to enhance the reuse and impact of marine citizen science data: (1) develop discipline-specific FAIR guidance, (2) establish minimum metadata standards, (3) create simplified training materials, and (4) support the development and deployment of low-cost sensors. This perspective article presents the EU-funded CS-MACH1 project’s approach to bridging marine citizen science initiatives with European data infrastructures, and highlights the community’s readiness to deliver FAIR, impactful in situ ocean observations.

#5 [paper] An institutional analysis and development perspective of Taiwan’s oceanographic data management: an orderly chaos
Authors: Hui-Yi Katherine Tseng, Huan-Sheng Tseng
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1867067
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Evaluation of Taiwan’s oceanographic data management to identify issues and prospects for development.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework; interviews with six databanks.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Taiwan’s oceanographic data management landscape, involving multiple databanks and the Ocean Affairs Council (OAC).
Abstract:
Using the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework, this research evaluates Taiwan’s oceanographic data management and identifies issues for the prospect of its development. Six databanks were interviewed. Taiwan’s oceanographic data management remains in an orderly chaos. On one hand, it is chaotic because there exist multiple actors with their own data management rules. The fact that these databanks enact their own data management rules and operate accordingly makes the whole context even more fragmented. Therefore, community attributes are a mixture of open data and limited free data usage because revenues of data processing can cover costs of bureaucratic operation and cybersecurity measures. On the other hand, it is orderly because all databanks view open data as a public good while recognizing the importance of data management. The UN initiative of Ocean Decade serves as a strong impetus in advancing Taiwan’s oceanographic data management. Given the situation, it is debated whether integrating oceanographic data and marine-related information to one single databank, National Ocean Database and Sharing System (NODASS) positioned under Ocean Affairs Council (OAC), is economically efficient. OAC also lacks a set of reward-and-punishment rules to enforce data submission to NODASS. Meanwhile, it is also debated whether OAC should be restructured as a ministry and enact a set of generally followed rules of data management. To further develop data management and facilitate data exchange with the international oceanography community, OAC will need to cultivate professional capability while enhancing inter-agency policy coordination.

#6 [paper] Sensoring the Oceans: The Argo Floats Array in the Governance of Science Data Infrastructures
Authors: Angelina Fisher, Benedict Kingsbury, Thomas Streinz
Venue: Cambridge University Press eBooks
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009425308.010
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
What role do governance arrangements, background legal rules, and the core infrastructures play in enabling collection and production of oceans data, and other data and knowledge of planetary significance? We explore this by focusing on Argo – an international program of research institutions and state agencies that deploys arrays of autonomous environmental sensor-equipped floats to collect and process ocean observation data that is then made freely available to all. We analyze the techniques and practices involved in planning, testing, calibrating, validating, and error-correcting that ultimately lead to the production, transmission, and dissemination of Argo data. We position Argo within the institutional governance of oceans, weather, climate and, most recently, earth systems to illustrate both the evolution of Argo’s role and its evolving and uneasy position within different governance approaches. In the conclusion, we highlight the advantages of organic network-based open science-data infrastructural initiatives in the development of planetary knowledge and governance, and point to some of the risks and trade-offs if this were to become subsumed into wider and more formalized international data-infrastructure hierarchies.

#7 [paper] Digital Tech Interventions in Marine Ecosystem Monitoring: An Integrative Review
Authors: Amina Hassan
Venue: Unveiling seven continents yearbook journal
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.65326/u7y.specsdg10003
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine ecosystems are changing faster than the observation systems designed to track them. This article presents an integrative review of digital technology interventions in marine ecosystem monitoring, synthesising peer-reviewed research on sensing platforms, molecular and acoustic methods, machine learning, and ocean data infrastructures published mainly between 2014 and 2026. The review addresses three questions: which classes of digital technology now support marine ecosystem monitoring and what ecological information each supplies; which recurring technical and institutional constraints limit their contribution to sustained, decision-relevant observation; and how these classes can be combined conceptually into an architecture linking sensing to management decisions. The synthesis shows that satellite remote sensing, autonomous platforms, environmental DNA, and passive acoustics have matured within largely separate research streams, each with distinctive observational strengths and each constrained by calibration demands, energy and sensor limits, interpretive uncertainty, or fragmented data practices. Machine learning relieves an analysis bottleneck created by high-volume sensing but introduces its own validation requirements. Building on these findings, the article proposes a four-layer sensing-to-decision architecture that connects observation, analytics, data integration, and governance through explicit feedback loops, using essential ocean variables as the prioritisation logic that binds the layers together. The framework offers monitoring programme designers and ocean governance bodies a structured basis for investment and evaluation decisions, and it identifies cost-effectiveness evidence, cross-domain interoperability, and institutional data governance as priorities for future research.

#8 [paper] A Comprehensive Analysis On Ocean Observation Systems And AI Integrated Technological Implementations In Ocean Science
Authors: Abhendra Pratap Singh, Nandini Sharma, Arpit Dwivedi, Vansh Garg, Saksham Aggarwal, Aakriti Sharma, Vanshika Dua
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21701082
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The integration of ocean observing networks and artificial intelligence is changing how and who access marine information. This review looks at technological and recent innovations along with uses from the Argo and Biogeochemical-Argo programs, satellite remote sensing, autonomous underwater vehicles, and cloud-native data architectures. This review assesses the integration of these systems with Artificial Intelligence, particularly large language models enhanced with vector-database retrieval systems and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This paper discusses the major hindrances to efficient ocean data utilization like data fragmentation, also throwing light on the intricate formats like NetCDF, scalability, and policy barriers. It highlights modern practices such as practical lakehouse architectures, cloud processing, and AI systems with semantic retrieval controls. Furthermore, the review describes and discusses AI prototypes and systems built from case studies designed to assist in disaster response and mitigation, monitor climate, and manage fisheries by transforming data on spectra, profiles, and images into concise answers and easy-to-understand visual response graphics. It also talks about the persisting questions of trust, explainability, provenance, multilingual support, and inclusive engagement at the community level as the foundation of new research. These systems anticipate the provision of standard metadata, uncertainty framing, AI systems, and ethically aligned deployment pathways. Integrating resilient observing systems with human centred AI and scalable infrastructure is essential to realize a transparent, operational, and community-driven ocean-observing ecosystem promoting further research in this domain.

#9 [paper] DESIGN AND APPLICATION OF A COMPREHENSIVE SUPERVISION PLATFORM FOR OCEAN PASTURES BASED ON THE INTERNET OF THINGS: A CASE STUDY OF DONGCHANG BAY, XUWEN COUNTY, ZHANJIANG CITY, GUANGDONG PROVINCE
Authors: HuiWen Deng, Wei Jiang
Venue: Frontiers in Environmental Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.61784/fer3055
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Ocean pastures in grassroots China suffer from low intelligent equipment coverage, weak environmental risk early warning capacity, and short industrial chains for industry integration.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Construction of a four-layer comprehensive supervision platform ('perception–transmission–decision–application') consisting of four modules: intelligent environmental monitoring, intelligent aquaculture management, risk early warning and emergency response, and resource and market matching.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Dongchang Bay, Xuwen County, Zhanjiang City, Guangdong Province; water quality monitoring (spring/autumn 2019 and 2021) and 372 questionnaires from aquaculture practitioners.
Abstract:
Ocean pastures are the core carrier for restoring offshore ecosystems and conserving fishery resources, and an important lever for advancing the building of the “Blue Granary”. At the grassroots level in China, however, ocean pastures generally suffer from practical weaknesses such as low coverage of intelligent equipment, weak capacity for environmental risk early warning and short industrial chains for the integration of the primary, secondary and tertiary industries. Taking the ocean pasture in Dongchang Bay, Xuwen County, Zhanjiang City, Guangdong Province as the research object, this study conducted water quality monitoring in the spring and autumn seasons of 2019 and 2021 and combined the results with 372 valid questionnaires answered by aquaculture practitioners to establish the environmental baseline characteristics of the sea area and the needs of practitioners, and on this basis constructed a four-layer comprehensive supervision platform covering “perception–transmission–decision–application”. The platform comprises four modules: intelligent environmental monitoring, intelligent aquaculture management, risk early warning and emergency response, and resource and market matching. Benefit estimation draws on validation data for the intelligent precision feeding system for fish developed by Huazhong Agricultural University in land-based recirculating aquaculture and pond modes (a 10%–15% reduction in the feed conversion ratio) and on survival-rate data for the local “land–sea relay” mode in Zhanjiang (above 95%). Combined with the actual feed and labor expenditure of farmers in Dongchang Bay, it is estimated that after platform deployment feed waste can be reduced by 10%–15% and the aquaculture survival rate can be raised by 5%–8%.

#10 [paper] Institutional effectiveness of regional environmental management plans for deep-sea mining: the Clarion-Clipperton Zone in the BBNJ era
Authors: Weiyu Wu
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1955654
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The extent to which the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ) regional environmental management plan (REMP) can effectively translate environmental protection mandates into operational mining constraints and ecological outcomes.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Qualitative analysis of ISA instruments, the 2025 standardized procedure for REMPs, draft exploitation regulations, scientific assessments, and policy literature across four dimensions: regulatory translation, ecological coherence, implementation capacity, and adaptive management.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ) within the International Seabed Authority (ISA) legal framework and the BBNJ era.
Abstract:
The International Seabed Authority (ISA) is negotiating rules for commercial exploitation in the Area, with particular significance for the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ), which contains most polymetallic nodule exploration contract areas. The CCZ regional environmental management plan (REMP) is intended to connect the environmental protection mandate in Article 145 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) with decisions on individual projects. Yet adoption alone does not show that a plan can shape mining activity, and ecological outcomes cannot be observed before exploitation begins. This article assesses the plan’s prospective institutional effectiveness through qualitative analysis of ISA instruments, the 2025 standardized procedure for REMPs, draft exploitation regulations, scientific assessments and policy literature across four dimensions: regulatory translation, ecological coherence, implementation capacity and adaptive management. The Agreement under UNCLOS on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), now in force, leaves the ISA legal framework intact while creating a setting in which REMP decision records may support cross-institutional coordination. The analysis finds partial institutional effectiveness. The plan is embedded in ISA decision-making, but it does more to shape whether an application is approved than to define what an approved contractor must do during operations. The network of areas of particular environmental interest (APEIs) has been expanded in response to scientific evidence, yet ecological criteria have only partly shaped spatial allocation, because existing contract and reserved areas constrained network design. Contractor-level supervision is more developed than regional assessment, where cumulative environmental change cannot yet be readily linked to regulatory consequences. Periodic review identifies occasions for reconsideration but does not specify which findings should initiate which responses. These limitations converge at three institutional transmission interfaces between regional objectives and contractor obligations, ecological evidence and spatial allocation, and monitoring findings and authorized decisions. The CCZ case yields three conditions for effective REMPs: contractor-facing regulatory force, ecologically justified spatial protection, and institutionalized monitoring, review and adaptive adjustment. These conditions offer a transferable basis for future REMPs while spatial and regulatory options remain open.

#13 [paper] A FAIR-driven framework for establishing and sharing virtual observatories based on the OGC standard SensorThings API: enabling replicability and re-imagining science datalife cycle?
Authors: Tom Loree, Hervé Squividant, Nicolás Le Moine, Fabrice Rodríguez, Zahra Thomas
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-6369

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The largely overlooked challenge of designing and building environmental observatories from the ground up, specifically how to apply FAIR principles to guide their construction and enable users without prior knowledge of data standards or database systems to easily build, explore, and use them.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A framework for the creation and sharing of environmental observatories centered on the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) SensorThings API (STA), which is FAIR by design and places the STA at the core of the entire data lifecycle from conception to dissemination.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Environmental observatories and time-series data.
Abstract:
Abstract. While numerous solutions exist for publishing time-series data from environmental observatories, the question of how to design and build such an observatory from the ground up remains a largely overlooked challenge. This study pursues two main objectives: 1) to demonstrate how FAIR principles can guide the construction of an environmental observatory in a straightforward and effective manner, and 2) to enable users with no prior knowledge of data standards or databases systems to easily build, explore, and use an observatory-including finding, accessing, downloading, and understanding the data. The same accessibility extends to external users, who must equally be able to understand how the observatory is structured and what scientific objectives it serves. To this end, we develop a framework for the creation and sharing of environmental observatories centred on the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) SensorThings API (STA). This approach is FAIR by design: by placing the STA at the core of the entire data lifecycle, it enables a unified and consistent handling of all stages, from observatory conception, data acquisition to dissemination.

#14 [paper] From Ocean Data to Strategic Decisions - Hydrospatial Knowledge and Institutional Capacity
Authors: Ocean Geopolitics Centre
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23919359
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The gap between the availability of marine information and its suitability for specific decisions, as well as the institutional capacity to use it responsibly.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of a conceptual framework informed by official hydrographic guidance and ocean information initiatives, structured around four dimensions: question definition, evidence suitability, analytical accountability, and institutional use.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Conceptual analysis of maritime contexts including navigation, infrastructure, environmental protection, and ocean space allocation; illustrated via hypothetical scenarios for cable planning, coastal planning, and offshore operations.
Abstract:
Marine information supports navigation, infrastructure, environmental protection and ocean space allocation. Its availability, however, does not establish its suitability for a particular decision or an institution’s ability to use it responsibly. This working paper examines the institutional conditions under which hydrospatial knowledge can support maritime choices and cooperation. The analysis develops a conceptual framework informed by official hydrographic guidance and ocean information initiatives. Hydrospatial knowledge is treated as a perspective connecting water related information, spatial context and application. The discussion distinguishes geographical coverage from evidential fitness and examines how resolution, provenance, metadata, uncertainty and temporal relevance influence interpretation. GIS, remote sensing and machine learning are considered within this relationship between analytical capability and institutional responsibility. The paper addresses reproducibility, validation and the limits of inference, emphasising that sophisticated processing cannot compensate automatically for unsuitable observations or poorly defined questions. Interoperability is examined alongside governance arrangements, access conditions, procurement and dependence on external expertise. Four dimensions structure the proposed assessment: question definition, evidence suitability, analytical accountability and institutional use. Together, they trace the connection between a decision requirement, the information supporting it, the analytical process and the authority responsible for acting. Hypothetical illustrations concern preliminary cable planning, coastal planning and offshore operations; they demonstrate analytical questions rather than validate particular applications. The contribution is a framework connecting marine data governance with institutional capacity and strategic autonomy. Practical implications include clearer commissioning, documented assumptions, proportionate quality assurance and retained competence to evaluate external services. Cooperation is understood as a means of strengthening informed agency rather than requiring complete technological independence. The paper does not certify datasets, assess surveys or test analytical systems. Comparative research, combining documentary evidence, interviews and specialist review, is proposed to examine whether the framework identifies consequential differences in capability and improves the transparency and defensibility of maritime decisions.

Abstract:
A persistent gap between marine decision-making and local government action limits the translation of ocean knowledge into practice. This case study shows how early-career marine social science research has been mobilized across the United Kingdom through the Local Government Ocean Recovery Declaration (‘Motion for the Ocean'), a voluntary, research–practice initiative that provides a framework for local government engagement in ocean recovery. To date, participating councils represent over five million people, demonstrating both reach and public mandate. The Motion has achieved international recognition, including presentation at the 2024 UN Ocean Decade Conference and inclusion in a High-Level Ocean Panel report. Drawing on 5 years of sustained collaboration, we trace the development and impact of this model and examine the role of co-production, voluntary contributions, and cross-sector partnership in enabling research impact. The case study highlights the often-overlooked dependence on in-kind contributions, and identifies key challenges and opportunities for policy, practice, and academia in scaling place-based ocean action.

#17 [paper] Operationalising accessibility in marine pollution science communication: the Zeropol Hub case study
Authors: Kathrin Köpke, Sonya Agnew, Thomas Heising, Lisa Devriese, Nina Vaupotič, Thomas Maes, Rian Ruhl, Sabine Pahl
Venue: Frontiers in Communication
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomm.2026.1913207

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine pollution communication resources are often fragmented across platforms and vary in language, format, audience orientation, and accessibility.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Implementation case study documenting the development and early deployment of the Zeropol Hub, including workflows for resource identification, screening, scientific validation, metadata classification, accessibility-oriented organisation, maintenance, and early monitoring.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Zeropol Hub, a digital repository for science communication and educational resources on microplastics, PFAS, nutrient pollution, and underwater noise.
Abstract:
Marine pollution is a major environmental challenge, and effective communication of scientific evidence is important for supporting public engagement, environmental governance, and evidence-based decision-making. Yet marine pollution communication resources are often fragmented across platforms and vary in language, format, audience orientation, and accessibility. This implementation case study describes the development and early deployment of the Zeropol Hub, an accessibility-oriented digital repository designed to curate validated science communication and educational resources on microplastics, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), nutrient pollution, and underwater noise. We document the repository workflow for resource identification, screening, scientific validation, metadata classification, accessibility-oriented organisation, maintenance, and early monitoring. During the initial implementation period, the repository expanded from 71 to 103 resources, representing more than 20 languages and multiple communication formats. Web analytics provide descriptive indicators of early use and geographic reach, but do not measure user comprehension, inclusivity, discoverability, behavioural outcomes, or science-policy-society impact. The case study therefore demonstrates how accessibility principles can be operationalised as repository design and governance features, rather than demonstrating that these intended outcomes have already been achieved. The study offers a documented implementation approach that may inform development and evaluation of comparable environmental science communication infrastructures, while identifying user-centred and longitudinal evaluation as priorities for future research.

#18 [paper] Tampa Bay observing network: a continuous data acquisition system in support of science and environmental management
Authors: Bo Yang, Yonggang Liu, Jason A. Law, Robert H. Weisberg, Samantha E. D’Angelo, Kaili Qiao, Marcus W. Beck, Edward T. Sherwood
Venue: Environmental Monitoring and Assessment
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10661-026-16007-4

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Low-frequency, monthly field sampling is inadequate for capturing rapid, high-frequency physical and biogeochemical processes and fails to provide continuous monitoring during acute disturbance events.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Implementation of the Tampa Bay observing network (TBON), an autonomous, continuous data acquisition system designed to supplement traditional sampling and bridge data gaps.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Tampa Bay estuary.
Abstract:
The Tampa Bay estuary is a vital ecological and economic hub, whose productive, shallow-water habitats are highly vulnerable to both chronic anthropogenic stress and acute environmental disturbance events (e.g., extreme weather, human incidents). Historically, the bay's health was monitored primarily through low-frequency, monthly field sampling that has provided a foundational baseline of water quality for the last fifty years. However, discrete sampling is inadequate for capturing the rapid, high-frequency processes that govern the bay's physics and biogeochemistry. Recent perturbations to the Tampa Bay system have exposed this shortcoming and illustrated clearly the need for an autonomous, continuous data acquisition system. This paper introduces the Tampa Bay observing network (TBON), a system designed for high-frequency environmental data acquisition. In addition to detailing its design and operation, case studies are reported to demonstrate its capacity to: (1) supplement traditional low-frequency field sampling, (2) bridge data gaps, and (3) provide continuous monitoring during acute disturbance events when field sampling is impractical. This work is also aimed at informing resource managers and stakeholders about TBON's capabilities and data availability, thereby facilitating its utilization for collaborative research, environmental protection, and effective policy formulation.

Abstract:
While documenting the data management ecosystem developed throughout the project, this Handbook is a practical guide for researchers and data managers working with polar oceanographic observations and related environmental datasets on the management and publication of research outputs produced within OCEAN ICE, with particular emphasis on in situ oceanographic observations and their integration into international marine data infrastructures. The Handbook captures the experience gained during OCEAN ICE and translates it into best practices and recommendations for researchers, data managers, and future research initiatives. Rather than providing a detailed technical description of individual software components, the report adopts the research data lifecycle perspective, showing how complementary services can integrate into a coherent and sustainable data ecosystem. The report describes the publication pathways adopted for different categories of research outputs, including observational datasets, model outputs, reanalysis products, software, scientific publications and project deliverables. It introduces the main components of the OCEAN ICE Data Ecosystem, including GeoNetwork, ERDDAP, Zenodo, SOOS, EMODnet and the OCEAN ICE Jupyter Notebooks, and explains how each contributes to metadata management, data dissemination, long-term preservation, international visibility and scientific reuse. Furthermore, the handbook synthesises key lessons learned and provides a practical handover of the OCEAN ICE approach, including technical documentation, reusable configuration resources and guidance for deploying the main data services and reusing the project's interactive notebooks. #20 [paper] OceanVerse: Evaluable 4D Ocean Element Reconstruction Dataset under Realistic Sparsity
Authors: Bin Lü, Jingjing Shen, Ze Zhao, Jianping Zhou, Haonan Qi, Luyu Han, Xiaoying Gan, Meng Jin
Venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3817534
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The vast oceans record the impacts of climate change and human activities on the Earth system. Over the past century, oceanographic scientists have collected extensive ocean profile data to reflect variations of oceanic elements, such as dissolved oxygen. However, due to the sophisticated measurements and high costs, historical ocean element observation data remains highly sparse and uneven across the global ocean, with the annual missing rate exceeding 90%. Thus, quantitatively understanding the four-dimensional (4D) spatiotemporal evolution of oceanic elements continues to pose a significant challenge. Machine learning (ML) techniques demonstrate superior capabilities in perceiving spatiotemporal variations within large-scale data, presenting promising opportunities to harness implicit correlations for global reconstruction. However, fragmented data and interdisciplinary differences create barriers to the availability of AI-ready open data, further hindering ML practitioners from designing specialized models. To solve this problem, we present the first oceanic 4D sparse observation reconstruction dataset, named OceanVerse. By integrating nearly 2 million real-world profiles since 1900 and three differentiated Earth system numerical simulation, we construct a comprehensively evaluable dataset with missing patterns that align with real-world conditions through a digital twin sampling. OceanVerse provides a novel large-scale (~100× nodes vs. existing datasets) dataset that meets the MNAR (Missing Not at Random) condition, supporting more effective model comparison, generalization evaluation and potential advancement of scientific reconstruction architectures. The OceanVerse dataset and codebase are publicly available. The OceanVerse resource is available at https://github.com/jingwei-sjtu/OceanVerse.

#2 [paper] Reply on RC2 Authors: Peihao Yang, Guodong Ye Year: 2026 Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-262-cc1 Still open/current: yes Abstract: Abstract. A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. After training on multiple CMIP6 ensemble members, the constructed models are evaluated for their predictive capacity regarding MHW in the SCS. The results also show that these machine learning-based methods can perform comparably to the existing dynamic models in terms of prediction performance, and in some cases even outperform the latter. Furthermore, by incorporating machine learning interpretability techniques, the key physical processes can also be elucidated from these predictions. That is to say, the new method is not a traditional "black box", but rather an effective tool that can possess certain physical transparency and scientific interpretability.

#3 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. #1 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Abstract:
The Fulbright-Hays DDRA Fellowship Program, funded by the U.S. Department of Education (ED) and administered by the International and Foreign Language Education (IFLE) Office, provides opportunities for graduate students to conduct full-time dissertation research abroad in modern foreign languages and area studies. ED defines "area studies" as a "program of comprehensive study of the aspects of a society or societies, including the study of their geography, history, culture, economy, politics, international relations, and languages." Eligible Regions and Countries: Allowable projects are those that focus on one or more of the following geographic areas: Africa, East Asia, Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands, South Asia, the Near East, Central and Eastern Europe and Eurasia, and the Western Hemisphere (excluding the United States and its territories). Note that it may be possible to conduct research in Western Europe, provided the project itself is focused on another world region. Projects in countries designated as "closed" by Fulbright-Hays are ineligible. See the "Maintenance Allowances" section in the FY 2025 DDRA Application Instructions for details. Applications for projects in countries currently designated by the Department of State with a Level 4 travel advisory may be submitted, but awardees may end up having their travel plans delayed or canceled due to travel restrictions. Applicants may propose research projects lasting from 6 to 12 consecutive months. Projects may begin as early as January 1, 2026 and must end by March 31, 2027. Students do not apply directly to the Department of Education for these awards. Instead, applications must be submitted on behalf of the applicant by the student's institution of higher education (IHE). #14 [paper] OTOLens: Development and validation of a mobile application for assessment of tympanic membrane and middle ear pathology.
Authors: Prakairungthong, Sarun, Limviriyakul, Siriporn, Thitisomboon, Wipaluk, Bhabhatsatam, Bhattaraprot, Thongyai, Kanthong, Atipas, Suvajana, Suvarnsit, Kanokrat
Venue: American journal of otolaryngology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42790172/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVE: Diagnosing tympanic membrane and middle ear pathology in primary care is challenging due to anatomical complexity, overlapping presentations, and limited access to specialized equipment. We developed and externally validated OTOLens, a smartphone-based mobile application classifying otoscopic images using deep learning. METHODS: In this prospective development and validation study, OTOLens combined three ResNet-based image classifiers (OME, TMP, and MYR) with a parallel gradient-boosted tabular classifier operating on PCA-reduced image features, integrated by a per-condition maximum and a 0.5 decision threshold (Apple Core ML/Create ML); the system was trained on 1011 annotated otoscopic images across five categories: normal tympanic membrane (n = 251), otitis media with effusion (OME; n = 227), myringitis (MYR; n = 210), other pathology (n = 197), and tympanic membrane perforation (TMP; n = 126), labeled by three fellowship-trained otolaryngologists via majority consensus. External validation used 180 prospectively acquired images reviewed independently by three otolaryngologists. Performance metrics included sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, F1 score, and AUROC; inter-rater reliability was assessed by Fleiss' κ; application agreement by Cohen's κ. RESULTS: Internal testing demonstrated class-wise accuracy of 58-81% with AUROC up to 0.89. External validation achieved 52.8% overall accuracy (Cohen's κ = 0.417; moderate agreement). Class-specific sensitivity was 86.7% for TMP, 48.9% for OME, 40.0% for MYR, and 35.6% for normal tympanic membrane; specificity was 100% for normal tympanic membrane and MYR. Expert inter-rater reliability was substantial (Fleiss' κ = 0.681, 95% CI: 0.619-0.738). CONCLUSIONS: OTOLens achieved high sensitivity for TMP, supporting its potential as a primary care triage aid. This single stronger result does not constitute broad clinical utility; the low sensitivities for normal TM, OME, and MYR and the modest OME PPV indicate that the application cannot reliably assess these categories and should not be used in isolation. Generalizability was constrained by domain shift, class imbalance, and limited TMP representation; multicenter validation with expanded datasets is required prior to clinical deployment.

#16 [paper] A multivariate analysis of the influence of soil conditions on wheat yields
Authors: Richard Gao, Akash Anand, Lucien Lin, Justin Nguyen, Arnav Sinha
Venue: STEM Fellowship Journal
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17975/sfj-2026-025
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Rapid global population growth has led to food demand out-pacing supply, increasing food insecurity. In light of this, the United Nations declared ending hunger as its Second Sustainable Development Goal in 2015. Environmental changes from pollution and climate change further threaten food security. In this study, machine learning regression models were employed to analyze the impact of fertilizer use, soil organic carbon displacement due to erosion, surface water conductivity, soil pH, and organic carbon content on wheat yields. Permutation feature importance scores were used to evaluate the importance of each variable. Through the application of a ridgeCV stacking regression model, we identified that soil pH was the most influential variable in determining wheat yields. In the regressions tested, all p-values were below 0.005, so the null hypothesis could be rejected. The study’s results suggest that regular pH monitoring, building organic carbon-boosting infrastructure, using drainage systems, and employing sustainable agricultural practices are necessary to maximize agricultural production efficiency. Soil pH could further be protected through directed future policymaking. To expand upon the research conducted in this study, investigating the effects of climate change on properties affecting soil quality could yield valuable information on strategies to promote sustainable agriculture. Furthermore, analyzing crops other than wheat would extend the study’s results to different agricultural practices, such as tropical agriculture.
