#1 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

#2 [paper] Data and code for: An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system for Mediterranean temperate reefs: forecasting climate-driven mortality under context-dependent local protection
Authors: Jairo Castro‐Gutiérrez, Mar Bosch‐Belmar, Francesco Paolo Mancuso, Sergio Dimarca, Mario Francesco Tantillo, Gianluca Sarà
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23476372
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Static conservation strategies are outpaced by accelerating marine heatwaves, threatening temperate reefs. There is a need for prospective tools that integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability and support climate-smart Marine Spatial Planning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system using a rigorous modelling framework. It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#3 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

#4 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#5 [paper] Coupled Coastal Hazard Prediction System (CCHaPS) Hindcast for Australia
Authors: Vanessa Hernaman, Ron Hoeke, Bryan Hally, Claire Trenham, Blake M. Seers, Ben Leighton, Alberto Meucci, Emilio R. Echevarría
Venue: CSIRO
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.25919/ersf-s538
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Simulating extreme sea levels, waves, and inundation events in the Australian region, including the Great Barrier Reef, over multiple decades at high spatial resolution.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A 2D hydrodynamic and wave model (SCHISM-WWMIII v5.9) using an unstructured triangular grid with over 1.4 million nodes, forced by downscaled ERA5 winds/pressure (BARRA-R2), ORAS5 water levels, TPXOv9.2 tides, and WHACS spectral wave forcing.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Australian coastline, including the Great Barrier Reef and extending to deep offshore waters and neighboring landmasses, with a grid extending overland to a 12m elevation contour. The hindcast covers the 40-year period 1981 to 2020, extended to 2025 as of September 2026.
Abstract:
CCHaPS, the Coupled Coastal Hazard Prediction System, is a 2D hydrodynamic and wave model (Semi-implicit Cross-scale Hydroscience Integrated System Model and Wind Wave Model III, SCHISM-WWMIII), configured around the Australian coastline including the Great Barrier Reef, and extending out to deep offshore waters or neighbouring landmasses. The model simulates water levels due to astronomical tides, weather, waves and aspects of wave-flow interaction over multiple decades, allowing for full consideration of the dynamics of extreme sea levels and waves in the Australian region, at high spatial resolution from ~7km off-shore down to ~250m at the coast, and ~100m in major river mouths. The model is run on an unstructured (triangular) grid comprising over 1.4 million nodes, which extends overland up to a 12m elevation contour, to enable modelling of inundation events and sea level rise. The CCHaPS hindcast covers the 40-year period 1981 to 2020. As of September 2026, this is extended to 2025. The hindcast is forced with downscaled ERA5 winds and mean sea level pressure produced by BARRA-R2, water levels from ORAS5, tides from TPXOv9.2, and spectral wave forcing from WHACS (see Lineage). The model used is SCHISM-WWMIII v5.9, using ST4 wave physics, run on NCI's Gadi supercomputer. The dataset comprises hourly netCDF data on an unstructured grid, compliant with CF, ACDD and UGRID metadata conventions. A notebook demonstrating how to interact with the data will be attached under Supporting Documentation. Variables included are: depth (non-time varying), sea surface height, wet-dry node, currents, significant wave height, mean wave direction, peak wave direction, directional spreading, t01 and t02 mean wave period, peak wave period, peak directional spreading, peak direction (rad), and orbital velocity. The data is also stored on CSIRO infrastructure in the {ev-acs-wp3-cchaps} volume, and at NCI in /g/data/ia39/WP3/release/CCHaPS. Examples of how to work with the data in Python are provided in the accompanying notebook "CCHaPS_examples.ipynb" (see Supporting Documentation) A manuscript describing this dataset (Hernaman et al, 2026) can be found at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocemod.2026.102731

#6 [paper] Understanding ecosystem responses to recurrent marine heatwaves
Authors: Emily Lester, Stanley Mastrantonis, Sharyn M. Hickey, Anna Lafratta, Jessica A. Benthuysen, Eben Afrifa-Yamoah, Arani Chandrapavan, martial depczynski
Venue: Biological Conservation
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2026.112016
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) have emerged as an increasingly severe disturbance to global marine ecosystems, with documented intensifications in both frequency and magnitude over the past century. Western Australia has experienced some of the most severe MHWs on record, causing widespread ecological impacts, including coral bleaching and mortality, local species extinctions, and socioeconomic impacts such as fishery closures, making the region a critical case study of climate-driven change in the marine domain. Most recently, a severe MHW during summer 2024/2025 has caused widespread disruption to marine life, reinforcing the region's vulnerability to repeated extreme events. While extensive research has documented the impacts of these events, most studies have examined individual heatwaves or specific taxonomic groups in isolation, limiting our understanding of cumulative and cascading effects across the ecosystem. Here, we combine a scoping review of published and emerging evidence with oceanographic analyses to assess the cumulative ecological impacts of MHWs across Western Australia. Using iconic MHWs as case studies, we reveal widespread ecological consequences, spanning habitat degradation, mass invertebrate mortality events, food web disruption, and spatial redistribution of fisheries' indicator species. Accordingly, we propose adaptive management strategies for future MHWs. These strategies include the relocation of vulnerable species, implementation of adaptive fisheries management frameworks, and development of rapid response monitoring programs targeting key benthic indicator groups. We emphasise that the successful implementation of such strategies hinges upon the accurate and timely prediction of future MHW events.

#7 [paper] Comparing Surface and Subsurface Marine Heatwaves in Ocean Reanalyses
Authors: Vincenzo de Toma, Andrea Storto, Ronan McAdam, Antonietta Capotondi, Chunxue Yang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5747
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The subsurface expression of marine heatwaves (MHWs) is poorly constrained due to sparse in situ observations.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Detection of MHWs across multiple depths (0.5–200 m) using a consistent percentile-based thresholding applied to three reanalysis members (CGLORSv7, GLORYS2v4, ORAS5) and evaluation against the ESA Climate Change Initiative SST dataset.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Copernicus Global Ocean Reanalysis Ensemble Product (GREP) covering various depths, including historical events in Western Australia (2011), Northeast Pacific (2015), and the Mediterranean Sea (2006).
Abstract:
Abstract. Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly recognised as major drivers of ecological and socio‑economic disruption, yet their subsurface expression remains poorly constrained due to sparse in situ observations. Here, we characterise properties such as the intensity, duration, and heterogeneity of subsurface MHWs using the Copernicus Global Ocean Reanalysis Ensemble Product (GREP). MHWs are detected across multiple depths (0.5–200 m) using a consistent percentile-based thresholding, applied to three reanalysis members (CGLORSv7, GLORYS2v4, ORAS5) and evaluated against well‑documented historical events. All reanalyses successfully capture the timing and general evolution of major, well-known surface expressions of MHW events when compared against the ESA Climate Change Initiative SST dataset in given areas of interest, such as, for example, events of 2011 in Western Australia, of 2015 in the Northeast Pacific Blob, and of 2006 in the Mediterranean Sea. Here, it is also shown that anomalies frequently penetrate below the mixed layer, down to 100–150 m. On a global scale, there is a positive bias of about 15 days in the mean duration for all the events with respect to satellite SST data, consistent with the limited eddy-resolving capability of the eddy-permitting GREP reanalyses, the additional smoothing introduced by ensemble averaging and the difference between the different representative depths of SST in satellite observations and models. Global diagnostics reveal that MHWs extending into the subsurface are more persistent, spatially heterogeneous, and characterised by sharper onset and decline rates than shallow events, particularly in the tropics, western boundary currents, and the Southern Ocean. Mixed‑layer variability strongly modulates the vertical propagation of anomalies, underscoring the role of vertical mixing in shaping subsurface extremes. Our results highlight both the value and limitations of current reanalyses for subsurface MHW characterisation, emphasising the need for ensemble‑based approaches to quantify uncertainty.

#8 [paper] A robust framework for evaluating marine heatwave risk in surface and seafloor waters.
Authors: Stephanie Helen Woolley, Moninya Roughan, Robert Mason, Nicholas R. Perkins, Timothy C. Ingleton, Skipton N. C. Woolley, Joel Williams
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10915846/v1
Still open/current: yes

#9 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#10 [paper] Deeper Structure of Marine Heatwaves: Glider-Detected Anomalies in the North Sea
Authors: Charlotte Z. Reed, Victor-Alexandru Darvariu, Nick Hawes, Helen Louise Johnson
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15009434/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Satellite-derived sea surface temperatures cannot always be used to estimate the spatial structure, duration, intensity, and drivers for temperatures below the ocean surface.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Comparison of near-continuous autonomous underwater glider observations with GLORYS12V1 ocean reanalysis and regional heat content analysis.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): North Sea, specifically off the East coast of Scotland and the area between the Shetland and Orkney Islands.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves are often characterized by sea surface temperatures derived from satellite data. However, surface anomalies cannot always be used to estimate the spatial structure, duration, intensity, and drivers for temperatures below the surface. In this study, we use near-continuous autonomous underwater glider observations from a deployment off the East coast of Scotland, accompanied by the GLORYS12V1 ocean reanalysis, to examine recent high temperature anomalies in the North Sea. Glider observations show that warm and cold anomalies can be stronger below the surface than what is represented in the reanalysis, and discrepancies are often associated with differences in the timing and depth of mixed layer depth changes. Regional heat content analysis indicates that anomalies within the mixed layer are strongly influenced by surface heat fluxes, while anomalies below are more closely associated with advective heat transport, particularly inflow from the North Atlantic between the Shetland and Orkney Islands. A prolonged anomaly in 2024-2026 persisted below the surface across multiple seasons, suggesting that subsurface heat storage may hold memory between surface events. Our results demonstrate that marine heatwaves in shelf seas can have substantial subsurface structure, even in a relatively shallow and seasonally well-mixed region. Sustained glider observations can provide key observations alongside satellite and reanalysis products, improving analysis and validation of subsurface temperature anomalies in shelf seas.

#11 [paper] Marine heatwave exposure is changing unevenly across Scottish aquaculture sites
Authors: Camila Toledo-Jaime, Jennifer A. Graham, Ben Hudson, David Andrew Moffat, Bryony L. Townhill, Steven J. Palmer
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1963854
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are an increasing climate hazard for coastal aquaculture, yet regional assessments may not resolve how exposure varies across the locations where farms operate. Methods Here, we analysed daily ~5-km OSTIA sea surface temperature data from 1990 to 2025 at the locations of 361 active Scottish finfish and shellfish farms, represented by 218 unique grid cells, and compared satellite temperatures with in situ records from eight farms. We used principal component analysis and hierarchical clustering to describe long-term MHW exposure, and mixed-effects models to assess temporal changes. Results Two broad exposure profiles were identified. Cluster 1 was characterised by higher mean, maximum and cumulative intensity, whereas differences in event duration and frequency between clusters were smaller. Temporal trends, however, differed more strongly. MHW frequency increased at similar rates in both clusters, while event duration, cumulative intensity and severity increased more rapidly in Cluster 2. Between 1990 -2019 and 2020 -2025, estimated event duration increased by 44.6% in Cluster 1 and 89.9% in Cluster 2, while cumulative intensity increased by 50.0% and approximately 127.5%, respectively (cluster × period, p < 0.001). The estimated probability of a Severe or Extreme event rose from 2.2% to 26.2% in Cluster 2, compared with 1.8% to 6.1% in Cluster 1 (cluster × period, p < 0.001). Mean event intensity changed comparatively little. Discussion These findings show that MHW exposure across Scottish aquaculture is multidimensional, spatially uneven and changing at different rates through time. The resulting hazard -exposure landscape helps bridge regional MHW assessments and individual-farm monitoring, providing a foundation for more targeted monitoring and future assessment of aquaculture vulnerability and climate risk.

#12 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#13 [paper] Vertical structure and evolution of large-scale subsurface marine heatwaves
Authors: Shujing Zhang, Neil J. Holbrook, Alex Sen Gupta, Annie Foppert, Zijie Zhao
Venue: npj Climate and Atmospheric Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01592-5
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The vertical structure and evolution of large-scale subsurface marine heatwaves (MHWs) are poorly understood due to sparse long-record subsurface observations and a lack of globally consistent characterization frameworks.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A four-dimensional event-tracking framework applied to ocean temperature reanalysis data, utilizing depth rescaling and cluster analysis to identify vertical structure types.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Ocean temperature reanalysis data for the upper 1000 m of the near-global ocean (60°N–60°S) from 1993–2020.
Abstract:
Abstract Subsurface marine heatwaves (MHWs) represent hidden thermal extremes that can strongly impact marine ecosystems, particularly when they are large-scale and long-lasting. Abstract:
Most of the ocean's life and biogeochemical activity is hidden from our satellite view, occurring in a vast vertical dimension that fundamentally governs marine ecosystems, the global carbon cycle, and Earth's climate. For decades, oceanography from space has been limited to a 2D surface perspective, with early light detection and ranging (lidar) offering tantalizing but quantitatively flawed glimpses into the ocean's interior. Here, we review the significant advancement driven by high-spectral-resolution lidar (HSRL), a technology that resolves this long-standing uncertainty. By directly measuring depth-resolved optical properties, HSRL transitions ocean profiling from estimation to quantitative measurement. The recent launches of the first spaceborne HSRL systems mark a major development in this new era. This technological step enables a "virtual constellation" in which HSRL provides the vertical backbone, hyperspectral sensors add biological complexity, and the Biogeochemical-Argo (BGC-Argo) network provides in situ biogeochemical context. This synergistic system is paving the way for 4D (3D space + time) ocean monitoring, providing the essential data streams to build a predictive "ocean digital twin"-a critical tool to advance our understanding of the ocean's response to climate change and to support global efforts in sustainable development.

Abstract:
The Momental Foundation, based in Redwood, CA, is dedicated to supporting social enterprises by developing programs that help researchers and startups advance the state of science and technology for the public good. Through that project, the fellow applies his/her knowledge to a specific science or technology problem that will help the startup develop a product with social impact. Projects are intended as extracurricular, and fellows are expected to dedicated approximately 100 hours to the project. #5 [paper] STEM-Based Fikih Learning Through Solar Shadow Prayer Time Schedule Project
Authors: Ahmad Syaifulloh
Venue: Journal of General Education and Humanities
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.58421/gehu.v5i5.1969
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study investigates the effectiveness of STEM-based Fikih learning through a solar shadow prayer time schedule project at MTs Khozinatul Ulum Blora. A true experimental design with posttest-only control group was employed, involving 60 eighth-grade students randomly assigned to experimental (STEM-based Project-Based Learning) and control (traditional demonstration) groups. Students in the experimental group engaged in a four-week sundial construction project involving astronomical observation, mathematical calculation, and jurisprudential integration for determining prayer times. Data were collected using a validated Prayer Times Calculation Achievement Test and analyzed using an independent-samples t-test in JAMOVI 2.3.28. Results revealed that the experimental group achieved significantly higher learning outcomes (M = 82.7, SD = 7.09) compared to the control group (M = 73.5, SD = 9.05), with t(58) = 4.37, p < .001, and a very large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.13). The findings demonstrate that integrating STEM methodologies with Islamic jurisprudence through authentic, culturally relevant projects substantially enhances student achievement while honoring Islamic intellectual heritage. This research provides empirical evidence for curriculum reforms integrating STEM pedagogies with traditional Islamic subjects in madrasah contexts.

evidence.text: #1 [paper] Reply on RC2 Authors: Peihao Yang, Guodong Ye Year: 2026 Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-262-cc1 Still open/current: yes Abstract: Abstract. A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. After training on multiple CMIP6 ensemble members, the constructed models are evaluated for their predictive capacity regarding MHW in the SCS. The results also show that these machine learning-based methods can perform comparably to the existing dynamic models in terms of prediction performance, and in some cases even outperform the latter. Furthermore, by incorporating machine learning interpretability techniques, the key physical processes can also be elucidated from these predictions. That is to say, the new method is not a traditional "black box", but rather an effective tool that can possess certain physical transparency and scientific interpretability.

#2 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#3 [paper] Rethinking Marine Heatwaves: Towards a Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress
Authors: Natalija Dunić, Krešimir Ruić, Ivica Vilibić
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15011394/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard marine heatwave (MHW) definitions rely on statistical temperature anomalies relative to a climatological baseline, which does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic examples used to demonstrate the estimation of response functions from biological observations and the derivation of binary event definitions.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

#4 [paper] Assessing Challenges for U.S.-Based Polar Early Career Scientists During Science Policy Changes
Authors: Fairuz Ishraque, Mohammad Afzal Shadab, Kevin Shionalyn, Neosha Narayanan, Meghan Schaberg, Shreyas Gaikwad, Izuchukwu Ezukanma, Olga Lauter
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5nr5s
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Early-career researchers (ECRs) play a critical role in sustaining polar and cryosphere research in the United States. Since January 2025, changes in U.S. science policy and federal research funding have created substantial uncertainty for researchers, particularly those in the early stages of their careers. To assess the impacts of these changes, we conducted a community-driven survey of U.S.-based polar and cryosphere ECRs examining concerns related to science policy, research funding, career trajectories, and workforce retention. Survey responses indicate widespread concern regarding recent changes in science policy and funding, with many respondents reporting negative effects on research productivity, motivation, and mental well-being. Respondents also expressed concern regarding future employment opportunities and the long-term health of the scientific enterprise. A substantial proportion reported considering employment opportunities outside the United States, leaving academia, or leaving polar and cryosphere research altogether. At the same time, respondents identified potential pathways for retention, including stable research funding, mentorship, professional support, and reversal of recent funding reductions. These findings provide a timely assessment of workforce sentiment during a period of rapid policy change and highlight factors that may influence the future sustainability of the U.S. polar and cryospheric research community.

#5 [paper] Constitutive Expression Differences and Thermal Responses of Stress-Associated Transcripts in Pacific Abalone.
Authors: Cui, Xuefan, Lan, Di, Lin, Huaqing, Yang, Weilong, Liu, Xin, Liu, Qiwen, Nian, Shushan, Li, Zhaoxian
Venue: Biology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42939486/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
We examined basal and exposure-associated transcript abundance in Pacific abalone. Pi3k, Akt, mTOR, Hsf1, Hsp70, and Hsp90 were compared across five anatomical samples and between heat-selected and common populations after identical two-week acclimation. Five transcripts were examined during adult exposure to 30 °C for up to 72 h and after a 15 min larval heat shock. Basal groups had three animal samples; population and adult groups had two or three analyzed samples. Larval groups comprised three pools of 500 individuals. Qualitative histology used three animals per condition. Welch tests on log2 values used Holm correction. Selected animals had higher hepatopancreatic Pi3k, Akt, mTOR, and Hsp70 levels. Hepatopancreatic Hsf1/Hsp70 means were highest at 12 h and Pi3k/Akt means at 24 h; peak times were not statistically compared. All five transcripts increased within late-veliger samples, without establishing a stage-by-treatment interaction. Histology showed local discontinuities, including in controls. These patterns identify candidate transcript-level indicators. One adult tank per condition, absent time-matched control comparisons, unverified larval culture independence, small samples, normalization uncertainty, population-history confounding, and absent protein endpoints and direct tolerance measurements limit interpretation.

#7 [paper] Submesoscale feedback suppresses marine heatwaves.
Authors: Dong, Jihai, Sun, Wenjin, Fox-Kemper, Baylor, Jing, Zhiyou, Dong, Changming
Venue: Science advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42905811/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are devastating extreme ocean temperature events whose frequency and severity have surged under global warming, threatening marine ecosystems and fisheries. Yet, the fundamental mechanisms that control their intensity and persistence remain incompletely understood. Here, using a submesoscale-permitting global model simulation validated by long-term observational and reanalysis data, this study reveals a previously overlooked submesoscale feedback that exerts a critical control on MHW severity. It is demonstrated that the submesoscale-induced vertical heat flux suppresses the intensity and persistence of atmosphere-driven MHWs in winter via a negative feedback mechanism. Enhanced air-sea net heat flux strengthens stratification and shoals the mixed layer, weakening submesoscale vertical heat transport by 19.4%, reducing MHW intensification by 18.1%, and accelerating decay by 21.7%. This missing regulatory mechanism indicates that models ignoring the submesoscale feedback likely overestimate MHW severity, with critical implications for future climate projections.

#8 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#9 [paper] High Temporal Resolution Gene Expression Analysis Reveals Contrasting Dynamics of Thermal Tolerance in the Coral Porites astreoides From the Florida Keys.
Authors: Parker, Katherine E, Locatelli, Nicolas S, Conn, Trinity L, Vlcek, Emma L, Radice, Veronica Z, Evensen, Nicolas R, Baums, Iliana B, Voolstra, Christian R
Venue: Molecular ecology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43031455/

Abstract:
Rising ocean temperatures threaten coral reefs, yet thermal tolerance varies among coral species and populations. Using the Coral Bleaching Automated Stress System (CBASS), we examined thermal thresholds and transcriptomic dynamics in two wild Porites astreoides populations from thermally contrasting habitats with documented differences in bleaching susceptibility: a more tolerant Inshore population vs. a more sensitive Offshore population. RNA-sequencing at six timepoints during a 19-h acute heat stress assay, coupled with photosynthetic efficiency measurements (Fv/Fm), revealed a higher standardized thermal tolerance threshold, that is, effective dose (ED50), in Inshore corals (37.77°C) compared to Offshore corals (36.94°C), supporting previous observed differences from a longer-term heat stress experiment. Importantly, at 34°C, the lowest heat stress applied, the Offshore population consistently exhibited more differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with a higher magnitude of change than the Inshore population. For example, during peak stress, there were 1136 DEGs expressed at higher magnitude in Offshore corals compared to just 50 Inshore. Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed temperature as the primary driver of transcriptional variation (explaining 30% of the variance along PC1), while population origin accounted for a smaller but significant proportion (21% along PC2). Inshore corals displayed a muted transcriptomic response and rapid recovery, whereas Offshore corals exhibited larger, delayed responses. We interpret these response differences as transcriptomic resilience and acclimation; two emerging mechanistic patterns associated with increased coral thermal tolerance. No evidence of gene expression frontloading was detected, suggesting epigenetic or post-transcriptional regulation may underlie the observed resilience differences. Our results demonstrate long-term, fine-scale population differences in resilience mechanisms, suggesting stable thermal tolerance strategies that can inform future conservation efforts.

#11 [paper] Deeper Structure of Marine Heatwaves: Glider-Detected Anomalies in the North Sea
Authors: Charlotte Z. Reed, Victor-Alexandru Darvariu, Nick Hawes, Helen Louise Johnson
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15009434/v1

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Satellite-derived sea surface temperatures cannot always be used to estimate the spatial structure, duration, intensity, and drivers for temperatures below the ocean surface.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Comparison of near-continuous autonomous underwater glider observations with GLORYS12V1 ocean reanalysis and regional heat content analysis.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): North Sea, specifically off the East coast of Scotland and the area between the Shetland and Orkney Islands.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves are often characterized by sea surface temperatures derived from satellite data. However, surface anomalies cannot always be used to estimate the spatial structure, duration, intensity, and drivers for temperatures below the surface. In this study, we use near-continuous autonomous underwater glider observations from a deployment off the East coast of Scotland, accompanied by the GLORYS12V1 ocean reanalysis, to examine recent high temperature anomalies in the North Sea. Glider observations show that warm and cold anomalies can be stronger below the surface than what is represented in the reanalysis, and discrepancies are often associated with differences in the timing and depth of mixed layer depth changes. Regional heat content analysis indicates that anomalies within the mixed layer are strongly influenced by surface heat fluxes, while anomalies below are more closely associated with advective heat transport, particularly inflow from the North Atlantic between the Shetland and Orkney Islands. A prolonged anomaly in 2024-2026 persisted below the surface across multiple seasons, suggesting that subsurface heat storage may hold memory between surface events. Our results demonstrate that marine heatwaves in shelf seas can have substantial subsurface structure, even in a relatively shallow and seasonally well-mixed region. Sustained glider observations can provide key observations alongside satellite and reanalysis products, improving analysis and validation of subsurface temperature anomalies in shelf seas.

#12 [paper] Comparing Surface and Subsurface Marine Heatwaves in Ocean Reanalyses
Authors: Vincenzo de Toma, Andrea Storto, Ronan McAdam, Antonietta Capotondi, Chunxue Yang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5747

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The subsurface expression of marine heatwaves (MHWs) is poorly constrained due to sparse in situ observations.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Detection of MHWs across multiple depths (0.5–200 m) using a consistent percentile-based thresholding applied to three reanalysis members (CGLORSv7, GLORYS2v4, ORAS5) and evaluation against the ESA Climate Change Initiative SST dataset.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Copernicus Global Ocean Reanalysis Ensemble Product (GREP) covering various depths, including historical events in Western Australia (2011), Northeast Pacific (2015), and the Mediterranean Sea (2006).
Abstract:
Abstract. Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly recognised as major drivers of ecological and socio‑economic disruption, yet their subsurface expression remains poorly constrained due to sparse in situ observations. Here, we characterise properties such as the intensity, duration, and heterogeneity of subsurface MHWs using the Copernicus Global Ocean Reanalysis Ensemble Product (GREP). MHWs are detected across multiple depths (0.5–200 m) using a consistent percentile-based thresholding, applied to three reanalysis members (CGLORSv7, GLORYS2v4, ORAS5) and evaluated against well‑documented historical events. All reanalyses successfully capture the timing and general evolution of major, well-known surface expressions of MHW events when compared against the ESA Climate Change Initiative SST dataset in given areas of interest, such as, for example, events of 2011 in Western Australia, of 2015 in the Northeast Pacific Blob, and of 2006 in the Mediterranean Sea. Here, it is also shown that anomalies frequently penetrate below the mixed layer, down to 100–150 m. On a global scale, there is a positive bias of about 15 days in the mean duration for all the events with respect to satellite SST data, consistent with the limited eddy-resolving capability of the eddy-permitting GREP reanalyses, the additional smoothing introduced by ensemble averaging and the difference between the different representative depths of SST in satellite observations and models. Global diagnostics reveal that MHWs extending into the subsurface are more persistent, spatially heterogeneous, and characterised by sharper onset and decline rates than shallow events, particularly in the tropics, western boundary currents, and the Southern Ocean. Mixed‑layer variability strongly modulates the vertical propagation of anomalies, underscoring the role of vertical mixing in shaping subsurface extremes. Our results highlight both the value and limitations of current reanalyses for subsurface MHW characterisation, emphasising the need for ensemble‑based approaches to quantify uncertainty.

#13 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

Abstract:
Abstract Recent studies have shown that marine heatwaves (MHWs) with similar surface signals can have distinct subsurface vertical structures; however, the processes associated with these differences remain an open question. MHW heat budgets have predominantly been examined at the mixed-layer scale, and the components of oceanic forcing in the subsurface have received less attention. We classified MHWs in the southwestern East Sea by their vertical structures and analyzed the associated heat transfer patterns. By applying K-means clustering to MHW events identified from detrended sea surface temperatures, we categorized the vertical structures into four types: subsurface-intensified, deep, shallow, and subsurface-reversed. We then analyzed the heat budget of each type by decomposing the lateral heat flux into dynamical (associated with velocity anomaly) and thermodynamical (associated with temperature anomaly) components. In the shallow type, the net surface heat flux term contributed most to the warming. In the subsurface-intensified and deep types, the dynamical component contributed more to the warming than the thermodynamical component, particularly in the subsurface-intensified type. In the subsurface layer, however, the thermodynamical component exerted a cooling effect, partially offsetting the dynamical warming. This study demonstrates that the dynamical and thermodynamical contributions to the lateral heat flux vary substantially among MHW types.

#19 [paper] Recent extreme heatwaves are no match for future events

Abstract:
Abstract In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21 st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. Abstract:
Abstract Subsurface marine heatwaves (MHWs) represent hidden thermal extremes that can strongly impact marine ecosystems, particularly when they are large-scale and long-lasting. Here we apply a four-dimensional event-tracking framework to ocean temperature reanalysis data to identify and characterize over 500 large-scale subsurface MHWs in the upper 1000 m of the near-global ocean (60°N–60°S) from 1993–2020. Method (Mycelium's reading): Developing a methodology to integrate machine learning (ML) with CFD models of OIDPs.

Abstract:
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has played a crucial role in providing an alternative bioequivalence (BE) approach for generic orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), in addition to comparative clinical endpoint or pharmacodynamic BE studies, as a relatively cost- and time-efficient complement to benchtop and clinical experiments that has been widely used in developing and assessing generic inhaler devices. However, despite the advances in the power of modern computers, there are still some bottlenecks in using CFD due to computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications. Machine learning (ML) has been gaining more attention as a potential tool to alleviate such limitations that arise in CFD. The purpose of this grant is to develop a methodology to integrate ML with CFD models of OIDPs to promote alternative BE studies to enhance and accelerate the development and approval of generic OIDPs.

Abstract Robocalls, spam texts, and scam calls all exploit one design assumption: anyone who knows a phone number, SIP URI, or messaging handle can attempt contact. Existing defences answer different questions. STIR/SHAKEN verifies who is calling, not whether that caller is permitted to reach this recipient now. Virtual and masked numbers hide the real number but stay dialable while active. OAuth delegates API access but defines no telecom reachability rules. Each inbound call, message, or notification is held as a candidate request until an enforcement point, such as a session border controller, SIP application server, IMS node, or CPaaS gateway, validates a recipient-scoped grant bound to sender, recipient, purpose or transaction, channel, expiry, attempt quota, revocation epoch, and audience, with replay protection and sender binding so that a copied grant is not a bearer credential. Only then does the phone ring or the message get delivered; otherwise the request is rejected (for example with SIP 403) before any communication takes effect. Three deployment profiles, blocked path, pre-routing authorization, and absent path, allow incremental rollout over existing E.164 numbering, SIP, IMS, and PSTN infrastructure, while emergency calls (911/112) and lawful intercept remain unaffected. The gap grows as AI agents and AI-native 6G networks originate contact at machine speed. The record includes use cases (map and directory enquiries, marketplaces, ride and delivery, AI assistants), a comparison with existing approaches, a candidate grant format, possible STIR/PASSporT, SIP, and OAuth encodings, security and privacy analysis, a 58-question telecom engineering FAQ, and five workflow charts. A reference implementation is publicly available. Its central principle: possession of a communication identifier is not, by itself, permission to communicate. Download the full PDF to review the workflow charts, grant format, deployment profiles, and complete FAQ. An AI system can give warranted answers and perform authorized, recoverable operations while the arrangement in which it works remains unjustified. The paper argues that where a consequential arrangement defended as supporting a person's agency helps shape the endorsements, preferences or evidence later cited for its continuing authority, those items cannot by themselves certify that authority unless their admissibility remains open to the person's challenge, directly or through a representative, by an effective route whose outcome does not depend solely on the criteria in dispute. The constraint applies a structure that Forst states for power in general, and Abukar for classification evidence, to endorsements an assistant helped produce; Lazar places AI's shaping of beliefs and desires within governing power. Building on work holding that legitimate acts do not aggregate into legitimate continuing authority and that power must answer to those subject to it, the paper offers a critical synthesis and internal correction of the program, not a new general theory. Of the three readings it withdraws, one was stated as a rule in the program's position paper and two were invited by its earlier formulations. It states five procedural specifications as design hypotheses: handoffs that reset neither a challenge nor its elapsed time; a terminal record of failed review that cannot be relabelled as a merits decision; a missed containment-review deadline treated as failure, not permission; continuity triage protecting separable assistance; and longitudinal comparison of the arrangement against a reference not controlled solely by the disputed profile. Constructed cases test the distinctions. The paper reports no empirical measurement of its own; §10.5 summarizes the confirmatory technical results of a preregistered companion study now in preparation, which, on its deposit, will carry the protocol, code and data: that study has confirmed the specifications' implementability and specified behaviour under scripted trajectories, and their normative work in real institutions remains untested. **Keywords:** AI delegation; answer entitlement; revisable authority; contestability; right to justification; influenceable preferences; endorsement; practical judgment; critique; human-AI interaction; MOBIUS. Release type: conceptual paper, a critical synthesis within the answer-entitlement program; the paper reports no empirical measurement of its own, and §10.5 summarizes the confirmatory technical results of the preregistered companion study (Toeda 2026g), which, on its deposit, will carry the protocol, code and data. Revisions in versions 0.2–0.4 responded to review comments that the author obtained from ChatGPT (OpenAI) and supplied to the drafting agent. #2 [paper] Computing Spectral Properties of Differential Operators on Surfaces
Authors: Gustav Conradie, Matthew J. Colbrook, Daniel Fortunato
Venue: arXiv (Cornell University)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2609.37764
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Computing spectra of differential operators on surfaces is crucial in many applications, ranging from medical image analysis to nanoscale quantum structures. However, discretization of the infinite-dimensional operator and the underlying surface can lead to inaccurate and misleading results. This paper introduces the SurfSpec suite of algorithms to compute eigenvalues and spectral measures of operators on surfaces with error control and convergence guarantees. We combine methods based on complex contour integration and residuals to compute discrete spectra and high-frequency eigenmodes, including of nonlinear eigenvalue problems. We then compute convolutions of spectral measures with rational kernels to deal with continuous spectra. In both cases, the key tool is the operator resolvent applied to functions, which is computed using high-order methods that solve surface PDEs. We illustrate our algorithms on a variety of differential operators and surfaces, including a triceratops.

#3 [paper] Optical architectures for information processing: advances in pattern recognition, phase imaging, and image encryption.
Authors: Mohapatra, Jyoti Bikash, Pal, Akash, Kumar, Ram, Kumar, Rahul, Rao, Sonu Kumar, Tripathi, Shivam, Nishchal, Naveen K
Venue: Journal of the Optical Society of America. A, Optics, image science, and vision
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42862992/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Optical information processing is a powerful paradigm due to its inherent parallelism, high speed, and multidimensional processing capability. This study provides a comprehensive overview of optical architectures for information processing, with particular focus on optical pattern recognition, phase retrieval techniques, and optical security frameworks. Optical correlators are among the most significant implementations of optical information processing for pattern recognition. They can correlate vast amounts of data simultaneously by exploiting the inherent parallelism of light, enabling processing at the speed of light. The unparalleled computational capability surpasses the performance limits of conventional electronic processors, making optical correlators highly suitable for real-time and high-throughput pattern recognition applications. Various parameters of the optical field provide distinctive and versatile means to encode information. Properties such as amplitude, phase, polarization, wavelength, and orbital angular momentum enable multidimensional data representation, thereby enhancing encoding capability, security, and transmission efficiency. Further, optical imaging techniques have advanced significantly, delivering improved resolution, contrast, and functional imaging capabilities. A significant contribution to this progress comes from phase retrieval techniques, which reconstruct phase information from intensity-only measurements. Collectively, these approaches demonstrate the potential of hybrid optical-digital systems for next-generation imaging and information processing applications.

Vibrational spectroscopy, specifically based on infrared absorption and Raman scattering, has emerged as a viable alternative to current biomedical diagnostic techniques, providing label-free, biochemically based early disease detection and precise diagnosis. #1 [grant] EIC Pre-accelerator - Widening
Amount: €500,000–€1,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-WIDERA-2027-01-WIDENING-01
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-11-18
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

This call will increase the innovation potential of deep-tech startups in the Widening countries and enable them to better attract private investments and scale up. It will further strengthen the innovation dimension of the widening component and increase the overall competitiveness of these countries.

The specific outcome expected of this action is increased business, investor, and technology readiness of high potential deep-tech startups in Widening countries to a level where they will:

- be successful in applying and attracting the EIC Accelerator funding and/or;

- manage to secure other private investment and/or;

- attract successfully national or regional funding as alternative funding sources (e.g. through Seal of Excellence programmes).

Scope:

This action focuses on early-stage deep-tech startups which 1) have high-impact innovation technology, product, service, or business model that could create new markets or disrupt existing ones, and 2) have the ambition and commitments to scale up.

The successful applicants need to work on deep tech innovation. Such companies often struggle to attract financing because the technology and investment risks are too high.

In the framework of this call, deep-tech[1] is technology that is based on cutting-edge scientific advances and discoveries and is characterised by the need to stay at the technological forefront by constant interaction with new ideas and results from the lab. Deep-tech innovations are understood to be those that have the potential to deliver transformative solutions, rooted in cutting-edge science, technology, and engineering, including innovation that combines advances in the physical, biological and digital spheres. Deep-tech is distinct from ‘high-tech’ which tends to refer only to R&D intensity[2].

This EIC Pre-accelerator - Widening call is designed to enable promising deep-tech startups to develop further their innovations (from TRL 4 to TRL 5/6)[3], attract the investment amounts needed for scale up in a shorter timeframe and successfully apply and attract funding from EIC Accelerator or other sources.

The applicants are expected to demonstrate in their application that they:

- have completed all elements of TRL 3 (Experimental proof of concept) and therefore the technology is currently at TRL 4 (Technology validated in lab);

- possess the necessary Intellectual Property Rights to ensure freedom to operate and adequate protection of the idea;

- have a clear vision on the intended pathway and route to market. This includes specific milestones together with concrete and verifiable KPIs to assess progress towards the market.

The support will be in awarded by grants max at 70% funding of the eligible costs. 30% co-funding to be covered by the beneficiary through its own resources.

An amount between EUR 500.000 and max EUR 1.000.000 in the form of a lump sum for a period of up to 2 years is considered appropriate.

The requested grant is expected to be used for:

- addressing the investor and market readiness towards commercialisation and deployment (market research, value proposition, business case and business model, prospects for growth, intellectual property protection, competitor analysis etc.) and if relevant, aspects of regulation, certification and standardisation, aimed at getting both the technology and the business idea investment ready and/or;

- the maturation and validation of novel technologies beyond proof of concept to viable demonstrators of the technology in the intended field of application (i.e., from minimum TRL 4 up to TRL 6).

At the end of the EIC Pre-accelerator project, it needs to:

- demonstrate that the technology component of their innovation has at least been validated in a relevant environment (e.g. at least completed all aspects of TRL 5);

- be ready to apply for EIC Accelerator and/or to seek other investors or sources of funding, to enter licensing or collaboration agreements with third parties

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to some or all of the following expected outcomes:

- Development of a mature technological solution addressing EU security policy priorities in the areas addressed by the Cluster 3 work programme and in particular the destination of fighting crime and terrorism, disaster resilient societies, border management and resilient infrastructure;

- Facilitate increased and sustained collaboration between small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), public research partners, and academia, leading to improved knowledge transfer within the European innovative SME ecosystem;

- Mitigate difficulties in access to finance and new international markets, thereby enhancing the growth and expansion of European innovative SMEs.

Scope:

Europe’s 25 million small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are the backbone of the EU economy. SMEs can bring innovation to societal challenges, including the security of EU citizens. Innovative SMEs and high-tech start-ups can transform and modernise EU security capabilities.

However, despite the innovation capacity of EU SMEs, these often experience difficulties in finding their way to the public markets. These include red tape in public contracts, access to new customers, access to finance, industrial competition and Intellectual Property (IP) valorisation. These difficulties are exacerbated in markets that show restrictions of different kind, as it is the case of security.

Knowing that SMEs require additional support to reach the security buyers and that the collaboration opportunities offered by the projects of the Pillar II of Horizon Europe can be a catalyst for uptake, this topic aims to offer a collaborative environment for small and medium innovators to tailor their innovations to the specific needs of civil security end-users, taking into account the urge to address the diverse needs of all citizens, regardless of gender, age or ability.

Applicants are invited to submit proposals for technology development along with the following principles:

- Focus on mature technological solutions addressing EU security policy priorities in the areas addressed by the Cluster 3 Work Programme;

- Fostering collaboration between SMEs from different Member States and Associated Countries;

- Involving security end-users in the role of validator and potential first-adopter of the proposed innovations;

- Fostering collaboration schemes between small companies and research and technology organisations and/or big industrial players aimed at fostering innovative technology transfer or creating innovative business models that facilitate access to market and strengthen the innovation capacity of EU SMEs and start-ups in the domain of civil security.

Examples of activities to plan in the proposed projects include, but are not limited to: assimilating market requirements; facilitating access to additional funding; approaching potential public buyers; assess competitive landscape; supporting in innovation management (methodological and process innovation, business model innovation, market innovation); assist in IP management and exploitation; provide guidance for expansion to future markets, etc.

The participation of research and technology organisations should not focus on own technology development but on supporting the small industrial players in accelerating the technology transfer of innovative security solutions for their further development and production.

It is encouraged that one SME takes the coordinator role[1]. If the coordinator is not an SME, this should be duly justified.

The projects should have a maximum estimated duration of 2 years.

Under this topic, projects should address one of the following areas addressed by the Cluster 3 work programme: Fighting Crime and Terrorism (FCT, Option A), Disaster-Resilient Society (DRS, Option B), Resilient Infrastructure (INFRA, Option C), Border Management (BM, Option D).
