#4 [paper] Risks of Mandatory Publications in International Scientific Journals in the Context of Ensuring National Security
Authors: Ihor F. Korzh
Venue: INFORMATION AND LAW
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.37750/2616-6798.2026.3(58).376741
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the problem of the mandatory publication of scientific results in journals indexed in the international scientometric databases Scopus and Web of Science, in the context of modern Ukrainian scientific discourse. The relevance of the study is due to the fact that these databases are increasingly perceived not only as a tool for integrating Ukrainian science into the global academic space, increasing the visibility of research results and ensuring certain quality standards, but also as a de facto mandatory condition for a scientific career, certification, accreditation of educational programs and defense of dissertations. Under such conditions, bibliometric indicators often begin to replace a substantive assessment of scientific novelty, methodological soundness and social significance of research, and publication activity itself becomes an end in itself. The paper proves that the problem of mandatory publication in Scopus and Web of Science cannot be considered only as a technical or administrative issue. It has a deep theoretical, methodological, institutional and ethical dimension. On the one hand, international indexing contributes to the openness of science, its inclusion in global communication networks, increased citations and dissemination of research results. On the other hand, excessive formalization of publication requirements creates risks of commodification of knowledge, when a scientific result is evaluated not so much by its truth, novelty or benefit to society, but by its ability to meet market and bureaucratic criteria. This, in turn, contributes to the spread of practices of academic capitalism, the emergence of a shadow market for intermediary services, as well as the intensification of the activities of so-called "predatory" publications that imitate scientific communication without proper peer review and compliance with ethical standards. Particular attention is paid to the methodological imbalance in the assessment of science. It is shown that a unified approach, based mainly on quantitative metrics - the number of publications, citations, Hirsch index, impact factor of journals, grant funding amounts - does not take into account the specifics of individual fields of knowledge. First of all, this applies to socio-humanitarian, artistic and some social disciplines, which are characterized by local issues, national and cultural conditioning of the subject, the importance of Ukrainian studies discourse and the need to use national languages ​​and professional publications. In such cases, focusing exclusively on English-language international journals is not always methodologically justified, and sometimes even narrows the possibilities of fully presenting research results that are important for national security, cultural identity and development of the state. The article also analyzes the institutional consequences of the introduction of strict requirements for publications in Scopus/WoS. It is established that the transformation of publication from a tool of scientific communication into a formal bureaucratic marker leads to a distortion of researchers' motivation, increased publication pressure, fragmentation of results, an increase in the number of formal or insignificant articles, as well as inefficient spending of budgetary and private funds. For many scientists, especially young researchers, postgraduate students and teachers, such a system creates additional barriers to reach academic recognition, forcing them to adapt to formal criteria that do not always adequately reflect the real scientific value of the work. Emphasis is placed on the financial pressures that accompany the modern publishing model. The text emphasizes that significant author's fees for publication in international journals, long review periods, as well as limited deadlines for the completion of scientific topics create unequal conditions for Ukrainian researchers. #7 [paper] Autonomy without immunity: conventionality control and the limits of sporting sovereignty in the Inter-American system
Authors: Roberto Leonardo Cruz-Núñez, Hugo Armando Aguilar Brito, Andherson Jhordan Aguirre-Lanegra, Nuccia Seminario-Hurtado
Venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2026.1949642
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Professional athletes and clubs can compete only if they accept the jurisdiction of an arbitral tribunal seated outside their own country. International federations rely on that arrangement to claim immunity from judicial review; this article calls that claim sporting sovereignty. European courts have narrowed it by holding that compulsory sports arbitration must satisfy fair-trial guarantees, but protection there still depends on the courts of the state where the federation is seated and on a narrow reading of public policy, so the substance of a discrimination complaint may go unexamined. This article asks how far Articles 8 and 25 of the American Convention on Human Rights limit the rule-making authority of transnational sports organisations in states parties, through conventionality control, the duty of every domestic authority to test the rules it applies against the treaty. It proceeds by doctrinal legal analysis and by comparing the European and Inter-American standards of review, and it examines four jurisdictions: Peru, Colombia, Chile and Brazil. Inter-American judicial guarantees attach to the function a body exercises rather than to its formal character; they reach private power through the state's duty to ensure rights; and every domestic authority must apply them of its own motion, wherever the federation is seated. The comparison shows that Brazil and Chile channel contractual and employment disputes between player and club to the state courts, and that Colombia protects players through the constitutional action of tutela, so that closure is confined to disciplinary, eligibility and competition matters; Peru is the exception, having legislated the primacy of federation rules without such limits. In the Peruvian and Colombian cases examined, the delays that harmed a club and a player came from federation bodies overrunning their own deadlines, which undermines the argument that speed requires exemption from review. Sporting sovereignty is thus a delegated and conditioned authority. The article proposes a criterion of conditioned autonomy under which the power of federations is legitimate where it pursues a permissible aim, observes procedural guarantees, decides while a decision can still serve the person affected, and respects the substantive limit of human dignity and non-discrimination.

Abstract:
The Graduate College's Dean’s Doctoral Fellowship (DDF) supports the recruitment of academically talented students whose educational pathways and experiences may include financial, institutional, or other barriers to graduate education. The fellowship reflects the Graduate College’s commitment to expanding access to graduate education and strengthening the Illinois graduate community by recruiting students from many educational, geographic, and familial backgrounds. The DDF provides financial support to students who demonstrate strong potential for success in graduate study and whose pathways to graduate education reflect significant barriers or nontraditional routes. Through this recruitment fellowship, the Graduate College seeks to expand opportunities for talented students to pursue doctoral education at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and to connect fellowship recipients with programs and resources that support their transition to and success in graduate education. Eligibility and Selection Criteria DDFs are intended as recruitment fellowships. To that end, only those students who are seeking admission to a doctoral program at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (Illinois) are eligible. Generally, this includes students at either one of two stages of study: students seeking first-time admission to a doctoral program, or students who have completed a master’s at Illinois and are now applying for admission to a doctoral program here at Illinois. Students in approved cost-recovery or self-supporting programs are not eligible for nomination. The list of such programs can be found here . Only those students intending to enter during the 2027-28 academic year are eligible. For students intending to enter in Spring 2028, their fellowship will not begin until Fall 2028. Full-time Illinois employees are ineligible. Students who have previously received a Graduate College Equity Master's Fellowship (EMF) or an Aspire Master's Fellowship remain eligible for consideration for the Dean’s Fellowship, provided they meet all other eligibility requirements. Candidates must be U.S. citizens, permanent residents, or approved domestic applicants . (If the student is tagged in Slate as "domestic," the student meets this criterion.) The Dean’s Doctoral Fellowship is open to newly admitted students in an Illinois doctoral degree program who: Demonstrate academic achievement and potential for success in graduate study (as assessed by the nominating department, transcript, honors, or other designation); and Have experienced financial hardship, are first generation in their families to attend college, experienced barriers to educational access, or followed a non-traditional path to graduate education; and Have demonstrated their ability to contribute to a community characterized by inclusion, belonging, respect, and productive collaboration. Candidates should provide an example of how they have engaged with students, colleagues, or communities with different perspectives, abilities, and experiences to achieve a positive outcome and reflect on what they learned from the experience. Award Structure – Two Versions: The DDF pays $75,000 in total stipend over the duration of the fellowship. However, there are two versions of the fellowship, each with its own payment structure. At the time of nomination, the department must select which version to offer the student. If awarded, students may not switch to the other version. Version 1: $25,000 annual stipend for three years, plus a full tuition waiver. This option is primarily for departments that intend for the fellowship to serve as the student’s main source of funding for the three “on fellowship” years. This version of the fellowship offers flexibility in that recipients have a five-year window within which to use the three years of support. #13 [paper] Point-of-Care Ultrasound After Medical Screening Exam Reduces Time to Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy Diagnosis and Surgery
Authors: Victoria L. Morris, Michael Vu, Yongsu Lee, Evelyn Park, Ravi Soni, Ryan Walsh, Rachel Bower, John Waller-Delarosa
Venue: Western Journal of Emergency Medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.53932
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction: Ectopic pregnancy remains the leading cause of first-trimester maternal mortality. Delays in diagnosis and operative management increase morbidity and may be exacerbated by emergency department (ED) crowding. We evaluated whether integration of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) into the medical screening exam of pregnant patients—the obstetric medical screening exam—was associated with improved timeliness of care for patients with surgically managed ectopic pregnancy. Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of adult patients undergoing operative management for ruptured ectopic pregnancy between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2023, at a county safety-net hospital. The obstetric screening exam was implemented July 12, 2021, and incorporated focused transabdominal pelvic and right upper quadrant ultrasound into the initial ED evaluation, often prior to bed assignment. The primary outcome was time from ED arrival to operating room (OR). Secondary outcomes included time to obstetric consultation, time to hospital admission, ED length of stay (LOS), and POCUS use. Nonparametric testing was used for skewed time data. Logistic regression evaluated the odds of reaching the OR within four hours. Patient-level interrupted time series analysis assessed temporal trends. Results: A total of 150 patients were included (87 pre- and 63 post-implementation). Median arrival-to-OR time decreased from 516 minutes (interquartile range [IQR] 324–709.5) to 391 minutes (IQR 220–619), a 125-minute reduction (P = .020; bootstrap 95% CI, 8–233). The proportion of patients reaching the OR within four hours increased from 16.1% to 31.8% (odds ratio 2.42; 95% CI, 1.11–5.29; P = .02). Time to obstetric consultation (210 vs 146 minutes; P = .003), time to hospital admission (345 vs 250 minutes; P = .005), and ED LOS (451 vs 367 minutes; P = .03) were all reduced. Point-of-care ultrasound use increased from 41.4% to 66.7% (P < .001), while the remainder underwent radiology ultrasound. Interrupted time series analysis demonstrated no significant immediate change after implementation (P = .790), but a significant postintervention trend toward reduced arrival-to-OR time (−0.45 minutes/day, P = .01). Conclusion: Embedding POCUS into the medical screening examination in triage was associated with sustained improvement in operative timeliness for ruptured ectopic pregnancy. #1 [paper] Shirking Responsibility and Accountability: Racial Capitalism, Biculturalism and the Ethics of the Crusaders Super Rugby Franchise’s Rebranding

Abstract:
This article examines the Crusaders Super Rugby franchise’s partial rebranding after the 15 March 2019 Christchurch mosque attacks as a case study in how sport reproduces settler/invader colonialism, racial capitalism and white possessive power in Aotearoa New Zealand. While the attacks prompted public scrutiny of the franchise’s name, medieval crusading symbolism and pre-match performance culture, New Zealand Rugby and the Crusaders retained the “Crusaders” name and substituted the horseman logo with koru-inspired branding. Drawing on Aileen Moreton-Robinson’s theorisation of the white possessive, the Doctrine of Discovery, critiques of bicultural containment, and Māori constitutional values, the article analyses media discourse, stakeholder consultation and branding decisions to show how symbolic reform can protect institutional authority while appearing responsive to racial harm. I argue that the rebrand commodified a history of Christian conquest and settler nostalgia for commercial profit, while marginalising Muslim concerns and avoiding deeper accountability for Islamophobia, white supremacy and colonial violence. The deployment of Māori design elements functioned as a settler move to innocence: bicultural aesthetics were used to soften critique, provide cultural legitimacy and redirect attention away from the franchise’s refusal to relinquish the name. Consultation processes similarly operated as performative inclusion, privileging majority sentiment, fan loyalty and brand equity over the experiences of communities most directly affected. By situating the controversy within longer histories of Indigenous dispossession, terra nullius-like logics in Te Waipounamu, racialised capitalism and the containment of mana motuhake, the article demonstrates that the issue was never simply one of branding or public sensitivity. Genuine transformation requires more than a redesigned logo. It requires decolonial accountability, Muslim–Māori solidarity, mana whenua narrative authority, and sporting governance grounded in tikanga, manaakitanga, pono, tika and mana motuhake.

Abstract In line with the priorities for the social alignment of technological innovations identified by the Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda and the Societal Readiness Pilot in Horizon Europe, this paper presents a comprehensive co-creation methodology for integrating Social Sciences and Humanities into CCAM. Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

- Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the new Extreme-Events Flagship Cluster. #3 [paper] Thomson: Continual Learning of Frontier Models for SovereignAI
Authors: Shengzhuang Chen, Jerrod Parker, Yejin Bang, Andrew M. Bean, Nabeel Seedat, S. Winzeck, Daniil Glazko, Jannik Zgraggen
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/25f93a6ad2540697a638a11c5b3b33d30ce29ee8
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The development of frontier models is commonly perceived to be the exclusive remit of a small number of heavily funded players, creating an information, economic and power asymmetry between developers and the diverse user base of modern AI. Recent public discourse acknowledges this concern, calling for SovereignAI (an organisation's capability to independently build, deploy and govern AI use), but offers little concrete advice on how this can be achieved in the short term under a diversity of funding settings. We argue that frontier performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models. Unlike limited approaches such as small-scale fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation of a frozen model, our approach exploits a modern mid-&post-training stack while introducing safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making the minimal number of high-impact interventions on the parameters. This yields gains comparable to those typically seen across multiple successive model generations, at compute and personnel budgets substantially lower than commonly thought, making ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values&data privacy) viable for far more actors. We demonstrate this with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model trained with an enhanced focus on high-stakes professional work. Thomson performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax&multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Evaluations show a distinctive $\pi$-shaped pattern: distinct improvements across a wide range of capabilities, including those not explicitly targeted, while almost completely eliminating the forgetting problem common to narrow domain adaptation.

Abstract:
Restoring the hazard-buffering ecosystems of the Western Ghats is essential to re-establish their natural capacity to attenuate runoff, stabilise slopes, and reduce disaster risk in a changing climate. This analytical paper proposes an integrated restoration framework that combines ecological priorities, technical bio-engineering, and institutional-financial reforms to transform fragmented conservation actions into a coherent, range-wide programme with measurable hazard-reduction outcomes. Ecologically, the paper emphasises targeted restoration of shola forests, montane grasslands (shola–grassland mosaics), wetlands, and riparian buffers, which collectively function as a “sponge and net” to delay peak flows and retain soil on steep terrain. It calls for active removal of invasive species such as Eucalyptus and Acacia to enable recovery of native vegetation and habitats, alongside large-scale native-tree planting and fire-prevention measures embedded within national schemes like the National Afforestation Programme and the Green India Mission. These actions aim to rebuild ecosystem mosaics that historically moderated hydrological extremes and maintained slope integrity across the Ghats. On the technical front, the paper advocates native-species bio-engineering on exposed, degraded slopes and road cuts, using deep-rooted indigenous plants to enhance slope cohesion and reduce infrastructure-induced failures at relatively low cost. It further recommends high-resolution, parcel-level GIS mapping to identify, safeguard, and restore critical wildlife corridors and riparian buffers, thereby aligning hazard mitigation with biodiversity connectivity and landscape-scale planning. Institutionally and financially, the analysis argues for replacing isolated, NGO- or division-led initiatives with a coordinated, range-wide ecosystem restoration programme underpinned by explicit hazard-reduction targets and dedicated funding. It proposes mobilising resources from CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management & Planning Authority) and other forestry or climate trusts through a performance-linked fiscal model, where disbursements are contingent on achieving quantifiable ecological indicators such as increases in native canopy cover. To ensure durability and local ownership, the framework integrates restoration with sustainable livelihoods—promoting agroforestry in transition zones and introducing payments for ecosystem services (PES) that provide Gram Sabhas and local communities with a direct economic stake in conservation outcomes. Together, these strategies offer a pathway to rebuild the Western Ghats’ natural hazard-buffering functions while strengthening rural livelihoods, institutional accountability, and climate resilience across one of India’s most critical mountain ecosystems. #6 [paper] Fair Access to Urban Water: Designing Population‐Sensitive Connection Fees Through a Welfare‐Informed Ability‐to‐Pay Approach
Authors: Seyedhossein Sajadifar, Masoud Alavian Sadr, Shahram Heydarian Samani, Ali Mazyaki, Alireza Pourebrahim

Year: 2026

Abstract:
ABSTRACT Setting urban water connection fees is a complex policy problem: Fees must balance affordability, equity, and adequate cost recovery. This study develops a two‐stage framework for setting urban water connection charges in Iran. A bottom‐up engineering model first establishes the full long‐run economic cost of a new connection; a distributive stage then allocates a target provincial average across six city population classes. The distributive stage is stated as a constrained social welfare program and solved exactly; under logarithmic utility, it yields corner solutions rather than a smooth gradient because the fee is a small share of household resources. The recommended schedule is therefore described as what it is: a proportional ability‐to‐pay allocation indexed to city size, whose formal relation to the welfare program is stated explicitly. Revenue neutrality is imposed on a connection‐weighted basis so that the utility collects the intended total rather than an unweighted average of six class fees. Using Household Expenditure and Income Survey data for all 31 provincial capitals, we test rather than assume the population proxy and find an income elasticity of about 0.13 with respect to city size: statistically significant, but explaining a minority of cross‐city variation. Equity claims are correspondingly framed at the intercity level. Applied to a representative province, the schedule is progressive with respect to ability to pay, holds first‐year revenue exactly at the target, and can be adjusted over time using the Consumer Price Index. The approach transfers to other water‐scarce settings under cost‐recovery pressure.

This dataset was created as part of the project Lettercraft and Epistolary Performance in Medieval Europe, a NWO-Vidi funded project based in the Department of Languages, Literature, and Culture at Utrecht University. The database came about in collaboration with Utrecht University’s Centre for Digital Humanities, who developed the online infrastructure, and with the help of students from Utrecht University Research Master’s Programme in Ancient, Medieval & Renaissance Studies, who joined the project as research apprentices. For more information about the project, visit the Lettercraft website. Here you can also browse the latest version of the data. About the project How did early medieval societies use the letter and who were among its users? The Lettercraft-project approaches the early medieval letter as a performative medium, whose communicative potential was defined principally by non-textual features: its materiality, its ability to be publicly read out and talked over, and its potential quickly to reach wide and diverse audiences. The project submits that the letter was a far more inclusive medium than is commonly assumed on the basis of its textual qualities. Literacy or social status were not required to participate in what the project calls lettercraft, i.e. the various performative actions (e.g. listening, speaking, negotiating, gossiping) that along with writing and reading made up epistolary communication. The project aims to show, moreover, that due to its public nature and social range, the letter was an essential tool of community-building and conflict-resolution in medieval society. As long as it was properly performed, a single letter could persuade an entire community. The project studies the performative potential of the letter in the context of the Merovingian Kingdoms, 476-751 CE, whose communicative networks covered much of Europe. Innovatively, it relies not on the surviving letter-collections, which showcase the literary exploits of elite ecclesiastical men, but rather on descriptions of lettercraft in Merovingian histories and saint-lives. The project proceeds along two complementary pathways. First, it has established an index of Merovingian epistolary terminology that is sensitive to all (textual and non-textual) aspects of lettercraft. This index can be consulted in the glossary provided on the Lettercraft website. We plan to include it in this dataset in the future. Second, the project is developing a new open access dataset of Merovingian epistolary communication, which records descriptions of letter-use documented in Merovingian narrative sources. Significantly, it is a dataset not of letters and their textual contents, but of the non-textual ‘metadata’ surrounding the epistolary process, including references to participants, delivery, performance, gift-giving, materiality, and audience. This enables users to analyses the social contexts in which early medieval epistolary communication took place, the diverse individuals and groups who participated in it, and the actions they performed. About the dataset Corpus – This dataset contains annotations on the use of letters in early medieval narrative texts. The project’s principal source are the eight volumes of Merovingian narrative texts edited by Bruno Krusch and Wilhelm Levison for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica under the header Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum (1885-1951), complemented with a smaller corpus of Merovingian texts not edited in this collection. Democratic self-defence, i.e. actions aimed at preventing, containing, resisting, or repairing democratic backsliding caused by domestic antidemocratic forces, can take many forms: from restrictions on candidacy rights to hate speech laws, and from street protests to welfare reforms. #15 [paper] Costing global biodiversity framework delivery in megadiverse Australia

Abstract:
Most nations worldwide face substantial funding gaps to halt biodiversity loss, yet many governments lack comprehensive cost estimates essential for effective budget allocation and implementation planning. Using interpretive principles and evidence from peer-reviewed literature, and spatial analysis, we derived actions, unit costs, and cost factors (the amount of each action required to achieve the GBF's targets). METHODS: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The review protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). A comprehensive search of major databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar) and grey literature was conducted. Eligible studies focused on dementia screening, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to evidence-based dementia care in primary healthcare settings across Africa. Study selection and data extraction were independently performed by three reviewers, and findings were synthesized using descriptive mapping. RESULTS: Of the 3,102 records identified, 16 studies met the inclusion criteria. Nine studies reported dementia screening practices using a range of screening tools, most commonly the Brief Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSID) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). The available evidence suggests that dementia screening was largely conducted within research settings rather than as part of routine primary healthcare. Six studies identified barriers to evidence-based dementia screening and care, including workforce shortages, limited infrastructure and funding, inadequate training, low policy prioritization, sociocultural stigma, and limited public awareness. Only one study evaluated the implementation of dementia risk reduction strategies in an African context, highlighting an important evidence gap. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence on dementia screening, risk reduction, and care integration in African primary healthcare remains limited. Key barriers include health system constraints, workforce shortages, inadequate infrastructure and funding, and sociocultural challenges. Future implementation research should evaluate culturally appropriate strategies to strengthen dementia detection, prevention, and integration of dementia services into primary healthcare across Africa.

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although the guidelines recommend opportunistic screening for adults ≥ 65 years, screening for atrial fibrillation (AF) remains underutilised in Australia. The absence of guidance on how often to screen has resulted in variable practice and missed opportunities for AF detection. Previous studies have focused on handheld devices rather than 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) devices that are readily available in primary-care settings, and the evidence supporting an annual AF screening programme in Australia is limited. The model included 11 health states capturing AF treatment and outcomes, and simulations were run using monthly cycles. A health system perspective and 10-year time horizon were applied. To account for uncertainty, a probabilistic sensitivity analysis with 1000 iterations was undertaken and the results were assessed against a cost-effectiveness threshold of 28,000 Australian dollars (AU$) per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Uncertainty was further examined through cost-effectiveness acceptability curves and scenario analyses to test the stability of findings under alternative assumptions. RESULTS: Annual screening increased costs by AU$4213 and gained 0.43 QALYs, yielding an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of AU$9797 per QALY gained. CONCLUSION: A structured annual screening approach for AF is likely to be a cost-effective strategy within the Australian primary-care setting. These findings highlight the benefits of more consistent screening practices for early AF detection and stroke prevention.

#20 [paper] Building a PET/CT Program in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Health-System Framework for Financing, Affordability, and Sustainable Implementation.
Authors: Mobit, Paul N, Mourad, Waleed F, Mosse, Wilfried B, Khair, Lana M, Njeh, Christopher F, Folefac, Edmund
Venue: Cancers
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43026854/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background: PET/CT is integral to modern oncology, yet access remains limited in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) because of capital requirements, radiopharmaceutical production complexity, workforce constraints, and weak reimbursement systems. We evaluated the modeled financial feasibility of a cyclotron-based PET/CT program using Cameroon as an illustrative national case and reframed implementation as a health-system planning problem rather than an equipment-purchase decision. Methods: A deterministic scenario model was developed over a 10-year horizon. The model was aligned conceptually with IAEA PET/cyclotron planning guidance, WHO OneHealth ingredients-based costing, and ISPOR principles for transparent decision modeling. The entry-level configuration comprised one PET/CT scanner, an 11-13 MeV negative-ion medical cyclotron, F-18 targetry, two synthesis modules, hot cells, a quality-control laboratory, backup power, and supporting infrastructure. Capital investment was modeled at USD 9 million as a planning estimate, with wide sensitivity analysis. Operating costs were separated into fixed, step-fixed, and variable components. Annual completed scan volumes of 500-5000 were evaluated, together with financing at 3%, 6%, 10%, and 12% APR, public capital support, operating subsidy, equipment availability, disease-specific demand, and alternative generator/satellite strategies. Results: At 6% financing, annual debt service for USD 9 million was USD 1.22 million. Modeled operating expenditure rose with activity from approximately USD 0.93 million at 500 completed scans to USD 1.77 million at 5000 scans because staffing and consumables were activity dependent. Total economic cost per completed scan declined from approximately USD 4311 at 500 scans to USD 598 at 5000 scans. If government provided the capital infrastructure, the operating cost to be recovered declined from USD 1865 to USD 353 per scan over the same activity range. A disease-specific incident-case model based on GLOBOCAN 2022 data for Cameroon showed that pathology confirmation, clinical eligibility, and referral completion materially constrain demand; at 30% histologic confirmation and 80% referral completion, approximately 1005 incident-case PET/CT examinations were generated under the base planning assumptions. Equipment availability of 80%, 90%, and 95% materially changed cost per completed scan in a 3000-slot program. Conclusions: Cyclotron-based PET/CT programs may achieve financial sustainability when patient throughput is sufficient, financing is appropriate, operations are reliable, and the surrounding cancer system can generate and act on evidence-based referrals. The model provides a transparent planning framework rather than empirical proof of sustainability and should be locally calibrated before investment decisions.

Secondary evaluation outcomes included quality monitoring performance, laboratory feedback on the ACORN-LAP and quality monitoring processes, and comparison of the ACORN-LAP and quality monitoring processes with existing laboratory assessment tools. FINDINGS: 20 laboratories completed the ACORN-LAP. The median time from initial contact with the laboratory to issuing recommendations was 3 months (IQR 3-4; range 1-8). The assessors identified 144 recommendations (median 6 per laboratory [IQR 3-8·5]; range 2-21), including 46 key and 98 non-key recommendations. Non-accredited laboratories received more recommendations per laboratory than accredited laboratories (median difference 5 [95% CI 1-11]; p=0·0062 and incidence rate ratio (IRR) 2·5 [95% CI 1·56-4·09]; p=0·0002). Non-accredited laboratories also received more key recommendations per laboratory (median difference 2 [95% CI 1-5]; p=0·0030) and IRR 4·75 [95% CI 2·11-11·84]; p=0·0003). 116 quality monitoring forms were completed (median 6 per laboratory [IQR 4-7]; range 2-9). 115 IQC and 59 scored EQA events were reported. Review of such quality monitoring data identified previously undetected IQC failures and led to improved IQC recording in some laboratories. Feedback showed that laboratories considered the assessment process useful although some laboratories found the assessment process labour intensive. INTERPRETATION: The findings support the use of structured laboratory assessment with ongoing quality monitoring to strengthen AMR surveillance, particularly in non-accredited laboratories. A simple, harmonised global online tool with integrated quality monitoring that assesses against a minimum standard could improve the quality and comparability of AMR surveillance data in low-income and middle-income countries. FUNDING: Wellcome Trust.

#3 [paper] Modeling dispersal and beaching of urban plastic waste along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire.
Authors: Amemou, Hilaire, Cecchi, Philippe, Koné, Vamara, Penven, Pierrick, Lett, Christophe
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42735662/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The processes governing the fate, dispersal, and coastal retention of urban plastic debris along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, which is vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO) to simulate the dispersal and beaching of plastic particles.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically focusing on the region around Abidjan and the broader Ivorian coast.
Abstract:
Plastic pollution is a growing concern in West Africa's marine environment, yet the processes governing its fate remain poorly understood. The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). We provide the first regional-scale assessment of seasonal beaching dynamics along the Ivorian coast using a high-resolution coupled hydrodynamic-Lagrangian framework. Simulations show that while a large fraction of particles is transported offshore (~52%), a substantial proportion (~48%) remains nearshore and beaches at least once. Persistent accumulation hotspots are identified around Abidjan, regardless of the release location. Seasonal variability strongly controls debris pathways. During the minor upwelling season (January-April), beaching occurs predominantly west of Abidjan, associated with weaker currents and enhanced coastal retention. In contrast, during the major upwelling season (June-September), intensified currents and mesoscale activity promote wider dispersal and shift beaching eastward. From October to December, beaching intensifies along the eastern coastline. These results highlight the dominant role of regional hydrodynamics in shaping marine debris distribution and demonstrate the value of high-resolution Lagrangian modeling for identifying pollution hotspots and supporting mitigation strategies in data-scarce coastal regions.

#5 [paper] Groundings of drifters in the Wadden Sea inform the transport of floating macroplastic
Authors: Marc Schneiter, Rolf Hut, Erik van Sebille
Venue: Ocean science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3595-2026
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the transport and coastal interaction dynamics of floating macroplastic in intertidal regions, specifically through the analysis of drifter groundings.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Field campaign involving the release and tracking of 24 shallow surface drifters in the Dutch Wadden Sea; manual and statistical automatic detection of drifter groundings; characterization of groundings relative to wind conditions, tides, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Dutch Wadden Sea, an intertidal region driven by semi-diurnal tides and wind.
Abstract:
Abstract. We study floating marine macro plastic pollution with a dedicated campaign where we released and tracked 24 shallow surface drifters in the Dutch Wadden Sea, an intertidal region where water dynamics are driven by semi-diurnal tides and wind. The campaign captured water surface transport patterns, and around 150 observations of the drifters interacting with the coast and mudflats, where groundings of varying durations occurred. We identify these transitions in the recorded trajectories from both manual inspection and by formulating and evaluating a statistical approach for automatic detection. We then characterize the transitions by relating them to the coinciding wind conditions and tides, and with the duration of the groundings. The results of this analysis generally agree with the intuitions that wind towards the coast increases the frequency of interactions and that the drifters are rarely re-floated during falling tides. Furthermore, we find that groundings tend to be shorter duration when they occur shorter before the next high tide. We present multiple visualizations that characterize the groundings in more detail. The results provide a statistical characterization of coastal interactions that can be integrated in models and used for the planning of beach-cleanups. They may be improved by considering the specific environmental conditions of the campaign, and by analyzing the influence of the weight and size of the drifters, which are both larger than typical floating macroplastic.

#1 [paper] Two-dimensional simulation of plastic bottles transport in a urban reach of the Arno River
Authors: Gabriella Petaccia, Elisabetta Persi, Francesco Paolo Contò, Diego Ravazzolo, Andrea Fenocchi, Stefano Sibilla, Lorenzo Innocenti, Mirco Mancini
Venue: Digital Water
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/28375807.2026.2724249
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Within the MINOSSE project (ManagINg plastic transpOrt in riverS and coaStal arEas), the 2D hydrodynamic numerical model ORSA2D_WT has been adapted to simulate the transport of plastic bottles, the most common macroplastic item transported in water bodies. Unlike smaller plastics, such as fragments or films, the shape and size of plastic bottles can significantly influence their inertia and fate. They may not follow flow velocity lines, so they must be modelled as discrete items, driven by the flow field and capable of interacting with surrounding elements (riverbed, riverbanks, bridge piers, vegetation, other debris of plastic or different nature). Thanks to the proposed 2D numerical approach, they are modelled as individual items floating on the water surface or being conveyed in the water column. The ORSA2D_WT model has been appled to simullate plastic bottles trajectories in a 7.6 km urban reach of the Arno River, during a winter event. Two different releases points were considered, the Affrco conflunece on the side of the river and a central point of the river close to the upstream section. The results of the model from the release points show a different behaviuor in the trajectories and in the stranding points. These first results qualitatively match the in situ observations, and show that the numerical model can help in identifying hot spots for plastic accumulation.

#4 [paper] Halting marine plastic inputs by 2050 is necessary but not sufficient to avoid microplastic accumulation
Authors: Takuro Uehara, Mateo Cordier, Laurent Lebreton
Venue: Communications Earth & Environment
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-026-04054-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic pollution threatens ecosystems, economies, and human health, yet economic literature overlooks the transport of plastic debris across marine ecosystem compartments and its natural breakdown. Here we show, using a system dynamics model, the global physical and economic efforts required to remove buoyant marine plastic debris by 2050. The model simulates the degradation, transport, and cleanup of macroplastics and their breakdown into microplastics across shoreline, coastal, and offshore zones. Scenario analyses explore varying rates of waste input reduction and cleanup intensity. Results indicate that halting new marine plastic inputs by 2050, as outlined in the G20 Implementation Framework for Actions on Marine Plastic Litter, and removing existing buoyant macroplastics may be insufficient to prevent substantial microplastic accumulation. Accelerating cleanup efforts can reduce microplastic generation, albeit at a higher cost. Estimated annual cleanup expenses range from €0.1–5.6 billion, representing 0.3–15.7% of national pollution abatement budgets and 0.0001–0.0052% of global GDP. Stopping new marine plastic inputs and removing buoyant macroplastics by 2050 may still leave substantial microplastic accumulation, and rapid cleanup to reduce microplastic generation would cost 0.1–5.6 billion euros annually, according to a system dynamics model.

#7 [paper] PlasticFADE: a predictive model for plastic fragmentation and degradation rates in the environment
Authors: Yibo Tang, Nadim Saadi, Jérôme Lavoie, Anne‐Marie Boulay
Venue: Microplastics and Nanoplastics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1186/s43591-026-00243-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Plastics are widespread across the globe, posing risks to environmental and human health. Fragmentation and degradation are key processes that govern the environmental fate and impacts of plastics, yet their rates remain poorly quantified. Life cycle assessment (LCA) is widely recognized as the standard framework for comprehensively evaluating the environmental performance of products and services. Accurately capturing the fate of plastics in natural environments therefore represents a critical priority for impact assessment modeling. However, the degradation and fragmentation mechanisms governing plastic polymer behavior remain poorly quantified in current life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) models, limiting their capacity to characterize the potential biodiversity impacts arising from plastic emissions to natural environments. In this study, experimental data on plastic fragmentation and degradation were systematically compiled from the literature. Using these data, PlasticFADE was developed as the first iteration of an empirical model to predict polymer-specific rate constants in various environmental compartments. The model predictions reveal that the rate constants vary considerably across polymers and compartments. Estimated lifespans of plastics range from several decades to over a millennium. Beaches are identified as hotspots for both fragmentation and degradation, whereas plastics are most likely to remain intact in the water column. Criteria are proposed for evaluating the reliability of the model outputs, which should be interpreted with due caution. Despite its limitations, the model offers valuable insights into plastic fate processes and offers significant potential for improving current LCIA methods for plastic emissions assessment.

Authors: Ali Farhadzadeh, Majid Ghayoomi, Tian-Jian Hsu, Seyedalireza Mirghafouri, Ahmad Klait, Pedro Lomónaco, Timothy B. Maddux
Venue: Texas Advanced Computing Center
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17603/ds2-71f8-sm86
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the interactions among extreme flood flow, soil, and structure that lead to foundation scour and failure in complex urban settings, including the effects of unsaturated soil mechanics and wave action.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A hybrid approach combining large-scale wave flume physical modeling, geotechnical centrifuge modeling, and numerical simulation (specifically enhancing an open-source Eulerian two-phase modeling framework with an extended effective stress-based sub-model and a revised solver for slight water compr…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Laboratory experiments (wave flume and geotechnical centrifuge) simulating extreme coastal flooding conditions, involving single and arrays of structures in low fines content soils of varying properties (composition, relative density, initial water content) and unsaturated ground.
Abstract:
Foundation scour is one of the primary causes of structural damage in coastal communities during flooding events. This project will leverage state-of-the-art in wave flume physical modeling, geotechnical centrifuge modeling, and numerical simulation to answer a number of critical and open questions related to the interactions among extreme flood flow, soil, and structure which lead to scour and foundation failure?shifting the paradigm in the current understanding of key physical processes in flood-induced scouring process in complex urban setting. Enhancement of open-source multi-physics computational tool for coastal hazard mitigation will provide a strong multi-disciplinary modeling platform to the broader civil and coastal engineering research community. The new parameterization set for extreme scour-liquefaction resulted from the fundamental knowledge-gain will benefit region-scale nearshore morphodynamic modeling and the state of foundation design in flood-prone areas. The education and outreach efforts will broaden the participation at all levels including: (1) recruitment, retention, and education of underrepresented students in three collaborating institutions; (2) engaging science teachers in three coastal states with different urban settings and population, in coastal infrastructure and community resiliency training; and (3) enhancing the well-being of the coastal residents through changing the design and hazard mitigation protocols. This project will bridge the state-of-the-art in sediment transport and scour, unsaturated and saturated soil mechanics, and hydrodynamics of flood flow. This goal will be achieved by correlating the spatiotemporal variations of scouring and loading with the dynamics of shallow flood flows within complex urban setting and water hysteresis in unsaturated soils around and underneath surface structures. The research objectives of this project are to understand: (1) scouring patterns of single and array of structures, under various flow and soil states; (2) initiation and progression of foundation scouring in low fines content soils of varying properties (i.e., composition, relative density, initial water content); (3) soil-foundation interaction response under simultaneous wave action and hydraulically-induced excess pore pressure; (4) rocking response of shallow foundations in unsaturated ground; (5) enhancement of an open-source Eulerian two-phase modeling framework for a complete description of seabed stability and scour; and (6) incorporating an extended effective stress-based sub-model and a revised solver for slight water compressibility to simulate soil behavior in partially drained and unsaturated condition with high overburden. The long-term goal of this project is to create public-domain tools for reliable scour predictions of complex urban and non-urban settings, under extreme coastal flooding conditions.

#6 [paper] Wave Overtopping of Rubble Mound Structures: The Combined Effects of Water Depth and Still Water Level
Authors: Anna Sansanelli, Carlos Coelho, Angela Di Leo, Fabio Dentale
Venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/jmse14222152
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The overtopping phenomenon is the main cause of coastal flooding and the susceptibility of coastal defense structures. Recent investigations have demonstrated that local hydrodynamics are considerably altered by progressive erosion and fluctuations in the water level in front of structures, with the direct impact of higher and more energetic waves on the structure increasing the overtopping volume. These studies show that the quantity of water that is overtopped is influenced by a variety of factors, including wave height, wave period, and sea water level. However, the fluctuation in the bottom elevation in front of coastal structures (due to coastal erosion, for instance) is one of the potential causes of the growth of this phenomenon over time. This work evaluates the impact of water depth variations in front of sea structures on overtopping. This paper introduces a numerical methodology that uses a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) method to verify the experimental results obtained in a two-dimensional hydraulic channel, on beach profiles in front of structures armored with Antifer-type blocks. Unlike traditional homogeneous porous media models, the individual blocks (Antifer) were discretized geometrically in 3D by superimposing them in the numerical domain. Additionally, the morpho dynamic evolution of the sandy beach in front of the structure was simulated. The purpose of this paper is to evaluate the efficacy of an advanced CFD methodology as a prediction and design tool for coastal defense systems. By comparing numerical results with physical models and mathematical formulas, this study assesses the accuracy of numerical approaches in reproducing beach evolution and the internal flow of coastal defense structures. While the CFD model demonstrates strong predictive capabilities under standard scenarios, notable discrepancies are observed under specific experimental conditions. These limitations and their implications for design practice are compared and discussed.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Bottlenecks in using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), including computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Developing a methodology to integrate machine learning (ML) with CFD models of OIDPs.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs) and generic inhaler devices.
Abstract:
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has played a crucial role in providing an alternative bioequivalence (BE) approach for generic orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), in addition to comparative clinical endpoint or pharmacodynamic BE studies, as a relatively cost- and time-efficient complement to benchtop and clinical experiments that has been widely used in developing and assessing generic inhaler devices. However, despite the advances in the power of modern computers, there are still some bottlenecks in using CFD due to computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications. Machine learning (ML) has been gaining more attention as a potential tool to alleviate such limitations that arise in CFD. The purpose of this grant is to develop a methodology to integrate ML with CFD models of OIDPs to promote alternative BE studies to enhance and accelerate the development and approval of generic OIDPs.

The Momental Foundation, based in Redwood, CA, is dedicated to supporting social enterprises by developing programs that help researchers and startups advance the state of science and technology for the public good. Offered by the Foundation, the Mistletoe Research Fellowship program provides professional development opportunities to postdoctoral fellows and, at some universities, to advanced PhD candidates. Specifically, the fellowship matches outstanding early-career researchers with startups that have a high potential for social and humanitarian impact. The fellowship has three main goals: Fund scientific research and provide a professional development & training opportunity for early-career academics. Help frontier startups advance nascent technologies. Create a bridge between the academic and entrepreneurship communities that may lead to further collaboration, partnerships, innovation, and employment. The fellowship has two components: Unfettered Research Grant - The fellowship offers $10,000 for use by the fellow for almost any university-approved research activity, including conference travel, equipment, software, database licenses, etc. The grant may not be used for salaries. Mistletoe Startup Collaboration - Each fellow is matched with a startup during a three-day workshop in the fall, then the fellow participates in an extended team project with that startup. Through that project, the fellow applies his/her knowledge to a specific science or technology problem that will help the startup develop a product with social impact. Projects are intended as extracurricular, and fellows are expected to dedicated approximately 100 hours to the project. The startups are divided into three focus areas: 1) Sustainability, 2) Autonomy/Mobility, and 3) Civil Society. Read more about the Mistletoe Startup Collaboration here .

#5 [paper] STEM-Based Fikih Learning Through Solar Shadow Prayer Time Schedule Project
Authors: Ahmad Syaifulloh
Venue: Journal of General Education and Humanities
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.58421/gehu.v5i5.1969
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study investigates the effectiveness of STEM-based Fikih learning through a solar shadow prayer time schedule project at MTs Khozinatul Ulum Blora. A true experimental design with posttest-only control group was employed, involving 60 eighth-grade students randomly assigned to experimental (STEM-based Project-Based Learning) and control (traditional demonstration) groups. Students in the experimental group engaged in a four-week sundial construction project involving astronomical observation, mathematical calculation, and jurisprudential integration for determining prayer times. Data were collected using a validated Prayer Times Calculation Achievement Test and analyzed using an independent-samples t-test in JAMOVI 2.3.28. Results revealed that the experimental group achieved significantly higher learning outcomes (M = 82.7, SD = 7.09) compared to the control group (M = 73.5, SD = 9.05), with t(58) = 4.37, p < .001, and a very large effect size (Cohen’s d = 1.13). The findings demonstrate that integrating STEM methodologies with Islamic jurisprudence through authentic, culturally relevant projects substantially enhances student achievement while honoring Islamic intellectual heritage. This research provides empirical evidence for curriculum reforms integrating STEM pedagogies with traditional Islamic subjects in madrasah contexts.

#1 [grant] Data sharing to support the training and development of AI foundation models in the energy sector
Amount: €4,500,000–€40,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2026-11-D3-23
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2026-12-01
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The quality of AI models in the energy sector depends strongly on the amount, quality, and representativeness of training data, requiring innovative methods for gathering, sharing, and using large datasets while ensuring privacy, security, and interoperability among energy actors.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Developing, training, and testing AI foundation models using extensive datasets; implementing data governance strategies such as data space connectors, federated training, synthetic data creation, or 'AI gym' approaches; performing in-depth testing and validation in lab demonstrators and real-life …
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The energy sector, specifically focusing on electricity grids, forecasting, congestion management, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, flexibility management, demand-side energy efficiency, and EV charging, utilizing data from energy utilities, grid operators, asset owners, …
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Projects are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- Effective and innovative methods for gathering, sharing and using large data sets in energy applications for the purpose of training AI models while ensuring privacy and security.

- Advanced and - wherever possible - open-source AI foundation models to support the digitalisation of the energy system, through improved grid observability, forecasting of supply and demand, advanced storage and renewables integration, demand side flexibility and energy efficiency.

- Enhanced cooperation, knowledge sharing and interoperability among energy system actors for secure and seamless data exchange.

- Advanced methodologies for AI model development ensuring that the results are FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) beyond the project ending, open source and accommodating for technology evolution.

Scope:

The quality of AI models depends strongly on the amount, quality, and representativeness of the data used for their training. Projects are expected to focus on developing, training and testing AI foundation models, using extensive data sets to accelerate the energy transition in key focus areas of the energy sector. Projects are expected to:

- Building on the results of previously funded projects on the Common European energy data space[1] as well as the ongoing work within the Data 4 Energy expert group, projects are expected to demonstrate innovative methods and data governance strategies for sharing data among various energy actors. Projects are expected to demonstrate that they have access to large relevant datasets at the time of submitting the proposal.

- Projects are expected to develop innovative strategies for sharing data in an effective, secure and transparent way to support the development of AI foundation models. An indicative non exhaustive list of strategies that can be explored is the use of data space connectors or federated training of models to allow the integration of confidential data; the creation of synthetic data as an intermediate step to fill data gaps or improve the quality of the data could also be explored. Projects could also explore other innovative data sharing strategies, such as an ‘AI gym’. The data governance strategies that will be developed in the project should be designed in a way to be scalable and operational even after the end of the project.

- Projects are expected to develop foundation models tailored for the energy sector, addressing at least one -or more- of the following use cases: planning and operation of electricity grids (including static power flow modelling and dynamic EMT modelling), forecasting, congestion management, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, flexibility management, demand-side energy efficiency, smart and bidirectional charging of EVs or other use cases that contribute to the objective of digitalisation of the energy system.

- Projects are expected to perform in-depth testing and validation of developed foundation models in lab demonstrators and real-life pilots, building on the results and using the facilities of previously funded projects on “AI testing and experimentation facilities (TEFs)”[2]. Regulatory sandboxes could also be considered for real-life pilot implementations.

#1 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

#2 [paper] Data and code for: An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system for Mediterranean temperate reefs: forecasting climate-driven mortality under context-dependent local protection
Authors: Jairo Castro‐Gutiérrez, Mar Bosch‐Belmar, Francesco Paolo Mancuso, Sergio Dimarca, Mario Francesco Tantillo, Gianluca Sarà
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23476372
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Static conservation strategies are outpaced by accelerating marine heatwaves, threatening temperate reefs. There is a need for prospective tools that integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability and support climate-smart Marine Spatial Planning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system using a rigorous modelling framework. It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#3 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

#4 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#5 [paper] Coupled Coastal Hazard Prediction System (CCHaPS) Hindcast for Australia
Authors: Vanessa Hernaman, Ron Hoeke, Bryan Hally, Claire Trenham, Blake M. Seers, Ben Leighton, Alberto Meucci, Emilio R. Echevarría
Venue: CSIRO
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.25919/ersf-s538
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Simulating extreme sea levels, waves, and inundation events in the Australian region, including the Great Barrier Reef, over multiple decades at high spatial resolution.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A 2D hydrodynamic and wave model (SCHISM-WWMIII v5.9) using an unstructured triangular grid with over 1.4 million nodes, forced by downscaled ERA5 winds/pressure (BARRA-R2), ORAS5 water levels, TPXOv9.2 tides, and WHACS spectral wave forcing.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Australian coastline, including the Great Barrier Reef and extending to deep offshore waters and neighboring landmasses, with a grid extending overland to a 12m elevation contour. The hindcast covers the 40-year period 1981 to 2020, extended to 2025 as of September 2026.
Abstract:
CCHaPS, the Coupled Coastal Hazard Prediction System, is a 2D hydrodynamic and wave model (Semi-implicit Cross-scale Hydroscience Integrated System Model and Wind Wave Model III, SCHISM-WWMIII), configured around the Australian coastline including the Great Barrier Reef, and extending out to deep offshore waters or neighbouring landmasses. The model simulates water levels due to astronomical tides, weather, waves and aspects of wave-flow interaction over multiple decades, allowing for full consideration of the dynamics of extreme sea levels and waves in the Australian region, at high spatial resolution from ~7km off-shore down to ~250m at the coast, and ~100m in major river mouths. The model is run on an unstructured (triangular) grid comprising over 1.4 million nodes, which extends overland up to a 12m elevation contour, to enable modelling of inundation events and sea level rise. The CCHaPS hindcast covers the 40-year period 1981 to 2020. As of September 2026, this is extended to 2025. The hindcast is forced with downscaled ERA5 winds and mean sea level pressure produced by BARRA-R2, water levels from ORAS5, tides from TPXOv9.2, and spectral wave forcing from WHACS (see Lineage). The model used is SCHISM-WWMIII v5.9, using ST4 wave physics, run on NCI's Gadi supercomputer. The dataset comprises hourly netCDF data on an unstructured grid, compliant with CF, ACDD and UGRID metadata conventions. A notebook demonstrating how to interact with the data will be attached under Supporting Documentation. Variables included are: depth (non-time varying), sea surface height, wet-dry node, currents, significant wave height, mean wave direction, peak wave direction, directional spreading, t01 and t02 mean wave period, peak wave period, peak directional spreading, peak direction (rad), and orbital velocity. The data is also stored on CSIRO infrastructure in the {ev-acs-wp3-cchaps} volume, and at NCI in /g/data/ia39/WP3/release/CCHaPS. Examples of how to work with the data in Python are provided in the accompanying notebook "CCHaPS_examples.ipynb" (see Supporting Documentation) A manuscript describing this dataset (Hernaman et al, 2026) can be found at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocemod.2026.102731

#6 [paper] Understanding ecosystem responses to recurrent marine heatwaves
Authors: Emily Lester, Stanley Mastrantonis, Sharyn M. Hickey, Anna Lafratta, Jessica A. Benthuysen, Eben Afrifa-Yamoah, Arani Chandrapavan, martial depczynski
Venue: Biological Conservation
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2026.112016
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) have emerged as an increasingly severe disturbance to global marine ecosystems, with documented intensifications in both frequency and magnitude over the past century. Western Australia has experienced some of the most severe MHWs on record, causing widespread ecological impacts, including coral bleaching and mortality, local species extinctions, and socioeconomic impacts such as fishery closures, making the region a critical case study of climate-driven change in the marine domain. Most recently, a severe MHW during summer 2024/2025 has caused widespread disruption to marine life, reinforcing the region's vulnerability to repeated extreme events.
