Here, we combine a scoping review of published and emerging evidence with oceanographic analyses to assess the cumulative ecological impacts of MHWs across Western Australia. Using iconic MHWs as case studies, we reveal widespread ecological consequences, spanning habitat degradation, mass invertebrate mortality events, food web disruption, and spatial redistribution of fisheries' indicator species. Accordingly, we propose adaptive management strategies for future MHWs. These strategies include the relocation of vulnerable species, implementation of adaptive fisheries management frameworks, and development of rapid response monitoring programs targeting key benthic indicator groups. We emphasise that the successful implementation of such strategies hinges upon the accurate and timely prediction of future MHW events.

Abstract:
Funders decide which science is paid for. Whether they also shape when it becomes public has been hard to test. Across 376,542 preprints on bioRxiv and medRxiv, the US share rose by 2.3 to 2.7 percentage points in the four weeks before due dates for the main research grant of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and dropped on the date. About one in eleven US preprints in those weeks was attributable to the deadline, and fields that depend least on NIH rose least. Among 15,906 funded investigators, the share of preprints posted in the four weeks before their own deadline was 9% higher than in other four-month cycles, and these preprints resembled the later grant without being more highly cited. Repeated before every due date, this individual surge matches the national peak's timing within a week. NIH's application calendar, like its funding, shapes when US biomedical science becomes public.

Abstract:
The time elapsed between the submission and publication of an article is an indicator of a journal's editorial workflow speed. This study aims to analyze the publication time of journals in the SciELO Brazil Collection, considering the stages of submission, acceptance, and publication, across different subject areas. The research is exploratory and descriptive in nature, based on data extracted from SciELO Analytics regarding 18.540 articles published in 2025 by 326 journals. Descriptive statistics were used to measure editorial times, alongside qualitative analyses to compare the results with existing literature. The results indicate that the average time between submission and acceptance was 192.4 days, and between acceptance and publication on SciELO, it was 165.5 days. The complete publication cycle ranged from 234.9 days in Engineering to 418.7 days in the Humanities, with an overall average of 357.9 days, exceeding the 180-day limit recommended by SciELO. The Humanities and Applied Social Sciences areas showed greater heterogeneity and timeframes exceeding 12 months, whereas Engineering and Biological Sciences demonstrated greater uniformity and shorter durations. It is concluded that the editorial workflows of the SciELO Brazil collection still face challenges related to delays in the review and production processes.

Drawing on the first-hand experiences of a multidisciplinary orthopaedic research team, it explains why laboratory timelines are often longer than expected, and offers practical guidance for working effectively alongside PhD-level scientists, postdoctoral researchers, research technicians, and their trainees - collaborators whose technical expertise is indispensable to experimental success. #12 [paper] Divergent responses to AI-era submission pressure: a comparative analysis of medicine and computer science, 2015–2026
Authors: KangWei Wang, Ce Shi
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11412416/v1

Abstract:
Abstract ChatGPT's release in late 2022 and the arrival of agentic AI systems from 2025 coincided with reports of rising manuscript volumes and editorial strain. Whether this pressure is uniform across research fields, or absorbed differently by each, has not been tested comparatively. We contrast two ecosystems with sharply different barriers to entry: computer science (CS), where submission carries almost no procedural cost, and medicine, where ethics review and data governance constrain what can be produced. Using open data for 2015–2026 — monthly submission and output volumes from arXiv, medRxiv, bioRxiv and PubMed; submission and acceptance figures for thirteen CS conferences; and review times for 38 medical journals — we measured AI-associated writing with a 95-word excess-vocabulary detector applied identically to 30,000 CS abstracts and 13,000–24,000 PubMed abstracts per year. CS preprint submissions rose 99.3% between 2022 and 2025, against 38–41% for the life-science preprint servers and 5.5% for PubMed-indexed output, and several medical specialties contracted; the divergence holds within arXiv itself. CS conferences absorbed the surge by expanding capacity, with NeurIPS submissions up 195% at an unchanged acceptance rate. Plankton underpins these processes by driving primary production, sustaining food webs, and mediating carbon sequestration. Setting (Mycelium's reading): Ocean sciences research literature covering physical oceanography, coastal hazards, marine biogeochemistry, ecology, remote sensing, acoustics, marine geology, and applied ocean engineering.
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly used in ocean sciences to analyze large, complex, and unevenly sampled datasets from satellites, autonomous platforms, sensors, vessels, and genomic tools. This review examines how AI and ML are being applied across major areas of ocean research, including physical oceanography, coastal hazards, marine biogeochemistry, ecology, remote sensing, acoustics, marine geology, and applied ocean engineering. Using a literature-synthesis workflow supported by Schlitsummarizer and full-text extraction methods, this paper identifies key applications, emerging trends, research gaps, and limitations in ocean-based ML. The review shows that ML is particularly useful for predicting surface currents, reconstructing subsurface ocean conditions, forecasting waves, estimating biogeochemical variables, classifying marine organisms and habitats, improving remote-sensing products, and supporting autonomous observing systems. Emerging trends include the growth of deep learning, physics-informed machine learning, explainable AI, data integration across observing platforms, and management-focused applications related to climate adaptation, coastal planning, fisheries, and environmental monitoring. However, major challenges remain, including sparse and biased ocean observations, limited data from deep-ocean and polar regions, validation bias, poor model transferability, class imbalance in ecological datasets, black-box model behavior, and uncertainty under changing climate conditions. Overall, this review argues that AI and ML are valuable tools for expanding ocean observation and prediction, but they must be used alongside oceanographic knowledge, careful validation, and transparent interpretation to ensure reliable scientific and management outcomes.

#14 [paper] Interpreting optical-biogeochemical associations underlying satellite nitrate retrieval in coastal waters using Explainable AI.
Authors: Yang, Keyi, Wu, Sensen, Qi, Jin, Yu, Xiaolong, Le, Chengfeng, Zhang, Xiaoyu, Ni, Sihan, Pu, Guantao

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of clarity regarding the mechanisms enabling the retrieval of optically inactive sea surface nitrate (SSN) from satellite observations, which limits the reliability of large-scale coastal eutrophication monitoring.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Application of an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model to identify latent associations between SSN and individual satellite spectral bands, quantifying spectral contributions in low- and high-turbidity waters.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Daily SSN distributions in the East China Sea, the Pearl River Estuary, and Chesapeake Bay.
Abstract:
Sea surface nitrate (SSN) monitoring is essential for understanding coastal eutrophication and anthropogenic water cycle. However, SSN is optically inactive, and the mechanisms that enable its retrieval from satellite observations remains unclear, limiting the reliability of large-scale and early diagnosis of coastal eutrophication from space. To address this gap, we employ an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) model to identify the latent associations between SSN and individual satellite spectral bands. By estimating daily SSN distributions in the East China Sea, the Pearl River Estuary, and Chesapeake Bay, the XAI model explicitly quantifies the spectral contributions and reveals the optical-biogeochemical association underlying SSN retrieval. According to optical complexity, the coastal waters are classified as low-turbidity water and high-turbidity water. In low-turbidity water, XAI reveals a distinct spectral fingerprint characterized by positive contributions from the red band near 673 nm and negative contributions from the violet band near 400 nm. Further analysis demonstrates that the red-band contribution reflects the biological nitrate uptake by phytoplankton, whereas the negative violet-band contribution is associated with shortwave absorption by CDOM and detrital material that co-vary with nitrate transport and enrichment. In high-turbidity water, strong particle scattering obscures the spectral fingerprint, indicating that satellite-derived SSN estimates should be interpreted with greater caution under highly turbid conditions. These findings highlight the optical-biogeochemical associations underlying satellite nitrate retrieval and provide both an explainable basis and practical guidance for future monitoring of coastal nutrient dynamics from space.

#15 [paper] Writing Nonhuman Agency

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The text explores the conceptual and historical connections between space exploration and oceanography, specifically examining how technological advancements in both fields (sonar, spacecraft) intersected with the American conservation movement and revealed Earth's uniqueness.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Historical narrative and literature review, citing secondary sources on the development of sonar, deep-sea exploration, and space missions.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Historical context of the mid-20th century, focusing on US technological developments in oceanography and space exploration.
Abstract:
Although space and the ocean on Earth may seem distant and unrelated, their unexpected connection emerges from the origins of water in the solar nebula that birthed our solar system, which ultimately found its way to our planet in liquid form ( Kunzig 2000 , 14–15). The Big Bang and the subsequent formation of stars and planets reveal the agential creativity of the universe, which is a self-organising dynamism that far exceeds human capacity for understanding. Both the vastness of outer space and the depths of the ocean remain mysterious realms that captivate human curiosity and symbolise the origins of our existence. After the two world wars, the second half of the twentieth century witnessed tremendous advancements in oceanography and space exploration in the United States. The development of the sonar system for seafloor mapping and submarine warfare emerged as a key surveillance technology during World War I. Constantin Chilowsky, a Russian scientist living in Switzerland, proposed using high-frequency sound for underwater detection and collaborated with French physicist Paul Langevin around 1915 to develop hydrophones ( Petersen 2012 , 241–242). In 1931, engineer Otis Barton and naturalist William Beebe became the first hydronauts to explore the depths of the ocean in the bathysphere, descending to a record 1,426 feet off the coast of Nonsuch Island, Bermuda, where they documented fascinating marine life in their natural habitat ( Cerka 2022 ). Sonar technology and deep-sea expeditions laid the foundation for modern oceanography. Post-war technological rivalry spurred efforts to explore outer space, with satellites and spacecraft sending early images of Earth in partial view, the first taken in 1946, followed by others that showcased the planet in its entirety ( Uri 2024 ). Among these, “The Blue Marble”, a well-known colour photograph taken by NASA astronauts on 7 December 1972 during their Apollo 17 mission, epitomised Earth's uniqueness as the only known life-inhabited planet ( Strickland 2022 ). The launch of NASA's Viking missions, which sent spacecraft to explore Mars in 1975 and 1976, was part of a broader initiative that began in the late 1940s and revealed the barrenness of Mars, further affirming Earth's special status ( NASA 2024 ). The scientific breakthroughs intersected with the emergence of the American conservation movement, a co-development that was by no means a coincidence.

#16 [paper] Many knowledges for One Ocean
Authors: Elizabeth Havice, Noella J. Gray, Oscar Hartman Davies, Nadège Legroux, JESSICA LEHMAN, Emily C. Melvin, Kimberley Peters, Teriitutea Quesnot
Venue: npj Ocean Sustainability
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s44183-026-00231-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract The international ocean community gathered in Nice, France, in June 2025 under a One Ocean framing that unified participants around work for sustainable and equitable oceans. We explore ways that the One Ocean Science shared at the One Ocean Science Congress (OOSC) – including new data technologies promising ‘complete’ ocean renderings – makes space for difference in ocean knowledges and ways of knowing. Drawing on our work on new data technologies, oceans governance, and our participant observation at OOSC and the Third United Nations Oceans Conference, we explore three sites where universalism and difference were evident at the meetings: the propensity to render the oceans technical rather than political; the persistence of gaps as a defining feature of One Ocean Science; and sciences and knowledges incommensurable with One Ocean Science universalism. We highlight that One Ocean Science universalism is, perhaps counterintuitively, constituted through differences and heterogeneities in scientific practices and politics. Manifesting the United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development’s goals of ocean science that fosters equity and sustainability will require holding space for difference within One Ocean, including by interrogating and redesigning the epistemological infrastructure of One Ocean Science so that pluralism becomes structural rather than residual.

#17 [paper] The evolving landscape of remote sensing employment: a data-driven analysis of requirements, skills, and responsibilities in earth observation roles
Authors: Christopher A. Ramezan, Ludwig Christian Schaupp, Cadence A. Wright, Aaron E. Maxwell
Venue: Geocarto International
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/10106049.2026.2717445
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Remote sensing and Earth observation technologies are expanding rapidly across scientific, commercial, and governmental domains, yet limited empirical research has examined how these roles are defined in practice. This study analyzes 250 public remote sensing job postings across 33 nations collected over an eight-month period in 2025. Using a hybrid approach combining manual information extraction and natural language processing (NLP), we evaluate qualifications, skills, and responsibilities in demand. Results indicate steep educational and experience requirements, strong demand for programming proficiency (especially Python), geospatial software expertise, and implementation of AI/ML/DL methods. Entry-level roles were rare, with most positions requiring over five years of experience. Soft communication and project-oriented skills were also frequently cited. Topic modeling identified five recurring role profiles: Remote Sensing Data Analyst, Image Specialist, Software Engineer, Research Scientist, and Sensor/Systems Specialist. Findings provide empirical insights to inform curriculum design, hiring practices, and workforce development.

Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of High-Resolution Sea Surface Height Anomaly (SSHA_HR) products from Jason-2, Saral/AltiKa, and Sentinel-3A to compare wavenumber spectra with SWOT Sea Surface Height Anomaly spectra.

Abstract:
Abstract. The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) wide-swath satellite altimetry mission represents a major advance over conventional nadir-pointing altimetry in resolving small-scale ocean dynamics. Here, we demonstrate the potential of conventional altimeters such as Jason-2, Saral/AltiKa, Sentinel-3A in observing small-scale ocean dynamics by using High-Resolution Sea Surface Height Anomaly (SSHA_HR) products instead of classical Low-Resolution products. We analyse SSHA_HR wavenumber spectra around New Caledonia in the southwestern tropical Pacific – an important study site in the context of SWOT. This region is characterized by complex ocean dynamics, featuring high mesoscale activity and internal tides. The comparison of SWOT Sea Surface Height Anomaly spectrum with Saral/Altika and Sentinel-3A SSHA_HR spectra shows a good consistency between both nadir altimetric measurements for small scales down to 20 km wavelength. SSHA_HR power spectra exhibit mesoscale spectral slopes extending down to 60 km wavelength, highlighting the dominant Surface Quasi-Geostrophic dynamics in the surface layers, particularly present in austral winter while Quasi-Geostrophic dynamics prevail in austral summer. A second k-2 spectral slope emerges at smaller scales down to 30 km wavelength in accordance with the Garret and Munk spectrum. The spectral signatures of internal tides are visible over a broad range of wavelengths up to 150 km in summer when submesoscale activity is less energetic. This study highlights the value of these high-resolution along-track data for documenting fine scale dynamics over a long time period and their integration into operational systems in conjunction with SWOT data or once the SWOT mission has been completed.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Satellite observations of sea surface chlorophyll-a (SChl) are subject to sampling bias in cloud-prone subpolar gyres due to the relationship between synoptic-scale wind speed and cloud cover.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Quantification of sampling bias by comparing SChl retrievals under high wind speed conditions versus low wind speed conditions using satellite SChl data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Satellite SChl data from 2010–2019 in the subpolar gyres of the North Atlantic and North Pacific.
Abstract:
Satellite observations of sea surface chlorophyll-a concentration (SChl) provide a basin-scale record for interpreting marine productivity and upper ocean biogeochemical variability. However, clouds and other observational limits create gaps in SChl retrieval, which can bias the SChl record, especially in cloud-prone subpolar gyres. Here, we use satellite SChl data from 2010–2019 to quantify sampling bias associated with synoptic-scale wind speed conditions. Compared with low wind speed conditions, high wind speed conditions are often cloudy, yielding fewer valid retrievals of SChl as well as lower observed SChl in subpolar gyres of North Atlantic and North Pacific. The wind-speed-dependent sampling asymmetry biases mean SChl upward; for instance, the largest SChl bias occurs in winter, with local values reaching over 10%. The resulting SChl bias also propagates into satellite-based estimates of ocean productivity.This archive provides the reproducibility package associated with the manuscript. #20 [paper] Three gaps for foundation models to address in satellite remote sensing of inland waters
Authors: Mortimer Werther, Stefan Simis, Jan Wegner, Daniel Odermatt
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5151t
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Discontinuities and trade-offs in satellite mission continuity, spectral/spatial/temporal coverage, and retrieval algorithm generalization constrain inland water remote sensing records.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Quantification of three gaps (mission, coverage, and generalization), definition of progress criteria for each, and assessment of 100 recent machine learning studies against these criteria.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 100 recent machine learning studies related to inland water remote sensing and existing generic Earth observation Foundation Models.
Abstract:
Long-term Earth observation of inland waters depends on continuity between satellite missions, adequate combinations of spectral, spatial and temporal resolution, and representative calibration and validation datasets. Discontinuities and trade-offs in these components constrain the records available for studying inland waters and their change. We examine three gaps affecting inland water remote sensing: a mission gap between comparable 300 m ocean colour observations from MERIS and OLCI during 2012–2016, a coverage gap in spectral, spatial and temporal sampling, and a generalisation gap when retrieval algorithm accuracy declines beyond bio-optical properties and atmospheric conditions represented during development. Foundation models (FMs) could help address these gaps by learning reusable representations from satellite archives before adaptation to a particular retrieval task. We hypothesise that relationships learned across overlapping satellite missions can support reconstruction of what a sensor would have measured during the mission gap, that combining complementary sensors can extend usable observation coverage, and that pretraining on satellite archives, which cover more water bodies and a wider range of bio-optical properties and atmospheric conditions than available field datasets, can improve retrieval algorithm generalisation. Testing these hypotheses requires criteria that define progress. We quantify the three gaps, define a progress criterion for each and assess 100 recent machine learning studies against the criteria. For the mission gap, three studies address continuity across sensor eras, and none recovers a record from a withheld mission period. For the coverage gap, 23 studies combine complementary observations, but only three test them on withheld water bodies or periods. For the generalisation gap, only seven studies withhold whole water bodies or later periods from all model development. Across all three gaps, none of the six studies that use pretraining compares it with the same architecture trained without pretraining on independent water bodies. The assumption common to all three hypotheses, that archive pretraining adds information beyond established methods, therefore remains untested. Applying the criteria to existing generic Earth observation FMs, then to FMs pretrained on inland waters, would determine which gaps pretraining can reduce.

#1 [paper] Shirking Responsibility and Accountability: Racial Capitalism, Biculturalism and the Ethics of the Crusaders Super Rugby Franchise’s Rebranding
Authors: Hemopereki Simon
Venue: Te Kaharoa
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.24135/tekaharoa.v19i1.497
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This article examines the Crusaders Super Rugby franchise’s partial rebranding after the 15 March 2019 Christchurch mosque attacks as a case study in how sport reproduces settler/invader colonialism, racial capitalism and white possessive power in Aotearoa New Zealand. While the attacks prompted public scrutiny of the franchise’s name, medieval crusading symbolism and pre-match performance culture, New Zealand Rugby and the Crusaders retained the “Crusaders” name and substituted the horseman logo with koru-inspired branding. Drawing on Aileen Moreton-Robinson’s theorisation of the white possessive, the Doctrine of Discovery, critiques of bicultural containment, and Māori constitutional values, the article analyses media discourse, stakeholder consultation and branding decisions to show how symbolic reform can protect institutional authority while appearing responsive to racial harm. I argue that the rebrand commodified a history of Christian conquest and settler nostalgia for commercial profit, while marginalising Muslim concerns and avoiding deeper accountability for Islamophobia, white supremacy and colonial violence. The deployment of Māori design elements functioned as a settler move to innocence: bicultural aesthetics were used to soften critique, provide cultural legitimacy and redirect attention away from the franchise’s refusal to relinquish the name. Consultation processes similarly operated as performative inclusion, privileging majority sentiment, fan loyalty and brand equity over the experiences of communities most directly affected. By situating the controversy within longer histories of Indigenous dispossession, terra nullius-like logics in Te Waipounamu, racialised capitalism and the containment of mana motuhake, the article demonstrates that the issue was never simply one of branding or public sensitivity. Genuine transformation requires more than a redesigned logo. It requires decolonial accountability, Muslim–Māori solidarity, mana whenua narrative authority, and sporting governance grounded in tikanga, manaakitanga, pono, tika and mana motuhake.

#3 [paper] International Conference on Hydrogen Horizons (ICH2) 2026 - Book of Abstracts
Authors: Carina B. Fialho, Renata Kércia Moreira Martins, Nuno Canha, Edgar C. Fernandes, HyLab Green Hydrogen Collaborative Laboratory, Instituto Superior Técnico
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This Book of Abstracts brings together the scientific and technical contributions from the International Conference on Hydrogen Horizons (ICH2 2026), held from 21 to 24 September 2026 at the Museu do Oriente, Lisbon, Portugal. Organised by HyLab – Green Hydrogen Collaborative Laboratory and IN+ – Center for Innovation, Technology and Policy Research, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, the conference provided an international platform for researchers, industry representatives, policymakers, and other stakeholders to exchange knowledge, share research findings, and discuss technological developments and challenges across the hydrogen value chain. ICH2 2026 was promoted within the framework of the H2 Green Valley Agenda (www.h2greenvalley.pt), funded under the Portuguese Recovery and Resilience Plan (PRR), with IAPMEI – Agency for Competitiveness and Innovation acting as the relevant implementing body. As part of the Agenda's dissemination and knowledge-sharing activities, the conference showcased relevant developments and achievements of H2 Green Valley while fostering dialogue with broader scientific, technological, regulatory, and industrial perspectives on hydrogen. The scientific programme was structured around five main thematic areas: H2 Economy; H2 Production; H2 Transport, Distribution and Storage; H2 End Use; and H2 Safety and Risk Assessment. The conference programme included 119 scheduled scientific contributions, comprising 57 oral presentations and 62 posters, covering topics ranging from fundamental research and materials development to hydrogen infrastructure, industrial applications, system modelling, safety, sustainability, economics, and policy. This publication provides a consolidated record of the scientific and technical work shared at ICH2 2026, supporting the dissemination of research results, the exchange of knowledge, and the development of new collaborations within the international hydrogen research and innovation community.

#5 [paper] Closing the Loop in CCAM Innovation: Advancing Holistic Co-creation Through Social Sciences and Humanities in the CONDUCTOR Project
Authors: François Brambati, Elisa Spiller, Paola Lanzi
Venue: Lecture notes in mobility
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37170-6_13
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In line with the priorities for the social alignment of technological innovations identified by the Strategic Research and Innovation Agenda and the Societal Readiness Pilot in Horizon Europe, this paper presents a comprehensive co-creation methodology for integrating Social Sciences and Humanities into CCAM. Building on the holistic Double Funnel Methodology introduced at TRA 2024, which merges top-down regulatory requirements with bottom-up user and stakeholder needs, the approach comprises four iterative steps. In the co-design phase, regulatory, social, stakeholder, and user needs are systematically elicited through policy analysis, interviews, and surveys. The co-development phase facilitates the interdisciplinary translation of the needs into technical specifications. The co-assessment phase involves validation activities with diverse user groups to assess key performance areas such as liability and human performance. Finally, the closing-the-loop phase critically reviews whether the implemented solutions fulfil the original expectations. Beyond outlining the methodological foundations and development process, the paper draws on five use cases within the CONDUCTOR project to present validation results and key conclusions. These findings demonstrate how incorporating SSH perspectives can shape user-centred CCAM policies and system designs, thereby providing an empirically grounded contribution to the field.

#6 [paper] A shared reflection report from award recipients at the European Health Psychology Society Conference 2025
Authors: Madeleine Warmer, Jennifer Tows, Lucia Volpi, Valentina Rossi, Abdulmalik Yemi Olaosebikan, Brona Mulligan, Dario Leanza, Rebecca Trower
Venue: European Health Psychologist
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.62696/8p07c762
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
In August 2025, the 39th Annual Conference of the European Health Psychology Society brought us together in Groningen, Netherlands, with more than 800 academics, researchers, students, and practitioners from over 50 countries participating. This year’s conference theme was “Putting Health Psychology to Work: Prevention, Practice, Policy”, focusing on the application of health psychology in practice and bridging the research with real-world practice. This reflection report, written from the perspective of conference grant award recipients, aims to provide insight into the experience of attending EHPS for early career researchers, future attendees, and prospective applicants. We reflect on key aspects of the conference, including participation in the CREATE workshop on open science, engagement with the scientific programme, and opportunities for networking and professional development. We were selected for these awards based on the relevance and quality of our ongoing research in health behaviour and intervention development, as well as our contribution to the conference programme. Receiving the conference grants allowed us to attend and fully engage with the event, including participation in the CREATE workshop on open science, with a particular focus on preregistration and registered reports. We highlight how the CREATE workshop supported the development of practical open science skills, how the scientific programme encouraged critical reflection on translating research into practice, and how informal and structured networking opportunities nurtured a strong sense of community within the field. Overall, this report outlines not only what we learned but also how the conference contributed to our development as early-career researchers within health psychology.

#7 [paper] Bridging science and sustainability by empowering the next generation of African researchers under the African Planet Prize
Authors: Rowland Staka Opisa, Cherif Farid Matta, Catherine Jane Ngila
Venue: Frontiers in Earth Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1898066
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The African Planet Prize (APP) was launched in 2025 as a collaboration between the African Academy of Sciences (AAS) and the Frontiers Research Foundation (FRF), conceived as an African-facing extension of the global Frontiers Planet Prize. The initiative recognises and supports early-career African researchers whose work addresses planetary boundary science, including climate instability, biodiversity loss, freshwater scarcity, and land degradation. This perspective offers a critical appraisal of the APP’s inaugural cycle, situating the project within the planetary boundary’s literature and within broader debates on research capacity asymmetries between Africa, and the rest of the world. Drawing on project documentation and independent reporting, the article examines the design logic of the APP, institutional mapping, sensitisation, open competition, and expert review, and weighs the strength of the evidence offered in support of its claimed outcomes. It finds that while the project’s institutional reach (over 100 institutions mapped across 22 countries) and its early monitoring and evaluation (MEL) commitments are genuine strengths. The perspective concludes with a balanced assessment of strengths and limitations, an account of sustainability risks that the project’s forward-looking narrative has yet to address explicitly, and a small set of concrete recommendations for strengthening the evidentiary basis, governance transparency, and continental scalability of future APP cycles.

#8 [paper] Ecumenical Heroism from Below: The Pastoral Witness of Sibongile and Fanyana Mhlophe in South African Church History
Authors: Thembelani E. Jentile
Venue: Studia historiae ecclesiasticae
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.25159/2412-4265/21954
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This article examines the Reverends Sibongile Jessie Mhlophe and Fanyana Peter Mhlophe as exemplars of grassroots ecumenical heroism in South African church history. Drawing on biographical material, oral narratives, and pastoral practice, it argues that their ministry embodied an ecumenical vision through everyday practices, including shared worship, interdenominational cooperation, social engagement, and prophetic witness, rather than through formal institutional structures. Challenging elite-centred accounts of ecumenism, the study shows how unity was enacted amid apartheid’s violence, poverty, and marginalisation. It proposes ecumenical heroism from below as a relational, embodied, and locally grounded framework that contributes to church history and ecumenical studies by rethinking Christian unity, leadership, and sanctity in contexts of struggle.

#9 [paper] Moving Targets in Collaborative Science: Boundary Spanning in Transdisciplinary Iterative Problem Formation
Authors: Andrew B. Neang, Will Sutherland, David Ribes, Charlotte P. Lee
Venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3816975
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The collaborative problems of nascence in transdisciplinary science, where frameworks and ways of working are often not mutually understood or are under contest or negotiation.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Ethnographic work.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A transdisciplinary scientific project spanning a number of subfields of oceanography.
Abstract:
While there is a great deal of excitement and concern around the prospects of transdisciplinary collaboration in the sciences, there has been little attention to the collaborative problems of nascence that such transdisciplinary visions entail. When working across disciplines or domains, the frameworks and ways of working that typically shape research and knowledge production are often not mutually understood or are under contest or negotiation. In this paper we draw on ethnographic work on a transdisciplinary scientific project spanning a number of subfields of oceanography, examining processes by which researchers give shape to a nascent transdisciplinary research project. We highlight two coordinative practices by which they accomplished this: data prioritization and pitching. These findings extend our understanding of coordinative practices in the contexts of nascence that are increasingly common to transdisciplinary science.

#12 [paper] Rural reconstruction and the 1951 Festival of Britain: The Dolhendre scheme and hill farm modernisation in Wales
Authors: Peter Merriman
Venue: Rural History
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/s095679332610034x
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In this article, I provide the first detailed study of the Dolhendre hill farm scheme on the Glanllyn Estate, which was the only ‘official exhibition’ staged in Wales for the 1951 Festival of Britain. I examine how Dolhendre was envisaged to provide a ‘live’ demonstration of hill farming that would parallel the Festival’s urban ‘live architecture’ exhibition in Poplar, East London. The article shows how the decision to rehabilitate three state-owned farms proved controversial amongst Welsh nationalists, and it examines how the scheme was ‘projected’ across Britain and the world in BBC radio programmes and newspapers. While many critical studies focus on how the Festival celebrated British traditions, achievements, and ways of life, this article examines how discourses of Britishness were distinctly absent in this scheme in rural Wales, supplanted by an emphasis on the Welshness of the area as reflected in its history, culture, language, and community values.

#13 [paper] Where Worlds Align: Insights from the Joint GGBN-ISBER Conference on Biodiversity and Biobanking, Cape Town, October 2025.
Authors: Astrin, Jonas J, Labuschagne, Kim, Avrili, Heather, Barker, Katharine, Burger, Anita L, Dhyani, Anurag, Escobari Vargas, Belén, Johnston, Puseletso
Venue: Biopreservation and biobanking
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42781813/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The 2025 Joint GGBN-ISBER Conference in Cape Town united biodiversity, environmental, and biomedical biobanking communities from 38 countries. The event highlighted biobanks as interdisciplinary and collaborative infrastructures for addressing global challenges-pandemics, biodiversity loss, and food security, among others. Recurring themes throughout the conference were as follows: (1) Harmonization and Quality-adoption of best practices and standards where possible to ensure global interoperability and sample integrity; (2) Equitable Governance-crafting flexible, transparent frameworks for sample and data sharing that uphold sovereignty and benefit local communities; (3) Technological and Data Integration-using artificial intelligence, omics technologies, and standardized metadata to transform physical specimens into scalable digital resources; and (4) Resilient Infrastructure-securing long-term investment in regional biobanking networks and targeted training to build enduring capacity, embedding sustainability by design and safeguarding local knowledge.

#14 [paper] Navigating the practice of co-produced convergence research: Lessons from projects funded by NSF's Coastlines and People (CoPe) program.
Authors: Tilt, Jenna H, Behl, Mona V, Moore, Laura J, Mosier, Samantha L, Auermuller, Lisa, Zarger, Rebecca
Venue: Cambridge prisms. Coastal futures
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43011587/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Convergent, co-produced coastal research engages researchers across disciplines and brings together researchers, practitioners and community representatives to co-create new knowledge and understanding to support community resilience while advancing scientific understanding. This type of research is increasingly required by funding agencies and yet it is relatively new. Given this, along with the expansive range of scholarly and lived expertise required to carry out this type of research, there are many epistemological, relational, temporal and institutional challenges for successful projects to overcome. Here we describe these challenges, along with strategies employed to overcome them, based on the work of multiple convergent, co-production research projects focused on coastal communities and environments, funded by the National Science Foundation's Coastlines and People (CoPe) Program. Our experience leads us to recommend that project leaders use inclusive communication practices; incorporate boundary spanners; build shared understanding; select the style and depth of co-production intentionally; focus on earning trust; tailor co-production approaches to the communities involved; equalize power dynamics; embrace and acknowledge the expanded timeline required; plan for delays; embrace flexibility; and build and sustain partnerships for the long haul. Additionally, supporting this type of work requires academic institutions to reward and value the best research practices and research products that emerge from convergent, community-engaged research, including revision of promotion and tenure guidelines to accommodate the expanded timelines required, and the different types of outcomes and products arising from these types of efforts. Further, we recommend that funders consider offering staged, progressive funding opportunities and longer funding timeframes, in recognition of the time it takes to build and sustain meaningful, trusting community partnerships and to plan research projects in a deeply collaborative way with community partners.

#15 [paper] Global Research Competitiveness of the Top Ten Asian Countries: A Bibliometric Analysis of Scopus-Indexed Publications (2020–2025)
Authors: Tahir Ahmed Batt, Priya Vaidya
Venue: International Journal of Computer Information Systems and Industrial Management Applications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.70917/ijcisim-2026-4959
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study presents a comprehensive bibliometric assessment of the scientific research performance of the ten leading Asian countries during the period 2020–2025. Using data retrieved from the Scopus database, the study evaluates publication productivity, citation impact, institutional contributions, international collaboration patterns, and emerging research themes to provide insights into the evolving scientific landscape of Asia. A total of 8,087,616 publications were analyzed using established bibliometric indicators. Co-citation analysis, keyword co-occurrence analysis, and network visualization techniques were conducted through VOSviewer and Biblioshiny to identify influential institutions, collaboration networks, and thematic research areas. The findings reveal that China remains the leading contributor to scientific output in Asia, followed by India, Japan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey. The Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences emerged as the most productive institutions. International research collaborations were particularly strong with the United States and Germany, highlighting the growing global integration of Asian research systems. Keyword analysis identified “scientific research output” as a prominent and recurring research theme, while journals such as Nature Communications, Scientific Reports, PLOS ONE, and Science of the Total Environment played a significant role in disseminating scholarly work. The study is limited to publications indexed in Scopus; therefore, future research may incorporate additional databases to provide broader coverage. The findings offer valuable evidence for policymakers, funding agencies, and research administrators in formulating strategies to enhance scientific productivity, research quality, and international collaboration. Overall, the study provides an updated comparative overview of scientific development across Asia and highlights the need for continued investment in research infrastructure, innovation, and global partnerships to strengthen scientific competitiveness and impact.

#17 [paper] The making of a one-world religion: From interfaith movements to the religious system of Revelation 17–18
Authors: Sixbert SANGWA
Venue: Open Journal of Stigmatized Knowledge & Suppressed Discourses
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.65655/ocp.ojsksd.169
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This historical-documentary and theological review investigates the internationalisation of interfaith activity, the relationship between public religious cooperation and doctrinal universalism, and their possible significance for a futurist reading of Revelation 17–18. The study traces Theosophical and parliamentary precursors, initiatives of the 1920s and 1930s, Alice Bailey’s published programme for a new world religion, postwar ecumenical and interfaith organisations, Vatican II, the United Nations’ religious-fraternity initiatives, and developments through October 2026. It gives special attention to the distinct Nigerian movements described as Chrislam, the 2019 Document on Human Fraternity, the UN General Assembly’s 2020 designation of 4 February as the International Day of Human Fraternity, and Abu Dhabi’s three-house Abrahamic Family House inaugurated in 2023. A structured comparison of founding records, official texts, published scholarship and the author’s previous works differentiates interreligious civic cooperation, religious mixing, pluralist soteriology, and compulsory worship. The historical evidence demonstrates institutional growth and some explicit projects of theological synthesis, but does not independently verify a single clandestine authority directing all initiatives. Biblical exegesis under Sola Scriptura identifies decisive incompatibilities between the Gospel and theories of interchangeable saving paths. Within the author’s premillennial, pre-tribulation futurism, the Great Prostitute is interpreted as a culminating apostate religious order allied with political power before being destroyed by the beast. Present initiatives are analysed as possible analogues or enabling conditions, not certified fulfilments. The Church is called to expose counterfeit gospels, defend conscience and neighbour-love, preach Christ’s unique saving work, and remain watchful without speculative certainty.

#18 [paper] Scripting the research process: didactic transposition and narrative design for a short documentary film around laboratory analysis of coastal sediments in Uruguay
Authors: Paulina Abre, Francisco Ignacio Lugo, Gonzalo Blanco
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5818
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. Geological literacy is critical for addressing modern socio-environmental challenges, yet geosciences remain marginalized within pre-university curricula globally due to the abstract nature of their processes and significant visualization barriers. This study examines a replicable framework for public science communication through the design, production, and multi-channel evaluation of the 17-minute place-based documentary “Arena negra, un misterio oculto en las playas de Uruguay”. Grounded in Place-Based Education (PBE) and Didactic Transposition frameworks, the scientific script was structured around a multi-scale narrative progression that transitions dynamically from macroscopic coastal landscapes down to laboratory processing (gravimetric and electromagnetic separation) and microscale single-grain mineralogical analysis using an electron microscope. Evaluation metrics over a 566-day digital tracking window yielded 35,704 views and 3124 cumulative playback hours. Algorithmic analysis revealed that 77.2 % of views were driven by YouTube’s Browse Features, indicating that the video successfully bridged a latent content-demand gap regarding regional Earth Sciences. Unexpectedly, hardware, metrics showed that Smart TVs were the dominant playback device (62 %), and demographic data indicated an inverted age profile where citizens ages 65 and older represent the primary consumer group. Qualitative analysis of user comments revealed deep-seated misconceptions regarding sediment color as well as environmental concerns that were successfully mitigated by the videos action-oriented pedagogical strategies and cultural analogies. Ultimately, this intervention demonstrates that translating rigorous laboratory workflows into dynamic, localized storytelling serves as a highly cost-effective, regional environmental awareness in territories with limited formal scientific infrastructure.

Abstract:
In the Persian-Arabian Gulf, conservation is uniquely complicated by transboundary ecosystems, migratory species, and anthropogenic pressures in the world’s hottest sea. Additionally, inadequate infrastructure, inconsistent data standards, and limited data interoperability complicate cross-border collaboration for science where geopolitical sensitivities, institutional fragmentation, and uneven capacities create a complex trust environment that can constrain cross-border collaboration. We propose a model for biodiversity data diplomacy inspired by the decentralized, reciprocal, and adaptive mycelium-like networks. While existing bodies such as the Regional Organization for the Protection of the Marine Environment (ROPME) play a role, we outline further steps, including regional data frameworks, capacity building, and inclusive governance. Like other examples of science diplomacy in complex trust geopolitical regions, we see renewed opportunities in the Gulf for politically neutral, equitable, and peer-driven spaces for data sharing. Most importantly, Gulf states and non-state actors can seize the opportunity to establish shared scientific priorities as foundations for broader diplomatic engagement, ecological resilience, climate adaptation, and scientific leadership.

Rather than producing a conventional academic account, the authors engage with what they call a karkhana way of collaborating—an iterative methodology inspired by South Asian arts laboratories, or ‘places of making’. Amount: €2,000,000–€3,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-JU-EUROHPC-2026-QML-07-01

Method (Mycelium's reading): The development, validation, and demonstration of quantum-enhanced AI approaches, including the design of quantum, quantum-inspired, or hybrid QML algorithms, performance modelling, complexity analysis, benchmarking, and the development of error-mitigation and noise-aware strategies tailored to QML…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The text describes a call for proposals for a research project rather than a specific dataset or cohort. The intended setting includes NISQ-era devices and application domains such as climate and environmental modelling, Earth observation, healthcare, materials discovery, finance, robotics, manufac…
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

- Integration of quantum computing into data pre-processing pipelines and learning workflows for data-heavy or computationally intensive tasks, demonstrating clear improvements in processing speed, computational complexity, modelling accuracy, and reduced sample requirements at scales achievable with NISQ-era devices,

- Reliable and scalable Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models and algorithms, integrated with existing AI frameworks and pipelines, enabling faster data processing, improved prediction accuracy, and enhanced computational capabilities,

- Validated quantum-enhanced AI methods demonstrating measurable improvements over classical baselines in terms of speed, accuracy, data efficiency, complexity, or scalability, supported by rigorous benchmarking and complexity analysis,

- Robust, noise-aware QML techniques suitable for NISQ hardware, including error-mitigation strategies and algorithmic adaptations that improve reliability, performance, and reproducibility on real quantum processors,

- Demonstrators or proof-of-concept applications showcasing the relevance of QML for real-world challenges (e.g. climate and environmental modelling, Earth observation, healthcare and life sciences, materials discovery, finance, robotics, manufacturing, and cybersecurity),

- Strengthened European leadership and technological sovereignty in quantum computing and trustworthy AI, supported by cross-sector collaboration, knowledge transfer, and contributions to emerging standards, benchmarks and best practices.

- Enhanced collaboration across quantum computing, machine learning and application domains, fostering a coordinated European QML research and innovation community.

Scope:

Proposals are expected to address multiple key research directions in Quantum Machine Learning (QML), targeting both scientific excellence and industrial relevance. Proposals should clearly outline how to contribute to the development, validation and demonstration of quantum-enhanced AI approaches, with clear pathways towards practical applications. The proposed work should strengthen Europe’s scientific and technological capabilities in quantum computing and accelerate the industrial uptake of quantum-enhanced AI solutions.

Activities may include, but are not limited to

- design and analysis of quantum, quantum-inspired or hybrid QML algorithms,

- performance modelling, complexity analysis and benchmarking of quantum-enhanced AI methods,

- development of error-mitigation and noise-aware strategies tailored to QML workloads,

Proposals should advance scalable QML algorithms capable of addressing large-scale, computationally intensive problems, this includes approaches that

- can manage massive data volumes and complex computational tasks,

- enable faster data processing and improved predictive performance in relevant application domains (e.g. hydrologic research, climate modelling, terrain classification from satellite remote sensing, drug discovery, and image-based medical diagnosis).

Many current QML methods remain closely inspired by classical algorithms and therefore do not yet achieve genuine quantum advantage, requiring further developments in

- quantum-native learning models,

- efficient quantum kernels and quantum feature mappings,

- algorithms demonstrating provable or empirical advantages over classical approaches.

Proposals may also include formal complexity analyses, identification of problem classes that can benefit from quantum acceleration.

Developments should address multiple of the following key research directions:

Quantum Supervised Learning (QSL):

Quantum Supervised Learning investigates how quantum algorithms can accelerate or improve the training of supervised learning models, offering novel opportunities to explore quantum–classical learning theories and enabling industry to shorten development cycles and enhance performance in data-intensive domains such as finance, healthcare, and Earth observation.

#1 [paper] AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
Authors: Sharath S. Girimaji
Venue: National Science Review
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1093/nsr/nwag654
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Applying AI/ML to turbulence modeling has yielded modest progress due to a lack of situation-aware deployment, leading to poor generalization of ML-RANS closures and unnecessary computational costs from misapplied ML-SRS.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The author proposes a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Reynolds number, Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ε), applying Weaver’s complexity framework to classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Turbulence modeling contexts, specifically Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) and scale-resolving simulations (SRS).
Abstract:
Abstract Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ε). By applying Weaver’s well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

#2 [paper] Event-based sensing for turbulent flows: A measurement science perspective on information-efficient estimation and control
Authors: Andrea Ianiro, Iacopo Tirelli, Stefano Discetti
Venue: Measurement Science and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6501/ae9783
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Event-based sensing offers a promising alternative to conventional frame-based measurement in turbulent flows, where intermittency, multiscale dynamics, and stringent latency constraints can make dense uniform sampling both expensive and redundant. Rather than acquiring less data, the goal is to acquire more-relevant data: measurements triggered by dynamically meaningful changes that reduce uncertainty in control-relevant flow coordinates. We leverage ideas from reduced-order modeling, sparse observability, biological mechanosensors, and event-based signal processing to outline a conceptual framework in which turbulent flows are sensed through asynchronous measurements, encoded at the hardware level, and processed by hybrid observers or neuromorphic architectures. A simple analytical argument shows that the estimation-error advantage of event-based encoding over uniform sampling scales directly with the temporal intermittency of the observable. Experimental demonstrations remain limited but encouraging. This perspective reframes the sensing bottleneck in turbulence as a problem of information relevance rather than sample count, and sets out a research agenda covering reduced-state targets, trigger policies, asynchronous observers, uncertainty quantification, and reproducible benchmarking.

#3 [paper] Modeling and simulating turbulent secondary flow in a streamwise-rotating channel with LLM-guided symbolic regression and physics-informed neural networks
Authors: Wei Zhang, Benlong WANG, Zheng Ma, Bing Zhu
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11375175/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The high computational expense of direct numerical simulation (DNS) for turbulent secondary flow in a streamwise-rotating channel, specifically the need for efficient closure models and flow simulation methods.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A two-stage AI framework: (1) LLM-guided Graph-Feynman (LGF) equation discovery to learn a closure for the secondary-flow covariance b23, compared against PySR; (2) Physics-informed spectral neural networks (PINNs) using the discovered closures to reconstruct the time-averaged Taylor–Görtler vortex…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Turbulent secondary flow in a streamwise-rotating channel; DNS statistics for rotation numbers Roτ = 7.5–150; simulation reconstruction at Roτ = 7.5, 30, and 75 on a desktop CPU.
Abstract:
Abstract Turbulent secondary flow in a streamwise-rotating channel is dominated by Taylor–Görtler (TG) vortices whose direct numerical simulation is expensive. This paper develops a two-stage artificial-intelligence framework that learns the closure and simulates the flow. In the first stage, the LGF (LLM-guided Graph-Feynman) equation discovery engine targets the single decisive anisotropy component, the secondary-flow covariance 𝑏23 = 〈𝑣𝑤〉/2𝑘: twenty discovery runs (four feature pools of rotation-variant tensor channels, two LGF operating arms, and PySR at three seeds) are scored against DNS statistics of five rotation numbers 𝑅𝑜𝜏 = 7.5–150. The guided search buys stability: the eight LGF runs hold the case-normalized error within 0.051–0.137 at 13–17 nodes, whereas the twelve PySR runs spread over 0.042–0.334 with seed-level variation up to eightfold at about 60% more nodes. The four selected closures (0.042–0.055, five to seven constants each) share one skeleton: a saturating function of the local rotation number, balancing Coriolis production against isotropization, crossed with a wall function of the wall distance. In the second stage they are carried through the mean-spanwise-profile balance into a physics-informed spectral network (PINN) that reconstructs the time-averaged TG-vortex field at 𝑅𝑜𝜏 = 7.5, 30 and 75 in minutes on a desktop CPU. All four reproduce the two-layer counter-rotating roll cells with secondary-flow amplitudes within 10% of the DNS despite mean-profile errors of order the profile itself: the reconstruction is robust to O(1) profile errors, identifying stress production and viscosity, not mean-flow advection, as the governing balance and completing a “discover–close–simulate” pipeline with compact learned closures.

#7 [paper] Momentum-scalar coupled turbulence with anomalous momentum and scalar diffusions. Part 2: with short-range external force and implementation in electrokinetic turbulence
Authors: Wei Zhao
Venue: Transport Phenomena
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1515/tp-2026-0130
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Extending the generalized anomalous diffusion framework to the short-range forcing regime (β > 2/3) in momentum-scalar coupled turbulence, specifically for electrokinetic (EK) turbulence, to determine velocity and scalar dissipation wavenumbers and identify new spectral subranges.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analytical derivation of relations for velocity and scalar dissipation wavenumbers (k_MD and k_SD) across four subranges of the Quad-cascade process, incorporating Golestanian’s predicted anomalous diffusion regimes for electrolytes to construct phase diagrams based on the scale-dependent anomalous…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Electrokinetic (EK) turbulence with β = 1, characterized by short-range external force and anomalous momentum and scalar diffusions.
Abstract:
Abstract We extend the generalized anomalous diffusion framework established in Part 1 to the short-range forcing regime ( β > 2/3), where the multiscale-force dominated (MFD) subrange is intercalated after the inertial subrange, competing directly with the dissipation ranges. Focusing on electrokinetic (EK) turbulence as the prototypical example with β = 1, we derive the relations for the velocity and scalar dissipation wavenumbers, k MD and k SD , across all four subranges of the Quad-cascade process (inertial, constant-Π u , constant-Π s , and variable flux). By incorporating Golestanian’s predicted anomalous diffusion regimes for electrolytes, we construct comprehensive phase diagrams showing how the relative magnitudes of k MD and k SD are governed by the scale-dependent anomalous Schmidt number Sc Z . We identify two new spectral subranges that emerge exclusively in this short-range forcing regime: (i) the convective-forcing-viscous subrange ( k MU ≪ k ≪ k CFVD ) for either Sc Z ≫ 1 or Sc Z ≪ 1 with γ > α , where the scalar field drives viscous flow through electric body force; and (ii) the diffusive-forcing-convective subrange ( k MU ≪ k ≪ k DFCD ) for Sc Z ≪ 1 and γ ≤ α , where the scalar structure dominated by diffusion determines electric body force, which in turn cause momentum convection. These results provide a complete analytical map of EK turbulence under anomalous diffusion, revealing how external parameters such as electric field strength and ionic diffusivity determine the cascade topology.

#8 [paper] The minimal attached eddy in wall turbulence: statistical foundations, inverse identification and influence kernels
Authors: Karthik Duraisamy
Venue: Journal of Fluid Mechanics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1017/jfm.2026.12182
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Townsend’s attached-eddy hypothesis models the logarithmic region of high-Reynolds-number wall turbulence as a random superposition of wall-attached, self-similar eddies whose sizes obey a scale-invariant population law. Building on the statistical framework of Woodcock & Marusic (2015 Phys. Fluids , vol. 27, no. 1, p. 015104), the present work (i) poses an inverse problem to infer the ideal single-eddy contribution (influence) functions for the mean velocity and Reynolds stresses from direct numerical simulations, (ii) uses these inferred kernels to guide a minimal Biot–Savart-consistent hairpin-type eddy built from Rankine vortex rods with an inviscid image system and (iii) introduces and infers a spectral influence kernel that maps a self-similar eddy footprint to its one-dimensional energy spectrum. The influence-kernel viewpoint yields an explanation for the emergence of the linear part of the energy spectrum, provides a clear scale-by-scale decomposition and helps rationalize why simple eddy templates can reproduce a broad set of log-layer statistics once the mean-flow anchoring is fixed. Closed-form expressions for the mean influence function and the Fourier-space streamwise velocity of a general straight-segment hairpin family with image are derived, revealing a mean-variance duality: for a rectangular hairpin, the horizontal head determines the entire mean kernel while the inclined legs dominate the spectral energy. It is shown that the rectangular hairpin yields a precise plateau in the influence function, resulting in a logarithmic mean velocity profile and desirable properties for the streamwise fluctuations. The model is further extended by calibrating the eddy population density as a function of scale, yielding accurate descriptions of mean velocity and streamwise variance across italic Re Subscript tau Baseline equals 6000 minus 20 000 Re τ = 6000 − 20 000 $\textit{Re}_{\tau }=6000{-}20\,000$ .

#9 [paper] Maximum likelihood reconstruction of particle trajectories in turbulent flows via sparse optimization
Authors: Griffin M. Kearney, Kasey Laurent, Makan Fardad
Venue: Scientific Reports
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-68853-4
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Extracting Lagrangian particle dynamics is essential for characterizing turbulent flows, but inferring particle acceleration from inherently noisy position data remains a significant challenge. Fluid particles in turbulence experience extreme, intermittent accelerations, resulting in heavy-tailed probability density functions (PDFs) that deviate strongly from Gaussian predictions. Existing filtering techniques, such as Gaussian kernels and penalized B-splines, implicitly assume Gaussian-distributed jerk, thereby penalizing sparse, high-magnitude acceleration changes and artificially suppressing the intermittent tails. In this work, we develop a novel maximum likelihood framework for filtering noisy particle tracks in turbulence that explicitly accounts for this non-Gaussian intermittency. By modeling the jerk with a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli–Gaussian prior in place of the usual Gaussian one, we obtain a sparse optimization problem, which we render tractable through a convex \(\ell _1\) -relaxation. To overcome the numerical stiffness associated with high-order difference operators, the problem is efficiently solved using an iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) algorithm. The proposed filter is evaluated against direct numerical simulation (DNS) data of homogeneous, isotropic turbulence ( \(\textrm{Re}_{\lambda } \simeq 433\) ) for the Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database. Results demonstrate that the IRLS approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art continuous MLE, discrete MLE, and B-spline methods, yielding systematic reductions in root-mean-squared error (RMSE) across position, velocity, and acceleration. Most importantly, the proposed framework succeeds in better recovering the heavy-tailed statistical structure of both acceleration and acceleration differences (jerk) across temporal scales, preserving the physical intermittency characteristic of high-Reynolds-number turbulent flows that baseline methods severely attenuate.

#10 [paper] On the Nature of Turbulence
Authors: Barry Kieran Radcliffe
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23173174
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The finite predictive horizon of turbulent systems and the question of whether coherent turbulent structures are best understood as isolated objects or as temporary localizations of distributed motion whose persistence depends on exchange with surrounding flow.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A relational interpretation framework (the "Relational Lens") in which turbulence is described as the continual emergence, persistence, transformation, and dissolution of distinguishable organization, tested through evolving-boundary descriptions, reorganization measurements, exchange variables, an…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four turbulent systems: forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence, experimental wall-bounded turbulence, buoyancy-driven Rayleigh–Taylor turbulence, and naturally occurring oceanic wake turbulence.
Abstract:
This paper presents a relational interpretation of turbulence in which coherent turbulent structures are treated not as isolated objects, but as temporary localizations of distributed motion whose persistence depends upon continuing exchange with the surrounding flow. Within this framework, turbulence is described as the continual emergence, persistence, transformation, and dissolution of distinguishable organization. The central hypothesis is that the useful predictive lifetime of turbulent structure depends upon the persistence of the relational organization that sustains its distinction. This proposition is examined across four substantially different turbulent systems: forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence, experimental wall-bounded turbulence, buoyancy-driven Rayleigh–Taylor turbulence, and naturally occurring oceanic wake turbulence. Across these systems, evolving-boundary descriptions improve prediction relative to fixed representations; greater reorganization is associated with reduced structural persistence; exchange variables improve prediction of future interface evolution beyond recent kinematics; and measurements of surrounding-flow organization add predictive information beyond localized state variables in held-out observations. The results are not uniformly strong across all systems, and one specific deformation model does not generalize universally, emphasizing that the Relational Lens should be distinguished from any single mathematical implementation. The paper proposes that turbulence may be understood as the continual formation and loss of distinction within distributed motion, and that the finite predictive horizon of turbulent systems may be interpreted in part as a finite lifetime of relational continuity.

#11 [paper] Lagrangian Statistics of Long Flexible Fibers in Wall-Bounded Turbulence
Authors: Darish Jeswin Dhas, Cristian Marchioli
Venue: Flow Turbulence and Combustion
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10494-026-00801-8
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the Lagrangian rotational and deformation dynamics of long flexible fibers in wall-bounded turbulence.
Method (Mycelium's reading): One-way coupled Euler-Lagrange direct numerical simulations (DNS) modeling fibers as chains of sub-Kolmogorov rod elements with prescribed bending stiffness.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Turbulent channel flow at a shear Reynolds number of 300, analyzing fibers spanning more than one order of magnitude in length across near-wall, log-layer, and bulk regions.
Abstract:
Abstract We investigate the Lagrangian rotational and deformation dynamics of long flexible fibers in a turbulent channel flow at a shear Reynolds number equal to 300, using one-way coupled Euler-Lagrange direct numerical simulations. The fibers, modeled as chains of sub-Kolmogorov rod elements with prescribed bending stiffness, span more than one order of magnitude in length and are analyzed in three wall-normal slabs covering the near-wall, log-layer and bulk regions. We compute autocorrelations of the tumbling and spinning rates, power spectra of the fiber’s end-to-end vector, and waiting-time distributions of intense tumbling events. Spinning decorrelates on a fixed multiple of the local Kolmogorov time, independent of fiber length, whereas tumbling develops a memory that grows with fiber length by factors of two to five, reversing the ordering of the two timescales between the shortest and longest fibers. Flapping spectra separate into a high-frequency regime in which all fiber lengths carry the same energy in absolute terms and a low-frequency regime in which the energy increases with fiber length. Intense tumbling exhibits approximately exponential, weakly clustered waiting-time statistics whose rescaled form is universal across slabs, fiber lengths and bending rigidities, whereas the event rate depends on both fiber length and rigidity.

#12 [paper] SIMR-NO: A Spectrally-Informed Multi-Resolution Neural Operator for Turbulent Flow Super-Resolution
Authors: Muhammad Abid, Omer San
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11514570/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Reconstructing high-resolution turbulent flow fields from severely under-resolved observations, specifically a 16x upscaling factor from 8x8 to 128x128 vorticity fields, which is an ill-posed inverse problem where classical interpolation and standard convolutional networks fail to recover missing f…
Method (Mycelium's reading): SIMR-NO, a hierarchical operator-learning framework that factorizes reconstruction across intermediate resolutions. Each stage combines a deterministic interpolation prior with a residual correction computed by Fourier layers with spectral multipliers modulated by a learned radial gate, and local c…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Two two-dimensional flows: statistically stationary Kolmogorov-forced turbulence and freely decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence at Reynolds numbers of 1000, 4000, and 8000. The task involves reconstructing 128x128 vorticity fields from 8x8 observations.
Abstract:
Abstract Reconstructing high-resolution turbulent flow fields from severely under-resolved observations is an ill-posed inverse problem of central importance in computational fluid dynamics. Classical interpolation cannot recover the missing fine scales, and convolutional super-resolution networks lack spectral and multiscale inductive biases suited to turbulence at large upscaling factors. We introduce the \textit{Spectrally-Informed Multi-Resolution Neural Operator} (SIMR-NO), a hierarchical operator-learning framework that factorizes the reconstruction across intermediate resolutions. Each stage combines a deterministic interpolation prior with a residual correction computed by Fourier layers whose spectral multipliers are modulated by a learned radial gate, and local convolutional refinement modules recover features beyond the truncated Fourier basis. SIMR-NO is evaluated on two two-dimensional flows with distinct dynamics, statistically stationary Kolmogorov-forced turbulence and freely decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence at Reynolds numbers of $1000$, $4000$, and $8000$, in which $128\times128$ vorticity fields are reconstructed from $8\times8$ observations, a $16\times$ upscaling factor. In comparison with bicubic interpolation, the Fourier neural operator, EDSR, and LapSRN, SIMR-NO achieves the lowest reconstruction error and the highest structural similarity for both flows and at every Reynolds number. On decaying turbulence, SIMR-NO attains a mean relative error of about $3\%$ at every Reynolds number, up to $55\%$ lower than that of the strongest baseline, and its accuracy is nearly insensitive to the Reynolds number. Spectral diagnostics, vorticity-conditioned error statistics, and localized comparisons show that these gains are accompanied by a more accurate reconstruction of intense vortex cores, fine-scale filaments, and high-wavenumber content.
