#4 [paper] Career Anxiety Among Students: Bibliometric Analysis of Scholarly Papers Published from 2016 to 2025
Authors: Tej Bahadur Karki
Venue: International Research Journal of MMC
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3126/irjmmc.v7i4.101373
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Career anxiety amongst students has emerged as a rather topical issue in the realm of psychology and education; however, at present, there is no comprehensive bibliometric analysis that would allow tracing the evolution of knowledge in this field. The purpose of this paper is to present the results of the bibliometric analysis of 525 peer-reviewed scientific papers on career anxiety amongst students, published freely in electronic form during 2016 – 2025. The search was carried out in the search engine Dimensions.ai using a search by title and abstract. The analysis was conducted taking into account the trends of publications and citations, subject areas, geographic distribution, institutional affiliation, and collaborative networks. It was found that the number of papers increased exponentially from 11 papers in 2017 to 168 papers in 2025, generating 1,550 citations in 2025. China has a considerable number of papers (61), but Poland, France, and the Netherlands have much greater impact per paper due to international collaboration. The Field-Weighted Citation Ratio decreased from 3.57 in 2018 to 1.46 in 2024, and only 33.33% of the papers in 2025 received citations, showing lower impact due to accelerated production. No institution published more than four papers, and there are no inter-institutional collaborations. There is a need in this area for creating international collaborations, bridging computing and economics disciplines, establishing research centers, and conducting research at different institutions in order to accumulate knowledge from the disjunctive output.

#5 [paper] Framing and accuracy of AMOC reporting in Dutch journalistic media: comparing scientific research papers and news articles
Authors: Yente M. J. te Koppele, Erik van Sebille
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-6433
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Current (AMOC) may be approaching a tipping point, with potentially significant environmental and societal consequences. Here, we examine the framing and accuracy of Dutch news articles reporting on the AMOC slowdown or potential collapse using peer-reviewed scientific research papers. In total, we analysed 17 scientific papers and 73 news articles published between 1999 and 2025 using qualitative coding, and eight scientists were interviewed to assess their opinion on the representation of their research in these news articles. Our analysis reveals that Dutch news articles often omit methodological detail and scientific uncertainties, while emphasizing the timing of an AMOC collapse. Dutch news articles simplify terminology, use types of exaggeration, and localize information to engage a broader public. Although most interviewed scientists consider the media coverage of their research adequate, they identify areas for improvement and propose solutions. Overall, Dutch journalistic media often accurately convey the core concepts of AMOC-related scientific research papers, but place strong emphasis on societal consequences and opportunities of an AMOC collapse.

The Journal of Argumentation in Context aims to publish high-quality papers about the role of argumentation in the various kinds of argumentative practices that have come into being in social life. These practices include, for instance, political, legal, medical, financial, commercial, academic, educational, problem-solving, and interpersonal communication. In all cases certain aspects of such practices will be analyzed from the perspective of argumentation theory with a view of gaining a better understanding of certain vital characteristics of these practices. This means that the journal has an empirical orientation and concentrates on real-life argumentation but is at the same time out to publish only papers that are informed by relevant insights from argumentation theory. These papers may also report on case studies concerning specific argumentative speech events. The journal aims to attract authors from various kinds of disciplinary background who are interested in studying argumentative practices in their fields of interest. #2 [paper] Modeling dispersal and beaching of urban plastic waste along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire.
Authors: Amemou, Hilaire, Cecchi, Philippe, Koné, Vamara, Penven, Pierrick, Lett, Christophe
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42735662/

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The processes governing the fate, dispersal, and coastal retention of urban plastic debris along the coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, which is vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO) to simulate the dispersal and beaching of plastic particles.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire, specifically focusing on the region around Abidjan and the broader Ivorian coast.
Abstract:
Plastic pollution is a growing concern in West Africa's marine environment, yet the processes governing its fate remain poorly understood. The coastline of Côte d'Ivoire is particularly vulnerable due to dense coastal populations and significant plastic inputs from rivers and lagoons. This study investigates the dispersal and coastal retention of urban plastic debris using a Lagrangian particle-tracking model (Ichthyop) forced by surface currents from a high-resolution ocean circulation model (CROCO). We provide the first regional-scale assessment of seasonal beaching dynamics along the Ivorian coast using a high-resolution coupled hydrodynamic-Lagrangian framework. Simulations show that while a large fraction of particles is transported offshore (~52%), a substantial proportion (~48%) remains nearshore and beaches at least once. Persistent accumulation hotspots are identified around Abidjan, regardless of the release location. Seasonal variability strongly controls debris pathways. During the minor upwelling season (January-April), beaching occurs predominantly west of Abidjan, associated with weaker currents and enhanced coastal retention. In contrast, during the major upwelling season (June-September), intensified currents and mesoscale activity promote wider dispersal and shift beaching eastward. From October to December, beaching intensifies along the eastern coastline. These results highlight the dominant role of regional hydrodynamics in shaping marine debris distribution and demonstrate the value of high-resolution Lagrangian modeling for identifying pollution hotspots and supporting mitigation strategies in data-scarce coastal regions.

#1 [grant] Integrating Machine Learning with Computational Fluid Dynamics Models of Orally Inhaled Drug Products (U01) Clinical Trials Not Allowed
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/351059

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Bottlenecks in using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), including computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Developing a methodology to integrate machine learning (ML) with CFD models of OIDPs.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs) and generic inhaler devices.
Abstract:
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has played a crucial role in providing an alternative bioequivalence (BE) approach for generic orally inhaled drug products (OIDPs), in addition to comparative clinical endpoint or pharmacodynamic BE studies, as a relatively cost- and time-efficient complement to benchtop and clinical experiments that has been widely used in developing and assessing generic inhaler devices. However, despite the advances in the power of modern computers, there are still some bottlenecks in using CFD due to computational time, limited grid resolution, pre- and post-processing of large simulation data sets, model parameter estimations, and uncertainty quantifications. Machine learning (ML) has been gaining more attention as a potential tool to alleviate such limitations that arise in CFD. The purpose of this grant is to develop a methodology to integrate ML with CFD models of OIDPs to promote alternative BE studies to enhance and accelerate the development and approval of generic OIDPs.

#5 [paper] Generating ACGME-constraint-aware surgery residency call schedule software with the assistance of agentic coding large language models
Authors: Isaac H. Lies, Meredith G. Rippy, Syamal Dave Bhattacharya, Wesley H. Giles
Venue: Global Surgical Education - Journal of the Association for Surgical Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s44186-026-00601-8
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Background Manual creation of a surgery residency call schedule is a labor-intensive process that adds to the administrative burden of a chief resident while often producing suboptimal fairness and work distribution. While commercial scheduling software exists, many programs struggle with inflexibility, high costs, and an inability to accommodate program-specific constraints. Methods We developed a scheduling software platform using AI-assisted development tools (Codex, Claude Code), both commercially available agentic coding environments. The system applies a rule-based, weekend-first assignment hierarchy with randomized tie-breaking under a search budget fixed in advance, then performs iterative weekday assignment, accommodating vacation requests and discrete call-shift swapping. The validation roster modeled a single general surgery residency program: 55 residents (32 categorical and 2 preliminary general surgery residents spanning PGY 1 through PGY 6; 20 off-service rotators from other programs; and 1 fellow) distributed across 10 call pools. Three prespecified call-related ACGME constraints were enforced (at least 4 days off per 28-day period, call no more frequently than every third night averaged over 4 weeks, and no consecutive 24-hour call). The 80-hour weekly maximum and the 24-hour period free of all clinical and educational responsibility were not evaluated, as both depend on activity the call calendar does not capture. We evaluated the system with 100 independent full-year runs (July 1 to June 30), each generated end-to-end across all call pools and months under an independently randomized vacation distribution. Compliance and fairness were evaluated at the level of the individual call-pool month (service-month), the unit at which a monthly schedule is produced; fairness and workload metrics were computed across the program’s in-program surgery residents. Results We generated 12,000 service-month schedules over 100 independent full-year runs. 99.2% (11,906) satisfied all prespecified call-related constraints with no violations detected by the internal validation engine. Forty-five of the 100 full-year runs required no manual intervention in any service-month, and none required it in more than 4 of its 120. Manual review of 120 randomly selected service-months by two authors, without reference to the validator’s output, agreed with it in 120 of 120 cases. Monthly fairness, defined within each call pool and month as the range (maximum minus minimum) of call shifts or weekends assigned per resident, showed a shift range ≤ 1 in 65.4% of service-months (mean 1.84, SD 2.15) and perfect weekend equity (range = 0) in 42.5%, with 86.6% achieving a weekend range ≤ 1 (mean 0.71, SD 0.70). Mean full-year generation time was 108.8 s (SD 59.1). Residents averaged 18.65 weekends (SD 3.13) and 78.23 call days (SD 5.49) per year. Conclusions This automated scheduling system generates resident call schedules that satisfy the prespecified call-related ACGME constraints, optimizes fairness across multiple dimensions, accommodates complex vacation requirements, handles cross-pool coordination, and flags the service-months it cannot resolve within its search budget rather than emitting a non-compliant schedule. These results provide construct validity evidence that optimization algorithms combined with careful constraint specification can eliminate the great majority of the administrative burden of manual scheduling while improving schedule quality and equity.

#6 [paper] Comparison of Sizing Methods to Optimize Device Selection for Percutaneous Closure of Atrial Septal Defects.
Authors: Vural, Çağdaş, Baykan, Ali, Doğan, Alper, Kum, Yunus Emre, Akay, Özge Pamukçu, Üzüm, Kazım, Narin, Nazmi
Venue: Cardiology research and practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42824356/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Accurate sizing of atrial septal defects (ASDs) is crucial for appropriate device selection during percutaneous transcatheter closure. Despite the availability of multiple imaging and sizing techniques, no consensus exists on the optimal method for determining device size. This study aimed to compare preprocedural ASD measurements obtained using different techniques with the final device waist diameter and to identify the measurement method demonstrating the most favorable agreement and reproducibility. METHODS: This retrospective study included 149 pediatric patients (64 males, 85 females) who underwent percutaneous transcatheter ASD closure. Preprocedural defect sizing was performed using transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), balloon sizing, and transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). TEE measurements were obtained in the four-chamber, aortic, and bicaval views. In addition to individual diameters, the arithmetic mean, cube root-derived diameter, and maximal TEE-measured diameter were calculated and compared with the final device waist diameter. The final device waist diameter, measured fluoroscopically after deployment, was used as the reference comparator, reflecting operator-selected device sizing rather than true anatomical defect dimensions. RESULTS: Among TEE-based measurements, both the cube root-derived diameter and the arithmetic mean of TEE measurements demonstrated high reproducibility and favorable agreement with the final device waist diameter, with only marginal numerical differences between the two methods. Bland-Altman analysis supported these findings by showing minimal bias and narrow limits of agreement, whereas TTE and balloon sizing demonstrated lower, though statistically significant, concordance with the final device waist diameter. CONCLUSION: Combining multiple measurement techniques improves agreement with the operator-selected device size during percutaneous ASD closure. While TTE alone may be sufficient in patients with simple defects and adequate acoustic windows, integrated approaches incorporating TEE and multiaxis measurements showed favorable agreement characteristics, particularly in anatomically heterogeneous defects or resource-limited settings. These findings should be interpreted as reflecting agreement with operator-selected device sizing rather than anatomical sizing accuracy, given the inherent circularity of using implanted device size as a reference standard.

#7 [paper] Frequent Callers to Emergency Medical Services: an observational cohort study from Region Zealand, Denmark (2018-2025).
Authors: Thiele-Nygaard, Amalie Elisabeth, Møller, Thea Palsgaard, Blomberg, Stig Nikolaj Fasmer, Andersen, Lars Bredevang, Jensen, Josefine Tangen, Ersbøll, Annette Kjaer, Christensen, Helle Collatz
Venue: BMC emergency medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43021062/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Frequent callers to Emergency Medical Services represent a small group of citizens who account for a substantial number of calls. Despite their impact, little is known about their characteristics and patterns of EMS use. This study aimed to examine frequency, dispatch outcomes, and characteristics of frequent callers in a prehospital setting. METHODS: We conducted an observational cohort study of calls to the Emergency Medical Dispatch Center in Region Zealand, Denmark, between 2018 and 2025. Calls without a civil register number and individuals younger than 18 years were excluded. Frequent callers were defined as individuals contacting 1-1-2 five or more times within 12 consecutive months. Calls from frequent callers were categorized as pre-frequent calls (before reaching the threshold) and post-threshold calls (from the fifth call onward). Descriptive statistics were used to compare frequent callers with non-frequent callers, as well as subgroups of frequent callers based on call frequency. RESULTS: Overall, 214 091 individuals made 443 977 calls. Of these, 3.0% (n = 6 415) were frequent callers, accounting for 19.9% (n = 88 260) of all calls. "Unclear problem" was the most common contact cause across all groups, whereas "Alcohol/intoxication/overdose" and "Psychiatry - Suicidal" were only among the five most common contact causes in the post-threshold groups with the highest call volumes. High-priority dispatch was assigned to 89.6% of non-frequent calls, 84.3% of pre-frequent calls, and 73.1% of post-threshold calls. Telephone resolution without ambulance dispatch increased across groups (7.3%, 12.5%, and 23.8%, respectively), as did non-conveyance after dispatch (19.2%, 20.8%, and 27.4%). Differences became more pronounced with increasing post-threshold call volume. CONCLUSIONS: Frequent callers accounted for a substantial proportion of contacts to the Emergency Medical Dispatch Center. While pre-frequent calls resembled calls from non-frequent callers, post-threshold calls were more often resolved over the phone and less often resulted in hospital transport. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Approval for performance of the study was given by the Emergency Medical Services in Region Zealand (p202519525).

#9 [paper] Knowing Your Number Is Not Permission to Call: Authorization-to-Reach for Spam-Free, Privacy-First Communication in the 6G and AI-Agent Era
Authors: Sangam Das
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23729617
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Robocalls, spam texts, and scam calls all exploit one design assumption: anyone who knows a phone number, SIP URI, or messaging handle can attempt contact. Once a number is shared with a business, a marketplace seller, a delivery driver, or a directory listing, it becomes a permanent, reusable route, and leaked or brokered contact data keeps that route open for anyone who obtains it. Existing defences answer different questions. STIR/SHAKEN verifies who is calling, not whether that caller is permitted to reach this recipient now. Virtual and masked numbers hide the real number but stay dialable while active. OAuth delegates API access but defines no telecom reachability rules. Spam scoring and call screening judge an attempt only after it has already been routed and signaled. This disclosure describes an authorization-to-reach model that separates knowing a contact identifier from permission to make contact. Each inbound call, message, or notification is held as a candidate request until an enforcement point, such as a session border controller, SIP application server, IMS node, or CPaaS gateway, validates a recipient-scoped grant bound to sender, recipient, purpose or transaction, channel, expiry, attempt quota, revocation epoch, and audience, with replay protection and sender binding so that a copied grant is not a bearer credential. Only then does the phone ring or the message get delivered; otherwise the request is rejected (for example with SIP 403) before any communication takes effect. Three deployment profiles, blocked path, pre-routing authorization, and absent path, allow incremental rollout over existing E.164 numbering, SIP, IMS, and PSTN infrastructure, while emergency calls (911/112) and lawful intercept remain unaffected. The gap grows as AI agents and AI-native 6G networks originate contact at machine speed. The record includes use cases (map and directory enquiries, marketplaces, ride and delivery, AI assistants), a comparison with existing approaches, a candidate grant format, possible STIR/PASSporT, SIP, and OAuth encodings, security and privacy analysis, a 58-question telecom engineering FAQ, and five workflow charts. A reference implementation is publicly available. Its central principle: possession of a communication identifier is not, by itself, permission to communicate. Download the full PDF to review the workflow charts, grant format, deployment profiles, and complete FAQ. Keywords: robocall prevention; spam call blocking; scam calls; SMS spam; caller ID spoofing; STIR/SHAKEN; PASSporT; SIP; IMS; session border controller; CPaaS; number masking; virtual numbers; privacy relay; consent to contact; contact data leakage; telecom fraud prevention; authorization-to-reach; purpose-scoped authorization; revocable grant; capability token; non-bearer token; OAuth RAR; DPoP; replay protection; zero-trust telecom; 6G; IMT-2030; AI-native networks; AI agents; machine-originated traffic; emergency call routing; TCPA; GDPR

#12 [paper] Dynamic Operator Allocation for Conversational AI Voice-Calling Systems

Link: https://doi.org/10.55640/ijaair-v03i07-07
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The article examines the dynamic allocation of outbound call launches in conversational AI voice-calling systems, where voice bots qualify customers before transferring them to human operators. The study aims to reduce customer hold time and operator idleness by replacing fixed-concurrency settings with a receding-horizon integer-programming controller. The relevance of the work stems from the growing use of AI voice agents in outbound contact centers, where stochastic answer behavior, delayed transfers, and scarce operator capacity create a control problem that static dialing rules cannot resolve. The novelty lies in modeling the bot-induced transfer delay as an empirical lag convolution and embedding this representation within a closed-loop optimization framework, validated through discrete-event simulation calibrated against production logs. The main results show that the proposed controller captures most of the throughput from aggressive dialing while reducing abandonment and hold times, and it unlocks unused operator capacity at higher staffing levels. The article will be useful to researchers, contact center engineers, operations managers, and developers of AI voice-calling platforms.

#14 [paper] An economic analysis of postoperative cataract consultation using remote self-assessment
Authors: Casper van der Zee, Janneau L. J. Claessens, Rudy M. M. A. Nuijts, Rob Wouters, Nicolaas J. Reus, Karl Boden, Oliver Findl, Saskia M. Imhof

Abstract:
To evaluate the potential savings realized by replacing the 4-6 weeks consultation following cataract surgery with remote self-assessment. In addition, we evaluated the costs associated with adverse events (AEs) from a societal perspective and evaluated the current cost of AEs based on published literature and publicly available datasets. We determined the cost reduction when replacing the in-person 4-6-week postoperative consultation visit with remote self-assessment using our previous clinical trial, publicly available healthcare resource databases, and threshold analysis to determine the effect on cost if the incidence of AEs is affected by conducting an online self-assessment. We collected AE probabilities and costs of AEs based on published literature and databases. and performed a threshold analysis to demonstrate the financial impact if the incidence of AEs is altered versus the savings due to replacing the 4-6 weeks in-person consultation with remote self-assessment. Remote self-assessments resulted in an average savings between -€83 and -€92 per patient. Physical consultations were less costly only if >80% of remote self-assessments warranted an in-person follow-up. The mean cost of AEs per patient was estimated to be €16.35 and were attributed primarily to rare but severe complications, including endophthalmitis and retinal detachment. Having patients participate in a remote self-assessment following cataract surgery is expected to reduce costs under a wide range of assumptions. Due to the lack of published data regarding the utility loss due to AEs, quality of life was not included in our analysis; nevertheless, these cost savings should be balanced by the clinical impact of potentially missing relatively rare AEs. #15 [paper] Reconstruction of Protective Clauses in Auction Minutes to Strengthen Legal Protection for Winners in Auctions of Receivables Secured by Mortgage Rights
Authors: Iwan Supriyanto, Ummi Maskanah

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.38035/gijlss.v4i4.1198
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study analyzes the legal position and evidentiary scope of Auction Minutes in auctions of receivables secured by Mortgage Rights and formulates a protective-document framework for good-faith auction winners. The research addresses the gap between the formal authenticity of Auction Minutes and the limited preventive protection available when disputes arise concerning the validity, assignment, notification, registration, or enforcement of receivables. It employs normative legal research using statutory, conceptual, and case approaches. Primary, secondary, and tertiary legal materials were collected through library research and analyzed through grammatical, systematic, teleological, and prescriptive legal reasoning. The findings show that Auction Minutes primarily authenticate the conduct and result of the auction but do not independently establish the substantive validity of the receivable or automatically confer an effective creditor position on the winner. Effective protection depends on valid assignment, debtor notification, transfer of supporting documents, and registration of the Mortgage Right. The novelty lies in a differentiated framework that distributes protective provisions among Auction Minutes, auction terms, seller representations, assignment instruments, debtor-notification documents, and registration records. This framework clarifies responsibilities, allocates risks proportionately, preserves lawful debtor defenses, and strengthens preventive legal protection without granting absolute immunity to the auction winner.

#16 [paper] When a Good Classifier Makes Bad Decisions: AUC as a Mann–Whitney Statistic, an Exact Variance Decomposition, and Cost-Optimal Thresholds Under Prior Shift in 41,188 Bank Marketing Calls
Authors: Manoj Kumar Aguru
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23609348
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Banks increasingly choose whom to call, lend to or review using machine-learning scores, and they judge these scores mainly by the area under the ROC curve (AUC). I prove three results and test them on the UCI Bank Marketing data (41,188 telemarketing calls of a Portuguese bank, 2008–2010), using the first 80% of calls in time order for training and the last 20% for testing. First, AUC equals the Mann–Whitney probability that a random positive outscores a random negative, so it does not change under monotone transformations of the score or under changes in class prevalence. Second, its variance decomposes exactly into the DeLong terms plus a remainder bounded by 1/(4mn). Third, the cost-minimising decision calls a customer when the calibrated probability exceeds r/(1+r), where r is the cost of a wasted call relative to a missed sale, and at that point the ROC slope equals r(1−π)/π. Between the training and test periods the success rate rose from 6.37% to 30.83%. A logistic regression kept an AUC of 0.7483 (DeLong s.e. 0.0057), while gradient boosting, the better model on a random split (0.8150 against 0.8062), fell to 0.6358; the paired DeLong z-statistic is −20.06. Using the Bayes threshold with uncorrected probabilities raised costs above the best achievable threshold by 8.5–16.5% for the logistic model and by 43–182% for boosting. AUC alone hides these losses; the decision depends on calibration.

ABSTRACT When managers revise earnings guidance between earnings announcements, they choose not only what to disclose but also where to disclose—in a standalone release, a guidance call, an investor conference, or an analyst/investor (A/I) day. These venues differ in audience, format, and visibility, raising the question of whether venue choice is a strategic communication decision. In a large sample of unbundled revisions, we find that managers use calls for relatively large negative revisions and when litigation risk is higher and that they use conferences and A/I days for smaller revisions and when analyst disagreement is greater. Our findings suggest that venue choice is a dimension of disclosure strategy for managers and an informative signal for investors.

METHODS: In this retrospective cross-sectional analysis, grant records were extracted from the NIH Research Portfolio Online Reporting Tools Expenditures and Results (RePORTER) database and filtered to PIs with an institutional department designation of "Radiation-Diagnostic/Oncology." Institutional funding, grant counts, unique investigators, grant mechanism portfolios, and career development awards were analyzed. RESULTS: A total of 437 unique clinician investigators (DR: 226; IR: 46; RO: 165) were identified, accounting for $1.65 billion in inflation-adjusted funding. NIH-funded clinicians were distributed across 47 institutions in DR, 29 in IR, and 45 in RO. The top five institutions accounted for 34.5% of grants and 38.4% of total funding, largely reflecting workforce size: institutional clinician PI count explained 82% of the variance in funding, and funding per clinician PI was more evenly distributed (Gini 0.38) than total funding (Gini 0.62). Stanford received the largest grant funding in DR ($134.9M), UC San Francisco in IR ($36.9M), and University of Michigan in RO ($68.1M). R01 awards were the dominant mechanism across all subspecialties. Forty new K-awards were issued across 21 institutions. CONCLUSIONS: NIH funding to radiology clinician investigators is concentrated at a small number of academic medical centers, principally because those centers host larger clinician investigator workforces, with a narrow clinician-scientist pipeline. These findings identify opportunities to broaden research capacity across the radiology workforce.

#7 [paper] Funding mechanisms as incentive systems: a role for science philanthropy
Authors: Lillian Parr, Nadia Sarfraz, Sylvina M. Raver, Nadia M. Penrod
Venue: Frontiers in Systems Biology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fsysb.2026.1939099
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Biomedical research is shaped not only by scientific questions, but also by the incentive structures that determine what scientists study, how they approach the work, and how success is defined. Current incentives often prioritize individual achievement as a pathway to career advancement, while undervaluing replication, data sharing, mentorship, collaboration, and shared infrastructure. This can make it challenging for scientists to prioritize these contributions, even when they recognize that they are essential for a strong scientific ecosystem. This article examines how funders and funding mechanisms create implicit incentives and argues that funding design is a powerful lever for shaping both scientific behavior and the broader research ecosystem. Philanthropy is uniquely positioned to experiment with funding design by supporting high-risk research, emerging areas, and investments in people, fields, norms, and shared infrastructure that other funders may be unable or unwilling to pursue, while also dedicating resources to learn from how these investments shape scientific behavior. Here, we highlight questions funders can ask about the incentives embedded in funding mechanisms, including what behaviors they encourage, who participates and benefits, and what persists beyond the award. For scientists, understanding funding goals, participating in evaluations, and making contributions beyond traditional outputs visible can strengthen the feedback between funding design and scientific practice. By treating funding mechanisms as design choices that can be tested and refined, philanthropy can generate evidence that informs future funding approaches and strengthens the scientific ecosystem.

#1 [paper] Advances in technologies across the marine plastic value chain in Europe: A critical review
Authors: Eimear Magee, Matheus C. dos Santos, Meriem Stimade, Jose Alvarez, Gerard Dooly, Vincent Mallet, Michel Bakni, Douglas Marques
Venue: Cleaner Engineering and Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clet.2026.101352

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Marine plastic pollution (MPP) driven by unsustainable production, ineffective waste management, and plastic persistence, requiring technologies to advance a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A critical review evaluating state-of-the-art technologies across the marine plastics value chain, including remote sensing, robotic platforms, machine-vision systems, downstream sorting (electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging, AI-driven classification), and mechanic…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe
Abstract:
Marine Plastic Pollution (MPP) is widely recognised as a significant global challenge, driven by unsustainable plastic production, ineffective waste management, and the long-term persistence of plastics in marine environments. MPP has become increasingly widespread across oceans, along coastlines and on the seafloor, resulting in an urgent need for the development of technologies capable of advancing a Circular Economy (CE) for marine-derived products. Advances in cleaner production technologies, including satellite and drone-based remote sensing, autonomous robotic platforms, and machine-vision systems, have improved the efficiency of plastic debris identification, classification, and recovery in complex marine environments. Similarly, innovations in downstream sorting, such as electrostatic separation, selective dissolution, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven classification, are enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of processing MPP. The review evaluates mechanical recycling methods with particular emphasis on recent advances in extrusion, moulding technologies, and additive manufacturing for converting MPP into high-value secondary materials in a CE framework in Europe. These technological developments demonstrate the potential for establishing viable and scalable valorisation routes. Overall, the review outlines key opportunities to strengthen a sustainable CE and guide future research and industrial adoption. In doing so, it provides a comprehensive examination of state-of-the-art technologies across the entire marine plastics value chain in Europe, from detection and recovery to separation, identification, and recycling.

#3 [paper] Remote sensing applications in solid waste monitoring and management.
Authors: Kozhikkodan Veettil, Bijeesh, Amangeldy, Nurzada, Puri, Vikram, Phuong, Tran Thi Nhu
Venue: Waste management & research : the journal of the International Solid Wastes and Public Cleansing Association, ISWA

Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Traditional solid waste monitoring methods are cost-effective and limited in spatial and temporal scope, necessitating more efficient monitoring solutions.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A comprehensive review and synthesis of remote sensing applications in solid waste management, covering technological developments over the past 20 years, including sensor platforms, data processing, machine learning workflows, and integration with GIS and IoT.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global solid waste management context, reviewing literature and applications from the last two decades.
Abstract:
The rapid growth of solid waste generation carries significant environmental and public health challenges globally. Traditional waste monitoring methods are not cost-effective and are limited in spatial and temporal scope. Remote sensing, encompassing satellite, aerial, and unmanned platforms, has emerged as a transformative approach to identify, monitor, and manage solid waste sites. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the state-of-the-art in remote sensing applications for solid waste monitoring and management, covering technological developments in the past 2 decades. We examine sensor platforms (optical, hyperspectral, thermal, synthetic aperture radar, light detection and ranging), data processing and machine learning workflows, major application domains (landfill mapping, illegal dumping detection, volumetric assessment, thermal anomaly detection, greenhouse gas monitoring, marine plastic tracking), and integration with geographic information system and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. The present study also evaluates operational successes, methodological challenges, policy implications, and outlines a research roadmap for enhancing the accuracy, scalability, and real-world adoption of remote sensing in waste management.

#4 [paper] UAV-based deep learning and spatial analysis for mapping coastal plastic debris distribution
Authors: Elnur Safarov, Эмиль Р. Байрамов, S.H. Safarov, Etibar Gahramanov, Saida Aliyeva, Zaur Imrani
Venue: Geocarto International
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/10106049.2026.2736384
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Plastic waste accumulation in enclosed and semi-enclosed coastal basins with restricted hydrodynamic exchange.
Method (Mycelium's reading): UAV imagery, YOLOv4-based detection, GPS field validation, and spatial analysis.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Neftchala shoreline of the western Caspian Sea.
Abstract:
Plastic waste accumulation is a major environmental challenge in enclosed and semi-enclosed coastal basins where restricted hydrodynamic exchange can promote long-term litter retention. This study assesses surface macroplastic litter along the Neftchala shoreline of the western Caspian Sea using UAV imagery, YOLOv4-based detection, GPS field validation, and spatial analysis. A total of 7,192 litter items were detected within approximately 0.385 km2, corresponding to an average density of 18,684 items/km2, while hotspot densities exceeded 60,000 items/km2. The distribution was strongly clustered, with a Nearest Neighbour Index of 0.49 and three shore-parallel accumulation zones. Detected litter was spatially associated with shoreline proximity, low-relief terrain, and reed-dominated vegetation, particularly desiccated reed belts exposed by recent Caspian Sea-level decline. Because the survey represents a single-date observation, these relationships are interpreted as spatial associations rather than direct causal mechanisms. The workflow supports targeted cleanup and monitoring across semi-enclosed coastal environments and broader evidence-based environmental management.

#5 [paper] CLEAR-RUN : AUTONOMOUS RUNWAY FOD DETECTION AND REMOVAL
Authors: Umair Raza
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23573169
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
CLEAR-RUN is a multi-phase research and engineering initiative at the National University of Sciences & Technology (NUST), aimed at transforming runway safety through intelligent, autonomous Foreign Object Debris (FOD) detection and removal. Moving beyond conventional detection-only systems, CLEAR-RUN integrates an AI-enabled aerial platform with RGB and thermal sensing, precision geolocation, a centralized ground control station, and an autonomous ground rover capable of locating and physically retrieving debris. The system employs edge AI, multi-agent coordination, and vision-guided retrieval to establish a complete detection-to-removal pipeline. Initial hardware development and field trials have demonstrated detection across 23 FOD classes and 93.3% retrieval success across 30 pickup trials. Subsequent phases aim to enhance localization accuracy, validate round-the-clock operational capability, and scale coordinated robotic deployment, advancing toward a cost-effective, operationally viable solution for autonomous runway clearance.

#6 [paper] Implementing AI in Ocean Waste Tracking and Management
Authors: MD Millen Singh
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21974811
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine pollution has emerged as a significant environmental challenge, with millions of tons of waste flowing intooceans each year, causing disruptions in marine ecosystems. Traditional methods for monitoring and addressing thispollution are inadequate in dealing with its ineffable complexity. Researchers are thoroughly investigating the potentialof artificial intelligence (AI) as a revolutionary tool for tracking and reducing ocean pollution. This literature reviewexplores the application of cutting-edge technology in tracking and mitigating marine pollution, such as plastic waste,oil spills, and wastewater contamination. A comprehensive review of recent research was performed, concentrating ontechniques that employ advanced technology for the detection, forecasting, and elimination of marine debris. Researchshows that advanced computer vision and machine learning techniques significantly boost the efficiency and precisionof pollution detection, such as recognizing plastic waste through satellite images, and improving clean-up strategies bydirecting collection vessels for maximum effectiveness. Efforts are underway to form partnerships among governmententities, industry players, and academic scholars to advance these data-centric solutions. However, obstacles persist;AI systems typically demand significant amounts of data and are subject to time limitations, and it is essential toconsider the environmental impacts of AI deployment, including energy use and electronic waste. This paper bringstogether current applications, assesses their effectiveness and limitations, and highlights gaps in the existing research.The ability of AI to transform ocean waste management is substantial; however, achieving its complete potentialnecessitates collaboration across disciplines, strict data governance, and thoughtful attention to sustainability in AIresearch.

#7 [paper] Infrared-visible space debris perception and detection with light-boosting convolution and cross-modal attention fusion
Authors: Yongqing Yang, Dalei Yao, Fan Bu, Yan Wen, Rongli Chen
Venue: Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fspas.2026.1930223
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction Space debris poses an increasing threat to the safety of spacecraft because reliable perception under complex illumination remains challenging for autonomous on-orbit operations. Existing visible-light methods are highly susceptible to low-light degradation, whereas infrared images preserve thermal information but lack sufficient structural details. Methods To address these limitations, we propose the Space Debris Perception and Detection Network (SPDNet), an end-to-end infrared-visible framework that jointly performs image enhancement, cross-modal feature fusion, and object detection. Specifically, a Light-Boosting Convolution module restores degraded visible features under weak illumination, a Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) module progressively exchanges complementary infrared and visible information during hierarchical feature extraction, and a Multi-Scale Adaptive Fusion (MSAF) module adaptively integrates multi-scale semantic features to improve both overall detection and small-object recognition. Experiments are conducted on a paired infrared-visible space debris dataset constructed from publicly available visible images and geometrically aligned simulated infrared imagery. Results The proposed SPDNet achieves an average gradient (AG) of 88.9, spatial frequency (SF) of 87.286, mutual information (MI) of 5.946, and Chen-Blum metric (QCB) of 0.941 for image fusion. For debris detection, SPDNet obtains 78.48% mAP, 98.74% mAP50, and 40.27% APsmall, outperforming representative image fusion methods under a unified detection framework. Discussion These results demonstrate that jointly optimized cross-modal feature enhancement and adaptive multi-scale fusion provide an effective solution for autonomous space debris perception under challenging illumination conditions.

#8 [paper] Multi-Task UAV Dataset for Floating Plastic Waste Detection in the Kashmir Region (AquaPlasticWaste 2026)
Authors: Veningston K, Ahsan Ul Haq, Shafiya Mushtaq, Dinesh Kumar R
Venue: Mendeley Data
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17632/zshjxgfmc3.1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
AquaPlasticWaste 2026 — Multi-Task UAV Dataset for Floating Plastic Waste Detection in the Kashmir Region — is a 5,000-image UAV aerial imagery dataset for automated plastic waste monitoring on Dal Lake, an ecologically important Himalayan freshwater lake in Srinagar, Kashmir, India, facing severe pollution pressure. Images were captured with a consumer-grade quadrotor UAV flown at a consistent altitude across open water, shoreline, houseboat clusters, and floating garden zones, under varied lighting conditions. It is the first multi-task, polygon-annotated UAV dataset targeting plastic pollution on a Himalayan lake surface. All images carry polygon-based instance segmentation masks, rather than bounding boxes, to capture the irregular shapes of floating litter (e.g., flattened bags, torn wrappers). Masks were created in CVAT and verified through a primary annotator, a second cross-checking annotator, a third adjudicator, and a final quality-control pass. Two labeling schemes are provided from the same masks: binary (plastic vs. non-plastic) and seven-class (background, bottle, cap, foam, polythene, shoe, wrapper). Annotations are exported in both COCO JSON and YOLO polygon/segmentation formats for direct use in standard detection and segmentation frameworks. Of the 5,000 images, 4,692 (93.8%) contain plastic and 308 (6.2%) are plastic-free, with 30,166 polygon instances annotated in total. Wrapper is the most common class (35.4% of instances, present in 63.2% of images); shoe is rarest (1.1% of instances, 4.8% of images). #9 [paper] Quantifying the long-term evolution of post-earthquake debris-flow activity in the epicentral area of the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, China

Abstract:

Abstract:
Diatoms are microscopic marine algae that are critical for global primary production, carbon sequestration, and fisheries productivity. However, select diatoms may form harmful algal blooms, which threaten marine ecosystems and the fisheries they sustain. Rapidly identifying harmful blooms is necessary to effectively manage marine resources, yet current identification methods are limited by expensive and labor-intensive in-situ point sampling. Hyperspectral remote sensing enables scalable monitoring, but its ability to resolve taxonomic shifts within phytoplankton groups (e.g. diatoms) is largely unknown. To investigate this uncertainty, we cultured four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including this system's most abundant harmful algae, Pseudo-nitzschia. The hyperspectral absorption and backscatter of these taxa were measured and used to model spectral reflectances that remote sensing platforms (satellites/drones) might detect. Differences between fingerprints of these taxa were quantified using vector-based and statistical analyses. Mean spectral differences of 48% were observed between the most dominant diatom, Thalassiosira, and the most toxic diatom, Pseudo-nitzschia. Differences of approximately 30% were found between Pseudo-nitzschia and the second and third most abundant diatoms, Chaetoceros and Asterionellopsis. Successful identification of Pseudo-nitzschia's reflectance fingerprint was driven by the presence of a unique feature around 560 nm. The distinct spectral fingerprint of Pseudo-nitzschia indicates that it can be distinguished from other diatom blooms using hyperspectral remote sensing platforms.

#1 [paper] Data and code for: An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system for Mediterranean temperate reefs: forecasting climate-driven mortality under context-dependent local protection
Authors: Jairo Castro‐Gutiérrez, Mar Bosch‐Belmar, Francesco Paolo Mancuso, Sergio Dimarca, Mario Francesco Tantillo, Gianluca Sarà

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Static conservation strategies are outpaced by accelerating marine heatwaves, threatening temperate reefs. There is a need for prospective tools that integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability and support climate-smart Marine Spatial Planning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system using a rigorous modelling framework. It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

Authors: Muhammad Zulhaikal Abdul Razak, Mohammad Hanif Hamden, A. H. M. Din, Fatin Nabihah Syahira Ridzuan, Amalina Izzati Abdul Hamid, Mohd Fadzil Mohd Akhir, Ku Nor Afiza Asnida Ku Mansor, Muhammad Syahrullah Fathulhuda

Abstract:
Heatwaves events is one of the consequences from the global warming and climate change. In a warming ocean temperature, sea level variations are expected to increase in correlation with the temperature fluctuations. Coastal flooding and erosion also occur significantly due to the sea level fluctuation, giving impacts towards economic and marine ecosystem. This study aims to investigate the impacts of heatwaves towards sea level and sea surface temperature using multi-mission satellite altimetry. #3 [paper] Model-Based Marine Heatwave Detection with Eddy Diagnostics in the Adriatic Sea: Regional Insights with Global Relevance

Year: 2026

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intensification, increasing frequency, and duration of marine heatwave (MHW) events, particularly in vulnerable semi-enclosed coastal basins like the Adriatic Sea.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Integration of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm and analysis of long-term observational temperature data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The Adriatic Sea (AS).
Abstract:
Marine heatwave (MHW) events are intensifying globally, doubling in frequency and increasing in duration and spatial distribution over recent decades. Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. In this study, we assess the capability of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to detect and simulate MHW events in the AS. We integrate this modeling framework with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm, alongside comprehensive analysis of long-term observational temperature data, to investigate the role of mesoscale eddies in modulating surface and subsurface MHW evolution. Results demonstrate that ROMS effectively reproduces the timing and spatial patterns of historical MHWs in the AS, showing strong agreement between modeled and observed MHWs, with eddy structures frequently coinciding with subsurface thermal anomalies preceding MHWs. These findings highlight the value of coupling regional ocean models with mesoscale eddy diagnostics to advance understanding of MHW occurrences and drivers, and to strengthen early-warning capabilities. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

#5 [paper] Understanding ecosystem responses to recurrent marine heatwaves
Authors: Emily Lester, Stanley Mastrantonis, Sharyn M. Hickey, Anna Lafratta, Jessica A. Benthuysen, Eben Afrifa-Yamoah, Arani Chandrapavan, martial depczynski
Venue: Biological Conservation
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2026.112016
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) have emerged as an increasingly severe disturbance to global marine ecosystems, with documented intensifications in both frequency and magnitude over the past century. Western Australia has experienced some of the most severe MHWs on record, causing widespread ecological impacts, including coral bleaching and mortality, local species extinctions, and socioeconomic impacts such as fishery closures, making the region a critical case study of climate-driven change in the marine domain. Most recently, a severe MHW during summer 2024/2025 has caused widespread disruption to marine life, reinforcing the region's vulnerability to repeated extreme events. While extensive research has documented the impacts of these events, most studies have examined individual heatwaves or specific taxonomic groups in isolation, limiting our understanding of cumulative and cascading effects across the ecosystem. Here, we combine a scoping review of published and emerging evidence with oceanographic analyses to assess the cumulative ecological impacts of MHWs across Western Australia. Using iconic MHWs as case studies, we reveal widespread ecological consequences, spanning habitat degradation, mass invertebrate mortality events, food web disruption, and spatial redistribution of fisheries' indicator species. Accordingly, we propose adaptive management strategies for future MHWs. These strategies include the relocation of vulnerable species, implementation of adaptive fisheries management frameworks, and development of rapid response monitoring programs targeting key benthic indicator groups. We emphasise that the successful implementation of such strategies hinges upon the accurate and timely prediction of future MHW events.

#6 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

#7 [paper] Rethinking Marine Heatwaves: Towards a Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress
Authors: Natalija Dunić, Krešimir Ruić, Ivica Vilibić
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15011394/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard marine heatwave (MHW) definitions rely on statistical temperature anomalies relative to a climatological baseline, which does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic examples used to demonstrate the estimation of response functions from biological observations and the derivation of binary event definitions.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

#8 [paper] Mitigating Summertime Marine Heatwaves via Targeted Marine Cloud Brightening
Authors: Matthew T. Luongo, Edward Blanchard‐Wrigglesworth, Kyle Armour, Haruki Hirasawa, Jacob Cohen, Aaron Donohoe
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5kv4t
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) negatively impact marine ecosystems and coastal economies. Here, we evaluate whether a preemptive, short-term, localized surface emission of sea salt aerosols (marine cloud brightening, MCB) can mitigate the impacts of a predicted MHW without creating significant effects beyond the intervention zone. As a case study, we apply MCB to the 2019 Northeast Pacific MHW, "The Blob 2.0," using a global climate model seasonal-to-multiyear predictability ensemble. Initiating MCB in May 2019 mitigates important negative consequences of the event, substantially reducing the MHW magnitude and limiting associated declines in surface oxygen. The impacts of this intervention are mostly local and limited to summer, even when MCB is extended into winter, with nonlocal climate effects smaller than internal variability. By demonstrating local efficacy and minor remote impacts for mitigating the Blob 2.0, this work motivates further study of whether localized and temporary climate interventions can safely and effectively mitigate MHWs.

#9 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#10 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350

Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#11 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

#12 [paper] Interview Materials for Comparing Decision-Makers' Interpretation and Use of Deterministic and Probabilistic Machine Learning Water Temperature Predictions for Cold-Stunning Event Management
Authors: Miranda White, Christopher D. Wirz, Mariana Goodall Cains, Julie L. Demuth, Philippe E. Tissot, Elisa R. Flores

Problem (Mycelium's reading): How adding probabilistic information to deterministic machine learning water temperature guidance shapes coastal decision-makers' interpretations, perceptions of event likelihood and certainty, and potential decisions and actions for cold-stunning event management.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Qualitative study using scenario-based interviews with returning and new participants, incorporating two interactive visualization activities: (1) comparing deterministic and probabilistic guidance for two scenarios, and (2) ranking five challenging scenarios using an interactive dashboard and slid…

Abstract:
Overview of Interview Materials This repository contains interview protocols and accompanying elicitation materials from a qualitative study of coastal decision-makers’ interpretation and use of deterministic and probabilistic machine learning water temperature predictions for cold-stunning event management along the Texas coast. Participants included natural resource managers, weather forecasting entities, and coastal economic operators involved in the Texas Marine Coldwater Response Collaborative (TCRC). The study builds upon prior work with TCRC members examining how users assess, interpret, and trust cold-stunning predictive information, including operational deterministic machine learning water temperature forecasts (White et al., 2026). Through scenario-based interviews with returning and new participants, this follow-up study examined how adding probabilistic information to deterministic guidance shaped interpretations, perceptions of event likelihood and certainty in the guidance, and potential decisions and actions. Materials include protocols for new and returning participants, links to two interactive visualization activities, and an accompanying scenario-ranking slide deck. Interview Protocols Two versions of the interview protocol accommodated participants with and without prior participation in the earlier interview study: New participants: Includes introductory questions about professional roles, organizational risks associated with cold-stunning events, information sources, preparedness and response actions, and communication pathways. Returning participants: Omits the introductory background questions and proceeds to the visualization activities following the interview preamble. Both versions include the following two activities and associated discussion questions. Activity 1: Interpretation and Comparison of Deterministic and Probabilistic Information Participants explored two potential cold-stunning event scenarios using an interactive dashboard. Within each scenario, participants first viewed deterministic water temperature guidance (Scenarios 1A and 2A), followed by probabilistic guidance for the same event (Scenarios 1B and 2B). The visualizations displayed observations and predictions, allowing participants to examine water temperature values over time. Interview questions explored participants’ interpretations, perceptions of certainty, potential actions and their timing, and the forecast features informing those assessments. Additional questions addressed interpretations of the shaded uncertainty ranges, strengths and weaknesses of each presentation format, forecast preferences, and perceived decision-making challenges. Access Activity 1: Deterministic and Probabilistic Scenario Comparisons Activity 2: Ranking Challenging Cold-Stunning Event Scenarios Participants compared probabilistic water temperature guidance across five potential cold-stunning event scenarios: the two scenarios examined in Activity 1 and three additional scenarios. Participants explored the forecasts using an interactive dashboard and used the accompanying PowerPoint slide deck to rank the scenarios from least to most challenging for decision-making. They were encouraged to think aloud while exploring and ranking the scenarios. Follow-up questions examined which forecast characteristics influenced their rankings and what made particular scenarios more or less challenging. Access Activity 2: Five-Scenario Exploration This material is based upon work supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation under Grant No. RISE-2019758 and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Adminstration, Office of Education Educational Partnership Program award (NA21SEC4810004).

#13 [paper] Intensifying concurrent marine–atmospheric heatwaves in the marginal seas of the Arabian Peninsula: implications for coral bleaching and ocean productivity
Authors: Waqar Ul Hassan, Md Saquib Saharward, Harikishan Gandham, Hari Prasad Dasari, Aneesh C. Subramanian, Vassilis P. Papadopoulos, Ibrahim Hoteit, Yasser Abualnaja
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1904418
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Marine (MHWs) and atmospheric heatwaves (AHWs) are intensifying with climate change, but their co-occurrence as concurrent heatwaves (CHWs) poses an even greater threat to marine ecosystems. This study examines the spatiotemporal variability, physical drivers, and ecological impacts of CHWs across the marginal seas of the Arabian Peninsula from 1982 to 2021. CHWs are most frequent in the northern Red Sea, Arabian Gulf, and western Arabian Sea, and least common in the southern Red Sea. Their frequency and duration have increased significantly, by up to 7.5 days per decade in the northern Red Sea. CHWs extend the duration of MHWs and AHWs by an average of 6 and 2.2 days, respectively, compounding ecological stress. Our findings show that CHWs are the dominant drivers of coral bleaching and productivity loss in the region, with 80–85% of severe bleaching events linked to CHWs. They also triggered more than 20% decline in chlorophyll-a concentrations – nearly 1.4 times that of standalone MHWs. These results underscore the critical role of atmospheric heat in marine impacts. Case studies from 1998 and 2010 highlight the influence of high-pressure anomalies and weakened winds in shaping the widespread CHWs. The study calls for integrating CHW risks into conservation strategies to build ecosystem resilience in a warming climate.

#14 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5

Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.
