Abstract:
Marine heatwave (MHW) events are intensifying globally, doubling in frequency and increasing in duration and spatial distribution over recent decades. Semi-enclosed coastal basins are particularly vulnerable, and the Adriatic Sea (AS) exemplifies a fast-reacting system, making it a natural laboratory for studying climate-driven ocean variability and impacts on ecosystems, fisheries, and aquaculture. In this study, we assess the capability of a high-resolution Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) to detect and simulate MHW events in the AS. We integrate this modeling framework with an eddy detection and tracking algorithm, alongside comprehensive analysis of long-term observational temperature data, to investigate the role of mesoscale eddies in modulating surface and subsurface MHW evolution. Results demonstrate that ROMS effectively reproduces the timing and spatial patterns of historical MHWs in the AS, showing strong agreement between modeled and observed MHWs, with eddy structures frequently coinciding with subsurface thermal anomalies preceding MHWs. Enhanced understanding of MHW precursors and eddy interactions in the AS provides a pathway for anticipating hazards, informing adaptive measures for coastal stakeholders, and improving regional climate resilience. Beyond the Adriatic, this framework offers a transferable approach to other semi-enclosed and shelf seas, where reliable detection of MHW drivers is essential. By linking detection with predictive understanding, this work contributes to broader efforts to improve preparedness for marine extremes and safeguard ecosystems and dependent economies in a warming ocean.

Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) have emerged as an increasingly severe disturbance to global marine ecosystems, with documented intensifications in both frequency and magnitude over the past century. Western Australia has experienced some of the most severe MHWs on record, causing widespread ecological impacts, including coral bleaching and mortality, local species extinctions, and socioeconomic impacts such as fishery closures, making the region a critical case study of climate-driven change in the marine domain. Most recently, a severe MHW during summer 2024/2025 has caused widespread disruption to marine life, reinforcing the region's vulnerability to repeated extreme events. Here, we combine a scoping review of published and emerging evidence with oceanographic analyses to assess the cumulative ecological impacts of MHWs across Western Australia. Accordingly, we propose adaptive management strategies for future MHWs. These strategies include the relocation of vulnerable species, implementation of adaptive fisheries management frameworks, and development of rapid response monitoring programs targeting key benthic indicator groups. Authors: Philipp Aglas-Leitner, S. Perkins-Kirkpatrick, Lukas Brunner, S. Undorf, F. Aglas-Leitner, E. Fischer, D. Stone
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76809-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21 st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

#1 [paper] An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast.
Authors: Zhang, Xiang, Cui, Yingzhe, Li, Furong, Zhou, Shenghui, Wu, Guangnan, Jing, Zhao, Wu, Lixin
Venue: Science advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43024702/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Machine learning ocean forecast models typically rely on initial conditions generated by traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs), making them unable to operate independently.
Method (Mycelium's reading): WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end machine-learning system that generates eddy-resolving global ocean forecasts directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global ocean forecast
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. WenHai-E2E outperforms a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS in the forecast accuracy. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

#1 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The quality of AI models in the energy sector depends strongly on the amount, quality, and representativeness of training data, requiring innovative methods for gathering, sharing, and using large datasets while ensuring privacy, security, and interoperability among energy actors.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Developing, training, and testing AI foundation models using extensive datasets; implementing data governance strategies such as data space connectors, federated training, synthetic data creation, or 'AI gym' approaches; performing in-depth testing and validation in lab demonstrators and real-life …
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The energy sector, specifically focusing on electricity grids, forecasting, congestion management, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, flexibility management, demand-side energy efficiency, and EV charging, utilizing data from energy utilities, grid operators, asset owners, …
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Projects are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- Effective and innovative methods for gathering, sharing and using large data sets in energy applications for the purpose of training AI models while ensuring privacy and security.

- Advanced and - wherever possible - open-source AI foundation models to support the digitalisation of the energy system, through improved grid observability, forecasting of supply and demand, advanced storage and renewables integration, demand side flexibility and energy efficiency.

- Enhanced cooperation, knowledge sharing and interoperability among energy system actors for secure and seamless data exchange.

- Advanced methodologies for AI model development ensuring that the results are FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) beyond the project ending, open source and accommodating for technology evolution.

Scope:

The quality of AI models depends strongly on the amount, quality, and representativeness of the data used for their training. Projects are expected to focus on developing, training and testing AI foundation models, using extensive data sets to accelerate the energy transition in key focus areas of the energy sector. Projects are expected to:

- Building on the results of previously funded projects on the Common European energy data space[1] as well as the ongoing work within the Data 4 Energy expert group, projects are expected to demonstrate innovative methods and data governance strategies for sharing data among various energy actors. Projects are expected to demonstrate that they have access to large relevant datasets at the time of submitting the proposal.

- Projects are expected to develop innovative strategies for sharing data in an effective, secure and transparent way to support the development of AI foundation models. An indicative non exhaustive list of strategies that can be explored is the use of data space connectors or federated training of models to allow the integration of confidential data; the creation of synthetic data as an intermediate step to fill data gaps or improve the quality of the data could also be explored. Projects could also explore other innovative data sharing strategies, such as an ‘AI gym’. The data governance strategies that will be developed in the project should be designed in a way to be scalable and operational even after the end of the project.

- Projects are expected to develop foundation models tailored for the energy sector, addressing at least one -or more- of the following use cases: planning and operation of electricity grids (including static power flow modelling and dynamic EMT modelling), forecasting, congestion management, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, flexibility management, demand-side energy efficiency, smart and bidirectional charging of EVs or other use cases that contribute to the objective of digitalisation of the energy system.

- Projects are expected to perform in-depth testing and validation of developed foundation models in lab demonstrators and real-life pilots, building on the results and using the facilities of previously funded projects on “AI testing and experimentation facilities (TEFs)”[2]. Regulatory sandboxes could also be considered for real-life pilot implementations.

- Projects are expected to bring together a wide group of stakeholders including data owners (for example energy utilities, grid operators, asset owners), application developers (for example startups, SMEs, hyperscalers) and model deployers (for example industry, grid operators, equipment manufacturers) providing a space of cooperation and collaborative data exchange.

- To scale up the training and development of the models, projects can benefit from the computing capacity of the AI factories that were recently announced by the European Commission[3], in particular the three AI factories that aim to develop AI applications for the energy sector.

#1 [paper] Funding deadlines act as a zeitgeber for science
Authors: Haining Wang, Jing Su
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.10.758253
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Funders decide which science is paid for. Whether they also shape when it becomes public has been hard to test. Across 376,542 preprints on bioRxiv and medRxiv, the US share rose by 2.3 to 2.7 percentage points in the four weeks before due dates for the main research grant of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and dropped on the date. About one in eleven US preprints in those weeks was attributable to the deadline, and fields that depend least on NIH rose least. Among 15,906 funded investigators, the share of preprints posted in the four weeks before their own deadline was 9% higher than in other four-month cycles, and these preprints resembled the later grant without being more highly cited. Repeated before every due date, this individual surge matches the national peak's timing within a week. NIH's application calendar, like its funding, shapes when US biomedical science becomes public.

#6 [paper] Alternative futures for laboratory medicine in 2050: scenarios and signposts for diagnostic capability contraction.
Authors: Yuji, Koichiro, Yuji, Wakako, Ohnishi, Hiroaki
Venue: Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42723619/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Laboratory medicine has begun to describe its own future, and the images it produces are almost uniformly expansionary. What they rarely contain is a collapse scenario: a future in which the field delivers less than today. A profession planning for 2050 needs one. CONTENT: We summarise what structured foresight offers a clinical readership, entering through the threats quadrant of a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) analysis, and treat the standard taxonomy of futures as a lens, not a required method. We define diagnostic capability contraction as progressive degradation rather than catastrophic disappearance, distinct from retiring tests that add nothing. Six drivers are specified: loss of laboratory-developed tests, reduced test availability, workforce attrition, supplier dependency, geographical access and payment. Evidence comes from three jurisdictions, including Japan, where one regulatory driver produced different outcomes in the same period. We set out four scenarios for 2050, one per generic image, and propose signposts as early-warning indicators, with action thresholds, for the contraction scenario. Estimates of likelihood attach to the indicators, not the futures. SUMMARY: The evidence base is uneven across drivers, and informatively so: what is not anticipated is not measured. The argument applies to our own prior work, expansionary in the same way. OUTLOOK: A set containing a contraction branch gives laboratory leadership what an expansionary set cannot: what to watch for, and when to act. A preferred future chosen without it comes from a shorter list than the field faces. Building a balanced set is work that no small group of authors can do alone.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The current knowledge of food chemical complexity is limited to a narrow set of approximately 150 components, leaving over 100,000 compounds and contaminants ('nutrient dark matter') unquantified and underexplored, creating a bottleneck for predictive nutrition and food safety.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development and testing of validated AI algorithms capable of interpreting and annotating high-throughput foodomics data (e.g., untargeted mass-spectrometry or nuclear magnetic resonance) and predicting/inferring compound presence and concentration via innovative approaches like phylogenetic relati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): High-throughput foodomics data involving hundreds of thousands of compounds across thousands of foods.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- an Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool able to accelerate the analysis of complex foodomics data to speed up the identification, structural characterisation, and quantification of chemicals present in food;

- improving capacity and synergies in foodomics research between academia, research infrastructures and industry.

Scope:

Through food and beverages, the population is exposed to an immense variety of chemicals (as contaminants and as ingredients). The “foodome” is the complete set of compounds present in a food sample at a given time; it includes both endogenous biomolecules (produced through a species' metabolic processes) and exogenous compounds (natural and synthetic substances from production, processing, handling, and packaging). The current knowledge is largely confined to a narrow set of approximately 150 food components catalogued by traditional databases. These components represent only a very small fraction of the total chemical complexity present in foods, while thousands (>100,000) of compounds and contaminants remain largely unquantified and underexplored. Understanding this “nutrient dark matter” would require identifying, cataloguing and quantifying the full spectrum of substances present in our food and present in accessible, AI-ready databases. The need for such information is today a bottleneck to make the nutrition field predictive and data driven, and has the potential to make food processing more efficient in bringing new foods items on the market. Efforts to create such datasets are underway but owing to the quantity of samples (hundreds of thousands of compounds across thousands of foods), such databases often rely on high-throughput experimental methods which do not allow a precise characterisation of the molecules identified.

Proposals should address the following activities:

- develop and test validated AI algorithms capable of interpreting and annotating high-throughput foodomics data, for instance from untargeted mass-spectrometry or nuclear magnetic resonance;

- the AI algorithms should be capable to predict or infer the presence and concentration of compounds based on (incomplete) foodomics data via innovative approaches, for instance by considering phylogenic relationships between species. Moreover, this should help identify analytical methods and potential food safety hazards based on their similarity to known compounds;

- develop a European research and innovation network between Member States and Associated Countries in food exposome research to support the development, standardization, valorisation and dissemination of the AI results and considering existing initiatives such as the Centre for Excellence in the Periodic Table of Food Initiative from Wageningen University.

The multi-actor approach is encouraged. Proposals should include industry in the consortia and academia, startups, SMEs and international initiatives. Collaboration with international partners is encouraged as well as with existing private companies in the EU/Associated countries.

Technology Readiness Level - Technology readiness level expected from completed projects

Activities are expected to start from TRL 5 in order to achieve TRL 7 by the end of the project – see General Annex B.

The National Institutes of Health (NIH) Tackling Acquisition of Language in Kids (TALK) initiative intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit research grant applications to improve the earliest steps in clinical practice for late talking children. #20 [paper] CY 2027 Medicare PFS and OPPS proposed rules: key implications for wound care across facility and non-facility settings
Authors: William H Tettelbach, Luis Arencibia, Diane Weiss
Venue: International Journal of Tissue Repair
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.63676/eya7yd09
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) CY 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) proposed rule contains several provisions with direct implications for wound care delivery. The proposals include lower physician conversion factors, a new 50% payment reduction when separately identifiable office/outpatient evaluation and management (E/M) services are furnished on the same day as 0-, 10-, or 90-day global procedures, replacement of HCPCS G2211 with percentage-based modifiers, continued evolution of cellular, acellular, and matrix-like product (CAMP) payment, national valuation of real-time bacterial fluorescence wound imaging, practice-expense reform, and changes to remote physiologic and therapeutic monitoring. The same-day E/M proposal is especially important for wound clinicians because interventions such as sharp surgical debridement are commonly performed and medically necessary during wound care encounters. Importantly, as currently drafted, the proposal is limited to office/outpatient E/M services, which in wound care are commonly furnished in private physician offices and hospital outpatient departments (HOPDs). It does not currently extend to appropriately reported home/residence or nursing-facility E/M services, including those furnished in POS 12, 13, 31, and 32. CMS is seeking comment on whether the policy should later extend to other E/M categories. Facility and non-facility effects also differ because hospital outpatient departments receive separate facility reimbursement while independent office and mobile practices bear practice expense directly. This summary reviews the proposed policies most relevant to wound care and distinguishes their expected application across common sites of service.

Proposals are expected to address multiple key research directions in Quantum Machine Learning (QML), targeting both scientific excellence and industrial relevance. Proposals should clearly outline how to contribute to the development, validation and demonstration of quantum-enhanced AI approaches, with clear pathways towards practical applications. The proposed work should strengthen Europe’s scientific and technological capabilities in quantum computing and accelerate the industrial uptake of quantum-enhanced AI solutions.

Activities may include, but are not limited to

- design and analysis of quantum, quantum-inspired or hybrid QML algorithms,

- performance modelling, complexity analysis and benchmarking of quantum-enhanced AI methods,

- development of error-mitigation and noise-aware strategies tailored to QML workloads,

Proposals should advance scalable QML algorithms capable of addressing large-scale, computationally intensive problems, this includes approaches that

- can manage massive data volumes and complex computational tasks,

- enable faster data processing and improved predictive performance in relevant application domains (e.g. hydrologic research, climate modelling, terrain classification from satellite remote sensing, drug discovery, and image-based medical diagnosis).

Many current QML methods remain closely inspired by classical algorithms and therefore do not yet achieve genuine quantum advantage, requiring further developments in

- quantum-native learning models,

- efficient quantum kernels and quantum feature mappings,

- algorithms demonstrating provable or empirical advantages over classical approaches.

Proposals may also include formal complexity analyses, identification of problem classes that can benefit from quantum acceleration.

Developments should address multiple of the following key research directions:

Quantum Supervised Learning (QSL):

Quantum Supervised Learning investigates how quantum algorithms can accelerate or improve the training of supervised learning models, offering novel opportunities to explore quantum–classical learning theories and enabling industry to shorten development cycles and enhance performance in data-intensive domains such as finance, healthcare, and Earth observation.

#1 [paper] Data and code for: An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system for Mediterranean temperate reefs: forecasting climate-driven mortality under context-dependent local protection

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Static conservation strategies are outpaced by accelerating marine heatwaves, threatening temperate reefs. There is a need for prospective tools that integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability and support climate-smart Marine Spatial Planning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system using a rigorous modelling framework. It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#2 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#3 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#6 [paper] Performance of the Heatwave ED Forecast Tool in the Emergency Department Network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland
Authors: Matteo Paganini, Ilaria Costantini, Ilenia Mascherona, Simone Cosci, Laura Di Domenico, Ana Maria Vicedo-Cabrera, Roberta Petrino

Year: 2026

Abstract:
Objectives: Heatwaves drive surges in acute care demand, yet heat-health action plans (HHAPs) lack tools to scale emergency care responses. This study validated a forecasting tool for heatwave-related emergency department (ED) demand across four clusters comprising the emergency care network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland. Methods: This retrospective, ecological, time-series study modeled daily mean temperature and ED presentations using a distributed lag non-linear model framework with autoregressive and calendar adjustment components. The model was trained on summers (June-August) 2016-2024 and tested on summer 2025, defining heatwaves as daily mean temperature >25 °C for ≥3 consecutive days. Results: A non-linear temperature-demand association was shown across the clusters, with ED visits increasing at higher temperatures. Model fit varied across clusters (R 2 0.389–0.672), and the reference model consistently outperformed naïve baselines. During two heatwaves in 2025, prediction errors remained within acceptable ranges. Baseline demand, heatwave occurrence, and model performance varied substantially within the canton. Conclusions: These findings have implications for the design of HHAPs, suggesting that emergency care preparedness should rely on locally calibrated demand forecast rather than standardized activation protocols.

#7 [paper] Mitigating Summertime Marine Heatwaves via Targeted Marine Cloud Brightening
Authors: Matthew T. Luongo, Edward Blanchard‐Wrigglesworth, Kyle Armour, Haruki Hirasawa, Jacob Cohen, Aaron Donohoe
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5kv4t
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) negatively impact marine ecosystems and coastal economies. Here, we evaluate whether a preemptive, short-term, localized surface emission of sea salt aerosols (marine cloud brightening, MCB) can mitigate the impacts of a predicted MHW without creating significant effects beyond the intervention zone. As a case study, we apply MCB to the 2019 Northeast Pacific MHW, "The Blob 2.0," using a global climate model seasonal-to-multiyear predictability ensemble. Initiating MCB in May 2019 mitigates important negative consequences of the event, substantially reducing the MHW magnitude and limiting associated declines in surface oxygen. The impacts of this intervention are mostly local and limited to summer, even when MCB is extended into winter, with nonlocal climate effects smaller than internal variability. By demonstrating local efficacy and minor remote impacts for mitigating the Blob 2.0, this work motivates further study of whether localized and temporary climate interventions can safely and effectively mitigate MHWs.

#9 [paper] The evolution of the Dutch heat early warning system (2007 - 2025)
Authors: Carolina Pereira Marghidan, Rob Sluijter, Justine Blanford, Hisso Homan, Peter Siegmund, Werner Hagens, Maarten van Aalst
Venue: Climate Services
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cliser.2026.100718
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Heat early warning systems (HEWS) are critical tools for anticipating hazardous heat and enabling timely response. While some of the earliest systems were developed over two decades ago, little is known about how and why systems have evolved in practice. This study therefore examines the evolution of the Dutch heat warning system from 2007 to 2025 and evaluates the future performance of current warning criteria. We analysed 18 operational documents, including seven post-event evaluations, to identify operational challenges and drivers of change. Current warning criteria were also applied to KNMI’23 climate scenarios to assess future warning frequency, duration, intensity, and season length. Results show that the warning system evolved from a single trigger for the national Heat-Health Action Plan into a tiered warning system, while the HHAP remained linked to lower warning levels, creating misalignment between warnings and actions. Criteria remained primarily climatological due to limited epidemiological evidence, and criteria changes, such as the removal of nighttime criteria, were driven primarily by operational considerations. Future projections indicate a substantial increase in heat warnings, from ~2 per year currently to 3.9–7 by 2050 and up to 29 by 2100. The findings provide lessons for meteorological and public health agencies by showing how operational, institutional, climate, and scientific factors shape the design of heat early warning systems.

#12 [paper] Multi-Hazard Disaster Prediction and Warning System Using Machine Learning
Authors: Kaustubh M. Patil, Rushikesh M. Patange, Siddhesh A. Nikam, Laxmikant M. Gholave
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24215741

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Headline accuracy in disaster early-warning studies often masks class imbalance, temporal drift, and spatial extrapolation error.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A leakage-aware evaluation protocol using chronological splits and spatial hold-outs, applying logistic regression for flood severity and histogram-based gradient boosting for heat-event proxies.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Two modules: 4,548 flood events from 155 gauges (split by time) and a heat-event proxy based on IMD gridded daily maximum temperature (1° grid, 1951–2024) across 338 eligible cells.
Abstract:
Disaster early-warning studies often report headline accuracy, which can hide class imbalance, temporal drift and spatial extrapolation error. This paper applies a leakage-aware evaluation protocol to two research modules. The first is flood severity classification among 4,548 recorded flood events from 155 gauges, evaluated with a chronological split (training before 2010, validation 2010–2014, test 2015–2020). The second is a heat-event proxy built from IMD gridded daily maximum temperature (1° grid, 1951–2024). A grid-cell day is positive when it belongs to a run of at least three consecutive hot days, where a hot day exceeds the cell's 1961–1990 calendar-day 90th percentile and its baseline climatological Tmax exceeds 35 °C. The proxy covers 338 eligible cells, April–June target dates and 1991–2024. It is not an official IMD declaration. For flood severity, validation PR-AUC selected logistic regression, which achieved test balanced accuracy 0.6445 and ROC-AUC 0.6483 against a majority-class balanced accuracy of 0.5000. For the heat-event proxy, histogram-based gradient boosting was selected by validation PR-AUC (0.5811). On the 2020–2024 test period it achieved balanced accuracy 88.82%, recall 90.36%, ROC-AUC 0.9548 and PR-AUC 0.5813, but produced 18,415 false positives at threshold 0.50. A simple persistence rule had higher F1 (0.591 against 0.457) and fewer false positives. A spatial hold-out over 51 unseen cells gave balanced accuracy 87.33%. Attributions are associations, not causes, and these results do not establish operational early-warning performance.

#14 [paper] INFLUENCE OF COMMUNITY-BASED EARLY WARNING SYSTEMS ON RESILIENCE-ORIENTED PROJECT PLANNING AMONG NANO, SMALL AND MICRO-ENTERPRISES IN MARSABIT COUNTY, KENYA
Authors: Abdi Rach Huka, Jennifer Wangari Wairiuko, Samuel Macharia
Venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.30574/wjarr.2026.31.3.2379
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Nano, Small and Micro Enterprises (NSMEs), represent the final linkage within last-mile delivery of food, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) commodities, in Kenya's arid and semi-arid regions; however, these entities remain excluded from formal disaster risk management and project planning frameworks. The objective of this study was to determine the extent to which Community Based Early Warning Systems (CBEWS) influence Resilience-Oriented Project Planning amongst NSMEs in Marsabit County, specifically regarding access to early warning information, translation of that information into preparedness, and mechanisms that enable such transition. Utilizing programmatic evidence from the B-READY Anticipatory Action Program, a Pre-Crisis Market Mapping and Analysis (PCMMA) of fifty NSMEs, Activation Ready Protocol (ARP) co-design forums, and associated anticipatory action plans; along with a literature review of CBEWS, anticipatory actions, and enterprise resiliency, the study developed a conceptual model relating access to early warnings to outcomes in planning through three constructs: Trust, Translation, and Actionability. The findings of the study indicated that while drought and flood forecasts have Increased their reach to Marsabit's trading community; access does not consistently translate into planning: fewer than half of the enterprises participated in the study used climate information to prepare for shocks, and almost none had written continuity plans. In addition to lacking sufficient working capital to withstand even short duration disruptions. Successful translation occurred primarily when scientific forecasting was integrated with locally trusted Indigenous Technical Knowledge, disseminated via trader networks and radio broadcasts, and coupled with trigger-based financing protocols. As such, it is recommended that county governments, humanitarian organizations, financial institutions and NSMEs treat early warning as an intermediate input requiring deliberate co-designed project components rather than a terminal product.

#15 [paper] The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
Authors: Catherine H. Gregory, Urs Hofmann Elizondo, Thibault Guinaldo, Thomas Lukas Frölicher
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78863-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

#16 [paper] Atmosphere-Driven Compound Extremes: Record Marine Heatwave and Phytoplankton Bloom in the Ross Sea During Summer 2022-2023
Authors: Zehao Wang, Shaoyin Wang, Zhu Zhu, Zixin Wei, Fukai Peng
Venue: Environmental Research Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1088/1748-9326/ae9780
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract We document an extreme marine heatwave (MHW) in the eastern Ross Sea during the 2022–2023 austral summer (DJF), the most intense thermal event in the satellite record. Using satellite-retrieved sea surface temperature (SST), ocean colour, sea ice, and atmospheric-oceanic reanalysis data, we show that the eastern Ross Sea experienced a Category IV (extreme) MHW during this season, with the regional-mean cumulative intensity reaching 127.22 °C·days in January 2023 and summer-mean SST anomalies locally peaking at approximately +2.5 °C above the climatological mean. Summer-mean chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) concentration reached 3.67 mg m⁻³, the highest value observed in the eastern Ross Sea since satellite ocean-colour records began in 1997. The ecological response followed a threshold-dependent sequence: early sea-ice retreat initially removed light limitation, followed later by a strong Chl-a increase as sustained warming and upper-ocean restratification favoured bloom development. In contrast, persistent ice cover in Terra Nova Bay prevented a comparable thermal or biological response. A meridional wind dipole drove divergent ice transport and the early expansion of the eastern Ross Sea polynya, while low-cloud cover decreased by up to 15.43%, increasing downward surface shortwave radiation by 64.09 W m⁻². Subsurface warming remained confined to the upper continental-shelf waters south of approximately 73°S, suggesting that local atmosphere–ice–radiation interactions contributed more strongly to the event than heat transport associated with ocean circulation. These results identify a distinctly polar pathway through which atmospheric forcing can generate compound thermal and biological extremes, highlighting the importance of local sea-ice coupling in shaping future Antarctic coastal productivity.

#19 [paper] Marine heat waves in vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable on multi-year timescales
Authors: Alexia Karwat, June‐Yi Lee, Christian L. E. Franzke, Yong‐Yub Kim, Eun Young Kwon, Sun‐Seon Lee
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78279-1

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The limited understanding of the predictability of marine heat waves (MHWs) in coral reef regions beyond seasonal timescales.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Analysis of Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments, and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020 to assess MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): 12 vulnerable coral reef regions across various ocean basins, using historical data from 1981 to 2020.
Abstract:
Marine heat waves (MHWs) increasingly threaten coral reefs, but their predictability beyond seasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here we assess the seasonal-to-multi-year predictability of MHW frequency, cumulative intensity, and duration across 12 coral reef regions. Using Community Earth System Model version 2 simulations, ocean-assimilated experiments and five-year hindcasts initialized annually from 1981 to 2020, we show that frequency and cumulative intensity are predictable for several months to multiple years across many ocean basins, with skill varying strongly by region and season. Anthropogenic warming is the dominant source of multi-year skill across most hotspots, while internal variability limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific. El Niño-Southern Oscillation and Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation further modulate regional forecasts through coupled ocean-atmosphere processes. These findings reveal strong regional contrasts in the sources and limits of forecast skill, identifying where advance warning can support timely, targeted regional preparedness, coral reef conservation and adaptation to escalating thermal stress. The study shows that marine heatwave frequency and cumulative intensity across vulnerable coral reef regions are skillfully predictable from months to years ahead, with long-term anthropogenic warming accounting for most multi-year forecast skill, while internal variability, particularly El Niño, limits predictability in the equatorial Pacific.

Abstract:
Abstract More than 50% of Oklahoma's surface water systems are classified as impaired by the US EPA, with limited funds designated toward surface water monitoring. Community science data can contribute to increasing the amount of quality‐controlled government water quality reporting. A framework is presented for implementing a community‐based approach to generating quality‐controlled water field data to support water quality monitoring by local and regional governments. This research focuses on the design and implementation of a water quality community science project in Oklahoma, USA. In this study, community scientists collected water samples and produced over 100 measurements of key water quality parameters, including alkalinity, conductivity, total dissolved solids, temperature, and selected metals (e.g., iron, manganese, mercury, cadmium, and lead). The frequency and resolution of these community‐generated data exceed those of conventional state government monitoring, demonstrating the potential for community science to provide cost‐effective, high‐frequency, and spatially expansive data sets, which fill monitoring gaps. Additionally, community science can act as a method to bridge the gap between stakeholders, scientists, and policy makers. This study highlights the quality‐controlled methods, tools, and community‐driven efforts shaping water quality research and public engagement in Oklahoma, a step forward in community‐driven data acquisition and water policy.

#2 [paper] Macrozoobenthos as a Bioindicator of Water Quality in the Coastal Waters of Merak Besar Island, Banten Province
Authors: Farhan Randi Darmawan, Muta Ali Khalifa, Erik Munandar
Venue: Barakuda 45 Jurnal Ilmu Perikanan dan Kelautan
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.47685/barakuda45.v8i1.875
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
High human activity in the coastal area of Merak Besar Island, Banten Province, such as tourism, port, and industrial activities, potentially degrades water quality and affects benthic organisms that serve as biological indicators of coastal ecosystem health. This study aimed to describe the physicochemical characteristics of the water, total organic matter (TOM), sediment texture, and macrozoobenthos community structure, and to determine the ecological condition of the waters using a macrozoobenthos bioindicator approach based on the AMBI (AZTI's Marine Biotic Index) method. Research was conducted spatially in January 2026 at four stations using 1x1 m² quadrat transects with different numbers of replicates per station, along with measurements of temperature, pH, DO, salinity, TOM, and sediment texture. Results showed physicochemical parameters at all stations remained stable and met seawater quality standards, although DO at one station was exactly at the minimum threshold. Twenty macrozoobenthos species were identified, comprising Group II (indifferent), Group III (tolerant), and Group IV (opportunistic) species, with no Group I or V species recorded, while Littoraria lutea had the highest abundance. Abundance ranged from 558-1,171 ind/m², highest at the least disturbed station. Species diversity was moderate, evenness high, and dominance low across all stations. Although physicochemical conditions were suitable for macrozoobenthos, AMBI values at all stations indicated a slightly polluted category, dominated by Group III. This confirms that macrozoobenthos can detect ecological stress not yet captured by instantaneous physicochemical parameters, making it a useful method for assessing the coastal environmental condition of Merak Besar Island.

Abstract:
Driven by warming and anthropogenic impacts, global coastal waters suffer from the escalating eutrophication crisis, making it essential to understand the dynamics of nutrient discharge and enrichment. While satellites can retrieve surface water optical properties, the estimation of coastal nutrients from space remains a long-standing challenge due to their non-optical properties. Recently, artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning, has enabled the spatiotemporal estimation of surface nutrients from satellite observations, which represents a potential breakthrough for sustainable water management. In this review, we summarize the mechanisms governing coastal biogeochemical cycling and identify the estimation complexity that international scholars have been striving to solve over the past decade. We demonstrate that data-driven methods have shown preliminary success in empowering remote sensing retrieval of nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon. Despite these advances, we note that significant challenges remain for effective monitoring of coastal eutrophication due to the limited interpretability of data-driven estimation and data scarcity. Ultimately, our aim is to advance satellite observations and data-driven estimation at the forefront of environmental science to develop the precise monitoring, assessment, and protection of coastal waters.

#1 [grant] GPD Grant Forecast

Abstract:
THIS IS NOT A NOTICE OF FUNDING. THIS IS A GENERAL FORECAST ONLY.

Grant and Per Diem (GPD) Program Introduction

The GPD Program is VA’s largest transitional housing program for Veterans experiencing homelessness and is permanently authorized under Public Law 109-461.

Since 1994, the GPD Program has awarded grants to community-based organizations to provide transitional housing with wraparound supportive services to assist vulnerable Veterans move into permanent housing. The grants are designed to meet Veterans at various stages as they move to stable housing. Community-based organizations receiving GPD grants offer focused transitional housing services through a variety of housing models targeted to different populations and needs of Veterans. The GPD program plays a vital role in the continuum of homeless services by providing supportive services to those Veterans who would otherwise be among the unsheltered homeless population. The result of GPD programs is that Veterans achieve residential stability, increase their skill levels and/or income, and obtain greater self-determination.

Types of GPD Grants

Transitional housing grants:

Per Diem Only (PDO) grants provide funding in the form of per diem payments to reimburse grantees for the cost of care provided to Veterans in transitional supportive housing.

Special Need grants target housing and services to specific populations of Veterans (e.g., women, Veterans with chronic mental illness, frail elderly Veterans, Veterans caring for minor dependents, terminally ill Veterans).

Transition-In-Place (TIP) grants offer Veteran residents housing in which supportive services transition out of the residence over time, rather than the resident. Upon completion of the TIP services, the resident retains the unit as their permanent housing with no requirement to move.

Other types of grants:

Case Management grants support Veterans who were previously experiencing homelessness or who are at risk for homelessness so that they may obtain or retain permanent housing.

Capital grants support the costs of acquiring, renovating, or constructing facilities and are only offered intermittently to improve existing facilities or to develop new transitional housing depending on VA's priorities and funding availability.

Lists of current grantees are available on the GPD website.

How to Apply for GPD Funding

Not all grant types are available annually. When available, notices of funding can be found at the following locations: www.grants.gov and https://www.va.gov/homeless/gpd.asp.

Application instructions are provided in each notice of funding.

Each notice of funding will clarify specific eligibility criteria, application requirements, funding limitations, and other requirements.

Applications are submitted through an online portal that is only available when there is an open notice of funding.

Potential applicants who wish to see what was required for previous applications may review past notices of funding, available on the GPD provider website and www.grants.gov. Past notices of funding are not a guarantee of future requirements.

Tentative Estimated GPD Award Schedule

Specific dates are not able to be forecast.

The follow tentative approximations are provided for general planning purposes.

FY 2026

Case Management – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2025 for case management awards starting approximately in FY 2026.

FY 2027

PDO – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2026 for PDO awards starting approximately in FY 2027.

TIP – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2026 for TIP awards starting approximately in FY 2027.

FY 2028

GPD tentatively does not expect to offer a notice of funding for this timeframe. GPD may update this forecast closer to the time.

THIS IS NOT A NOTICE OF FUNDING. THIS IS A GENERAL FORECAST ONLY.

Through this Disaster NOFO, EDA will award investments in regions experiencing severe economic distress or other economic harm resulting from hurricanes, wildfires, tornadoes, floods, and other natural disasters occurring in calendar years 2023 and 2024. EDA’s goal under this NOFO is to assist communities recovering from a disaster by realizing opportunities to recover and change the economic trajectory of the community for the better. In other words, EDA funding seeks to help communities recover and set them on a path to exceed their previous pre-disaster baseline. EDA seeks projects that are responsive to community needs post-disaster by engaging all aspects of the community, with special focus on private industry partners.

This Disaster NOFO provides funding through three pathways:

Readiness Path – Standalone non-construction projects designed to increase a community’s readiness to apply for or implement disaster recovery funding from private and public sources including, but not limited to, future EDA NOFOs and the Implementation or Industry Transformation Paths under this NOFO. Projects will fund strategy development, capacity building, and/or predevelopment costs necessary for future recovery projects.

Implementation Path – Standalone construction or non-construction projects designed to address the economic challenges faced by a community recovering from a natural disaster and improve economic trajectories beyond pre-disaster economic conditions.

Industry Transformation Path – Led by a coalition of regional stakeholders, a portfolio of large-scale, multicomponent construction and non-construction projects designed to fundamentally transform the economic trajectory of a region through the development or acceleration of an industry.

#20 [grant] Advancing Screening, Diagnosis, and Referral for Late Talking Children
Amount: $500,000
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/362352
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-10-15
Abstract:
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) Tackling Acquisition of Language in Kids (TALK) initiative intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit research grant applications to improve the earliest steps in clinical practice for late talking children. The overarching purpose of this funding opportunity is to inform, develop, and evaluate evidence-based practices and implementation strategies to (1) effectively and efficiently identify early signs of late talking and (2) successfully guide parents, caregivers, and professionals in supporting the needs of late talking children at the first point of concern.

For this NOFO late talking is defined as a child, usually over the age of 18 months, not meeting expressive language milestones, for any reason. Populations of interest include, but are not limited to, children at higher risk for late talking due to premature birth, exposure to maltreatment or trauma, neurological conditions, motor and sensory disorders, emotional and behavioral disorders, and intellectual and developmental disorders. Children who present as late talkers for no other known reason and with no other symptoms also are of interest for this NOFO.

For this NOFO, the early steps for services for children age birth to three years that are of interest include screening and developmental surveillance of late talking, referral and follow through for specialized services, and in-depth evaluation and diagnosis of language and other contributing delays/disorders. These services typically occur in primary care, specialty care, educational settings, and early childhood community settings. The research will need to be conducted in a relevant setting.

Research focusing on children as well as their parents, caregivers, and supporting community professionals is of interest, including how to support successfully navigating from initial concern to effective care. Community partnerships and community engaged research approaches will be a key requirement for this opportunity.

Applications are not being solicited at this time. Notice is being provided to allow potential applicants sufficient time to develop meaningful collaborations and responsive projects.

Investigators with expertise and insights into early language learning, late talking, early childhood education, early intervention, and primary care are encouraged to begin to consider applying for this new NOFO. In addition, collaborative investigations combining expertise in clinical practice research, dissemination and implementation science, or community engaged research will be encouraged and these investigators should also begin considering applying for this application.

The working group provides scientific advice on 25 assessment units, including stocks of deep-water species and those on deep shelf areas. Available time-series for international landings and discards, fishing effort, survey indices, and biological information were updated for all stocks and are presented in this report. Working documents and presentations on intersessional work undertaken since the last WGDEEP meeting were discussed during plenary sessions at the 2026 meeting, including exploratory assessments and reports on research on relevant stocks. These were used to inform the assessments and conclusions outlined in this report. Overall, there are a few changes in the perception of the health of the stocks and fisheries since the previous reporting period. Non-straddling fish stocks in the northwestern Northeast Atlantic Ocean that were historically assessed by WGDEEP, including Greater silver smelt (aru.27.5a14), Blue ling (bli.27.5a14), Atlantic wolffish (caa.27.5a), Ling (lin.27.5a), and Tusk (usk.27.5a14), were assessed in 2026 by the Northwestern Working Group (NWWG). Available information to WGDEEP is indicative that deep-water stocks account for a small proportion of catches in the NEAFC Regulatory Area (RA). Spatial and seasonal management measures, including specific measures for the protection of Vulnerable Marine Ecosystems, are considered important factors that contribute to the reduction of fishing effort for deep-water species within those areas. No new emerging deep-water fisheries were detected with the available data from the NEAFC RA. The working group notes that the limited fisheries-independent data are not considered appropriate to assess the stock and exploitation status of many stocks across the Northeast Atlantic and Arctic Ocean, which limits the ability to understand climate-related and fisheries effects on deep-water fish stocks. The uncertainty over the landings and stock status of several stocks is a major limitation to the provision of fisheries advice to support the recovery of depleted stocks. Abstract:
The rapid convergence of neurotechnology and artificial intelligence (AI) has moved beyond the isolation of clinical laboratories and IT factories to become a transformative force capable, in the long-term, of redefining the human experience. In the wake of brain-machine interaction technologies, human and cognitive enhancement and even transhumanism perspectives, this evolution has given rise to the concept of the hybrid mind, a state where biological cognitive systems merge seamlessly with artificial ones, blurring traditional boundaries of identity, agency, autonomy, and consciousness. While these advances offer unprecedented potential to restore sensory and motor functions, they simultaneously challenge our foundational understandings of cognitive liberty, mental integrity, neuroethics and conventional privacy paradigms. This Research Topic, hosted by Frontiers in Human Dynamics -Digital Impacts and cross-listed across seven participating journals, includingFrontiers in Sociology, Neurology, and Neurorobotics, serves as a multidisciplinary research collection that aims to connect different fields and backgrounds with a common frame. It also archives the overall findings that emerged from the international conference "The Hybrid Mind: Ethics and Regulation of Intelligent Neuroprostheses", that took place in October 2023 in Berlin, Germany. Under the stewardship of the editors spanning legal, ethical, medical, and IT backgrounds, the collection features the work of 39 authors, and reflects a rigorous selection process, resulting in a competitive acceptance rate of 46%. In terms of typology of scientific research, the contributions, from 3 reviews, 2 conceptual analyses and 1 study protocol to 3 perspectives and 2 original research papers, paint an articulated, yet still homogeneous spectrum of different research perspectives that pivot around the neuroprivacy topic. The impact of this collection is already evident from the numbers of citations, research topic views, article views, and article downloads.The 11 articles in this collection can be organised into four thematic clusters (plus one focus) that reveal a productive tension between the drive for therapeutic "super-human" capabilities and the necessity of safeguarding the "most intimate personal corner": the mind.The collection provides a firm grounding in current medical progress, establishing a baseline for the technical capabilities that now interact with the human mind. Deng and colleagues provide a comprehensive twenty-year bibliometric analysis of Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS) for stroke rehabilitation, documenting a clear transition from basic pathophysiological research toward translational studies focused on neuroplasticity. Their findings highlight how non-invasive methods, such as transauricular VNS, are gaining traction as safer and more cost-effective alternatives to surgical intervention. Complementing this technical trajectory, Kim et al. present a double-blinded randomised control pilot trial protocol utilising the RecoveriX PRO system. Their work aims to verify that motor imagery-contingent neurofeedback is superior to sham feedback in subacute stroke rehabilitation, asserting that the closed-loop connection between intention and feedback is essential for the effective reorganisation of neural circuits. The trial aims to resolve a current research gap by directly comparing the superiority of "real BCI" (MI-contingent feedback) over "sham BCI" (MIirrelevant feedback) specifically for patients in the subacute phase of stroke. The protocol uniquely combines clinical evaluations with neurophysiological tools like EEG (functional connectivity) and TMS (cortical excitability) to assess brain reorganization from the cerebral cortex down to the endeffector. #5 [paper] Mapping Global Trends in Higher Education Admission Strategies Over the Last Decade: A Bibliometric Analysis
Authors: Noormawanti -, Agus Pahrudin, Eti Hadiati, Muhammad Afif Amrullah
Venue: Journal Human Research in Rehabilitation
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21554/hrr.092604
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study examines global trends and thematic developments in research on higher education student admission strategies from 2016 to 2025, amid increasingly complex selection policies and expanding digital influence. Using a bibliometric analysis of 487 Scopus-indexed documents, metadata were refined with OpenRefine and analyzed using Biblioshiny R and VOSviewer to map publication patterns, collaborations, and keyword networks. Results show a significant rise in publications since 2018, peaking in 2024. Leading sources include Academic Medicine and ASEE Annual Conference Proceedings, with prominent contributors such as Glazer, James-Maceachern, Nesterov, and Sin. Five main thematic clusters emerged: student recruitment policy, professional education, cultural diversity, educational psychology, and academic evaluation. Emerging topics include machine learning applications, sustainability-oriented admissions, and digital justice. These developments highlight the growing need to integrate technological innovation with social equity to promote inclusive and transparent global admission practices.

#6 [paper] Factors Associated With Interview Offer Rates in Otolaryngology Residency Applications.
Authors: Nanu, Douglas P, Maley, Grace E, Khan, Sofia, Ibrahim, Alexa F, Nguyen, Shaun A, Carr, Michele M
Venue: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42934850/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association of preference signaling on interview offer rates in otolaryngology residency applications, comparing applicant type (MD vs DO), geographic status (in-state vs out-of-state), and international status (US vs non-US IMGs) across US programs and regions. STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional analysis. SETTING: All US otolaryngology residency programs with interview data participating in the 2024 to 2025 match cycle. METHODS: Data were obtained from the AAMC Residency Explorer Tool. Programs reporting interview rates for both signaled and nonsignaled applicants were included. Mean rates (±SD) were compared using Welch's t-tests. Effect sizes were calculated with Cohen's d. Regional differences (Midwest, South, Northeast, West) were analyzed using one-way ANOVA. RESULTS: Of 133 programs, 82 (61.7%) reported complete data. Programs invited signaled applicants at markedly higher rates than nonsignaled applicants (41.8% vs 5.0%, P < .001). Programs demonstrated significantly higher interview offer rates for MD and in-state applicants than DO and out-of-state applicants, respectively, across all regions (all P < .01). Differences between US and non-US IMGs were smaller and less consistent. No significant regional differences were observed in the magnitude of these effects. CONCLUSION: Preference signaling and applicant background were strongly associated with interview offer rates in the 2024 to 2025 OHNS cycle, with programs demonstrating significantly higher interview offer rates for MD, in-state, and signaled applicants across all regions. These findings highlight disparities in interview selection observed in the 2024 to 2025 cycle and emphasize the continued influence of both signaling and applicant characteristics on residency competitiveness.

Factors other than greenhouse gas emissions have caused observed warming to date of 1.2°C . No. There is consensus among scientists that the warming to date above preindustrial levels (observed at weather stations and confirmed by satellite data) is from atmospheric accumulations of human-induced, heat-trapping gases, rather than other factors like changes in solar radiation and volcanic activity or urban heat absorption (see Chapter 2 ). Myth 2. Global warming is not a major concern because people can adapt, for example, by adopting air conditioning, drought-resistant crops, and moving to cooler climates . No. Global warming is causing a diverse range of climate risks such as greater frequency and intensity of heat waves, shifting precipitation patterns (which puts at risk water systems, agriculture, and ecosystems), droughts, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes—these risks are escalating because warming causes more energy and water vapor in the atmosphere. Higher atmospheric CO 2 concentrations also eat away at the minerals used by marine life to build their shells and skeletons. And there is an escalating risk of crossing (poorly understood) tipping points in the Earth’s climate system such as permafrost melting (which could turn on an unstoppable gas tap of CO 2 and methane), long-term collapse of major ice sheets (which could raise global sea levels several meters), changes in ocean circulation (which could radically change temperature and precipitation patterns around the world), and forest dieback (which could transform the Amazon into dry savanna) (see Chapter 2 ). Myth 3. Near-term mitigation action in advanced economies can largely get global emissions on track with temperature goals . No. Global emissions need to be cut 25–50 percent below 2019 levels by 2030 to get on track with limiting warming to 2°C and 1.5°C, respectively. This will not be possible without substantial emissions reductions in developing countries given they account for nearly 70 percent of global baseline CO 2 emissions in 2030 (see Chapter 2 ). Proportionate emissions cuts should however be larger in advanced economies, and international climate finance should support low-carbon energy transitions in low-income countries. Myth 4. The Paris process is on track for achieving global temperature goals . No. Even if fully achieved, current mitigation targets in Nationally Determined Contributions would only reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by 12 percent below 2019 level by 2030. Put another way, new measures equivalent to a global carbon price upward of $80 per ton are needed by 2030 to be on track with keeping warming below 2°C (the current global average carbon price is $5 per ton). If the required emissions reductions are not achieved by 2030, emissions will need to be cut even more drastically after 2030, rapidly raising the costs of low-carbon energy transitions and potentially putting temperature goals permanently beyond reach (see Chapters 2 and 9 ). Myth 5. Low-carbon technology subsidies and mandates can mimic many of the mitigation responses from carbon pricing . No. Carbon pricing can promote the full range of behavioral responses to cut emissions across fuels, sectors, firms, and households—and cost-effectively, because it equates the cost of the last ton reduced across responses. Low-carbon technology subsidies and mandates promote a much narrower range of responses. For example, in the power sector carbon pricing will reduce electricity demand, encourage operational efficiencies, promote switching from coal to gas and from fossil fuels to nuclear and hydro, adoption of carbon capture technologies, and switching from fossil fuels to wind and solar.
