#8 [paper] The impact of presentations in scientific conferences: Publication and citation rates in trauma surgery.
Authors: Touponse, Gavin, Bidwell, Serena, Shank, Amei, Tai, Jesse, Poe, James, Berg, Alexander, Khan, Hason, Tian, Lu
Venue: The journal of trauma and acute care surgery
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42912484/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Understanding the publication rates and citation patterns of conference abstracts is critical for program committees and investigators alike. However, the downstream scholarly outcome of conference abstracts remains poorly characterized. We hypothesized that across contemporary US trauma-related scientific meetings, a substantial proportion of conference abstracts would not progress to peer-reviewed publications, and that publication rates and citation patterns would vary by presentation format and conference. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of abstracts presented at four major US trauma surgery conferences from 2017 to 2019. We identified peer-reviewed manuscripts associated with conference abstracts via Google Scholar and PubMed. We collected presentation format, publishing journal, 2024 journal impact factor, and citation count. A cohort of directly submitted peer-reviewed manuscripts was also analyzed. Mixed-effects Poisson regression models assessed the association between presentation and citation counts, adjusting for publication timing. RESULTS: Of 1,157 abstracts, 762 (66%) were published as peer-reviewed manuscripts. Most manuscripts were published in the Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery (JTACS) (55%), with 5 in journals with a higher-impact factor than JTACS. On regression analysis, abstracts presented as oral presentations, and published in journals with an impact factor higher than JTACS, were associated with a greater number of citations. When comparing manuscripts presented as abstracts to directly submitted peer-reviewed manuscripts, abstract presentation was associated with 22% more citations (incidence rate ratio: 1.22; 95% CI [1.16-1.29]; p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This cross-sectional study of four trauma societies found that approximately a third of presented abstracts did not progress to peer-reviewed publication, with publication rates varying by conference and presentation format. Exploratory analyses found that among those published in JTACS, published manuscripts originating from presented abstracts demonstrated a modestly higher citation count compared with directly submitted manuscripts. Our findings highlight an opportunity to better understand how conference time and investigator effort translate into downstream scholarly output. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic/Epidemiological; Level IV.

#9 [paper] A Decision Support System for Conference Session Selection using Natural Language Processing and Machine Learning
Authors: Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, Tillman Erb, SLO Cal Poly, Puneet Agarwal, Sumona Mukhopadhyay
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21872/annual2025_6180
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Conference attendees are often faced with selecting from hundreds of presentations and sessions in pursuit of new findings and methods relevant to their area of interest, an overwhelming amount of information from which to clearly make a decision. To address this, we aim to develop a tool leveraging machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) techniques such as topic modeling (BERTopic) and semantic matching. By creating and matching embeddings of conference presentation abstracts and titles, the tool will provide improved query matching compared to keyword searching. Attendees can select from a variety of input types, including keyword selection and natural language query, and receive a collection of presentations with abstracts semantically matching the input. Notably, users can input an abstract of a paper most relevant to their area of interest and receive a collection of relevant conference presentations. We hope that this tool will enable academics and practitioners to rapidly identify relevant presentations, fostering knowledge exchange and professional network exploration.

#10 [paper] Fair, Explainable Early Warning for First-Year Student Dropout: Accuracy, Group Equity and Support Allocation
Authors: FNU Sumaiya
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23487386

Abstract:
Working paper (v1.0, October 2026). Not peer reviewed; results are preliminary and may contain errors. Colleges use early-warning systems to decide which students receive outreach, tutoring and advising, yet published audits show these tools can be inaccurate and unequal across student groups. This working paper asks three questions an institution should answer before relying on such a tool: Is a transparent model accurate enough? Is it equally accurate for every student group? And who should receive support when capacity is limited? Using public records for 4,424 students (UCI Predict Students’ Dropout and Academic Success), we compare transparent logistic and multinomial-logit models, built at enrollment and after the first semester, against a grades-only baseline. We audit their errors across four student groups, and we formulate the allocation of limited support as an optimization problem with fairness quotas, proving that a simple greedy rule solves it optimally. Key findings (means across five data splits): A first-semester model that never sees demographic attributes reached AUC 0.897 and caught 66.8% of eventual dropouts at a 5.5% false-alarm rate. Entry grades alone reached AUC 0.564. The model under-detected dropouts among scholarship holders by 27 percentage points and among younger students by 25 points, consistently across splits. Group-specific thresholds narrowed these gaps but sharply increased false alarms. With support capacity for 10% of students, model-based targeting reached three times as many eventual dropouts as random selection. Fairness quotas cost about 2 of 132 support slots. Files: the working paper (PDF), and fair-early-warning.zip, which contains R code that reproduces every table and figure (base R only). The data are available from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.24432/C5MC89) and are not redistributed here.

#12 [paper] Reapplication and Credential Completion Among Non-Selected Community College Health Science Applicants: A Social Stratification Perspective
Authors: Donna G Whitehouse
Venue: Digital Commons - East Tennessee State University (East Tennessee State University)
Year: 2026
Link: https://dc.etsu.edu/etd/4736
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Reapplication and Credential Completion Among Non-Selected Community College Health Science Applicants: A Social Stratification Perspective by Donna Whitehouse Community colleges serve as primary access points for healthcare workforce preparation, yet thousands of qualified applicants are not selected for competitive admission health science programs each year. Research on what happens to these students following non-selection is limited, and existing studies focus almost exclusively on nursing, leaving allied health programs largely absent from the literature. This study addressed that gap by examining the reapplication behavior and credential completion outcomes among 2,604 applicants to three competitive admission health science programs, Nursing, Occupational Therapy Assistant, and Surgical Technology, at a single public, urban, community college in the southeastern United States. Social stratification theory, rooted in the frameworks of Weber (1946) and Bourdieu (1986), provided the theoretical foundation for this study. This perspective holds that educational institutions, such as community colleges with open access missions, can still function as sites where existing social hierarchies are reproduced through seemingly neutral selection processes. Social stratification theory suggests that competitive admission processes, while operationally necessary given program capacity constraints, may function as filters whose consequences fall unevenly across demographic groups, reflecting pre-existing structural inequalities rather than 6 academic potential alone. This study examined whether that pattern was observable in the reapplication and credential completion outcomes of non-selected applicants. Using a descriptive longitudinal design and binary logistic regression, the study tracked student outcomes over a three-year window following initial application. Pell grant eligibility emerged as the most consistent predictor across every research question, with Pell-eligible applicants reapplying and completing credentials at higher rates than their non-Pell-eligible peers, a counterintuitive finding that resists straightforward theoretical explanation. Race and ethnicity were associated with lower odds of credential completion among Black and Other/Unknown applicants relative to White applicants, particularly in models with sufficient statistical power to detect the effect. Selection status was the strongest predictor of credential completion, with selected applicants more than five times more likely to complete a credential within three years than non-selected peers. Findings suggest that competitive admission processes at community colleges may unintentionally replicate broader societal stratification patterns. Implications for enrollment management practice, institutional data tracking, and equitable access to health science education are discussed.

#13 [paper] Enrollment, Graduation, and Dropout Trends in Nepalese Higher Education: A Mathematical and Statistical Analysis
Authors: Kranti Thakur, Suresh Kumar Sahani
Venue: MASALIQ
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.58578/masaliq.v6i6.12248
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Rapid enrolment growth in Nepalese higher education has coincided with persistently weak graduation and completion outcomes. This study examined enrolment trends, faculty and funding capacity, pass and graduation rates, and dropout dynamics across central and provincial universities. Secondary data from University Grants Commission Nepal Education Management Information System reports, national newspapers, and peer-reviewed studies were analysed using ordinary least-squares regression and log-linear exponential growth models. A four-state absorbing Markov chain representing active enrolment, delayed or repeated study, graduation, and dropout was calibrated to Tribhuvan University’s reported aggregate pass rate of 29.3%. Enrolment increased from approximately 371,000 students in 2016/17 to over 633,000 in 2023/24. The linear model showed a strong fit (R² = 0.933), while the estimated enrolment compound annual growth rate was 7.93%, compared with 3.81% for faculty and 11.07% for government funding. The Markov model estimated a long-run dropout absorption probability of approximately 43% for first-attempt cohorts. Additional analyses characterized institutional fragmentation through the distribution of affiliated colleges by enrolment size and examined outbound student mobility, with more than 100,000 students annually obtaining No-Objection Certificates for overseas study. The findings indicate that enrolment growth has outpaced faculty expansion, while completion outcomes remain weak despite increased government funding. The study provides an integrated quantitative assessment to inform policies addressing imbalances between enrolment expansion, institutional capacity, and completion efficiency.

#14 [paper] Emergency Ultrasound Fellowship Match Outcomes: Unfilled Positions and Implications over Eight Years.
Authors: Boivin, Zachary, Coneybeare, Di, Salerno, Alexis, Werner, Sandra, She, Trent
Venue: The western journal of emergency medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43023757/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Advanced emergency ultrasound (AEMUS) fellowships recently experienced an unexpected decrease in the number of positions filled in the match. Our study aimed to characterize this trend over an eight-year period. METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional observational study of AEMUS fellowships participating in the National Resident Matching Program (NRMP) from the 2019-2026 match cycles, cross-referencing the publicly available database from the Society of Clinical Ultrasound Fellowships. The primary outcome was both the proportion of AEMUS fellowship positions filled and a program complement fill percentage. Secondary outcomes included stratification by geography and duration since program establishment. RESULTS: We included a total of 138 of the 141 programs listed in the NRMP Match. From 2019 to 2026, there was a 28.2% increase in the number of programs and a 34.5% increase in available positions. There was a general increase in the percentage of positions filled from 2019 to 2022, with 53.7% (87/162) of positions filled to 74.4% (145/195), peaking at 81.1% (137/169) in 2021. This upward trend reversed in 2023 with a decrease to 65.1% (142/218). The percentage of positions filled has continued to decrease through 2026, with a fill rate of only 56.0% (122/218). In the eight years of NRMP data, 97 of the 138 programs (70.3%) went unfilled at least once. Programs participating in the Match for a longer period had a statistically significant higher fill percentage, with 27 programs in the 1- to 4-year group with a total fill percentage of 46.0%, 32 programs in the 5- to 7-year group with a fill percentage of 59.0%, and 79 programs in the ≥ 8-year group with a fill percentage of 72.8% (P < .01) using a Kruskal-Wallis test. Spearman correlation analysis found no association between geographic proximity and likelihood of a program being fully filled. CONCLUSION: This cross-sectional study of NRMP data showed a decrease in the percentage of positions filled for adult AEMUS fellowships starting in 2023, which continued through 2026. Programs with greater longevity exhibited higher fill percentages, showing resilience in the face of this pattern.

#15 [paper] Decreasing Reviewer Engagement Trends at Two STFM Journals
Authors: Christopher P. Morley, José E. Rodríguez, Joel J. Heidelbaugh, Sam Grammer
Venue: Family Medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22454/fammed.2026.0268
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Securing peer reviewers for scholarly manuscripts is essential to journal operations but has become increasingly challenging. We sought to describe trends in acceptance of reviewer invitations and review completion at two journals sponsored by the Society of Teachers of Family Medicine: PRiMER and Family Medicine. METHODS: We conducted retrospective quality assurance of reviewer invitation outcomes for research manuscripts submitted to either journal from January 2010 to April 2026. Data were extracted from ScholarOne. We calculated odds ratios (ORs) for agreement to review and for review completion for each year via binary logistic regression, employing the generalized estimating equation to control for individual reviewer behavior, journal, and article type. RESULTS: We included 16,905 discrete invitations to review 2,574 manuscripts. Agreement rates at Family Medicine ranged from 70.99% in 2010, to a low of 41.80% in 2025, and 37.99% through April 2026; PRiMER agreement ranged from 74.36% in 2016, to 42.79% in 2025, and 20.23% in partial 2026. Combined completion rates dropped from 89.90% in 2010, to 82.20% in 2025, and to 73.90% in partial 2026. Using 2010 as the reference year, ORs for agreement to review dropped markedly, with the odds of accepting a review invitation in 2026 only 15.9% of the 2010 (2026: OR = 0.159, P<0.001) and the odds of review completion in 2026 falling to 32.9% of 2010 (OR = 0.329, P<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Reviewer engagement is declining across both journals. New, innovative strategies to recruit, engage, and incentivize reviewers will be necessary to sustain peer review.

#17 [paper] Cutoff Trend Prediction for Engineering Admis-sions Using Machine Learning
Authors: Mule Darshan Dipak, Bhosale Sachin Bajirao, Bangar Abhishek Popat
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23801960
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Engineering admission in Maharashtra is carried out through merit-based Centralised Admission Process (CAP) rounds, in which every college, branch and reservation category closes at a different cutoff percentile each year. Students usually rely on the previous year's cutoff list to decide their preference order, but cutoffs move from year to year because of changes in seat matrices, examination difficulty, branch demand and category-wise competition. Existing college-predictor tools mostly compare a candidate's score with last year's closing val-ues and rarely model how the cutoff itself is changing. This paper reviews five selected studies on admission prediction, cutoff-based college prediction and time-series forecasting, and iden-tifies gaps in temporal modelling, validation and uncertainty reporting. Based on these findings, a Machine Learning Framework for Cutoff Trend Prediction is proposed. The framework con-verts official CAP cutoff lists into a structured dataset of about 239,840 records, derives lag-based and trend features for every college-branch-category-round combination, and trains re-gression models such as Ridge regression, Random Forest and gradient boosting, with LSTM and ARIMA considered as optional time-series baselines. The forecast cutoff for the coming year is compared with a student's percentile to group colleges as Safe, Target or Dream. A pro-totype web application with search, prediction and history modules has been developed to de-liver the results. The framework aims to improve the accuracy, transparency and practical use-fulness of cutoff information for engineering aspirants. Quantitative evaluation of the proposed models is identified as future work.

#18 [paper] Predictive Validity of Entrance Selection Tests for Academic Performance and Study Completion in Postgraduate Education
Authors: Sendi Ramdhani, Amalia Saprıatı, Kristanti Ambar Puspitasari
Venue: International Journal of Education and Teaching Zone
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.57092/ijetz.v5i3.843
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study examined the predictive validity of postgraduate entrance-test scores for cumulative grade point average (GPA) and study duration at the Postgraduate School of Universitas Terbuka, Indonesia. Using retrospective institutional records, the study included 112 alumni admitted under comparable testing procedures implemented from 2021 onward; analyses involving English proficiency were based on 111 cases because one score was recorded on a non-comparable scale. Pearson correlations and multiple linear regression were used to assess predictive relationships. Numerical reasoning showed the strongest bivariate association with GPA (r = .227, p = .016), followed by verbal reasoning (r = .195, p = .040). No entrance-test component was significantly associated with study duration. In the multivariable model, English proficiency (β = −.233, p = .011), numerical reasoning (β = .271, p = .017), and figural reasoning (β = −.286, p = .004) were significant predictors of GPA, with the model explaining 17.9% of its variance (adjusted R² = .139). However, after adjustment for study program, only numerical reasoning remained statistically significant (β = .230, p = .044). Entrance-test scores provided little evidence of predictive utility for study duration after program adjustment. Overall, the findings indicate limited and component-specific predictive validity, with program-level heterogeneity influencing the observed relationships. These results highlight the need to evaluate entrance-test components in relation to specific academic outcomes and institutional contexts rather than treating aggregate test performance as a uniformly reliable predictor of postgraduate success.

#19 [paper] Divergent responses to AI-era submission pressure: a comparative analysis of medicine and computer science, 2015–2026
Authors: KangWei Wang, Ce Shi
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11412416/v1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract ChatGPT's release in late 2022 and the arrival of agentic AI systems from 2025 coincided with reports of rising manuscript volumes and editorial strain. Whether this pressure is uniform across research fields, or absorbed differently by each, has not been tested comparatively. We contrast two ecosystems with sharply different barriers to entry: computer science (CS), where submission carries almost no procedural cost, and medicine, where ethics review and data governance constrain what can be produced. Using open data for 2015–2026 — monthly submission and output volumes from arXiv, medRxiv, bioRxiv and PubMed; submission and acceptance figures for thirteen CS conferences; and review times for 38 medical journals — we measured AI-associated writing with a 95-word excess-vocabulary detector applied identically to 30,000 CS abstracts and 13,000–24,000 PubMed abstracts per year. CS preprint submissions rose 99.3% between 2022 and 2025, against 38–41% for the life-science preprint servers and 5.5% for PubMed-indexed output, and several medical specialties contracted; the divergence holds within arXiv itself. CS conferences absorbed the surge by expanding capacity, with NeurIPS submissions up 195% at an unchanged acceptance rate. AI-associated writing rose sharply from 2023 in both fields, the proportional increase nearly identical from a higher CS baseline, with the break appearing in all eight medical specialties tested. Review time for accepted papers showed no aggregate change. Medicine and CS therefore experienced comparable growth in AI-associated writing but opposite responses: CS expanded output and review capacity, while biomedicine held output flat and routed the pressure into editorial triage.

#21 [paper] Predicting Timely Graduation for Evidence-Based Higher Education Management: An Explainable Machine Learning Approach
Authors: Sunda Ariana, Devi Udariansyah, Bosya Perdana, Rosmiani Aprian
Venue: International Journal of Engineering Science and Information Technology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.52088/ijesty.v6i4.1977
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Higher education institutions increasingly use predictive analytics to identify students who may require academic support, yet predictive accuracy alone does not determine how model outputs should inform responsible management action. This study evaluates an explainable machine-learning framework for timely graduation decision support using routine academic records through Semester 4 and proposes a Role-Differentiated Action Translation Layer (R-ATL). Historical academic records were reconstructed into student-level trajectories, with timely graduation defined as completion by the end of the eighth semester. The analytical sample comprised 1,711 students from the 2019–2021 cohorts. Models were developed using the 2019–2020 cohorts and temporally tested on the untouched 2021 cohort. Random Forest achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.755, balanced accuracy of 0.670, and Brier score of 0.190, while XGBoost achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.761, with the small difference not statistically resolved. TreeSHAP identified a mixed performance–progression profile dominated by weighted IPS, Semester-4 IPS, early credit accumulation, and Semester-3 IPS. Informative missingness in the 2024 cohort limited complete-trajectory scoring to 438 of 604 students; these results were therefore treated as a current-cohort scoring demonstration rather than external validation. R-ATL translates explanation patterns into proposed role-specific information for students, academic advisors, program managers, and institutional leaders while retaining human review. The framework received complete content validity agreement from six experts. External validation, end-user usability and actionability testing, and intervention-outcome evaluation remain necessary for further empirical assessment and confirmation of the framework’s practical effectiveness across diverse higher education contexts and student populations

#1 [grant] Advancing understanding, modelling and prediction of extreme events in a changing climate
Amount: €3,000,000–€15,000,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2027-01-D1-07
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-03-04
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding, modelling, and predicting extreme events (isolated, compound, or cascading) in a changing climate, including their interaction, likelihood, and impact on resilience.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Utilizing a hierarchy of models (including high-resolution Earth system models and digital twins), data from past and recent climate, AI-based approaches, quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, and case studies to improve prediction, projection, and attribution capabilities across s…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Europe and globally, encompassing large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena, with specific focus on EU and national/regional actors, low- to middle-income countries, and integration with initiatives like Copernicus and Destination Earth.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Improved understanding of past and present extreme events in the context of climate change in Europe and globally, as well as the interaction between different hazards, their cumulative and/or cascading effects.

- Enhanced seamless prediction and projection modelling and attribution capabilities for extreme events and their likelihood to support preparedness, response and resilience to climate change by EU and national and regional actors. The EU Union Preparedness Strategy, the EU Adaptation Strategy and the European Climate Adaptation Plan can act as a guidance in these efforts.

- Up-to-date contributions towards latest climate science, risk assessments, adaptation strategies and policies and improved early warning systems for single and multi-hazard events.

Scope:

Climate change is intensifying the frequency and severity of extreme events. Understanding and predicting extreme events and the interaction between different types of hazards is critical for building resilience and safeguarding communities.

Actions are expected to draw upon multiple lines of evidence from a hierarchy of models (including high resolution Earth system models and digital twins) and data of past and recent climate to further our understanding of processes, pre-conditioning and causality driving extreme events under climate change conditions, including anthropogenic factors and internal variability. Other innovative and efficient modelling and analysis methods, including AI-based approaches, to better predict, emulate and reveal climate change related extreme and unprecedented high impact events, and to capture their likelihood are particularly welcome.

Extreme events should be addressed in their broadest sense and types, encompassing isolated, compound or cascading events affecting lives, livelihoods, ecosystems, socio-economic sectors and infrastructures, from large-scale continental to local-scale phenomena.

Actions should encompass quantitative intercomparisons, retrospective analyses, lessons learned and case studies of recent emblematic and diverse extreme events, and demonstrate the corresponding progress offered by the project in terms of improved understanding, comprehensive integration of multiple lines of evidence, and seamless (e.g. from short-term weather to sub-seasonal and multi-decadal scales) prediction and projection capabilities and skills.

The work is expected to support the future European Climate Risk Assessment (EUCRA)[1], for example through storylines on extremes or other approaches. Project outcomes should demonstrate clear benefits for the prediction and attribution of extreme events and contribute to the activities of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change.

Cooperation with global, EU, national and regional actors in the field of Disaster Risk Reduction and climate adaptation, including through integration into or interoperability with Copernicus, Destination Earth and other relevant initiatives is encouraged. In addition, international cooperation with low- to middle-income countries automatically eligible for Horizon Europe funding[2] is encouraged in support of climate resilience efforts, especially for capacity building.

Selected proposals may consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) whose contribution could consist of scientific advice and technical support in the context of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service and transfer of relevant research outcomes to operations.

This topic is part of a coordination initiative between ESA and the European Commission on Earth System Science (ESSI) under the new Extreme-Events Flagship Cluster. Successful consortia will be asked to coordinate with projects to be selected under ESA's FutureEO programme to facilitate access to and uptake of satellite data products and related tools or methodologies. #3 [paper] Thomson: Continual Learning of Frontier Models for SovereignAI
Authors: Shengzhuang Chen, Jerrod Parker, Yejin Bang, Andrew M. Bean, Nabeel Seedat, S. Winzeck, Daniil Glazko, Jannik Zgraggen
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/25f93a6ad2540697a638a11c5b3b33d30ce29ee8
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The development of frontier models is commonly perceived to be the exclusive remit of a small number of heavily funded players, creating an information, economic and power asymmetry between developers and the diverse user base of modern AI. Recent public discourse acknowledges this concern, calling for SovereignAI (an organisation's capability to independently build, deploy and govern AI use), but offers little concrete advice on how this can be achieved in the short term under a diversity of funding settings. We argue that frontier performance is achievable by a wide range of institutions through Continual Learning on readily available open-weight models. Unlike limited approaches such as small-scale fine-tuning, prompt engineering, or tool-augmentation of a frozen model, our approach exploits a modern mid-&post-training stack while introducing safeguards that preserve both plasticity and stability at each stage, making the minimal number of high-impact interventions on the parameters. This yields gains comparable to those typically seen across multiple successive model generations, at compute and personnel budgets substantially lower than commonly thought, making ownership of large parts of the SovereignAI stack (model, tool infrastructure, values&data privacy) viable for far more actors. We demonstrate this with Thomson, a general-purpose frontier model trained with an enhanced focus on high-stakes professional work. Thomson performs competitively with recent frontier models across agentic tasks, safety, legal, tax&multilingualism, and large-scale Deep Research. Evaluations show a distinctive $\pi$-shaped pattern: distinct improvements across a wide range of capabilities, including those not explicitly targeted, while almost completely eliminating the forgetting problem common to narrow domain adaptation.

#5 [paper] Monsoon’s Edge: Rain-Rock & Ruin Western Ghats-The Breaking Point
Authors: Dr NR Jagannath
Venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.55041/ijcope.v2i9.030
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Restoring the hazard-buffering ecosystems of the Western Ghats is essential to re-establish their natural capacity to attenuate runoff, stabilise slopes, and reduce disaster risk in a changing climate. This analytical paper proposes an integrated restoration framework that combines ecological priorities, technical bio-engineering, and institutional-financial reforms to transform fragmented conservation actions into a coherent, range-wide programme with measurable hazard-reduction outcomes. Ecologically, the paper emphasises targeted restoration of shola forests, montane grasslands (shola–grassland mosaics), wetlands, and riparian buffers, which collectively function as a “sponge and net” to delay peak flows and retain soil on steep terrain. It calls for active removal of invasive species such as Eucalyptus and Acacia to enable recovery of native vegetation and habitats, alongside large-scale native-tree planting and fire-prevention measures embedded within national schemes like the National Afforestation Programme and the Green India Mission. These actions aim to rebuild ecosystem mosaics that historically moderated hydrological extremes and maintained slope integrity across the Ghats. On the technical front, the paper advocates native-species bio-engineering on exposed, degraded slopes and road cuts, using deep-rooted indigenous plants to enhance slope cohesion and reduce infrastructure-induced failures at relatively low cost. It further recommends high-resolution, parcel-level GIS mapping to identify, safeguard, and restore critical wildlife corridors and riparian buffers, thereby aligning hazard mitigation with biodiversity connectivity and landscape-scale planning. Institutionally and financially, the analysis argues for replacing isolated, NGO- or division-led initiatives with a coordinated, range-wide ecosystem restoration programme underpinned by explicit hazard-reduction targets and dedicated funding. It proposes mobilising resources from CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management & Planning Authority) and other forestry or climate trusts through a performance-linked fiscal model, where disbursements are contingent on achieving quantifiable ecological indicators such as increases in native canopy cover. To ensure durability and local ownership, the framework integrates restoration with sustainable livelihoods—promoting agroforestry in transition zones and introducing payments for ecosystem services (PES) that provide Gram Sabhas and local communities with a direct economic stake in conservation outcomes. Together, these strategies offer a pathway to rebuild the Western Ghats’ natural hazard-buffering functions while strengthening rural livelihoods, institutional accountability, and climate resilience across one of India’s most critical mountain ecosystems. Keywords: Western Ghats; disaster risk reduction; landslides; Ecologically Sensitive Area; Gadgil report; Kasturirangan report; land-use zoning; cumulative impact assessment; ecosystem restoration; climate resilience; trans-boundary governance; ecological fiscal transfers

#6 [paper] Fair Access to Urban Water: Designing Population‐Sensitive Connection Fees Through a Welfare‐Informed Ability‐to‐Pay Approach
Authors: Seyedhossein Sajadifar, Masoud Alavian Sadr, Shahram Heydarian Samani, Ali Mazyaki, Alireza Pourebrahim
Venue: World Water Policy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1002/wwp2.70115
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
ABSTRACT Setting urban water connection fees is a complex policy problem: Fees must balance affordability, equity, and adequate cost recovery. This study develops a two‐stage framework for setting urban water connection charges in Iran. A bottom‐up engineering model first establishes the full long‐run economic cost of a new connection; a distributive stage then allocates a target provincial average across six city population classes. The distributive stage is stated as a constrained social welfare program and solved exactly; under logarithmic utility, it yields corner solutions rather than a smooth gradient because the fee is a small share of household resources. The recommended schedule is therefore described as what it is: a proportional ability‐to‐pay allocation indexed to city size, whose formal relation to the welfare program is stated explicitly. Revenue neutrality is imposed on a connection‐weighted basis so that the utility collects the intended total rather than an unweighted average of six class fees. Using Household Expenditure and Income Survey data for all 31 provincial capitals, we test rather than assume the population proxy and find an income elasticity of about 0.13 with respect to city size: statistically significant, but explaining a minority of cross‐city variation. Equity claims are correspondingly framed at the intercity level. Applied to a representative province, the schedule is progressive with respect to ability to pay, holds first‐year revenue exactly at the target, and can be adjusted over time using the Consumer Price Index. The approach transfers to other water‐scarce settings under cost‐recovery pressure.

#7 [paper] THE STORIES BEHIND THE DATA: 30 YEARS OF SNOWPACK SURVEYS ON NIWOT RIDGE
Authors: Jennifer Frances Morse
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.15788/1790099397
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
My work is a case study about the co-development of an academic field safety program with a high alpine fine-scale snow depth and snow profile record spanning 30 years in the Front Range of the Southern Rocky Mountains.The Niwot Ridge Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) Project maintains a long-term snow data set through a mid-May snow survey designed to capture peak snowpack.Up to 20 volunteers overnight at a high alpine laboratory (3,505 m) to access the otherwise restricted City of Boulder Watershed.Over three days they record ~ 500 snow depth points and six 2 m snow pit profiles across the upper Green Lakes Valley (3,567 m to 4,042 m).This record has been used to understand how snow redistributes across mountain terrain, develop an index of wind drifting and scouring, inform a model of wind slab release, validate satellite products, and track one of the leading abiotic drivers of a changing mountain watershed.I first joined the survey as a volunteer in 2007.By then, it had run for over a decade in remote, highelevation avalanche terrain, with no formal safety or avalanche protocols or training requirements.Coming from ski patrol, I found this alarming.After several years in academia, I learned it was unremarkable.Field safety provision was, and in places remains, uneven.Programs operating through polar or international logistics organizations had real requirements, while local fieldwork had whatever an individual investigator thought to provide.Field leaders in academia were trained as scientists, not practitioners, with few bridges between the two.Field safety was not taught, if it was addressed at all.Proposal budgets did not include funding for it.When I joined the program in 2010, I brought some knowledge of standard operational practices: protocols, training, and the habit of using close calls as data.Beyond bridging research and practice, this presentation describes the circular evolution between them.Field practice enabled the continuation and consistency of annual data collection in a remote, high-risk environment.The ongoing data collection improved the field practice through building years of experience from which to learn and improve.The results are an increasingly robust field safety program, enabling one of the longest fine-scale records of high alpine snowpack in the Rocky Mountains.

#9 [paper] Lettercraft dataset
Authors: Robert Flierman, Hope Williard, Luka van der Plas, Xander Vertegaal, Sam English, Alexander de Graaf, Wouter Hofland, Ellen Joosten
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22896398
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This dataset was created as part of the project Lettercraft and Epistolary Performance in Medieval Europe, a NWO-Vidi funded project based in the Department of Languages, Literature, and Culture at Utrecht University. The database came about in collaboration with Utrecht University’s Centre for Digital Humanities, who developed the online infrastructure, and with the help of students from Utrecht University Research Master’s Programme in Ancient, Medieval & Renaissance Studies, who joined the project as research apprentices. For more information about the project, visit the Lettercraft website. Here you can also browse the latest version of the data. About the project How did early medieval societies use the letter and who were among its users? The Lettercraft-project approaches the early medieval letter as a performative medium, whose communicative potential was defined principally by non-textual features: its materiality, its ability to be publicly read out and talked over, and its potential quickly to reach wide and diverse audiences. The project submits that the letter was a far more inclusive medium than is commonly assumed on the basis of its textual qualities. Literacy or social status were not required to participate in what the project calls lettercraft, i.e. the various performative actions (e.g. listening, speaking, negotiating, gossiping) that along with writing and reading made up epistolary communication. The project aims to show, moreover, that due to its public nature and social range, the letter was an essential tool of community-building and conflict-resolution in medieval society. As long as it was properly performed, a single letter could persuade an entire community. The project studies the performative potential of the letter in the context of the Merovingian Kingdoms, 476-751 CE, whose communicative networks covered much of Europe. Innovatively, it relies not on the surviving letter-collections, which showcase the literary exploits of elite ecclesiastical men, but rather on descriptions of lettercraft in Merovingian histories and saint-lives. The project proceeds along two complementary pathways. First, it has established an index of Merovingian epistolary terminology that is sensitive to all (textual and non-textual) aspects of lettercraft. This index can be consulted in the glossary provided on the Lettercraft website. We plan to include it in this dataset in the future. Second, the project is developing a new open access dataset of Merovingian epistolary communication, which records descriptions of letter-use documented in Merovingian narrative sources. Significantly, it is a dataset not of letters and their textual contents, but of the non-textual ‘metadata’ surrounding the epistolary process, including references to participants, delivery, performance, gift-giving, materiality, and audience. This enables users to analyses the social contexts in which early medieval epistolary communication took place, the diverse individuals and groups who participated in it, and the actions they performed. About the dataset Corpus – This dataset contains annotations on the use of letters in early medieval narrative texts. The project’s principal source are the eight volumes of Merovingian narrative texts edited by Bruno Krusch and Wilhelm Levison for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica under the header Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum (1885-1951), complemented with a smaller corpus of Merovingian texts not edited in this collection. NB: the annotation of this corpus is still ongoing. Specific information on date, authorship, editions and translations is given with each individual text. In terms of provenance, most of the texts in the dataset can be said to have originated in the Frankish kingdoms under Merovingian rule in the period 450-750, but we have followed the MGH editions in not keeping to a strict chronological or geographical demarcation. The dataset thus includes texts from later times, especially the Caroli

#10 [paper] Ten simple rules for preparing and delivering effective funding pitches in competitive grant applications
Authors: Andy Göbel, Tilman D. Rachner
Venue: PLoS Computational Biology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014840
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
In grant applications, oral presentations can be an integral part of the evaluation process. Funding pitches are a specific form of pitch presentations delivered during competitive review procedures to complement a written proposal. Their goal is to convince reviewers of both your project's strength and excellence as well as your suitability as a researcher. This paper offers ten simple rules on how to prepare and deliver effective funding pitches, with a particular focus on content selection, clear structuring, and convincing scientific argumentation. We also highlight the importance of practice and feedback and share practical strategies on how to handle questions and critical discussion professionally.

#13 [paper] Linguistic diversity and theory in psychological science
Authors: Kenny R. Coventry
Venue: Frontiers in Psychology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1866037
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
When it comes to understanding the human mind and behaviour, theory is often generated from and tested via samples that are not representative of the population as a whole. Over twenty years ago, this problem was brought into sharp focus with a number of authors calling for research in the cognitive and psychological sciences to be more aware of diversity and representativeness (e.g. Atran, Medin, & Ross, 2005;Norenzayan & Heine, 2005;Rozin, 2001) -a point also more recently recognised in comparative cognition (Andrews & Monsó, 2025). 'WEIRD' -Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic (Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan, 2010) -was coined as an acronym to raise awareness that most findings in psychological science and related fields are gleaned from studies with limited participant pools. Over a decade later, the extent to which such concerns have resulted in changes to practice can be questioned (e.g. Apicella, Norenzayen, & Henrich, 2020), and a coherent framework to embed linguistic and cultural diversity in psychological theorizing and empirical testing has yet to be established.In tandem with the recognition of a problem with representativeness in psychological science, two other major issues have emerged as ongoing concerns. First, there is the 'reproducibility crisis', pulling together a range of methodological and statistical issues, including worries regarding sample sizes, statistical reporting, questionable research practices (e.g. p-hacking) and publication bias (e.g. Open Science Collaboration, 2015). Second, a range of concerns have been expressed regarding the very nature of theorizing in the psychological sciences. Some have drawn attention to the lack of specificity of theories as one of the origins of the replication crisis itself, calling for more formal theories to be de rigour in the discipline (e.g. Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019;van Dongen et al., 2025), while others point the finger at the absence of an overarching theory formulation framework that may help to constrain theories to become more appropriately testable (e.g. van Rooij & Baggio, 2021,) akin to the 'levels of explanation' approach proposed by Marr (1982).In this article I consider how these three major concerns interconnect in consideration of one of the most essential elements of WEIRDness -the failure to embrace linguistic diversity in both theoretical and empirical psychological science.There are over 7,000 spoken and signed languages across the globe (Ethnologue, 2026), In contrast to the assumption from generative linguistics that languages share universal features (e.g. Chomsky, 1986;Pinker, 1996), a body of (largely) anthropological linguistic studies has shown that languages vary in significant ways, with diversity found at almost every level of linguistic organisation (Evans & Levinson, 2009). For example, languages differ across dimensions including sound systems, phonology, morphology, grammar, orthography, and semantics, leading Evans and Levinson (2009) to conclude that diversity is the most remarkable property of language. If the goal of the cognitive and psychological sciences is to identify and study universal psychological processes, akin to Newton's universal laws of physics (Kroupin, Davis & Henrich, 2025), then such linguistic diversity may challenge the very nature of the focus on universals (see Levinson, 2012 for discussion).In light of this linguistic diversity, one can ask how the cognitive and psychological sciences are doing prior and since Evans and Levinson (2009) in terms of sampling speakers of diverse languages. The answer is not very well. The cognitive and psychological sciences have been dominated with publication in English and testing of English-speaking participants. Authors: Anthoula Malkopoulou

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The rise of far-right antidemocratic actors in consolidated democracies, specifically the challenge of defending democracy against actors who use lawful, often invisible tactics, and the normative dilemma of choosing between repressive measures and other strategies.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A comparative normative political theory approach that defines and analyzes three ideal types of democratic self-defence: militant (restrictive), tolerant (liberal-procedural), and social (addressing structural injustices). Setting (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical analysis grounded in contemporary political contexts, with specific reference to the case of the Greek neo-fascist party Golden Dawn and its legal and political trajectory, as well as broader European and global contexts of democratic backsliding.
Abstract:
Associate Professor, Department of Government The rise of far-right antidemocratic actors in many consolidated democracies today poses a unique challenge. Political parties and leaders who enjoy popular support risk tearing apart the democratic fabric through tactics that appear lawful and are often invisible. What options do democracies have to defend themselves against such actors? Democratic self-defence, i.e. actions aimed at preventing, containing, resisting, or repairing democratic backsliding caused by domestic antidemocratic forces, can take many forms: from restrictions on candidacy rights to hate speech laws, and from street protests to welfare reforms. Political parties may exclude antidemocratic parties from coalitions, or they may choose to include them while seeking to moderate their positions. Alternatively, they may focus on expanding social protections in order to address the structural injustices that antidemocratic actors exploit. Such choices raise difficult normative questions. This book offers conceptual tools for making these choices intelligible and brings to light the principles that animate them. Political theorists addressing these issues have paid a great deal of attention to justifying repressive measures. Militant democracy, which includes the pre-emptive restriction of political and civil rights, has received so much attention in the past decade that one would be forgiven for thinking there is no alternative. This book is partly a reaction to this one-sided engagement with repressive measures. It examines less-known approaches to democratic self-defence that prioritise toleration and social integration respectively, strategies that are used as much, if not more, than militant restrictions. The three rationales of democratic self-defence that emerge –militant, tolerant, and social– are presented as ideal types. Unlike much theorising on democratic self-defence, which is prescriptive and advances a single normative framework, this book adopts a deliberately comparative approach that examines the strengths and weaknesses of each ideal type, as well as their connections and contrasts. It proposes conceptual definitions and analyses the normative justifications underpinning each type. The aim is to clarify the principles embodied in practices of democratic self-defence, enabling actors to better understand the normative commitments behind their choices and to make decisions that are ethically justified, democratically legitimate, and consistent with the values they seek to defend. The book also seeks to move the discussion beyond legal instruments and state responses by bringing broader societal and public actors into view. At the same time, it remains focused on agency: on both defenders of democracy and those who seek to undermine it. In doing so, it resists the tendency to portray democracy as a quasi-natural system whose resilience must simply be enhanced. Unlike many studies framed around the concept of democratic resilience, this book foregrounds human agency and the diverse actors who actively defend democracy across multiple spheres. Decisions about whether and how to confront antidemocratic actors do not fall exclusively on any single category of actor. They concern government authorities, courts, state agencies, municipal leaders, business actors, journalists, academics, and others. Democratic self-defence should therefore be understood as a form of agency distributed across a variety of actors. #15 [paper] Costing global biodiversity framework delivery in megadiverse Australia
Authors: Paul Elton, Sarah Clément, Michelle Ward, Martine Maron
Venue: Journal of Environmental Management
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.130756
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Most nations worldwide face substantial funding gaps to halt biodiversity loss, yet many governments lack comprehensive cost estimates essential for effective budget allocation and implementation planning. This study provides a comprehensive estimate of the costs Australian governments would need to bear to deliver the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework in Australia. Using interpretive principles and evidence from peer-reviewed literature, and spatial analysis, we derived actions, unit costs, and cost factors (the amount of each action required to achieve the GBF's targets). We populated an automated model with these inputs to produce national and jurisdictional government cost estimates to inform planning and cost-sharing between national and subnational governments. Our method captures cost efficiencies from actions that benefit multiple targets. Our model estimates that delivering GBF targets in Australia will cost governments approximately AU$28.5 billion per annum from 2025 to 2050. At 1.1 per cent of GDP, this estimate shows comprehensive biodiversity conservation is arguably fiscally realistic. Our cost factor data can be disaggregated at various scales—such as bioregions, ecosystems, or Indigenous nations—to inform biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning. Our analysis and cost model offer a replicable methodology for other national governments to quantify their financial resourcing requirements for GBF implementation.

#16 [paper] Current state of dementia screening, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to the uptake of evidence-based dementia care in primary healthcare in Africa: a scoping review and call for implementation
Authors: Debela, Mitiku Bonsa, Krell-Roesch, Janina, Geda, Yonas, Bekele, Kebebe, Assefa, Tesfaye, Zenbaba, Demisu, Oljira, Lemessa, Takele, Abulie
Venue: BMC psychiatry
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43026524/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Dementia is a growing public health challenge worldwide, particularly in Africa. Although various screening tools have been used across different settings in the region, evidence on dementia screening practices, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to evidence-based dementia care has not been systematically mapped. This scoping review aimed to map the available evidence on dementia screening practices, risk reduction approaches, and barriers to dementia care across Africa. METHODS: This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The review protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). A comprehensive search of major databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar) and grey literature was conducted. Eligible studies focused on dementia screening, risk reduction strategies, and barriers to evidence-based dementia care in primary healthcare settings across Africa. Study selection and data extraction were independently performed by three reviewers, and findings were synthesized using descriptive mapping. RESULTS: Of the 3,102 records identified, 16 studies met the inclusion criteria. Nine studies reported dementia screening practices using a range of screening tools, most commonly the Brief Community Screening Instrument for Dementia (CSID) and the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). The available evidence suggests that dementia screening was largely conducted within research settings rather than as part of routine primary healthcare. Six studies identified barriers to evidence-based dementia screening and care, including workforce shortages, limited infrastructure and funding, inadequate training, low policy prioritization, sociocultural stigma, and limited public awareness. Only one study evaluated the implementation of dementia risk reduction strategies in an African context, highlighting an important evidence gap. CONCLUSIONS: Evidence on dementia screening, risk reduction, and care integration in African primary healthcare remains limited. Key barriers include health system constraints, workforce shortages, inadequate infrastructure and funding, and sociocultural challenges. Future implementation research should evaluate culturally appropriate strategies to strengthen dementia detection, prevention, and integration of dementia services into primary healthcare across Africa.

#17 [paper] Cost-Effectiveness of Annual Atrial Fibrillation Screening Compared with Current Opportunistic Screening in Australian Primary Care: A Model-Based Economic Evaluation
Authors: Ureni Halahakone, Sameera Senanayake, Victoria McCreanor, William Parsonage, David Brain
Venue: Applied Health Economics and Health Policy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40258-026-01073-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although the guidelines recommend opportunistic screening for adults ≥ 65 years, screening for atrial fibrillation (AF) remains underutilised in Australia. The absence of guidance on how often to screen has resulted in variable practice and missed opportunities for AF detection. Previous studies have focused on handheld devices rather than 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) devices that are readily available in primary-care settings, and the evidence supporting an annual AF screening programme in Australia is limited. Therefore, the aim of this study is to compare the cost-effectiveness of an annual, structured, higher‑coverage opportunistic ECG screening approach (annual screening) with current unstructured opportunistic screening (current screening) in older adults in Australia. METHODS: A Markov model was developed to evaluate two strategies for adults ≥ 65 years: (1) annual screening using 12-lead ECG and (2) current opportunistic screening. The model included 11 health states capturing AF treatment and outcomes, and simulations were run using monthly cycles. A health system perspective and 10-year time horizon were applied. To account for uncertainty, a probabilistic sensitivity analysis with 1000 iterations was undertaken and the results were assessed against a cost-effectiveness threshold of 28,000 Australian dollars (AU$) per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Uncertainty was further examined through cost-effectiveness acceptability curves and scenario analyses to test the stability of findings under alternative assumptions. RESULTS: Annual screening increased costs by AU$4213 and gained 0.43 QALYs, yielding an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of AU$9797 per QALY gained. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis demonstrated that 100% of simulations yielded a positive incremental net monetary benefit. Scenario analyses demonstrated that both higher screening costs and less frequent 3-yearly screening were cost-effective in comparison to the current opportunistic screening, with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios below the cost-effectiveness threshold and positive incremental net monetary benefits in all scenarios. CONCLUSION: A structured annual screening approach for AF is likely to be a cost-effective strategy within the Australian primary-care setting. These findings highlight the benefits of more consistent screening practices for early AF detection and stroke prevention.

#20 [paper] Building a PET/CT Program in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Health-System Framework for Financing, Affordability, and Sustainable Implementation.
Authors: Mobit, Paul N, Mourad, Waleed F, Mosse, Wilfried B, Khair, Lana M, Njeh, Christopher F, Folefac, Edmund
Venue: Cancers
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43026854/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background: PET/CT is integral to modern oncology, yet access remains limited in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) because of capital requirements, radiopharmaceutical production complexity, workforce constraints, and weak reimbursement systems. We evaluated the modeled financial feasibility of a cyclotron-based PET/CT program using Cameroon as an illustrative national case and reframed implementation as a health-system planning problem rather than an equipment-purchase decision. Methods: A deterministic scenario model was developed over a 10-year horizon. The model was aligned conceptually with IAEA PET/cyclotron planning guidance, WHO OneHealth ingredients-based costing, and ISPOR principles for transparent decision modeling. The entry-level configuration comprised one PET/CT scanner, an 11-13 MeV negative-ion medical cyclotron, F-18 targetry, two synthesis modules, hot cells, a quality-control laboratory, backup power, and supporting infrastructure. Capital investment was modeled at USD 9 million as a planning estimate, with wide sensitivity analysis. Operating costs were separated into fixed, step-fixed, and variable components. Annual completed scan volumes of 500-5000 were evaluated, together with financing at 3%, 6%, 10%, and 12% APR, public capital support, operating subsidy, equipment availability, disease-specific demand, and alternative generator/satellite strategies. Results: At 6% financing, annual debt service for USD 9 million was USD 1.22 million. Modeled operating expenditure rose with activity from approximately USD 0.93 million at 500 completed scans to USD 1.77 million at 5000 scans because staffing and consumables were activity dependent. Total economic cost per completed scan declined from approximately USD 4311 at 500 scans to USD 598 at 5000 scans. If government provided the capital infrastructure, the operating cost to be recovered declined from USD 1865 to USD 353 per scan over the same activity range. A disease-specific incident-case model based on GLOBOCAN 2022 data for Cameroon showed that pathology confirmation, clinical eligibility, and referral completion materially constrain demand; at 30% histologic confirmation and 80% referral completion, approximately 1005 incident-case PET/CT examinations were generated under the base planning assumptions. Equipment availability of 80%, 90%, and 95% materially changed cost per completed scan in a 3000-slot program. Conclusions: Cyclotron-based PET/CT programs may achieve financial sustainability when patient throughput is sufficient, financing is appropriate, operations are reliable, and the surrounding cancer system can generate and act on evidence-based referrals. The model provides a transparent planning framework rather than empirical proof of sustainability and should be locally calibrated before investment decisions.

#21 [paper] Evaluation of the laboratory assessment process for A Clinically Oriented Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network (ACORN-LAP) in low-income and middle-income countries: a multicountry, cross-sec
Authors: ACORN Laboratory Investigators
Venue: The Lancet. Microbe
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42810374/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-quality microbiology laboratory data underpin effective antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance. Laboratory assessments are useful for ensuring the quality of microbiology data used for AMR surveillance, especially in low-income and middle-income countries where accreditation might not be feasible. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the microbiology laboratory assessment and quality monitoring tools developed to assess laboratories participating in A Clinically Oriented Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network 2 (ACORN2). METHODS: We conducted a multicountry observational study of microbiology laboratories participating in the ACORN2 surveillance project, including a baseline cross-sectional laboratory assessment process (ACORN-LAP) with longitudinal quality monitoring and follow-up. Between Sept 21, 2021, to Nov 25, 2024, all laboratories of hospitals identified as ACORN2 sites identified through investigator networks were invited to complete the ACORN-LAP. These laboratories were from nine countries across Asia and Africa. The assessment included an online REDCap-based assessment, and document-based and video call-based reviews by two selected ACORN assessors. The laboratories participated in quarterly quality monitoring processes, including the review of internal quality control (IQC) and external quality assessment (EQA) results. Anonymous feedback was collected, and an in-person feedback session was conducted during the study. The primary evaluation outcome was the findings of the ACORN-LAP, including the number of key and non-key recommendations identified. Secondary evaluation outcomes included quality monitoring performance, laboratory feedback on the ACORN-LAP and quality monitoring processes, and comparison of the ACORN-LAP and quality monitoring processes with existing laboratory assessment tools. FINDINGS: 20 laboratories completed the ACORN-LAP. The median time from initial contact with the laboratory to issuing recommendations was 3 months (IQR 3-4; range 1-8). The assessors identified 144 recommendations (median 6 per laboratory [IQR 3-8·5]; range 2-21), including 46 key and 98 non-key recommendations. Non-accredited laboratories received more recommendations per laboratory than accredited laboratories (median difference 5 [95% CI 1-11]; p=0·0062 and incidence rate ratio (IRR) 2·5 [95% CI 1·56-4·09]; p=0·0002). Non-accredited laboratories also received more key recommendations per laboratory (median difference 2 [95% CI 1-5]; p=0·0030) and IRR 4·75 [95% CI 2·11-11·84]; p=0·0003). 116 quality monitoring forms were completed (median 6 per laboratory [IQR 4-7]; range 2-9). 115 IQC and 59 scored EQA events were reported. Review of such quality monitoring data identified previously undetected IQC failures and led to improved IQC recording in some laboratories. Feedback showed that laboratories considered the assessment process useful although some laboratories found the assessment process labour intensive. INTERPRETATION: The findings support the use of structured laboratory assessment with ongoing quality monitoring to strengthen AMR surveillance, particularly in non-accredited laboratories. A simple, harmonised global online tool with integrated quality monitoring that assesses against a minimum standard could improve the quality and comparability of AMR surveillance data in low-income and middle-income countries. FUNDING: Wellcome Trust.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Method (Mycelium's reading): An adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine utilizing probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods (such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) to dynamically queue, activate, or inhibit sensor payload…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned aerial and ground platforms conducting standoff reconnaissance for subsurface WMD devices, chemical/biological munitions, and radiological dispersal device components in diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
Abstract:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.

A proactive system is required to answer:

"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"

This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.

The Marine Geology and Geophysics Core Program supports research on all aspects of the geology and geophysics of the present ocean basins and margins, as well as those of the Great Lakes.

- Structure, composition, tectonics, and evolution of the oceanic lithosphere

- Paleoceanography, paleoclimate, and sea level change

- Submarine volcanology, petrology and geochemistry of the oceanic crust and upper mantle lithosphere

- Marine hydrogeology, water-rock interaction, seeps and gas hydrates

- Hydrothermal venting and in situ fluid processes, and associated geochemistry

- Geochemical indicators of life operating below the seafloor

- Marine sedimentology, stratigraphy, sediment transport, and diagenesis

- Mid-ocean ridge spreading, back-arc rifting, transform processes, and ocean island/seamount formation and evolution

- Submarine components of subduction zone systems and passive margins

- Marine geohazards (e.g., earthquakes, faulting, mass wasting, geological aspects of tsunamis)

- Coastal processes (e.g., geological aspects of hurricanes, sea-level change, erosion, offshore deposition)

The Marine Geology and Geophysics Program supports acquisition of new field data and the leveraging of and/or synthesis of existing data. Abstract:
International Ocean Discovery Program Operations

The International Ocean Discovery Program (IODP) serves to advance basic research in the marine geosciences and is supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and its international partners. The science plan, Illuminating Earth's Past, Present, and Future: The International Ocean Discovery Program Science Plan for 2013-2023, provides justification for the United States' participation in the IODP and reflects the top priorities of the international science community. A multi-platform approach is required to address the goals outlined in the IODP science plan, including a non-riser vessel to collect widely-distributed high-resolution cores to address climate, environmental, crustal and observatory science objectives; a heavy riser-equipped vessel to reach the deep sedimentary and crustal layers; and mission-specific platforms to support high-latitude and shallow-water projects.

The light drillship, JOIDES Resolution, is provided by the U.S. National Science Foundation. Science operations for the JOIDES Resolution are conducted through a Cooperative Agreement with Texas A&M University with scientific planning conducted by the JOIDES Resolution Facility Board.

The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) of Japan provides the heavy drillship, Chikyu (Earth), to conduct the deep drilling projects in the new program. The Center for Deep Earth Exploration of the Independent Administrative Institution, Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC) operates the vessel for IODP. Scientific planning for Chikyu IODP operations is conducted by the Chikyu IODP Board.

Mission Specific Platforms (MSP) are provided by the European Consortium for Ocean Research Drilling (ECORD). The ECORD Facility Board conducts scientific planning for MSP expeditions and the platforms themselves are operated by the European Science Operator (ESO).

A Science Support Office (SSO) is provided by Scripps Institution of Oceanography, University of California San Diego under a Cooperative Agreement with the National Science Foundation. The SSO’s primary tasks include:

- providing logistical support for the JOIDES Resolution Facility Board and its advisory panels

- overseeing the proposal submission and review process

- managing the Site Survey Data Bank

- providing a gateway website to IODP scientific planning

U.S. scientific community involvement in IODP is facilitated by the United States Science Support Program (USSSP) for Ocean Drilling. USSSP is run by Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory of Columbia University under a Cooperative Agreement with the National Science Foundation. USSSP’s primary tasks are:

- support for U.S.-based researchers to participate on IODP expeditions, participate on the IODP advisory panels, and conduct initial post-expedition research

- support for planning and thematic workshops and pre-drilling activities to collect, refine, and/or integrate site specific and/or regional data that aid in planning drilling expeditions

- support outreach activities on IODP drilling platforms, for graduate students fellowships, and an IODP-themed lecture series.
