#6 [grant] Persistent, Geochemically-Driven Low-Temperature Power Systems for Subsea Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13137
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsea ISR nodes and UUV docking stations rely on lithium-chemistry batteries that suffer from capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess toxic chemistries, and require resource-intensive physical replacement in contested or ice-covered environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters that generate electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between anoxic marine sediment and oxygenated overlying seawater, utilizing abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode …
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Sub-zero Arctic subsea environments, specifically the interface between marine sediment and overlying seawater.
Abstract:
The Department of the Navy’s expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries. These legacy power sources present severe logistical and operational limitations: they suffer from rapid capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess highly toxic/hazardous chemistries, and require frequent, resource-intensive physical replacement (battery swapping) in highly contested or ice-covered environments.

To achieve persistent, logistics-free ISR, the Navy has a critical need for an environmentally benign, deploy-and-forget power architecture. This STTR topic seeks the development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters to generate continuous electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between the anoxic marine sediment (mud) and the oxygenated overlying seawater. The proposed approach must demonstrate a credible path to 5W power and 24-month endurance in sub-zero Arctic conditions through a ruggedized seabed electrochemical power-harvesting architecture that maximizes long-term energy extraction while using only indigenous sediment microbial communities and naturally occurring geochemical gradients. Proposed solutions may use abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode design, power management, and optimum emplacement.

Biocatalytic Prioritization & Environmental Strictures:

While purely abiotic electrochemical approaches will be considered, approaches that leverage biologically-mediated processes (e.g., utilizing natural biocatalysis to enhance electron transfer at the anode) will be prioritized due to their potential for higher power density and self-renewing longevity.

However, to prevent any risk of ecological disruption to fragile Arctic ecosystems, solutions must strictly rely on harnessing the naturally occurring, indigenous populations already present in the local sediment. The introduction, deployment, or seeding of any exogenous, synthetic, lab-grown, or non-native biological agents (microbes/bacteria) is strictly prohibited.

By utilizing advanced electrode materials that naturally synergize with the local subsea environment, the system must reduce or avoid reliance on deployable primary batteries for the supported payload while ensuring operational viability in extreme cold and high-pressure conditions.

#7 [grant] Self-Sustaining Wave Energy Capture for Persistent Autonomous Ocean-Going Systems
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13132
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles require a reliable, self-sustaining power source for recharging when operating far from human contact, specifically a wave energy capture device (WECD) that is portable, deployable in various depths, and stealthy.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Open water environments ranging from depths of 100 meters to full ocean depth, with sea states ranging from calm to Sea State 8.
Abstract:
Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles need regular recharging, and since they often operate far from human contact, their charging systems require a reliable, self-sustaining power source. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) believes the ideal power source will be a wave energy capture device (WECD). WECDs capture kinetic and potential energy generated by the movement of ocean waves on or near the surface of open water.

The desired WECD must be portable, specifically, designed as a set of components that can each be carried by one or two people who must be able to quickly assemble and disassemble those components. Components designed for one-person carry should weigh no more than 14 kg with largest dimension no greater than 1.9 m, while components designed for two-person carry should weigh no more than 45.4 kg with largest dimension no greater than 2.3 m. The WECD must be able to be relocated to areas of very different depths, including full ocean depth so the WECD’s design cannot require placement or anchoring on the sea floor. And since the WECD may need to deploy near the shore, its design must allow it to function in waters as shallow as 100 meters.

Ocean weather conditions can be challenging. The WECD should function reliably at Sea State 6 or less (very rough seas, with wave heights of 4 to 6 meters), and it should be able to survive conditions up to Sea State 8 (very high seas, with wave heights of 9 to 14 meters).

ONR assumes the WECD will be tethered to some device at or near the surface of the water. That tethered system may be an autonomous vehicle in loiter mode, and since loitering involves continuous vehicle movement, the WECD should operate reliably while in motion, and its design should leverage such motion to increase energy capture.

The WECD should produce a minimum of 20 kilowatt-hours (kWh) per day, but more is highly desirable. ONR believes 100+ kWh per day is achievable. Even in calm seas, the ideal WECD should produce sufficient electricity to charge a 2-kWh battery in 6 hours or less. Vehicle movement may be considered when ensuring this minimum level of power generation.

The desired WECD may be needed in areas where human assembly is impractical. Thus, the deliverables must include a prototype device capable of deploying the assembled WECD from the deck of a medium or large autonomous surface vessel. Like the WECD itself, the deployment device (DD) should function reliably in challenging weather conditions: Sea State 4 or less (moderate seas with wave heights of 1.25 to 2.5 meters).

Once deployed, very little of the WECD itself should be visible at the surface of the water. The WECD should minimize any increase in the visibility of the vehicle it is tethered to. This includes surface and airborne observation, both optically and by radar. Acoustic noise generated by the WECD should either be minimized or disguised to seem environmental or biological.

Cost for the WECD and associated DD should be minimized. ONR expects that under certain environmental conditions or mission requirements, WECDs may not be recoverable. At full-rate production, the ideal price will allow for multiple units per million dollars.

Under normal operating conditions, including Sea States of 6 or less, the expected operational duration of the deployed WECD should be at least one month, with three months or more expected if Sea State 4 or less is maintained.

#9 [grant] Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO)
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13159
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Abstract:
Army formations, including XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) and its subordinate formations, operating in Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO) face increasingly capable adversary intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) systems that can exploit electromagnetic emissions to detect, characterize, locate, and target command posts, platforms, and other mission-critical nodes. The proliferation of networked sensors and increasingly rapid sensor-to-shooter processes creates a need for affordable and scalable capabilities that reduce the effectiveness of adversary electromagnetic sensing and targeting.

XVIII ABC requires capabilities that can be rapidly employed and distributed across formations to improve electromagnetic signature management and enhance survivability and freedom of maneuver in contested environments. This topic seeks innovative approaches for Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO), a low-cost, modular, distributed, and attritable capability for electromagnetic signature management. The desired solution should enable multiple software-configurable nodes to operate cooperatively across an operational area to sense the local electromagnetic environment and generate controlled electromagnetic activity that increases ambiguity and uncertainty for adversary ISR and targeting processes. Potential approaches may include distributed electromagnetic signature shaping, configurable RF effects representations, coordinated emissions, and adaptive management of distributed nodes. Proposed solutions should address the ability to sense and characterize the local electromagnetic environment, coordinate activity across distributed nodes, generate Government-authorized RF effects representations, and dynamically adapt system behavior as the electromagnetic environment changes.

The solution should emphasize low cost, low size, weight, and power (SWaP), modularity, scalability, software configurability, distributed operation, and interoperability with Army command-and-control architectures at Corp and Division. Innovative approaches to autonomous coordination, AI-enabled processing, electromagnetic environment awareness, and dynamic signature management are encouraged. The capability should be scalable from individual nodes to distributed networks and adaptable to different platforms and operational environments. Offerors should characterize key trades including frequency coverage, bandwidth, processing requirements, network latency and synchronization, RF-generation capability, SWaP, node density, and unit cost. Solutions should demonstrate a credible pathway toward a fielded node cost below $50,000, with $30,000 desired where technically feasible.

The desired outcome is a prototype capability that demonstrates how XVIII ABC and Army formations can employ distributed, attritable electromagnetic spectrum technologies to improve survivability and freedom of maneuver by complicating adversary ISR, reducing confidence in electromagnetic-derived targeting information, and degrading adversary decision-making and targeting cycles during LSCO.

Throughout the SBIR|STTR Phase I and Phase II, CEMA CAMO prototype capabilities will be demonstrated in partnership with Joint Innovation Out Post (JIOP) through XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) experimentation to assess operational effectiveness, inform capability refinement, and demonstrate integration with Army formations and command-and-control architectures.

#10 [grant] Dynamic Sensor-Tasking and Routing System for Subsurface Hazard Detection
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13082
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsurface hazard detection systems suffer from a 'collect everything' bottleneck, where static, pre-programmed sensor scripts flood tactical networks with raw data, ignore environmental degradation of sensor modalities, and lack the real-time adaptability to optimize sensor tasking and rou…
Method (Mycelium's reading): An adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine utilizing probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods (such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) to dynamically queue, activate, or inhibit sensor payload…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned aerial and ground platforms conducting standoff reconnaissance for subsurface WMD devices, chemical/biological munitions, and radiological dispersal device components in diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
Abstract:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.

A proactive system is required to answer:

"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"

This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.

Method (Mycelium's reading): Developing, training, and testing AI foundation models using extensive datasets; implementing data governance strategies such as data space connectors, federated training, synthetic data creation, or 'AI gym' approaches; performing in-depth testing and validation in lab demonstrators and real-life …

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Projects are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- Effective and innovative methods for gathering, sharing and using large data sets in energy applications for the purpose of training AI models while ensuring privacy and security.

- Advanced and - wherever possible - open-source AI foundation models to support the digitalisation of the energy system, through improved grid observability, forecasting of supply and demand, advanced storage and renewables integration, demand side flexibility and energy efficiency.

- Enhanced cooperation, knowledge sharing and interoperability among energy system actors for secure and seamless data exchange.

- Advanced methodologies for AI model development ensuring that the results are FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) beyond the project ending, open source and accommodating for technology evolution.

Scope:

The quality of AI models depends strongly on the amount, quality, and representativeness of the data used for their training. Projects are expected to focus on developing, training and testing AI foundation models, using extensive data sets to accelerate the energy transition in key focus areas of the energy sector. Projects are expected to:

- Building on the results of previously funded projects on the Common European energy data space[1] as well as the ongoing work within the Data 4 Energy expert group, projects are expected to demonstrate innovative methods and data governance strategies for sharing data among various energy actors. Projects are expected to demonstrate that they have access to large relevant datasets at the time of submitting the proposal.

- Projects are expected to develop innovative strategies for sharing data in an effective, secure and transparent way to support the development of AI foundation models. An indicative non exhaustive list of strategies that can be explored is the use of data space connectors or federated training of models to allow the integration of confidential data; the creation of synthetic data as an intermediate step to fill data gaps or improve the quality of the data could also be explored. Projects could also explore other innovative data sharing strategies, such as an ‘AI gym’. The data governance strategies that will be developed in the project should be designed in a way to be scalable and operational even after the end of the project.

- Projects are expected to develop foundation models tailored for the energy sector, addressing at least one -or more- of the following use cases: planning and operation of electricity grids (including static power flow modelling and dynamic EMT modelling), forecasting, congestion management, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, flexibility management, demand-side energy efficiency, smart and bidirectional charging of EVs or other use cases that contribute to the objective of digitalisation of the energy system.

- Projects are expected to perform in-depth testing and validation of developed foundation models in lab demonstrators and real-life pilots, building on the results and using the facilities of previously funded projects on “AI testing and experimentation facilities (TEFs)”[2]. Regulatory sandboxes could also be considered for real-life pilot implementations.

- Projects are expected to bring together a wide group of stakeholders including data owners (for example energy utilities, grid operators, asset owners), application developers (for example startups, SMEs, hyperscalers) and model deployers (for example industry, grid operators, equipment manufacturers) providing a space of cooperation and collaborative data exchange.

- To scale up the training and development of the models, projects can benefit from the computing capacity of the AI factories that were recently announced by the European Commission[3], in particular the three AI factories that aim to develop AI applications for the energy sector.

#2 [paper] The impact of personalized deadline reminders via Microsoft Teams and Moodle calendar on assignment submission and completion rates
Authors: Ahmad Alfailakawi, Abdulaziz Alenizi
Venue: Frontiers in Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943550
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Objectives This study investigated the effectiveness of two digital deadline reminder strategies—a researcher-authored, friendly-toned announcement delivered through Microsoft Teams and a standard automated calendar/email notification generated by Moodle—compared with a control condition receiving no additional reminders. The study examined differences in on-time assignment submission rates and average submission delays among higher education students. Methodology An A/B/C comparative design with random assignment was employed involving 138 male and female students enrolled in the Introduction to Educational Technology course at the College of Basic Education in Kuwait during the second semester of the 2024–2025 academic year. Participants were allocated equally to three groups: a researcher-authored Microsoft Teams reminder group, an automated Moodle reminder group, and a control group. Five assignments were monitored over a ten-week intervention period, and submission data were obtained from Moodle activity logs. Results Statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups. Students receiving researcher-authored, friendly-toned reminders through Microsoft Teams demonstrated the highest mean on-time submission rate (94.22%) and the shortest mean submission delay (5.18 h). Students receiving automated Moodle reminders recorded an on-time submission rate of 85.65% and an average delay of 15.45 h, while the control group recorded 75.22% and 30.89 h, respectively. The effect sizes were substantial ( η 2 = 0.289 for on-time submission and η 2 = 0.639 for submission delay), although the latter estimate requires cautious interpretation because of the distributional characteristics of the delay variable. Conclusion The findings suggest that proactive digital reminder strategies can support students’ adherence to assignment deadlines. The researcher-authored, friendly-toned reminder strategy delivered through Microsoft Teams was associated with more favorable submission outcomes than the default automated Moodle reminder strategy. However, because the interventions differed simultaneously in communication platform, message content, authorship, and delivery format, the observed differences cannot be attributed to platform characteristics alone. The findings highlight the potential importance of reminder design and delivery practices while emphasizing the need for future research that independently examines the contributions of individual reminder components.

#3 [paper] QNFO Funding Strategy — Verified Funder Landscape & Shortlist
Authors: Rowan Brad Quni-Gudzinas

Abstract:
This paper presents a verified funder landscape and fit-score shortlist for sustaining QNFO, a two-year-old, solo-run, AI-assisted research platform that has produced an open corpus of approximately 1,000 method papers across seven program areas. Every funder fact was verified by live HTTP retrieval on 2026-08-13 across twenty-six pages spanning Web3 and IPFS ecosystem grantors, open-science philanthropy, and decentralized-science programs; anything not verified live is explicitly flagged. The analysis scores eleven funders on eligibility for an unaffiliated individual, topical fit with decentralized and epistemics-oriented research, and application friction, yielding a weighted ranking led by NLnet NGI Zero (calls open September 3, 2026; deadline November 3, 2026, 12:00 CEST) and Emergent Ventures, followed by the Foresight Institute, Filecoin Foundation, the Ethereum Ecosystem Support Program, Gitcoin, and the Effective Altruism funds. A sequencing calendar spans August 2026 through 2027, including the Sovereign Tech Agency Fellowship cycle. The paper documents application-readiness gaps (legal entity, residency, tax position, public identity), per-funder pitch skeletons, and framing cautions, including the risk of presenting corpus volume as rigor. It closes with an agent-executable action plan.

#4 [paper] AI Governance Readiness Map: Evidence Records, Roles and Missing Work
Authors: Dmytro Nasyrov
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026

Abstract:
AI Governance Readiness Map version 1.0.0 preserves an evidence worksheet for one AI system. Twelve controls connect ownership, artifact references and review records. The output identifies missing work and exports every control, including exclusions. Pharos Production AI engineering developed the worksheet to make those record requirements inspectable before a team treats a governance plan as implemented. A complete worksheet still returns DRAFT_REQUIRES_REVIEW. The counts describe entered records. They do not establish that an artifact exists, supports the declared control or has received a valid independent review. Evidence records and roles Catalog entries cover inventory, jurisdiction and use-case review, risk acceptance, accountability, training, suppliers, data provenance, validation, oversight, traceability, monitoring and incident triage. Controls carry editorial references to the GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE functions of NIST AI RMF, alongside prompts for a separate EU applicability review. The 12-control selection is original planning guidance. Each row records a status and eight text fields: responsible, accountable, consulted, informed, evidenceRef, reviewer, reviewedOn and rationale. The five statuses are unknown, planned, evidence-recorded, review-recorded and not-applicable. Responsible and accountable are required for ordinary rows. Evidence-recorded also needs an evidence reference. A reviewed row needs the owners, evidence reference, reviewer and review date. An exclusion instead needs an accountable owner, reviewer, review date and rationale. Consulted and informed stay optional. Only complete review-recorded rows increment reviewed. Only complete not-applicable rows increment excluded. Every other row needs attention, including a planned row with all its fields filled. Missing-field lists and next actions explain what remains. Scope warnings separately flag missing system purpose, jurisdiction review or an unresolved EU role. They do not determine a legal risk class or notification deadline. Six reproducible synthetic scenarios Six scenarios provide a blank worksheet, the unchanged original mixed example, an all-review-recorded worksheet and three boundary variants. The blank worksheet reports 12 rows needing attention and three scope warnings. The original example records two reviewed rows, one exclusion and nine rows needing attention, with one unresolved scope warning. All-review-recorded reports 12 reviewed rows while retaining the draft status. The remaining variants remove an exclusion rationale, omit the responsible owner of an evidence record or change a complete row to planned. Each reports 11 reviewed rows and one needing attention. All names, memos and dates used as review records are fictional. The original example retains September 11, 2026 inputs. Added examples use October 12, 2026 as a fixed assessment label. The reproduction command checks six scenarios and writes 25 files for comparison. No package dependencies, model calls or credentials are needed. JSON preserves exact entered values. #5 [paper] DESIGN AND SIMULATION OF A TASK REMINDER WITH SPACED REVIEW AND DEADLINE PRESSURE DETECTION
Authors: Hizba Muhammad Falah, Anggi Rizky Windra Putri, Tasiu Abdullahi Yusuf
Venue: International Journal of Cyber Engineering
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.68404/ijce.v2i1.26
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Describe Task reminders commonly indicate when an assignment is due, but deadline counts alone do not describe the effort required before each due date. Moreover, repeated notifications are not equivalent to retrieval-based spaced review. This study develops an explicit scheduling specification for an existing task-reminder prototype and evaluates a separate executable reference engine. The design combines a recall-dependent review rule, a cumulative deadline-pressure calculation, and an event resolver that distinguishes review prompts from deadline checks. Evaluation comprises 23 functional checks, three scripted review sequences, and 300 synthetic workload scenarios containing 1,150 task records. All functional checks passed. At an assumed capacity of two hours per day and a 72-hour horizon, count-based, aggregate-load, and cumulative deadline-pressure rules flagged 100, 100, and 150 scenarios, respectively. In 50 deliberately constructed early-bottleneck scenarios, only the cumulative rule flagged insufficient capacity before the earliest deadline. Conversely, all 50 light clustered workloads triggered the count rule without exceeding the assumed capacity. An independent exhaustive scheduling oracle agreed with the cumulative rule in all 300 scenarios; agreement was 50.0% for the count rule and 83.3% for the aggregate rule. These results verify logic under the stated capacity model. They do not establish improved retention, productivity, or student well-being. The contribution is a reproducible prototype extension with transparent assumptions and an evidence-based separation of reminder functionality from educational effectiveness.

The fellowship reflects the Graduate College’s commitment to expanding access to graduate education and strengthening the Illinois graduate community by recruiting students from many educational, geographic, and familial backgrounds. The DDF provides financial support to students who demonstrate strong potential for success in graduate study and whose pathways to graduate education reflect significant barriers or nontraditional routes. Through this recruitment fellowship, the Graduate College seeks to expand opportunities for talented students to pursue doctoral education at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and to connect fellowship recipients with programs and resources that support their transition to and success in graduate education. Eligibility and Selection Criteria DDFs are intended as recruitment fellowships. To that end, only those students who are seeking admission to a doctoral program at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (Illinois) are eligible. Generally, this includes students at either one of two stages of study: students seeking first-time admission to a doctoral program, or students who have completed a master’s at Illinois and are now applying for admission to a doctoral program here at Illinois. #13 [paper] Do Firms Expect the Deadline to Move? Expiry Dates, Repeated Extensions, and AI Decision-Makers in Japanese Corporate Tax Special Measures
Authors: 勉 矢作
Venue: Open Science Framework
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/dsm7j
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Many tax incentives carry an expiry date. A deadline should pull investment forward into the final year before expiry (a time notch in the sense of Slemrod 2013). If a measure has been extended many times, however, firms may expect another extension, and the deadline may stop working as a deadline. The literature on time notches (Slemrod 2013; House and Shapiro 2008; Cashin and Unayama 2016) and the literature on transition policy (Kaplow 1986, 2003; Shaviro 2000) have developed separately. This study links them by asking whether the history of extensions changes the response to an expiry date. Study 1 uses the annual reports that the Minister of Finance submits to the Diet under the Act on Transparency of Special Tax Measures (2010). These reports give, for each corporate tax special measure, the number of corporations applying it and the amount applied, for fiscal years ending on or after 1 April 2011. Study 2 asks how large language models (LLMs), acting as managers of a small firm, respond to the same kind of deadline. As firms delegate tax and investment decisions to AI, the response to deadlines may change. Study 2 tests the prediction, registered in OSF pw5fz, that LLM agents follow what is written: they respond to the expiry date stated in the statute and ignore an extension history unless it is written in front of them.

#14 [paper] Just Another Manic Monday in the Call Center: When Equal Demand Does Not Produce Equal Service
Authors: Michael Douglas, Eric Kyper
Venue: Archives of Business Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.14738/abr.1410.12332
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Call centers ordinarily explain service-level variation through demand, service time, staffing, routing, and customer patience. Yet performance may also vary systematically by weekday even when workload is comparable. This study examines a Monday effect in operational data from a large U.S. insurance-service organization. The dataset contained 13,024 intraday records across 32 business days, 37 reporting queues, and 20 business groups. Because call counts were cumulative within day, the primary analysis used each queue’s final daily snapshot, producing 1,127 active queue-day observations. Monday service level averaged .658, compared with .715 on Tuesday, although log-transformed call volume did not differ significantly between the two days. Ordinary least squares models with queue-clustered standard errors showed that Monday remained associated with a 5.1-percentage-point reduction in service level after controlling for call volume, average handle time, and business-group fixed effects. The result persisted across all-weekday, logit-transformed, volume-threshold, nonboundary, weighted, paired-queue, and nonparametric sensitivity analyses. The findings distinguish workload effects from weekday effects and suggest that start-of-week operational frictions may impair service beyond what volume alone explains. Because staffing, schedule adherence, absence, backlog, and call-mix measures were unavailable, the analysis identifies a robust temporal pattern rather than a causal mechanism. The study contributes to service-operations research by treating weekday as an operational state variable and offers managers a focused diagnostic agenda for Monday readiness.

Abstract:
Abstract Background Manual creation of a surgery residency call schedule is a labor-intensive process that adds to the administrative burden of a chief resident while often producing suboptimal fairness and work distribution. While commercial scheduling software exists, many programs struggle with inflexibility, high costs, and an inability to accommodate program-specific constraints. Methods We developed a scheduling software platform using AI-assisted development tools (Codex, Claude Code), both commercially available agentic coding environments. The system applies a rule-based, weekend-first assignment hierarchy with randomized tie-breaking under a search budget fixed in advance, then performs iterative weekday assignment, accommodating vacation requests and discrete call-shift swapping. The validation roster modeled a single general surgery residency program: 55 residents (32 categorical and 2 preliminary general surgery residents spanning PGY 1 through PGY 6; 20 off-service rotators from other programs; and 1 fellow) distributed across 10 call pools. Three prespecified call-related ACGME constraints were enforced (at least 4 days off per 28-day period, call no more frequently than every third night averaged over 4 weeks, and no consecutive 24-hour call). The 80-hour weekly maximum and the 24-hour period free of all clinical and educational responsibility were not evaluated, as both depend on activity the call calendar does not capture. We evaluated the system with 100 independent full-year runs (July 1 to June 30), each generated end-to-end across all call pools and months under an independently randomized vacation distribution. Compliance and fairness were evaluated at the level of the individual call-pool month (service-month), the unit at which a monthly schedule is produced; fairness and workload metrics were computed across the program’s in-program surgery residents. Results We generated 12,000 service-month schedules over 100 independent full-year runs. 99.2% (11,906) satisfied all prespecified call-related constraints with no violations detected by the internal validation engine. Forty-five of the 100 full-year runs required no manual intervention in any service-month, and none required it in more than 4 of its 120. Manual review of 120 randomly selected service-months by two authors, without reference to the validator’s output, agreed with it in 120 of 120 cases. Monthly fairness, defined within each call pool and month as the range (maximum minus minimum) of call shifts or weekends assigned per resident, showed a shift range ≤ 1 in 65.4% of service-months (mean 1.84, SD 2.15) and perfect weekend equity (range = 0) in 42.5%, with 86.6% achieving a weekend range ≤ 1 (mean 0.71, SD 0.70). Mean full-year generation time was 108.8 s (SD 59.1). Residents averaged 18.65 weekends (SD 3.13) and 78.23 call days (SD 5.49) per year. Conclusions This automated scheduling system generates resident call schedules that satisfy the prespecified call-related ACGME constraints, optimizes fairness across multiple dimensions, accommodates complex vacation requirements, handles cross-pool coordination, and flags the service-months it cannot resolve within its search budget rather than emitting a non-compliant schedule. These results provide construct validity evidence that optimization algorithms combined with careful constraint specification can eliminate the great majority of the administrative burden of manual scheduling while improving schedule quality and equity.

Introduction: Ectopic pregnancy remains the leading cause of first-trimester maternal mortality. The obstetric screening exam was implemented July 12, 2021, and incorporated focused transabdominal pelvic and right upper quadrant ultrasound into the initial ED evaluation, often prior to bed assignment. The primary outcome was time from ED arrival to operating room (OR). Secondary outcomes included time to obstetric consultation, time to hospital admission, ED length of stay (LOS), and POCUS use. Nonparametric testing was used for skewed time data. Logistic regression evaluated the odds of reaching the OR within four hours. Patient-level interrupted time series analysis assessed temporal trends. Results: A total of 150 patients were included (87 pre- and 63 post-implementation). Median arrival-to-OR time decreased from 516 minutes (interquartile range [IQR] 324–709.5) to 391 minutes (IQR 220–619), a 125-minute reduction (P = .020; bootstrap 95% CI, 8–233). The proportion of patients reaching the OR within four hours increased from 16.1% to 31.8% (odds ratio 2.42; 95% CI, 1.11–5.29; P = .02). Time to obstetric consultation (210 vs 146 minutes; P = .003), time to hospital admission (345 vs 250 minutes; P = .005), and ED LOS (451 vs 367 minutes; P = .03) were all reduced. Point-of-care ultrasound use increased from 41.4% to 66.7% (P < .001), while the remainder underwent radiology ultrasound. #1 [paper] Funding deadlines act as a zeitgeber for science
Authors: Haining Wang, Jing Su
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.10.758253
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Funders decide which science is paid for. Whether they also shape when it becomes public has been hard to test. Across 376,542 preprints on bioRxiv and medRxiv, the US share rose by 2.3 to 2.7 percentage points in the four weeks before due dates for the main research grant of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and dropped on the date. About one in eleven US preprints in those weeks was attributable to the deadline, and fields that depend least on NIH rose least. Among 15,906 funded investigators, the share of preprints posted in the four weeks before their own deadline was 9% higher than in other four-month cycles, and these preprints resembled the later grant without being more highly cited. Repeated before every due date, this individual surge matches the national peak's timing within a week. NIH's application calendar, like its funding, shapes when US biomedical science becomes public.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The current knowledge of food chemical complexity is limited to a narrow set of approximately 150 components, leaving over 100,000 compounds and contaminants ('nutrient dark matter') unquantified and underexplored, creating a bottleneck for predictive nutrition and food safety.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development and testing of validated AI algorithms capable of interpreting and annotating high-throughput foodomics data (e.g., untargeted mass-spectrometry or nuclear magnetic resonance) and predicting/inferring compound presence and concentration via innovative approaches like phylogenetic relati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): High-throughput foodomics data involving hundreds of thousands of compounds across thousands of foods.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- an Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool able to accelerate the analysis of complex foodomics data to speed up the identification, structural characterisation, and quantification of chemicals present in food;

- improving capacity and synergies in foodomics research between academia, research infrastructures and industry.

Scope:

Through food and beverages, the population is exposed to an immense variety of chemicals (as contaminants and as ingredients). The “foodome” is the complete set of compounds present in a food sample at a given time; it includes both endogenous biomolecules (produced through a species' metabolic processes) and exogenous compounds (natural and synthetic substances from production, processing, handling, and packaging). The current knowledge is largely confined to a narrow set of approximately 150 food components catalogued by traditional databases. These components represent only a very small fraction of the total chemical complexity present in foods, while thousands (>100,000) of compounds and contaminants remain largely unquantified and underexplored. Understanding this “nutrient dark matter” would require identifying, cataloguing and quantifying the full spectrum of substances present in our food and present in accessible, AI-ready databases. The need for such information is today a bottleneck to make the nutrition field predictive and data driven, and has the potential to make food processing more efficient in bringing new foods items on the market. Efforts to create such datasets are underway but owing to the quantity of samples (hundreds of thousands of compounds across thousands of foods), such databases often rely on high-throughput experimental methods which do not allow a precise characterisation of the molecules identified.

Proposals should address the following activities:

- develop and test validated AI algorithms capable of interpreting and annotating high-throughput foodomics data, for instance from untargeted mass-spectrometry or nuclear magnetic resonance;

- the AI algorithms should be capable to predict or infer the presence and concentration of compounds based on (incomplete) foodomics data via innovative approaches, for instance by considering phylogenic relationships between species. Moreover, this should help identify analytical methods and potential food safety hazards based on their similarity to known compounds;

- develop a European research and innovation network between Member States and Associated Countries in food exposome research to support the development, standardization, valorisation and dissemination of the AI results and considering existing initiatives such as the Centre for Excellence in the Periodic Table of Food Initiative from Wageningen University.

The multi-actor approach is encouraged. Proposals should include industry in the consortia and academia, startups, SMEs and international initiatives. Collaboration with international partners is encouraged as well as with existing private companies in the EU/Associated countries.

Technology Readiness Level - Technology readiness level expected from completed projects

Activities are expected to start from TRL 5 in order to achieve TRL 7 by the end of the project – see General Annex B.

#9 [paper] Alternative futures for laboratory medicine in 2050: scenarios and signposts for diagnostic capability contraction.
Authors: Yuji, Koichiro, Yuji, Wakako, Ohnishi, Hiroaki
Venue: Clinical chemistry and laboratory medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42723619/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Laboratory medicine has begun to describe its own future, and the images it produces are almost uniformly expansionary. What they rarely contain is a collapse scenario: a future in which the field delivers less than today. A profession planning for 2050 needs one. CONTENT: We summarise what structured foresight offers a clinical readership, entering through the threats quadrant of a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) analysis, and treat the standard taxonomy of futures as a lens, not a required method. We define diagnostic capability contraction as progressive degradation rather than catastrophic disappearance, distinct from retiring tests that add nothing. Six drivers are specified: loss of laboratory-developed tests, reduced test availability, workforce attrition, supplier dependency, geographical access and payment. Evidence comes from three jurisdictions, including Japan, where one regulatory driver produced different outcomes in the same period. We set out four scenarios for 2050, one per generic image, and propose signposts as early-warning indicators, with action thresholds, for the contraction scenario. Estimates of likelihood attach to the indicators, not the futures. SUMMARY: The evidence base is uneven across drivers, and informatively so: what is not anticipated is not measured. The argument applies to our own prior work, expansionary in the same way. OUTLOOK: A set containing a contraction branch gives laboratory leadership what an expansionary set cannot: what to watch for, and when to act. A preferred future chosen without it comes from a shorter list than the field faces. Building a balanced set is work that no small group of authors can do alone.

Abstract:
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) Tackling Acquisition of Language in Kids (TALK) initiative intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit research grant applications to improve the earliest steps in clinical practice for late talking children. The overarching purpose of this funding opportunity is to inform, develop, and evaluate evidence-based practices and implementation strategies to (1) effectively and efficiently identify early signs of late talking and (2) successfully guide parents, caregivers, and professionals in supporting the needs of late talking children at the first point of concern.

For this NOFO late talking is defined as a child, usually over the age of 18 months, not meeting expressive language milestones, for any reason. Populations of interest include, but are not limited to, children at higher risk for late talking due to premature birth, exposure to maltreatment or trauma, neurological conditions, motor and sensory disorders, emotional and behavioral disorders, and intellectual and developmental disorders. Children who present as late talkers for no other known reason and with no other symptoms also are of interest for this NOFO.

For this NOFO, the early steps for services for children age birth to three years that are of interest include screening and developmental surveillance of late talking, referral and follow through for specialized services, and in-depth evaluation and diagnosis of language and other contributing delays/disorders. These services typically occur in primary care, specialty care, educational settings, and early childhood community settings. The research will need to be conducted in a relevant setting.

Research focusing on children as well as their parents, caregivers, and supporting community professionals is of interest, including how to support successfully navigating from initial concern to effective care. Community partnerships and community engaged research approaches will be a key requirement for this opportunity.

Applications are not being solicited at this time. Notice is being provided to allow potential applicants sufficient time to develop meaningful collaborations and responsive projects.

Investigators with expertise and insights into early language learning, late talking, early childhood education, early intervention, and primary care are encouraged to begin to consider applying for this new NOFO. #18 [paper] Assessing Challenges for U.S.-Based Polar Early Career Scientists During Science Policy Changes
Authors: Fairuz Ishraque, Mohammad Afzal Shadab, Kevin Shionalyn, Neosha Narayanan, Meghan Schaberg, Shreyas Gaikwad, Izuchukwu Ezukanma, Olga Lauter
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31223/x5nr5s
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Early-career researchers (ECRs) play a critical role in sustaining polar and cryosphere research in the United States. Since January 2025, changes in U.S. science policy and federal research funding have created substantial uncertainty for researchers, particularly those in the early stages of their careers. To assess the impacts of these changes, we conducted a community-driven survey of U.S.-based polar and cryosphere ECRs examining concerns related to science policy, research funding, career trajectories, and workforce retention. Survey responses indicate widespread concern regarding recent changes in science policy and funding, with many respondents reporting negative effects on research productivity, motivation, and mental well-being. Respondents also expressed concern regarding future employment opportunities and the long-term health of the scientific enterprise. A substantial proportion reported considering employment opportunities outside the United States, leaving academia, or leaving polar and cryosphere research altogether. At the same time, respondents identified potential pathways for retention, including stable research funding, mentorship, professional support, and reversal of recent funding reductions. These findings provide a timely assessment of workforce sentiment during a period of rapid policy change and highlight factors that may influence the future sustainability of the U.S. polar and cryospheric research community.

#2 [grant] GPD Grant Forecast
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/356629
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 
Abstract:
THIS IS NOT A NOTICE OF FUNDING. THIS IS A GENERAL FORECAST ONLY.

Grant and Per Diem (GPD) Program Introduction

The GPD Program is VA’s largest transitional housing program for Veterans experiencing homelessness and is permanently authorized under Public Law 109-461.

Since 1994, the GPD Program has awarded grants to community-based organizations to provide transitional housing with wraparound supportive services to assist vulnerable Veterans move into permanent housing. The grants are designed to meet Veterans at various stages as they move to stable housing. Community-based organizations receiving GPD grants offer focused transitional housing services through a variety of housing models targeted to different populations and needs of Veterans. The GPD program plays a vital role in the continuum of homeless services by providing supportive services to those Veterans who would otherwise be among the unsheltered homeless population. The result of GPD programs is that Veterans achieve residential stability, increase their skill levels and/or income, and obtain greater self-determination.

Types of GPD Grants

Transitional housing grants:

Per Diem Only (PDO) grants provide funding in the form of per diem payments to reimburse grantees for the cost of care provided to Veterans in transitional supportive housing.

Special Need grants target housing and services to specific populations of Veterans (e.g., women, Veterans with chronic mental illness, frail elderly Veterans, Veterans caring for minor dependents, terminally ill Veterans).

Transition-In-Place (TIP) grants offer Veteran residents housing in which supportive services transition out of the residence over time, rather than the resident. Upon completion of the TIP services, the resident retains the unit as their permanent housing with no requirement to move.

Other types of grants:

Case Management grants support Veterans who were previously experiencing homelessness or who are at risk for homelessness so that they may obtain or retain permanent housing.

Capital grants support the costs of acquiring, renovating, or constructing facilities and are only offered intermittently to improve existing facilities or to develop new transitional housing depending on VA's priorities and funding availability.

Lists of current grantees are available on the GPD website.

How to Apply for GPD Funding

Not all grant types are available annually. When available, notices of funding can be found at the following locations: www.grants.gov and https://www.va.gov/homeless/gpd.asp.

Application instructions are provided in each notice of funding.

Each notice of funding will clarify specific eligibility criteria, application requirements, funding limitations, and other requirements.

Applications are submitted through an online portal that is only available when there is an open notice of funding.

Potential applicants who wish to see what was required for previous applications may review past notices of funding, available on the GPD provider website and www.grants.gov. Past notices of funding are not a guarantee of future requirements.

Tentative Estimated GPD Award Schedule

Specific dates are not able to be forecast.

The follow tentative approximations are provided for general planning purposes.

FY 2026

Case Management – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2025 for case management awards starting approximately in FY 2026.

FY 2027

PDO – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2026 for PDO awards starting approximately in FY 2027.

TIP – GPD tentatively expects to offer a notice of funding around FY 2026 for TIP awards starting approximately in FY 2027.

FY 2028

GPD tentatively does not expect to offer a notice of funding for this timeframe. GPD may update this forecast closer to the time.

THIS IS NOT A NOTICE OF FUNDING. THIS IS A GENERAL FORECAST ONLY.

GPD Fact sheet

#13 [grant] Advancing Screening, Diagnosis, and Referral for Late Talking Children
Amount: $500,000
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/362352
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-10-15
Abstract:
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) Tackling Acquisition of Language in Kids (TALK) initiative intends to publish a Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) to solicit research grant applications to improve the earliest steps in clinical practice for late talking children. The overarching purpose of this funding opportunity is to inform, develop, and evaluate evidence-based practices and implementation strategies to (1) effectively and efficiently identify early signs of late talking and (2) successfully guide parents, caregivers, and professionals in supporting the needs of late talking children at the first point of concern.

For this NOFO late talking is defined as a child, usually over the age of 18 months, not meeting expressive language milestones, for any reason. Populations of interest include, but are not limited to, children at higher risk for late talking due to premature birth, exposure to maltreatment or trauma, neurological conditions, motor and sensory disorders, emotional and behavioral disorders, and intellectual and developmental disorders. Children who present as late talkers for no other known reason and with no other symptoms also are of interest for this NOFO.

For this NOFO, the early steps for services for children age birth to three years that are of interest include screening and developmental surveillance of late talking, referral and follow through for specialized services, and in-depth evaluation and diagnosis of language and other contributing delays/disorders. These services typically occur in primary care, specialty care, educational settings, and early childhood community settings. The research will need to be conducted in a relevant setting.

Research focusing on children as well as their parents, caregivers, and supporting community professionals is of interest, including how to support successfully navigating from initial concern to effective care. Community partnerships and community engaged research approaches will be a key requirement for this opportunity.

Applications are not being solicited at this time. Notice is being provided to allow potential applicants sufficient time to develop meaningful collaborations and responsive projects.

Investigators with expertise and insights into early language learning, late talking, early childhood education, early intervention, and primary care are encouraged to begin to consider applying for this new NOFO. In addition, collaborative investigations combining expertise in clinical practice research, dissemination and implementation science, or community engaged research will be encouraged and these investigators should also begin considering applying for this application.

Abstract:
Through this Disaster NOFO, EDA will award investments in regions experiencing severe economic distress or other economic harm resulting from hurricanes, wildfires, tornadoes, floods, and other natural disasters occurring in calendar years 2023 and 2024. EDA’s goal under this NOFO is to assist communities recovering from a disaster by realizing opportunities to recover and change the economic trajectory of the community for the better. In other words, EDA funding seeks to help communities recover and set them on a path to exceed their previous pre-disaster baseline. EDA seeks projects that are responsive to community needs post-disaster by engaging all aspects of the community, with special focus on private industry partners.

This Disaster NOFO provides funding through three pathways:

Readiness Path – Standalone non-construction projects designed to increase a community’s readiness to apply for or implement disaster recovery funding from private and public sources including, but not limited to, future EDA NOFOs and the Implementation or Industry Transformation Paths under this NOFO. Projects will fund strategy development, capacity building, and/or predevelopment costs necessary for future recovery projects.

Implementation Path – Standalone construction or non-construction projects designed to address the economic challenges faced by a community recovering from a natural disaster and improve economic trajectories beyond pre-disaster economic conditions.

Industry Transformation Path – Led by a coalition of regional stakeholders, a portfolio of large-scale, multicomponent construction and non-construction projects designed to fundamentally transform the economic trajectory of a region through the development or acceleration of an industry.

#7 [paper] Valuing education for limited-resource audiences using a willingness to accept experiment
Authors: Russell Tronstad, Ibrahima Sall
Venue: PLoS ONE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0348858
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Education grants often target audiences that have limited-resources relative to their peers, such as beginning farmers, who arguably have the most to gain from more education. Yet, charging even modest fees to these participants is discouraged, creating a challenge for funding entities that desire to have a dollar value for the education provided. To measure this value, we conducted an experiment using a willingness-to-accept (WTA) approach. Participants chose a minimum cash payout from seven different options to voluntarily leave a training session before receiving any instruction or educational materials. The design is constructed so that each option has an equal expected payout. Cash payouts were not advertised or known to any participants before the training. Results show that average WTA values are $277.44 per training (about 4 hours of instruction), which is 2.11 to 4.74 times more than participants' self-reported willingness to pay (WTP), depending on how travel costs and time of participants are valued. WTP consistently and significantly explains much of the variation in WTA. In sharp contrast, detailed travel cost estimates in various forms were consistently insignificant for explaining WTA values. Beginning farmers and ranchers, our targeted limited-resource audience, reported WTA and WTP values that were $81.18 and $22.73 more per training, respectively, than those of non-beginning farmers.

#9 [paper] Answering Service Price Index (answeringservicequotes.com)
Authors: Joseph Ellul
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23141746
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The median published figure in the Answering Service Price Index is 68.95 USD across 23 sources' own pages (range 5 to 399 USD), read 26 September 2026. Coverage. 23 of the 70 named sources read in full publish a figure; 47 publish none, read 26 September 2026. Methodology. Every row is a verbatim sentence read from the named source's own page through the estate's fetch service on the date shown, hash-pinned to the stored read (the sha of the page's visible text; the raw page is mirrored to R2). 23 of the 70 named sources that could be read published a usable figure; 47 published none and are recorded as not published, never filled in; 3 could not be read (blocked, dead or unreachable) and count nowhere. #10 [paper] An economic analysis of postoperative cataract consultation using remote self-assessment
Authors: Casper van der Zee, Janneau L. J. Claessens, Rudy M. M. A. Nuijts, Rob Wouters, Nicolaas J. Reus, Karl Boden, Oliver Findl, Saskia M. Imhof

Abstract:
To evaluate the potential savings realized by replacing the 4-6 weeks consultation following cataract surgery with remote self-assessment. In addition, we evaluated the costs associated with adverse events (AEs) from a societal perspective and evaluated the current cost of AEs based on published literature and publicly available datasets. We determined the cost reduction when replacing the in-person 4-6-week postoperative consultation visit with remote self-assessment using our previous clinical trial, publicly available healthcare resource databases, and threshold analysis to determine the effect on cost if the incidence of AEs is affected by conducting an online self-assessment. We collected AE probabilities and costs of AEs based on published literature and databases. and performed a threshold analysis to demonstrate the financial impact if the incidence of AEs is altered versus the savings due to replacing the 4-6 weeks in-person consultation with remote self-assessment. Remote self-assessments resulted in an average savings between -€83 and -€92 per patient. Physical consultations were less costly only if >80% of remote self-assessments warranted an in-person follow-up. The mean cost of AEs per patient was estimated to be €16.35 and were attributed primarily to rare but severe complications, including endophthalmitis and retinal detachment. Perceived price is how much a donor believes it costs, in dollars given, to deliver a dollar of program benefit to the organization's beneficiaries, and it rises as more of a gift is expected to go to overhead. Prior work shows that both effectiveness signals and overhead ratios shape giving, yet few studies test whether effectiveness signals work by way of donors' beliefs about the price of their gift. In partnership with a small, newly established nonprofit, an online survey experiment was conducted (total N = 1862). The experiment manipulated reputational effectiveness across control, low, and high conditions and measured the perceived price of giving, giving intentions, and a small‐stakes incentivized donation decision. The perceived price of giving mediated the response to the low‐effectiveness (reach) cue, but there was little evidence that it mediated the response to the high‐effectiveness (outcome) cue; the mediation was clearest for stated giving intentions and weaker for the amount donors were willing to give and for the small‐stakes donation decision. Because the high and low conditions differed in dimension as well as in valence, we do not attribute this asymmetry to the sign of the signal alone. For fundraising practice, how an organization communicates its effectiveness can shift what donors believe a gift will accomplish (a lever available even to organizations without audited financial figures), though this belief is one mechanism among several rather than the whole story.

One such intervention is the use of random selection. The method has been trialled by a number of funders, but the organisational motivations for its use have until now, not been explored empirically. This qualitative study aims to address this evidence gap. Methods This study is part of a collaborative research initiative between research funders, technologists and researchers ‘The Research on Research Institute’ (RoRI). #18 [paper] Cost-Effectiveness of Annual Atrial Fibrillation Screening Compared with Current Opportunistic Screening in Australian Primary Care: A Model-Based Economic Evaluation

Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although the guidelines recommend opportunistic screening for adults ≥ 65 years, screening for atrial fibrillation (AF) remains underutilised in Australia. Previous studies have focused on handheld devices rather than 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) devices that are readily available in primary-care settings, and the evidence supporting an annual AF screening programme in Australia is limited. Therefore, the aim of this study is to compare the cost-effectiveness of an annual, structured, higher‑coverage opportunistic ECG screening approach (annual screening) with current unstructured opportunistic screening (current screening) in older adults in Australia. METHODS: A Markov model was developed to evaluate two strategies for adults ≥ 65 years: (1) annual screening using 12-lead ECG and (2) current opportunistic screening. The model included 11 health states capturing AF treatment and outcomes, and simulations were run using monthly cycles. A health system perspective and 10-year time horizon were applied. To account for uncertainty, a probabilistic sensitivity analysis with 1000 iterations was undertaken and the results were assessed against a cost-effectiveness threshold of 28,000 Australian dollars (AU$) per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Uncertainty was further examined through cost-effectiveness acceptability curves and scenario analyses to test the stability of findings under alternative assumptions. RESULTS: Annual screening increased costs by AU$4213 and gained 0.43 QALYs, yielding an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of AU$9797 per QALY gained. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis demonstrated that 100% of simulations yielded a positive incremental net monetary benefit. Setting (Mycelium's reading): Russian Arctic coastlines using high-resolution airphotos.
Abstract:
Marine litter beach accumulation is a pressing issue not only for urban coastal areas but also for remote and uninhabited regions such as the Arctic. Existing manual litter collection and identification methods remain labor-intensive. An assessment of the volume and composition of marine litter was conducted for the Russian Arctic coastlines using high-resolution airphotos. The method is based on training the You Only Look Once (YOLOv8, 2023) convolutional neural network (CNN) in the Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) configuration to recognize plastic, metal, fishing gear, wood, and other types of marine litter on images. The best detection performance was obtained for metal and plastic-large, visually contrasting litter items. The worst performance was obtained for wood and other debris, primarily due to their similarity to the natural background. Machine learning (ML) methods combined with remote sensing data represent a new high-precision tool for large-scale environmental monitoring in the Arctic.

The findings reveal a substantial increase in scientific production, particularly after 2015, demonstrating the rapid expansion of this interdisciplinary research domain. China, the United States, and several European and Asian countries emerged as the leading contributors to scientific productivity and international collaboration, while Marine Pollution Bulletin and Science of the Total Environment ranked among the most productive publication sources. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive knowledge map of the field, highlighting the growing integration of digital technologies and sustainable waste management strategies. The findings offer valuable insights for researchers, policymakers, and environmental practitioners in identifying research priorities, strengthening international collaboration, and advancing technology-driven solutions for sustainable ocean plastic waste management.

Authors: Eviatar Bach

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of theoretical foundations for using analysis increments (the difference between analysis and forecast) to diagnose and correct model bias in weather and climate prediction, particularly when using machine learning for state-dependent corrections.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical analysis of Kalman filters with constant and state-dependent biases, including proofs of what averaged increments measure and the limits of bias identification for linear dynamics, supplemented by numerical experiments on linear models and the nonlinear Lorenz'96 model.

Abstract:
A common method for diagnosing and correcting model bias in weather and climate prediction is based on analysis increments: the difference between the analysis and the forecast at each data assimilation cycle. Their time average is used to estimate and correct the bias, and machine learning is increasingly used to map the forecast state to the increments, giving a state-dependent correction. Despite its widespread use, the method lacks theoretical foundations. We first analyse a Kalman filter whose forecast model has a constant bias. We show what the averaged increment measures, and prove that iterating the correction removes all of the bias seen through the observations; for linear dynamics, no method can identify the rest. We then extend the analysis to state-dependent biases. For linear dynamics, each increment records the model error over the filter's memory, as seen through the observations. We use this to determine what the increments measure when averaged over a long period, averaged over periods with similar slowly varying conditions, and used without averaging, as in machine-learned corrections. Numerical experiments confirm the theory for a linear model and suggest that its main conclusions carry over to the nonlinear Lorenz'96 model, including for a correction learned by a neural network.

Method (Mycelium's reading): Culturing four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, measuring their hyperspectral absorption and backscatter, modeling spectral reflectances detectable by remote sensing platforms, and quantifying differences between taxonomic fingerprints using vector-based and stat…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including Pseudo-nitzschia, Thalassiosira, Chaetoceros, and Asterionellopsis.
Abstract:
Diatoms are microscopic marine algae that are critical for global primary production, carbon sequestration, and fisheries productivity. However, select diatoms may form harmful algal blooms, which threaten marine ecosystems and the fisheries they sustain. Rapidly identifying harmful blooms is necessary to effectively manage marine resources, yet current identification methods are limited by expensive and labor-intensive in-situ point sampling. Hyperspectral remote sensing enables scalable monitoring, but its ability to resolve taxonomic shifts within phytoplankton groups (e.g. diatoms) is largely unknown. To investigate this uncertainty, we cultured four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including this system's most abundant harmful algae, Pseudo-nitzschia. The hyperspectral absorption and backscatter of these taxa were measured and used to model spectral reflectances that remote sensing platforms (satellites/drones) might detect. Differences between fingerprints of these taxa were quantified using vector-based and statistical analyses. Mean spectral differences of 48% were observed between the most dominant diatom, Thalassiosira, and the most toxic diatom, Pseudo-nitzschia. Differences of approximately 30% were found between Pseudo-nitzschia and the second and third most abundant diatoms, Chaetoceros and Asterionellopsis. Successful identification of Pseudo-nitzschia's reflectance fingerprint was driven by the presence of a unique feature around 560 nm. The distinct spectral fingerprint of Pseudo-nitzschia indicates that it can be distinguished from other diatom blooms using hyperspectral remote sensing platforms.

A primary challenge of machine learning to predict marine heatwave (MHW) for the south China sea (SCS) is the limited availability of observational data for model training. To address this issue, this study explores the viability of leveraging multi-member ensemble simulations from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6), to construct an extensive, physically consistent training dataset for various machine learning models. After training on multiple CMIP6 ensemble members, the constructed models are evaluated for their predictive capacity regarding MHW in the SCS. #3 [paper] Beyond a Better Score: Long-Horizon Agentic ML Development and Evaluation Protocol for Physics Time Series
Authors: Yajun Ma, Lucas Venetoulias, Akbota Assan, A. Li

Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23071121

Abstract:
Physics time-series data are central to fundamental discoveries involving dark matter, neutrinos, and gravitational waves. Machine learning has shown strong potential to recover weak scientific signals buried in complex noise. Recent LLM-agent systems further automate ML development, but existing approaches are often driven primarily by one or a few numerical scores. In pursuit of a better score, agents may exploit shortcuts, trigger mode collapse, or game the evaluation procedure, producing models that achieve high scores but are scientifically invalid. We introduce SIDERIUS, an LLM agent system designed to move beyond a better score toward scientifically valid, long-horizon ML development. SIDERIUS combines contract-defined composable capabilities for flexible orchestration and human-in-the-loop, a multi-layer scientific evaluation protocol that distinguishes valid models from unhealthy or gaming models, and resource-aware exploration for computationally expensive scientific ML. In our TIDMAD benchmark, SIDERIUS with a GPT-based orchestrator achieves the highest Valid-model proposal rate of 63.8% and the best valid denoising score of 2.744, compared with 1.6% and −0.647, respectively, for the same GPT model using the general-purpose Codex coding agent. We further benchmark SIDERIUS on three additional physics time-series datasets, demonstrating its reuse and performance across different tasks. Together, these results suggest that progress in agentic scientific ML should be measured beyond a better score, by how an agent explores and by whether the models it produces can be trusted as science.

Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Abstract:

Cold-stunning events (or periods when water temperatures drop to threatening levels for wildlife) pose substantial risks to coastal systems in Texas. In response, the Texas Marine Coldwater Response Collaborative (TCRC) was established to coordinate cold-stunning response across organizations with diverse priorities and interests. A machine learning (ML) water temperature prediction model has been used to guide the cold-stunning advisory process; however, little is known about how users within the TCRC interpret and act on this information in complex, time-sensitive decision environments. Structured interviews, which incorporated an interactive activity presenting various forms of predictive information at several stages before and during a simulated cold-stunning event, were conducted with 15 TCRC members, encompassing natural resource managers, coastal economic operators, and weather forecasters. How and when users placed trust in the predictive information also varied across users and decision contexts, shaped by familiarity with the predictive tools, relationships with model developers, consistency with other information sources, and the stakes associated with particular decisions.
