#20 [paper] Storm surge dynamics in the northern Adriatic Sea: comparing AI emulators with high-resolution numerical simulations
Authors: Rodrigo Campos-Caba, Paula Camus, Andrea Mazzino, Michalis Vousdoukas, Massimo Tondello, Iván Federico, Salvatore Causio, Lorenzo Mentaschi
Venue: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-26-3683-2026
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract. Accurate storm surge forecasting is vital for protecting coastal regions, particularly in the northern Adriatic Sea where sea-level rise and increasingly severe storm events pose growing risks. Machine Learning (ML) approaches offer compelling speed and flexibility, yet their ability to emulate high-resolution dynamic models, especially for extreme surge events, has not been sufficiently assessed across methods and loss functions. In this study, a range of ML emulators, from Multivariate Linear Regression (MLR) to Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, is benchmarked against a high-resolution hydrodynamic model optimized for extreme surge representation. We also evaluate the impact of training loss functions, comparing the conventional Mean Squared Error (MSE) with the corrected Mean Absolute Deviation squared (MADc²), designed to better capture surge peaks. Results show that even simple models like MLR, when trained with MADc², achieve performance comparable to advanced neural networks while remaining orders of magnitude faster. These findings demonstrate that with appropriate training strategies, data-driven emulators can rival physics-based models in reproducing extremes. The MLR-MADc² configuration emerges as a practical balance between computational efficiency and accuracy, underscoring the potential of ML emulators for coastal forecasting and risk assessment.

#3 [paper] Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for Satellite Trajectory-Based Reconstruction: Applications to Grad-Shafranov and Magneto-Hydrostatic Equilibria
Authors: Kyoung-Joo Hwang, Kyunghwan Dokgo, Hiroshi Hasegawa, 최은진, James Burch
Venue: AIP Publishing
Year: 2026

Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Reconstructing continuous two-dimensional Grad-Shafranov (GS) and magneto-hydrostatic (MHS) equilibrium structures from limited, sparsely sampled trajectory-like satellite measurements without explicit boundary conditions.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) utilizing a Sinusoidal Representation Networks (SIREN)-enhanced architecture and uncertainty weighting for balanced optimization of physical constraints.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic, noise-free trajectory-like data representative of satellite measurements under GS and MHS constraints.
Abstract:
This study demonstrates the effectiveness of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for reconstructing Grad-Shafranov (GS) equilibrium structures from synthetic, noise-free trajectory-like data representative of satellite measurements under both GS and magnetohydrostatic (MHS) constraints. The proposed framework focuses on inferring continuous two-dimensional equilibrium structures from limited and sparsely sampled measurements along trajectories analogous to satellite sampling using static equilibrium solutions without explicitly provided boundary conditions. The Sinusoidal Representation Networks (SIREN)-enhanced architecture played a key role in capturing fine-scale structures. By incorporating uncertainty weighting, the model ensured balanced optimization, leading to higher accuracy and more effective enforcement of physical constraints. Additionally, the study highlights the importance of diverse training data, including multi-component measurements and data from multiple trajectories. The integration of such data significantly improved model performance by reducing errors and uncertainty while stabilizing training dynamics. These findings suggest that, even in the absence of explicit boundary conditions, which are commonly incorporated in PINN research, multi-component and multi-trajectory data can provide additional directional information that guides the solution process, reduces reconstruction ambiguity, and improves the reliability of the reconstructed solution.

#12 [paper] Accuracy and CPU speed gains across lightweight YOLO generations under downstream uncertainty
Authors: Ge Yang

Abstract:
Abstract Each new lightweight YOLO release reports higher COCO accuracy and lower CPU latency, and applied studies commonly build on the newest release. Recent multi-dataset comparisons show that a newer release need not win downstream, but they rarely separate a model difference from training-seed and test-set variability. We trained six nano-scale generations with three seeds on floating-debris and PASCAL VOC subsamples and three generations on VisDrone (49 runs), and compared them with paired test-image resampling. YOLO26n led YOLOv8n by 5.98 percentage points of mAP@0.5:0.95 on VOC but trailed it by 1.62 points on floating debris and 0.69 points on VisDrone, with all three bootstrap intervals excluding zero. The floating-debris deficit occurred in every object-size stratum and persisted under the default training recipe. These pairwise contrasts were stable, whereas the complete six-model ranking survived in only 55.1% and 16.4% of resamples. On three CPUs, randomized interleaved timing gave latency reductions of 1–12% from YOLOv8n to YOLO11n and 14–22% from YOLO11n to YOLO26n, against about 30% and 31% implied by the published tables. A release-level gain is therefore a hypothesis to test on the target data and processor. Pairwise intervals, not full rankings, should decide an upgrade or a baseline.

Frontline Demonstrations also recorded consistently higher benefit-cost ratios than farmers’ practices, confirming the economic viability of the improved production packages. Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23000728
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
With this dataset, we benchmarked random forest, XGBoost, convolutional neural network (CNN), and Transformer classifiers using Raman spectra from six wound-associated bacterial species and five Staphylococcus aureus/Pseudomonas aeruginosa mixture ratios. Unsupervised dimensionality reduction showed substantial overlap among classes. The CNN achieved the highest clean-test accuracy for species identification (98.74%) and mixture-ratio classification (97.04%) and remained stable after synthetic white-noise perturbation; all models showed less than 0.5 percentage-point degradation, and noise-augmented retraining improved performance. These results establish a reproducible benchmark for supervised analysis of Raman bacterial spectra and show that mixture ratios can be discriminated in laboratory-prepared samples. The dataset, trained models, and preprocessing code are openly available to support validation on more complex mixtures and clinical wound specimens and can be found here: https://github.com/Tissue-Engineering-BioImaging-Lab/ML-Benchmark-for-Species-Identification-and-Polymicrobial-Mixture-Quantification/tree/main

#17 [paper] Machine Learning-based Ground Motion Prediction Models for Indonesia: A Performance Evaluation of XGBoost and Random Forest Against Conventional GMPE
Authors: Rayhan Irfan Hielmy, Edy Santoso, Muzli Muzli, Sigit Pramono, Setyoajie Prayoedhie
Venue: Jurnal Meteorologi dan Geofisika
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.31172/jmg.v27i1.1233
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Accurate ground motion prediction is critical for seismic hazard mitigation in Indonesia, a region characterized by complex tectonic settings. Conventional Ground Motion Prediction Equations (GMPEs) often struggle to capture the non-linear attenuation characteristics of local seismicity. This study develops national-scale Machine Learning (ML) models—specifically XGBoost and Random Forest (RF)—to predict Peak Ground Acceleration (PGA) and benchmarks them against the widely used Zhao et al. [23] model. The dataset comprises 20,287 strong-motion records from 1,573 events (M 1.6–7.9) recorded by 667 stations across Indonesia between January 2023 and April 2025. Performance evaluation reveals that the XGBoost model outperforms both RF and the conventional GMPE, achieving the lowest Mean Squared Error (MSE) of 0.8885. In contrast, the conventional model showed less reliability with a significantly higher MSE of 1.5905. Feature importance analysis indicates that hypocentral distance and magnitude are the dominant predictors, while site condition (Vs30) plays a secondary role. Validation on independent test sets and recent significant seismic events confirms the model's robust generalization capability compared to conventional approaches. These findings demonstrate that ML-based approaches provide a more reliable alternative for estimating ground motion in Indonesia, offering significant potential for improving early warning systems and hazard maps.

#19 [paper] Machine Learning-Enhanced Generic Raman Model for Commercial-Scale Cell Culture Process Monitoring.
Authors: Shen, Yunfei, Wan, Yuxiang, Wu, Sijun, Yan, Xu, Chen, Hang, Chen, Zhenhua, Wang, Haibin, Qu, Haibin
Venue: Biotechnology journal
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42764603/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Continuous monitoring of therapeutic cell cultures via Raman spectroscopy traditionally relies on product-specific calibration models, which often fail to generalize across diverse commercial processes when process parameter or cell lines change. To overcome the need for extensive recalibration, an integrated generic Raman modeling framework was developed by aggregating in-line spectra from four distinct 1500-L commercial Chinese hamster ovary fed-batch processes. Fifteen combinations of regression algorithms and feature selection strategies were first evaluated under sample-level splitting, and representative pipelines were subsequently assessed through repeated batch-level validation splits. A Support Vector Machine combined with the interval whale optimization algorithm demonstrated competitive performance on validation and test sets. The model achieved high prediction accuracy for glucose, lactate, and viable cell density, with R2 values exceeding 0.94 and low prediction errors observed on the independent test set. Shapley Additive Explanations and permutation importance analyses indicated that the retained intervals were consistent with chemically plausible vibrational regions. Transfer to a fifth unseen commercial process further demonstrated the applicability limits of the global model and the potential of local updating with limited labeled spectra. The integration of machine learning algorithms and feature selection provides a practical strategy for multiproduct Raman PAT development in commercial biopharmaceutical manufacturing.

#1 [paper] Comment on egusphere-2026-5844
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5194/egusphere-2026-5844-rc2
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Providing seasonal ocean forecasts for the Northeast Pacific to support marine resource management and ecosystem variability assessment.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A seasonal ocean forecasting system based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model, forced by GFDL-SPEAR global climate forecasts, with a ~10 km horizontal re…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Northeast Pacific region extending from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea; evaluation uses a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months, assessed against ocean reanalyses and in situ observations.
Abstract:
Abstract. Seasonal ocean forecasts offer critical insights for marine resource management, particularly in regions like the Northeast Pacific where ecosystem variability can have profound impacts on marine life, fisheries, and coastal communities. Under NOAA’s Changing Ecosystems and Fisheries Initiative, we developed a seasonal ocean forecasting system for the Northeast Pacific based on the Modular Ocean Model version 6 (MOM6) ocean model coupled to the Sea Ice Simulator version 2 (SIS2) sea ice model and the Carbon, Ocean Biogeochemistry, and Lower Trophics (COBALT) biogeochemical model. The model domain extends from south of Baja California to the Chukchi Sea with ~10 km horizontal resolution. To evaluate forecast skill, we produced a 32-year set of retrospective forecasts with 10 ensemble members, four initializations per year, and lead times up to 12 months. Forcing for the forecasts was derived from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory's Seamless System for Prediction and Earth System Research (GFDL-SPEAR) global climate forecast system. Forecasts were assessed using ocean reanalyses and in situ observations, focusing on three ecologically- and societally-relevant variables: sea surface temperature, bottom temperature, and bottom oxygen concentration. Forecast skill varies by region, variable, and season, but generally remains high (anomaly correlation coefficient; ACC>0.5) for lead times of at least several months across all variables and regions. The downscaled forecasts reduce errors relative to the SPEAR global forecasts and in some cases increase ACC, while also enabling predictions of biogeochemical variables. These new forecasts compare favorably to previous downscaled ocean forecasts off the U.S. west coast, with increased ACC and small forecast errors that may be reduced further by future methodological changes. Routine real-time forecasts, available starting in October 2026, will support proactive decision making by managers, industry, and coastal communities.

Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). #3 [paper] Rethinking Marine Heatwaves: Towards a Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress
Authors: Natalija Dunić, Krešimir Ruić, Ivica Vilibić
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.22541/essoar.15011394/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Standard marine heatwave (MHW) definitions rely on statistical temperature anomalies relative to a climatological baseline, which does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences.
Method (Mycelium's reading): The Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Synthetic examples used to demonstrate the estimation of response functions from biological observations and the derivation of binary event definitions.
Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are commonly defined as statistically extreme temperature events relative to a climatological baseline. While this approach provides a consistent description of ocean temperature extremes, it does not directly account for the thermal exposure experienced by marine organisms or its biological consequences. Here, we propose the Probabilistic Marine Heat Stress Wave (PMHSW) framework, which shifts the focus from temperature anomalies toward biologically relevant thermal exposure. The framework integrates temperature exceedance above a biological threshold across time and depth to estimate cumulative thermal exposure and relates this exposure to the probability of a defined biological response. The probabilistic formulation allows differences among organisms, habitats and thermal tolerances to be represented while retaining a continuous description of biological heat stress. Using synthetic examples, we demonstrate how the response function can be estimated from biological observations and how a binary event definition can be obtained when needed. The PMHSW framework is intended as a complementary approach to existing MHW definitions, particularly when the objective is to assess the potential biological consequences of marine thermal extremes under present and future climate conditions.

Abstract:
Early-career researchers (ECRs) play a critical role in sustaining polar and cryosphere research in the United States. Since January 2025, changes in U.S. science policy and federal research funding have created substantial uncertainty for researchers, particularly those in the early stages of their careers. To assess the impacts of these changes, we conducted a community-driven survey of U.S.-based polar and cryosphere ECRs examining concerns related to science policy, research funding, career trajectories, and workforce retention. Survey responses indicate widespread concern regarding recent changes in science policy and funding, with many respondents reporting negative effects on research productivity, motivation, and mental well-being. At the same time, respondents identified potential pathways for retention, including stable research funding, mentorship, professional support, and reversal of recent funding reductions. These findings provide a timely assessment of workforce sentiment during a period of rapid policy change and highlight factors that may influence the future sustainability of the U.S. polar and cryospheric research community.

#7 [paper] Submesoscale feedback suppresses marine heatwaves.
Authors: Dong, Jihai, Sun, Wenjin, Fox-Kemper, Baylor, Jing, Zhiyou, Dong, Changming
Venue: Science advances
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42905811/

Abstract:
Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are devastating extreme ocean temperature events whose frequency and severity have surged under global warming, threatening marine ecosystems and fisheries. Yet, the fundamental mechanisms that control their intensity and persistence remain incompletely understood. Here, using a submesoscale-permitting global model simulation validated by long-term observational and reanalysis data, this study reveals a previously overlooked submesoscale feedback that exerts a critical control on MHW severity. It is demonstrated that the submesoscale-induced vertical heat flux suppresses the intensity and persistence of atmosphere-driven MHWs in winter via a negative feedback mechanism. Abstract:

Abstract:
Marine heatwaves are often characterized by sea surface temperatures derived from satellite data. Our results demonstrate that marine heatwaves in shelf seas can have substantial subsurface structure, even in a relatively shallow and seasonally well-mixed region. Sustained glider observations can provide key observations alongside satellite and reanalysis products, improving analysis and validation of subsurface temperature anomalies in shelf seas.

MHWs are detected across multiple depths (0.5–200 m) using a consistent percentile-based thresholding, applied to three reanalysis members (CGLORSv7, GLORYS2v4, ORAS5) and evaluated against well‑documented historical events. All reanalyses successfully capture the timing and general evolution of major, well-known surface expressions of MHW events when compared against the ESA Climate Change Initiative SST dataset in given areas of interest, such as, for example, events of 2011 in Western Australia, of 2015 in the Northeast Pacific Blob, and of 2006 in the Mediterranean Sea. Our results highlight both the value and limitations of current reanalyses for subsurface MHW characterisation, emphasising the need for ensemble‑based approaches to quantify uncertainty.

Abstract:
Abstract In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. #18 [paper] Heat transfer patterns of marine heatwaves with distinct vertical structures in the southwestern East Sea (Japan Sea)
Authors: Jae‐Heon Lee, Cheol-Ho Kim, Daeho Kim, Chang You-Soon
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11285976/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The processes associated with the distinct subsurface vertical structures of marine heatwaves (MHWs) with similar surface signals remain an open question, particularly regarding the components of oceanic forcing in the subsurface.
Method (Mycelium's reading): K-means clustering to categorize MHW vertical structures into four types (subsurface-intensified, deep, shallow, and subsurface-reversed), followed by a heat budget analysis decomposing lateral heat flux into dynamical (velocity anomaly) and thermodynamical (temperature anomaly) components.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Southwestern East Sea (Japan Sea), using detrended sea surface temperatures.
Abstract:
Abstract Recent studies have shown that marine heatwaves (MHWs) with similar surface signals can have distinct subsurface vertical structures; however, the processes associated with these differences remain an open question. MHW heat budgets have predominantly been examined at the mixed-layer scale, and the components of oceanic forcing in the subsurface have received less attention. We classified MHWs in the southwestern East Sea by their vertical structures and analyzed the associated heat transfer patterns. By applying K-means clustering to MHW events identified from detrended sea surface temperatures, we categorized the vertical structures into four types: subsurface-intensified, deep, shallow, and subsurface-reversed. We then analyzed the heat budget of each type by decomposing the lateral heat flux into dynamical (associated with velocity anomaly) and thermodynamical (associated with temperature anomaly) components. In the shallow type, the net surface heat flux term contributed most to the warming. In the subsurface-intensified and deep types, the dynamical component contributed more to the warming than the thermodynamical component, particularly in the subsurface-intensified type. In the subsurface layer, however, the thermodynamical component exerted a cooling effect, partially offsetting the dynamical warming. This study demonstrates that the dynamical and thermodynamical contributions to the lateral heat flux vary substantially among MHW types.

#19 [paper] Recent extreme heatwaves are no match for future events
Authors: Philipp Aglas-Leitner, S. Perkins-Kirkpatrick, Lukas Brunner, S. Undorf, F. Aglas-Leitner, E. Fischer, D. Stone
Venue: Nature Communications
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76809-5
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract In recent years, record-breaking heatwaves have occurred over many regions of the Earth causing serious impacts to human and natural systems. Here we show that recently observed exceptional heatwaves are no match to potential future 21 st century events based on multiple metrics. For several observed heatwaves, this holds even under low- and medium-emissions scenarios. In a high- to very high-emissions future, many regions are projected to experience heatwaves that generate several times more cumulative heat and are many times longer (up to several months) than the observed heatwaves. Should the Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement not be implemented, in most regions a concerningly large proportion of projected heatwaves exceeds all analyzed heatwave characteristics at once. Our results underscore the crucial need for substantial emissions reduction and have important implications for adaptation measures, as a substantial proportion of projected heatwaves is well outside the recent lived experience.

#20 [paper] Vertical structure and evolution of large-scale subsurface marine heatwaves
Authors: Shujing Zhang, Neil J. Holbrook, Alex Sen Gupta, Annie Foppert, Zijie Zhao
Venue: npj Climate and Atmospheric Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01592-5
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The vertical structure and evolution of large-scale subsurface marine heatwaves (MHWs) are poorly understood due to sparse long-record subsurface observations and a lack of globally consistent characterization frameworks.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A four-dimensional event-tracking framework applied to ocean temperature reanalysis data, utilizing depth rescaling and cluster analysis to identify vertical structure types.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Ocean temperature reanalysis data for the upper 1000 m of the near-global ocean (60°N–60°S) from 1993–2020.
Abstract:
Abstract Subsurface marine heatwaves (MHWs) represent hidden thermal extremes that can strongly impact marine ecosystems, particularly when they are large-scale and long-lasting. Although they evolve across time and space, their vertical structure and evolution remain poorly understood because of sparse long-record subsurface observations and the limited application of globally consistent frameworks to characterize them. Here we apply a four-dimensional event-tracking framework to ocean temperature reanalysis data to identify and characterize over 500 large-scale subsurface MHWs in the upper 1000 m of the near-global ocean (60°N–60°S) from 1993–2020. Occurrences are highest in equatorial regions and lowest in the subtropics. The framework captures extensive subsurface expressions of major events, including the northeast Pacific Blob, which penetrated hundreds of metres below the surface, and the Ningaloo Niño, whose subsurface structure extended beyond its traditionally defined surface footprint. Using depth rescaling and cluster analysis, we identify seven recurring vertical structure types, with five significantly associated with El Niño–Southern Oscillation phases. MHWs generally maintain their vertical structure for months to years, with limited propagation across the mixed layer and thermocline. Together, these findings link subsurface MHW evolution to large-scale climate variability and ocean stratification, providing a basis for improved detection and potential predictability.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems to harmonize omics-based and in-situ data with remote sensing, socio-ecological, and climatic data; design data integration approaches for predictive analytics and AI; and deliver FAIR data, harmonisation workfl…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

To address these challenges, proposals should:

- develop and validate fit-for-purpose multisensory biodiversity data integration systems, to enable omics-based and in-situ data harmonization and integration with remote sensing data from space or sub-orbital platforms, as well as socio-ecological and climatic data for enhancing assessment of ecosystem condition and degradation, and the predictive modelling of biodiversity trends at international, regional and European scales;

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. To this end, proposals should identify and prioritise critical biodiversity knowledge gaps and their data needs, with a focus on predictive analytics and the use of AI, and address them by designing data integration approaches that support scientific and policy needs, including biodiversity protection, restoration, and sustainable use goals and targets, as well as other related policy objectives;

- develop demonstration and verification cases focusing on specific ecosystems under the EU ecosystem typology[1] and habitats, including ecotones[2], identified as those under pressure or as restoration priorities. Proposals should take into account socio-economic pressures and activities impacting ecosystems, including land and sea use and emissions of pollutants (e.g. agriculture, aquaculture, urbanization, resource exploitation and management practices). Demonstration cases should be relevant to EO applications, such as AI-assisted ecosystem and habitat mapping, ensuring interoperability with European and global frameworks such as the Global Ecosystem Typology as well as EUNIS, and aligned with reporting requirements under the Habitats Directive, Birds Directive, Marine Strategy Framewor

#1 [paper] Hyperspectral remote sensing for harmful algal bloom detection: Pseudo-nitzschia in the Northeast Pacific.
Authors: Bailess, Alexander L, Baetge, Nicholas, Barnard, Andrew H, Tufillaro, Nicholas, Behrenfeld, Michael, Bill, Brian, Kudela, Raphael, Graff, Jason
Venue: Harmful algae
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/43020539/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The need for rapid, scalable identification of harmful algal blooms, specifically Pseudo-nitzschia, to manage marine resources, given that current in-situ point sampling methods are expensive and labor-intensive.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Culturing four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, measuring their hyperspectral absorption and backscatter, modeling spectral reflectances detectable by remote sensing platforms, and quantifying differences between taxonomic fingerprints using vector-based and stat…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including Pseudo-nitzschia, Thalassiosira, Chaetoceros, and Asterionellopsis.
Abstract:
Diatoms are microscopic marine algae that are critical for global primary production, carbon sequestration, and fisheries productivity. However, select diatoms may form harmful algal blooms, which threaten marine ecosystems and the fisheries they sustain. Rapidly identifying harmful blooms is necessary to effectively manage marine resources, yet current identification methods are limited by expensive and labor-intensive in-situ point sampling. Hyperspectral remote sensing enables scalable monitoring, but its ability to resolve taxonomic shifts within phytoplankton groups (e.g. diatoms) is largely unknown. To investigate this uncertainty, we cultured four dominant diatom genera from the California Current upwelling system, including this system's most abundant harmful algae, Pseudo-nitzschia. The hyperspectral absorption and backscatter of these taxa were measured and used to model spectral reflectances that remote sensing platforms (satellites/drones) might detect. Differences between fingerprints of these taxa were quantified using vector-based and statistical analyses. Mean spectral differences of 48% were observed between the most dominant diatom, Thalassiosira, and the most toxic diatom, Pseudo-nitzschia. Differences of approximately 30% were found between Pseudo-nitzschia and the second and third most abundant diatoms, Chaetoceros and Asterionellopsis. Successful identification of Pseudo-nitzschia's reflectance fingerprint was driven by the presence of a unique feature around 560 nm. The distinct spectral fingerprint of Pseudo-nitzschia indicates that it can be distinguished from other diatom blooms using hyperspectral remote sensing platforms.

#2 [paper] Global and National Dynamics of Scopus-Indexed Data Paper Publishing: A Bibliometric Analysis With Evidence From Ukraine
Authors: Павло Кузнєцов, Olha Biedunkova, Oleg Pinchuk
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11256137/v1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract This article examines the global evolution and national differentiation of Data Papers in the context of the development of open science, with a particular focus on Ukraine. The aim of the study was to determine the temporal dynamics, geographic and disciplinary distribution, major publishing platforms, and the characteristics of Ukraine’s positioning within the global research data publication landscape. The analysis was conducted based on Scopus data using the distinct “Data Paper” document type. Publications from 2014 to 2026 were analyzed on a global scale, and those from 2016 to 2026 were analyzed for Ukraine; subject areas, journals, open access models, and mechanisms for waiving publication fees were examined separately. An overall upward global trend in Data Papers was observed, with a peak annual figure of approximately 2,300 documents in 2024. At the same time, Ukrainian activity remains low in volume and volatile: only 57 documents were identified during the study period, with a maximum of 10 publications in 2022. Global publication activity is concentrated primarily in the United States, China, and leading European research systems. The Ukrainian landscape is characterized by a unique combination of computer science, mathematics, social sciences, management and analytics, and natural sciences. The results indicate that Ukraine is already integrated into the Data Paper segment; however, its trajectory differs significantly from the global one in terms of scale and stability. #3 [paper] Career Anxiety Among Students: Bibliometric Analysis of Scholarly Papers Published from 2016 to 2025
Authors: Tej Bahadur Karki
Venue: International Research Journal of MMC
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3126/irjmmc.v7i4.101373
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Career anxiety amongst students has emerged as a rather topical issue in the realm of psychology and education; however, at present, there is no comprehensive bibliometric analysis that would allow tracing the evolution of knowledge in this field. The purpose of this paper is to present the results of the bibliometric analysis of 525 peer-reviewed scientific papers on career anxiety amongst students, published freely in electronic form during 2016 – 2025. The search was carried out in the search engine Dimensions.ai using a search by title and abstract. The analysis was conducted taking into account the trends of publications and citations, subject areas, geographic distribution, institutional affiliation, and collaborative networks. It was found that the number of papers increased exponentially from 11 papers in 2017 to 168 papers in 2025, generating 1,550 citations in 2025. China has a considerable number of papers (61), but Poland, France, and the Netherlands have much greater impact per paper due to international collaboration. The Field-Weighted Citation Ratio decreased from 3.57 in 2018 to 1.46 in 2024, and only 33.33% of the papers in 2025 received citations, showing lower impact due to accelerated production. No institution published more than four papers, and there are no inter-institutional collaborations. There is a need in this area for creating international collaborations, bridging computing and economics disciplines, establishing research centers, and conducting research at different institutions in order to accumulate knowledge from the disjunctive output.

#4 [paper] Bibliometric Analysis of the 20-Year Transformation of Educational Technology Articles: A Case Study of the Journal of Theory and Practice in Education
Authors: ÖZDEN ŞAHİN İZMİRLİ, Asmin Murat, Tülay Akbıyık Koç, Giunai Abdulla Kyzy, Sarvinoz Abdinazarova, Ege İnal
Venue: Eğitimde Kuram ve Uygulama
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.17244/eku.1982476
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The purpose of this study is to examine papers in the field of educational technologies published in the Journal of Theory and Practice in Education (EKU) between 2005 and 2025. Using bibliometric analysis, it determines the journal's thematic, methodological, and sample-based publication trends. Seventy papers were identified through a manual systematic review, and citation counts, keyword patterns, study designs, and participant categories were analysed. RAWGraphs and VOSviewer software were then used to visualise the data. The results indicate that the journal underwent a period of rapid growth between 2013 and 2017, a hiatus in publication in 2021, and achieved publication consistency after 2022. Keyword analyses revealed clusters centred on technology, distance education, virtual reality, and multimedia. However, the study reveals a relative scarcity of cross-disciplinary integration. From a methodological perspective, qualitative and quantitative studies were shown to occur with similar frequency, while mixed designs remained relatively limited. Participants were primarily pre-service teachers. This study reveals the 20-year evolution of the EKU Journal in the field of educational technologies and provides evidence-based guidance for editors and researchers.

#5 [paper] New visual culture of science: analysis of graphical abstracts in the life science journal “Cell”
Authors: Kana Ariga
Venue: History & Philosophy of the Life Sciences
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40656-026-00763-0
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Driven by the shift towards online journal publishing, many academic journals have introduced graphical abstracts (GAs) since the 2000s to convey the primary findings of research papers. This study investigated this visual culture in life sciences by analyzing GAs with focus on content, representation, and background. In total, 333 GAs were collected from articles published in the journal Cell in 2021 and analyzed. Among these, 295 GAs (88.6%) explained the results and models and succinctly presented the key findings, and 251 GAs (75.4%) used a layout that divided the area into two or more sections. New graphics that were not present in the main text were featured in 222 GAs (66.7%), indicating substantial investment in their creation. The GAs shared commonalities with modern infographics commonly seen on the internet, which emphasize clarity. The increased used of GAs may be attributed to the need for "instant comprehension," which is an epistemic virtue reinforced by authors, readers, and journals and driven by the scientific self of "surviving researchers and journals" in a competitive scientific environment.

#6 [paper] Journal of Argumentation in Context
Authors: Menno H. Reijven
Venue: Journal of Argumentation in Context
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1075/jaic
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The Journal of Argumentation in Context aims to publish high-quality papers about the role of argumentation in the various kinds of argumentative practices that have come into being in social life. These practices include, for instance, political, legal, medical, financial, commercial, academic, educational, problem-solving, and interpersonal communication. In all cases certain aspects of such practices will be analyzed from the perspective of argumentation theory with a view of gaining a better understanding of certain vital characteristics of these practices. This means that the journal has an empirical orientation and concentrates on real-life argumentation but is at the same time out to publish only papers that are informed by relevant insights from argumentation theory. These papers may also report on case studies concerning specific argumentative speech events. The journal aims to attract authors from various kinds of disciplinary background who are interested in studying argumentative practices in their fields of interest. In all cases, in papers published in the journal an interesting and revealing connection should be established between certain insights from argumentation theory and some particular context of argumentative practice.

#7 [paper] High Article Processing Charges and the Expansion of Predatory Publishing in the Generative AI Era: Implications for Research Integrity and Global Scholarly Inclusion
Authors: A. O. Alli
Venue: Research Square
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-11540134/v1
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The intersection of high article processing charges (APCs), generative AI-driven publication pressures, and the expansion of predatory publishing, and their impact on research integrity and global scholarly inclusion.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A critical review based on a purposive selection of interdisciplinary literature in scholarly communication, higher education, information science, research ethics, and science policy, utilizing reference snowballing and thematic relevance.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Interdisciplinary literature in scholarly communication, higher education, information science, research ethics, and science policy.
Abstract:
Abstract The transition to open access publishing was intended to democratize knowledge, yet the dominance of article processing charge models has created new financial stratifications that disproportionately affect researchers in low- and middle-income countries. Concurrently, generative artificial intelligence has lowered barriers to manuscript production while amplifying editorial overload and predatory publishing vulnerabilities. This critical review examines the interconnected dynamics among article processing charge inflation, generative artificial intelligence-driven publication pressures, predatory publishing expansion, and global scholarly inequality, with alignment to Sustainable Development Goals 4, 9, 10, 16, and 17. The review is based on a purposive selection of interdisciplinary literature in scholarly communication, higher education, information science, research ethics, and science policy. Literature was selected through reference snowballing and thematic relevance to the five research objectives rather than systematic database searching. Findings indicate that global spending on article processing charges has escalated significantly, with average charges for high-impact journals exceeding several thousand United States dollars, creating conditions that increase susceptibility to predatory journals. Abstract:
AI in education is changing faster than conventional academic publishing can follow. A paper that takes a year to reach print may describe tools, policies and evidence that have already been superseded. This article describes an experiment in doing things differently. #13 [paper] The disclosure gap: why mandating AI transparency without protecting honesty is a leadership failure

Abstract:
Universities and journals have answered generative artificial intelligence (AI) with one main instrument: mandatory disclosure. Ask researchers to declare what they used, and transparency should follow. The evidence says it does not. Across 5,114 journals and 5.2 million papers, about 70% of journals now require disclosure, yet only around 0.1% of papers published since 2023 declare AI use, and journals with policies show no less AI adoption than journals without them. Submission data from two major publishers tell the same story: 5.7 and 3.3% disclosure, against surveys where between 28 and 76% of researchers say they use these tools. This Perspective argues that the gap is not a compliance failure to be fixed with firmer rules. It is what happens when institutions ask people to volunteer information that carries a real cost, and then do nothing about that cost. Experiments show that AI users are judged less competent and less motivated; researchers have named the effect AI shaming and the punishment of honesty. The paper argues that this cost falls unevenly, that the evidence on how it falls is messier than a simple centre-periphery story allows, and that the problem belongs to institutional leaders rather than journal editors. It sets out what owning it would mean.

The authors matched 72,644 bioRxiv preprints posted between 2018 and 2025 to their eventual journal-published versions by DOI, then used an LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to extract one primary and two secondary claims from each abstract and classify how much the content, claim type, and certainty shifted between the two versions. The main finding reported by the work is that most claims remain stable: 39.8% of primary claims in the preprints were unchanged in the published version, 50.0% underwent only minor revision, and just 10.2% saw major changes, meaning approximately 90% of claims stayed the same or shifted only slightly. #16 [paper] Signed and anonymous referee reports and AI-associated language in open peer review: a within-manuscript difference-in-differences study of Copernicus journals

Abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) are now used to write scientific papers and peer review reports. Corpus-level studies have estimated their footprint in abstracts (Kobak et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2025) and in reviews for machine learning conferences (Liang et al., 2024; Russo et al., 2025). Sharma et al. (2026) examined whether LLM-assisted reviews treat LLM-assisted papers differently and found that an apparent interaction disappears once paper quality is controlled. Publishers have responded with rules. The AI policy of Copernicus journals does not allow referees to have AI tools generate their comments or reports, allows assistance with language, and asks referees not to upload manuscripts or reports to AI tools (for example, Ocean Science AI policy). One proposed safeguard is open identity: a referee who signs a report is personally accountable for its content. Accountability theory predicts that identifiable people take more care over their judgements (Lerner and Tetlock, 1999), and signed reviews have long been studied for their quality, tone and recommendations (van Rooyen et al., 1999; Bravo et al., 2019; van Sambeek and Lakens, 2021). The same theory also predicts more attention to how one appears to an audience, and a named referee may have more reason to polish the language of a report. Signed and anonymous reviews have also been compared for tone in journals where referees choose to sign (Sahakyan and AlShebli, 2025). To our knowledge no study has compared AI-associated vocabulary in signed and anonymous referee reports (literature searches to 28 October 2026). Copernicus journals allow this comparison. Their interactive public discussion publishes every referee report, and each referee chooses whether to sign or to remain anonymous. Signed and anonymous reports therefore appear side by side on the same manuscripts, and this has been the case since well before ChatGPT was released on 30 November 2022 (Bornmann et al., 2010, used the same system to study peer review). Crossref holds structured metadata for every report, including the referee's recommendation and the link to the final article. The study compares, within the same manuscript, the change in AI-associated vocabulary between signed and anonymous referee reports from before to after the release of ChatGPT. Comparing reports on the same manuscript holds the manuscript, its quality, its topic and its authors constant. The measure is lexical: it captures LLM-styled text, which includes text generated, polished or translated with LLM tools, and it cannot tell these uses apart.

#17 [paper] From journal validation to quality governance: a policy analysis of India's transition from UGC-CARE to quality-oriented research assessment and its implications for medical and dental education

Abstract:
Background The University Grants Commission (UGC) announced the discontinuation of the UGC-CARE Reference List through a Public Notice dated 11 February 2025, following the Commission's decision taken at its 584th meeting on 3 October 2024, marking a major shift in India's approach to research quality governance. Introduced in 2019 to address predatory publishing, the UGC-CARE framework provided a centralized mechanism for identifying credible publication venues. The transition to quality-oriented research assessment emphasizing publication ethics, peer review integrity, editorial transparency, and institutional accountability has generated considerable debate, yet its implications for research integrity and health professions education remain insufficiently explored. Methods A narrative policy analysis was conducted using publicly available UGC policy documents, regulatory reports, international responsible research assessment frameworks, and peer reviewed literature. Guided by Walt and Gilson's Policy Analysis Triangle, the analysis examined the policy context, content, process, and key actors associated with India's transition from the UGC-CARE framework to quality-oriented research assessment. Evidence was synthesized into four thematic domains: journal quality governance, research integrity, stakeholder implications, and educational implications. Results The findings were organized into four thematic domains. First, the post-CARE framework reflects a transition from centralized journal vetting to decentralized quality governance. Second, greater emphasis is placed on researcher responsibility, institutional accountability, and publication literacy. Third, the reform has important implications for researchers, institutions, and research assessment practices. Fourth, it creates opportunities to strengthen publication ethics, journal evaluation, and responsible scholarly communication within medical and dental education. Based on these findings, publication literacy is proposed as a competency supporting competency-based medical education (CBME). Conclusions India's post-CARE reforms represent an evolution toward responsible research assessment and institutional accountability rather than a return to the pre-CARE era. Strengthening publication literacy, research integrity culture, and faculty development may support successful implementation of the emerging quality-oriented research assessment framework.

#21 [paper] Paper mill or paper mine? A tentative answer to the sharp increase in research papers based on the Global Burden of Disease database.
Authors: Degen, Peter Methys, Riebler, Andrea, Held, Leonhard
Venue: Journal of clinical epidemiology
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42624337/

Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Recent studies have raised concerns arising from the exploitation ("mining") of public health databases for low-quality, mass-produced papers. However, it remains challenging to disambiguate whether such papers originate from paper mills (commercial entities that sell authorships on mass-produced papers) or from the uncoordinated action of individuals facilitated by AI tools and templated workflows. Our study aims to address this question for one particular database, the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD). We selected this database after noticing that one of our papers on Bayesian age-period-cohort models has recently been experiencing a rapid surge in geographically clustered citations from GBD papers with Chinese affiliations. METHODS: We collected bibliometric and article-level metadata from GBD papers to search for indicators of mass-produced research. Moreover, we assessed 713 full-text articles for reported R versions, availability of code and data, and declaration of generative AI use. For 180 articles, we qualitatively screened the figures for graphical similarities. Finally, we conducted an exploratory scoping investigation of online platforms (social media sites, vendor websites) dedicated to do-it-yourself workflows for secondary analyses of public health data. RESULTS: Although we cannot rule out paper mill involvement, our findings suggest that the geographically clustered increase in GBD publications from China is at least partially driven by independent authors. The wide variety of R versions listed in 477 articles points against centralized paper production. Moreover, despite broad graphical similarities in figure styles that suggest the use of shared visualization tools, substantial variation in ancillary details suggest independent authors finalizing figures. This is corroborated by the identification of an online ecosystem of proprietary tools and services specializing in streamlined do-it-yourself workflows for conducting, writing, and publishing secondary analyses of public health data. CONCLUSION: Appropriate efforts should be directed towards evaluating the quality of the identified workflows. Stakeholders in scientific integrity should monitor online platforms dedicated to the rapid production of papers, especially in light of the increasing focus on AI-assisted workflows. Code sharing should be mandated for data-driven secondary analyses. Paywalls and proprietary software licenses hinder transparency and reusability, underscoring the importance of free and open-source software for trustworthy and reproducible research.

Abstract:
The article provides a comprehensive analysis of the problem of the mandatory publication of scientific results in journals indexed in the international scientometric databases Scopus and Web of Science, in the context of modern Ukrainian scientific discourse. The relevance of the study is due to the fact that these databases are increasingly perceived not only as a tool for integrating Ukrainian science into the global academic space, increasing the visibility of research results and ensuring certain quality standards, but also as a de facto mandatory condition for a scientific career, certification, accreditation of educational programs and defense of dissertations. Under such conditions, bibliometric indicators often begin to replace a substantive assessment of scientific novelty, methodological soundness and social significance of research, and publication activity itself becomes an end in itself. The paper proves that the problem of mandatory publication in Scopus and Web of Science cannot be considered only as a technical or administrative issue. It has a deep theoretical, methodological, institutional and ethical dimension. On the one hand, international indexing contributes to the openness of science, its inclusion in global communication networks, increased citations and dissemination of research results. On the other hand, excessive formalization of publication requirements creates risks of commodification of knowledge, when a scientific result is evaluated not so much by its truth, novelty or benefit to society, but by its ability to meet market and bureaucratic criteria. This, in turn, contributes to the spread of practices of academic capitalism, the emergence of a shadow market for intermediary services, as well as the intensification of the activities of so-called "predatory" publications that imitate scientific communication without proper peer review and compliance with ethical standards. Particular attention is paid to the methodological imbalance in the assessment of science. It is shown that a unified approach, based mainly on quantitative metrics - the number of publications, citations, Hirsch index, impact factor of journals, grant funding amounts - does not take into account the specifics of individual fields of knowledge. First of all, this applies to socio-humanitarian, artistic and some social disciplines, which are characterized by local issues, national and cultural conditioning of the subject, the importance of Ukrainian studies discourse and the need to use national languages ​​and professional publications. In such cases, focusing exclusively on English-language international journals is not always methodologically justified, and sometimes even narrows the possibilities of fully presenting research results that are important for national security, cultural identity and development of the state. The article also analyzes the institutional consequences of the introduction of strict requirements for publications in Scopus/WoS. It is established that the transformation of publication from a tool of scientific communication into a formal bureaucratic marker leads to a distortion of researchers' motivation, increased publication pressure, fragmentation of results, an increase in the number of formal or insignificant articles, as well as inefficient spending of budgetary and private funds. For many scientists, especially young researchers, postgraduate students and teachers, such a system creates additional barriers to reach academic recognition, forcing them to adapt to formal criteria that do not always adequately reflect the real scientific value of the work. Emphasis is placed on the financial pressures that accompany the modern publishing model. The text emphasizes that significant author's fees for publication in international journals, long review periods, as well as limited deadlines for the completion of scientific topics create unequal conditions for Ukrainian researchers. #6 [paper] Autonomy without immunity: conventionality control and the limits of sporting sovereignty in the Inter-American system
Authors: Roberto Leonardo Cruz-Núñez, Hugo Armando Aguilar Brito, Andherson Jhordan Aguirre-Lanegra, Nuccia Seminario-Hurtado
Venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fspor.2026.1949642
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Professional athletes and clubs can compete only if they accept the jurisdiction of an arbitral tribunal seated outside their own country. International federations rely on that arrangement to claim immunity from judicial review; this article calls that claim sporting sovereignty. European courts have narrowed it by holding that compulsory sports arbitration must satisfy fair-trial guarantees, but protection there still depends on the courts of the state where the federation is seated and on a narrow reading of public policy, so the substance of a discrimination complaint may go unexamined. This article asks how far Articles 8 and 25 of the American Convention on Human Rights limit the rule-making authority of transnational sports organisations in states parties, through conventionality control, the duty of every domestic authority to test the rules it applies against the treaty. It proceeds by doctrinal legal analysis and by comparing the European and Inter-American standards of review, and it examines four jurisdictions: Peru, Colombia, Chile and Brazil. Inter-American judicial guarantees attach to the function a body exercises rather than to its formal character; they reach private power through the state's duty to ensure rights; and every domestic authority must apply them of its own motion, wherever the federation is seated. The comparison shows that Brazil and Chile channel contractual and employment disputes between player and club to the state courts, and that Colombia protects players through the constitutional action of tutela, so that closure is confined to disciplinary, eligibility and competition matters; Peru is the exception, having legislated the primacy of federation rules without such limits. In the Peruvian and Colombian cases examined, the delays that harmed a club and a player came from federation bodies overrunning their own deadlines, which undermines the argument that speed requires exemption from review. Sporting sovereignty is thus a delegated and conditioned authority. The article proposes a criterion of conditioned autonomy under which the power of federations is legitimate where it pursues a permissible aim, observes procedural guarantees, decides while a decision can still serve the person affected, and respects the substantive limit of human dignity and non-discrimination.

#13 [paper] Point-of-Care Ultrasound After Medical Screening Exam Reduces Time to Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy Diagnosis and Surgery
Authors: Victoria L. Morris, Michael Vu, Yongsu Lee, Evelyn Park, Ravi Soni, Ryan Walsh, Rachel Bower, John Waller-Delarosa
Venue: Western Journal of Emergency Medicine
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.53932
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction: Ectopic pregnancy remains the leading cause of first-trimester maternal mortality. Delays in diagnosis and operative management increase morbidity and may be exacerbated by emergency department (ED) crowding. We evaluated whether integration of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) into the medical screening exam of pregnant patients—the obstetric medical screening exam—was associated with improved timeliness of care for patients with surgically managed ectopic pregnancy. Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of adult patients undergoing operative management for ruptured ectopic pregnancy between January 1, 2019, and December 31, 2023, at a county safety-net hospital. The obstetric screening exam was implemented July 12, 2021, and incorporated focused transabdominal pelvic and right upper quadrant ultrasound into the initial ED evaluation, often prior to bed assignment. The primary outcome was time from ED arrival to operating room (OR). Secondary outcomes included time to obstetric consultation, time to hospital admission, ED length of stay (LOS), and POCUS use. Nonparametric testing was used for skewed time data. Logistic regression evaluated the odds of reaching the OR within four hours. Patient-level interrupted time series analysis assessed temporal trends. Results: A total of 150 patients were included (87 pre- and 63 post-implementation). Median arrival-to-OR time decreased from 516 minutes (interquartile range [IQR] 324–709.5) to 391 minutes (IQR 220–619), a 125-minute reduction (P = .020; bootstrap 95% CI, 8–233). The proportion of patients reaching the OR within four hours increased from 16.1% to 31.8% (odds ratio 2.42; 95% CI, 1.11–5.29; P = .02). Time to obstetric consultation (210 vs 146 minutes; P = .003), time to hospital admission (345 vs 250 minutes; P = .005), and ED LOS (451 vs 367 minutes; P = .03) were all reduced. Point-of-care ultrasound use increased from 41.4% to 66.7% (P < .001), while the remainder underwent radiology ultrasound. Interrupted time series analysis demonstrated no significant immediate change after implementation (P = .790), but a significant postintervention trend toward reduced arrival-to-OR time (−0.45 minutes/day, P = .01). Conclusion: Embedding POCUS into the medical screening examination in triage was associated with sustained improvement in operative timeliness for ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Early diagnostic integration within ED workflow may mitigate system-level delays in time-sensitive obstetric emergencies.

#14 [paper] Generating ACGME-constraint-aware surgery residency call schedule software with the assistance of agentic coding large language models

Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s44186-026-00601-8

Abstract:
Abstract Background Manual creation of a surgery residency call schedule is a labor-intensive process that adds to the administrative burden of a chief resident while often producing suboptimal fairness and work distribution. While commercial scheduling software exists, many programs struggle with inflexibility, high costs, and an inability to accommodate program-specific constraints. Methods We developed a scheduling software platform using AI-assisted development tools (Codex, Claude Code), both commercially available agentic coding environments. The system applies a rule-based, weekend-first assignment hierarchy with randomized tie-breaking under a search budget fixed in advance, then performs iterative weekday assignment, accommodating vacation requests and discrete call-shift swapping. The validation roster modeled a single general surgery residency program: 55 residents (32 categorical and 2 preliminary general surgery residents spanning PGY 1 through PGY 6; 20 off-service rotators from other programs; and 1 fellow) distributed across 10 call pools. Three prespecified call-related ACGME constraints were enforced (at least 4 days off per 28-day period, call no more frequently than every third night averaged over 4 weeks, and no consecutive 24-hour call). The 80-hour weekly maximum and the 24-hour period free of all clinical and educational responsibility were not evaluated, as both depend on activity the call calendar does not capture. We evaluated the system with 100 independent full-year runs (July 1 to June 30), each generated end-to-end across all call pools and months under an independently randomized vacation distribution. Compliance and fairness were evaluated at the level of the individual call-pool month (service-month), the unit at which a monthly schedule is produced; fairness and workload metrics were computed across the program’s in-program surgery residents. Results We generated 12,000 service-month schedules over 100 independent full-year runs. 99.2% (11,906) satisfied all prespecified call-related constraints with no violations detected by the internal validation engine. Forty-five of the 100 full-year runs required no manual intervention in any service-month, and none required it in more than 4 of its 120. Manual review of 120 randomly selected service-months by two authors, without reference to the validator’s output, agreed with it in 120 of 120 cases. Monthly fairness, defined within each call pool and month as the range (maximum minus minimum) of call shifts or weekends assigned per resident, showed a shift range ≤ 1 in 65.4% of service-months (mean 1.84, SD 2.15) and perfect weekend equity (range = 0) in 42.5%, with 86.6% achieving a weekend range ≤ 1 (mean 0.71, SD 0.70). Mean full-year generation time was 108.8 s (SD 59.1). Residents averaged 18.65 weekends (SD 3.13) and 78.23 call days (SD 5.49) per year. Conclusions This automated scheduling system generates resident call schedules that satisfy the prespecified call-related ACGME constraints, optimizes fairness across multiple dimensions, accommodates complex vacation requirements, handles cross-pool coordination, and flags the service-months it cannot resolve within its search budget rather than emitting a non-compliant schedule. These results provide construct validity evidence that optimization algorithms combined with careful constraint specification can eliminate the great majority of the administrative burden of manual scheduling while improving schedule quality and equity.

#15 [paper] Just Another Manic Monday in the Call Center: When Equal Demand Does Not Produce Equal Service
Authors: Michael Douglas, Eric Kyper
Venue: Archives of Business Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.14738/abr.1410.12332
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Call centers ordinarily explain service-level variation through demand, service time, staffing, routing, and customer patience. Yet performance may also vary systematically by weekday even when workload is comparable. This study examines a Monday effect in operational data from a large U.S. insurance-service organization. The dataset contained 13,024 intraday records across 32 business days, 37 reporting queues, and 20 business groups. Because call counts were cumulative within day, the primary analysis used each queue’s final daily snapshot, producing 1,127 active queue-day observations. Monday service level averaged .658, compared with .715 on Tuesday, although log-transformed call volume did not differ significantly between the two days. Ordinary least squares models with queue-clustered standard errors showed that Monday remained associated with a 5.1-percentage-point reduction in service level after controlling for call volume, average handle time, and business-group fixed effects. The result persisted across all-weekday, logit-transformed, volume-threshold, nonboundary, weighted, paired-queue, and nonparametric sensitivity analyses. The findings distinguish workload effects from weekday effects and suggest that start-of-week operational frictions may impair service beyond what volume alone explains. Because staffing, schedule adherence, absence, backlog, and call-mix measures were unavailable, the analysis identifies a robust temporal pattern rather than a causal mechanism. The study contributes to service-operations research by treating weekday as an operational state variable and offers managers a focused diagnostic agenda for Monday readiness.

#17 [paper] Do Firms Expect the Deadline to Move? Expiry Dates, Repeated Extensions, and AI Decision-Makers in Japanese Corporate Tax Special Measures

Abstract:
Many tax incentives carry an expiry date. A deadline should pull investment forward into the final year before expiry (a time notch in the sense of Slemrod 2013). If a measure has been extended many times, however, firms may expect another extension, and the deadline may stop working as a deadline. The literature on time notches (Slemrod 2013; House and Shapiro 2008; Cashin and Unayama 2016) and the literature on transition policy (Kaplow 1986, 2003; Shaviro 2000) have developed separately. This study links them by asking whether the history of extensions changes the response to an expiry date. Study 1 uses the annual reports that the Minister of Finance submits to the Diet under the Act on Transparency of Special Tax Measures (2010). These reports give, for each corporate tax special measure, the number of corporations applying it and the amount applied, for fiscal years ending on or after 1 April 2011. Study 2 asks how large language models (LLMs), acting as managers of a small firm, respond to the same kind of deadline. As firms delegate tax and investment decisions to AI, the response to deadlines may change. Study 2 tests the prediction, registered in OSF pw5fz, that LLM agents follow what is written: they respond to the expiry date stated in the statute and ignore an extension history unless it is written in front of them.

The Pareto results show that long parking time (49.9%) and unloading schedule (41.1%) caused 91.0% of the delays. Based on FMEA, the highest Risk Priority Number (RPN) belongs to the absence of a joint arrival scheduling mechanism with receivers (336), followed by the absence of an estimated arrival notification procedure (168) and a standard maximum stopping time (120). Joint arrival scheduling with receivers should be the priority for improvement.

#20 [paper] The impact of personalized deadline reminders via Microsoft Teams and Moodle calendar on assignment submission and completion rates
Authors: Ahmad Alfailakawi, Abdulaziz Alenizi
Venue: Frontiers in Education
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943550
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Objectives This study investigated the effectiveness of two digital deadline reminder strategies—a researcher-authored, friendly-toned announcement delivered through Microsoft Teams and a standard automated calendar/email notification generated by Moodle—compared with a control condition receiving no additional reminders. The study examined differences in on-time assignment submission rates and average submission delays among higher education students. Methodology An A/B/C comparative design with random assignment was employed involving 138 male and female students enrolled in the Introduction to Educational Technology course at the College of Basic Education in Kuwait during the second semester of the 2024–2025 academic year. Participants were allocated equally to three groups: a researcher-authored Microsoft Teams reminder group, an automated Moodle reminder group, and a control group. Five assignments were monitored over a ten-week intervention period, and submission data were obtained from Moodle activity logs. Results Statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups. Students receiving researcher-authored, friendly-toned reminders through Microsoft Teams demonstrated the highest mean on-time submission rate (94.22%) and the shortest mean submission delay (5.18 h). Students receiving automated Moodle reminders recorded an on-time submission rate of 85.65% and an average delay of 15.45 h, while the control group recorded 75.22% and 30.89 h, respectively. The effect sizes were substantial ( η 2 = 0.289 for on-time submission and η 2 = 0.639 for submission delay), although the latter estimate requires cautious interpretation because of the distributional characteristics of the delay variable. Conclusion The findings suggest that proactive digital reminder strategies can support students’ adherence to assignment deadlines. The researcher-authored, friendly-toned reminder strategy delivered through Microsoft Teams was associated with more favorable submission outcomes than the default automated Moodle reminder strategy. However, because the interventions differed simultaneously in communication platform, message content, authorship, and delivery format, the observed differences cannot be attributed to platform characteristics alone. The findings highlight the potential importance of reminder design and delivery practices while emphasizing the need for future research that independently examines the contributions of individual reminder components.
