#1 [paper] Public knowledge of plastic-related chemical risks and intention to reduce exposure: a secondary analysis of an international randomized controlled trial
Authors: Danya Sandler, Rivka Green, Carly Goodman, Christine Till, Bruce Lanphear
Venue: BMC Public Health
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-29140-z
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Background Endocrine-disrupting chemicals in plastics are linked to earlier puberty, adverse birth outcomes, and reduced cognitive function, yet public awareness of these risks remains low. We examined whether a brief educational video could increase knowledge about plastic-related hazards and intention to reduce plastic use. Methods This secondary analysis draws from a parallel-group randomized controlled trial [1] in which 15 761 participants aged 18–45 were recruited from Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, India, and Australia via CloudResearch's Prime Panels®. After completing baseline demographic and knowledge measures, participants were randomly assigned to watch a 7-minute educational video about toxic chemicals and neurodevelopment (n = 9135) or to view a blank screen (n = 6626). Immediate outcomes included three plastic-related knowledge items and one behavioural intention item assessing their likelihood of reducing plastic use in the next month. Following exclusions, 12 818 participants were included in analyses (intervention: n = 6427; control: n = 6391). Six weeks later, 3879 participants completed a follow-up assessing prevention attitudes and self-reported behaviour change. Results Participants who viewed the video were significantly more likely to report that plastics are harmful, disrupt hormone activity, and affect children’s cognitive development (rank-biserial r = .34–.38, all p < .001). They also reported greater intention to reduce plastic compared with controls (51% vs. 44.8%, (rank-biserial r = .06, p < .001). Intention was most strongly predicted by the belief that plastic chemicals disrupt hormone activity (OR = 1.99, p < .001). At six-week follow-up, higher baseline intention predicted greater self-reported reductions in plastic use (OR = 1.56, p < .001), with no significant difference by group. Effects varied across demographic subgroups, with stronger responses among participants in India, urban residents, South Asian participants, those with higher education or fewer children, and right-leaning participants. Conclusions A brief educational video improved plastics-related knowledge and short-term intentions to reduce exposure. However, behaviour change at follow-up was more strongly associated with baseline intention than with intervention status, highlighting the role of motivation and contextual factors in sustained behaviour change. Future interventions should consider baseline motivation and structural barriers alongside educational content.

#2 [paper] Selecting Materials Outreach Topics from Community Repair Demand: Organizational Weighting, Temporal Transfer and Local Fit
Authors: Chahn Yong Jung
Venue: Journal of Materials Education (Electronic)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.71448/jme2026346
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Community repair events bring materials science into contact with familiar products, but outreach teams must decide which objects deserve limited preparation time. This study evaluates topic selection under two representation rules: equal influence for each recorded repair attempt and equal influence for each repair group. The Open Repair Alliance collection contains 48,669 attempts. Selection used 17,805 attempts from 95 groups, followed by evaluation on 18,802 attempts from 126 groups. The four topics selected by attempt weighting were laptops, lamps, separate audio equipment and coffee makers. Group weighting replaced the latter two with mobile phones and small kitchen appliances. Its selection-period advantage in average group coverage contracted from 3.09 to 0.43 percentage points in the following year. Network-stratified group resampling gave a 95% interval of −1.29 to 2.28 points for that contrast, while attempt coverage decreased by 3.27 points. Local differences had opposing signs: 58 groups gained coverage, 63 lost coverage and five were unchanged. Resampling the selection groups recovered the complete topic sets in only 19.28% and 35.84% of draws. Increasing the kit to eight topics made the two rules select identical categories; ten topics were needed to exceed one-half of average group demand. These results establish the consequences of representation choices without attributing learning gains to category matching. A shared materials kit therefore requires an explicit intended beneficiary, host-specific preparation and an educational assessment independent of repair completion.

#3 [paper] Developing the Styrofoam Systems Education Model (SSEM): An Integrative Critical Review and Conceptual Framework for Mitigating Polystyrene Foam Pollution
Authors: Leo C. Osuji, Rosemary C. Ugonwa, Christiana Uzoaru Okorie, Nnennaya Kalu-Uche, Theresa Obiajulu Egbuchunam, Chisom C. Umeileka, Ozioma J. Anekwe-Nwekeaku
Venue: Asian Journal of Current Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.56557/ajocr/2026/v11i411197
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Background: Foamed polystyrene, widely known by the colloquial name Styrofoam, is a lightweight, low-cost material whose physical properties make it unusually prone to fragmentation, wind and water transport, and poor recovery once it escapes waste systems. Regulatory bans have expanded, yet the educational dimension of mitigation has received little systematic attention, and plastic-pollution education is rarely designed around the material-specific, life-cycle and behavioural features of a single problematic product class. Purpose and Scope: This integrative critical review examines environmental, health, life-cycle, policy, behavioural and educational evidence relevant to polystyrene foam, and uses the synthesis to develop a conceptual framework, the Styrofoam Systems Education Model. Approach: A critical narrative design was used, drawing on education, environmental science, behavioural science and policy literature identified through multidisciplinary scholarly indexes, institutional sources and citation chasing, with the final search completed on 27 July 2026. Principal Findings: Evidence that polystyrene foam fragments readily, carries hazardous additives such as brominated flame retardants, and resists economic recovery is comparatively strong. Evidence on human health risk from food-contact use is less conclusive, and comparative life cycle studies show that substitute materials are not automatically preferable. Insect-mediated and photochemical degradation findings are scientifically important but remain distant from field-scale remediation. Plastic-pollution education reliably improves knowledge, whereas effects on observed behaviour are weaker, frequently self-reported and seldom followed over time. Systems-thinking, life-cycle and action-competence research offers the most coherent theoretical foundation for education that addresses these gaps. Framework: The proposed model links five components, namely material literacy, life-cycle systems reasoning, evidence and uncertainty appraisal, action competence, and institutional and community coupling, and distinguishes relationships supported by empirical research from those that remain hypothesised. Implications and Unresolved Questions: The model offers a testable structure for curriculum design, teacher education and evaluation, but its effect on foam consumption and leakage has not been demonstrated. Conclusion: Education is best positioned as a complement to regulation, infrastructure and product redesign, and the model requires staged empirical validation across educational levels, sectors and socio-economic settings.

#4 [paper] An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
Authors: Borja Nogué-Algueró, Richard York, Stefano B. Longo, Ekaterina Chertkovskaya, Patrick Trent Greiner
Venue: Ecological Economics
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolecon.2026.109264
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This survey synthesizes insights from environmental social sciences to recast the plastics crisis as a structural feature of growth-dependent economies instead of a problem solvable by consumer choice or incremental technologies. Rather than a within-field review of ecological economics, it maps adjacent literatures to specify what this field could study and how, clarifying researchable questions, suitable methods, and tractable indicators. The synthesis foregrounds connections between expansionary political-economic dynamics, globally uneven socio-ecological burdens across the plastics life cycle, and the power and knowledge relations that shape what is produced, measured, and governed. It calls for comparative, mixed-methods, multi-scalar work and for open, standardized data on plastics flows to strengthen causal inference and comparability. Shifting attention upstream—from end-of-pipe fixes to the transformation of provisioning systems—the paper charts lines of inquiry capable of aligning social metabolism with biophysical limits and human needs, providing a roadmap for ecological economics to organize and accelerate research beyond consumer or techno-managerial framings.

Authors: Shengyan Xu
Venue: Mathematical Modeling and Algorithm Application

Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): transforming unstructured online DIY content into structured design knowledge for sustainable reuse
Method (Mycelium's reading): collecting unstructured data from the Internet, extracting key information through lightweight natural language processing, normalizing data into a unified model, and implementing a human-in-the-loop pipeline with interactive segmentation code linking material understanding to robot operations
Setting (Mycelium's reading): an unfinished prototype system designed for personal creativity support, maker education, and community recycling
Abstract:
This article investigates and explores the prototype of a material based project generation system, aiming to transform online DIY content into structured design knowledge for sustainable reuse. Based on an unfinished system developed by the author in his early years, this work reviews the methods of collecting unstructured data from the Internet, extracts key information through lightweight natural language processing, and normalizes it into a unified model suitable for automatic generation. Discussed baseline strategies for retrieving and editing project generation, as well as evaluation metrics that consider constraint satisfaction, feasibility, and user experience. The paper also investigates practical applications in personal creativity support, maker education, and community recycling, supported by initial human in the loop implementation and interactive segmentation code that links material understanding with basic robot operations. The challenges of multimodal alignment, richer constraint modeling, and robust dataset construction have been identified, highlighting opportunities for future integration with digital twins and automated assembly. Although the original system is still incomplete, the study concludes that a practical and impactful pipeline is achievable, demonstrating how artificial intelligence can help users recycle materials more effectively and contribute to sustainable, resource-saving designs.

#2 [paper] "Where the Money Goes: Institutional Distribution of NIH Funding Among Radiology Clinician-Scientists (2012-2025)".
Authors: Malhotra, Ajay, Kandala, Keervani, Tegtmeyer, Kyle, Gomez, Paul Timothy, Singhania, Siddhi, Wu, Xiao, Mohan, Suyash, Payabvash, Seyedmehdi
Venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42957078/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prior analyses of National Institutes of Health (NIH) funding to radiology departments have characterized aggregate grant volume and funding levels but have not systematically examined the institutional landscape of clinician-led research. This study characterized the institutional distribution of NIH funding awarded to clinician principal investigators (PIs) in diagnostic radiology (DR), interventional radiology (IR), and radiation oncology (RO) from fiscal years 2012 through 2025. METHODS: In this retrospective cross-sectional analysis, grant records were extracted from the NIH Research Portfolio Online Reporting Tools Expenditures and Results (RePORTER) database and filtered to PIs with an institutional department designation of "Radiation-Diagnostic/Oncology." Clinician investigators were identified by cross-referencing with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) datasets. Institutional funding, grant counts, unique investigators, grant mechanism portfolios, and career development awards were analyzed. RESULTS: A total of 437 unique clinician investigators (DR: 226; IR: 46; RO: 165) were identified, accounting for $1.65 billion in inflation-adjusted funding. NIH-funded clinicians were distributed across 47 institutions in DR, 29 in IR, and 45 in RO. The top five institutions accounted for 34.5% of grants and 38.4% of total funding, largely reflecting workforce size: institutional clinician PI count explained 82% of the variance in funding, and funding per clinician PI was more evenly distributed (Gini 0.38) than total funding (Gini 0.62). Stanford received the largest grant funding in DR ($134.9M), UC San Francisco in IR ($36.9M), and University of Michigan in RO ($68.1M). R01 awards were the dominant mechanism across all subspecialties. Forty new K-awards were issued across 21 institutions. CONCLUSIONS: NIH funding to radiology clinician investigators is concentrated at a small number of academic medical centers, principally because those centers host larger clinician investigator workforces, with a narrow clinician-scientist pipeline. These findings identify opportunities to broaden research capacity across the radiology workforce.

Abstract:
This Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) encourages grant applications for Animal and Biological Material Resource Centers. These Centers provide support for special colonies of laboratory animals and associated services, as well as other resources such as informatics tools, reagents, cultures (cells, tissues, and organs) and genetic stocks that serve the biomedical research community in a variety of research areas on a local, regional, and national basis. The goal of projects supported by this NOFO is to provide research resources that facilitate optimization and enhancement of scientific rigor, transparency, and experimental reproducibility of biomedical research. Proposed Animal and Biological Material Resource Centers must have broad application to multiple NIH Institutes or Centers (ICs) to align with the ORIP"s NIH-wide mission (https://orip.nih.gov/about-orip). This funding opportunity is designed to support both continuation of existing resources and to develop new ones when appropriate. Of special interest of the announcement is a requirement of the Center"s close coordination with efforts to develop new approach methodologies (NAMs) that complement traditional animal-based research. #6 [paper] Funding mechanisms as incentive systems: a role for science philanthropy
Authors: Lillian Parr, Nadia Sarfraz, Sylvina M. Raver, Nadia M. Penrod
Venue: Frontiers in Systems Biology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fsysb.2026.1939099
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Biomedical research is shaped not only by scientific questions, but also by the incentive structures that determine what scientists study, how they approach the work, and how success is defined. Current incentives often prioritize individual achievement as a pathway to career advancement, while undervaluing replication, data sharing, mentorship, collaboration, and shared infrastructure. This can make it challenging for scientists to prioritize these contributions, even when they recognize that they are essential for a strong scientific ecosystem. This article examines how funders and funding mechanisms create implicit incentives and argues that funding design is a powerful lever for shaping both scientific behavior and the broader research ecosystem. Philanthropy is uniquely positioned to experiment with funding design by supporting high-risk research, emerging areas, and investments in people, fields, norms, and shared infrastructure that other funders may be unable or unwilling to pursue, while also dedicating resources to learn from how these investments shape scientific behavior. Here, we highlight questions funders can ask about the incentives embedded in funding mechanisms, including what behaviors they encourage, who participates and benefits, and what persists beyond the award. For scientists, understanding funding goals, participating in evaluations, and making contributions beyond traditional outputs visible can strengthen the feedback between funding design and scientific practice. By treating funding mechanisms as design choices that can be tested and refined, philanthropy can generate evidence that informs future funding approaches and strengthens the scientific ecosystem.

Abstract:
This article provides an input–output-based estimate of the economic impact of U.S. federal laboratory licensing from 2011–2020. Federal laboratory earned royalty data are used to estimate licensed product sales. These estimated sales, plus federal laboratory license income data and Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) data on patterns of production and employment, are then used in the economic‑impact calculations of Gross Industry Output (GO), Gross Domestic Output (GDP) and jobs. Reported earned royalties on licensed product sales provide a clearly attributable, visible and quantitative estimate of the economic impact of federal laboratory research and industry-federal laboratory engagement, but an incomplete one. Because of the potential for missed sales, this article also provides GO, GDP and jobs multipliers per billion (2017) dollars of such sales. Reasons for unseen sales are explored and discussed. Persistent government and corporate commitments to fund research absent readily calculable near-term returns on investment are highlighted and discussed as evidence of a shared public-private belief in the future benefits of research that are not fully apparent at the time of research funding. Policy and legal frameworks which may lead to more technology transfer and more visible technology transfer are discussed.

Abstract:
Abstract The proposed scholarly and societal metrics reflect the output efficiency of extramural research funded by the US National Cancer Institute. The productivity of awards or investigators (AoIs) expressed as output COst INdexes (COINs) were calculated based on AoI-linked qualified research articles (qRA) published in single years that follow the AoI-funded years. The outputs for qualified years manifested as either qRA counts or sums of qRA-specific impact values were normalized by the total multi-year amount of funding and, for fractional metrics, by the number of the qRA funders and co-authors. Calculations of the basic (overall) COINs (B-COINs) included all qRAs while translational COINs (T-COINs) were based on a subset of qRAs cited by clinical practice guidelines published by major professional cancer associations. Higher B-COIN values were associated with Early Stage Investigator (ESI) group as compared to non-ESIs. The Outstanding Investigator designation correlated with B-COIN decrease. The highest T-COINs were associated with awards supporting late phase clinical trials, intermediate values noted for programs focused on early translation (SPOREs), followed by P01 and Research Project Grants (R01). #14 [paper] Feed-based delivery of plasmid DNA using milk-derived extracellular vesicle-polyethylenimine complexes enables hepatic transgene expression in goldfish
Authors: Qiwen Zheng, Hiu Mai, Wenliangyu Li, Shuisheng Li, Binbin Zheng
Venue: bioRxiv (Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.20.760587
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Oral administration through feed offers a non-invasive, cost-effective, and scalable approach for gene delivery in aquaculture. However, gastrointestinal degradation and intestinal barriers severely limit the oral delivery of plasmid DNA (pDNA). In this study, we developed a ternary nanocarrier composed of bovine milk-derived extracellular vesicles (MEVs), polyethylenimine (PEI), and pDNA (MPPs) to investigate its potential for functional gene delivery to the goldfish (Carassius auratus) liver (hepatopancreas). The resulting MPPs exhibited a relatively uniform particle size, high pDNA loading efficiency, and protection against nuclease-mediated degradation. Formulation optimization in HEK293T cells identified an MEV:PEI:pDNA mass ratio of 16.7:4.1:1, which supported robust EGFP reporter expression. Following oral administration of DiD-labeled MEVs through feed, fluorescence signals were detected in the goldfish hepatopancreas within 2 h and remained detectable at 6 h. After a single feeding of MPP-containing feed, hepatic luciferase mRNA expression peaked at 24 h and gradually declined to near-baseline levels by 72 h. During 14 consecutive days of feeding, luciferase protein expression was detectable from day 3, with progressively increased protein abundance and enzymatic activity observed on days 7 and 14. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of feed-based MPP administration for inducing functional transgene expression in the goldfish hepatopancreas, providing a promising foundation for developing non-invasive nucleic acid delivery strategies in aquaculture.

Authors: J. E. Naranjo Arroyave, Mike D Tokach, Jason C Woodworth, Joel M DeRouchey, Robert D Goodband, Katelyn N. Gaffield, Jordan T Gebhardt, Jorge Estrada

Abstract:
This experiment was conducted in a commercial research facility to validate the results of a previous study conducted at Kansas State University swine facilities that observed no difference in overall growth performance, but better economic outcomes, when the feed budgets for the more complex diets (phases 1 and 2) were reduced and the simple diet (phase 3) budget increased. A total of 1,170 pigs (initially 12.5 ± 0.70 lb) were randomly assigned to one of three nursery phase feeding budgets under a randomized complete block design. There were 26 pigs per pen and 15 pens per treatment. The feed budgets for high, medium, and low programs were 4, 2, and 0 lb/pig for phase 1 and 12, 8, and 4 lb/pig for phase 2, respectively. All pigs were then fed common phase 3 and 4 diets thereafter. Phase 1 was formulated with specialty animal protein and lactose products and was formulated to contain 18.0% lactose with 16.3% soybean meal. In phase 2, specialty protein sources and the lactose level were reduced, with diets containing 7.2% lactose and 22.5% soybean meal. Phase 3 and 4 diets were corn-soybean meal-based with no specialty protein or lactose sources. Pigs were weighed and feed disappearance was measured on d 0, 7, 14, 21, 33, 42, and 63 to calculate ADG, ADFI, and F/G. Pigs fed the high-budget program tended (P < 0.10) to have increased ADG and ADFI during period 2 (d 14 to 33); however, by d 63, no differences between nursery budget programs were observed for any of the response criteria, removals, or mortality. Feed cost and feed cost per lb of gain decreased (P < 0.001) as the budget for phases 1 and 2 was reduced. Pigs fed the high-budget program had greater (P = 0.049) revenue than those fed the medium-budget program, with intermediate values observed in the low-budget program, which resulted in greater income over feed cost (IOFC; P = 0.004) for pigs fed the low-budget program compared with those fed the medium- or high-budget programs. Pigs fed the low-budget program had numerically lower fecal dry matter (DM) compared with pigs fed the medium- or high-budget programs. In conclusion, under commercial conditions, reducing the feed budget amounts of phases 1 and 2 of the nursery feeding program had minimal effects on pig growth performance and lowered feed cost and feed cost per unit of gain, resulting in greater IOFC.

Abstract:
Abstract Macro indicators of Research and Development (R&D) such as numbers of journal publications and citation rates, patents, impact factors, and R&D expenditures have become proxies for economic competitiveness. But quantifying relationships between macro-indicators and budgets supporting these indirect metrics of R&D are sparse, and some factors critical to the holistic university, such as expenditures on libraries, have been missed. We quantified post-1945 relationships between federal research and development (R&D) funding to large universities and individual university rankings and regional economic prosperity in the United States. Empirical data, substantiated by a principal component analysis of multiple additional university-specific factors, reveals that there are $21.34 of R&D expenditures for each $1 of library expenditures at 71 public universities; arts and humanities programs are a positive influence for acquiring R&D funds. University rankings for > 90 universities are also positively correlated to R&D expenditures. There is a $1:$264 ratio of state-wide R&D expenditures to state’s gross economic production ( R 2 = 0.86), and a $1:$59 ratio for a state’s per capita R&D expenditure vs. per capita income ( R 2 = 0.34). These empirical relationships can guide budget decisions. They support the conclusion that effective university R&D is fostered by a holistic framework espousing scholarship through research, teaching, and public service benefiting state-scale populations, and are currently at risk.

Abstract:
This publication introduces Funding as Research, a methodological framework for treating research funding opportunities, calls for proposals, and RFPs as external research-development specifications rather than solely as sources of financial support.The framework proposes a structured process through which an emerging research infrastructure can examine a funding opportunity, decompose its objectives and evaluation criteria, compare them with existing capabilities, identify methodological and technical gaps, define a new development phase, and document the resulting analysis as an independent open research object.The proposed workflow is:FUNDING SIGNAL → RFP ANALYSIS → FIT MATRIX → GAP ANALYSIS → PHASE DEVELOPMENT → OPEN PUBLICATION → APPLICATION / NON-APPLICATION → LEARNThe methodology is particularly relevant to emerging research areas involving AI accountability, agentic AI, AI safety, research provenance, institutional observation, digital evidence, citizen auditing, open science, interoperability, verification, and reproducible research infrastructure.The publication develops the concept of Funding as Research as an extension of Research Infrastructure Evolution. Under this approach, a funding call can function as an external maturity signal: its requirements may reveal existing capabilities, missing infrastructure components, implementation challenges, measurable development objectives, and potential future research questions.The framework does not require researchers to reshape their work artificially around a particular funder. Instead, funding criteria are treated as an external analytical reference. The resulting fit analysis may lead to a formal application, further research and infrastructure development before application, or a documented decision not to apply. All three outcomes can generate methodological learning.The approach also proposes that funding-analysis records can become persistent research objects containing the relevant RFP version, analytical criteria, fit matrix, identified gaps, proposed development roadmap, application decision, external response, and subsequent methodological learning. Repeated application of the methodology could therefore support the development of a longitudinal Funding & Research Infrastructure Alignment Corpus.In the context of AI accountability, the framework further explores how funding-driven research development can contribute to open infrastructure for AI identity, authorization, observation, evidence preservation, verification, cross-checking, and research provenance.References to external funding organizations, programs, or RFPs are used solely as analytical inputs. Their inclusion does not imply endorsement, partnership, eligibility, institutional validation, or funding commitment.The primary contribution of this publication is therefore methodological: it proposes that funding environments themselves can become observable components of research infrastructure evolution, providing structured signals for identifying where a research infrastructure currently stands, what it needs to develop next, and what evidence supports that development.

#1 [paper] Expert insight on the design, implementation, and monitoring of future community benefit funds within the energy transition
Authors: E. Boyle, A. Revez, Aoife Deane, B. Ó. Gallachóir
Venue: Discover Energy
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/0255d82aaededef457ac0966198f350485bcdc76
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Increasingly, citizen and public participation are considered central to achieving the energy transition to a low carbon future. Such participation has different dimensions in new energy infrastructure, in terms of both renewable energy installations and additional electricity grid developments. Participation includes active involvement in decision making, the ability to invest in developer-led projects, and capacity for community owned renewable energy projects. This also includes community benefit funding (CBF), whereby a local fund is established by the developer and provided to communities impacted by infrastructural developments. There is a growing body of experience with CBF, but it has not received much attention in the scientific literature. In addition, there is a paucity of analysis of the design, implementation, and evaluation of CBF schemes. This research intervention addresses this gap using a modified Delphi panel approach to explore areas of consensus and divergence on these dimensions of CBF programs. We bring together national and international experts on community benefit funding who work on key areas of relevance such as policy formation, strategy design, fund administration, and community development to deliberate on the role of CBF in supporting future developments towards energy system change. Abstract:

Abstract:

Results The findings show that donor agencies significantly shaped WEFH governance across six action situations: policy formulation, program design, resource allocation, inter-ministerial coordination, monitoring, and international policy alignment. While ministries maintained formal authority, donor funding and technical assistance influenced policy priorities, where programs were implemented, and resource distribution. Rules-in-use, particularly boundary, choice, and payoff rules, were redefined through donor conditions. Participation also remained asymmetric, with local governments and non-core ministries excluded from upstream decision-making. These interactions led to varying governance outcomes: improved coordination efficiency, enhanced attention to equity and inclusion, strengthened institutional capacity and policy alignment with frameworks. However, they also reinforced fragmentation, spatial inequities, accountability tensions, and sustainability challenges beyond donor project cycles. Discussion These findings show that donor-recipient interactions are not merely financing relationships, but governance mechanisms that shape decision-making, participation, resource allocation, reporting, and accountability in WEFH systems. Externally funded governance can create hybrid action situations in which formal state authority and donor practical leverage diverge. Strengthening WEFH governance therefore requires earlier inclusion of subnational actors in upstream decision-making, harmonized reporting systems across donors and ministries, equitable financing arrangements, and stronger alignment of donor support with national priorities and local realities.

Abstract:
The emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini is reshaping research, education, and industry. Recent workforce data indicate a widening gap between declining junior-level opportunities and rising demand for senior-level expertise, underscoring the urgent need to adapt undergraduate chemistry curricula to prepare students for an AI-enabled workforce. To address this challenge, we designed a series of Python-based laboratory experiments for General Chemistry that integrate generative AI with instructor guidance to enhance student learning. The modules focus on (1) using AI tools to support conceptual understanding, (2) applying AI-assisted coding for data visualization and analysis, and (3) introducing machine learning workflows to solve real-world chemistry problems. All activities are implemented in Google Colaboratory, a cloud-based programming platform now integrated with Gemini, which helps students, particularly those without prior programming experience, complete coding tasks with step-by-step instructor guidance. We compare student attitudes toward the use of AI and programming at the beginning and end of the semesters, observing a more positive attitude toward AI use and increased confidence in programming. To demonstrate scalability, three PhD graduate students, two of whom had no prior programming background, successfully led the laboratory sessions using these AI-supported materials, confirming that instructors across a wide range of computational skill levels can teach the experiments. This work demonstrates how generative AI can create more prosperous and equitable learning experiences, equipping students with transferable skills essential for research and industry careers, as well as the evolving STEM workforce.

#15 [paper] Embedding Responsible AI in a Technical Machine Learning Course
Authors: Stefania Zourlidou, Frank Hopfgartner
Venue: European Conference on e-Learning
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.34190/ecel.25.1.5151
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) courses in higher education usually emphasise mathematical foundations and algorithmic methods, while ethical and societal questions are often treated as separate or optional topics. This paper reports a small-scale practice-based evaluation of a blended design that embedded responsible AI within a Master’s-level ML and Data Mining course at a German university in winter semester 2025/26. The design combined fifteen on-campus lectures on core ML topics, including one lecture on fairness as a technical topic, fifteen optional weekly assignments discussed in tutorials, and an eight-module microlearning course on AI literacy and responsible AI. Completion of at least half of the microlearning and a mandatory practical assignment were required for exam eligibility. The study analyses an anonymous end-of-course survey, using only responses from students who explicitly consented to research use (n=35). Student perceptions were generally positive: 78% reported a good balance between theory and practice, 75% found the weekly assignments important for understanding, and 59% judged the microlearning to fit well with the on-campus lectures. For responsible AI, around two thirds reported greater confidence in identifying fairness issues, feeling better prepared to discuss ethics professionally, or perceiving ethics as integrated rather than added on. 75% intended to consider fairness and ethical implications in future ML projects, with no respondent disagreeing. Open responses suggested perceived transfer, with students naming hiring systems, facial recognition, student-risk prediction and credit or loan decision-making, and often using technical vocabulary such as training data, optimisation objectives and evaluation metrics. The paper does not claim causal impact, and findings should be interpreted in light of the small voluntary sample, the single-cohort single-institution setting, and the possibility of social-desirability bias on an end-of-course survey on ethics. Instead, it offers descriptive evidence that a lightweight microlearning layer, combined with a technical fairness lecture, can be a feasible way to connect technical ML learning with ethical reflection in practice. It also identifies revisions for the next iteration: reduce workload tension, add explicit ethical-reflection prompts to assignments, and include more practical coding work.

#16 [paper] Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
Authors: Elhocine Mansouri, Eiki Kimura, Masatoshi Koga, Keigo Arai
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/cecdb34a7d3e95180e270f1fb1888def6a606b1c
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.

#18 [paper] MIRA: Towards a General AI Scientist
Authors: Deep Principle
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21930641
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Artificial intelligence now reaches into much of scientific practice, yet a gap persists between systems that answer scientific questions and systems that advance science. Scientific discovery is not a single response but an iterative loop that runs from hypothesis generation through execution to interpretation, carried out under uncertainty and accountable to reproducible evidence. We present MIRA, an AI scientist tailored for the physical sciences, to operationalize this loop end to end. MIRA is organized as a squad of agents with different harnesses and tools that mirror how a human research team divides and coordinates its work. It frames research directions and mines the published literature and a team’s internal data to propose grounded, testable hypotheses; it executes pre- or user-defined simulation workflows on cloud compute infrastructure; and it drives physical experiments through our in-house automated laboratory, the AI Materials Factory, carrying a hypothesis from plan to bench. MIRA consolidates results into calibrated conclusions, states its uncertainty explicitly, and compiles each completed project into a persistent memory and a maintained scientific wiki, so that reasoning, provenance, and negative results remain available to later work. On two external benchmarks MIRA attains the highest score at the lowest cost per task among seven agents compared, and leads four of five task categories on a specialized drug-discovery suite, exceeding agents purpose-built for that domain. This report details MIRA’s architecture and stage-by-stage design, and demonstrates it across chemistry, materials, and energy as a generalist that accelerates research and discovery while remaining reliable and auditable.

#19 [paper] Machine Learning – Supported Pedagogy in Computer Engineering: A Proposed Framework for Learner Modeling, Adaptive Support, and Controlled Empirical Evaluation
Authors: Hillary Mae De Guzman
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23126049
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Students in Computer Engineering courses often progress unevenly across diverse subject areas, and instructors lack sufficient time to provide individual feedback.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A pedagogical framework that converts course records and learning-activity data into learner features, uses a lightweight predictive model to estimate mastery and flag students needing help, and employs a recommender to suggest targeted support activities for instructor review.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Computer Engineering courses involving programming, digital logic, mathematics, and hardware laboratories.
Abstract:
Computer Engineering courses combine programming, digital logic, mathematics, and hardware laboratories, so students often progress unevenly and instructors have little time for individual feedback. Machine Learning (ML) has recently been explored to predict student performance, personalize learning support, and provide scalable feedback. This paper presents the design of an ML-supported pedagogical framework in which course records and learning-activity data are converted into learner features, a lightweight predictive model estimates mastery and flags students who may need help, and a recommender suggests targeted support activities that the instructor reviews before use. Effectiveness is evaluated in a controlled comparison with conventional instruction using concept assessments, normalized learning gain, prediction quality, and fairness checks across student subgroups. Privacy, informed consent, human oversight, and verification of any generative-AI output are treated as hard constraints rather than optional features. The study is structured for validation in a real course and does not claim measured improvement until the experiments are completed.

#1 [paper] Data and code for: An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system for Mediterranean temperate reefs: forecasting climate-driven mortality under context-dependent local protection
Authors: Jairo Castro‐Gutiérrez, Mar Bosch‐Belmar, Francesco Paolo Mancuso, Sergio Dimarca, Mario Francesco Tantillo, Gianluca Sarà
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23476372
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Static conservation strategies are outpaced by accelerating marine heatwaves, threatening temperate reefs. There is a need for prospective tools that integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability and support climate-smart Marine Spatial Planning.
Method (Mycelium's reading): An explainable, policy-aware early-warning system using a rigorous modelling framework. It leverages historical mass mortality data (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk. The model is validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020) and uses interpretability methods to identify modulati…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Mediterranean coralligenous reefs, utilizing a historical record of mass mortality events from 1986 to 2020.
Abstract:
Accelerating marine heatwaves are outpacing static conservation strategies, threatening the functional integrity of temperate reefs globally. Implementing “climate-smart” Marine Spatial Planning requires moving beyond retrospective impact assessment toward prospective tools that can integrate local context to anticipate vulnerability. This study presents an explainable, policy-aware early warning system that leverages the most comprehensive historical record of mass mortality events (1986-2020) to forecast site-level risk in the Mediterranean coralligenous reefs. Using a rigorous modelling framework validated on independent prospective test data (2019-2020), the model achieves high forecasting skill (average precision = 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect and the baseline is 0.70) and maintains temporal robustness by simulating real-world forecasting across the historical record. Model interpretability indicates that macroclimatic thermal stress is modulated by local factors such as depth and spatial protection. For instance, each decade since marine protected area (MPA) designation corresponds to an estimated ~48% decrease in the odds of elevated mortality (95% CI: 17–72%) under high heat stress, although this modulating signal was statistically detectable primarily in the Western Mediterranean and does not imply absolute resistance against extreme thermal anomalies. By translating these complex, context-dependent predictions into equitable, subregion-balanced alerts through an open-access interactive decision-support platform, this study provides a practical forecasting tool blueprint to optimize monitoring surveys, guide proactive triage, and support climate-adaptive Marine Spatial Planning under accelerating ocean warming.

#2 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#3 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

#6 [paper] Performance of the Heatwave ED Forecast Tool in the Emergency Department Network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland
Authors: Matteo Paganini, Ilaria Costantini, Ilenia Mascherona, Simone Cosci, Laura Di Domenico, Ana Maria Vicedo-Cabrera, Roberta Petrino
Venue: medRxiv
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.10.11.26365239
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Objectives: Heatwaves drive surges in acute care demand, yet heat-health action plans (HHAPs) lack tools to scale emergency care responses. This study validated a forecasting tool for heatwave-related emergency department (ED) demand across four clusters comprising the emergency care network of Ticino Canton, Switzerland. Methods: This retrospective, ecological, time-series study modeled daily mean temperature and ED presentations using a distributed lag non-linear model framework with autoregressive and calendar adjustment components. The model was trained on summers (June-August) 2016-2024 and tested on summer 2025, defining heatwaves as daily mean temperature >25 °C for ≥3 consecutive days. Results: A non-linear temperature-demand association was shown across the clusters, with ED visits increasing at higher temperatures. #34 [grant] Coupling, Energetics, and Dynamics of Atmospheric Regions
Amount: $100,000–$750,000
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/357105
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-03-03
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Understanding the behavior, coupling, energetics, chemistry, and dynamics of atmospheric regions from the middle atmosphere upward through the thermosphere and ionosphere into the exosphere, including responses to lower atmospheric perturbations and solar radiation/particle inputs.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Observations from ground-based and space-based platforms, theory and modeling of the upper atmosphere of the Earth and other planets, and the application of AI and ML tools.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): The upper atmosphere of the Earth and other planets in the solar system, specifically from the middle atmosphere upward through the thermosphere and ionosphere into the exosphere.
Abstract:
The Coupling, Energetics, and Dynamics of Atmospheric Regions (CEDAR) program supports research to increase our understanding of the behavior of atmospheric regions from the middle atmosphere upward through the thermosphere and ionosphere into the exosphere. Projects explore coupling, energetics, chemistry, and dynamics on regional and global scales. The research topics include investigations of upper atmosphere responses due to a) processes driven by the lower atmospheric perturbations and (b) solar radiation and particle inputs from above. The activities supported by this program include observations from ground-based and space-based platforms, as well as theory and modeling of the upper atmosphere of the Earth and other planets in our solar systems. Novel approaches that include AI and ML tools and open data and open science practices are encouraged.

NSF Publication 25-510

#35 [grant] STARBASE Cherry Point
Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/358672
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Assessing the feasibility of soliciting a non-profit organization to operate and manage the Department of Defense STARBASE program at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Request for Information (RFI) process requiring non-profit organizations to submit a 5-page technical response detailing capability, prior experience, teaming arrangements, and certifications, without cost or pricing information.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina; DoD STARBASE program; non-profit organizations meeting DoD Instruction 1025.07.
Abstract:
This is a Request for Information (RFI) only. The responses will be used to assess the feasibility of the Government soliciting this requirement from a non-profit organization that meets the applicable regulations and qualifications outlined in the attached DRAFT Performance Requirements Statement (PRS) for the operation and management of the Department of Defense (DoD) STARBASE program at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina.

Please refer to the attached draft PRS for additional details. This requirement is for ONLY non-profit organizations in accordance with DoD Instruction 1025.07.

SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS AND FORMATING REQUIREMENTS:

- Responses to the RFI are due by 5:00pm Eastern Time on 16 May 2025 to the following email address/es: jessica.d.franceschini.civ@us.navy.mil and kara.m.ridgell.civ@us.navy.mil. Any response received after this date will also be considered but may not be included in initial reporting or assessment.

- All responses should be unclassified. All information received in response to this RFI that is marked proprietary will be handled accordingly. Responses to this notice will not be returned.

- All responses should be in Adobe PDF or Microsoft (MS) Word format. Format specifications include 12-point font, single-spaced, 8.5 by 11 inches paper, with 1-inch margins in either Adobe PDF or MS Word. Responses should not exceed 5 pages.

-Cover page (1 page) with RFI Number and name, address, company/institution, Point of Contact (POC) including name, phone number, and email address, and date. The Cover Page shall also specify the business type (i.e. Non-Profit Organization).

-Technical Data and Approach (4 pages): This should specifically address, and demonstrate the capability to meet, the required capabilities for the operation and management of the DoD STARBASE program at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina. In addition, the response should address relevant prior experience (as a prime or subcontractor) on similar requirements. This should include the size, scope, complexity, timeframe, and whether the work was for government or commercial clients. As well, include pertinent certifications that may help in evaluating your capabilities. Teaming and/or subcontracting arrangements should be clearly delineated and previous experience in teaming must be provided.

- No cost or pricing information should be provided. Any received will be deleted and destroyed.

- Due to email constraints, the size of the submission is limited to 10 MB.

DISCLAIMER

This RFI is not a solicitation and should not be construed as a commitment by the Government. This notice is issued solely for information and planning purposes and does not constitute a solicitation. Responses in any form are not offers and the Government is under no obligation to award a cooperative agreement as a result of this RFI. Responses to this RFI will not be returned. Responders are solely responsible for all expenses associated with responding to this RFI. No funds are available to pay for preparation of responses to this announcement. Any information submitted by responders to this RFI are strictly voluntary. The Government does not guarantee any action beyond this RFI. The Government may not respond to questions posed in company/institution responses.

ATTENTION

Although this is a RFI notice only, interested parties must be registered with the System for Award Management (SAM) to be eligible for award or payment if the Government chooses to make an award. Information on registration and annual confirmation requirements may be obtained via https://www.sam.gov

#36 [grant] Demonstration for Long-duration Battery Energy Storage Systems (BATT4EU Partnership)
Amount: €5,000,000–€9,400,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2027-05-D2-08
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-15
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Dependence on critical raw materials and the need for grid stability, resilience, and flexibility in Europe through long-duration (> 8 hours) battery energy storage systems.
Method (Mycelium's reading): System-level demonstrations of non-commercialized technologies (e.g., novel redox flow, high-temperature, metal-air, or multivalent chemistries) integrated with advanced digital technologies for SOC/SOH predictions and techno-economic analysis of CAPEX/OPEX.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European utility-scale energy systems or large industrial consumers.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Projects are expected to contribute to all of the following outcomes:

- Demonstrated system-level long-duration energy storage (LDES) solutions, explicitly aimed at enhancing grid stability, resilience, and flexibility in Europe.

- Substantial reduction of Europe's dependence on critical raw materials through the use of abundant, low-cost, and sustainable materials.

- Contribute to strategic insights for a coherent EU-wide stationary storage deployment strategy, enhancing European energy autonomy and sustainability.

- Sufficient and reproducible operational data and insights to serve as reliable input towards detailed technoeconomic analyses.

Scope:

Proposals should focus on system-level demonstrations of innovative long-duration (> 8 hours) battery storage concepts that can effectively support utility-scale energy systems or industrial consumers in achieving energy security and operational sustainability.

Projects are expected to cover all the following points:

- Demonstration of advanced long-duration storage technologies not yet on the market such as novel redox flow batteries (standard or mediated), high-temperature systems, metal-air systems, multivalent chemistries (organic or aqueous), or other non-commercialised technologies or architectures.

- Assessment and definition of use case(s) intended for the proposed technology (front-of-the-meter grid-scale storage, behind-the-meter large industrial energy consumer, firming of renewable generation) along with quantified impact on improved grid resilience, reduced emissions, safety, and lowered energy storage cost.

- Assessment of hybridization potential of complementary energy storage technologies (e.g., redox flow batteries with supercapacitors) to optimize overall system performance for the intended use case(s) and extending system lifecycle.

- Utilization of abundant, low-cost, and sustainable materials, explicitly prioritizing materials with reliable and scalable European supply chains, accompanied by realistic and detailed pathways to production routes at scale.

- Integration of advanced digital technologies, for accurate state-of-charge (SOC), state-of-health (SOH), and lifetime predictions, optimizing battery management systems (BMS), energy management systems (EMS), and overall component performance for extended system longevity.

- Comprehensive techno-economic analyses, including realistic assessments of CAPEX, OPEX, based on measured technical performance metrics (e.g., self-discharge rates, calendar life, cycle life, round-trip efficiency, necessary safety investments) to clearly establish economic viability and competitiveness for the intended use-case in comparison to the commercial, incumbent technology.

- Comprehensive safety assessment at system-level, documenting potential concerns (e.g. flammability, toxicity, explosion potential) and mitigation strategies ahead of widescale adoption of technology.

The Commission initiative for Safe and Sustainable by Design[1] (SSbD) sets a framework for assessing the safety and sustainability of chemicals and materials which should be considered as a reference for project proposals.

Whenever the expected exploitation of project results entails developing, creating, manufacturing and marketing a product or process, or in creating and providing a service, the plan for the exploitation and dissemination of results must include a strategy for such exploitation. The exploitation plans are expected to include preliminary plans for scalability, commercialisation, and deployment (feasibility study, business plan) indicating the possible funding sources to be potentially used (in particular the Innovation Fund).

Proposals could consider the involvement of the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC)[2] whose contribution could consist of performing experimental or desk-top research on battery performance or safety. For further information on the JRC’s possible contribution to the projec

Amount: €2,000,000–€13,500,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2027-03-D5-06
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-04-14
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Public concern and potential fire hazards associated with Electric Vehicles (EVs) in constrained spaces such as underground parking lots, garages, ferryboats, and depots.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of a comprehensive European fire accident database, on-board/off-board detection and suppression systems, real-time monitoring for early warning, firefighting protocols integrated with ISO/NFPA standards, and the use of Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) disciplines for public percept…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Constrained spaces (underground/built-in parking lots, garages, ferryboats, depots) involving EV categories M1, N1, HDV, and L-category vehicles with 400V-AC or DC charging connectors.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Standardised fire risk assessment for EVs’[1] fire hazards in constrained spaces and areas such as underground/ built-in parking lots, garages, ferryboats and depots with and without charging facilities and during mono- or bidirectional charging.

- Innovative on-board and/or off-board affordable fire-detection, suppression, and containment measures and techniques.

- Standardised fire protocols and open evaluation frameworks.

- Enhanced public perception of fire safety across all EV categories.

Scope:

The overall fire safety risks associated with Electric Vehicles (EVs) are substantially lower compared to those of Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) vehicles. However, public concerns and perceptions about EV fire safety may still persist. This necessitates a thorough examination and addressing of potential causes of EV fire to alleviate any remaining worries. This necessitates a thorough examination and addressing of potential causes of EV fire to alleviate any remaining worries..

Proposed actions are expected to address all of the following aspects:

- Development of the most comprehensive database about fire accidents involving all EV categories at the European level.

- Mitigation measures and solutions in case of thermal runaway of batteries, if not prevented in the first place, by appropriate design or by active measures to effectively avoid open fire and its possible progression.

- A clear recognition of EV risks by improved on-board diagnosis and real-time monitoring, leading to early warning and to appropriate countermeasures.

- Development of innovative and affordable fire detection, prevention and optionally suppression solutions for constrained spaces and areas such as underground/ built-in parking lots, garages, ferryboats and depots with and without charging facilities and during mono- or bidirectional charging. This can include e.g. measures for thermal runaway, fire-resistant systems/materials, easy and safe access to the battery for removal from the vehicle.

- Development of firefighting protocols to deal with EVs on fire in narrow situations, essential for quick and effective intervention, including integration with existing safety standards (e.g., ISO, NFPA) to ensure smooth adoption and compatibility.

- Social awareness for a transparent, informed public perception of the safety level of all EV categories, also with the development of a European based platform for dissemination and information with direct involvement of main stakeholders.

This topic requires the effective contribution of Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) disciplines and the involvement of SSH experts, institutions as well as the inclusion of relevant SSH expertise, in order to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related research activities.

This topic implements the co-programmed European Partnership on ‘Towards zero emission road transport’ (2ZERO). As such, projects resulting from this topic will be expected to report on the results to the European Partnership ‘Towards zero emission road transport’ (2ZERO) in support of the monitoring of its KPIs.

The topic is open to international collaboration, and the funded project are expected to seek synergies with the Sustainable Transport Forum[2] and with the EV TCP Task 49[3].

Technology Readiness Level - Technology readiness level expected from completed projects

Activities are expected to achieve TRL 6 by the end of the project – see General Annex B. Activities may start at any TRL.

[1] The focus of this topic is on vehicles in categories, M1, N1 and HDV including L-category vehicles as far as commercially available with 400V-AC or DC charging connectors

[2] In particular on fire safety issues, see e.g. “Guidance of fire safety for electric vehicles parked and charging infrastructure in covered parking spaces”, doi:10.2832/668117

Still open/current: yes

Abstract:
This Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) invites applications for the Readiness and Recreation Initiative (RARI), administered by the National Park Service (NPS). The purpose of the program is to: 1) provide outdoor recreation opportunities, and 2) promote or support compatible land uses and avoid incompatible development in areas in the vicinity of, or ecologically related to, a military installation or military airspace, and/or to maintain or enhance disaster resilience. RARI is a program within the Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF). State and Local Assistance Program. RARI funding is available in addition to traditional LWCF state formula grants and does not affect state apportionments. RARI operates in partnership with the Department of War (DOW) and seeks to leverage funding across departments to benefit the general public and military communities. RARI is dollar for dollar match, meaning it covers up to 50% of all project costs and applicants are responsible for funding the remaining 50% of project costs. However, for RARI projects, DOW Readiness and Environmental Protection Integration (REPI) funds are allowable to meet the LWCF Act's cost-share requirement (10 U.S.C. 2684a). Therefore, 100% of project costs could be funded through these two federal programs. To be eligible, proposed projects must: Include a land acquisition component. Be in a Readiness and Environmental Protection Integration (REPI) Partnership Opportunity Area or Sentinel Landscape. Have a Letter of Support from a Military Installation or Range commander.1 Additional LWCF requirements for the RARI program: Perpetuity Requirement - Projects assisted through RARI must be maintained and accessible exclusively for public outdoor recreation use in perpetuity. This applies to the assisted park or site in its entirety, not just the area assisted by the grant funds. Alignment with LWCF Law and Policy - As an LWCF program, RARI projects must align with the purposes and requirements of the LWCF Act and LWCF Manual. This includes meeting a priority need or goal identified in the Statewide Comprehensive Outdoor Recreation Plan (SCORP). Alignment with National Priorities – Projects must be responsive to Executive and National priorities, including those outlined in Executive Order 14313, "Establishing the President's Make America Beautiful Again Commission" and Secretarial Order 3442, "Land and Water Conservation Fund Implementation by the U.S. Department of the Interior."

#39 [grant] Persistent, Geochemically-Driven Low-Temperature Power Systems for Subsea Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13137
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current subsea ISR nodes and UUV docking stations rely on lithium-chemistry batteries that suffer from capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess toxic chemistries, and require resource-intensive physical replacement in contested or ice-covered environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters that generate electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between anoxic marine sediment and oxygenated overlying seawater, utilizing abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode …
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Sub-zero Arctic subsea environments, specifically the interface between marine sediment and overlying seawater.
Abstract:
The Department of the Navy’s expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries. These legacy power sources present severe logistical and operational limitations: they suffer from rapid capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess highly toxic/hazardous chemistries, and require frequent, resource-intensive physical replacement (battery swapping) in highly contested or ice-covered environments.

To achieve persistent, logistics-free ISR, the Navy has a critical need for an environmentally benign, deploy-and-forget power architecture. This STTR topic seeks the development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters to generate continuous electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between the anoxic marine sediment (mud) and the oxygenated overlying seawater. The proposed approach must demonstrate a credible path to 5W power and 24-month endurance in sub-zero Arctic conditions through a ruggedized seabed electrochemical power-harvesting architecture that maximizes long-term energy extraction while using only indigenous sediment microbial communities and naturally occurring geochemical gradients. Proposed solutions may use abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode design, power management, and optimum emplacement.

Biocatalytic Prioritization & Environmental Strictures:

While purely abiotic electrochemical approaches will be considered, approaches that leverage biologically-mediated processes (e.g., utilizing natural biocatalysis to enhance electron transfer at the anode) will be prioritized due to their potential for higher power density and self-renewing longevity.

However, to prevent any risk of ecological disruption to fragile Arctic ecosystems, solutions must strictly rely on harnessing the naturally occurring, indigenous populations already present in the local sediment. The introduction, deployment, or seeding of any exogenous, synthetic, lab-grown, or non-native biological agents (microbes/bacteria) is strictly prohibited.

By utilizing advanced electrode materials that naturally synergize with the local subsea environment, the system must reduce or avoid reliance on deployable primary batteries for the supported payload while ensuring operational viability in extreme cold and high-pressure conditions.

#40 [grant] Self-Sustaining Wave Energy Capture for Persistent Autonomous Ocean-Going Systems
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13132
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles require a reliable, self-sustaining power source for recharging when operating far from human contact, specifically a wave energy capture device (WECD) that is portable, deployable in various depths, and stealthy.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Open water environments ranging from depths of 100 meters to full ocean depth, with sea states ranging from calm to Sea State 8.
Abstract:
Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles need regular recharging, and since they often operate far from human contact, their charging systems require a reliable, self-sustaining power source. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) believes the ideal power source will be a wave energy capture device (WECD). WECDs capture kinetic and potential energy generated by the movement of ocean waves on or near the surface of open water.

The desired WECD must be portable, specifically, designed as a set of components that can each be carried by one or two people who must be able to quickly assemble and disassemble those components. Components designed for one-person carry should weigh no more than 14 kg with largest dimension no greater than 1.9 m, while components designed for two-person carry should weigh no more than 45.4 kg with largest dimension no greater than 2.3 m. The WECD must be able to be relocated to areas of very different depths, including full ocean depth so the WECD’s design cannot require placement or anchoring on the sea floor. And since the WECD may need to deploy near the shore, its design must allow it to function in waters as shallow as 100 meters.

Ocean weather conditions can be challenging. The WECD should function reliably at Sea State 6 or less (very rough seas, with wave heights of 4 to 6 meters), and it should be able to survive conditions up to Sea State 8 (very high seas, with wave heights of 9 to 14 meters).

ONR assumes the WECD will be tethered to some device at or near the surface of the water. That tethered system may be an autonomous vehicle in loiter mode, and since loitering involves continuous vehicle movement, the WECD should operate reliably while in motion, and its design should leverage such motion to increase energy capture.

The WECD should produce a minimum of 20 kilowatt-hours (kWh) per day, but more is highly desirable. ONR believes 100+ kWh per day is achievable. Even in calm seas, the ideal WECD should produce sufficient electricity to charge a 2-kWh battery in 6 hours or less. Vehicle movement may be considered when ensuring this minimum level of power generation.

The desired WECD may be needed in areas where human assembly is impractical. Thus, the deliverables must include a prototype device capable of deploying the assembled WECD from the deck of a medium or large autonomous surface vessel. Like the WECD itself, the deployment device (DD) should function reliably in challenging weather conditions: Sea State 4 or less (moderate seas with wave heights of 1.25 to 2.5 meters).

Once deployed, very little of the WECD itself should be visible at the surface of the water. The WECD should minimize any increase in the visibility of the vehicle it is tethered to. This includes surface and airborne observation, both optically and by radar. Acoustic noise generated by the WECD should either be minimized or disguised to seem environmental or biological.

Cost for the WECD and associated DD should be minimized. ONR expects that under certain environmental conditions or mission requirements, WECDs may not be recoverable. At full-rate production, the ideal price will allow for multiple units per million dollars.

Under normal operating conditions, including Sea States of 6 or less, the expected operational duration of the deployed WECD should be at least one month, with three months or more expected if Sea State 4 or less is maintained.
