Link: https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/362715
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2030-11-01
Abstract:
This Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) invites applications for the Outdoor Recreation Legacy Partnership (ORLP) Program, administered by the National Park Service (NPS). ORLP provides funding to 1) to acquire land and water for parks and other outdoor recreation purposes in qualifying areas, and 2) to develop new or renovate existing outdoor recreation facilities that provide outdoor recreation opportunities to the public in qualifying areas. ORLP is a program within the Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF) State and Local Assistance Program, which provides matching grants to States. ORLP funding is available in addition to traditional LWCF state formula grants and does not affect state apportionments.

ORLP projects must be within a Qualifying Area, defined as:

- an urban area that has a population of 25,000 or more in the most recent census, or

- 2 or more adjacent urban areas with a combined population of 25,000 or more in the most recent census; or

- an area administered by a federally recognized Indian Tribe or an Alaska Native or Native Hawaiian community organization.

Additional requirements under the ORLP program:

- Matching Requirement - ORLP is dollar for dollar match, meaning it covers up to 50% of all project costs. Applicants are responsible for providing non-federal funds for at least 50% of project costs.

- Perpetuity Requirement - Projects assisted through ORLP must be maintained and accessible for public outdoor recreation use in perpetuity. This applies to the assisted park or site in its entirety, not just the area assisted by the grant funds.

- Alignment with LWCF Law and Policy - As an LWCF program, ORLP projects must align with the purposes and requirements of the LWCF Act and LWCF Manual.

- Alignment with National Priorities – Projects must be responsive to Executive and National priorities, including those outlined in Executive Order 14313, "Establishing the President's Make America Beautiful Again Commission" and Secretarial Order 3442, "Land and Water Conservation Fund Implementation by the U.S. Department of the Interior."

#1 [paper] From Stream to State: Engaging Communities in Approved Water Monitoring Frameworks
Authors: Lauren A. Haygood, Todd Halihan
Venue: Community Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1029/2026csj000186
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract More than 50% of Oklahoma's surface water systems are classified as impaired by the US EPA, with limited funds designated toward surface water monitoring. Community science data can contribute to increasing the amount of quality‐controlled government water quality reporting. A framework is presented for implementing a community‐based approach to generating quality‐controlled water field data to support water quality monitoring by local and regional governments. This research focuses on the design and implementation of a water quality community science project in Oklahoma, USA. In this study, community scientists collected water samples and produced over 100 measurements of key water quality parameters, including alkalinity, conductivity, total dissolved solids, temperature, and selected metals (e.g., iron, manganese, mercury, cadmium, and lead). The frequency and resolution of these community‐generated data exceed those of conventional state government monitoring, demonstrating the potential for community science to provide cost‐effective, high‐frequency, and spatially expansive data sets, which fill monitoring gaps. Additionally, community science can act as a method to bridge the gap between stakeholders, scientists, and policy makers. This study highlights the quality‐controlled methods, tools, and community‐driven efforts shaping water quality research and public engagement in Oklahoma, a step forward in community‐driven data acquisition and water policy.

#2 [paper] Macrozoobenthos as a Bioindicator of Water Quality in the Coastal Waters of Merak Besar Island, Banten Province
Authors: Farhan Randi Darmawan, Muta Ali Khalifa, Erik Munandar
Venue: Barakuda 45 Jurnal Ilmu Perikanan dan Kelautan
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.47685/barakuda45.v8i1.875
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
High human activity in the coastal area of Merak Besar Island, Banten Province, such as tourism, port, and industrial activities, potentially degrades water quality and affects benthic organisms that serve as biological indicators of coastal ecosystem health. This study aimed to describe the physicochemical characteristics of the water, total organic matter (TOM), sediment texture, and macrozoobenthos community structure, and to determine the ecological condition of the waters using a macrozoobenthos bioindicator approach based on the AMBI (AZTI's Marine Biotic Index) method. Research was conducted spatially in January 2026 at four stations using 1x1 m² quadrat transects with different numbers of replicates per station, along with measurements of temperature, pH, DO, salinity, TOM, and sediment texture. Results showed physicochemical parameters at all stations remained stable and met seawater quality standards, although DO at one station was exactly at the minimum threshold. Twenty macrozoobenthos species were identified, comprising Group II (indifferent), Group III (tolerant), and Group IV (opportunistic) species, with no Group I or V species recorded, while Littoraria lutea had the highest abundance. Abundance ranged from 558-1,171 ind/m², highest at the least disturbed station. Species diversity was moderate, evenness high, and dominance low across all stations. Although physicochemical conditions were suitable for macrozoobenthos, AMBI values at all stations indicated a slightly polluted category, dominated by Group III. This confirms that macrozoobenthos can detect ecological stress not yet captured by instantaneous physicochemical parameters, making it a useful method for assessing the coastal environmental condition of Merak Besar Island.

#5 [paper] Data-driven coastal nutrients estimation: current status, research gaps, and future developments.
Authors: Ni, Sihan, Qi, Jin, Ran, Xiangbin, Liu, Zhiqiang, Wu, Sensen, Wang, Minyu, Yang, Keyi, Le, Chengfeng
Venue: Water research
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42748610/
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The estimation of coastal nutrients from satellite observations remains a challenge because nutrients lack direct optical properties, and current data-driven methods face issues with interpretability and data scarcity.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A review of the mechanisms governing coastal biogeochemical cycling, the development of data-driven methods for remote sensing retrieval of nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon, and an analysis of the integration of machine learning with marine biogeochemical mechanisms.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global coastal waters and satellite-based remote sensing observations.
Abstract:
Driven by warming and anthropogenic impacts, global coastal waters suffer from the escalating eutrophication crisis, making it essential to understand the dynamics of nutrient discharge and enrichment. While satellites can retrieve surface water optical properties, the estimation of coastal nutrients from space remains a long-standing challenge due to their non-optical properties. Recently, artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning, has enabled the spatiotemporal estimation of surface nutrients from satellite observations, which represents a potential breakthrough for sustainable water management. In this review, we summarize the mechanisms governing coastal biogeochemical cycling and identify the estimation complexity that international scholars have been striving to solve over the past decade. We demonstrate that data-driven methods have shown preliminary success in empowering remote sensing retrieval of nitrogen, phosphorus, and silicon. Despite these advances, we note that significant challenges remain for effective monitoring of coastal eutrophication due to the limited interpretability of data-driven estimation and data scarcity. A thorough analysis is provided on the developments and limitations of nutrient retrieval, the potential of integrating data-driven methods with marine biogeochemical mechanisms, and future opportunities to enhance marine ecosystem dynamic models. Ultimately, our aim is to advance satellite observations and data-driven estimation at the forefront of environmental science to develop the precise monitoring, assessment, and protection of coastal waters.

#6 [paper] Reimagining coastal water quality forecasting with hydrodynamic simulation and advanced machine learning.
Authors: Hashemi Monfared, Seyed Arman, Jafari-Asl, Jafar, Behzadian, Kourosh, Thi Hoang, Thu-Huong, Nazari, Rouzbeh, Sharifi, Soroosh, Abolfathi, Soroush
Venue: Journal of environmental management
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42580284/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Effective and sustainable management of coastal ecosystems relies on accurate water quality monitoring and forecasting, particularly in regions facing heavy pollutant loads. Phosphate and nitrate play crucial roles in coastal water quality and ecosystem health. However, predicting their concentrations remains challenging due to complex spatiotemporally varying environmental interactions. Leveraging advanced numerical modelling and artificial intelligence (AI), this study introduces a novel hybrid machine learning (ML) framework based on least-squares support vector regression (LSSVR) to simulate coastal water quality using physically grounded simulation data generated by the TELEMAC-WAQTEL numerical framework, calibrated against field-measured boundary and initial conditions. The proposed model is applied to Ha Long Bay, Vietnam, utilizing a dataset comprising 8760 hourly samples collected over one year (2021-2022). The data was generated through a two-dimensional TELEMAC hydrodynamic model integrated with a water quality module. Key hydrodynamic variables, including free surface elevation (FS), velocity (U), and flow direction (α), serve as inputs to predict nitrate (NO3) and phosphate (PO4) concentrations. To optimize the LSSVR hyperparameters, we introduced the Improved Dragonfly Algorithm (IDA), which integrates Cauchy walk mutation and adaptive inertia weighting to enhance convergence, global search efficiency, and robustness. Benchmarking against Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), ε- LSSVR, ANN, Random Forest, and Model Tree demonstrate the superior predictive capability of IDA-LSSVR. On an independent testing dataset comprising 20% of the total samples (1752 observations), IDA-LSSVR achieved the lowest RMSE (NO3 = 1.55E-02 mg/L, PO4 = 5.88E-04 mg/L), MAE (NO3 = 3.45E-07 mg/L, PO4 = 2.39E-04 mg/L), and MAPE (NO3 = 3.41, PO4 = 4.49E-04), coupled with the highest R2 (NO3 = 0.95, PO4 = 0.97). By coupling high-resolution physics-based hydrodynamic simulations with advanced machine learning and optimisation techniques, the proposed framework provides an accurate, computationally efficient, and reliable tool for coastal water quality forecasting. The integration of physically consistent simulation data with robust uncertainty-aware prediction offers valuable decision-support capabilities for nutrient management, eutrophication risk assessment, and environmental monitoring in dynamic coastal environments. The framework therefore presents a promising approach for supporting sustainable coastal ecosystem management and protecting vulnerable marine systems from nutrient-driven degradation.

#8 [paper] Satellites reveal how extreme rainfall affects coastal water quality in the Bohai Sea: Implications for marine environmental management.
Authors: Zheng, Longxiao, Guo, Wei, Zhao, Ning, Yu, Yonggui, A, Runa, Cheah, Wee, Zhang, Qian, Chen, Yanlong
Venue: Journal of environmental management
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42772159/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Extreme rainfall is intensifying globally as the climate continues to warm. Yet how such events affect coastal water quality and potentially influence assessments of water quality improvement remains poorly understood. This study uses time-series optical satellite observations to characterize the response and recovery of coastal water quality following the 2023 extreme rainfall event in the Bohai Sea and to evaluate how this short-term disturbance influences monthly assessments of water quality improvement. The event substantially increased suspended particulate matter (SPM), chlorophyll-a, colored dissolved organic matter, and Forel-Ule Index values, while reducing water transparency (Secchi disk depth, ZSD) and sea surface salinity. In particular, SPM increased by 173% relative to the pre-rainfall baseline. The proportions of highly turbid and diluted waters increased by 27 and 10 percentage points (pp), respectively. Across all indicators, the strongest changes were found in estuaries and nearshore waters. Responses peaked five days after the event, and all indicators returned to the pre-rainfall level within two weeks. Such dramatic and prolonged changes in water quality can alter monthly means, with the monthly ZSD assessment for August 2023 showing a sensitivity of 13 pp to disturbance-period observations. This finding emphasizes the importance to distinguish event-driven variability from longer-term water quality changes in marine environmental management.

#9 [paper] Dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), total alkalinity, pH on total scale, nutrients, water temperature, salinity and other variables collected from profile and discrete samples observations during the NO
Authors: Leticia Barbero, Rik H. Wanninkhof, Denis Pierrot, Donald Christopher Melrose, Paula S. Fratantoni, Harvey J. Walsh, David W. Townsend, Maura A. Thomas
Venue: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.25921/4xq9-qp20
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This dataset consists of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), total alkalinity, pH on total scale, nutrients, water temperature, salinity and other variables collected from profile and discrete samples observations during the NOAA Ship Pisces cruise PC2601 (EXPOCODE 334B20251022) in the New York Bight, Northeast U.S. Shelf, North Atlantic Ocean from from 2025-10-23 to 2025-11-07. Increasing amounts of atmospheric carbon dioxide from human industrial activities are causing changes in global ocean carbon chemistry ultimately resulting in a reduction in pH, a process termed ocean acidification. Studies have demonstrated adverse effects on calcifying organisms, particularly some invertebrates, corals, sea urchins, pteropods, and coccolithophores, but also on species of commercial interest such as oysters or crabs. In support of the coastal monitoring and research objectives of the NOAA Ocean Acidification Program (OAP), the Ecosystem Monitoring Cruises (ECOMON) are utilized to collect water samples to measure water column inorganic carbon and hydrographic parameters including nutrients. Samples are collected at three depths (surface, mid-depth and near bottom) at select stations on a quarterly basis in the northeastern Atlantic continental shelf region off the United States. Water samples are sent to and analyzed by scientists at the Atlantic Oceanographic & Meteorological Laboratory (AOML) for dissolved inorganic carbon, pH and total alkalinity concentrations. Additional samples are analyzed for nutrient concentrations at the University of Maine. These data are used to monitor short-long term coastal ocean acidification trends.

#10 [paper] Optical measurements for surface water samples collected within South San Francisco Bay in support of mercury modeling
Authors: Angela M. Hansen, Jacob A. Fleck, Diana M Oros, Niky C. Taylor, Patrick C Dellwo, Mark C. Marvin-DiPasquale, Brian A. Bergamaschi, Kristin B. Byrd
Venue: USGS DOI Tool Production Environment
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5066/p13joxxa
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Little is known about mercury concentrations at bay margins, and how climate change, including changes in temperature and precipitation, will affect mercury exposure and methylmercury (MeHg) production. In addition, the San Francisco South Bay Salt Ponds Restoration Program (SBSPRP) needs more efficient and effective mercury monitoring approaches at larger spatial scales to understand changes in mercury at a regional level. The goal of this new project, a collaboration between the USGS Western Geographic Science Center, Water Mission Area, and the California Water Science Center (CAWSC), is to develop the capacity to map total mercury (THg) and MeHg in South San Francisco Bay (SFB) through the satellite remote sensing (Sentinel-2) of two known mercury indicators: total suspended solids (TSS) and colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM). In addition to quantifying the accuracy of this approach, this research aims in South SFB using the Sentinel-2 satellite in order to 1) improve understanding of region-wide mercury spatial and temporal trends associated with weather events and wetland restoration management activities, and 2) improve mercury monitoring efficiencies and capabilities moving forward. One main project objective is to assess the capacity to detect anomalies in remotely sensed TSS, CDOM, and mercury species associated with recent weather events or restoration activities through time series analysis. The optical measurements reported here were collected to aid in the characterization of water sources and mixtures and establish proxies (surrogates) for mercury and methylmercury concentrations and to provide ground-truthing for remotely sensed models of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations. Data are compiled into five tables: 1) full fluorescence spectra in vectorized format (LSB_Hg_RS_EEMs_vectors.csv), 2) full absorbance spectra for 1 centimeter (cm) path measurements (LSB_Hg_RS_1cm_ABS_scans.csv), 3) full absorbance spectra for 10 cm path measurements (SSFB_Hg_RS_10cm_ABS_scans.csv), 4) absorption coefficients derived from the 10cm path measurements (SSFB_Hg_RS_10cm_ag_scans.csv), and 5) summary file of commonly extracted optical indicators and calculated wavelength-array values derived from the optical data that correspond to arrays measured by field-based sensors for use in statistical analyses and model development (LSB_Hg_RS_OMRL_Sample_Summary.csv).

#11 [paper] Editorial: Anthropogenic footprints on marine ecosystems: insights into biogeochemical shifts
Authors: Sreenivasulu Ganugapenta, Upendra Badimela, Effi Helmy Ariffin, Krishnan Anoop Krishnan, Jayaraju Nadimikeri
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1988736
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Transitional Water Systems (TWS) including estuaries, lagoons and coastal embayment regulate the exchange of water, sediments, nutrients and contaminants between terrestrial and marine environments (Chilton et al., 2021). As a result, they play a critical role in marine biogeochemical cycles and support diverse and productive ecosystems (Li et al., 2024).However, these systems are increasingly being altered by urbanisation, industrialisation, climate change and pollution with cascading impacts on habitat quality, food webs and ecosystem services (He and Silliman, 2019). This Research Topic in Frontiers in Marine Science brings together ten peer reviewed studies that examine how anthropogenic activities are modifying biogeochemical processes and pathways in vulnerable coastal environments.Collectively, these studies highlight the importance of integrated monitoring, modelling and effective policy approaches to better understand environmental changes, support ecosystem conservation and promote sustainable coastal development.The Topic welcomes original and innovative studies on biogeochemical evidence and anthropogenic impacts in coastal zones, spanning: This Research Topic underscores the urgent need to address anthropogenic pressures on marine biogeochemical cycles in TWS. The contributing studies reveal a consistent pattern in which human activities such as nutrient loading, sediment modification, contaminant discharge and climate forcing are altering the fundamental processes that regulate coastal ecosystem functioning. At the same time, the collection highlights potential pathways forward.Strengthened monitoring networks, integrated modelling frameworks and evidence based policies can support more effective management and help balance biodiversity conservation with sustainable coastal development. As editors, we hope that this Research Topic will stimulate further interdisciplinary research and contribute to management strategies that safeguard the health, resilience and long-term sustainability of marine and coastal ecosystems for future generations.

#12 [paper] A source-to-sea decision-support framework for wet-weather wastewater load management: evidence from Jiaozhou Bay
Authors: Longjiang Han, Shunshun Zhao, Yong Liu, Liting Yin, Dewen Ding
Venue: Ocean & Coastal Management
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocecoaman.2026.108405
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Coastal concentration compliance may overlook increased wastewater throughput during wet weather events.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A five-stage source-to-sea decision-support framework involving source-record auditing, hydraulic and concentration decomposition, benchmark comparison, and source–receptor chronology.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Jiaozhou Bay, China, using 2019–2022 wastewater, river, and marine observations, including data from the Loushan wastewater treatment plant.
Abstract:
Coastal concentration compliance can overlook increased wastewater throughput during wet weather. We developed a source-to-sea decision-support framework using 2019–2022 wastewater, river, and marine observations from Jiaozhou Bay, China. The analysis combined source-record auditing, hydraulic and concentration decomposition, benchmark comparison, and source–receptor chronology. At Loushan wastewater treatment plant, throughput increased by 87.5% from the second to the third quarter of 2020 while total phosphorus remained low at 0.06–0.07 mg L −1 . The corresponding operational loading estimate increased by 118.8%. Hydraulic amplification persisted across seven benchmarks, whereas the direction of estimated load change depended on the reference concentration. Earlier biological surveys characterized receiving-water conditions and informed subsequent monitoring design. The resulting five-stage framework connects data validation, hydraulic review, synchronized source-to-sea monitoring, sediment and benthic follow-up, and adaptive evaluation. It uses hydraulic amplification to prioritize representative effluent sampling and assigns each stage to existing source, river, or marine monitoring functions. Explicit benchmark rules and a proposed sampling timetable make the workflow reproducible and operationally interpretable. The framework provides a practical route from sparse concentration records to coordinated coastal load management, with operational estimates used for screening and representative measurements required for regulatory load assessment.

#13 [paper] Prediction of fecal coliform concentration in coastal surface water using machine learning algorithms and water quality parameters.
Authors: Basak, Jayanta Kumar, Hasan, Shihab, Ismail, Mohammad, Sonet, Sanjay Saha, Chowdhury, Pinaki, Paudel, Bhola
Venue: Journal of microbiological methods
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42702291/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Fecal coliform (FC) is a key indicator of surface water contamination from animal and human waste, and elevated FC levels are associated with waterborne diseases, which remain major public health concerns. However, existing studies are often limited by sparse sampling, time-consuming laboratory analyses, and inadequate representation of complex nonlinear relationships among water quality parameters (WQPs) influencing FC dynamics. Therefore, this study aims to apply and compare machine learning models for predicting FC concentrations using physicochemical WQPs, including pH, salinity (WS), water temperature (WT), electrical conductivity (EC), total dissolved solids (TDS), dissolved oxygen (DO), turbidity (Turb), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), and water hardness (WH), while evaluating their predictive contributions and interactions in coastal Bangladesh. FC concentrations ranged from 188 to 1620 CFU/100 mL, with a mean of 765.57 CFU/100 mL. Pearson correlation analysis ranked the predictors as Turb > BOD > DO > pH > WS > WH > WT > TDS > EC. Among the models, the multilayer perceptron (MLP) outperformed random forest regression (RFR), multiple linear regression (MLR), extreme gradient boosting (XGB), and support vector regression (SVR). During testing, MLP achieved the highest R2 (0.822), with the lowest RMSE (109.48 CFU/100 mL) and MAE (99.95 CFU/100 mL). Notably, the optimal input combination (IC-5), comprising only five WQPs (Turb, BOD, DO, pH, and WS), explained 80.8% of the variability in FC concentrations and achieved 98.30% of the R2 obtained using all nine WQPs. These findings may provide a useful basis for microbial water-quality assessment in comparable coastal environments.

#14 [paper] Quantifying Nitrogen Removal Potential from Oyster Aquaculture in Massachusetts Estuaries
Authors: Micheline S. Labrie, Miles A. Sundermeyer, Brian L. Howes
Venue: Journal of Shellfish Research
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.2983/035.045.0206
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Compliance with the United States Clean Water Act requires states and municipalities to reduce nitrogen (N) pollution and document the effectiveness of mitigation efforts. Oyster aquaculture is a cost-effective and sustainable approach to N removal; however, direct measurement of oyster N content is time- and resource-intensive. Meanwhile, existing predictive models are either broadly general or developed for specific regions outside of Massachusetts (MA). Consequently, the MA Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) requires site-specific measurements. In this study, oysters from 21 southeastern MA estuaries were analyzed as a case study to quantify region-specific relationships of N content, calculated as both mass and percent of whole oyster dry weight, in relation to oyster size, deployment method (surface versus bottom), and water quality metrics. A nonlinear model was used to estimate oyster N mass from shell height (SH), whereas a stepwise linear regression model was used to identify tissue weight, shell weight, water column total N, and oyster deployment method as significant predictors of percent N content. A potential benefit of regional models is to provide a better fit to local data than a general model that incorporated data from across a broader range (e.g., in the present case North Carolina to Maine), particularly for the upper range of oyster SH. These region-specific models enable municipalities to estimate N removal from harvests without laboratory analyses, supporting state level DEP-approved nutrient crediting.

#19 [paper] Temporal changes in estuarine water quality during decentralized wastewater treatment implementation in the Paranaguá estuarine system, southern Brazil.
Authors: Portella, Ana Karine K, Lubiana, Karoline Magalhães Ferreira, Armani, Fernando Augusto Silveira, Lagreze-Squella, Francisco José, Melegari, Silvia Pedroso
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42762762/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study investigates the temporal response of estuarine water quality to progressive implementation of decentralized wastewater treatment systems (DWWTS) in Eufrasina, a traditional community within the Paranaguá Estuarine System (PES), southern Brazil. Monthly monitoring was conducted over 20-months period (September 2024-April 2026) at four fixed sampling stations. Coastal Water Quality Index (CWQI), adapted from the Canadian Council of Ministers of the Environment framework, was applied to integrate physicochemical and microbiological variables and track temporal trends. Principal Component Analysis revealed seasonal structuring with summer campaigns associated with higher continental inputs and spring campaigns with greater microbiological contamination. CWQI showed a significant improving trend during the implementation phase (Mann-Kendall τ = 0.515, p = 0.024), rising from "Bad/Regular" to "Good/Excellent" as coverage expanded. Lagged correlations indicated that Escherichia coli and total coliforms had the strongest negative associations with cumulative sanitation coverage (lag 0-3), whereas enterococci, phosphate, and DO showed no significant associations, a pattern consistent with non-point sources and biogeochemical processes not addressed by household-level treatment. CWQI values declined episodically during periods of peak seasonal occupancy and rainfall, indicating that residual contamination. Water quality improved measurably even at early stage of DWWTS implementation, which highlights the value of monitoring designs that account for response lags when assessing delayed environmental responses to sanitation interventions. By showing that community-scale sanitation interventions can produce measurable reductions in estuarine pollution, this work provides evidence relevant to SDG 6 and 14, and United Nations Ocean Decade's call for science-based solutions to coastal and marine pollution.

#20 [paper] Survey and literature review dataset for: Fresh, salty, and still not talking? Assessing and addressing the limnology-oceanography research divide
Authors: Osiris Díaz-Torres, Danielle Robinson, Alejandra Zazueta, Helen R. Powley, Gabriela López‐González, Taylor Maavara

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The research divide and 'collaboration ceiling' between the limnology and oceanography communities regarding freshwater-marine interdisciplinary research.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A combination of an anonymized survey of aquatic researchers and a systematic literature review of papers published in Limnology & Oceanography between 2015-2025.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Anonymized survey responses from 101 English-speaking (76%) and Spanish-speaking (24%) aquatic researchers from 27 countries, and a literature review of 320 papers from Limnology & Oceanography.
Abstract:
This dataset contains the complete raw data supporting the analyses presented in the paper in processing"Fresh, salty, and still not talking? Assessing and addressing the limnology-oceanography research divide" (Díaz-Torres et al., 2026). The dataset includes three Excel files: 1. RivertoOcean_Summary_English.xlsx: Anonymized survey responses from 78 English-speaking aquatic researchers (76% of total respondents) from 27 countries. The survey was conducted between October 2024 and January 2025 and collected information on research backgrounds, collaboration patterns, perceived barriers, and priorities for freshwater-marine interdisciplinary research. 2. RivertoOcean_Summary_Spanish.xlsx: Anonymized survey responses from 25 Spanish-speaking aquatic researchers (24% of total respondents), primarily from Latin America. The Spanish version of the survey enabled inclusion of perspectives often underrepresented in international assessments. 3. LO_26_0181_literature_review.xlsx: Systematic literature review of 320 papers published in Limnology & Oceanography between 2015-2025 (approximately 17% of all regular issue papers in that period_). Each entry includes classification by field (limnology, oceanography, coastal, estuary, both), whether the paper mentions the other field, and whether it demonstrates substantive interdisciplinary engagement (knowledge exchange or land-ocean aquatic continuum research). Together, these datasets provide the empirical foundation for identifying the "collaboration ceiling" between limnology and oceanography communities, revealing that while 49% of papers mention both fields, only 25% demonstrate meaningful interdisciplinary collaboration. The survey was approved by the University of Leeds Faculty of Environment Research Ethics Committee (reference: 1620). All data are anonymized with no personally identifiable information. Corresponding authors: Taylor Maavara (maavarat@caryinstitute.org), Osiris Díaz-Torres (osiris.diaz@udlap.mx)

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The rise of far-right antidemocratic actors in consolidated democracies, specifically the challenge of defending democracy against actors who use lawful, often invisible tactics, and the normative dilemma of choosing between repressive measures and other strategies.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A comparative normative political theory approach that defines and analyzes three ideal types of democratic self-defence: militant (restrictive), tolerant (liberal-procedural), and social (addressing structural injustices). The method involves providing conceptual definitions, analyzing normative j…
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical analysis grounded in contemporary political contexts, with specific reference to the case of the Greek neo-fascist party Golden Dawn and its legal and political trajectory, as well as broader European and global contexts of democratic backsliding.
Abstract:
Associate Professor, Department of Government The rise of far-right antidemocratic actors in many consolidated democracies today poses a unique challenge. Political parties and leaders who enjoy popular support risk tearing apart the democratic fabric through tactics that appear lawful and are often invisible. What options do democracies have to defend themselves against such actors? Democratic self-defence, i.e. actions aimed at preventing, containing, resisting, or repairing democratic backsliding caused by domestic antidemocratic forces, can take many forms: from restrictions on candidacy rights to hate speech laws, and from street protests to welfare reforms. Political parties may exclude antidemocratic parties from coalitions, or they may choose to include them while seeking to moderate their positions. Alternatively, they may focus on expanding social protections in order to address the structural injustices that antidemocratic actors exploit. Such choices raise difficult normative questions. This book offers conceptual tools for making these choices intelligible and brings to light the principles that animate them. Political theorists addressing these issues have paid a great deal of attention to justifying repressive measures. Militant democracy, which includes the pre-emptive restriction of political and civil rights, has received so much attention in the past decade that one would be forgiven for thinking there is no alternative. This book is partly a reaction to this one-sided engagement with repressive measures. It examines less-known approaches to democratic self-defence that prioritise toleration and social integration respectively, strategies that are used as much, if not more, than militant restrictions. The three rationales of democratic self-defence that emerge –militant, tolerant, and social– are presented as ideal types. Unlike much theorising on democratic self-defence, which is prescriptive and advances a single normative framework, this book adopts a deliberately comparative approach that examines the strengths and weaknesses of each ideal type, as well as their connections and contrasts. It proposes conceptual definitions and analyses the normative justifications underpinning each type. The aim is to clarify the principles embodied in practices of democratic self-defence, enabling actors to better understand the normative commitments behind their choices and to make decisions that are ethically justified, democratically legitimate, and consistent with the values they seek to defend. The book also seeks to move the discussion beyond legal instruments and state responses by bringing broader societal and public actors into view. At the same time, it remains focused on agency: on both defenders of democracy and those who seek to undermine it. In doing so, it resists the tendency to portray democracy as a quasi-natural system whose resilience must simply be enhanced. Unlike many studies framed around the concept of democratic resilience, this book foregrounds human agency and the diverse actors who actively defend democracy across multiple spheres. Decisions about whether and how to confront antidemocratic actors do not fall exclusively on any single category of actor. They concern government authorities, courts, state agencies, municipal leaders, business actors, journalists, academics, and others. Democratic self-defence should therefore be understood as a form of agency distributed across a variety of actors. This book grew out of an article I co-authored in 2017 with my dear colleague Ludvig Norman, ‘Three Models of Democratic Self-defence: Militant Democracy and Its Alternatives’ published the year after in Political Studies. In that article, Ludvig and I challenged the dominance of militant democracy in debates on democratic self-defence by exploring two alternative perspectives: a tolerant approach (which we then called liberal-procedural) and a social approach, which we ultimately defended. Abstract:
This dataset was created as part of the project Lettercraft and Epistolary Performance in Medieval Europe, a NWO-Vidi funded project based in the Department of Languages, Literature, and Culture at Utrecht University. The database came about in collaboration with Utrecht University’s Centre for Digital Humanities, who developed the online infrastructure, and with the help of students from Utrecht University Research Master’s Programme in Ancient, Medieval & Renaissance Studies, who joined the project as research apprentices. For more information about the project, visit the Lettercraft website. Here you can also browse the latest version of the data. About the project How did early medieval societies use the letter and who were among its users? The Lettercraft-project approaches the early medieval letter as a performative medium, whose communicative potential was defined principally by non-textual features: its materiality, its ability to be publicly read out and talked over, and its potential quickly to reach wide and diverse audiences. The project submits that the letter was a far more inclusive medium than is commonly assumed on the basis of its textual qualities. Literacy or social status were not required to participate in what the project calls lettercraft, i.e. the various performative actions (e.g. listening, speaking, negotiating, gossiping) that along with writing and reading made up epistolary communication. The project aims to show, moreover, that due to its public nature and social range, the letter was an essential tool of community-building and conflict-resolution in medieval society. As long as it was properly performed, a single letter could persuade an entire community. The project studies the performative potential of the letter in the context of the Merovingian Kingdoms, 476-751 CE, whose communicative networks covered much of Europe. Innovatively, it relies not on the surviving letter-collections, which showcase the literary exploits of elite ecclesiastical men, but rather on descriptions of lettercraft in Merovingian histories and saint-lives. The project proceeds along two complementary pathways. First, it has established an index of Merovingian epistolary terminology that is sensitive to all (textual and non-textual) aspects of lettercraft. This index can be consulted in the glossary provided on the Lettercraft website. We plan to include it in this dataset in the future. Second, the project is developing a new open access dataset of Merovingian epistolary communication, which records descriptions of letter-use documented in Merovingian narrative sources. Significantly, it is a dataset not of letters and their textual contents, but of the non-textual ‘metadata’ surrounding the epistolary process, including references to participants, delivery, performance, gift-giving, materiality, and audience. This enables users to analyses the social contexts in which early medieval epistolary communication took place, the diverse individuals and groups who participated in it, and the actions they performed. About the dataset Corpus – This dataset contains annotations on the use of letters in early medieval narrative texts. The project’s principal source are the eight volumes of Merovingian narrative texts edited by Bruno Krusch and Wilhelm Levison for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica under the header Scriptores rerum Merovingicarum (1885-1951), complemented with a smaller corpus of Merovingian texts not edited in this collection. NB: the annotation of this corpus is still ongoing. Specific information on date, authorship, editions and translations is given with each individual text. In terms of provenance, most of the texts in the dataset can be said to have originated in the Frankish kingdoms under Merovingian rule in the period 450-750, but we have followed the MGH editions in not keeping to a strict chronological or geographical demarcation. #8 [paper] Fair Access to Urban Water: Designing Population‐Sensitive Connection Fees Through a Welfare‐Informed Ability‐to‐Pay Approach
Authors: Seyedhossein Sajadifar, Masoud Alavian Sadr, Shahram Heydarian Samani, Ali Mazyaki, Alireza Pourebrahim
Venue: World Water Policy
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1002/wwp2.70115
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
ABSTRACT Setting urban water connection fees is a complex policy problem: Fees must balance affordability, equity, and adequate cost recovery. This study develops a two‐stage framework for setting urban water connection charges in Iran. A bottom‐up engineering model first establishes the full long‐run economic cost of a new connection; a distributive stage then allocates a target provincial average across six city population classes. The distributive stage is stated as a constrained social welfare program and solved exactly; under logarithmic utility, it yields corner solutions rather than a smooth gradient because the fee is a small share of household resources. The recommended schedule is therefore described as what it is: a proportional ability‐to‐pay allocation indexed to city size, whose formal relation to the welfare program is stated explicitly. Revenue neutrality is imposed on a connection‐weighted basis so that the utility collects the intended total rather than an unweighted average of six class fees. Using Household Expenditure and Income Survey data for all 31 provincial capitals, we test rather than assume the population proxy and find an income elasticity of about 0.13 with respect to city size: statistically significant, but explaining a minority of cross‐city variation. Equity claims are correspondingly framed at the intercity level. Applied to a representative province, the schedule is progressive with respect to ability to pay, holds first‐year revenue exactly at the target, and can be adjusted over time using the Consumer Price Index. The approach transfers to other water‐scarce settings under cost‐recovery pressure.

Abstract:
Health-related decisions should be made based on best available evidence. Synthesizing evidence from health governance and health systems research is necessary to support health policy-making and health systems strengthening: “Decision-makers request reviews of the effectiveness of health policies and health systems interventions, but they also require contextual evidence, for example, to support the implementation of an intervention in their own setting or to assess stakeholders' perceptions and views of specific health system challenges and policy options. Rapid delivery of this information is also thought to increase the adoption of evidence-informed decision-making” (Langlois et al., 2018).Evidence synthesis from health governance and health systems research could be conducted using a variety of methods based on a type of research question and its aim. Recent WHO discussion paper argues that “by enabling faster synthesis and analysis of diverse, large-scale data, AI promises to expand the evidence base available to policymakers, enhance scenario modelling and simulation, and support adaptive and responsive decision-making. These capabilities can accelerate the development of policies, improve the effectiveness of implementation and facilitate both continuous monitoring and refinement in complex and dynamic health contexts” (WHO, 2026).IJHG encourages publication of evidence synthesis papers (literature reviews with systematic approach) (Ibragimova and Phagava, 2023, 2024). In this section, we look at two recent evidence synthesis papers published in the IJHG – one systematic and one scoping review.This review is based on the article “Factors supporting organizational and individual resilience for healthcare professionals and informal caregivers in elderly care settings – a systematic review” (Knutsen Glette et al., 2026).The authors explain that the reasons for their evidence synthesis are the growing of elderly population and mismatch between health staff capacity and demand due to “workload imbalances, limited resources, role ambiguity, which result in stress, burnout, uncertainty and diminished mental health and well-being among healthcare professionals and leaders, as well as informal caregivers” and the need to support the providers of the elderly care “with tailored, integrated healthcare interventions that emphasize resilience as a protective factor” (Knutsen Glette et al., 2026). The authors state that research on resilience in healthcare has predominantly treated individual and organizational resilience as separate constructs, and there remains a lack of research integrating these two dimensions of resilience. Databases were selected for their coverage of the subject areas and validated through test searches. Abstract:
The median published figure in the Answering Service Price Index is 68.95 USD across 23 sources' own pages (range 5 to 399 USD), read 26 September 2026. Coverage. 23 of the 70 named sources read in full publish a figure; 47 publish none, read 26 September 2026. Methodology. Every row is a verbatim sentence read from the named source's own page through the estate's fetch service on the date shown, hash-pinned to the stored read (the sha of the page's visible text; the raw page is mirrored to R2). 23 of the 70 named sources that could be read published a usable figure; 47 published none and are recorded as not published, never filled in; 3 could not be read (blocked, dead or unreachable) and count nowhere. The headline figures (median, minimum, maximum, quartiles) are over ONE figure per source in USD (a source's median where its page yielded several accepted sentences), so N counts sources, never sentences; 343 candidate sentence(s) were refused by a reviewer with the reason recorded. Derivation as chartered: one row per provider per plan: the base fee, the METER (per minute, per call, per unique caller, per conversation, per agent hour, flat, per seat), the included allowance, the overage rate, the setup fee and whether a contract is required. Across them, the figures nobody publishes: the median and spread of the entry price at each meter; the share of providers publishing a rate AT ALL against the share quoting only, which the harvest already puts near half; the EFFECTIVE cost per answered call at 50, 200 and 500 calls a month, which is the only way plans on five different meters can be compared and which no provider will ever compute because it is the comparison they lose; the AI-priced tier against the human-staffed tier for the same call volume; and the bilingual surcharge, which some providers charge, some bundle and most do not mention. #11 [paper] Ten simple rules for preparing and delivering effective funding pitches in competitive grant applications
Authors: Andy Göbel, Tilman D. Rachner
Venue: PLoS Computational Biology

Abstract:
In grant applications, oral presentations can be an integral part of the evaluation process. Funding pitches are a specific form of pitch presentations delivered during competitive review procedures to complement a written proposal. Their goal is to convince reviewers of both your project's strength and excellence as well as your suitability as a researcher. This paper offers ten simple rules on how to prepare and deliver effective funding pitches, with a particular focus on content selection, clear structuring, and convincing scientific argumentation. We also highlight the importance of practice and feedback and share practical strategies on how to handle questions and critical discussion professionally.

#12 [paper] Valuing education for limited-resource audiences using a willingness to accept experiment
Authors: Russell Tronstad, Ibrahima Sall
Venue: PLoS ONE
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0348858
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Education grants often target audiences that have limited-resources relative to their peers, such as beginning farmers, who arguably have the most to gain from more education. Yet, charging even modest fees to these participants is discouraged, creating a challenge for funding entities that desire to have a dollar value for the education provided. To measure this value, we conducted an experiment using a willingness-to-accept (WTA) approach. Participants chose a minimum cash payout from seven different options to voluntarily leave a training session before receiving any instruction or educational materials. The design is constructed so that each option has an equal expected payout. Cash payouts were not advertised or known to any participants before the training. Results show that average WTA values are $277.44 per training (about 4 hours of instruction), which is 2.11 to 4.74 times more than participants' self-reported willingness to pay (WTP), depending on how travel costs and time of participants are valued. WTP consistently and significantly explains much of the variation in WTA. In sharp contrast, detailed travel cost estimates in various forms were consistently insignificant for explaining WTA values. Beginning farmers and ranchers, our targeted limited-resource audience, reported WTA and WTP values that were $81.18 and $22.73 more per training, respectively, than those of non-beginning farmers.

#13 [paper] An economic analysis of postoperative cataract consultation using remote self-assessment
Authors: Casper van der Zee, Janneau L. J. Claessens, Rudy M. M. A. Nuijts, Rob Wouters, Nicolaas J. Reus, Karl Boden, Oliver Findl, Saskia M. Imhof
Venue: PLOS Digital Health
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pdig.0001617
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
To evaluate the potential savings realized by replacing the 4-6 weeks consultation following cataract surgery with remote self-assessment. In addition, we evaluated the costs associated with adverse events (AEs) from a societal perspective and evaluated the current cost of AEs based on published literature and publicly available datasets. We determined the cost reduction when replacing the in-person 4-6-week postoperative consultation visit with remote self-assessment using our previous clinical trial, publicly available healthcare resource databases, and threshold analysis to determine the effect on cost if the incidence of AEs is affected by conducting an online self-assessment. We collected AE probabilities and costs of AEs based on published literature and databases. and performed a threshold analysis to demonstrate the financial impact if the incidence of AEs is altered versus the savings due to replacing the 4-6 weeks in-person consultation with remote self-assessment. Remote self-assessments resulted in an average savings between -€83 and -€92 per patient. Physical consultations were less costly only if >80% of remote self-assessments warranted an in-person follow-up. The mean cost of AEs per patient was estimated to be €16.35 and were attributed primarily to rare but severe complications, including endophthalmitis and retinal detachment. Having patients participate in a remote self-assessment following cataract surgery is expected to reduce costs under a wide range of assumptions. Due to the lack of published data regarding the utility loss due to AEs, quality of life was not included in our analysis; nevertheless, these cost savings should be balanced by the clinical impact of potentially missing relatively rare AEs. These findings contribute to the ongoing discussion regarding appropriate care following cataract surgery.

#14 [paper] Financial implications of post-transcarotid artery revascularization duplex surveillance.
Authors: AbuRahma, Ali, Cragon, Robert, AbuRahma, Zachary, Dees, Kory, Fong, Suy Sen Hong, Dargy, Noah, Veith, Christina, Dean, Scott
Venue: Seminars in vascular surgery
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42735964/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study analyzes the financial and clinical implications of routine post-transcarotid artery revascularization (TCAR) surveillance (PTS). In this retrospective analysis, patients who underwent TCAR in a single institution during an 8-year period (2016 to 2024) were included. All patients underwent postoperative duplex ultrasound (DUS) repeated at 1, 6, and every 12 months. Previously validated carotid DUS criteria were used to define in-stent restenosis. Hospital charges for carotid DUS were captured to estimate charges for long-term PTS. The number of duplex examinations was used to calculate cost charge per reimbursement. A total of 301 patients with TCAR were analyzed. In a mean follow-up of 30 months, 21 patients had >50% in-stent restenosis (7%). Of these, 9 were associated with >80% and only 2 had ipsilateral strokes. The rates of freedom from >50% and >80% restenosis at 12, 24, and 36 months were 94%, 90%, and 89% and 97%, 96%, and 95%, respectively. The total number of duplex examinations was 938. Estimated hospital charges for all DUS examinations were $1,017,730. However, the estimated reimbursement was $272,345. Based on the Society for Vascular Surgery guideline recommendation that most asymptomatic (>70% to 80%) restenosis should be treated medically and do not need re-intervention, this surveillance would have detected only 2 patients associated with >80% restenosis. If the patients had undergone re-intervention, 2 potential strokes at the cost of $1,017,730 per $272,345 reimbursement may have been prevented. Based on this study, PTS is probably costly and perhaps should be performed selectively. Further studies are needed to clarify this finding.

#15 [paper] Cotton Producers’ Willingness to Pay for Agricultural Advisory Services and the Estimated Financial Potential: The Case of Şanlıurfa Province
Authors: İpek Yücel, Gönül Sevinç
Venue: Türk Tarım ve Doğa Bilimleri Dergisi
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.30910/turkjans.1940917
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This study was conducted to determine the information sources used by cotton producers in Şanlıurfa Province, their levels of satisfaction, and their willingness to pay for quality agricultural advisory services. The primary data for the study consist of data collected through face-to-face questionnaire interviews with 168 cotton producers. The respondents were recruited using a non-probability convenience sampling approach with voluntary participation. In addition to descriptive statistics, independent samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and the Kruskal-Wallis H test were used in the statistical analysis of the data. It was found that 95.8% of producers received consulting services, but that nearly all of these services were provided free of charge by input suppliers (dealers). Despite the dominant role of dealers, it was determined that the institution meeting expectations at the highest level was universities (2.48/3.00). 80.3% of producers are willing to pay an average of 199.33 ₺ per decare annually for the advisory services they request. This amount corresponds to approximately 4.9% of the average annual net income from cotton production. Applying the survey-derived willingness-to-pay estimates—an 80.3% willingness-to-pay rate and a mean stated willingness to pay of 199.33 ₺ per decare per year—to the approximately 2.42 million decares of cotton cultivation area in Şanlıurfa during the 2022 production season yields a scenario-based annual payment potential of approximately 388.1 million ₺ for professional agricultural advisory services. This scenario suggests that the region may have an economic basis for developing a university-led, producer-participatory, and sustainable advisory model, although the estimate is based on stated willingness to pay and should be interpreted cautiously.

#19 [paper] Indigenous Consultation-Fee Disclosure and Subsequent Biomedical Referral Among Togolese Ewe Diviners: A Factorial Vignette Estimation of Payment Framing and Referral Deferral
Authors: Ousmane Faye, Khady Sarr
Venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23549792
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
The study treats referral deferral as a decision-theoretic outcome under conditions of fee dependency and reputational risk, and proposes a factorial vignette design capable of estimating the causal effect of payment framing on deferral. Because no primary observational data were collected, the analysis characterises the operating characteristics of a before-after-control-impact estimator under a declared variance structure: between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, residual standard deviation of 4.5, and intraclass correlation of 0.64. Power was estimated across 2000 design cells spanning cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design achieves 80% power to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 54 clusters. Fee disclosure is not a neutral administrative act but a framing device that alters the perceived cost of referral, and that the proposed design can identify this framing effect while accommodating the clustered structure of diviner practice. The contribution is a methodologically explicit framework for studying referral behaviour in indigenous therapeutic systems without requiring the researcher to treat diviners as either gatekeepers or obstacles to biomedical care.

#20 [paper] Cost drivers of cancer sequencing technologies
Authors: Sanjeeth Rajaram, Kevin Alan Schulman, Tian Yi Zhang
Venue: npj Precision Oncology
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41698-026-01724-3
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is widely recommended for cancer diagnosis and monitoring, but is perceived as prohibitively expensive. Using Medicare reimbursement data and microcosting analysis in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), we find that sequencing alone costs less than the ~$1000 reimbursement, while library preparation ($12–$154/sample), driven by oligonucleotide synthesis, comprises an increasing share of cost. Expanding NGS access may depend more on cheaper library preparation and systems-level centralization.

#21 [paper] Generating a national snapshot of all publicly reported investments in ecosystem and species conservation across public, private, and philanthropic finance
Authors: Alice Stuart, Sophus zu Ermgassen
Venue: AMBIO
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1007/s13280-026-02464-1
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Abstract Scaling up investment in ecosystems is a national and international public policy priority. Evaluations of the total amount spent have been severely criticised, with a lack of transparent reporting, especially of private finance flows, a known limitation. We provide a country-wide snapshot of investment in nature in the UK based on publicly available data, estimating total annual nature finance flows in the UK of ~£1.15bn. Public investment in agri-environment (£389.1m) and grant schemes (£314.8m) accounted for over 60% of identified flows. Private financial flows (£142.4m) consisted of corporate philanthropy (£71.5m), return-seeking investment and loans (£50.7m), and credit and unit purchases (£20.2m). Estimated flows from NGOs and philanthropic grants totalled £388.5m. Interactions between flows mean double counting must be considered when summing. We find major public transparency gaps in nature finance flows, undermining efforts to understand the both the extent of nature finance flows and their effectiveness for nature recovery.

#1 [paper] Analysis increments for model bias diagnosis and correction: Theoretical foundations
Authors: Eviatar Bach
Year: 2026
Link: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/102fc24308c75c70cf2bd8e0ed3659c9af62e97e
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The lack of theoretical foundations for using analysis increments (the difference between analysis and forecast) to diagnose and correct model bias in weather and climate prediction, particularly when using machine learning for state-dependent corrections.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical analysis of Kalman filters with constant and state-dependent biases, including proofs of what averaged increments measure and the limits of bias identification for linear dynamics, supplemented by numerical experiments on linear models and the nonlinear Lorenz'96 model.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Theoretical Kalman filter models with constant and state-dependent biases, and numerical experiments using a linear model and the nonlinear Lorenz'96 model.
Abstract:
A common method for diagnosing and correcting model bias in weather and climate prediction is based on analysis increments: the difference between the analysis and the forecast at each data assimilation cycle. Their time average is used to estimate and correct the bias, and machine learning is increasingly used to map the forecast state to the increments, giving a state-dependent correction. Despite its widespread use, the method lacks theoretical foundations. We first analyse a Kalman filter whose forecast model has a constant bias. We show what the averaged increment measures, and prove that iterating the correction removes all of the bias seen through the observations; for linear dynamics, no method can identify the rest. We then extend the analysis to state-dependent biases. For linear dynamics, each increment records the model error over the filter's memory, as seen through the observations. We use this to determine what the increments measure when averaged over a long period, averaged over periods with similar slowly varying conditions, and used without averaging, as in machine-learned corrections. Numerical experiments confirm the theory for a linear model and suggest that its main conclusions carry over to the nonlinear Lorenz'96 model, including for a correction learned by a neural network.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Projects are expected to contribute to all the following expected outcomes:

- Effective and innovative methods for gathering, sharing and using large data sets in energy applications for the purpose of training AI models while ensuring privacy and security.

- Advanced and - wherever possible - open-source AI foundation models to support the digitalisation of the energy system, through improved grid observability, forecasting of supply and demand, advanced storage and renewables integration, demand side flexibility and energy efficiency.

- Enhanced cooperation, knowledge sharing and interoperability among energy system actors for secure and seamless data exchange.

- Advanced methodologies for AI model development ensuring that the results are FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) beyond the project ending, open source and accommodating for technology evolution.

Scope:

The quality of AI models depends strongly on the amount, quality, and representativeness of the data used for their training. Projects are expected to focus on developing, training and testing AI foundation models, using extensive data sets to accelerate the energy transition in key focus areas of the energy sector. Projects are expected to:

- Building on the results of previously funded projects on the Common European energy data space[1] as well as the ongoing work within the Data 4 Energy expert group, projects are expected to demonstrate innovative methods and data governance strategies for sharing data among various energy actors. Projects are expected to demonstrate that they have access to large relevant datasets at the time of submitting the proposal.

- Projects are expected to develop innovative strategies for sharing data in an effective, secure and transparent way to support the development of AI foundation models. An indicative non exhaustive list of strategies that can be explored is the use of data space connectors or federated training of models to allow the integration of confidential data; the creation of synthetic data as an intermediate step to fill data gaps or improve the quality of the data could also be explored. Projects could also explore other innovative data sharing strategies, such as an ‘AI gym’. The data governance strategies that will be developed in the project should be designed in a way to be scalable and operational even after the end of the project.

- Projects are expected to develop foundation models tailored for the energy sector, addressing at least one -or more- of the following use cases: planning and operation of electricity grids (including static power flow modelling and dynamic EMT modelling), forecasting, congestion management, anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, flexibility management, demand-side energy efficiency, smart and bidirectional charging of EVs or other use cases that contribute to the objective of digitalisation of the energy system.

- Projects are expected to perform in-depth testing and validation of developed foundation models in lab demonstrators and real-life pilots, building on the results and using the facilities of previously funded projects on “AI testing and experimentation facilities (TEFs)”[2]. Regulatory sandboxes could also be considered for real-life pilot implementations.

- Projects are expected to bring together a wide group of stakeholders including data owners (for example energy utilities, grid operators, asset owners), application developers (for example startups, SMEs, hyperscalers) and model deployers (for example industry, grid operators, equipment manufacturers) providing a space of cooperation and collaborative data exchange.

- To scale up the training and development of the models, projects can benefit from the computing capacity of the AI factories that were recently announced by the European Commission[3], in particular the three AI factories that aim to develop AI applications for the energy sector.
